title: Scenario Proofs for Verification of Distributed Protocols
what: Introduces scenario proofs: regular-expression-like representative executions with ghost variables, guards, phases, and loops; coverage modulo sound semi-commutation plus Hoare-style correctness replaces monolithic inductive-invariant discovery. The semantics has structure, variable, feasibility, and commutativity layers. Coverage is reduced to syntax-directed inclusions J1K⊆JsK and Js·aK⊆JsK; correctness checks only feasible representatives using weakest preconditions and supplied loop invariants; local pairwise soundness of semi-commutation justifies reordering. The Paxos scenario defers negative Promise/Accept actions, orders positive rounds ascending, and proves agreement because each later round sees a quorum intersection with completed earlier rounds. Additional appendixed proofs cover two-phase commit, a decentralized lock (empty commutativity), and two Ivy multisignature-payment variants.

assumptions_limits: Protocols are modeled as finite-action transition systems with feasible runs; semi-commutation must preserve feasibility and final states and is checked locally. title: Modeling and Reasoning over Distributed Systems using Aspect-Oriented Graph Grammars
what: Defines aspect-oriented graph grammars (AOGGs) for modular system-wide policies over graph-rewriting distributed systems, gives an encoding into a single typed graph grammar, and uses AGG critical-pair analysis to detect conflicts and dependencies in aspect weaving. The base model uses DPO graph rules for a client-server system; aspects are rule-level spans with pointcuts, interfaces and effects. Log and security aspects respectively add execution tracing and read/write permissions. Weaving is non-reentrant and ordered, yielding a concrete graph grammar. Encoding operations R1–R3 represent rule spans as typed nodes/edges, and S1–S3 encode concrete rules/advices; the resulting typed graph lets AGG analyze both execution and weaving. In the case study, ExecuteSET/ExecuteGET conflict on shared data, while log/security advices are conflict-free, implying aspect-order confluence for that model.

title: APE-Bench: Evaluating Automated Proof Engineering for Formal Math Libraries
what: Defines Automated Proof Engineering (APE) for repository-scale Lean/Mathlib maintenance and releases APE-Bench plus APE-Harness. Contracts pin repository/toolchain, objectives, access boundaries and verification protocols. APE-Bench mines real Mathlib commits, synthesizes natural-language instructions and validates patches with dual checks: Lean compilation and LLM-judge semantic requirement/scope validation. APE-Harness provides isolated workspaces, version-scoped retrieval, execution services and interchangeable APE-Agent, Claude Code and Codex scaffolds. The benchmark contains 100 tasks from 67 Mathlib commits (2026-01-06–12), 10–284 changed lines, 17 mathematical domains, and is evaluated against miniCTX (334 tasks) and miniF2F (244). Under $3 and 100 turns per task, Gemini 3 Flash reaches 47% APE-Bench success, Gemini 3 Pro 24%, GPT-5.2 27%; miniCTX reaches 87.1%, 80.5%, 71.9%. Static gold-solution analysis finds 95/100 tasks require declarations from other files (median nine declarations across eight files). Difficulty declines with diff size and cross-file sources. Three judges achieve 90.6% overall semantic accuracy (92.2% correctness, 93.8% requirement alignment, 89.1% scope). APE-Agent outperforms Claude/Codex by 15–23 points; content-addressable storage cuts 480 GB to 71 GB and retrieval annotation cost $12.9K to $197. Limitations are Lean/Mathlib-only, single-file modifications and LLM-judge scope errors. Appendix A traces a sqrt continuity/filter task solved in 32 turns and $0.79, while Appendix B gives judges accepting unauthorized declaration deletions and rejecting benign refactoring; these cases explain why compilation and LLM consensus still need calibrated scope checks.

title: APKeep: Realtime Network Verification for Real Networks
what: APKeep incrementally checks a symbolic model of network forwarding, filtering and header rewriting. Its Port-Predicate Map separates logical functions and their applications, and maintains Boolean packet equivalence classes by splitting only for changed behavior and merging equal port sets. An informal inductive proof establishes a minimum partition for the basic immediate-merge algorithm; experiments measure update-plus-loop-check cost, partition sizes, memory, link-failure queries and synthetic NAT updates. Records the precise EC equivalence relation, rule priority/hit analysis, split/transfer/merge algorithm, rewrite closure, delayed merging and separate partition optimizations, invariant and policy traversal, vendor PBR case, all dataset and comparison tables, partial-run counting and synthesized workloads. Distinguishes the basic minimum-partition theorem from optimized execution and exposes printed formula/pseudocode/data inconsistencies without inferring implementation faults.
assumptions_limits: §2.1: Every element sends each header to exactly one logical action port. Headers in an EC must select the same port at every element, even elements the header never reaches. This partition can be finer than physical device behavior or reachable paths. An element topology node is an application of a logical element; one ACL applied twice has two nodes but one shared model update. §2.1/§3.2/Appendix A: Disjoint ECs cover all headers. Minimum partition additionally requires equal port vectors to imply same EC. Appendix A uses informal induction over split/transfer/merge and rule updates; it is not machine checked and does not prove fidelity of parsers, Java code, device behavior or every invariant checker. §3.2/Algorithm 1: Rule hit subtracts higher-priority matches; identify only action changes, including default. Pseudocode uses strict priority comparisons and assumes a well-defined priority order. Rule deletion omitted; modification represented by delete plus insert. No detailed argument for atomic multi-device update semantics. §3.2/Algorithm 2: Split predicates on partial overlap; copy port sets, transfer changed part, merge equal port sets and propagate transferred-set D. BDDs encode arbitrary sets rather than header rectangles. Equality is model forwarding/action equality, not observational equivalence of stateful network executions. §3.4/Algorithm 3: Rewriting to constants existentially forgets overwritten bits then constrains new values. Maintain pre-to-post predicate table; recursively split images until rewrites are representable by current predicates. This closure can require additional splits beyond the simple port-vector partition. Appendix A does not explicitly extend its minimum-partition induction to rewrite closure. §3.4 Eq.(2), visually confirmed: printed existential quantification joins true/false cofactors with conjunction. Existential elimination mathematically requires disjunction. Treat as a printed formula error, not evidence that JDD implementation uses wrong operation. Algorithm 3 calls UpdateRW although prose calls this Algorithm 2; rewrite-table notation abbreviates rule association. §3.5: Delayed merging records candidates and merges only when predicate count exceeds 500 by default. The immediate-minimum theorem does not literally describe states between these merges. Forwarding and ACL partitions are updated separately; loop validation checks a nonempty conjunction of one predicate from each, avoiding cross-product false positives. Minimum per component does not imply a globally minimum joint partition. §3.3/Appendix B: Incremental delta forwarding graph uses transferred predicates; loop means revisiting a device without modification, blackhole means no forwarding rule. Intentional ACL denial is not this blackhole definition. Printed traversal remembers graph nodes; device-versus-element, topology applications, ingress reachability and rewrite-aware history are abstracted rather than fully formalized. Appendix B/Algorithms 4–5: Construct graph from ports holding D, with virtual default node. Traverse from updated element applications, carrying predicate intersections/history. Algorithm 5 line 4 passes undefined predicates after initializing pset; default-edge check precedes edge intersection, apparently allowing an empty-intersection edge to flag. These are presentation concerns; no executable bug reproduced. §3.3/§5.1: BDD match plus regular-expression path policies/automata described, but implementation reports only loop/blackhole invariant checker and what-if link analyzer. No policy-checker experiment or formal soundness/completeness theorem for the full checker. §4: Vendor PBR redirect can be modeled by cascading classifiers and connecting permit to redirect, deny to ordinary forwarding. Extra symbolic length/time fields can encode static conditions. Traffic statistics, mirroring, rate limiting and congestion avoidance are explicitly outside the model; stateful middlebox semantics not evaluated. §5.1: Around 5K Java/JDD lines; configuration parsers for three vendors, update parser for one, JSON intermediate form. title: Synthesizing Approximate Implementations for Unrealizable Specifications
what: Synthesizes reactive implementations against environments whose infinite input words have bounded ultimately periodic representations. A k-lasso-precise implementation satisfies the specification for every input word represented by a lasso of length at most k. An ε-k approximation instead satisfies it on at least a 1−ε fraction of those distinct input words. Sections 3–4 formalize transition systems, lassos and the difference between bounding input words and bounding environment state. Proposition 1 connects the two using an implementation-size factor. A deterministic automaton recognizes bounded-lasso prefixes; an exponential lower bound shows why this recognition is costly. Composing it with a deterministic parity specification yields an exact synthesis algorithm. Section 5 gives a bounded-state QBF encoding with O(|φ|+n²+k²) formula size as stated by the paper, with input-alphabet size present in the variable count. Section 6 reduces approximation to maximum model counting over transition/output choices and input words. Auxiliary unrollings of length 2k prevent double counting different lassos that denote the same infinite word. Section 7 implements the encodings with CAQE and MaxCount and evaluates greedy and round-robin arbiters.

assumptions_limits: All correctness and approximation claims are relative to bounded input lassos, not unrestricted environments or an empirical probability distribution. A bounded environment state space and bounded lasso length are related but distinct restrictions. The automata algorithms are exponential in k; symbolic instances also grow quickly with state bound and process count. Table 1 contains timeouts and an approximate solver result of 0.88 even for a case where exact QBF synthesis succeeds, so the reported MaxCount solutions need not reach the optimal rate. Hardware and timeout duration are not specified in the experimental section.
use_for_goal: Shows how to make an unrealizable temporal specification usable by stating an explicit environment restriction or a precisely counted loss of satisfaction. For LLM-generated distributed specifications, the transferable lesson is to record the bounded environment and approximation denominator; these guarantees must not be relabeled as unrestricted protocol correctness.

title: Abstract Framework for All-Path Reachability Analysis toward Safety and Liveness Verification (Full Version)
what: Reformulates all-path reachability (APR) proof rules for abstract reduction systems so they correspond one-to-one with LCTRS rules, adapts cyclic APR proofs, reduces safety properties to partial APR validity, and introduces total validity that quantifies over finite and infinite execution paths for liveness. Defines DVP+ and a complete disproof rule DVP-bottom, proves equivalence with the original DVP, and formalizes finite APR pre-proofs, bud/companion links and proof graphs. Safety APR predicates characterize non-reachability of error states, illustrated with Peterson mutual exclusion. For liveness, Theorem 6.3 proves that an APR proof graph is acyclic iff the APR predicate is totally valid; the Peterson starvation-freedom example obtains an acyclic proof. Appendices establish decidability under finite reachable closure and detail limitations of reduction and cyclic generalization.

title: Backward Reachability of Array-Based Systems by SMT Solving: Termination and Invariant Synthesis
what: Develops a declarative SMT-based backward-reachability framework for infinite-state array systems. First-order formulas over separate index/data theories represent states; preimages, safety and fixpoint checks are mechanized with quantifier instantiation. Model-theoretic embeddings and well-quasi-order conditions yield termination results, while a dual invariant-synthesis method is complete under corresponding hypotheses. The paper separates symbolic and semantic tracks, defines array-based transition systems and theory conditions for closure/decidability, presents a tableaux-like calculus, and proves undecidability outside restricted classes. It integrates resource-bounded invariant guessing (index and signature abstraction) with exact backward search, checking candidate invariants before pruning. mcmt experiments cover mutual exclusion, cache coherence, imperative array programs and miscellaneous protocols, comparing default and tuned settings.

assumptions_limits: Termination and completeness require theory-specific local-finiteness, quantifier-elimination/instantiation and well-quasi-order hypotheses; unrestricted safety and satisfiability are undecidable. Quantified SMT is difficult, and mcmt uses Yices plus heuristic instantiation. Invariant synthesis is theoretically complete but can have a huge finite search space; experiments are on selected translated benchmarks and old hardware, with tuned settings potentially non-global best.
use_for_goal: Foundational symbolic verification work directly relevant to formal distributed systems: declarative array models, SMT proof obligations, termination conditions and invariant synthesis support automated safety checking of parameterized protocols. It predates Verus but offers comparable specification-to-proof automation and explicit limits.

title: AssertCoder: LLM-Based Assertion Generation via Multimodal Specification Extraction
what: Introduces AssertCoder, a pipeline that classifies PDF specification blocks, extracts signal-level semantics from text/tables/diagrams/formulas, synthesizes SystemVerilog assertions through structured multi-step prompting, and iteratively refines them using mutation-based model checking feedback. The framework uses LayoutParser plus an LLM to label modality and semantic categories, converts blocks to a unified intermediate representation, and decomposes each assertion into precondition, consequence, timing, pattern selection, temporal binding and syntax synthesis. Design-aware retrieval supplies patterns; SymbiYosys checks assertions and Mantra injects roughly 100–300 mutants per DUT. The mutation score averages detected mutants per assertion, while MDR is the fraction of mutants detected by any assertion and FPR manually distinguishes semantically wrong failures from real DUT bugs. On I2C, AES and Openmsp430, AssertCoder averages 97.8% syntax correctness, 87.6% functional correctness, 85.6% MDR and 3.2% FPR, beating AssertLLM (79.2% functional, 79.8% MDR, 5.5% FPR) and zero-shot GPT-4o (17.2%, 38.1%, 21.7%). Ablations show CoT most affects correctness and iterative refinement most affects mutation detection; RAG has comparatively small impact.

title: Towards Formal Verification of LLM-Generated Code from Natural Language Prompts
what: Introduces Astrogator, a verifier for LLM-generated Ansible programs. A user-readable Formal Query Language gives a precise, reviewable specification of natural-language intent; a State Calculus models stateful system effects; a symbolic interpreter and unifier compare generated playbook behavior with the query and report extra assumptions/actions. The formalization separates user intent U from an approved but possibly under-specified query semantics and explicitly defines the unresolved gap p∖s for user review. The State Calculus models attributes, nested elements, stateful functions, reads, writes, conditionals, cases and symbolic loops; unknown reads branch over possibilities, and symbolic lists are approximated by one representative element. Ansible modules are specified in a small module-definition language, while a hand-curated knowledge base maps high-level descriptions such as apache server or zsh configuration file to OS-specific packages and paths. On 1,260 generated playbooks from six LLMs, Astrogator accepts most test-correct programs and rejects most incorrect ones, but under-specified queries permit incorrect programs unless users review reported assumptions.

title: Formal Verification of Self-Assembling Systems
what: Interprets bounded Abstract Tile Assembly Model systems in CTL and gives a polynomial algorithm for rectilinear systems: either a counterexample to rectilinearity or verification of unique terminal assembly. Partial-order reduction cuts search from exponential to O(n²) for an n×n surface; SMART Petri-net checking runs O(|T|·n⁴). Defines assembly transition systems and CTL encodings for legal tile additions, studies terminality and unique terminal assemblies, and translates TAS simulator files to SMART Petri nets. It proposes a tailored front-end to exploit tile locality and discusses extension toward larger surfaces.

what: Describes Attestor, an automated Java/bytecode verifier for dynamic pointer structures. title: Autoformalizing Euclidean Geometry
what: Introduces LeanEuclid, 173 manually formalized Euclidean geometry statement/proof/diagram examples, and a Lean implementation of a variant of system E. A symbolic SMT engine fills implicit diagrammatic proof gaps and evaluates statement equivalence as E3. January2024 GPT-4/GPT-4V few-shot experiments report up to21.0% solver-proved statement equivalence and23.1% proof acceptance across the143-item evaluation set. SMT answers are admitted through an explicitly unsound axiom rather than reconstructed as Lean proof terms, so results require trusting the translation and SMT solvers as well as the Lean kernel. Separates explicit construction steps, chosen by humans/models, from non-construction diagrammatic/metric/transfer reasoning handled by SMT refutation. euclid_apply instantiates a rule, proves missing premises with SMT, and adds conclusions/witnesses; euclid_finish/assert discharge goals. E3 checks both implication directions plus contradiction detection; approximate comparison requires matching numbers/types of bound variables, selects top-n renamings by string similarity, and counts four directions of pre/postcondition obligations, adding preconditions to postcondition comparisons only after precondition equivalence. Dataset contains all48 Elements BookI propositions and125 UniGeo examples (25 each in five categories); texts are manually augmented/abridged. Appendices give a full axiom catalogue, a missing-case reconstruction for Elements24, formalization comparisons, exact prompts, partial semantic outcomes, and before/after repair scripts.
assumptions_limits: Correctness is relative to the chosen geometric axioms and Lean-to-SMT encoding. AppendixC explicitly introduces an unsound axiom to admit successful SMT queries; there is no end-to-end kernel certification or SMT proof reconstruction. The reader did not audit or execute the released implementation. SystemE soundness/completeness is attributed to Avigad etal for its original axioms. This implementation adds construction, diagrammatic and transfer rules, strengthens one construction rule, and uses SMT real-number theories. The supplied paper does not mechanize a soundness proof of the modified implementation. The diagrammatic engine uses diagrammatic,metric,transfer rules. Equivalence checking additionally uses nine simple construction rules. Limited construction/instantiation makes E3 incomplete; failure to establish equivalence is not proof of inequivalence. Logical equivalence of closed true theorems can be weaker than faithful correspondence of hypotheses,objects and informal meaning. The paper itself reports a logically equivalent but unfaithful quadrilateral/parallelism example; success should not be read as comprehensive intent validation. Approximate equivalence is a bounded heuristic over variable unifications and clause counts, not a semantic distance with a correctness theorem. It excludes formulas with differing variable counts/types and depends on chosen clauses and names. Evaluation uses gpt-4-1106-preview and gpt-4-1106-vision-preview in January2024, one domain, manually prepared prompts and a small curated test split. No significance intervals or multiple-run variance are reported. Proof autoformalization receives a correct formal statement and informal proof, whereas statement autoformalization is evaluated separately. Proof success cannot establish an end-to-end informal-statement-to-correct-proof rate. Manual Elements repairs use ground-truth proofs and a minimum-change preference; Levenshtein ratios measure textual alteration, not time,semantic effort,independent automation success or proof validity. Data-contamination improbability is the authors inference from LeanEuclid being unpublished at experiment time. Models may have seen Elements/UniGeo or other formalizations; no pretraining audit is supplied. No distributed systems,Verus,Rust or TLA+ evaluation occurs. Reuse of domain rules and semantic equivalence checks in those settings is a reader hypothesis, not established transfer.
use_for_goal: Useful for specification/proof agents because it separates specification meaning from syntax and proof acceptance,and shows how explicit construction with domain-specific implicit reasoning can simplify generation. Its admission of SMT results demonstrates why checker acceptance must include the trusted rules/translation. For distributed verification, analogous equivalence checks would require an appropriate temporal/concurrent semantics and a certified or explicitly trusted backend;none is evaluated here.

title: Autoformalizing Mathematical Statements by Symbolic Equivalence and Semantic Consistency
what: Ranks ten LLM-generated Isabelle/HOL mathematical statement candidates using symbolic self-consistency (ATP-proved equivalence classes) and semantic consistency (BERT cosine similarity between original text and LLM back-translation). Combines normalized scores by log, linear or quadratic weighting. Log-comb with alpha=.5 generally improves selected-candidate accuracy on 400 MATH and 488 miniF2F problems across five models. It evaluates statement translation and ranking, not autonomous proof discovery of intended informal mathematics. Decomposes statements into premises P and conclusions Q, tests equivalence of both after variable standardization, and checks inconsistent premises by attempting P→False. Numeric conclusions introduce an auxiliary alpha equal to a numerical expression; other cases partially enumerate variable alignments using edit-distance-weighted bipartite matching. Equivalent candidate frequency supplies SymEq score; BERT cosine of original and back-translated text supplies SemCo score. Worst-case comparison cost is k(k−1)/2, with transitivity used to skip tests. For multiple outputs, remove the selected candidate and its equivalence class before repeating ranking. Uses scala-isabelle, 12 tactics including Sledgehammer timeout 300s, and Z3/CVC5. Baselines use LLM log-probabilities or prompted ranking for Codex/GPT-4, ATP-provability filtering, and adaptive KMeans on formal-text BERT embeddings. No model training is required.
assumptions_limits: miniF2F correctness is assigned by ATP symbolic equivalence to its oracle; MATH outputs are manually labeled. The method and automatic metric share an equivalence checker, while oracle mistakes and incomplete proving can change labels. Formal provability and candidate agreement cannot establish that a theorem matches human intent. Appendix B says human grounding remains necessary even with ideal ATPs and embeddings; oversimplified geometry is an example. Semantic consistency assumes back-translation is more reliable than forward translation and embeddings preserve consequential mathematical differences. The authors acknowledge that embeddings can miss single-symbol changes; correlated round-trip errors remain possible. A finite ATP failure does not establish inequivalence or satisfiable premises. Limited variable matching and numerical standardization are heuristics; the paper gives no completeness theorem or full quantifier treatment for auxiliary variables. The study uses mathematical statements in Isabelle/HOL, not program semantics, distributed protocols, Verus, Rust or TLA+. Lean 4 support is future work. Five models are Mistral-7B, Llemma-34B, DeepSeek-V2, Codex completion API and GPT-4 (version 0710 as printed), temperature .7, k=10 and eight-shot prompting as reported. MATH 400 is randomly sampled; no seed, error bars or significance analysis is supplied. The checklist declines statistical significance because of evaluation cost. Alpha=.5 is selected from the reported GPT-4 MATH curve; no separate held-out tuning population is identified. BERT checkpoint/pooling details, Isabelle version, full costs and the nonnumerical matching enumeration budget are not specified in this PDF. Human labeling efficiency is inferred from a rank-based formula, not a user study or measured human time. It omits ATP/LLM computation costs and rests on correctness labels subject to the same caveats. The source asserts code/data availability at github.com/Miracle-Messi/Isa-AutoFormal; the repository and supplemental compute details were not inspected. Appendix F gives two templates but does not enumerate the complete eight-example demonstration sequence.
use_for_goal: Relevant to specification-writing agents because proving a specification does not establish that it matches intent. The paper combines formal relations between multiple translation candidates with a separate check against the informal source. For Verus/TLA+, candidate clustering plus semantic review is a transfer hypothesis, not an evaluated result. The study shows how oracle labels, grounding, domain constraints and logical vacuity can undermine automatic assessment.

title: AutoHyper: Explicit-State Model Checking for HyperLTL
what: Presents AutoHyper, a complete explicit-state model checker for arbitrary HyperLTL quantifier prefixes, using automata quantifier elimination and practical language-inclusion backends. HyperLTL trace quantifiers are eliminated inductively into T-equivalent Büchi automata; existential elimination composes with the transition system, while universal elimination is negation plus complementation. Proposition 1 replaces the outermost complementation by inclusion L(A_T^n)⊆L(A_φ), enabling spot, RABIT, BAIT and FORKLIFT. AutoHyper is implemented in F# with symbolic alphabets and text interfaces. Experiments compare explicit-state inclusion checking with HyperQube BMC on Boolean programs, NuSMV models, SNARK linearizability, mutation tests and grid path-planning hyperproperties; it is complete and often as fast or faster. Random formulas with up to four alternations show practical growth milder than worst-case theory. A complete AutoHyper baseline quantifies strategy-based verification's incompleteness and runtime trade-offs.
numbers: On the HyperQube benchmark table, AutoHyper handles Bakery, SNARK, thread, NRP and mutation instances; HyperQube returns wrong results for Bakery3 φS3 and NRP:Tincorrect.
For grids, AutoHyper solves 60×60 shortest path in 88.83 s and robust path in 3.70 s, while HyperQube times out; 40×40 robust path takes 1.58 s versus HyperQube 265 s.
Strategy verification succeeds on 60.4% of random instances whose properties hold in 61.1% of cases.
All experiments use an Intel Core i3 Mac Mini with 16 GB RAM and spot 2.11.1 plus four inclusion backends.
assumptions_limits: The model is finite-state, formulas are closed HyperLTL formulas over infinite traces, and explicit-state methods can exhaust the generated state space. Language inclusion remains PSPACE-complete in theory; backend performance depends on automata representation and checker. BMC may be faster on shallow cases but is incomplete for many alternated properties (for example GNI), while AutoHyper's completeness does not remove worst-case state explosion. Evaluation uses a Mac Mini i3/16GB, selected benchmark instances, fixed HyperQube bounds and semantics, and an unoptimized strategy-based engine; results may not generalize to larger systems or optimized competitors.
use_for_goal: AutoHyper is a concrete example of a complete, proof-oriented model checker for hyperproperties with quantifier alternation. Its automata construction, inclusion reduction, complete-versus-bounded comparison, and empirical SBV study provide useful evidence for evaluating automated specification/proof tools and their completeness claims.

title: Automated and Modular Refinement Reasoning for Concurrent Programs
what: Introduces civl, a Boogie extension that proves multi-layer refinement of concurrent shared-memory programs. Cooperative yield semantics, mover-type automata, location invariants, linear permissions and modular ownership reduce preemptive concurrency reasoning to automated per-procedure obligations. A high-level atomic action is refined by a procedure whose paths contain exactly one implementing atomic block; other blocks preserve visible state. Mover types and the yield sufficiency automaton justify cooperative reasoning for sequentially consistent preemptive execution. Linear variables guarantee distinct thread identifiers or disjoint permission sets across threads. Location invariants are checked for sequential correctness and non-interference; modules own disjoint globals so quadratic checks are per module. A soundness theorem chains layers from safe high-level program to low-level implementation. Implementation infers verification conditions and atomic blocks, computes graph simulations in O(n·m), and supports variable hiding/data refinement.

assumptions_limits: The paper focuses on sequential consistency and leaves weak memory models future work. Safety guarantee requires high-level safety, valid refinement, sequential/non-interference invariants, linear typing, pairwise commutativity, sufficient yields, and infinitely frequent yields on infinite executions. The full formalization is in a technical report. Modules require strict global-variable ownership. Location invariants cannot refer to other threads and can be incomplete. The approach verifies safety/refinement, not liveness or arbitrary functional properties.
use_for_goal: A close precedent for modular distributed/concurrent verification and refinement layering. Its atomic actions, ownership, permissions and explicit safety assumptions map naturally to TLA+ refinement and can inform Verus contracts for concurrent Rust, although civl targets Boogie and sequential consistency.

quotes.text: civl veriﬁes that the safety of the cooperative semantics of P implies the safety of the preemptive semantics of P . This veriﬁcation is done by computing an automata-theoretic simulation check

Finally, civl provides a simple module system. Modules can be veriﬁed sep- arately, in parallel or at diﬀerent times, since the module system soundly does away with checks that pertain to cross-module interactions. This feature is signif- icant since commutativity checks and non-interference checks for location invari- ants are quadratic, whole program checks involving all pairs of yield locations and atomic blocks, or all pairs of actions from a program. Using the module system, the number of checks is reduced; they become quadratic in the number of yields and atomic blocks within each module rather than the entire program

We can combine the veriﬁcation techniques described above to verify the safety of a program Prog lo . Speciﬁcally, we can guarantee that Prog lo is safe (i.e., all atomic actions will satisfy their gates when run) if the following conditions hold: 1. Prog hi is safe when executed with preemptive semantics. 2. Prog lo is a valid reﬁnement of Prog hi , according to the rules for reﬁnement in civl. Speciﬁcally, for any atomic action A in Prog hi implemented by a procedure P in Prog lo , any path from entry to exit of P must contain exactly one atomic block that implements the action A; all other atomic blocks on the path must leave the global and thread-local state unchanged. Furthermore, all calls to A in Prog hi are replaced by calls to P in Prog lo . 3. The invariants of Prog lo satisfy sequential correctness and non-interference with respect to cooperative semantics. 4. Prog lo is well-typed with respect to linearity. Speciﬁcally, Prog lo does not try to duplicate any linear variables, and linear variables passed to procedures calls and atomic actions are available as expected by the type checker. 5. The atomic actions in Prog lo satisfy the pairwise commutativity checks. 6. The yield statements in Prog lo are suﬃcient, according to the yield suﬃciency automaton in Fig. 2. 7. Any inﬁnite execution of Prog lo must visit a yield statement inﬁnitely often

We automated the simulation relation check used for yield suﬃciency in Sect. 3 by adapting an algorithm by Henzinger et al. [24] for computing the similarity relation of labeled graphs. The complexity of the algorithm is O(n∗m), where n and m are the number of control-ﬂow graph nodes and edges. In practice, this part of the veriﬁcation is fast

title: Automated Theorem Proving for Metamath
what: Builds Metamath-to-ATP translations through MM0/HOL, three higher-order encodings and one first-order class encoding. Evaluates proof search on 40,556 translated set.mm problems, then adds chronological nearest-neighbor premise selection and Prover9/IVY-to-Metamath reconstruction in mm-hammer. Combined ATP success with human proof dependencies is 27,436/40,556 (67.65%). Reports around 30% hammer success with four 60-second premise slices and replay of roughly 15k Prover9 proofs with human premises. These are distinct evaluation settings; no LLM or distributed-protocol evaluation. Separates theorem bundling/unbundling, syntactic versus semantic encodings, known-proof premise access, chronological training, variable time-budget solver unions, first-order reconstruction restriction, full hammer claims and proof-size explosion. Preserves all table data, successful concrete examples and unsolved general lemmas, artifact pointers, hardware/version details and metric ambiguities.
assumptions_limits: §§2–3: Metamath stores explicit proofs over token sequences. Metavariable substitution can bundle multiple alpha-equivalence classes in one theorem. MM0 splits these, parses constructor trees and makes set-variable dependencies explicit. Open formulas become higher-order functions. Unbundling increases task count without adding independently authored mathematics. §§3–4: translation chain is set.mm→MM0→HOL Lisp→TPTP TH0. Formula, class and set-variable types become truth values o, predicates iota→o and individuals iota. No constructor returns a set variable, so such terms are variables. v1 leaves constructors uninterpreted; v2 interprets 10 logical constructors; v3 interprets 11 more, including ternary conjunction, substitution and class abstraction. Deeper interpretation can ease search while making replay harder. §§4/6: benchmark axioms are earlier facts extracted from each theorem’s actual MM0 proof. This gives access to human proof dependencies. It is different from automatic premise selection over the whole library. Sequent antecedents are also distinguished from external facts used in proofs. Some alias problems are trivial because a supplied fact equals the goal. §5: first-order encoding represents formulas/classes as classes of context-tuples. It uses var constants for bound variables, cv for coercion, eval for composition/application, all for binding and predicate p for truth in empty context. Logic remains largely uninterpreted. Certain identities needed to expose intended semantic consequences are deliberately omitted, limiting provability of some generated tasks. §6: set.mm snapshot June 24, 2022, commit d75c0dbe. Original 40,338 theorems become 40,556 MM0 theorems, including 218 additional alpha-degenerate variants. Each of v1/v2/v3 has 40,556 tasks, plus a first-order version. Encodings overlap; they are not independent samples. No later-library or separate held-out library evaluation is provided. §7.1: server has 36 hyperthreading Intel Xeon Gold 6140 cores at 2.30GHz and 256GB RAM. Systems are E2.6, Vampire5980 and ZipperpositionCASC20, with portfolios and selected extra strategies. Most limits are 60s, with initial 10s runs, full runs up to 280s, and 600/1200s runs on previously unsolved tasks. The 67.65% union combines heterogeneous methods and budgets. §7.1: E at 10s solves 11,456 v1 versus 20,352 v2 problems; v1 adds only 46 unique solutions. Best full run is Zipperposition v3 at 280s with 25,420 (62.68%). Its v2 runs solve 24,959 at 280s and 23,518 at 140s. E at 60s slightly prefers v2 (21,001) over v3 (20,799). Deeper encoding does not uniformly improve every prover. §7.2: first-order successes with human premises are Vampire 15,938, E 15,136 and Prover9 14,693. Tasks are Horn with small dependency sets. Authors attribute similar results and weak complementarity to that structure. The paper compares these to Vampire’s higher-order 60s result but gives no separate full configuration table for first-order runs. §7.3: the whole-earlier-library setting allows all facts before the target theorem. Vampire at 60s solves 8,509 v3 tasks in LTB/SInE mode and 4,013 in hol mode. Distance-weighted nearest-neighbor selection trains incrementally on preceding human proofs. Seven parameters/slice sizes are 10,20,40,80,120,160,240. Future facts and proofs are excluded. Feature encoding, distance weights and tuning holdout are not detailed here. §7.3.1: seven higher-order 60s slices together solve 14,787 tasks; three complementary slices 120/240/20 solve 14,113, with nominal sequential budgets seven/three minutes. Best listed single slice, 120, solves 12,043. Parallel execution changes resource use; these unions are not one 60-second CPU run. §7.3.2: seven first-order standard slices plus 480/960 solve 12,373 unique tasks. Four slices 480/960/80/240 solve 12,089, about 30%. Sizes 480/960 alone solve 10,726/10,593. These are Vampire search results. No separate table gives final Metamath replay counts/timing for each slice. §11 calls the full tool 30% successful with four parallel 60s selections; retain that author claim without inventing a separately measured replay denominator. §8: Vampire proofs lack sufficient detail for reconstruction, so Vampire minimizes premises and Prover9 supplies IVY proofs. Reconstructed inputs and goals are Horn clauses. Instantiation/resolution preserve Horn; observed propositional steps remove duplicate assumptions. new_symbol, flip and paramod do not occur in reconstructed proofs. This is not replay of arbitrary classical or higher-order ATP proofs. §8: interpret Horn clauses as functions in minimal logic/simply typed lambda calculus. A headed clause maps conjunction of assumptions to its head; a negative clause maps to fresh F. Negated goal introduces the only constructor thm:B′→F. Resolution becomes function composition, instantiation substitutes terms, and duplicate removal repeats arguments. Normalize the proof of F to thm(p), remove thm, and emit Metamath applications. This argument relies on the restricted grammar and source facts; no full mechanized translator-correctness theorem is supplied. §8.1: normalization pushes instantiations to leaf applications. Restricting output to one theorem proof can duplicate intermediate work. mercolem6 expands from 674 IVY steps to 5,660,830 Metamath lines. Named auxiliary lemmas would avoid replication but are future work. Other listed reconstructed lengths are 849,77,50,45. Proof size can dominate search cost. §§9–11: benchmark https://github.com/ai4reason/mm-atp-benchmark and tool https://github.com/digama0/mm-hammer are published. Tool includes installer, premise selection, provers and reconstruction. Authors report replay of all roughly 15k Prover9 proofs with human premises. No artifact was executed for this record. No Verus/Rust/TLA+, distributed-protocol specification, LLM training or LLM-agent experiment.

Finding a translated proof differs from emitting a checked proof; supplied human premises differ from automatic selection; encodings, solver unions and time budgets need explicit reporting. Chronological training limits future-proof leakage. Proof-assistant replay can check external search, but unsupported inferences and proof-size explosion affect usability. The paper provides no evidence of specification writing or verification of distributed systems, Verus, TLA+ or Rust, and is not an LLM-agent study.

title: Automated Verification for Real-Time Systems via Implicit Clocks and an Extended Antimirov Algorithm
what: Defines the core timed language C_t, the Timed Effects (TimEffs) specification logic, a Hoare-style forward verifier, and an extended Antimirov term-rewriting system (TRS) that checks timed-language inclusion. The implementation verifies source-level temporal behavior with implicit, input-dependent clocks and concurrency constructs. TimEffs combines regular-expression traces with dependent arithmetic bounds, event absence, guards, waiting, deadlines, interrupts, parallel composition and shared mutable state. title: Automated Verification of Idempotence for Stateful Serverless Applications
what: Flux verifies retry transparency for concurrent stateful serverless applications using symbolic execution and SMT-checked simulation. Idempotence consistency requires retrying executions to match event histories and final database states of some retry-free execution. A stronger per-function simulation supports composition; inferred rely conditions and failure reduction limit checking to one retry after state changes. A logging advisor chooses protected operations, reducing overhead compared with logging all operations. Evaluation covers27 applications/79 functions and eight selected performance workloads. Records exact event/failure/API semantics, annotation and NoSQL assumptions, stable pre/post rules, restricted loop treatment, paper-only metatheory and omitted proof, heuristic mapping/advisor incompleteness, unsupported-loop fallback, concrete bug patterns and HDFS extension limits. Saves complete27-row application counts/times, every latency label, comparison settings/ports, plot estimates and adverse raw/timeout cases. Preserves the source’s inverted Table1 legend and distinguishes correctness definitions from atomicity/liveness.
assumptions_limits: §3 Definition1: Observable behavior is ordered invocation/response/side-effecting-service events plus final shared database state. For every retrying execution from any initial state, some retry-free execution must produce the same behavior. The retry-free execution may have a different interleaving; this is not deterministic replay or exactly-once execution of each database operation. §3: Failures discard only the failed instance’s local state; persistent database state and other instances’ local states survive. Retry restarts at the first statement with the same invocation ID and arguments and generates no new invocation event. Correctness is relative to this retry/failure model, not arbitrary database corruption, lost acknowledged writes or overlapping duplicate workers outside the model. §§1,4.2,5,9: Shared state is modeled as persistent NoSQL key-value pairs, and APIs become atomic read/write steps (a conditional update’s read/write pair is atomic). Prototype supports Java via Java Pathfinder and DynamoDB. File descriptors, shared process memory, other database semantics and other languages need new models/engineering. §§3,5,5.1: Developers must supply names and side-effect bits for third-party services; optional unique-variable annotations exclude other instances from accessing corresponding keys. These annotations and modeled semantics must be accurate. Thus entirely automated means generated reasoning conditions after these inputs, not zero human semantic input or automatic validation of service uniqueness. §4.1 Theorem1/AppendixA: Per-function simulation is sufficient, stronger than application consistency. Every retry step must match zero/more retry-free steps with the same event and database state, stable under the environment relation. Composition needs rely conditions covering actual concurrent effects: AppendixA uses (D,D′)∈R to preserve the other component’s simulation. Do not interpret the existential R in the abbreviated theorem as permission to choose an arbitrary underapproximation. §4.2: Rely inference has only read-only, arbitrary-update and same-constant-update classes. Symbolic-key writes may modify arbitrary data. Read-only reads and invariant constant writes permit stable facts; otherwise facts remain unchanged. This is conservative and incomplete; it does not infer every useful invariant or semantic relation. §4.3 Theorem2/AppendixC: Non-writing unbounded loops are replaced by uninterpreted functions returning arbitrary values. Writing loops require retry-invariant iteration count and inputs, idempotence simulation for prefix/body/suffix and no further state effect after each successfully executed component. These restrictions exclude loops whose writes/iteration counts change on retry. No general automatic loop invariant synthesis or termination proof. §4.4/AppendixB: Theorems3–4 reduce arbitrary finite retry counts to one retry and state-changing cut points using simulation induction/transitivity. AppendixB explicitly omits a formal proof of the state-changing-cut condition as intuitive. Theorems/lemmas are paper proofs; no mechanized metatheory or independently checked implementation-soundness proof is reported. Eventful third-party APIs must be modeled consistently with this reduction; the paper does not separately prove that boundary. §5 Algorithms1–2: Symbolic traces start with true conditions for unconstrained inputs/database states. SMT checks operation-parameter equalities under path-condition conjunctions, matches observable events and carries equalities between same-key reads. Verification relies on trace generation, API model, implication construction and solver correctness. No independently checkable proof certificate or complete trusted-component inventory is supplied. §5.2: Step mapping uses a preferred prefix/retry-to-nop heuristic, with random alternative mappings if needed; it can miss valid mappings. Four incompleteness sources are stronger-than-needed per-function simulation, unsupported writing loops, missed mappings and limited inferred conditions. Sound/no-missed-bug statements are authors’ guarantees under assumptions, not empirical proof of implementation soundness. No false positives in evaluated cases does not establish completeness. §6: Brute-force advisor checks2^n candidate sets and minimizes estimated logging cost among verifier-accepted sets. Greedy advisor checksO(n) sets, keeps any log whose removal fails verification and need not find a global minimum. A retained log can reflect incompleteness rather than a necessary bug fix. Unsupported loops trigger conservative all-operation logging before/inside the loop except reads of read-only data. §6 Table1: The table’s candidate columns are get/update/put=[0,1,1],[1,0,1],[1,1,0] with results false,false,true. The prose says0means logged/1not logged but also says get=0 removes its log, contradicting that legend. The algorithm/example outcome consistently keeps get/update logs and removes put. Preserve printed cells and flag the inversion instead of silently choosing a legend. §7.1: Applications are adapted from public repositories/benchmarks; AWS repository selection requires≥1000deployments and omits stateless/microbenchmark cases. The authors manually port Java applications to Go for Beldi/Boki performance; semantic equivalence is asserted, not formally verified. Selection/adaptation limits generalization to all serverless applications. §§7.1–7.2 Table2: Fifteen applications classified consistent, twelve inconsistent;21functions have issues;8issue confirmations are reported, not27independently proved diagnoses. SPECjbb verification times out on unsupported loops. Authors say its unverified functions are buggy and use advisor fallback; this is not successful verification of all79functions. Table2 does not give timeout threshold. §§7.1,7.4: Beldi uses AWS Lambda1GB instances/DynamoDB/CloudWatch; Boki uses its own platform. Transactions in comparison runtimes are disabled to compare idempotence costs. Boki cannot precisely report throughput and does not support the needed read-modify-write guarantee for Alexa/SPECjbb; those cases are excluded. Do not attribute Beldi throughput results to Boki. §7.4: wrk2 load runs seven minutes; eight selected applications supply Beldi plots, six Boki plots at1RPS. Further800RPS and Java results are prose-only. Median/p99 are request latency statistics, not repeated-experiment confidence intervals. Repetition counts/warm-up policy and raw runs are not stated. Raw may be incorrect, and Type-II protection retains overhead relative to it. §9: Idempotence consistency permits partial updates visible to other functions and does not guarantee atomicity, serializability, availability, termination or eventual retry success. HDFS truncate example illustrates the definition’s reach, but Flux’s Java/NoSQL algorithm is not shown verifying all HDFS. Applying it elsewhere needs state models and exactly-once mechanisms. §§8–10: Relevant to retry specifications, compositional verification and evaluating automated proofs. Comparisons to CHL/Yggdrasil/Perennial/RGSim concern stated methods and scope. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. No Flux artifact appendix/repository pointer in this PDF; cited benchmark/tool/bug sources are not a replay.
use_for_goal: Direct distributed retry-specification case: event/final-state inclusion is weaker than atomicity and stronger per-function simulation enables automation. Concrete annotation/model/trusted-tool boundaries, omitted proof and heuristic incompleteness are useful checks for agent-generated specifications and proof claims. Empirical results distinguish verifier rejection/timeout, confirmed bugs, conservative protection and measured overhead. No direct Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent result.

title: Automated Verification of Network Function Binaries
what: Klint checks x86_64 network-function binaries against Python specifications by symbolic execution with trusted environment/data-structure contracts. Ghost maps express both specifications and contracts, separating known key/value/presence triples from unknown-item invariants and translating operations into quantifier-free bitvector constraints. Candidate invariants are inferred across maps and weakened to a packet-loop fixed point. Optional full-stack verification follows NIC register actions and separately proved data structures/allocator. Records operation formulas, persistence layers and recursive lookup shortcut, forall incompleteness/nontermination, invariant relaxation and cross-map candidates, dynamic-link/memory/event restrictions, NIC action preconditions, precise full-stack trust boundary, all verification/performance tables and BPF scope, concrete configuration/standard bugs, appendix property obligations and get algorithm.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: Core technique assumes correctly implemented, delineated data structures with map-based contracts. Binary must expose calls/symbols for environment operations and known parameter types/calling convention. No source/debug symbols needed for NF, but this is not arbitrary opaque whole-binary verification without contracts. §2.1: Single-threaded, initialization then packet processing; no shared-state multi-thread verification. Code executes only on init/packet arrival; timers must be checked within handler. Capability allocation only at initialization and may fail externally, e.g.OOM. Later operations may fail through misuse, not arbitrary external environment failure. §5: Mutable memory after init confined to stack and map-modeled heap; other memory read-only. calloc-like allocations return symbolic pointers. State/data-structure separation is enforced, and excessive unabstracted paths reach configurable instruction threshold. No general unbounded-loop termination proof. §§3.2–3.4: Decidability concerns generated quantifier-free bitvector formulas, not completeness or termination of all host-level map/invariant processing. forall false gives no constraints on future unknown items. Recursion shortcut handles reciprocal maps but other recursive invariants may recurse infinitely; introduction always-proof-or-counterexample claim is explicitly qualified by §3.4 and execution limits. Failed checking can be incompleteness/threshold/timeout rather than an actual implementation bug. §3.4: Unknown-item invariant applies only to unknown keys, not every known item; equality consistency handles aliases and KnownSize constrains distinct present known keys. Map layers share base unknown state and lazily transform known entries so later reads on old/new versions remain related. Ordered queues/stacks are expressible but authors believe poorly suited to inference. §4: Candidate constraints from initialized/known items are relaxed until inductive over each packet path; cross-map FK,FV,FP functions are discovered from known items and checked against unknown invariants. Shrinking candidate set is paper convergence argument; this does not establish inference of every useful invariant or remove §3.4 recursive-operation nontermination. §5: Specification map matching tries candidates heuristically and rejects only after all possibilities violate spec. §6.1 requires struct field order in spec to match implementation; values can be abstracted with ellipsis. Specifications/environment contracts remain human adequacy obligations. §5: Full stack verifies driver/most minimal OS against manually encoded NIC DSL/actions from public hardware documentation. Register writes must match feasible action and preconditions; hardware semantics and model faithfulness remain trusted. Does not prove physical NIC correctness or distributed network behavior. §5: Full-stack TCB explicitly includes Klint,angr,Z3,bootloader,hardware,VeriFast and C compiler for source-verified data structures/allocator. Ordinary core-contract mode assumes those implementations correct. Abstract assertion of no trusted software except Klint omits this detailed boundary. §§5,7: Environment compiled separately, linked without LTO to retain symbols; dynamically linked data-structure operations cost calls/lost inlining. NF+driver can compile together. Containers use Linux environment/contracts and trust container runtime/Linux implementation, enlarging TCB. §§6.3,7: Seven functionally checked binaries are six C functions plus one Rust policer; five existing BPF programs receive memory safety/crash freedom only because functional specifications unavailable. Native assembly dumped from kernel-compiled BPF is analyzed with BPF-map contracts. Rust example validates one compiled binary relative to contracts/spec, not Rust language/compiler correctness or a Verus proof. §7: Correct implementation of specification is not proof of protocol properties such as absence of infinite network-message loops. No distributed consensus/liveness/linearizability/durability theorem, no TLA+ or LLM-generated specification/proof evaluation. §6.1: Verification timing from one specified CPU; solver heuristics can change times by dozens of seconds, no repetitions/confidence intervals stated. Table1 excludes additional~15minutes/fullstack/function. Router0s cells are printed values, not measured zero computational work. §6.2/Table2/Figure5: All10Gbps Klint throughput cells are link-saturated censored measurements, not true maximum capacities. TinyNF replaces original Vigor DPDK subset in principal comparison. Implementations/allocator/driver/inline assembly differ and Klint bridge adds STP; performance is not controlled same-code cost of verification. Curves show median and5th/95th percentiles, not statistical confidence intervals. §6.3/Table3: No extra inputs comparison excludes shared prerequisites: NF specification plus data-structure/environment contracts still required. Historical Rust bug-tracker69unsoundissues and BPF loop restrictions are source-time claims, not current facts. External repository/proofs unrun.
use_for_goal: Binary/refinement evidence for trusted-contract system verification, including one Rustpolicer. Useful for distributed-system/LLMproof evaluation: separate protocol adequacy from implementation refinement, assumptions from checkedcode, solverdecidability from tooltermination, functional from crash/memorychecks, symbolicconfiguration coverage from concretetestsettings, and linklimitedbenchmarks from actualcapacity. No direct Verus,TLA+orLLMresult.

title: Automated Verification of Robot Software Models with Assume-Guarantee Reasoning in Isabelle/HOL
what: Defines a coinductive CSP deadlock-freedom specification and reports its equivalence to a failures-divergences refinement specification in Isabelle/HOL. Builds proof tactics for RoboChart transition processes enriched with active-node parameters and invariant assumption/guarantee checks. Demonstrates automated component transition proofs and guard-gap counterexamples,including models with real-valued state. Full state-machine/controller composition and environment compatibility remain future work. Gives explicit assume and guarantee processes with observable violation events,normalization laws and sufficient proof-reduction rules. Reduces recursive-process deadlock goals by coinduction,node case splits,universally quantified inputs,invariant hypotheses,guard coverage and proofs of every enabled continuation. A second tactic exposes guard-gap formulas to Nitpick/Quickcheck. Cases show invariant dependence,a corrected navigation guard gap and symbolic verification where finite-state FDR runs out of memory.
assumptions_limits: Target is the transition behaviour process,not complete communicating controllers or robot physical safety. Trigger events are treated as available; synchronization/event availability and compatibility of component contracts need separate system-level proofs. Exactly one simple leaf node is active; composite states with multiple active nodes are excluded. Invariant I is supplied manually as a design/environment assumption. Initial satisfaction and preservation by other components are environmental obligations. Checking a component under I does not establish that the deployed sensor/memory/environment enforces I or that interacting components are mutually consistent. The CSP notion permits successful termination through Skip. It is the deadlock_freeSKIPS variant,not the usual never-terminating deadlock-free CSP process. Coinductive DFI requires a nonempty observable event sequence before recursion,while DFI* permits empty sequences after progress is already accounted for. Correctly distinguishing those variants prevents unguarded circular proof. Isabelle/HOL and the HOL-CSP semantic libraries support kernel-checked proofs of generated logical terms. Model translation runs through Eclipse EOL RoboChart→Circus and EGL Circus→HOL-CSP; the paper claims semantic faithfulness but does not give a machine-checked end-to-end translator correctness theorem. Enrichment adds an explicit active-node parameter,final-state branch and assume/guar wrappers. Equivalence to the original process is conditional on successful contracts and surrounding operational structure. Assuming an invariant is a meaningful restriction on admissible inputs,not an unconditional theorem about the original unrestricted model. False assume emits aviol and recurses to a fallback; false guar emits gviol then STOP. These behaviors differ. Component proofs distinguish environmental violations from internal errors; a deadlock-free enriched process can still rely on an unrealized environment contract. Automation is specialized to the prototypical Trans structure and available normalization/reduction rules. Simple logical/arithmetic goals use simp,auto or Sledgehammer. A failed tactic does not establish a deadlock; Nitpick/Quickcheck witnesses of uncovered guards must be assessed for reachability,environment assumptions and the actual original model. Counterexample search concentrates on enabled-guard coverage. It does not claim completeness for arbitrary transition action failure,interacting process deadlock or infinite-state reachability. Real-valued symbolic proofs avoid enumeration but still require dischargeable mathematical obligations. Authors declare GenAI only for language polishing: technical content,proofs and formalization are human work. The study evaluates theorem-prover automation,not LLM-generated specifications/proofs or agents. No Verus,Rust or TLA+case is included.
use_for_goal: Relevant to verified concurrent models and evaluation: precise separation of kernel-checked logical results,manual invariants,translation faithfulness,environment assumptions and full composition. Gives coinductive progress proof patterns potentially useful for Verus/distributed verification and concrete specification pitfalls for LLM agents to detect. Its demonstrated result remains conditional transition deadlock freedom in Isabelle/HOL,with system-level deadlock freedom and implementation links unresolved.

title: Automatic Test-Case Reduction in Proof Assistants: A Case Study in Coq
what: Coq-specific test-case reducer integrated into compatibility-testing workflows. Repeatedly transforms a failing development while testing that it still fails under the changed Coq version and passes under the baseline. Uses proof admission, definition-block deletion, module/name handling and dependency inlining to obtain smaller self-contained reproductions. Deployment study measures reduction outcomes; the reducer itself is not formally verified. Explains the behavioral oracle, admission/transparency pitfalls, section dependencies, inaccurate globalization metadata and non-linearizable global state. Separates initial-run success, standalone success on a smaller measured subset, elapsed workflow time and final compilation time. Provides exact denominator accounting and explicitly rejects using its evolving-tool observational results as a comparative benchmark.
assumptions_limits: Reverse dependency compatibility testing (RDCT) uses external projects as tests of a modified proof assistant. Standard reducer oracle is baseline success and modified-version failure with a normalized matching error message. That preserves a chosen symptom, not a proof of identical root cause or semantic equivalence between original and reduced files. Error matching deliberately groups universe inconsistencies, forgotten-universe errors and unsatisfied-constraint errors, ignores filenames/positions/wrapping and often numbering. It preserves numeric information for universe-instance length errors. Such relaxations trade reduction freedom against possible slippage to another bug. Replacing proofs with Admitted, Admit Obligations or an existing axiom is intentional for debugging. A reduced file with admissions is not a newly verified theorem or a successful proof-generation outcome. A kernel-acceptance bug needs an explicit observable test symptom, not merely a generic compiler error oracle. Greedy syntax-unit and definition-block removal can stop at local minima; minimal means reduced under tested heuristics, not globally shortest or a proved minimal reproducer. Program obligations, modules, imports and section variables create dependencies that single-line deletion misses. Coq cannot fully isolate every global setting when files are inlined. Module wrapping, selective name resolution and trying alternate insertion positions are heuristic workarounds; no guarantee exists that every dependency tree can be flattened while reproducing behavior. Globalization .glob metadata is incomplete/inaccurate, including missing tactic and notation resolution. The implementation selectively resolves Require/Import/Export and lets Coq handle other names; it does not use a complete verified Coq parser or resolver. Production bot automatically PROPOSES minimization after internal tests pass and external tests fail relative to a successful base. §9.1 describes a comment from someone triggering the run. Abstract automatic-trigger phrasing should not be read as unattended execution of every CI failure. Six-hour GitHub Action timeout causes restart from the latest reduced file. A retry can repeat indefinitely if no progress is made before timeout. The study includes four manually cancelled loops; retrying is not itself evidence of eventual completion. Dataset is observational, selected by developers requesting minimization, excludes PRs opened by first author, and deduplicates to first trigger per PR/project. Tool changed in response to these same cases. This is feasibility evidence, not a fixed-version unbiased comparison against alternative reducers. Standalone means no dependency beyond Coq standard library, not no dependencies whatsoever. 89% uses only 47 recent SUCCESSFUL runs with inlining metadata; detailed size/time/ratio results mostly use 42 known standalone cases. These are distinct from all 191 requested first runs. Elapsed reduction duration includes queue/VM setup, not pure reducer CPU time. Final-case compile time comes from reducer header estimates, not a new independently controlled rerun. Hardware, language-version-specific controls and dispersion are not given here. Record reads the publication, not supplementary CSV/Jupyter code or current repository behavior. No efficacy measurement on Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-generated specifications/proofs is reported; generalization to other assistants is an author expectation.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly useful for evaluating and maintaining automated proof workflows. Preserving the actual failing symptom, recording environments, distinguishing admissions from checked proofs, separating infrastructure failures and using correct conditional denominators apply to LLM agents generating specs/proofs. The study supplies real Coq ecosystem evidence but no distributed-system proof, Verus/verified-Rust/TLA+ workflow or LLM-agent benchmark.

title: Automatically Generalizing Proofs and Statements
what: Lean proof-term generalization tactic that takes an existing proof and a selected constant, then returns a more abstract statement with a proof when transformation typechecks. It generalizes repeated occurrences independently, discovers related constants through type mismatches/antiunification, and abstracts composite proof fragments into hypotheses. Demonstrations include arithmetic, set cardinality, algebraic cancellation and Bézout. Six-stage description explains separate metavariables per occurrence, hypothesis abstraction from inferred types, iterative detection of dependent constants, unification to recover required equalities, metavariable-to-binder extraction, and type inference for the resulting statement. Contrasts accepted proof with useful/general/nonvacuous generalization, and shows how definitional computation or opaque proof steps obstruct extraction. Distinguishes implemented tactic from ideal future proof-discovery uses.
assumptions_limits: Requires an existing formal Lean proof and user-selected expression/constant, optionally occurrence controls. Soundness relies on successful final proof typechecking in its Lean environment and the assumptions of referenced declarations. It is not a stand-alone axiomatic proof of the algorithm, an audit of input axioms, or a guarantee that a formal statement matches human intent. Accepted result is a provable conditional statement. This alone does not establish weakest hypotheses, nonvacuity, strict generality, novelty, usefulness or a canonical mathematical abstraction. Paper explicitly describes a true output hypothesis that forces n=2 and thus adds no genuine generality. Outputs depend on the exact proof, including how facts are encoded, not just the original theorem statement. The transformation operates on proof terms and loses tactic-script structure. Default abstracts all occurrences; coincidental equality may change output, and user can restrict occurrences. Dependent-constant search uses syntactic antiunification and a heuristic favoring fewer metavariables. No completeness, optimality, termination or runtime complexity theorem is reported. Related mismatches may remain unresolved, especially when generalized types lose definitional equality. Definitional-equality example fails when generalizing integers because divisibility no longer unfolds as the required existential. An explicit rewrite via Int.dvd_def records the connection as a proof step and permits an added divisibility-definition hypothesis. Merely unfold does not change the proof term and therefore does not provide that evidence. Computation can erase the dependency trace needed for abstraction:paper’s reduceMul example leaves 6 rather than how 2*3 produced it. Generalizing proofs cannot independently solve newly exposed mathematical subproblems. Original specialized computations may need to become hypotheses instead. Bézout output is a long collection of sufficient algebraic/size/quotient/remainder conditions from a particular proof, not a recovered canonical Euclidean-domain definition. Typeclass simplification and simultaneous generalization from two proofs are future work. Several application sections discuss an ideal algorithm or mathematical motivation rather than demonstrated execution:inductive proof discovery, intermediate-value abstraction, conjecture generation, learning from counterexamples, and interesting-question generation. No integrated LLM/automated proof-discovery evaluation is reported.
use_for_goal: Relevant non-LLM component for specification/proof agents:reuse a checked proof to expose parameters and required assumptions, then separately judge nonvacuity, usefulness and statement fidelity. Provides failure cases for evaluating proof transformations and illustrates why kernel acceptance alone is insufficient for specification quality. No Verus/Rust, distributed-system, TLA+ or LLM experiment is reported; transfer to those workflows is reader inference.

title: Automating and Mechanizing Cutoff-based Verification of Distributed Protocols
what: Formalizes cutoff-based verification for parametric distributed protocols in the Relational Modeling Language (RML). A finite cutoff instance is sufficient when every safety violation in any larger instance can be simulated by a trace of the cutoff; the paper encodes this simulation in first-order logic and uses SMT to check it. The paper gives initial, step, and safety simulation conditions and a first-violation refinement that removes the need to simulate behavior after a violation. A backward static analysis starts from instantiated negated safety clauses, follows action updates into guards to a fixed point, and emits the relevant action set, simulation relation, and lockstep. In the sharded key-value example, the analysis reduces eight actions to four and proves a two-node cutoff. The implementation checks the formulas with Z3 and handles seven protocols: four cutoffs are synthesized automatically; three require small manual changes. Two-phase commit exposes a limit: universally quantified guards force actions of all larger-instance nodes into the simulation, requiring an extra failure-simulating node and constraints.

assumptions_limits: RML domains are finite per instance but may have infinitely many valid interpretations; safety properties are assumed universally quantified. The result is for safety, not liveness. Cutoff correctness depends on a simulation relation for every valid larger interpretation and on a safe finite cutoff. Automatic synthesis can fail when universal guards or side effects conflict, as in two-phase commit, and the basic key-value store needs an added precondition.

Its cutoff and backward-relevance approach complements inductive-invariant methods, while the manual repairs and universal-guard failures identify assumptions an automated Verus/TLA+ workflow must expose.

title: An Automaton Learning Approach to Solving Safety Games over Infinite Graphs.
short_name: Automaton learning for infinite safety games
what: Learns finite-state winning controllers for safety games over infinite or very large graphs. Rational arenas encode vertex sets as regular languages and edges as rational relations; an ICE-like teacher returns positive, negative, existential-implication or universal-implication counterexamples, and a SAT-based learner constructs minimal consistent DFAs. The paper proves closure properties of rational relations, defines winning sets and a generic automata-theoretic teacher, and gives SAT encodings whose satisfiability is equivalent to existence of an n-state DFA consistent with the sample. The minimal-consistent-DFA algorithm increments n and terminates at the minimum; the full learner terminates with a winning set when one exists. An RPNI heuristic is sound but incomplete and restricted to finite out-degree. Examples include unary encodings of grid positions, implication counterexamples, diagonal/box/evasion/follow games and program repair.
numbers: SAT learner solved all infinite-arena games; RPNI all but Follow
9×9 planning: 7.8 s SAT, 2.1 s RPNI, 5.4 s TuLiP
300 s timeout and 16 GiB memory
roughly 2m vertices in scalability game
assumptions_limits: Winner determination for rational safety games is undecidable, so the method is a semi-algorithm and assumes a winning set exists for the termination theorem. The SAT learner's passive DFA identification is NP-complete in general; RPNI cannot guarantee minimality or completeness and handles only finite implication languages. Experiments use regular-language/transducer encodings and finite-state safety objectives; results do not establish liveness synthesis or arbitrary infinite-state game classes.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for CEGIS-style controller/specification synthesis over infinite-state abstractions. The explicit implication counterexamples, minimal-DFA encoding and semi-decision boundary inform agent-generated distributed specifications and the need to distinguish soundness from guaranteed termination.
