title: AutoQ: An Automata-Based Quantum Circuit Verifier.
what: Presents C++ automated Hoare-style quantum-circuit checking with tree-automata sets of pure states, symbolic amplitude expressions and predicate-valued postconditions. Extends prior exact gate transformations with relational symbolic specifications and an antichain entailment procedure invoking Z3. Reports Hadamard identity, real-amplitude checks, full Grover probability checks for fixed/all encoded oracles and a weaker single-iteration amplification check, plus two injected bugs. No new machine-checked verifier correctness proof or empirical proof-writing agent is supplied. Defines symbolic-tree entailment and a compact high-level language with basis patterns, existential index and tensor products. Exact algebraic-number representation supports a finite gate set; the main new entailment step checks constraint-implied leaf predicates during bottom-up TA inclusion. Benchmark details expose how oracle quantification and weaker properties change scale and bottlenecks. Reader checks separate printed algebra/size defects from artifact correctness and distinguish the defined uniform symbolic-tree entailment from ordinary valuation-dependent set inclusion.
assumptions_limits: Hoare input{P,phi}C{Q} has a finite OpenQASM gate sequence C, term-leaf precondition TA P, formula phi over shared symbolic values and term/predicate-leaf postcondition Q. It operates on pure-state amplitudes and unitary supported gate sequences; no measurement branching, noisy/mixed-state evolution, dynamic loops or physical-device correspondence is established. Exactness is relative to represented states and supported transformations. Each n-qubit vector is a depth-n binary decision tree, ordered by qubits, with amplitudes at2^nleaves. Tree automata share substructure and can represent all computational basis states with O(n)states/transitions. This compactness is for structured families, not a general polynomial representation of arbitrary quantum-state sets; executing gates and entailment can still grow exponentially. Introductory two-symbol construction assigns one marked amplitude vh and the same vl to every other basis. The text describes this as all states with one more probable basis, but it only covers that equal-unmarked-amplitude subclass, not arbitrary unequal lower amplitudes. A more general TA/specification may encode other structures; the displayed construction itself is restricted. High-level grammar supports fixed basis patterns with default other-basis term, existential bitstring index, finite spec unions and tensor products. Free indices, repeated bases and mixed lengths are ill-formed. Reusing an existential index across tensor factors encodes oracle/work-register relationships. This is user-authored specification automation, not automatic discovery that the postcondition captures the intended quantum algorithm. Concrete gate coefficients use(1/sqrt2)^k*(a+b*omega+c*omega²+d*omega³),integer a,b,c,d and omega=exp(i*pi/4). Supported gates:X,H,Y,Z,S,T,Rx(pi/2),Ry(pi/2),CNOT,CZ,Toffoli. This countable ring supports a universal approximation basis, not exact arbitrary-angle rotations. Solovay–Kitaev approximation for other rotations does not by itself certify the original ideal circuit/property or propagate an error budget. Precondition leaves share a normalization exponent k, omitted using normalization of the full state; relative exponent kc is tracked through gates and applied to final leaves. This depends on normalized-state/common-scale interpretation. The paper does not supply a full symbolic normalization-validation procedure or arithmetic-overflow audit. Integer symbolic terms and exact gate constants do not prove the whole C++/SMT pipeline correct. Visually confirmed formula defect on p.145: expansion first contains +c*i, but squared imaginary component is printed(b*sqrt2/2−c+d*sqrt2/2)² instead of+c. Reader example(a,b,c,d)=(0,1,1,0): |omega+i|²=2+sqrt2, whereas printed formula yields2−sqrt2. The real-amplitude condition c=0,b=−d remains valid; artifact arithmetic was not inspected and no implementation bug is inferred. Tree entailment requires each term leaf either match syntactically or satisfy phi=>postpredicate after substitution. Automaton entailment is forall source symbolic trees exists a post tree whose every leaf implication is valid under all phi-valuations. This quantifier order requires one post-tree choice uniformly across those valuations, stronger than allowing post-tree choice per concrete valuation. It is the defined check, not completeness for arbitrary extensional unions of concrete states. Reader quantifier example: identity on v|0>+(1−v)|1>,integer v∈{0,1}; postcondition is a union of predicate trees describing exactly|0> and exactly|1>. Every concrete output belongs to that union, yet neither fixed post tree matches both valuations under leafwise implication. Defined entailment can fail without a concrete physical violation under that different set interpretation. Do not treat bug found as an independently validated counterexample for every broader intended semantics. Algorithm1 initializes pairs(sourceleafstate,setofmatchingpostleafstates), combines pairs bottom-up along the same qubit label, rejects if a source root has no post root, and returns true when the worklist empties. Antichain Min/subsumption/simulation prune states; details are delegated to refs4/10. Visual line4 is Worklist!=empty; raw extraction loses the slash. Qr/Qq notation in some lines is inconsistent with Sr/Sq, not evidence of an implementation fault. C++ pipeline preprocesses .aut/.hsl/.smt/.qasm, applies imported gate transformations with symbolic leaf updates and outputs reachable TA R, then checks entailment. Uses VATA for term-only TA inclusion and Z3 for predicate implications; experiments use QF_NIRA. Allowing any Z3-supported theory is not a claim that every theory is decidable or that unknown/timeouts imply a bug. Such result handling and proof certificates are not described. Hadamard-square case uses arbitrary symbolic quadruples for both input amplitudes and phi=true, preserving each amplitude. One altered H gate is detected. Bernstein–Vazirani cases check only zero imaginary parts, not the full correct secret output, although the worked three-qubit example yields|010>. An injected BV bug violates that property. A different erroneous circuit could retain real amplitudes and evade this weaker specification. GroverSingle fixes an oracle satisfying bitstring and starts all work/ancilla bits zero; postcondition requires correct-work-basis probability>.9, other basis probabilities<.1, real amplitudes and zero ancillas. GroverAll stores an arbitrary basis-index oracle in an additional register and relates it to the work-register answer using the same index. It covers all encoded unique-solution bitstrings at a fixed n, not all Boolean functions/multiple-solution oracles or coherent superpositions of distinct oracle indices. GroverIter assumes all unmarked amplitudes are the same positive real vl, marked amplitude vh>0 and(2^n−1)*vl>vh. The postcondition increases marked magnitude and decreases every unmarked magnitude, preserves real amplitudes and zero ancillas. This avoids Grover overshoot and proves one iteration on that structured region, not overall search success for arbitrary input vectors, alliterationcounts or probability>.9. Table1 has18selected rows:16OKand2Bug. BV reaches1000qubits/2500gates in198m28s; that property is only real amplitudes. Full GroverAll reaches n9(27totalqubits),1492gates,25m16s; GroverSingle reaches n20(40qubits),141527gates,19m57s. GroverIter reaches n100(200qubits),895gates,10m53s for its weaker property. A fixed-size verification does not establish a parameterized theorem for alln. Printed GroverIter(2) row lists3qubits/13gates while Section5.4 describes a4-qubit two-work/two-ancilla circuit. Preserve the table and note the discrepancy; do not silently repair either without artifact comparison. n>=100scaling language is supported here by an n100row, not an unbounded sequence of measured results. Maximum peak memory is reported52MiB for GroverAll9. Entailment is usually negligible but costs138of198seconds for All8(~70percent) and1296of1516seconds for All9(~85percent). These are different-instance bottlenecks, not a controlled asymptotic proof. The paper supplies no CPU/RAM/OS, repeated trials, seeds, variance, timeout criterion or competitor benchmark table; previous evaluation is delegated to ref14. Artifact https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7966542 and repository https://github.com/alan23273850/AutoQ are linked. A predecessor caught a Qcec bug according to footnote2/ref3, not a newly reproduced result here. No new formal correctness theorem/proof, independent artifact execution or full trust audit is provided in this reading. Relevance is automated relational specification checking, exact symbolic arithmetic and evaluation of property strength/negative cases. No LLM writes specs/proofs, no Verus/verified Rust or TLA+ pipeline, and no distributed-system protocol is verified. Claims about tool priority/manual-proof alternatives are author statements rather than an independent exhaustive comparison. Reader qualification after independent review: Grover probability/amplification predicates are printed using only coefficient a (square-a placeholder), not the full real amplitude a+sqrt(2)*b allowed by psi_Im (c=0,b=−d). Interpreting a as the entire real amplitude needs an a-only invariant for these cases or an unstated shorthand. This is a specification-presentation limitation; no circuit or artifact error is inferred.
use_for_goal: Useful comparison for specification/proof-agent evaluation: user-authored relational predicates, automated symbolic execution, exact-number boundaries, stronger symbolic quantifiers, fixed-instance versus parameterized claims, injected negative cases and property-strength-dependent scale. No LLM-agent,Verus/Rust,TLA+or distributed correctness result.

title: AVR: Abstractly Verifying Reachability.
what: Presents AVR, a push-button word-level model checker for source-level transition systems. It combines syntax-guided abstraction/refinement with word-level IC3, SMT backends, BMC and interpolation, and emits independently checkable inductive-invariant certificates or BTOR2 counterexample witnesses. The paper details AVR architecture and interfaces (Verilog/Yosys, VMT/MathSAT, BTOR2/Btor2Tools), IC3+SA abstraction atoms, incremental refinement and caching, data abstraction, property-directed splitting, interpolation and extract/concat handling. Proof certificates are SMT-LIB inductive invariants externally checked by Z3/Yices; failed properties produce simulator-checkable BTOR2 traces. A multi-engine proof race runs configurations in parallel. Case studies cover patched Apache buffer overflows, Needham–Schroeder authentication, and finite-to-unbounded distributed-protocol invariant generalization.
numbers: less than one minute for each Apache case
3 initiators and 3 responders in Needham–Schroeder instance
HWMCC 2019 single-bit-vector track
assumptions_limits: Targets primarily safety properties over quantifier-free bit-vectors, arrays, uninterpreted functions and linear integer arithmetic. Word-level abstraction can be ineffective when bit-precise data dominates; current support is limited for nonlinear arithmetic, floating point, quantifiers, liveness and fairness. Distributed-protocol generalization is preliminary and requires human/generalization reasoning beyond finite AVR runs. Certificates rely on an external SMT checker and traces on a witness simulator.
use_for_goal: A concrete source-level IC3/SMT workflow for distributed-protocol and hardware safety verification, with independently checkable certificates and explicit abstraction limits.

quotes.text: Upon termination, AVR will either produce a proof certificate, in the form of a state formula representing an inductive invariant, if the safety property holds or a counterexample execution trace if it fails.
AVR prints such proof certificates directly in the SMT-LIB format, which allows for independent checking of their correctness using an external SMT solver like Yices 2 or Z3.
proof race initiates multiple AVR instances and terminates execution as soon as one of these instances successfully races to the result.
In less than a minute, AVR successfully verifies that both of these buffer overflow exploits are unreachable in the patched versions for any buffer size.
properties beyond safety (such as liveness and fairness) have limited support in the current tool implementation.

title: Regular Model Checking Upside-Down: An Invariant-Based Approach
what: Reverses regular model checking direction: intersects all inductive b-invariants represented by CNF formulas with at most b clauses, obtaining regular over-approximations converging to reachability. Defines regular transition systems with finite-word configurations and length-preserving transducers, then constructs automata for IndInv_b. For every b, unsafe-intersection emptiness is in EXPSPACE; b=1 has an exponential NFA and PSPACE-completeness. The proof uses tables/separation languages and a reduction from polynomial-space Turing machines. MONA experiments compute minimal DFAs for IndInv_1 across classic parameterized protocols and inspect cases needing b>1.

title: Formalization of a Realistic Verification-Condition Generator for an Intermediate Verification Language
what: Reports Dafny definitions and soundness proofs for a B3 intermediate verification language, an executable verification-condition generator (VCG), and a coinductive reference semantics supporting nondeterminism, unbounded loops, scopes, abrupt exits and recursive calls. Proves valid generated conditions imply procedure correctness for a closed set of procedures. A structural invariant/specification semantics makes most proofs amenable to SMT automation; a separate coinductive refinement connects it to reference execution. The authors report Cursor auto-completion only, without an LLM evaluation. Postcondition stacks model escape depth while continuation stacks guide VCG control flow and variable removal. Fresh variable incarnations distinguish assignment histories from current program states. The general statement theorem connects an arbitrary symbolic context, incarnation map and continuation stack to a reconstructed scoped statement; procedure soundness is derived from an assume-pre/body/check-post wrapper. Mutual coinduction handles both recursive procedure calls and loop unrolling. The paper explicitly separates the verified formal generator from incremental SMT interaction and evolved public B3, and excludes user axiom definitions.
numbers: No runtime or benchmark evaluation is reported in the extracted text. The only quantitative proof-engineering datum is that coinductive proofs required about 100 lines of manually supplied Dafny proofs outside existing automation.
assumptions_limits: Only source-IVL-to-VC generation is proved sound. Source-to-B3 translation, B3-expression-to-SMT translation and actual solver validity remain outside the theorem. The conclusion is conditional on mathematical validity of every generated VC, not on any unchecked SMT response. Dafny, its own verification pipeline, logic and underlying SMT automation are trusted for the author-reported proofs; no independently checked small-kernel certificate or self-verifier proof is supplied here. The paper simplifies the grammar: Boolean/integer/uninterpreted types; mathematical operations, quantified expressions and function calls; check/assume, assignment, nondeterministic choice, conditionals, unbounded loop, vars scopes and escape depths. It assumes unique variable declarations with no shadowing. Only distinct-variable inout parameters are shown; the accompanying formal implementation handles all parameter kinds, as does B3. Interpreted-function semantics and expression refinements are described but omitted from printed formal definitions. Correctness is partial: nontermination is permitted, and the work does not prove termination of B3 loops or recursive source procedures. VCG itself is reported terminating by measures on statements and continuations. Assertions must hold on relevant execution prefixes; reference omnisemantics is not merely an arbitrary overapproximation that can hide a failing check, since Check demands both the expression and post-state membership. Omnisemantics relates a statement and initial state to a sequence of overapproximating post-state sets. Its head handles normal completion; index i handles escape i. A scope duplicates the current head, adds arbitrarily initialized fresh locals, and lifts every post-set by allowing those locals and projecting them away. An escape does not execute the rest of its current statement sequence: it targets the indexed enclosing-scope postcondition. Escape zero is a no-op. A loop introduces no control-flow scope. To break out, wrap it in vars and use escape 1. Structural loop semantics existentially chooses any suitable invariant state set containing the initial state and preserved by normal body completion; body escapes still answer to the unchanged tail of enclosing postconditions. The syntactic invariant annotation is ignored by the semantics and is separately validated by VCG. Reference loop semantics instead unrolls body;loop using a greatest fixed point. Structural call semantics checks the instantiated precondition and universally considers post-states satisfying the instantiated postcondition, with the same domain and all nonargument variables unchanged. It omits checking the callee body. Reference call semantics adds RefMeetsSpec for the callee. A procedure without a body is treated as meeting its specification; its specification remains an assumption, not a proved implementation. Aliased inout actuals are excluded by the displayed distinct-variable requirement. Theorem 1 requires a closed set of procedures: every called procedure belongs to that set. Valid VCs for every procedure imply all reference MeetsSpec predicates. Recursive specifications may be assumed modularly only because all available bodies are checked and the mutually recursive reference predicates are coinductive. The article does not present a global liveness theorem or a termination argument for arbitrary recursion. Proof decomposition: Lemma 2 derives structural MeetsSpec from one procedure’s valid VCs; Lemma 3 derives reference MeetsSpec for a closed, structurally correct procedure set. Theorem 4 is the generalized statement-level VCG invariant used for Lemma 2. Several prose cross-references call Lemmas 2/3 Theorems 2/3; the numbered statement labels remain Lemma 2 and Lemma 3. VCG state contains incarnation map I, symbolic path context C and stack B of (introduced variables, continuation statements). Check generates C implies substituted E and leaves C unchanged; assume conjoins substituted E. Assignment creates a globally fresh incarnation xprime, constrains it to E evaluated under the old map, then updates I. This freshness and substitution bookkeeping is part of soundness, not a source-level assignment simplification. Conditional generation follows each branch with its continuation under opposite guard assumptions and unions the VC sets. Scope entry allocates local incarnations and pushes its following statement with its local-variable set. Normal and abrupt scope exit remove local entries from I, while accumulated formulas may still mention their incarnation values. The paper describes this symbolic-execution choice as more stable for automation but potentially producing more VCs; it gives no comparative measurement. Theorem 4 assumes all free variables in S and B are mapped by I; each jump depth fits its corresponding continuation suffix; the stated VCG judgment holds; every VC is valid; and incarnation state ist satisfies C. It concludes structural correctness of mkScope(S,B) from AdjustState(ist,I) against the universal post-set. AdjustState projects current program values from I-selected incarnations; conflating it with the full symbolic-history state would misstate the theorem. Printed equation (2) gives mkScope(S,B)=mkScope(Bprime,(vars nu in S);Sprime) in the nonempty case, reversing the declared statement/continuation argument order. Reader diagnosis: the type-consistent intended recurrence is mkScope((vars nu in S);Sprime,Bprime). This is a presentation issue; no claim is made that the Dafny implementation contains the same error. The detailed inductive proof of Theorem 4 is delegated to the artifact. Coinductive SemRefine and MeetsSpecRefine are mutually recursive greatest lemmas. Structural loop-unrolling first proves Sem(body;loop,...); the coinductive hypothesis gives RefSem of that unrolling. Calls invoke the procedure refinement, which in turn invokes statement refinement for all precondition states. Recursive interpreted expressions require a similar omitted refinement. About 100 manually supplied proof lines connect the semantics; this is not the size of the full soundness proof. The formal AST/state, semantics, generator and proofs total about 4.7 kLoC: about 2.0 kLoC AST/state, 660 LoC omnisemantics, and about 2.0 kLoC VCG/proofs. Roughly 1.5 kLoC are actual code and 3 kLoC annotations/proofs. Authors report four months by one person previously inexperienced with Dafny proofs. These are rounded development-effort reports without timing trials, benchmark corpus, proof acceptance rates or independent reproduction. Manual proof work concentrated in incarnation/substitution chains, sequence folds for continuation unwinding, and quantified/uninterpreted expression semantics. The paper calls these higher-order semantics difficult for SMT. It does not measure how much automation replaced manual work or compare alternative provers. The GenAI declaration says only Cursor auto-completion was used; it gives no model, prompts, accepted-completion counts or agent autonomy evidence. The formalized VCG stays close to the public B3 generator but is not a verified release of every public-tool path. Public B3 sends branch contexts incrementally to SMT and has evolved; integrating proofs into a release remains future work. User-defined axiom definitions are excluded; public lazy delivery of axioms and interpreted-function definitions is also future work. Thus the abstract phrase realistic features does not mean all current B3 features are covered. Artifact is linked at https://github.com/dafny-lang/b3, Software Heritage swh:1:dir:1795668a148637332f93759bb96a4cd4283d6e32, DOI 10.4230/artifacts.27039. No artifact files, source-build logs, generated binary or model of the compiler/runtime were inspected. Related claims about HOL4/Dafny, core Why3, Viper, Boogie certification and Featherweight VeriFast are author comparisons, not independent re-evaluations in this reading.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to the trust boundary of tools used for formal verification, including Verus-style SMT pipelines. Reader inference: evaluating an LLM-written proof or specification requires separating source translation, VC generation, solver encoding/validity and implementation integration; successful VCs alone do not prove those components. Also offers concrete tests for state renaming, scope unwinding, recursion and nontermination. Uses Dafny/B3 rather than verified Rust, Verus or TLA+ and verifies no distributed protocol. Cursor auto-completion is a qualitative declaration, not an evaluated autonomous proof agent.

title: Basilisk: Using Provenance Invariants to Automate Proofs of Undecidable Protocols
what: A Dafny-based tool generates history-preserving asynchronous protocol models and mechanically checked provenance, monotonicity and ownership invariants. Atomic sharding traces current local values or collection entries to past steps and messages. Users supply host definitions, selected hints/labels and final safety proofs. Evaluation reports 16 protocol-model proofs, with 10 Kondo comparisons, final proof sizes and verifier times. Reconstructs host/network provenance and the atomic-shard algorithm, collection correlation failure and epoch-reset counterexample. Records formal safety obligations, all 16 protocol properties and every numerical comparison cell. Separates generated invariant proofs from user safety proofs, model correctness from implementation correspondence, and measured final LOC from development effort. Preserves incompleteness, syntax restrictions and all trust limits.

assumptions_limits: §§3,5.2: Model has arbitrary host counts, nondeterministic single-host atomic steps, history of all Hosts snapshots and a monotonically growing set of sent messages. Receive selects an addressed message already sent; repeat selection and nondelivery overapproximate duplication, delay, reordering and loss. Messages carry sender identities; arbitrary Byzantine forgery or compromised hosts are not modeled. History is proof state, not a measured runtime logging cost. §3: Network provenance links a sent message to an adjacent pair of historical sender states and a matching send step. Host provenance for witness q requires q now, no initial state satisfying q, and a historical crossing from not-q to q through a candidate modifying step. These statements concern well-formed initialized protocol executions, not arbitrary malformed history sequences. §§3.3,5.3: Provenance alone identifies a past producing event. Monotonicity/non-equivocation invariants are needed to move from past sender conditions to present facts. Ownership invariants/labels are inherited from Kondo; generated invariants are individually/local mechanically checked, not assertions trusted merely because the generator produced them. §4.1: An atomic shard is a subset of local variables always modified together. If the current tuple is not an admissible initial tuple, it was established in one candidate update step. Maximal shards retain shared-message correlations lost by independent singleton witnesses. This does not mean every member of a collection remains correlated with the latest scalar value. §4.2: Static footprints overapproximate variables a step may update; excess candidates weaken the resulting provenance disjunction. Underestimating footprints would produce incorrect invariants. Prototype rejects a step updating different variables under different conditions, e.g. if c then x:=5 else y:=6. User must split this into separately guarded steps. §§4.2,5.3: Collection fields also receive refined singleton shards, allowing each noninitial set/map entry to be traced to its insertion step. Prototype supports explicit Dafny record-update syntax only, rather than general relational updates. A step can receive and send together; multiple sends/broadcasts in one step are described as an easy extension but not implemented or evaluated. §5.4 reader qualification: Formal obligations are Init⇒I∧φ and I∧φ∧Next⇒I′∧φ′. Thus the actual method proves safety with induction on I∧φ and may use current φ in the step proof. Figure 5/prose describing a proof that I implies safety must not be read as requiring or establishing the stronger standalone I⇒φ in every example. The final safety proof remains user-written. §§5.4,6.4: Failure may reflect a too-weak generated invariant or an unsafe model; the verifier points to the failing host-step obligation, but does not automatically decide which explanation is true. Reader qualification: SMT proof failure can also arise from solver incompleteness. Additional provenance witnesses or manually written invariant clauses may be needed; Basilisk is explicitly incomplete for undecidable logics. §6: First six protocols were used to develop/refine provenance and atomic sharding; the remaining ten were applied later. All sixteen models/invariants are reported outside EPR. This is an author-built benchmark suite, not a blinded independent user study or proof of completeness for all protocols outside EPR. §§6.1–6.2: Zero manually supplied invariant clauses across 16 does not mean zero user reasoning. Six of 64 host-provenance invariants need explicit witness hints, across Paxos-Dynamic, Raft election and Multi-Paxos; monotonicity annotations, ownership labels and safety lemmas remain. Distributed Lock and both ShardedKV variants already had fully automatic Kondo ownership proofs. §6.2: Kondo comparisons cover only ten protocols and modify models to split receive/send; Kondo also needs synchronous protocol definitions. Final proof LOC excludes failed/revised proof attempts and does not measure person-time, cognitive difficulty or novice success. Basilisk uses more proof LOC for some simple cases and is not faster for every ownership example. §6.3: Timings check final history-preserving asynchronous proofs including generated/user invariants and lemmas; Kondo synchronous-proof verification is excluded. Invariant generation is under two seconds in every case. Table 1 reports Multi-Paxos 61.5 seconds; the prose phrase in a minute is approximate, not a strict sub-60-second bound. No repetitions/variance or controlled proof-authoring experiment is reported. §6.4: Epoch resets create implicit multi-step relations that sharding cannot infer. Adding an event at current year and clearing events on year increment requires a witness relating every current entry to current year; merely finding its historic insertion year is too weak. All three hinted benchmark protocols have collection resets at epoch changes. Footprint imprecision is another possible weakness, not observed by authors in these protocols. §6.4: Safety specification is trusted. The user must trust the model describes actual code or separately prove correspondence; this work does not verify production implementations. Dafny, dependencies and hardware are trusted. Crash-fault safety is the scope; no liveness or Byzantine correctness proof is provided. §§6–8,Appendix A: No runtime throughput, production bug-finding or LLM-agent experiment is evaluated. Artifact developed/tested on M3 MacBook Pro with MacOS Sequoia; this appendix statement is not an explicit platform declaration for every published timing. Artifact and external proof bodies were not executed in this reading.

title: Bayesian Inference of Temporal Task Specifications from Demonstrations
what: Defines a Bayesian model that infers LTL task specifications from positive state-only demonstrations. Formulas combine global invariants, eventual subtask completion and DAG-based temporal ordering. Three priors sample order structures (permutation, sets of chains, forests); a domain-independent complexity-based likelihood penalizes conjunctive complexity while allowing occasional nonconforming demonstrations; webPPL MCMC yields a posterior over formulas. The method assumes propositions and their labeling functions are known, reducing inference to selecting subsets of global predicates, eventual subtasks and ordering relations. Hyperparameters are fixed (pE=pG=0.8, ppart=0.3, Nnew=5), with epsilon chosen so one violating example offsets four satisfying examples; 10,000 MCMC samples and 100 burn-in samples are used. Similarity is Jaccard overlap of true/inferred clause sets; posterior concentration and top-5 recovery are reported. Complexity-based likelihood outperforms a complexity-independent alternative by avoiding overly simple formulas.

assumptions_limits: Only positive demonstrations are assumed acceptable; actions and dynamics are not observed. Candidate formulas are restricted to three template families and known proposition sets/conditions; true formulas outside the template cannot be recovered. MCMC runtime grows with demonstrations and formula size. In the dinner-table data, extra inferred ordering can over-constrain behavior even when all but a few demonstrations satisfy it.

title: Two Variable vs. Linear Temporal Logic in Model Checking and Games
what: Compares two-variable first-order logic (FO2) and linear temporal logic (LTL), including unary temporal logic UTL, stutter-free fragments, and the combined FO2[LTL]. It gives three formula-to-automata translations and derives tight or near-tight verification bounds for nondeterministic, recursive, probabilistic, and game models. Translation I relates UTL/FO2 to unambiguous limit-deterministic Büchi automata; Translation II exploits polynomially many FO2[<] subformula types under a unary-alphabet restriction; Translation III builds deterministic parity automata for FO2 using small-model representatives. These constructions yield NP for FO2[<] on Kripke/HSM/RSM, NEXP for FO2 on RSM, 2EXPTIME-complete two-player games, #P/PEXP probability bounds on Markov chains, PSPACE for FO2[<] on recursive Markov chains, and 2EXPTIME quantitative MDP bounds. FO2[LTL] inherits the maximum complexity of its components, while Let definitions make FO2[<] exponentially harder.

title: Beyond Theorem Proving: Formulation, Framework and Benchmark for Formal Problem-Solving
what: Introduces FPS, a Lean 4 metaprogramming DSL that synthesizes an answer term together with its correctness proof, and D-FPS, which synthesizes an answer proposition by forward implication and then verifies the reverse implication. Provides mathematical soundness/expressiveness arguments, 1,086 formal problems across three benchmarks, restricted-tactic answer comparison RPE, and evaluations of existing specialist provers and generalist LLMs. Crucially, D-FPS experiments run only forward reasoning plus RPE, not the framework’s complete backward soundness stage. FPS elaborates to a dependent function returning an answer/proof pair, with Answer and Proof goals; extract_answer/extract_proof recover terms and certificates. D-FPS changes the unknown to Prop and separates Ψ→A from A→Ψ: forward completeness captures all original solutions, backward soundness excludes spurious ones. Appendix E derives these conditional guarantees from completed proof terms and a correct canonical ground truth, rather than proving a new general-purpose solving algorithm. RPE accepts equality of generated/canonical answer objects only when a fixed tactic set proves it: rw_search, rfl, norm_num, aesop, ring_nf. Expert-in-loop benchmark construction checks contradictory hypotheses and known-answer provability, then performs dual expert review. Benchmarks and evaluations expose unsimplified or tautological answer terms that satisfy a specification while missing the desired answer representation.
assumptions_limits: FPS soundness is relative to the formal specification, admitted axioms, Lean kernel and extraction/metaprogram implementation. The paper does not supply a machine-checked correctness proof of that implementation or a detailed adversarial proof-bypass audit. This reader did not execute it. Assumption 3.4 requires a solution whenever the hypotheses hold. D-FPS completeness/soundness additionally assumes the canonical ground truth is equivalent to the formal problem. The expressiveness argument for unique answers requires uniqueness; for solution sets it requires a globally complete characterization. None establishes fidelity to informal intent automatically. Only forward reasoning is run for D-FPS in Appendix I.1. Thus its experimental Typecheck% is forward-proof acceptance, which can be satisfied by True, rather than completion of both implications. RPE separately compares the resulting answer against the canonical one. Backward soundness follows after the backward proof is completed. Appendix E.4 also claims an exception for unique answers represented as a=â; this needs â to be independent of the original queried variable a, which the printed D-FPS dependency rules do not explicitly enforce. RPE is an operational criterion of bounded tactic provability, not complete semantic equality or a theorem that a representation is human-preferred. Mathematically equivalent but less simplified answers can be deliberately rejected. Success establishes formal equality under the chosen environment; failure does not establish mathematical inequality. No general theorem gives a universal human-alignment guarantee, transitivity, or freedom from canonical-answer shortcuts. The 300-example xVerify validation includes xFinder answer extraction and DeepSeek-V3 four-shot translation before symbolic checking. Thus the symbolic tactic phase is deterministic, but this evaluation is not an LLM-free semantic-fidelity test. Zero observed false positives is finite empirical evidence, not a universal bound. Benchmarks focus on canonical/closed-form answers: 387 FormalMath500, 375 MiniF2F-Solving, 324 PutnamBench-Solving. Geometry and Counting & Probability are excluded from FormalMath500; generic find-one witnesses and open conjectures remain future work. Existing public benchmark/model training exposure is not audited here. Experiments evaluate existing provers/prompts without task-specific training. Whole-proof, search, DSP+, FPS prompting and D-FPS prompting use different sample/search/token budgets, so cross-method rates are not equal-compute efficiency comparisons. Table 1 reports mean±std for selected methods but the supplied settings do not state the number of independent runs. Preference evidence uses two learned preference models on commonly solved problems with comments removed, not a direct blinded human study of full reasoning. Formal proof steps certify logical claims, not faithfulness of informal comments or the model’s hidden reasoning process. No distributed-system implementation, Verus/Rust proof, TLA+ model, concurrency/liveness task, or agent-generated systems specification is evaluated. Transfer to those topics is reader inference.
use_for_goal: Directly useful for evaluating proof/specification agents: distinguish existence of an accepted proof from synthesis of a useful answer, preserve formal-to-informal fidelity, and report which proof obligations were actually discharged. The forward/backward split suggests separate completeness/soundness checks for generated systems specifications; that transfer remains untested. For Verus/Rust/TLA+, canonical-answer checking would need domain-specific semantics and hypotheses rather than importing these Lean arithmetic tactics.

title: BFS-Prover-V2: Scaling up Multi-Turn Off-Policy RL and Multi-Agent Tree Search for LLM Step-Provers
what: A Lean4 step prover combines success-trajectory supervised expert iteration with tactic-surprisal filtering and periodic retraining from a base checkpoint. At inference a separate Gemini2.5Pro planner proposes intermediate lemmas; parallel best-first provers race on one active subgoal and reuse solved proofs. Authors report95.08% miniF2F-test with32B+planner and41.4% ProofNet-test with32B pure search, both accumulated across search settings. Describes inner-loop one-epoch updates and outer-loop corpus re-synthesis,more aggressive filtering and three-epoch base-model resets. Filters both highly predictable and highly surprising successful tactics rather than only selecting theorem-level difficulty. The planner produces have statements, augments context after verified subgoals and replans at bottlenecks. All provers focus on the same current lemma; first success populates a shared cache and cancels redundant searches, after which the group advances. Long examples compare concise tactics/library reuse with whole-proof scripts and exhibit dynamic decomposition of a finite trigonometric sum into a nonzero sinusoid.
assumptions_limits: Formal acceptance concerns supplied Lean theorem statements under Lean4.10.0,Mathlib/imported axioms and verification infrastructure. Planner suggestions and autoformalizations are untrusted proposals; checking syntax with sorry does not establish semantic fidelity or prove the theorem. The paper does not supply an independent final-artifact trust/admission audit. Training uses roughly3million autoformalized statements from NuminaMath-CoT,NuminaMath1.5 and Goedel-PsetV1; GPT4o/Claude3.7Sonnet help formalize statements. Base models are Qwen2.5Math7B and Qwen2.5-32B with initialization from BFS-ProverV1. Distillation-free refers to the self-generated prover training loop, not absence of external statement formalizers or the Gemini planner. Only successful proof trajectories train the policy after filtering. Failed searches,compiler errors and negative tactics are not systematically incorporated. Off-policy RL here is an expert-iteration/search-and-supervised-learning framework; no value-network or policy-gradient objective is developed in this paper. Filtering retains central tactic-surprisal quantiles:approximately15% removed from each tail during ordinary iterations,20% each during resets. Curating a successful tactic out of training does not invalidate its source proof. Interpretations of low/high surprisal as trivial/noisy are empirical hypotheses, not a certified classification. Accumulated results are unions over expansion widths{2,3,4,8} and depth rewards{0,1,2},with8192 passes evaluated separately per configuration. A planner pass counts cumulative cooperating prover instances sharing cache; pure-search passes count independent searches. Each instance has600seconds including Lean interactions. These are different experiments from8192 independent whole-proof samples. The named planner is Gemini2.5Pro,additional model capacity beyond the reported7B/32B prover. Planner calls,cost,latency,total inference GPU hours and concurrency are not fully accounted for. Comparisons with much larger whole-proof models are not compute/model-system matched. Authors label ProofNet an out-of-distribution benchmark relative to Olympiad-style training, but do not give a corpus-level leakage/deduplication audit. Public benchmark adaptation and unknown model pretraining overlap limit generalization claims. Training reset decisions use new solved counts and downstream miniF2F accuracy;Figure4 explicitly plots miniF2F-test throughout training. Thus the reported test is adaptively monitored rather than clearly untouched by training-method selection. Training cost250–300 A100GPUhours per7B epoch,1500–1800 per32B epoch;reset uses3epochs. Cost prevents independent full-pipeline random-seed repetitions and comprehensive end-to-end ablations. Plateau recovery is primarily an observed trajectory,not a controlled causal experiment. The planner and prover are separately optimized. Parallelism races independent searches on a single active lemma; it does not concurrently expand one search tree or prove all dependent lemmas at once. There is no general search-complexity,completeness or convergence theorem.
use_for_goal: Relevant to proof-agent architecture and evaluation:demonstrates tactical interaction,success-data filtering,model resets,goal decomposition,shared checked lemmas and adaptive search. Highlights benchmark budget definitions,external-planner capacity,test monitoring,statement fidelity and final trust checks. Transfer to long distributed-system invariants,Verus/Rust specifications or TLA+ temporal proofs is a reader research direction;this paper evaluates Lean mathematical theorem proving only.

what: Presents a runtime QoS prediction architecture that continuously updates a parameterized probabilistic model from monitored data and uses PRISM to estimate near-future SLA violation probabilities. A queue-length abstraction maps KPI intervals to an M/M/1 CTMC; transition rates are updated with an EWMA of observed interval changes, while queue bounds are doubled/halved at thresholds. A CEP extracts Smart Grid energy-balance indicators, generates the finite model, and PRISM checks bounded reachability probabilities in a repeated loop. title: BlueCov: Integrating Test Coverage and Model Checking with JBMC
what: Introduces BlueCov, a Java bytecode coverage tool that consumes JBMC’s own coverage goals, instruments exactly those bytecode locations, records runtime hit counts and feeds uncovered goals back to JBMC for incremental test generation. This avoids criterion mismatches and redundant tests when formal test generation augments an existing suite. JBMC translates Java bytecode through CProver GOTO, inserts assert(false) goals for location/branch/path/MC-DC criteria, and synthesizes inputs; a greedy subset-cover heuristic minimizes generated tests. BlueCov takes JBMC’s JSON goals, instruments bytecode with ASM 6 using bytecode indices, records hits in an in-memory map, persists them with MapDB and uses a JVM shutdown hook. A FloatTools.sign example maps nine goals to three existing tests, then uses a NaN input to reach otherwise apparently dead code and complete coverage. The implementation discusses Java interfaces, erased generics, modeled JCL functions, exceptional termination, Maven integration and the difference between source lines and bytecode goals.

Test generation is NP-hard subset cover approximated greedily and object construction is proprietary/outside the paper. BlueCov records coverage rather than percentages, and persistence depends on shutdown-hook execution. title: Bounded Model Checking for Asynchronous Hyperproperties
what: Generalizes asynchronous HyperLTL (A-HLTL) with nested trajectory quantifiers and gives a QBF-based bounded model checker for a fragment, with complexity results for acyclic Kripke structures and case-study experiments. The extended logic quantifies traces and trajectories independently, where trajectories choose which traces advance or stutter and must be fair. The bounded encoding unrolls Kripke structures to depth k and trajectory schedules to m, with pessimistic and optimistic halting semantics; Theorem 1 establishes equivalence at the structure diameter and a finite trajectory bound. For acyclic frames, one trajectory quantifier gives NL/coNP-polynomial-hierarchy bounds depending on trace alternation, while nested trajectory quantifiers raise complexity one level; arbitrary trace alternation with one trajectory remains PSPACE. The HyperQB implementation translates the encoding to QuABs QBF and finds security counterexamples and classifications in concurrent, speculative, compiler, and cache examples.

title: Bounded Model Checking for Probabilistic Programs?
what: Develops an on-the-fly bounded model-checking method for conditional probabilistic programs. Each finite unrolling constructs a finite operational MDP, and monotonic growth of conditional reachability probabilities and expected rewards yields sound lower bounds; parametric iterations can permanently classify valuations that already violate a property. The paper gives SOS semantics for a cpGCL language with probabilistic/nondeterministic choices, observations, divergence and post-expectation rewards. It treats universal scheduler semantics for MDP properties and explains finite expansion, model-checking calls and parameter-valuation elimination. Five benchmark families (Crowds, Herman, Robot, Predator, Coupon Collector and observation variants) show that useful bounds can arise before full expansion, while expected-reward queries currently permit only one unfolding step.

title: Bounded Model Checking of RISC-V Machine Code with Context-Free-Language Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams
what: Presents rotor, which generates BTOR2 bit-precise models of user-space 32/64-bit RISC-V integer machines, and bitme, which unrolls those models for bounded checking using Z3/Bitwuzla and byte-oriented ADD/CFLOBDD domain propagation. The paper defines rotor models as (states, initial states, transition, bad states, good constraints), k-satisfiability, and a reachability correspondence proposition, while explicitly marking formal proof of rotor correctness as future work. Bitme tracker algebra maps bounded input domains to state values; soundness/completeness are conditional on correct BDD and SMT implementations and only hold modulo timeout and bound k. Arrays are flattened to bitvectors for propagation. In 18 microbenchmarks, most samples time out under SMT or constant propagation but finish with BDD propagation; ROABVDD is faster, whereas CFLOBVDD memory scales better on increasing input complexity. The study also identifies regressions and array-unfolding limitations.

The reachability proposition assumes read consumes one byte per call. Bounded checking says nothing beyond k. Domain propagation is limited to input bitvectors up to 8 bits and arrays are not natively handled; fixed input order can cause exponential BDD growth. Experiments average three runs, use an unreported 18-program supplementary suite, and impose a 900-second timeout.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for bit-precise bounded verification, conditional soundness claims, and practical tradeoffs among SMT and decision-diagram backends. It provides concrete proof obligations and limitations relevant to verified Rust/Verus machine-level reasoning, while its unproved rotor/bitme correctness and bounded scope caution against treating tool output as a full proof.

title: Model Checking Existential Logic on Partially Ordered Sets
what: Classifies existential first-order model checking and embedding on finite posets by structural invariants, proving fixed-parameter tractability for bounded width and polynomial-time isomorphism there, while establishing hardness for neighboring bounded invariants. The bounded-width algorithm computes a chain partition, compiles tuples of chains into semilattice structures, uses perfect hash families/color coding to reduce embeddings to polynomial-time homomorphism instances, and runs in 2^{O(k log k)} n^{O(1)} for pattern size k. A proposition equates existential model checking and embedding in parameterized complexity. Reductions from Clique give W[1]-hardness at bounded cover-degree, and SAT encodings give NP-hard embedding at bounded width and bounded degree in classical complexity. A distributive-lattice construction solves isomorphism in polynomial time on bounded-width posets.

title: Bridging Arrays and ADTs in Recursive Proofs.
short_name: Bridging arrays and ADTs in recursive proofs
what: Presents a fully automatic method for synthesizing recursively defined relational invariants that prove equivalence of paired object implementations when one uses arrays and the other algebraic data types (ADTs). The method encodes initialization, paired transitions, applicability and output equality as CHCs; Algorithm 1 builds a recursive invariant schema, Algorithm 2/3 bridge producer/consumer operations for linear scans, and Algorithm 4/5 use noop observations for sets/maps. Candidate relations are validated by structural induction with AdtInd/Z3. The paper formalizes equivalence as an inductive invariant over a composition of two deterministic objects, with initialization, consecution for every paired operation, precondition applicability in both directions, and output equality. It defines producer/consumer/noop classifications via a partial ordering on ADT states and synthesizes a Skolem-like updated array state plus matching constraints. Recipe 1 handles stacks/queues with an index and can infer loop invariants; Recipe 2 handles sets, multisets and maps by updating only the observed array cell while preserving all other inputs. Validation is structural induction rather than recursion-free SMT checking, and user lemmas are optional (one multiset lemma was needed in evaluation).

title: Brief Announcement: Generalising Concurrent Correctness to Weak Memory
what: Defines causal atomicity for partially ordered object executions, extending the authors' causal linearizability work to transactional memory. States compositionality for objects with disjoint operation alphabets and client abstraction. Defines causal opacity by combining transaction operations into atomic blocks; outlines an operational specification adapted from TMS2 for simulation proofs. An execution structure has a finite event set, strict precedence order and a communication relation satisfying three coherence axioms. A valid logical order must include precedence and be contained in communication; every total extension of that order must be a legal sequential execution. Thus checking one arbitrary linearization is insufficient. The stack/STM example shows why cross-object communication and the third coherence axiom matter: a transaction that observes written values induces communication, which forces Push before an empty Pop and exposes the stack violation. The client theorem compares compatible orders on client-local events. The final paragraph describes a transactional sequential specification whose causally atomic executions remain atomic after transaction-block abstraction.
assumptions_limits: Finite event structures over fixed operation alphabets; Theorem 3 requires disjoint alphabets for the two sequential objects. Communication captures synchronization between low-level operations; precedence alone does not characterize correctness under weak memory. The three-page brief states theorems without supplying full proofs or concrete STM implementations. The client abstraction statement concerns matching observations with compatible local-event orders; the brief does not claim arbitrary hyperproperty preservation. Causal atomicity here differs from Farzan–Madhusudan's same-named notion, which the footnote says is not compositional.
use_for_goal: Relevant when a distributed or concurrent Rust implementation relies on weak-memory synchronization. A high-level atomic-object proof must account for low-level communication and compositionality; the record supplies a precise correctness target rather than an implementation in Verus/TLA+. No LLM evaluation.

title: BrokenMath: A Benchmark for Sycophancy in Theorem Proving with LLMs
what: Introduces BrokenMath, a 504-item benchmark of plausible false mathematics statements for testing whether LLMs challenge a user’s incorrect theorem request. It combines 321 proof-style and 183 final-answer items from 2025 competitions, LLM-generated perturbations, expert review, and a four-way LLM-judge label (Ideal,Corrected,Detected,Sycophant). Across eleven models,GPT-5 has the lowest reported sycophancy at29.0%,but still attempts false proofs often. Proof-style tasks and unsolved originals increase sycophancy;prompting,best-of-n,self-verification,confidence heuristics and fine-tuning reduce but do not eliminate it. Perturbations are context-sensitive false answers,nonexistent counterexamples,inverted properties or semantic inversions rather than simple contradictory constraints. Original and corrupted theorem plus generated response are jointly given to a judge. Non-sycophantic labels distinguish detecting falsehood from recovering the original theorem. Utility uses parsed answers or OPC-R1-8B proof judging. GPT-5-mini majority judge gets95% granular/98% binary agreement on240 human labels;an alternate Grok judge gives nearly identical scores. Difficulty is measured by solving original problems with OPC-R1-8B;proof problems are subsampled per model to match final-answer accuracy. Self-sycophancy replaces a model’s generated theorem with a corrupted benchmark item in a three-turn dialogue. Agent tests use four-candidate tournament or up to four self-verification rounds. Qwen3-4B fine-tuning uses a13,000-sample filtered dataset from roughly15,000 source problems,including roughly8,000 sampled from a35,000-problem competition pool,90% sycophancy-focused,5% each valid final-answer/proof.
assumptions_limits: The benchmark’s falsehood and original correctness rely on human-curated competition problems,LLM perturbations and expert annotation. A 100-item secondary review found97% agreement,but two near-trivial and one potentially true perturbation were identified;all models attempted the latter,so absolute scores and residual label noise remain possible. The main judge is an LLM. It is validated on240 responses but can confuse Corrected and Detected;five sycophant/non-sycophant errors remain. OPC-R1-8B judges proof utility and is explicitly “not infallible”;neither judge supplies formal proof certificates. The operational sycophancy label concerns attempting a false proof or missing a flaw,not direct measurement of internal belief. §4.4 finds97.7% Qwen3-4B responses follow a prompt to disprove the false statement;this measures disproof intent and instruction following,not formally checked correctness of the disproof. The authors infer sycophancy from the prompt contrast. Coverage is competition mathematics up to undergraduate level,not research mathematics,program verification or distributed systems. Agentic/self-sycophancy experiments use only selected models because of cost. Utility and sycophancy are measured on different outputs and judged with different procedures;reported Pearson correlation −0.65 is observational. Proof/final-answer comparison subsamples per model to approximate equal original accuracy,so denominators differ. The difficulty-control prose reports an average selected proof count as95%,an unclear/inconsistent unit;the record does not infer a corrected sample count. Prompt engineering,confidence and fine-tuning results use selected models and settings. Black-box confidence AUC reaches0.75 at best;white-box Qwen3-4B metrics AUC0.61–0.66. Fine-tuning two epochs on four H200s changes Qwen3-4B sycophancy55.6→51.0% and utility33.4→37.9%,not elimination. No external artifact or API output was rerun.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for LLM agents writing mathematical specifications/proofs: a model can produce a polished proof for a user-imposed false statement,especially when the original problem is hard. The four-way distinction and disproof-intent test suggest evaluating Verus/TLA+/Rust agents on false specifications and adversarial user framing,with formal checkers plus human specification review. This paper does not test machine-checked Lean/Verus artifacts or distributed protocols.

title: Sound Statistical Model Checking for Probabilities and Expected Rewards
what: Surveys statistical methods used by SMC tools, identifies unsound confidence procedures, recommends Clopper–Pearson for probabilities and DKW for bounded rewards, and introduces theoretical bounding-set and limit-PAC methods for unbounded reachability rewards implemented in modes. The paper distinguishes fixed-k and sequential PAC settings and requires worst-case coverage over all true probabilities, exposing why CLT/Wald, Wilson/CC and Chow–Robbins procedures can be unsound. It proves the DKW confidence band yields a tighter expected-reward interval than Hoeffding, derives bounds for instantaneous, cumulative and reachability rewards, and shows a finite-state DTMC geometric path-length construction is theoretically sufficient but often unusably large. DKW-E-Lower is a new lower-bound procedure for any nonnegative finite-expectation random variable, with a limit-PAC theorem. A survey of tools shows no sound and efficient default for sequential probabilities or fixed reward estimation before their modes implementation.

assumptions_limits: PAC guarantees assume independent samples and known confidence level. Unbounded expected rewards cannot have sound finite-sample two-sided intervals without additional structure; reachability construction assumes finite DTMC, almost-sure goal reachability, lower-bounded transition probabilities and bounded state rewards, and can be astronomically conservative. DKW/Hoeffding require known support bounds for two-sided reward intervals. Empirical QVBS evaluation turns unbounded reachability rewards into manually bounded ones, uses DTMC semantics for MDPs, excludes unsupported models, and does not establish universal practical convergence.
use_for_goal: Useful evidence for rigorous probabilistic verification claims: confidence guarantees depend on statistical assumptions, and apparent model-checking results can be unsound. The explicit PAC definitions, tool survey and reproducible evaluation inform specification and evaluation of distributed-system verification and LLM-generated proofs.

title: BWoS: Formally Verified Block-based Work Stealing for Parallel Processing
what: BWoS splits bounded per-owner work-stealing queues into blocks with independent metadata. Block takeover/grant separates get from steal, amortizes synchronization, and reduces cache interference. FIFO permits stealing from the middle; LIFO steals from bottom. Random block sampling approximates size-proportional victim choice and combines with NUMA preference. GenMC/VSync check and optimize C memory-order choices for small IMM/RC11 clients; benchmarks evaluate C/C++/Rust/Go/Kotlin implementations and Java/Go/Tokio integrations. Records all four block invariants, atomic takeover thresholds, completion counter and packed rounds, exact probabilistic premise versus sampled approximation, bounded model/client/sum assertion and three-day expanded check, found reset race/barrier counts, verification versus runtime-port boundary, complete tables and benchmark settings/results including negative cases, source wording discrepancy and assertion-coverage concern.

Do not infer strict global FIFO linearizability for a general shared queue from this scheduler design. §3.1: Invariants forbid overwriting unconsumed data, duplicate or same-item get/steal reads, and an in-progress steal preventing owner get takeover. These are algorithm design requirements; model check establishes checked-client properties, not a parameterized invariant proof for every capacity/thread/round count. §3.4: Exact victim probability proportional to size follows ideal accept probability S/C with uniform queue selection and equal capacities. Implementation samples whether random block has stealable data, only approximating S/C; owner-private partial block and low occupancy matter. NUMA-biased selector changes selection probabilities. No universal load-balance/tail-latency theorem or runtime fairness proof provided. §4.2: Metadata has finite index/round packed into64bits. Paper describes wraparound of block pointer/next rounds but gives no all-time proof or exhaustive lifetime bound against round-number overflow/ABA. Paper explicitly says properties of individual operations were not verified. No unrestricted linearizability, wait-freedom or scheduler eventual-service guarantee should be inferred. §5.1 Figure9: Two2-entry blocks, owner3 rounds of3put/2get,4put/3get,5put/4get, two thieves performing1and2steals, then sequential drain. Reader inference: sum equality alone is not a complete multiset oracle if duplicates and losses coexist (e.g. duplicate1plus2 can compensate missing4:1+1+2=4); other properties/algorithm constraints would be needed to rule out such compensation. title: Formal Verification of Blockchain Byzantine Fault Tolerance
what: Surveys blockchain-consensus vulnerabilities and formally verifies two Red Belly Blockchain components with the ByMC threshold-automata model checker: binary-value broadcast and a DBFT-style Byzantine consensus variant. title: Cameleer: A Deductive Verification Tool for OCaml.
what: Translates GOSPEL-annotated OCaml programs to WhyML and invokes Why3 verification-condition generation and SMT solvers. Extends GOSPEL from interface contracts to implementation annotations including loop invariants and ghost code. Supports a bounded-mutability subset with basic modules/functors; reports a26-case verified gallery. Proof success concerns supplied specifications and translated semantics,conditional on front-end/solver correctness and assumptions. Shows higher-order and functor binary search with loop variants and exceptional postconditions;maps OCaml attributes,ghost code,type invariants and module namespaces into WhyML. Integrates OCaml as a Why3 input format using the Why3 API/session tools,and uses extraction to erase ghost code. Explicitly documents rejection of recursive mutable Queue cells under Why3’s alias discipline,and gives line counts,VC counts,replay times and manual-interaction flags across realistic library fragments and textbook algorithms.
assumptions_limits: Programmer supplies contracts,invariants,termination variants,ghost functions and sometimes manual auxiliary induction/case splits. Discharged VCs prove those formal requirements,not that the requirements express all intended behavior. Axioms in module signatures constrain admissible implementations and must be justified at instantiation. Cameleer trusts its GOSPEL parser/type-checker and OCaml-to-WhyML translator,Why3 typing/effect analysis/VC generation and external solvers. The paper refers to inductive translation rules in the longer report but does not present a machine-checked compiler/refinement correctness theorem in this chapter. Higher-order comparison arguments used in specifications are assumed pure. WhyML’s bounded-mutability discipline requires aliases to be statically known. Effectful higher-order code and recursive mutable data types are limited;arbitrary OCaml pointers/aliasing are not handled by this translation. Supported subset roughly corresponds to caml-light plus basic modules/functors. Objects,GADTs and polymorphic variants are unsupported. Viper/CFML integration and richer heap reasoning are future work in this2021paper,not implemented capabilities established by the case studies. Source integer overflow and precise machine-integer correspondence are not explained in the supplied chapter. Do not infer that mathematical arithmetic VCs automatically prove every OCaml machine arithmetic corner case without checking library models and translation. Case-study proof replay is measured after contracts,lemmas and proof sessions have been developed. “Immediate” means no extra IDE interaction after annotation,not no human proof design. Manual sessions are retained for six cases. No failed-case population,annotation time or developer-effort study is reported. Quoted comparison of tool usability/language suitability reflects author opinion and2021tool scope. Related-work mentions Prusti and Tezos proofs in other tools;neither is an evaluated Cameleer Rust/blockchain case.
use_for_goal: Useful comparator for Verus and LLM-assisted implementation proofs: source-language contracts,ghost code,module assumptions,backend limitations and proof replay versus proof construction. Concrete comparator/record snippets illustrate that valid formal obligations must still match original source semantics and intended contracts. It supplies verified sequential OCaml examples,not a distributed-system or LLM-agent case.

title: CaMeLoT: CaMeL orchestrated with Temporal logic for static verification and liveness
what: CaMeLoT extends the CaMeL agent-defense framework with pre-execution verification of generated plans. title: Can Large Language Models Reason about Program Invariants?
what: Fine-tunes 430M, 1B, and 5B-parameter code language models to predict 18 classes of Java program invariants at function entry/exit and loop points. A scratchpad prompt predicts invariants at successive program points and then the target; the paper interprets this as learning in an abstract invariant space. On Code Contests Java programs, the best models reach about 86% precision and recall and outperform Daikon when Daikon receives at most five traces. The dataset is generated by instrumenting Java submissions with dummy loop calls, running Daikon on 200 available inputs, and splitting by problem to prevent near-duplicate leakage. The authors report 1,600,158 train, 86,346 validation and 24,509 test examples. Evaluation uses Jaccard similarity, precision, recall and F1 against 200-trace Daikon targets; models use greedy decoding, 20,000 steps, batch 128 on 64 TPU-v4 cores. Table 3 shows Daikon F1 .721 with one trace, .857 with five, .868 with six and 1.00 with 200. For ordered 5B scratchpad forward prediction, F1 is .858 in both combined and separated training; combined shuffled 5B scratchpad reaches .863. Oracle reaches .867 forward and up to .877 backward across settings. GPT-4 zero-shot is weak (listed pilot precision .44, recall .384 on paper listings and no ground-truth invariants for ten random test prompts). Case listings show model-discovered valid invariants omitted by Daikon, but also spurious predictions and dependence on model scale. The paper is empirical invariant prediction, not proof: Daikon targets are treated as ground truth although dynamic analysis can miss valid invariants or produce false positives. The oracle receives the Daikon target invariants at program points preceding its target and therefore uses dynamic information, unlike direct and scratchpad inference. Backward prediction also changes the dataset: it excludes the final program point and introduces class invariants, yielding 1,284,492 training, 61,431 validation and 21,576 test examples; forward/backward scores thus have different target and example populations.

assumptions_limits: An invariant is a Boolean predicate true whenever execution reaches a specified program point; the task is undecidable in general. Ground truth is the set Daikon emits from 200 inputs; the authors explicitly note this can miss invariants and overfit finite traces. The dataset consists of Java competitive-programming submissions with available inputs, not distributed protocols, Rust/Verus code or TLA+ specifications. Direct and scratchpad inference is static with respect to the target program and uses greedy decoding, but training labels come from dynamic traces. Oracle inference receives intermediate Daikon target invariants as additional dynamic information and is not a purely static comparator. The paper reports offline experiments and does not establish semantic correctness of model outputs beyond comparison with Daikon/manual inspection.
use_for_goal: For LLM agents writing distributed-system specifications or Verus/TLA+ proofs, this is evidence that code-trained LLMs can infer useful candidate predicates from source and intermediate points, but evaluation against dynamic-analyzer labels is weaker than solver-checked proof. It supplies no Rust, Verus, TLA+, distributed-system or proof-completion experiment; applying the method to those domains would require semantic checking and independent labels.

title: Can LLMs Reason Like Automated Theorem Provers for Rust Verification? VCoT-Bench: Evaluating via Verification Chain of Thought
kind: Verus proof-reasoning benchmark and proof-lifting framework
what: Introduces VCoT-Lift, which transforms low-level Z3 proof traces into explicit Verus-level proof steps, and VCoT-Bench, 1,988 completion tasks with semantic proof holes. It evaluates whether LLMs reconstruct missing invariant, assertion and lemma reasoning, rather than merely causing a verifier to pass. The four-stage pipeline uses a global proof transformer, rule-specific checker agents for high-level Z3 rules, a pruner for trivial/redundant steps, and a repair agent that compiles/checks transformed Verus proofs. A 36-rule Z3 hierarchy groups high/medium/low importance. Checker mappings must explicitly associate Z3 steps with Verus steps; a transformer-checker loop keeps global context while applying partial checks. VCoT-Bench derives 1,159 ratio tasks, 439 proof-type tasks and 390 location tasks from 150 verified Verus programs. Overall accuracy weights semantic and syntactic correctness (1, 0.5, 0.25, 0 for levels 3 through 0). GPT-5 mini is selected as semantic judge after 100-task, eight-judge validation.

assumptions_limits: The benchmark relies on Z3 proof traces, Verus syntax and a specialized GPT-5-mini semantic judge, so semantic accuracy is not itself a verifier theorem. The checker assesses only selected high-level rules; low-level steps are abstracted/pruned as trivial or redundant. Models are zero-shot and outputs are judged on completion tasks derived from existing verified programs, not independently generated distributed protocols. Context removal can overrepresent small one-block programs at 100%. The study reports current-model fragility and does not show that VCoT-Lift guarantees complete semantic equivalence for arbitrary proofs. Overall Acc gives partial credit (0.5 for semantically correct but syntactically invalid; 0.25 for syntactically valid but semantically incorrect); it is not the fraction of fully correct verified completions.
use_for_goal: Directly targets LLM-generated Verus proofs and gives a finer diagnostic than pass/fail. Its middle-step and assertion weaknesses matter for agents proving distributed invariants, while the reliance on an LLM semantic judge and existing benchmarks marks a limit on assurance.

quotes.text: we introduce VCoTLift, a framework that lifts low-level solver reasoning into high-level, human-readable verification steps. By exposing solver-level reasoning as an explicit Verification Chain-of-Thought, VCoTLift provides a concrete ground truth for finegrained evaluation. Leveraging VCoT-Lift, we introduce VCoT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark of 1,988 VCoT completion tasks for rigorously evaluating LLMs’ ability to reconstruct the entire verification process. VCoT-Bench measures performance along three orthogonal dimensions: robustness to varying degrees of missing proofs, competence across different proof types, and sensitivity to proof locations. Evaluation of ten state-of-the-art models reveals severe fragility, indicating that current LLMs fall well short of the reasoning capabilities exhibited by automated theorem provers

The pipeline starts with an iterative transformer–checker loop that improves proof completeness: the transformer synthesizes Verus proofs from Z3 proofs, and the checker evaluates their completeness until predefined criteria are met. Next, the Proof Pruner removes trivial or redundant steps to improve conciseness. Finally, Proof Repair enforces soundness by interacting with Verus to detect and fix syntactic and semantic errors

With the semantic blocks, we construct the full VCoT-Bench suite with 1,988 VCoT completion tasks. To rigorously evaluate LLMs’ ability to reconstruct the entire verification process, we organize these tasks along three orthogonal dimensions, Ratio, Type, and Location. Detailed statistics of VCoT-Bench are provided in Figure 6. t/output limits, and semantic-judge costs are reported in Appendix B.5. Evaluation Metrics. To evaluate LLM performance on VCoT completion tasks, we employ three metrics: Syntactic Accuracy (SynAcc), Semantic Accuracy (SemAcc), and Overall Accuracy (Acc). Syntactic correctness is checked by invoking Verus in syntax-only mode (-no-verify). Semantic correctness is evaluated by a specialized LLM-based judge, guided by a detailed protocol with curated examples to align its decisions with human judgment. We use GPT-5 mini as the final judge. Specifically, we randomly sample 100 stratified tasks from VCoT-Bench and evaluate eight judge candidates, covering the strongest LLMs available at submission time from four model families: OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek. Each judge is evaluated on outputs from all ten models, with accuracy measured against author consensus. Detailed results are reported in Appendix D.1. GPT-5 mini achieves the highest overall accuracy (92.7%) and is therefore selected as the semantic judge. VCoT-Bench-Ratio. This sub-benchmark evaluates an LLM’s ability to recover missing verification steps under varying degrees of information loss, quantified by the ratio of removed semantic blocks. For each program in VCoTBench-Org containing N semantic blocks, we generate N variants by randomly removing between 1 and N blocks and computing the corresponding removal ratios. This procedure yields a total of 1,159 VCoT completion tasks. VCoT-Bench-Type. This sub-benchmark evaluates an LLM’s ability to reconstruct specific proof types. For each program, we generate up to three variants by removing all blocks of a given type: Invariant-removal (all loop invariants), Assertion-removal (all inline assertions), and Lemmaremoval (all lemma functions). This procedure yields 439 VCoT completion tasks. For overall accuracy, inspired by CodeBLEU (Ren et al., 2020), we define a weighted accuracy metric that emphasizes semantic correctness over syntactic correctness. Each prediction is categorized into one of four levels: • Level 3: Both semantically and syntactically correct. • Level 2: Semantically correct but syntactically incorrect. • Level 1: Syntactically correct but semantically incorrect. • Level 0: Incorrect in both dimensions. Overall accuracy is computed as VCoT-Bench-Loc. The order of the VCoT is critical. This sub-benchmark evaluates how the position of missing reasoning steps affects a model’s ability to recover the underlying logic

Syntactic correctness is checked by invoking Verus in syntax-only mode (-no-verify). Semantic correctness is evaluated by a specialized LLM-based judge, guided by a detailed protocol with curated examples to align its decisions with human judgment. We use GPT-5 mini as the final judge. Specifically, we randomly sample 100 stratified tasks from VCoT-Bench and evaluate eight judge candidates, covering the strongest LLMs available at submission time from four model families: OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek. Each judge is evaluated on outputs from all ten models, with accuracy measured against author consensus. Detailed results are reported in Appendix D.1. GPT-5 mini achieves the highest overall accuracy (92.7%) and is therefore selected as the semantic judge

When all blocks are removed (100%), turning the task into full VCoT construction, performance collapses: Claude Sonnet 4.5 falls to 17.22% and Qwen 3 think to near zero (0.66%). This shows that current LLMs do not reason from first principles but rely heavily on local pattern matching and syntactic scaffolding; once this context Decoding Strategy. Once introduced, these hallucinated elements propagate through the remaining chain and lead to syntactic or semantic errors. In contrast, the non-thinking variant tends to stay closer to local contextual patterns and is therefore less exposed to these cascading deviations. These behaviors indicate a mismatch between generic CoT-style reasoning and formal verification.
