title: Candle: A Verified Implementation of HOL Light
what: A HOL Light-like interactive theorem prover whose soundness theorem reaches from higher-order-logic inference rules through source/kernel/REPL/compiler to modeled machine-code execution. Exported statements on a dedicated kernel-controlled channel must encode derivable HOL sequents and contexts. Implements runtime compilation of user declarations using CakeML Eval,with safety and datatype-protection proofs in HOL4. Combines a prior verified HOL kernel with whole-program simulation preserving soundness-critical values,syntactic restrictions that protect constructors/references/export channels,an interactively verified Eval-based REPL,and in-logic compilation. Distinguishes unverified user-customized display/input behavior from a verified invertible theorem-export format. Shows actual HOL Light-style sessions and documents incompatible language/library features and required wrappers.
assumptions_limits: Top theorem is conditional on repl_ready_to_run:the generated code is installed in the prescribed machine state with correct entry point and FFI setup,plus other compiler/runtime premises hidden in that predicate. It is a theorem about machine_sem with basis_ffi,not a proof of physical processor/OS behavior or arbitrary binary loading. Guarantee concerns special kernel_ffi events. Ordinary stdout can contain any theorem-looking string;pretty printing is customizable and mostly unverified. Only the protected export,which includes a recoverable context and sequent,has the stated semantic guarantee. Logical result is THM ctxt th:derivability in the encoded HOL calculus relative to a context,connected through prior kernel/semantic soundness work. It does not establish that a human’s intended theorem was faithfully parsed/formalized or that arbitrary printed prose is true. Safe declarations cannot directly call protected constructors or kernel FFI,and cannot obtain writable kernel references;pattern matching and kernel-function calls are allowed. Runtime checks,environment/type-stamp freshness and valid-state invariants protect this boundary. Unrestricted native code/unsafe operations are not granted to arbitrary users. REPL theorem rules out Fail,meaning a stuck/type-error behavior in the formal semantics. It does not guarantee termination,successful compilation of every declaration,absence of exceptions,resource sufficiency or eventual theorem production. Compiler refinement permits early resource-limit exits. REPL functional input-output correctness is deliberately not proved. A parser,quote filter or pretty-printer could choose the wrong intended statement while the exported formal sequent remains sound. Verifying safety suffices for this soundness theorem,but not for full user-interface equivalence. Eval is integrated into CakeML compiler/proofs but not typeable in the source type system used to validate user code;users therefore cannot mention Eval. Its detailed verification is deferred to another publication. Current top-level proof uses interactive reasoning rather than ordinary whole-REPL type inference. 2022 HOL Light library port is incomplete. Some record-using files omitted;open/include unsupported,polymorphic comparison/hash rewritten or removed,value restriction affects code,and parser needs explicit arguments in let rec. No drop-in compatibility/completeness theorem or performance study is reported. Proofs developed in HOL4 depend on the correctness of the host prover and formal logic/machine/compiler/FFI models. The paper uses prior kernel,CakeML compiler/type-inference/bootstrap results;it does not independently re-prove their entire development here.
use_for_goal: Strong trust-chain example for evaluating generated proofs and verified systems:separates kernel acceptance,proof-value integrity,source execution,verified compilation,machine model and theorem serialization. Suggests LLM proof agents should retain exact protected sequent/context exports and independently audit statement fidelity. This is a HOL/CakeML prover infrastructure result,not a Verus/Rust,TLA+,distributed-consensus or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: Canonical for Automated Theorem Proving in Lean
what: Presents Canonical, a Rust implementation of backward type-inhabitation search linked to Lean, using beta-normal eta-long terms, explicit substitutions, equational constraints, arbitrary argument refinement order and entropy-guided parallel iterative deepening. On an adapted Natural Number Game with manually selected premises, solves 62/74 statements versus Aesop 27 and Duper 45; reports 51 seconds for the 62 successes. Also solves 46 of the first 50 Lean Prelude statements under a specified inhabitant-equality criterion. Search supports higher-order premises, indexed types and induction, but the translation omits universes and quotients, and default iota pruning is incomplete. Separates source-dependent type theory, Rust search, translation obligations and returned Lean terms; records universe-erasure unsoundness admitted by the authors, iota/structure-eta incompleteness, manually chosen premises and benchmark adaptations, per-world results, exact proof-size metric, successful-proof timing denominator, Prelude success definition, and examples requiring supplied lemmas or generalized recursors. Distinguishes proposed LLM integration from measured proof search.
assumptions_limits: §§3.1–3.2, pp.5–6: terms are beta-normal eta-long and have parameter bindings, simultaneous let declarations, a local head and arguments. Types annotate bindings. Parameters/lets may refer to each other circularly; the encoder must supply a signature valid in the target theory. A missing variable type prevents its use in proof construction; a missing let body makes it an opaque constant. Recursor and projection annotations add reduction behavior. Static arity is an input-format property, not a general property of Lean expressions. §3.2, p.6: start with a goal metavariable, choose a local head and create all its argument metavariables together. Refinement creates typing and definitional-equality constraints. Violations undo a head assignment; metavariable choice need not be backtracked because any completed term admits arbitrary refinement order. This is a structural algorithm argument, not a mechanized implementation-correctness theorem. §3.3, pp.6–7: de Bruijn indices with explicit substitutions permit partial beta reduction without knowing a metavariable’s eventual free variables. Reduction either exposes a rigid head/arguments or becomes stuck. Different rigid heads violate equality; equal heads yield subterm equations. Refinement revisits equations stuck on that metavariable and undo restores them. There is no separate dedicated unification algorithm; constraints guide the same search. §3.3.1, p.8: equality of a blocked recursor/projection and a rigid term may become true after the major argument is instantiated. Default mode treats it as violated, deliberately sacrificing completeness. Program-synthesis mode (+synth) treats it as stuck, admitting more search. A constructor cannot be chosen as the major-argument head of a recursor/projection because that would create a reducible term outside canonical form. This paper does not establish completeness for all Lean definitional equality. §§3.4–3.4.1, pp.8–9: iterative deepening DFS bounds a custom entropy product, mutates assignments in place and runs large branches with fork-join parallelism. Successive thresholds aim to double node counts. Refined metavariables contribute branching factors; unrefined ones use empirical completion estimates from bins keyed by source type ignoring explicit substitution and rigid-equation status. Estimated chance of later rigid equality mixes entropy 1 with average completion refinements; each metavariable estimate is capped at 1000, and unsuccessful refinements incur an extra penalty. Independence is an estimating assumption, not a proved property of dependent subgoals. §3.4.2, pp.9–10: prefer rigid equations for propagation and early failure, then statistically likely impossible metavariables, then high estimated entropy and later arguments whose types constrain earlier values. Meta-level choice and head-level choice serve different purposes. No general theorem of optimality, fair coverage under changing statistics, or global resource bound accompanies this heuristic. §4, pp.10–11: Rust solver communicates through Lean FFI and translated Term/Typ structures. Translation follows Lean Expr constructors, uses lets to retain beta-redexes, and replaces universe-indexed sorts by a single declaration Sort : Sort. The authors explicitly admit possible unsoundness by Girard’s paradox. This affects the search abstraction; a returned term accepted by Lean’s kernel would still have to satisfy Lean’s original universe rules. The paper supplies no mechanized translator-correctness proof or separate measured return-path/kernel-rejection experiment. Rust implementation alone is not evidence of verified Rust or Verus use. §§4–4.1, p.11: Pi structure packages function-valued terms to enforce static arity, with Pi.f/Pi.mk wrappers and eta expansion. Unfolds Set, Not, reducible definitions and typeclass instances where possible to avoid excess wrappers. Literal constants are generally opaque; only natural literals at most 5 receive constructor definitions. Quotient types and universe levels are outside the translation’s supported scope. §4.2, p.12: recursively include constant definitions down to primitives; provide recursor definitions as usable abstractions while hiding types of certain definition-only constants to reduce redundant expressions. Inductive declarations bring constructors/recursors, structures bring projections; local assumptions are included and users supply extra constants in brackets. Recursive expansion can violate abstraction and explode for real numbers. Relevance filtering and automatic premise selection over all Mathlib are outside scope. §5, pp.12–13: Natural Number Game has 79 levels across 9 worlds but 74 unique statements. Authors replace its pedagogical custom naturals/axiomatic operations with standard Nat. Premises are manually selected, mostly from reference solutions and earlier levels. Added Nat.le.intro/dest convert inequality definitions; one level needs Classical.byContradiction; an If structure lets Canonical encode implication induction predicates. Report results for this adapted benchmark, not the untouched game or an unseen randomly sampled theorem library. §5, p.13: Aesop uses default options, Duper portfolio mode, Canonical timeout 15 seconds. Natural-number simp attributes are removed until the corresponding game level, while Duper gets needed definitional equations. Hardware Mac Mini M4 Pro, 24GB RAM; Lean/Mathlib 4.16.0, Duper 0.0.23. No complete matching CPU/thread/time budget table for all solvers. Artifact reference 45 names CanonicalLean v4.22.0, distinct from the benchmark Lean version. §5, pp.13–14: 62/74 Canonical, 27/74 Aesop, 45/74 Duper. Authors attribute much advantage to induction support absent from the compared tactics. 51 seconds is explicitly the time to generate 62 successful proofs; it does not include all failed attempts as a benchmark-total wall-time measurement. On nine successes taking over one second, averages are 23 million attempted refinements/s, 2.1 million/s without equation violation and 1.2 million/s below threshold, branching factor 1.6, final iteration 17% of solve time. §5, p.14: proof length counts constants, free/bound variables, sorts, literals and projections, excluding lambda/let binder types. On common successes Canonical proofs average 251 times shorter than Duper and 18 times shorter than Aesop. Available constants and use of domain-specific lemmas differ. This metric does not measure human readability, checking time, bytes, or whole-benchmark proof-size performance. §5, p.14: Prelude test uses first 50 statements, not a random held-out set. Nonpropositions allow multiple generated inhabitants; success requires one definitionally equal to the library implementation. Constructor-disequality proofs supplied instead of noConfusion. 46 successes; three failures due to missing structure eta encoding, one due to iota incompleteness. Per-problem timeouts and count limits are not comprehensively tabulated. §§6–8, pp.15–16: compares its approach with sauto, Agda inhabitant tools, TWELF, hammers and tactic prediction. Cut-free backward search does not invent local lemmas, call domain solvers on partially instantiated goals, share conflict clauses or table results; branches mostly share statistics. Learned forward reasoning, tactic integration, other DTT languages, AI data generation and LLM use are future directions, not evaluated contributions. No distributed protocol, TLA+, Verus or LLM-agent experiment.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful proof-agent baseline for separating foundational search, premise access, higher-order induction, generated proof terms and original-kernel acceptance. Gives concrete evaluation pitfalls: adapted benchmark, reference-derived premises, incomplete reduction, unsound universe abstraction, solved-subset proof lengths and success-only timing. Can serve as a tactic for later LLM agents, but that integration is proposed rather than tested. Rust implementation supplies no Verus or verified-Rust evidence; no distributed-specification/TLA+ case.

title: Invariant Verification of Nonlinear Hybrid Automata Networks of Cardiac Cells.
what: Presents a simulation-based algorithm that soundly over-approximates bounded-time reach sets of networks of deterministic nonlinear hybrid automata, using automatically computed modular input-to-state (IS) discrepancy functions and simulations of a lower-dimensional model. The method starts from validated simulations at representative initial states, computes bloating factors through IS discrepancy functions, and systematically discovers guard crossings that may invalidate the simulated location sequence. When a bloated tube intersects another guard, the algorithm generates simulations for the newly possible location sequence, retaining sound over-approximation. The paper defines robustness under c-perturbations of initial sets and dynamics and proves relative completeness for robust invariants: refinement of initial-state sampling and discrepancy bounds terminates when a positive robustness margin exists. HA composition plugs module inputs into other modules' state variables; transitions are urgent and deterministic, and trajectories use Lipschitz ODE mappings. An FHN example models fast/slow currents, diffusion coupling and periodic stimulation in a ring of cells.
numbers: Prototype checks bounded-time invariants for five cells (20 continuous variables, 295 locations) typically in under 15 minutes for reasonable horizons; it finds counterexamples for eight-cell networks in about two minutes. The paper states these measurements in §1; no additional benchmark table is present in the extracted Sections 1-3.
assumptions_limits: The formal setting assumes deterministic urgent discrete transitions, Lipschitz continuous ODE dynamics, piecewise-continuous inputs and no transition synchronization between modules. Guarantees concern bounded-time robust invariants; exact reachability is undecidable and non-robust properties need not terminate. The network abstraction relies on module annotations/discrepancy functions (although the paper gives automatic computation techniques), validated numerical simulation and over-approximation, so spurious states/counterexamples are possible. The available extraction contains Sections 1-3 only; detailed algorithm pseudocode and cardiac experiments from later sections are summarized in the abstract/introduction rather than present as full tables.
use_for_goal: Useful architecture for Verus-style verification of nonlinear cyber-physical networks: modular contracts/discrepancy bounds plus verifier-guided exploration provide sound bounded-time safety while exposing assumptions needed for relative completeness. Cardiac scale and runtime numbers show feasibility, but robustness and deterministic-urgent semantics limit direct transfer to distributed asynchronous systems.

quotes.text: We present an algorithm for over-approximating reach sets of networks of nonlinear HA which can be used for sound and relatively complete invariant checking.
The algorithm is sound; it systematically discovers possible transitions and then generates new simulations for different location sequences.

For networks with 5 cells, each with 4 dimensions and 29 locations, and multi-affine dynamics (total of 20 continuous variables, 295 locations), invariants for up to reasonable time horizons are established typically in less than 15 minutes.
In two minutes, it finds counter-examples of networks with 8 cells.
We assume that the discrete transitions are urgent and deterministic.
In this paper we will present semi-decision procedures for bounded-time robust invariant checking of networks of deterministic nonlinear HA.

title: A Fully Verified Executable LTL Model Checker
what: Presents CAVA, an executable LTL model checker whose complete functional correctness is proved in Isabelle/HOL. The automata-theoretic checker translates Boolean programs and negated LTL to Büchi automata, forms their product, and uses nested DFS; abstract set-based algorithms are refined to red-black trees, lists and arrays before ML code generation. The paper gives the full correctness decomposition: Gerth tableau translation to generalized Büchi, generalized-to-ordinary Büchi conversion with acceptance-index states, product-language intersection, lasso characterization and nested-DFS emptiness. It states the Isabelle refinement workflow and interface lemmas, including the exact NO-LASSO specification. Boolean programs are intentionally small (Boolean guarded commands, no arrays/bounded integers), compiled to an interpreted assembly language with always-infinite runs. The 16,000-line Isabelle development (plus 30,000-line Collections and 10,000-line Refinement frameworks) generates about 4,900 ML lines and is benchmarked against SPIN.

assumptions_limits: Input programs are finite-state Boolean guarded-command programs; variables are Booleans and the formal language omits arrays and bounded integers. The model semantics forces every program to have an infinite run, and correctness is for the generated ML code under Isabelle’s trusted kernel/code generator. Functional verification is complete but performance is below optimized C tools: state-space compilation can create extra states, and SPIN uses more mature reductions/simplification. Experiments consider only properties that hold and compare unoptimized SPIN, so timings are reference-implementation evidence rather than broad performance claims.
use_for_goal: A directly relevant verified reference implementation: it shows how mechanized refinement can make a trustworthy executable model checker practical enough to test faster tools, while exposing the modelling and performance limits that matter for verified distributed-system infrastructure.

title: Smart Casual Verification of the Confidential Consortium Framework (CCF)
what: Industrial experience applying TLA+ specification/model checking, weighted simulation and implementation trace validation to the existing C++ Confidential Consortium Framework. Separate node-consensus and client-history specifications are aligned with production protocol details and incorporated in CI. The paper reports six consensus bugs found/fixed and a clarified read-only consistency limitation, plus tooling/effort and state-exploration measurements. Reconstructs all six safety/liveness cases and the unsuccessful first fix, distinguishes trace compatibility from universal implementation refinement, records granularity alignment via composition/stuttering and incomplete-state reconstruction. Saves all scale/coverage rows, effort figures, counterexample sizes and issue pointers. Preserves TEE/model trust, bounded exploration and non-linearizable read-only semantics; no all-executions C++ correctness theorem is claimed.
numbers: Six subtle bugs found, five concerning safety and one liveness
400 LoC Trace spec; 88 commits to it and 107 changes to the consensus spec; implementation 63 kLoC C++
six subtle bugs found
63 kLoC in C++ (§2)
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: CCF runs application logic inside trusted execution environments while treating operators, host OS/hypervisor, network and storage as corruptible. This paper checks distributed protocol behavior under modeled failures, not hardware/firmware isolation, enclave security, cryptography, all 63k C++ LOC, or arbitrary Byzantine behavior of the protected consensus code. Production use in Azure Confidential Ledger is context, not evidence that every production behavior is covered. §§1.1,4,8: Smart casual verification combines formal specification, finite model checking/simulation and tests/trace checks. Consensus spec is unbounded but exhaustive checking restricts terms, requests and reconfiguration sequences. No TLAPS safety/liveness proof for all sizes or universal code-refinement proof is reported. Most CI exploration relies on bounded simulations because sufficiently realistic exhaustive exploration is too expensive. §2: CCF returns transaction results before replication; clients separately query Pending/Committed/Invalid status. A returned result may later be invalidated. Committed read-write transactions are strictly serializable; committed read-only transactions are serializable and may be stale. Pending branches offer fork-like consistency rather than arbitrary results. Broad prose about all committed transactions being linearizable needs the explicit read-only exception. §2: Transaction IDs are lexicographic term/index pairs. If two transactions commit, ID ordering agrees with execution ordering. Ancestor Commit says committed <t,i> implies same-term <t,j>, j≤i, committed. This concerns transaction identity/status, not a proof that any stale read immediately observes the newest committed write. §2.1: CCF customizes Raft with signed Merkle-root transactions, messaging without RPC correspondence, optimistic sentIndex advances, express catch-up, CheckQuorum, bootstrapping/reconfiguration and retirement/ProposeVote. A transaction is committed only after a subsequent signature is committed. The actual combined protocol needs verification; citing the base Raft proof does not establish these extensions. §2.1 reader qualification: Early description says an AE-ACK carries the last transaction in the follower log, while the Inaccurate AE-ACK bug/fix later constrains that index to the end of the received AE. The historical/protocol-description distinction must be retained rather than treating the early sentence as the final safe response rule. §§2.1,4: Reconfiguration needs majorities in each active configuration, rather than a majority of their union. A removed node remains retiring until retirement information is safely committed for future leaders. CheckQuorum steps down an isolated leader, but absent delivery/scheduling assumptions this is not a theorem that all executions make progress. §4: Consensus has 17 actions/13 variables, 12 local-state mappings plus network. Parameterization includes every nonempty initial node subset with any member as initial leader. Locally initiated timeout/signature/candidacy/step-down choices impose no clock synchrony. LogInv compares pairwise committed-log prefixes; AppendOnlyProp prevents committed-prefix rollback over time. Another 27 properties include MonoLogInv, requiring term increases only after signatures. §4: Simulation explores behaviors to bounded depth under a time quota; authors manually downweight failures to promote forward progress. Q-learning was implemented in TLC but no state-hash feature set beat manual weighting. More progress-rich traces may help find bugs but do not constitute exhaustive failure coverage or proof of liveness. §5: Client model uses append-only history and logBranches, independent of node count. History includes read-only/read-write requests/responses and status responses, but omits status requests/Pending replies. A simple shared value appends transaction identifiers so conflicts and observations are visible. It is a deliberately selected application workload, not a proved reduction of all arbitrary CCF application semantics. §5: A new branch can be any prefix of an existing branch containing the last committed transaction. Requests may execute at any still-active leader/term. PrevCommittedInv checks same-term committed ancestor statuses; ObservedRoInv demands that a subsequently committed read-only response observe a read-write transaction whose response preceded its request. The latter expectation is falsified and documented, not a proved CCF invariant. §6.1: Scenario driver serializes consensus execution deterministically and mocks governance/networking/other components, injecting loss/reordering/partition/delay. Original 13 scenarios and about 1.6k unit-test/2k Python end-to-end LOC precede the effort; Table 1 gives later exact scope counts. Initial fuzzing was abandoned for insufficient interesting coverage. Driver/mock accuracy is a boundary, as demonstrated by retirement bugs. §6.1: Driver uses a global logical ordering clock; distributed Lamport/vector alternatives are suggested but not implemented here. Fifteen added logging statements capture stable states at message and role-change points, immediately after a global lock for state changes. Constant-space values such as log lengths are recorded, not full log entries. Production logging compiles out, so the checks use instrumented test executions rather than continuous production monitoring. §6.1/§6.5: Traces initially remove/deduplicate bootstrapping events because early consensus spec omits that phase; later specification is expanded to model bootstrapping more faithfully. These describe successive coverage stages. A successful preprocessed trace validates only its retained observations and modeling assumptions, not excluded initialization behavior. §6.2: Trace spec checks existence of a spec behavior consistent with observed events/values: T∩S is nonempty. Nondeterministically reconstructed hidden state is existential. A successful finite trace check is evidence for those observations, not proof that all completions, all execution traces or unlogged state transitions meet the spec. If logging or mappings omit a decisive distinction, an incorrect implementation could remain compatible. §6.2: Send actions constrain current state, invoke high-level action and assert matching successor messages. Network changes from set to multiset to represent duplicate/resend occurrences. Trace network abstractions also explore ordering/duplication/loss guarantees. Such abstraction choices affect what is observable and accepted; they are not runtime network guarantees inferred from traces. §6.2.1 Listing 5: UpdateTerm·HandleAppendEntriesReq composes two model actions into one implementation receive. IsFault·Next admits unlogged network faults before a step; send-response events may stutter high-level variables when already modeled by another action. Composition hides intermediate states and stuttering changes observation granularity, so correctness depends on the mapping retaining semantically important events. Merely making a mismatch disappear is not an independent proof. §6.2.2–6.3: Start with a happy-path trace, add many assertions and cross-references, debug source and formulas. Invalid traces may indicate bogus logging, incorrect mapping, specification error or implementation bug; failure lacks an ordinary model-checking counterexample. Longest matching prefixes, unreachable-state graphs, failing subformulas and an unsatisfied breakpoint support diagnosis. §6.4: DFS stops after finding one compatible behavior, avoiding BFS enumeration of alternatives; a consistency trace goes from about one hour to under a second. This is an author example without trace-size distribution or controlled speedup suite, and does not mean all traces validate in under a second. Existential acceptance is essential to that optimization. §6.5: Logging/driver enhancements took about one day. Consensus alignment/tooling took two engineer-months over four months, including TLC composition/DFS/debug support, discrepancy diagnosis and abstraction design. Writing about 400 lines of Trace was minor; Table 1 counts 369. Trace saw 88 commits and consensus spec 107 changes. This is observed project effort, not a controlled productivity study. §6.5: Client consistency validation uses REST observations without source instrumentation, reconstructs other clients’ hidden transactions from observed IDs, and took about one engineer-week over two weeks, mainly by CCF experts. Smaller spec, previous experience and reused TLC changes confound a simple comparison with initial consensus effort. §7 Table 1: Approximate state counts/rates are measured on Azure DC8s v3. A log line is largely equivalent to a model action, according to authors, not a formal equality of semantic coverage. Different abstraction sizes, bounds, durations and distinct/generated-state counting prevent treating orders-of-magnitude state counts as a calibrated defect-detection probability. §7: Six serious consensus bugs comprise five safety issues and one liveness issue, found by combined modeling, source scrutiny, trace mismatch, simulation and functional/end-to-end reproduction. They are not six independent discoveries by model checking alone. Read-only non-linearizability is an additional documented consistency ambiguity and accepted behavior, not a seventh fixed consensus bug. §§7–8: Authors report all six fixed before user impact/customer reports; software had already been deployed. One-node-at-a-time operational reconfiguration masked the election bug, and absence of an incident from the first bad commit fix was attributed to chance. No external incident audit, current repository verification or independent bug reproduction was done in this reading. §§8–9: Paper chooses model checking for developer accessibility rather than deductive proof, despite compute cost. AI-assisted proof search is future possibility with a reference to neural theorem proving, not an experiment using LLM agents. Related-work sentence says IronFleet and Verdi both proved Raft; reader qualification: IronFleet uses a Paxos-based replicated state machine, so do not propagate that comparison as fact.
use_for_goal: Direct industrial evidence for TLA+, specification-to-implementation trace mapping, model/spec drift, mutable protocol extensions and reproducible bug evaluation. A useful target for LLM specification agents: require real-trace correspondence, independent safety/consistency expectations and reproduced counterexamples; report search bounds, instrumentation trust and failed fixes. No verified Rust/Verus or actual LLM-agent experiment is reported.

title: A Safety and Liveness Theory for Total Reversibility?
what: Defines CCSroll, a CCS extension with totally ordered keyed reductions and programmed rollback, and characterizes safety and liveness preorders using forward traces, rollback barbs and tree refusals. The syntax/semantics records memories and dependency histories so a rollback of key k deterministically returns all later reductions to the state before k. The authors prove rollback determinism and rollback/forward correspondence, then identify two semantic properties enabling forward-only reasoning. Observable trace inclusion is shown sound and complete for inverse may-testing safety; a rollback-aware tree-refusal model is sound and complete for should-testing liveness. Examples M1–M6 show safety conservatively extends CCS while rollback distinguishes systems that CCS cannot distinguish; the paper also gives compositional LTS, trace zipping/unzipping, and characteristic tests.
numbers: two semantic properties underpin forward models
Theorem 1 safety conservativity
Theorem 3 trace soundness/completeness
Theorem 4 refusal soundness/completeness

No empirical evaluation is reported. Formal results include deterministic rollback (Lemma 1), rollback-forward recovery (Lemma 2), forward-reduction properties, Theorem 1 (CCS safety conservativity), Theorem 3 (trace soundness/completeness), and Theorem 4 (refusal soundness/completeness).
assumptions_limits: CCSroll reductions are totally ordered, rollback is controlled by explicit rlh keys, and proofs rely on the two stated reachability properties, including the difficult liveness property. Liveness should-testing is justified under a fairness assumption that infinitely enabled outputs eventually happen. Results are semantic theorems, not mechanized proofs or implementation measurements; the authors leave applicability of the second property to other causal-reversibility calculi open. The theory concerns CCS-like processes and does not model data, failures or real distributed timing.
use_for_goal: Formalizes how rollback changes safety/liveness reasoning and when forward-only traces suffice. The explicit fairness and reachability assumptions are useful specification obligations for reversible or recovery-oriented distributed systems, while the open generalization points to proof gaps for mechanized Verus models.

title: Automated Formal Synthesis of Digital Controllers for State-Space Physical Plants
what: Synthesizes safe finite-precision state-feedback controllers for discretized linear time-invariant plants. A CEGIS loop combines stability-constrained controller search with either multi-stage bounded verification up to a completeness threshold or abstraction/refinement with abstract acceleration and explicit quantization/noise bounds. The paper models ADC/DAC, fixed-point arithmetic, plant representation and rounding errors as bounded nondeterministic noise and interval operations. The baseline synthesizes on one initial state, then checks all hypercube vertices, precision soundness and a stability-derived completeness threshold; convexity proves vertex sufficiency. The abstraction backend accelerates all closed-loop powers into an infinite reach-tube, returns iteration/initial-state counterexamples, and refines eigenvalue constraints. Worked examples show successive counterexamples and precision increases; ten control benchmarks compare both backends.

title: Central Limit Model Checking
what: Develops scalable approximate model checking for time-bounded CSL and reward properties of CTMCs induced by stochastic reaction networks. A central-limit/Gaussian process approximation is projected onto linear combinations defining convex-polytope targets, discretized into a low-dimensional time-inhomogeneous DTMC, and checked numerically with convergence guarantees as population size grows. The paper formalizes density-dependent SRNs, CTMC/CME semantics, Gaussian CLA equations, convex predicates, CSL syntax/semantics and reward operators. Time and space discretization produce DTMC transition kernels; Theorems 2–4 establish convergence/soundness for reachability abstraction and Theorem 5 extends convergence to CSL. Reward propositions cover instantaneous, cumulative and bounded-reachability rewards. Case studies compare Matlab CLA results with PRISM statistical model checking: gene-expression reachability where mean-field methods fail, and a seven-species phosphorelay at N=400/800. Errors decrease with smaller timestep and larger population; for N=800,h=0.1, average relative error is 0.0015 and max 0.0217, while PRISM’s 30,000 simulations take hours.

assumptions_limits: The SRN rates are real analytic and density dependent; CLA convergence is asymptotic in population size and only finite-time. Targets must be convex polytopes expressed by linear inequalities, and discretization introduces timestep/grid error. The Gaussian approximation can be inaccurate at low populations or in tails; time-unbounded properties are excluded. Results depend on well-mixed stochastic kinetics and bounded/continuous reward assumptions, and exact CTMC uniformization remains infeasible for evaluated models.
use_for_goal: A rigorous example of replacing an intractable distributed stochastic state space with a low-dimensional approximate model plus asymptotic convergence proofs. It is relevant to probabilistic verification workflows and makes approximation assumptions explicit, but finite-time Gaussian limits and discretization errors prevent unconditional correctness claims.

title: CertiFlash: A Formal Verification Framework for Flash Translation Layers in Computational Solid State Drives
what: CertiFlash models FTLs as deterministic state machines with a global invariant covering mapping, isolation, integrity, ownership, and allocation, then packages reusable Rocq proofs so modified FTLs discharge five design-specific hypotheses instead of re-proving the full invariant. The framework proves invariant preservation, stepwise simulation, command precondition soundness, read-after-write correctness, and cross-address non-interference. Four case studies cover new state, reimplemented operations, new operations, and changed invariants; inherited proofs and local obligations are measured in lines.

title: Characteristic Formulae for Liveness Properties of Non-Terminating CakeML Programs
what: Extends CakeML characteristic formulae and Hoare triples to prove total-correctness liveness properties of diverging programs. Divergent results carry lazy I/O traces; a clocked big-step semantics defines divergence as timeout at every clock and the supremum of finite-clock I/O prefixes. A transfinite-induction rule for repeat loops reduces proofs to terminating loop-body triples plus a limit-stream equation. A verified source transformation rewrites tail-recursive functions to repeat form. The framework is mechanized in HOL4 and integrated with CakeML. The semantics adds Div and FFIDiv results and POSTd predicates while preserving local separation reasoning. The repeat rule has base, successor and limit cases and a limited_parts side condition controlling all FFI resources. The transformation injects a runtime error in non-tail return branches so a transformed terminating function cannot be incorrectly treated as diverging; it is proved sound only for POSTd. Examples include silent pureLoop, conditional condLoop, infinite/finite catLoop over lazy input, cyclic pointerLoop, uncurried myRepeat, and a seL4 UAV filter. The filter proof shrinks from 1,971 lines of direct operational-semantics HOL to 1,479 lines with CF and yields an operational theorem; compiler liveness transfer remains conditional on no out-of-memory.
numbers: {'printed_pages': 19, 'filter_cf_hol_lines': 1479, 'filter_direct_hol_lines': 1971, 'filter_message_bound': 256, 'myrepeat_proof_lines': 8, 'cat_proof_approx_lines': 90}
assumptions_limits: Divergence semantics is a supremum of I/O traces over all clock values; divergent runs have no final heap state. The repeat transformation currently handles single-argument tail-recursive, non-mutually-recursive functions; mutual recursion, curried/multiple arguments and recursion through store are future work. The induction principle requires limited_parts to bound possible FFI calls and user proofs of each terminating iteration and the infinite trace equation. The seL4 filter assumes infinite input, null termination and message length ≤256; the paper says the communication backend enforces these. Binary liveness after CakeML compilation is conditional on not running out of memory; no unconditional space bound is proved here. Formal results are HOL4/CakeML proofs, not Verus/Rust or TLA+ specifications and not LLM-generated proofs.
use_for_goal: This is a strong precedent for proof-producing liveness specifications of non-terminating distributed components: explicit I/O traces, environmental assumptions and compiler transfer are made part of the theorem. It complements Verus/Rust safety proofs and TLA+ temporal specifications by showing how divergence can be handled in a mechanized Hoare framework. It does not evaluate LLM agents or distributed protocols directly.

quotes.text: This work has been developed in the HOL4 theorem prover and has been integrated into the ecosystem of proof tools surrounding the CakeML programming language.
Few Hoare logics can state (let alone prove) that the yes program (1) will not terminate and (2) will produce a never-ending stream of y characters as output.
The approach is inspired by transfinite induction rather than coinduction, and does not require non-terminating loops to be productive.
When a program diverges, it exhibits a possibly infinite trace of I/O events, represented as a lazy list.
This extends the soundness result of Guéneau et al. [15] to total-correctness Hoare triples about divergent programs.
In the limit case, we need to show that the least upper bound of events – or in other words, the I/O events after infinitely many iterations of fv – satisfies Q.

title: Temporal Logic and Model Checking for Operator Precedence Languages
what: Introduces Operator Precedence Temporal Logic (OPTL) for expressing and automatically checking properties of operator-precedence languages, whose hidden parse structure strictly generalizes visibly pushdown languages. It defines operator-precedence automata (OPA), chain and summary/hierarchical temporal operators, and an automata construction for model checking finite and infinite words. Sections 2–4 define OPA stack semantics and the non-visible chain relation, then give examples of matching-next/back, summary until/since, and hierarchical modalities for handlers and nested procedure traces. Every NWTL formula is translated linearly to OPTL on an encoding of nested words; hierarchical operators can be eliminated with exponential formula blowup. Section 5 gives closure/atom construction rules for automata, stack auxiliaries for maximal chains, summary and hierarchical operators, and a generalized Büchi extension for infinite words.
numbers: OPA size 2^O(|formula|)
NWTL-to-OPTL translation linear in formula length
hierarchical-elimination translation O(n^2 2^n |alpha|)
OPTL automata support finite and omega words
assumptions_limits: The OPM on atomic-proposition sets supplies the word structure; complete matrices are needed for universal languages, and formulas rely on compatible chains. The construction is exponential in formula length (2^O(|phi|)); translating hierarchical operators can itself be exponential. Infinite-word checking is only sketched via generalized Büchi acceptance and requires extra bookkeeping for obligations buried forever on the stack. The paper reports no implementation or empirical benchmark and leaves expressiveness completeness and user-friendly requirements open.
use_for_goal: Provides a formal temporal-logic/model-checking design for hidden stack structure beyond visibly pushdown words. Its explicit automaton construction, chain obligations, complexity, and finite/infinite semantics are useful comparison points for TLA+, Verus specifications, and automated proof workflows.

title: Quorum Tree Abstractions of Consensus Protocols
what: Introduces Quorum Tree (QTree), a sequential rooted-tree abstraction whose add and commit operations model quorum observations in consensus rounds. It proves safety of QTree and shows Paxos, HotStuff, PBFT, Raft, and Multi-Paxos refine one or more QTree instances via fixed linearization points. QTree nodes carry round, value, parent, and ADDED/GHOST/COMMITTED status. Predicates enforce unique rounds, parent links, trunk extension, and (for single-decree consensus) parent-value preservation. Theorem 1 characterizes correct successful invocation sequences using four checkable properties, including the key prohibition on committing a lower conflicting round after a higher branch is added. Paxos refinement marks PROPOSE as add and DECIDE as commit; safety follows from quorum intersection between vote and later join quorums. HotStuff uses valid PRECOMMIT and DECIDE certificates under 3f+1 Byzantine processes and 2f+1 quorums. PBFT maps each sequence number to an independent QTree. A table relates protocol phases to add/commit quorum phases and exposes quorum optimization opportunities.

assumptions_limits: Refinement proofs assume round-based protocols with identifiable phases, fixed code locations as linearization points, honest processes for Paxos/Raft and cryptographically constrained Byzantine behavior for HotStuff/PBFT. Validity additionally requires client-value broadcast or equivalent checks. QTree is a safety abstraction; the authors do not establish liveness and note protocols without round decomposition (e.g., Texel) may not fit. Multi-decree protocols require independent QTree instances, and removing valueConstraint changes validity interpretation for state-machine replication.
use_for_goal: A compact operational specification and refinement proof pattern for distributed consensus. It is useful for Verus/TLA+ work because fixed linearization points and quorum obligations turn complex protocol executions into checkable safety properties.

title: Cloud Deployment Tradeoffs for the Analysis of Spatially-Distributed Systems of Internet-of-Things
what: Builds a runtime spatial-verification architecture for resource-constrained IoT systems. Trajectory-derived accessibility graphs become closure spaces evaluated with Spatial Logic for Closure Spaces (SLCS); model checking is packaged as microservices and deployed on VMs, containers, AWS Lambda FaaS, or a hybrid. The paper explains how points of interest and trajectories induce a quasi-discrete closure model, how SLCS closure/surround operators express bike-sharing requirements, and how services maintain model/state updates. It compares monolithic VM, containerized ECS, FaaS and hybrid load balancing, using a Beijing taxi trace and a 30-second SLA. A mobile-device baseline averages 99 seconds per invocation. Lambda stays near 12 seconds across load rates; monolith is 9–12 seconds through 20× load but violates SLA at higher peaks; containers time out at 20× or more due to scale-up; hybrid splits 65–35% monolith/FaaS at 60× and has about 20 seconds median calls, with load-balancer overhead under 300 ms.
numbers: 15,456 propositions / 5,152 nodes
30-second SLA

536 requests in peak experiment
5×–60× workload rates
<300 ms hybrid load-balancer overhead
assumptions_limits: The spatial model is finite, graph-derived and qualitative; only three properties and one model checker are evaluated. Cloud resources are assumed available, and cost/SLA conclusions depend on AWS instance sizes, 30-second SLA choice, taxi workload shape and preallocation. The hybrid is a proof of concept with tunable threshold/cache policies. The architecture centralizes verification and can suffer network latency, privacy and single-point-of-failure issues; edge decentralization and quantitative/metric properties are future work.
use_for_goal: Concrete evidence that runtime formal checking for spatial distributed systems must be co-designed with deployment elasticity, cost and latency. The workflow illustrates specification-to-checker service integration, while narrow workloads and centralized assumptions constrain generalization to distributed proof systems.

title: Parameterizing the quantification of CMSO: model checking on minor-closed graph classes
what: Introduces CMSO/tw, a fragment of counting monadic second-order logic whose set quantifiers range over sets of bounded annotated treewidth, and proves an algorithmic meta-theorem for CMSO/tw+dp on H-minor-free graphs. The paper defines annotated treewidth and the bounded quantifiers, develops annotated types and flat railed annuli, and proves local-global irrelevance to construct the meta-algorithm. The main theorem decides a CMSO/tw+dp formula on an H-minor-free graph in f(|φ|,|H|)|G|² time. The conclusion argues treewidth is the best possible minor-monotone parameter for this style of result and identifies extensions beyond minor-closedness as open directions.
numbers: quadratic |G|² dependence in the main theorem
algorithm factor f(|φ|, |H|)
bounded-treewidth quantifier parameter k included in formula length
assumptions_limits: The theorem is parameterized by formula length and excluded-minor size and applies to non-trivial minor-closed classes (or H-minor-free graphs); it is a theoretical construction with no empirical runtime evaluation. The optimality discussion rules out analogous AMTs for parameters not functionally larger than treewidth, while topological-minor and alternative-parameter extensions remain open.
use_for_goal: Provides a rigorous tractability boundary and parameterized logic design for graph model checking, relevant to understanding how structural annotations can make otherwise expressive verification logics algorithmically manageable.

title: Cost-Efficient Theorem Proving via Agent Orchestration in Program Verification
what: Introduces CoCo-Prover, a cost-aware Lean 4 program prover that treats proving as metalevel decision-making over a two-level proof graph: intra-declaration AND/OR proof hypergraphs and an inter-lemma dependency DAG. A symbolic scheduler exposes dependency-ready goals, while an evidence-grounded router purchases actions from deterministic automation, Proof Writer, Lemma Planner, and Recovery Reviewer agents. The formal model defines state, frontier scheduling, action outcomes/costs, a Bellman objective 1[solve]-lambda C, and regret decomposition. The implementation clusters goals, bypasses model calls for definition-nested goals, tracks provisional lemmas and rollback, rejects cyclic/unelaborated helpers, and uses Lean as proof authority. The evaluation fixes theorem statements and implementations, compares against Ax-Prover-Base, Humanize, and coding agents on CLEVER, VERINA, AlgoVeri, NTP4VC, and Vero with GPT-5.6-Terra, Gemini-3.5-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. CoCo-Prover reaches 100% on CLEVER/VERINA in several settings, up to 60.5% on Vero versus at most 7% coding-agent, and lowers cost up to 30.9% against Humanize on commonly solved tasks. Ablations show removing routing raises cost 39.9% and removing lemma planning 41.6%; case studies show shared lemmas solve 56 interdependent Vero obligations. Independent review checks no holes, unchanged statements, no new axioms, automated review, and manual audits.

assumptions_limits: Theory assumes finite reachable abstractions, finite admissible computations/text vocabularies, Markov specialist outputs, bounded positive paid costs, deterministic verifier transitions, proper policies, and an explicit stop. The deployed router is not proved low-regret; semantic decisions rely on LLM judgment. Evaluation is Lean 4 only, proof-only with fixed implementations/specifications, and repository-scale evidence uses two benchmarks. Local computation, Lean checking, retrieval, and wall-clock costs are not charged; CoCo-Prover can be slower in wall-clock time. Shared-helper savings assume equal success probability and can be lost to false or abandoned lemmas.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for LLM agents writing machine-checked program proofs: symbolic scheduling, reusable lemma graphs, verifier-gated progress, and cost-aware routing improve repository-scale verification. It provides concrete evaluation methodology and exposes assumptions relevant to Verus/Rust and TLA+ proof automation.

title: Compile to Compress: Boosting Formal Theorem Provers by Compiler Outputs
what: Introduces a learning-to-refine framework for Lean theorem proving that treats compiler diagnostics as a lossy many-to-one compression of failed programs into recurring error modes. It trains provers on direct solutions plus compiler-conditioned repair traces, uses expert iteration to collect on-policy failures, and performs random or value-guided tree search that alternates fresh proof generation with local refinement. On MiniF2F-test, ProofNet, MathOlympiadBench and PutnamBench, Kimina-Expert and Goedel-Expert generally improve over direct baselines; Goedel-Expert value search reaches 110 solved PutnamBench problems at budget 256 and Kimina-Expert reaches 25. Defines programs C, compiler messages M, verifier Φ:C→M, equivalence classes Ψ(c) of programs sharing feedback, and a refinement supervision operator that maps correct programs to synthesis targets and failures to repaired programs. The chain-of-distributions view models each next program as conditioned on current program, compiler message and problem. Markovian refinement discards long interaction histories while retaining the failed code and diagnostics. Cold-start data pairs base-prover failures with base-prover correct solutions and Claude-3.7-Sonnet-generated explanatory traces; direct examples are subsampled to balance refinement data. Expert iteration repeatedly refines on-policy failures and trains a value head from pairwise preferences along successful and failed trajectories. Compiler messages are inserted at reported source lines using <error> delimiters; insertion beats appending in a one-direct-plus-one-refinement MiniF2F comparison (279 versus272 solved after one epoch,and284 versus246 after two epochs).
assumptions_limits: The compiler projection is explicitly lossy: the paper says messages ‘do not capture full semantic context’; shared error signatures are an inductive bias, not a proof that all programs in a class share a repair. The Markov treatment assumes each refinement step depends only on the current failed program, its compiler feedback and the problem, with history ‘implicitly encoded in Lean semantics’. This is a modeling choice and is not established as a theorem. The chain-of-distributions claim that refinement can reach solutions outside direct-generation support is supported by edit-distance energy tests and MDS visualizations. Edit distance is syntactic, and MDS is a low-dimensional visualization; these do not establish semantic support escape. The authors call the synthesized pipeline ‘hallucination-free’ because corrected solutions are validated by Lean and come from base-prover failures; Claude supplies explanatory traces, not executable repairs. This does not make the natural-language reasoning truthful or independently verified. Main evaluation uses Lean v4.15.0, a pinned Mathlib snapshot, Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B and Goedel-Prover-V2-32B, and four mathematics benchmarks. It does not evaluate Verus, Rust, TLA+, concurrency or distributed systems. Reported Pass/solved counts use different sampling budgets and methods. PutnamBench is described as 660 problems, while the leaderboard includes an Aleph result of 668; this apparent version/scope mismatch is preserved rather than reconciled. Goedel-V2 already supports non-Markovian refinement, so the main experiments use only its direct generation ability as a base; direct-vs-refinement comparisons therefore are not a uniform comparison of all native capabilities. Error-type correction probabilities aggregate occurrences and treat multiple errors independently; they do not measure transition-node success. Training frequency alone does not imply repairability. The Claude ablation and Table 16 use fixed budgets and selected datasets. Expert iteration, not cold-start SFT or Claude traces alone, accounts for most reported gains, but this is an ablation interpretation rather than a causal decomposition over all possible training procedures. No external artifact or proof checker was rerun here; quoted correctness of the worked repair is the paper's report that the generated Lean program compiled.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to verified proof agents: compiler or verifier diagnostics can define reusable failure classes, and on-policy repair plus adaptive search can reduce dependence on long proof histories. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ systems, the transferable idea is a checker-feedback-conditioned refinement policy; transfer is an inference because the paper studies only Lean mathematics and does not test code, concurrency or distributed protocols.

title: A Complete Method for Symmetry Reduction in Safety Verification
short_name: Complete symmetry reduction in safety verification
what: Introduces a complete symmetry-reduction method for safety verification of finite, parametrically defined multi-process systems without precomputed global symmetry. It defines weak symmetry relative to the safety property, learns state interpolants backward over the interleaving tree, transforms interpolants by process permutations, and prunes states whose symmetric future is covered. The DFS algorithm handles cycles with fixpoint interpolation. Weak symmetry compares program-counter tuples, safety truth under a permutation, and bijective matching of enabled/scheduled transitions while deliberately ignoring shared-variable values; strong symmetry additionally requires full state equality. The algorithm memoizes interpolants per program point, recursively conjoins weakest-precondition approximations for enabled and disabled transitions, detects cycles and computes path-invariant fixpoints, then prunes if a permuted memoized interpolant holds. Theorem 1 proves pruning sound; Theorem 2 proves completeness with respect to weak symmetry when precondition computation is monotonic and symmetry preserving. Examples show pruning despite differing sums and process IDs.

title: Compositional Probabilistic Model Checking with String Diagrams of MDPs
what: Defines CompMDP, a compositional probabilistic model-checking algorithm for open Markov decision processes composed as string diagrams, computing optimal expected cumulative rewards while retaining reachability probabilities and scheduler alternatives. The paper formalizes open MDPs with entrances/exits, rewards, transition probabilities and almost-sure termination, then derives decomposition equalities for reachability and expected rewards under sequential composition and loops. A categorical construction builds solution functors from rightward Markov chains to MDPs and bidirectional diagrams; semantic arrows retain pairs of reachability probability and expected reward for each memoryless scheduler, with a meager subsumption optimization. CompMDP implements this in Python, supports freezing subdiagrams and delegates frozen components to PRISM, and records an optimal scheduler result. Experiments on Patrol, Wholesale and Packets test reuse, freezing and scale, including models with 10^8 positions.

title: Computing Adequately Permissive Assumptions for Synthesis.
what: . We automatically compute a new class of environment as- sumptions in two-player turn-based finite graph games which character- ize an “adequate cooperation” needed from the environment to allow the system player to win. Given an ω-regular winning condition Φ for the system player, we compute an ω-regular assumption Ψ for the environ- ment player, such that (i) every environment strategy compliant with Ψ allows the system to fulfill Φ (sufficiency), (ii) Ψ can be fulfilled by the environment for every strategy of the system (implementability), and (iii) Ψ does not prevent any cooperative strategy choice (permissiveness).

title: Modular Verification of Concurrent Programs via Sequential Model Checking
what: Introduces CoMuS, a fully automatic reduction of safety verification for a fixed number of concurrent threads to sequential model-checking tasks, with lazy environment learning and a hierarchy-aware verification order. The main-thread program inserts env_move at interleaving cut-points and initially havocs environment-written shared variables. Counterexample paths induce ReachE(alpha,beta) queries; infeasible queries generalize alpha/beta and refine env_move, while feasible queries produce promises of error that become assertions and may expose environment locals or pcE as new variables. Environment queries are answered by a sequential environment program using try_start to model reachable non-initial computations. The algorithm maintains an overapproximation invariant, is sound for Safe and Real Violation outcomes, and makes progress by shrinking represented environment transitions or expanding states known to lead to errors. It is guaranteed to terminate for finite variable domains but not generally for infinite domains.
numbers: CoMuS was compared with Threader, VVT, and UL-CSeq using SeaHorn/CPAChecker backends on Ubuntu 16.04, 8GB RAM, with 3600-second timeouts for dynamic-program benchmarks and 1200 seconds for fib-bench. In chain-structured dynamic programs CoMuS scaled best as thread count increased; all tools failed on ring instances with at least four threads while CoMuS verified all tested chain instances. On the general benchmark subset CoMuS was typically outperformed.
assumptions_limits: Semantics is sequentially consistent interleaving with a fixed number of threads; synchronization is modeled atomically. Safety assertions are placed in the main thread, and cut-point/interleaving reduction must preserve safety. The prototype supports only a C subset, lacks alias analysis and dynamic thread creation, and depends on the sequential checker (SeaHorn) for infinite-state capabilities. Termination is not guaranteed over infinite domains; hierarchy-sensitive performance degrades on rings/general programs.
use_for_goal: A concrete compositional verification architecture that reuses sequential checkers and learns rely-like environment assumptions automatically. It is relevant to automated distributed/concurrent verification methodology, but does not verify Verus/Rust or TLA+ and has prototype limitations.

title: Conditional Model Checking
what: Reformulates a failed model-checking run to return a condition Ψ describing the state space verified: the program satisfies the specification as long as it stays within Ψ. Conditions can restrict later runs, preserve partial work after timeout, and combine complementary analyses. Defines condition-aware outcomes, resource/progress monitors, and conditions such as path length, repeating locations, time limits, and assumption automata. Experiments combine CBMC shallow BMC with CPACHECKER explicit-value and predicate analyses, feeding generated assumptions between runs for bug finding, regression checking, and coverage.

Best pipeline used CBMC, then 10-second explicit analysis, then 15-minute predicate analysis (§V)
assumptions_limits: Software model checking remains undecidable; a condition summarizes verified regions rather than proving the whole program. Effectiveness depends on useful predicates/conditions and tool configurations. Experiments use bounded analyses and benchmark-specific thresholds; conditions can exclude states and leave a residual region requiring another method.
use_for_goal: Provides a practical way to preserve partial verification progress and compose bounded, explicit, and predicate analyses. Conditions improve coverage and resource use but do not remove undecidability or guarantee completion of the residual state space.

title: Verifying Global Two-Safety Properties in Neural Networks with Confidence
what: Defines confidence-based global 2-safety properties unifying robustness and fairness, and verifies them by self-composing a DNN and replacing softmax with a sound piecewise-linear over-approximation checked by Marabou. The property compares every sufficiently close input pair when at least one output has confidence above a threshold, allowing class changes near low-confidence decision boundaries while requiring high-confidence predictions to agree. The paper proves soundness and bounds softmax approximation error, gives a complete Marabou-based counterexample procedure for the approximated network, and uses binary search to synthesize minimum robust/fair confidence. Experiments cover German Credit, Adult, Law School and COMPAS models with global robustness and sensitive-attribute fairness queries.

Four datasets; fully connected ReLU models with up to 50 neurons; accuracies German Credit 0.71, COMPAS 0.74, Law 0.94, Adult 0.77. German Credit robustness becomes unsat above κ=0.75 (binary search finds 0.75 in 45 s). Adult, Law and COMPAS are 2-safe above κ=0.5 with proofs in ≤50 s. Fairness: German Credit Gender κ=0.5 unsat 10.232 s; Age 0.5 unsat 11.478 s; COMPAS Gender 0.5 sat 7.423 s; Ethnicity 0.5 sat 18.293 s, 0.99 sat 25.846 s, 0.999 unsat 171 min 15 s. For COMPAS, certified fair above 0.999, unfair below 0.969, undecided in between due to 0.171 error.
assumptions_limits: Networks are feed-forward ReLU models with a small output layer; the linear softmax abstraction has no error for two outputs but about 0.171 error for three outputs, producing an undecidable confidence interval for COMPAS. Marabou completeness removes solver false positives, but abstraction can produce spurious counterexamples. High confidence as a precondition can make poorly calibrated networks vacuously safe; current method handles roughly two to five outputs and does not establish training-data generalization.
use_for_goal: Relevant to automated proof and specification generation: it turns a relational neural property into self-composition plus a formally justified abstraction, and clearly separates sound certification from approximate counterexamples. The output-count and calibration limits are important when judging generated verification claims.

It intersects policies inferred from sampled forwarding states with a candidate set, then uses grouped symbolic control-plane queries to verify remaining policies or produce counterexamples. Two runtime predictors choose between sampling and verification; policy-aware sampling, topology cuts and prefix grouping reduce work. A handwritten argument establishes exactness and termination conditional on exact terminating component tools and correct environment enumeration. Evaluation measures runtime, query reduction and specification size. title: Optimal Stateless Model Checking for Causal Consistency
what: Develops a stateless model-checking framework for causal consistency variants CC, CCv and CM. The DPOR algorithm explores executions represented by program-order (po) and reads-from (rf) relations, maintaining model-specific consistency edges; it is sound, complete and optimal because each consistent po-rf trace is explored once. Conschecker implements the algorithm at LLVM IR level and reports assertion violations. The paper formally defines CC overwrite cycles, CCv conflict/arbitration cycles and CM happened-before cycles, then gives a uniform trace semantics and DPOR schedule construction. Conschecker extends Nidhugg and validates outcomes against Herd simulations. Evaluation spans 9,815 litmus tests, SV-COMP stress tests, five database applications, classical anomaly benchmarks and parameterized programs; model strength differs (e.g., Delivery Order unsafe under CC/CCv but safe under CM).

The method explores terminating executions and detects user assertions, not liveness, memory safety or implementation correctness beyond the modeled semantics. Trace consistency checking can be expensive: SV-COMP examples generate millions of traces and parameterized scaling reaches 13 processes/variables in reported cases.

title: Context-Bounded Verification of Liveness Properties for Multithreaded Shared-Memory Programs
what: Proves decidability and complexity results for termination, fair non-termination and fair starvation of dynamically spawning recursive threads under a fixed context-switch bound, introducing VASS with balloons as the key intermediate model. The paper formalizes Dynamic Networks of Concurrent Pushdown Systems (DCPS), thread identities, scheduler swaps/resumptions and fairness. Ordinary termination reduces through downward closures to VASS non-termination, yielding the 2EXPSPACE result. Fairness is not downward-closure preserving, so VASS with balloons stores semi-linear multisets of future spawns; progressive runs and a shallow-run theorem reduce DCPS fair behavior to VASSB reachability, then to ordinary VASS reachability. A separate Ramsey/pumping and consistency construction reduces starvation to fair termination. The paper gives proof machinery rather than an implementation or empirical benchmark.

assumptions_limits: The bound K is fixed per decision instance and fairness means every thread ready infinitely often is eventually scheduled (with identity-equivalence subtleties handled by an angelic scheduler argument). Results concern the DCPS model: finite global state, pushdown stacks, shared global control and restricted scheduler rules. Fair problems are decidable but non-elementary; unbounded context switching remains outside the decidability claim.
use_for_goal: This is a foundational formal-verification result for concurrent distributed-style programs: it precisely separates decidable context-bounded liveness from highly undecidable unrestricted fairness and gives a reduction architecture that preserves spawning and recursive stacks. It informs verification of distributed runtimes where bounded scheduling and fairness are explicit assumptions.

title: Safety Verification of Decision-Tree Policies in Continuous Time
what: Introduces the first direct continuous-time reachability algorithm for systems controlled by decision trees. It propagates set enclosures through policy branches and nonlinear ODEs, using Taylor models for dynamics and axis-aligned predicate splitting for the tree, thereby detecting between-sample safety violations. A DTCS samples a tree every control period while applying the selected action continuously. Algorithm 1 queues state sets, postT partitions them among actions, and postf computes interval and endpoint enclosures; Theorem 1 proves termination/soundness and relative completeness under exact post procedures. The implementation uses TaylorModels.jl/JuliaReach and handles fixpoints for unbounded-time results. Even state-independent dynamics f(x,u)=u yield PSPACE-complete bounded-time reach-avoid and undecidable unbounded-time reachability via reductions from LBAs and two-counter machines. Experiments distill trees from neural policies: a depth-10 six-dimensional quadrotor is verified in 6.5 minutes; cart-pole is proved safe forever by a fixpoint; acrobot policies reach goal in about 100–112s; mountain-car reaches its goal within 132 steps in 16s. A generic hybrid-automata tool stalls at bisections, showing the value of exploiting tree structure.

assumptions_limits: Solutions to ODE initial-value problems are assumed unique; predicates are axis-aligned xi≤c; Taylor-model overapproximations and bisections can accumulate wrapping error. Fixpoint checking is for time-invariant systems and may be hard with general Taylor sets. The proof-of-concept focuses on relatively small trees and simple tasks; nonlinear reachability remains undecidable in general and exactness depends on post procedures.
use_for_goal: Direct formal verification of learned control policies with sound set-based reachability and explicit complexity limits; highly relevant to formal safety guarantees, though not distributed protocols.

title: A Convex Relaxation Barrier to Tight Robustness Verification of Neural Networks
what: Unifies LP-relaxed neural-network verifiers in a layer-wise convex-relaxation framework and characterizes the optimal relaxation within that framework. The primal and dual formulations are shown equivalent through convex conjugacy and layer-wise bounds. LP-ALL computes tight preactivation bounds in parallel, then solves the final LP exactly; LP-GREEDY and LP-LAST are weaker baselines. Large experiments compare these relaxations against PGD and MILP on normally and robustly trained MNIST/CIFAR networks. Even the optimal layer-wise relaxation only modestly improves existing relaxed bounds, leaving a persistent gap to PGD/MILP and motivating methods beyond this framework.

assumptions_limits: The barrier applies to methods expressible as layer-wise convex relaxations, especially ReLU networks; it does not rule out non-convex, branch-and-bound, or other verification methods. LP-ALL requires many per-neuron LPs and large parallel compute. MILP comparisons use time limits, and PGD is an attack upper bound rather than a proof. title: Correctly Compiling Proofs About Programs Without Proving Compilers Correct
what: PotPie compiles an embedded source program, its Hoare proof and its specification into a related target language, preserving a selected partial specification even when the program compiler changes other behavior. Gives a correct-by-construction CC workflow and a Tree workflow with an untrusted certificate generator or a less-assured boolean checker. Coq formalization proves conditional soundness; toy examples include deliberate miscompilation. Makes specification meaning preservation explicit via state correspondence and bidirectional assertion semantics, separately from target proof validity. Uses a manually translated implication database for consequence rules and structural compiler equations to transport other Hoare rules. Details source/target well-formedness, stack-purity obligations, certificate-versus-boolean trust, localized UIP axioms and partial-correctness/termination boundaries.
assumptions_limits: Languages are simple related imperative calculi Imp and Stack, with natural-number arithmetic, functions and different variable models. They are embedded semantics, not C/Rust/assembly or machine-word execution. Practical lower-level logics, pointers, optimizing control-flow passes and scalability are future work. Partial correctness of a selected postcondition does not establish full behavioral equivalence, termination or any property omitted from that specification. Helper multiplication/exponentiation need separate termination proofs, and target termination is reproved rather than automatically transported. No total correctness of the approximation algorithms is established by their Hoare triples. Definition3 requires pre/postcondition meaning equivalence on source stores and target stacks related by the chosen bijective variable mapping. Compiling both assertions toFalse could yield a valid target Hoare triple without preserving intended meaning. CC requires specification soundness; Tree certificate validity alone does not supply it. Users manually translate a valid source implication database and prove corresponding target implications. These finite assertions can be preserved even if the whole compiler is incorrect. Automatic generation of these obligations via weakest preconditions is proposed but not implemented. CC needs structural equations for assignment/substitution, skip, sequence, if and while, plus source well-formedness and stack-preserving compiled expressions/functions. Thus arbitrary semantics-preserving control-flow transformations do not automatically qualify. Completeness language is conditional on the stated proof obligations and supported structure. Stack expressions in assignments and branch/loop tests must preserve the stack. Function-call effects/arity/stack shape require proofs. Source functions are mutation-free outside locals and immutable parameters, while target calls can access the whole stack. Definition1 constrains mapped variables/parameters but leaves extra stack suffix unconstrained. CC trust includes Coq kernel, mechanized semantics/Hoare definitions and two localized UIP axioms for assertion and function-environment types. It does not assume universal UIP. Opaque CC proof terms may retain dependency on source semantics. Tree certificate path constructs stk_valid_tree, whose Coq checking plus valid_tree_can_construct_hl_stk gives a target Hoare proof without UIP. OCaml certificate generation is untrusted for accepted checked certificates. Boolean fallback adds an unverified OCaml checker to the trust base and is not formal correctness evidence. Certificate generation can fail on mutually recursive functions or malformed trees. A boolean fallback for modular stack-purity checks does not repair this certificate limitation. Target specification preservation still needs its own user proof even if a certificate typechecks. Square-root example’s printed formal postcondition is a pair of cross-multiplied natural-number inequalities under preconditionTrue. Interpreting it as rational approximation additionally requires nonzero relevant denominators (b,y,epsilon denominator); these are not in the displayed precondition. The mathematical reading must not silently replace the stated encoded relation.
use_for_goal: Clarifies three evaluation questions for proof/specification agents: is the target proof valid, does the formal specification retain its meaning, and does it state the desired property? Offers a route to preserving partial verified properties across an untrusted compiler, with explicit trust/termination limits. Relevant to verified Rust/Verus build-chain questions by inference; no direct Rust, Verus, distributed-system, TLA+ or LLM experiment.

venue: Logical Methods in Computer Science 18(3), Article 26
what: Introduces Prophecize, which adds history and frozen prophecy variables during CEGAR refinement to target array terms at future time steps. The array abstraction and refinement reduce many quantified, array-valued invariant proofs to quantifier-free, array-free reasoning, implemented in prophic3. The paper proves soundness and no false positives for the refinement, describes weak versus strong array abstraction, unsat-core filtering of axioms, large-value abstraction, and a pre-state-property heuristic. The approach needs only a small number of relevant index instantiations close to a potential violation; prophecy variables average 1.2 (median 1) on solved quantified cases.
