title: Efficient Reachability Analysis of Büchi Pushdown Systems for Hardware/Software Co-verification
kind: reachability reduction algorithm and driver co-verification study
what: Proves a static partial-order reduction preserving reachability when combining a finite hardware Büchi automaton with labeled pushdown software, implements it in CoVer, and checks two original Windows C drivers against manually written device models. §3 defines enabledness, indistinguishability, independence and commutativity for hardware/software transitions. §4 converts the product into a standard pushdown system; its SensitiveSet retains the initial software head and heads reached after dependent transitions. Algorithm 1 removes asynchronous diagonal transitions and allows hardware-only steps only at sensitive heads, while retaining synchronous transitions and software steps. Theorem 1 proves reachability preservation by moving a removed independent hardware step backward to the last sensitive point; the reverse direction follows from transition-set inclusion. §4 analyzes reduction size and warns that a giant symbolic transition rule defeats reduction. §5 translates this to synchronization points after register access and where interrupt effects matter. modelC describes bounded-register, static-memory hardware transactions; CoVer instruments original driver C with hardware execution loops at those points, then uses SLAM abstraction/refinement and SLIC safety rules. §6 reports four PIO-24 and three Ethernet bugs, with examples of inconsistent global I/O status, interrupt storms and a successful-return flag despite device initialization failure.
numbers: PIO-24 driver 1724 lines/model 1232 lines; Ethernet 14406 lines/model 3518 lines
7 properties proved and 7 previously undiscovered bugs reported across 14 selected checks
PIO-24 InvalidRead 589.4s/132MB without vs 91.3s/66MB with reduction
PIO-24 IsrCallDpc timeout vs 700.5s/218MB
Ethernet DoubleRUC spaceout vs 1797.3s/231MB; ProperReset timeout vs 86.9s/71MB
Ethernet DevD0Entry 1328.3s/758MB vs 367.1s/182MB
assumptions_limits: Reachability/safety properties only; Büchi acceptance is unused and nondeterministic unbounded delay loops do not establish liveness. Hardware is a manually specified transaction-level model derived from interface documents, not verified RTL. Transactions are atomic to software and terminating; ISRs are atomic relative to lower-priority routines, with interrupts suppressed while one ISR runs. Driver statements are assumed preprocessed to be atomic from hardware’s view. Hardware integers are bounded and its global state has no dynamic allocation. Correct dependency/synchronization-point identification and faithful device/interface/harness models are required. Original driver code is analyzed, but claims are conditional on these abstractions and SLAM/tool correctness. Two sample drivers and selected rules do not establish complete driver correctness.
use_for_goal: Transfers directly as a method for reducing asynchronous component interleavings without changing a reachability target, relevant to distributed protocol model checking and evaluating generated models. The explicit atomicity and model-fidelity assumptions are useful when comparing a TLA+ model result with verified Rust/Verus code. It does not provide a distributed protocol implementation proof or evaluate LLM-generated specifications.

title: Cross-Entropy Optimisation of Importance Sampling Parameters for Statistical Model Checking
what: Statistical model checking avoids the exponential growth of states associated with probabilistic model checking by estimating prop- erties from multiple executions of a system and by giving results within confidence bounds. title: CSolve: Verifying C with Liquid Types
what: C memory-safety verifier combining physical heap-layout/pointer types with SMT-checked liquid refinement types. Infers predicates from a user/library qualifier vocabulary, generating subtyping constraints and solving them by predicate-abstraction fixed point. Demonstrates bounded string manipulation and recursive list-field invariants. Separates layout inference from bounds inference, explains modular checking of annotated library functions versus caller-driven inference, and tracks potential aliasing through named location parameters. Recursive list type ties each node’s string capacity to its length field using @offset expressions, allowing unbounded list contents to carry dependent bounds without individual-node enumeration.
assumptions_limits: §2: CIL frontend and SSA simplify mutable locals; physical types checked before unknown refinement variables/subtyping constraints are generated. Fixed-point solver uses Z3. This paper describes the architecture, not a new full soundness proof or independently checked compiler/solver implementation. §§1/2/3: refinement candidates are conjunctions of instantiated logical qualifiers from a supplied file plus standard library. Low annotation burden is the authors’ claim, conditional on adequate qualifiers/specifications; not annotation-free arbitrary invariant discovery. No completeness or success guarantee beyond this hypothesis space is shown. §3: CHECK_TYPE checks a function against its declared augmented type rather than inferring contract solely from uses. extern types are assumed for omitted bodies. A verified caller depends on those contracts and trusted malloc/library models; body omission is not proof of an external implementation. §3 pp.748–749: example relies on a malloc type yielding a non-NULL 12-byte allocated region, with no NULL check in printed caller. This is allocation-success/library-specification scope, not demonstrated handling of ISO C malloc failure. 12-byte structure and offsets 0/4/8 assume illustrated four-byte field/pointer layout; not a portable arbitrary-ABI theorem. §3: SAFE(p)=p>0 ∧ BS(p)≤p<BE(p); SIZE_GE(n) requires BE(p)−p≥n. STRINGPTR combines array shape with this pointer safety, not a proved zero-terminated string predicate. strntolower explicitly bounds accesses using n and short-circuit evaluation, so actual zero termination is not needed for the demonstrated bounds reasoning. §3: default nonaliasing assumption for separate function pointer arguments/returns is checked against bodies, and LOC/INST annotations describe may-alias sets. They permit possible aliases, not Rust-style unique ownership or proof that every member is the identical object. An omitted extern body’s stated alias contract remains assumed. §3: demonstration proves described access/type safety under the source model and contracts. It does not establish CSV parser functional correctness, list acyclicity, termination, leak freedom, deallocation/lifetime correctness or all ISO C undefined-behavior obligations. tolower is modeled as returning arbitrary char; text does not verify its standard argument-domain requirement. §3 p.749: full surrounding input routine omitted. The paper explicitly assumes inferred line/len types at call site before demonstrating propagated constraints. Do not claim an independently shown end-to-end verified input-reading implementation. §2: failed type checking may indicate physical/refinement type inability, with unsolved constraints; this is not a guaranteed concrete bug/counterexample. Multi-file makefile/drop-in GCC compatibility is a tool-interface claim, not proof of support for every GCC extension or arbitrary C program. Entire paper: no benchmark collection, timing, annotation counts, failure rates, hardware, solver-version details or comparative evaluation. No source artifact was run here. Detailed low-level liquid type theory is in cited POPL2010 work, not reproduced or counted as read.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: relevant precursor for automatic Verus/Rust contracts, invariant inference and evaluating LLM-generated specifications: qualifier expressiveness, assumed extern contracts, alias information and dependent field bounds define what a verification success means. Distinguishes memory access safety from intended parser behavior and allocation assumptions. Paper itself contains no distributed algorithm, concurrent proof, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM evaluation.

title: CTL* Model Checking on Infinite Families of Finite-State Labeled Transition Systems
what: Develops compositional CTL* model checking for infinite families of finite-state labeled transition systems represented by hyperedge replacement grammars (HRGs). A Büchi-automaton-based M-equivalence and M-behaviour abstraction recolors grammar nodes while preserving family structure. The method decomposes a generated graph as context J, production rule R, and component graphs K, then summarizes exposed-node traces with finite M-behaviours. Theorem 2 proves M-equivalence is an HGV congruence; Theorem 3 proves sound and complete recoloring. LTL recoloring uses bottom-up and top-down fixed points, and CTL* recursively recolors subformulae; HRG minimization controls growth. The complexity bound is exponential in automaton state count, rule hyperedges, and arity.

title: Verifying That a Compiler Preserves Concurrent Value-Dependent Information-Flow Security
what: Decomposes a two-execution secure-refinement obligation for concurrent value-dependent noninterference (CVDNI) into an ordinary simulation plus checks for consistent execution pace, stopping behavior and a concrete coupling invariant. Uses the principle to verify in Isabelle/HOL a proof-of-concept compiler from a locking While language to generic RISC-style assembly. Section 2 defines low-equivalence modulo access modes, memory-dependent classifications, per-thread bisimulation and closure under permitted interference. Secure refinement preserves all shared memory, not only low observations. Section 3 introduces a pacing function and proves the decomposition sound in Theorem 9. Section 4 reduces one hand-written refinement proof from about 3.6 kLOC to 2 kLOC. Section 5 implements the wr-compiler with a register-expression map and an assumption record; locks identify variables and classification-control variables that remain stable, enabling redundant-load removal while rejecting unsafe expressions and inconsistent mode changes. A refinement relation, 0/1-step pacing and same-program/same-PC coupling invariant establish CVDNI preservation for non-High-branching source bisimulations. Theorem 17 connects successful compilation and consistent initial states to that relation. Section 6 executes compilation on both threads of a desktop-compositor model and composes their security results.
numbers: proof comparison: ~3.6k → ~2k proof lines, 44% reduction
example: 9 source commands → 16 concrete commands
wr-compiler ~7k lines
CDDC verification + compilation ~1.6k proof-script lines
2 CDDC threads, ~150 While lines → ~250 RISC instructions
assumptions_limits: Other threads must obey the synchronization discipline and satisfy their own security obligations. Source and target hide program locations/code/registers from other threads and the attacker. Shared memory is modeled as a finite variable set with total maps and deterministic per-thread steps; weak-memory effects are not considered. Microarchitectural side channels are omitted, with the paper discussing hardware/OS partitioning assumptions. Source/target languages lack pointers and arrays; enough registers are assumed and spilling is future work. The compiler result excludes branching on sensitive values even though the general decomposition handles a hand-written example that branches on a secret. The lock interpretation and classification function must satisfy stated conditions. The case study is a two-thread model, not the later three-thread CDDC model requiring shared-data invariants.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to compositional verification of concurrent systems and to the limits of semantics-preserving compilation as a security argument. The transferable proof structure separates simulation from two-run timing/termination conditions and makes interference assumptions explicit. For Verus/Rust systems this is evidence about proof obligations and trust boundaries, not a theorem about Rust or its compiler.

title: A Behavioral Theory for Distributed Systems with Weak Recovery
what: Introduces DπFR, a distributed pi-calculus with dynamic nodes and links, crash failures, weak recovery, imperfect local knowledge, and incarnation numbers; defines reduction and labelled-transition semantics and proves weak bisimilarity fully abstracts weak barbed congruence. The calculus models recovery by restarting a location with an arbitrary process set and a higher incarnation number, while local views may be stale. Network state explicitly tracks alive/dead incarnation, links, and per-node beliefs; spawn succeeds only when links and incarnation beliefs align. The authors prove preservation of closed well-formed systems, define weak barbs and an LTS including external network actions, and prove Theorem 4.11 (weak barbed congruence iff weak bisimilarity). Case analyses show the ideal server servD is bisimilar to a fault-masking recovered server servDFR, whereas stale-view variants are distinguishable. Docker/Erlang experiments reproduce a rapid unlink/kill/recreate/relink sequence where a spawn targets an old incarnation and fails, matching the calculus trace.

title: Towards the verification of a generic interlocking logic: Dafny meets parameterized model checking
what: Encodes a generic railway interlocking logic as modular Dafny classes and combines template-style contracts with an SMT-based parameterized model checker to infer inductive invariants over arbitrary station configurations. title: Verifying the DaisyNFS concurrent and crash-safe file system with sequential reasoning
what: DaisyNFS is a Go NFS server with sequential Dafny-verified file-system methods on the Coq/Perennial-verified GoTxn transaction system. A simulation-transfer theorem converts sequential operation refinement plus safe transaction use into concurrent crash-safe trace refinement. GoTxn extends GoJournal with two-phase locking and an allocator; each visible NFS operation runs in one transaction; space reclamation uses separate transactions that are logical no-ops. Evaluation measures throughput/scaling, proof sizes, development changes and trusted-code/specification bugs found by testing. Reconstructs the four theorem/lemma roles, trusted Dafny/Coq correspondence and safe-use check, local two-phase-locking footprint invariant, nondeterministic allocator validation, rename retries and zero/free checks. Saves full API scope, proof/LOC, eleven bug and four change-effort entries, benchmark baselines and visual estimates. Distinguishes modeled network-trace correctness from wire code/spec intent, crash safety from liveness, and final LOC ratios from controlled productivity evidence.

unverified NFS wrapper is 1,144 lines (Figure 12, PDF p.12)
assumptions_limits: §§3–4.2: The top-level theorem is network-request/response trace inclusion for a modeled server loop, not verification of every byte in the daisy-nfsd binary. Unverified Go dispatch must parse/decode correctly, call the correct method and encode results; GetRequest/SendReply are abstract I/O events. Each request executes in its own goroutine. Dafny-generated Go methods link with directly written GoTxn verified through Goose/Perennial in Coq. §§4.2,9.3: Disk reads/writes of 4KB blocks are assumed atomic; written data must persist without corruption. Initial implementation/spec disks are all zero and same size; initialize on an empty disk and run recovery after every boot. Crashes may recur and erase memory. This theorem does not cover malicious disk corruption or executions violating the assumed language/disk model. §4.1: Formal NFS state is inode→regular-byte-file/directory map plus attributes; directory names are bytes and clients resolve paths. The model is links, not an enforced directory tree. Out-of-space failures and any chosen current timestamp are nondeterministic. All specified errors leave state unchanged, which authors state is stronger than RFC 1813. Proving this model does not prove it captures the intended RFC. §4.1 Figure 6: Verified file/directory operations are GETATTR,SETATTR,READ,WRITE,CREATE,REMOVE,MKDIR,RENAME,LOOKUP,READDIR; NULL/COMMIT are verified trivial operations. READLINK,SYMLINK,LINK,MKNOD,READDIRPLUS,ACCESS are unsupported. FSINFO/PATHCONF return implemented constants without specification; FSSTAT has no meaningful specification. No NFS unstable writes or paginated READDIR support is supplied. §5.1: Sequential refinement requires an abstraction relation preserved by every operation Hoare triple, initial-state relation and boundary crash simulation. Mid-operation crash/concurrency reasoning is delegated to transaction correctness. Simulation transfer applies to arbitrary spec programs only if each operation body is both sequentially correct and safe, then wrapped atomically and linked to GoTxn. §§5.1–5.2,9.3: Safe transactions cannot observe/mutate outside shared state through arbitrary global heap access; otherwise replaying the body at commit can change behavior. Two trusted composition assumptions remain: Dafny encoding/transaction semantics correctly imply Coq sequential refinement; every Dafny body satisfies safe. Authors use a simple syntactic mutable-state check rather than a verified cross-language compiler/translation theorem. §§6.1–6.2: Each read/write acquires the corresponding object lock and retains it until commit/abort; disjoint transactions can prepare in parallel and commit batching comes from GoJournal. The linearization point is commit. Abort discards buffered writes. The proof tracks initial footprint J and buffered J′; every accessed address remains locked, and replay from any state agreeing with J on that footprint can reproduce the same partial execution. §§3.2,6.2: Allocator calls are concurrent but do not keep locks until transaction end, so allocation is not transactional atomicity. Its deliberately weak spec can return any value, not necessarily currently free. File system validates allocation candidates against durable bitmap through transaction reads, and updates both volatile allocator and persistent bits on free. This validation preserves safety while neither successful allocation nor progress is guaranteed. §§1,3.2,7.1.1: No liveness or transaction deadlock-freedom proof. GoTxn imposes no global lock order or dynamic deadlock detection. File-system code orders inodes numerically and retries RENAME with discovered inode hints; this described strategy is not a mechanized eventual-completion guarantee. §§3.1,7.1.2: Underlying write-ahead log is 513 blocks; transaction update limit is 511 blocks. Large file operations must stay within limits. Separate ZeroFreeSpace transactions may stop early and are proved to have no visible file-system effect. Their general specification permits arbitrary writes to unused space; the strong verified zero-check is what prevents stale data becoming visible when extending a file. §§7.2–8,9.3: Efficient mutable byte slices and integer-to-byte primitives use 558 lines of trusted Dafny interface specification backed by Go, tested rather than proved. Serialized metadata is updated in place; machine uint64 arithmetic requires bounds/overflow proofs. Reader qualification: Dafny/Coq/Perennial and language/compiler/runtime correctness are toolchain assumptions; this paper does not establish an end-to-end compiler theorem. §8 Figure 12: File-system proof 6787 LOC over 4051 implementation LOC gives about 1.68×, rounded in prose to 2×. Transaction extension alone is 10000/250=40×; reader inference: the prose 20× is consistent with including reused GoJournal 39000/1669≈23×, rather than the extension row alone. LOC ratios are final artifact measures, not proof effort per unit of equally difficult functionality. §§9.1–9.2: Main comparison uses Linux NFS/ext4 data=journal for synchronous durable RPCs; data=ordered log bypass is a weaker-crash-guarantee performance alternative. Both use Linux NFS client. No unstable writes in DaisyNFS. Plot values not numerically printed are saved as approximate visual estimates, and graph claims do not imply equal functionality, production robustness or every workload speed. §9.1: Measurements use Linux 5.15, Go 1.18.1, EC2 i3.metal 72 cores/512GB/local 1.9TB NVMe, restricted to one 36-core socket with turbo/sleep states disabled. Coefficient of variation is reported below 5%; exact repetitions and confidence intervals are not stated. In-memory smallfile parity is prose-only and not graphed. §9.3: fsstress, fsx-linux, Linux/macOS use and all supported two-operation CrashMonkey tests are empirical checks, not exhaustive RFC or crash proof. CrashMonkey found no bugs within that bounded supported suite. Independent collaborator Robert Morris used a wider-range NFS-specific tool; methodology omitted for space. Eleven reported trust/spec bugs show the theorem alone does not validate specification intent or callers. §9.4: One author developed/verified the initial runnable prototype over three months. Four later changes report days and combined implementation/proof LOC, without controlled comparison or independent participant study. No Verus/Rust implementation, TLA+ tool experiment or LLM-agent proof/specification experiment is reported; artifacts/external thesis proofs were not executed.
use_for_goal: Concrete method for isolating crash/concurrency proof obligations behind a transaction refinement interface and using sequential automation above it. Provides useful specification-agent evaluation cases: unsafe caller assumptions, missing rename constraints, weak allocator contracts with validation, trusted cross-tool boundaries and bounded testing after proof. Network-visible trace refinement relates directly to distributed service correctness, although this is one-server storage rather than consensus; no Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment.

title: SoS contract verification using statistical model checking
what: Presents the DANSE toolchain for statistical model checking of heterogeneous systems of systems. UPDM/SysML models are extended with stochastic attributes and GCSL contracts; contracts translate to bounded temporal logic for PLASMA, while DESYRE simulates heterogeneous components through FMI. The tool estimates contract satisfaction to support architectural tradeoffs. The paper specifies random-variable stereotypes (uniform, normal, custom) whose String parameters can depend on model state, and GCSL as OCL plus SPEEDS contract patterns with quantification over component collections. PLASMA compiles model/property programs to bytecode and uses Monte Carlo, Chernoff-Hoeffding error-bounded estimation, or sequential ratio hypothesis testing; it stores only bounded trace fragments. DESYRE supplies hierarchical component simulation, fault injection, tracing, monitor synthesis, and FMI model exchange. The authors discuss projection of dynamic SoS state and why open systems with changing variables require future quantifier/search support.
numbers: three SMC analysis techniques: Monte Carlo, Chernoff-Hoeffding, SPRT
PLASMA bounded temporal logic
UPDM/SysML + GCSL + DESYRE/FMI integration
assumptions_limits: The approach deliberately limits itself to performance and non-critical structural/temporal constraints so statistical inference remains scalable; SMC estimates probabilities rather than exhaustively proving properties. GCSL only handles a subset of OCL and cannot specify interactions between anonymous components without added quantification. PLASMA's current focus is discrete time and bounded temporal logic. Closed systems are easiest; dynamic open systems are acknowledged as unresolved engineering work. The paper describes architecture and integration, not a quantitative benchmark or industrial case study.

title: Shield Decentralization for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
what: Defines decentralized multi-agent shielding and decomposes a centralized DFA shield into per-agent shields that require no communication while preserving safety. The paper identifies two requirements for communication-free shields: Cartesian safe action sets so any combination of local choices is safe, and unambiguous local state transitions inferable from each agent’s label and action. Algorithm 1 starts from one safe joint action, greedily adds individual actions only when the induced Cartesian set is safe and next-state mapping remains unambiguous; Algorithms 2–3 compile these sets into transient and interface-compatible individual shields. Theorem 1 proves safety preservation for environments with all actions enabled. If the input shield is Cartesian and unambiguous, the result is maximally permissive; otherwise it is at least the trivial one-action solution. Gridworld experiments retain 22.07 of 23.30 average safe joint actions, and Q-learning obtains zero violations; a momentum particle task shows zero violations even under partial observability.

State explosion is severe (71,130 gridworld and 170,348 particle shield states before reduction); asymmetric observations may lack a shared label set. Evaluation is simulated tabular Q-learning/DQN, not physical systems.

title: Decompose, Structure, and Repair: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Autoformalization via Operator Trees
what: Presents DSR, a statement-autoformalization pipeline: Gemini 3.0-Pro decomposes informal mathematics into conditions and conclusion, a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct formalizer produces Lean components and operator trees, and Qwen3-Max repairs compiler-localized subtrees before a mandatory whole-statement semantic review. Introduces PRIME, 156 manually formalized textbook statements with informal proofs. Reports highest LeanScorer consistency scores among main Table 2 methods (84.00/79.51/67.95% on ProverBench/ProofNet/PRIME), while syntax scores and supplementary FATE results are more mixed. This evaluates statements ending in admitted proofs, not completed verified theorem proofs. Operator trees are labeled ordered scope trees derived with ASSESS/Lean Language Server, adapted to component granularity with parentheses retained. Training constructs 283,958 NL-component/Lean-component/tree triples from 120,627 NuminaMath-LEAN+ATLAS-Synthetic statements, using Qwen3-Max backtranslation. It filters extreme tree complexity, retains 281,209 examples in simple/moderate/complex tiers, and applies four one-epoch LoRA phases with replay. Assembly prioritizes tree reconstruction and falls back to linear components for malformed trees. Repair maps compiler row/column to a tree node, expands bottom-up from parent subtrees through component and full statement, with one pass per repair attempt. Local prompts omit informal text; component prompts see the informal component; the final whole-statement prompt restores full informal context and checks semantics even when compilation succeeds.
assumptions_limits: Syntax Check (SC) is Lean 4 v4.15.0 compilability. Outputs intentionally end in by sorry; passing SC establishes a well-formed admitted statement, not its truth, consistency of premises, semantic correspondence or a proved theorem. Consistency Check (CC) is LeanScorer using DeepSeek-V3.2 at threshold 0.6, not a kernel certificate of NL/Lean equivalence. The framework uses larger external models: Gemini 3.0-Pro for decomposition, Qwen3-Max for backtranslation and repair, and DeepSeek-V3.2 for evaluation. Calling the system 7B describes only its trained formalizer. No all-components fixed-parameter comparison follows from the smaller formalizer. Decomposition may infer missing domains or assumptions incorrectly; the source explicitly acknowledges error propagation. A 90-item manual sample reports 95.56% decomposition accuracy for Gemini versus 87.78% Qwen3-Max, not universal correctness. The final semantic check is another LLM repair call and supplies no formal semantic guarantee. PRIME covers 156 textbook theorems, not distributed-system specifications. Expert formal statements and informal proofs are supplied, but no full formal proofs or independent statement-quality audit is reported here. Textbook/domain selection and judge limitations constrain generalization. Appendix B.1 says PRIME Lean references were private/manual and shares only 4 conceptual overlaps with FATE-M. Domain separation and new reference strings do not exclude semantic overlap, textbook NL pretraining exposure, reuse of library facts or alternative formalizations; no exhaustive model-training-data audit is supplied. The stated four-call budget measures calls, not tokens, dollars or equal model compute. Calls differ across decomposition, component generation and local/global repair; exact component batching/counting and strict per-problem truncation are insufficiently specified. §4.2 says four total calls, but §4.4.2 says four refinements following initial generation. No seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests accompany the small main CC margins. On PRIME the best external main baseline is66.67% versus 67.95% DSR, roughly two of 156 items. Benchmark-level differences do not isolate structural complexity as the cause. Tree construction details are delegated to ASSESS; source lacks full LoRA rank/alpha, hardware, decoding and complexity-tier threshold/combination details. Table 1 specifies one epoch per phase, batch 128/128/128/64, learning rates 2e−4/1e−4/5e−5/1e−5 and replay ratios, but not every reproducibility choice. All results are author-reported. No model, benchmark repository, LeanScorer, compilation trace or proof artifact was rerun by this reader.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to agents writing formal specifications: decompose conditions/goals, retain a structured statement tree, localize verifier feedback, and recheck whole-statement intent after syntactic repairs. Its important evaluation boundary is SC versus LLM-assessed CC, with admitted outputs and examples that alter assumptions. Applying these ideas to Verus/Rust contracts or TLA+ protocol specifications is a reader hypothesis; no distributed-system, verified-Rust or proof-completion evaluation is performed.

title: Dependently Sorted Theorem Proving for Mathematical Foundations
what: DiaToM is a proof-of-concept LCF-style SML prover for classical first-order logic with term-dependent sorts, formula-schema variables and a configurable equality/specification policy. Authors encode ETCS and SEAR and demonstrate proof-producing bounded comprehension translation, quotients and group homomorphisms, natural numbers/integers/lists/co-lists, a simulation-preservation characterization of modal formulas, and a set receiving injections from every finite powerset iterate of any given set. The body explains explicit context tracking for possibly empty dependent sorts, the danger of evaluating arbitrary relations as functions, specification unique up to a chosen equivalence, and proof-producing conversion from external bounded formulas to categorical internal logic. Quotient elimination requires a nonempty witness; co-list heads use option values because carriers may be empty. Concrete modal quantification and powerset-collection statements show what the chosen foundation adds, while a 2,443-line kernel and elementary SML infrastructure give qualitative implementation evidence.
assumptions_limits: Classical first-order ambient logic; sorts s(t0,…,tn) depend on terms of earlier sorts, with each term storing its unique sort. Formula variables encode axiom schemas by instantiation, not ordinary higher-order quantified predicates. Only foundation-approved sorts support equality: no primitive object equality in ETCS or set equality in SEAR. Heterogeneous equality between differently sorted members is not expressible. Theorem Γ,A⊢φ retains all needed variables in Γ, including dependency information, so possibly empty sorts are not silently inhabited. Universal specialization adds free variables of its witness; generalization checks assumptions, sort dependencies and schema-sort lists. Substitution/matching must preserve well-formed dependent sorts; equality transport is deliberately restricted rather than a full dependent type theory. New function symbols require nonemptiness of output sorts plus unique existence modulo an equivalence with reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity proofs. Which equivalences are permitted is a foundational choice. Allowing the universal true relation imports choice. A proof-of-concept LCF architecture is reported; neither kernel implementation correctness nor consistency of newly added axioms is independently established in this paper. Semantic explanation erases sort dependencies into ordinary sorted FOL, adding domain/codomain projection functions and guarded function-symbol axioms. Quantifiers and theorem contexts gain guards. Conservative elimination of formula variables and proof-theory mechanization are reported as separate work not described here; validity of rules is sketched with universal generalization. No completeness theorem, detailed full soundness proof or metatheory artifact evaluation is supplied in this article. ETCS uses object/arrow sorts, choice and bounded internal comprehension; SEAR uses set/member/relation sorts, unrestricted formula-schema comprehension and collection, without choice as a base axiom. A new function subsort ensures Eval only accepts relations already represented as total single-valued functions. The authors call this extension conservative and cite Shulman’s personal agreement; no independent metatheory checked here. SEAR plus choice and restriction to bounded comprehension is compared in strength to ETCS. The unmodified foundations are not ordered by this sentence alone because their choice assumptions differ. The common constructions are shown in SEAR after §4; the text says ETCS analogues work except the all-model modal result and large-set construction, but does not print duplicate developments. Internalization accepts bounded formulas with appropriate element arguments and registered external/internal symbol correspondences. User-defined predicates require manually supplied correspondence theorems. It constructs a predicate arrow and a correctness theorem by derived rules, not an unchecked syntax translation or unrestricted comprehension axiom for ETCS. Quotient construction uses full equivalence relations; partial equivalences first restrict their domain. Defining a total left inverse requires a default point of the source. Empty quotient statements are handled through explicit hypotheses, not HOL’s built-in type nonemptiness. Card of an infinite subset is defined as zero, so Card(s)=0 alone does not characterize the empty subset. Modal theorem is PUS(φ) iff φ is equivalent over all set-carrier Kripke models to a positive existential formula. Quantification over sets supplies what ordinary HOL type variables cannot quantify over directly. The comparison concerns that direct unbounded all-carriers statement, not a claim that HOL cannot encode modal syntax, fixed-carrier results, selected universes or extensions with type quantification. Related work explicitly discusses extended HOL systems. Large-set statement is ∀A ∃P ∀n∈N ∃i:Pow^n(A)→P. Inj(i). It gives a common receiving set, not necessarily the least such set, a literal union of all iterates, or a completed Beth-cardinal development. Selection up to bijection and collection are essential. Minimality/replacement/Beth-cardinal work is future work. Abstract’s V_(ω+ω) comparison is a foundational expressiveness claim under its standard HOL interpretation, not a demonstrated impossibility for every HOL encoding. Printed formulas have local notation defects: §2.3.2’s variable-sort guard uses t_n under index i where t_i is intended; its concluding ∀ step is called elimination instead of introduction. Table1’s first three connective rows omit explicit equality-to-⊤ on their left sides. §8 uses unbound A instead of V in model parameters and f0 instead of φ0 in the final existential. §9’s successor construction writes i(xs) for xs∈Pow(X) although declared i:Pow(B)→Pow(X); intended argument is in Pow(B). These are source display issues, not established artifact errors. Further printed typing slips: §3’s respectful-isomorphism equations have f∘g=Id(B),g∘f=Id(B′) although f:B→B′ and g:B′→B, so identity objects are interchanged. §6 says qhom(N)∈ghom(g,qgrp(g)), where qgrp takes N not g. §5’s product-quotient paragraph labels (a,b)∈Q1×Q2 while they are elements of A×B in its membership equation. Correct intended typings are used for explanation; implementation not inspected. No runtime benchmarks, proof-time comparisons, memory results, automation success rates, user study, distributed protocol verification, Verus/Rust/TLA+ model or LLM agent evaluation. Implementation line counts are reported measurements of source size, not performance evidence. Claims of efficient checking and convenient rewriting are qualitative.
use_for_goal: Indirect foundations/tool-design relevance: dependent specifications and explicit inhabitedness can prevent malformed proof goals, while LCF derived rules can turn automatic model transformations into checked theorems. For proof-writing agents, useful obligations are empty-domain witnesses, allowed equality, choice assumptions, correspondence theorems and direct-statement expressiveness. Mathematical induction/coinduction and modal simulation examples could inform specification methodology; no distributed-system correctness result or direct Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM evaluation.

title: Deriving Semantic Checkers from Tests to Detect Silent Failures in Production Distributed Systems
what: T2C transforms existing distributed-system tests into runtime semantic checkers. It slices assertions into parameterized functions, obtains symbolic triggering histories and constraints from instrumented test execution, mutates these histories, then filters candidates by compilation, JVM verification, self-validation and cross-validation. A production monitor matches traces and invokes checkers. The paper measures checker generation, detection after known failures are triggered, false alarms and performance; it does not prove transformation or checker soundness. Records exact extraction/precondition/mutation mechanisms, observational filtering and unsoundness, four validation levels, trace matching and distributed adapters, all study and generation counts, all twenty failure outcomes/times and issue identities, manual integration effort, false alarm denominators/counts, full cost tables, missed cases and newly added HB2 test, and a distinct newly reported ZooKeeper defect.
assumptions_limits: §§2–3,8: Existing assertions encode useful intended semantics, and test-derived checks generalize beyond their original inputs/configurations. This is an explicit empirical assumption, not established for every test. The study randomly samples 35 tests per system, 210 total; subsequent percentages use only 183 assertion-bearing tests. Equal per-system sampling does not estimate the pooled distribution of all tests by test-count weight. §4.1: Backward data/control slicing preserves relevant branches, explicit aliases, local computations and assertion dependencies. It stops at operations classified as side-effecting by purity analysis plus manually supplied exclusions. No soundness guarantee; missed effects can survive. Section 4.1 says validation exposes missed operations, whereas §8 expressly denies a full guarantee of freedom from side effects. No formal refinement between a test and generated checker is established. §§4.2–4.3: Trigger preconditions are observed server-side call sequences before assertions, excluding operations performed by the checker itself. They are not Hoare-logic weakest preconditions. Analysis depends on chosen instrumentation, recorded execution, API wrappers and manual parsing/adapters. Unobserved paths and system configurations may affect applicability. Enum arguments remain concrete by default. §4.2.2: Equality of observed constants yields shared symbols; accidental equality can over-constrain and suppress checker activation. Simple less-than/contains constraints supported, arbitrary semantic relationships not inferred. Missing complex constraints or broad mutation can over-generalize and cause false alarms. Reduce/insert-wildcard/duplicate/reorder mutations are bounded enumeration; bounds, completeness and global coverage are not established. §4.4: The paper calls 672 outputs verified, meaning they passed empirical/syntactic filters: compilation, JVM sanity checks, rerunning source tests with the checker, then other passing-test workloads. Neither JVM verification nor passing tests proves semantic validity, absence of false positives, complete detection or freedom from side effects. Cross-validation assumes passing-test executions are suitable nonfailure examples; unexpected alerts could also expose real defects, a reader inference not systematically studied here. §5: Circular-buffer trace expiry bounds memory but can discard needed history; precise buffer capacity and complete-coverage guarantee are not given. Reversed precondition trie matches current trace suffix. Configuration requirements checked at startup, with no general claim of adaptation to later configuration changes. Instrumentation, runtime matcher, target methods queried, assertions, adapters, Java/Soot/Javassist and trace transport are trusted operational components. §5: Multiple clients may collectively supply a trigger sequence; cluster mode forwards traces and invokes assertions on respective nodes via RPC. No theorem establishing causal ordering, globally consistent observation, race-free semantic checking across arbitrary interleavings or distributed snapshot correctness. The runtime architecture avoids worker/evaluator buffer races according to authors; that claim is narrower than distributed checker soundness. Special concurrency properties still need carefully designed checks. §§6–7: Implementation is Java only; C/C++ port through LLVM is proposed, not evaluated. Setup includes core classes, about six unsafe operations and about three utility-adapter classes per system, beyond 42-line average configuration. HBase integration one person-week. Claims of little manual effort concern this measured support, not zero domain knowledge. §7.2: Tests selected by system-test package groups, excluding low-level data structure tests and assertion-free performance/stress tests. Target-test denominator 2172, generated functions for 2019, healthy 1933 and final 672. Final outputs cover available test semantics only. Section 4.1 describes one checker per assertion while §7.2 reports 4.3 assertions per checker; paper does not reconcile granularity, so both statements retained. §7.3: Benchmark construction starts with keyword-filtered issues, then 56 randomly inspected, 24 qualifying silent failures and 20 reproducible cases; four lack reproduction information. Reported 15/20 detection is conditional on failures already triggered, not a bug-triggering success rate or representative prevalence estimate. Reproduction takes about one week per case. Generation excludes tests reproducing benchmark failures, but baseline event checkers use historical failure examples; no universal equivalence of training information is claimed. §7.3: Missed five cases include absent semantic coverage and poor/non-generalizable assertions. HB2 only becomes detected after authors add a new test; this does not change original 15/20 result. New ZooKeeper 3.9.2 bug is a separate fault-injection finding, not an additional benchmark hit. Source calls version latest at publication; no current-version claim. §7.4: False alarm ratios use checker invocations in failure-free scenarios over 30 minutes, with Jepsen network faults every 10s. They are not alarms per hour or precision among alerts, and do not estimate arbitrary production workloads. 56% average checker activation leaves many checkers unexercised. No repetitions, confidence intervals or broad deployment duration reported. No noticeable harmful checker effects observed is empirical, not a safety theorem. §7.5: Four benchmark workloads give throughput losses 1.4/9.1/3.8/1.5%, mean 3.95% rounded 4.0. Low activation contributes to low overhead and also limits exercised semantics. No universal cost bound or worst-case under high checker activation. CPU percentages sum across cores; increases must not be read as fractions of a single total CPU. Offline build/validation take hours despite slicing taking minutes. Tables1–2: Same-version study/generation test counts differ (ZooKeeper 434 vs428, Cassandra 4118 vs3283, HDFS 3265 vs4304), without reconciliation. Table1 prints CephFS 1.11.0 and Mesos 18.2.0; preserved as printed rather than silently correcting versions. These are source discrepancies/labels, not independently checked software inventories. §8: LLM-assisted analysis, sandboxing and formal verification of generated checkers are future work. Paper evaluates no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-written proof system, and establishes no universal distributed-system correctness theorem.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for obtaining executable semantic checks from distributed-system tests, useful as an independent evaluation route for agent-written specifications and proofs. It illustrates that executable assertions plus inferred triggers require separate validation: a program compiling or passing a JVM verifier does not prove its intended property or side-effect safety. Its controlled failure benchmark, false-alarm denominator and test-age exclusion inform evaluation design. LLM use and formal verification of checkers are future work; no direct Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ results.

title: Design and Verification of the Arm Confidential Compute Architecture
what: Arm CCA isolates Realm VMs from malicious hypervisors using a separate hardware physical-address space and verified RMM/EL3 monitor firmware. VIA verifies an early concurrent C/Arm-assembly prototype through Coq refinement and simulation of an ideal model with explicit declassification. Techniques combine local CPU rely/guarantee with movers, program-specific conditions transferring SC proofs to relaxed Arm memory, and ABI-based accounting for registers hidden by C. Functional tests use an architectural Fast Model; preliminary performance uses modified non-CCA Arm hardware. Records delegation/GPT/GST/PAR semantics and all RMI operations, exact mover/log and RTT uniqueness proof, all six permutation conditions and real reordering bug, detailed ABI/inline-assembly restrictions, six declassification rules and three simulation relations, unverified initialization/crypto/compiler/hardware boundaries, concrete bugs, complete Coq and benchmark tables, workload settings and qualified bar estimates. Preserves 43-versus-45 layer and seven-versus-eight hypercall-register wording differences and distinguishes secure functional model from insecure performance emulation.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: Protects confidentiality/integrity of VM registers and memory against compromised hypervisor/other VMs, memory remapping/aliasing and DMA under GPT enforcement. VM must not itself disclose private data. No availability guarantee; hypervisor can stop scheduling or reclaim memory, causing protected accesses to halt. Physical attacks, DRAM probing/replay/cold boot, side channels and software-error injection are excluded or require separate mitigations. §3: Hardware must correctly implement Realm/NS/Root/Secure PAS checks, GPT, exception/virtualization and DMA checks. Root EL3M may access all PAS; RMM controls Realm VMs at Realm EL2. Firmware verification does not verify hardware or microarchitecture. Paper focuses NS/Realm interactions; detailed Secure-world behavior is omitted. §3: Hypervisor controls all dynamic resources but must delegate zeroed granules before RMM use. GPT is hardware permission state; separate GST is software bookkeeping for granule use. Protected addresses inside PAR map only private Realm Data; outside PAR may deliberately access shared NS/device data. Untrusted I/O payloads are not covered as confidential private memory. §3: Reclaim zeros and unmaps private memory; future access faults/halts. A previously backed protected IPA cannot be remapped without Realm permission. This is integrity against observing unauthorized changes, not durable data availability or prevention of every malicious deallocation. Remote-attestation initialization hashes IPA/data but relies on unverified crypto. §4.1: Global logical event log abstracts interleaved CPUs. Per-CPU environment oracle yields unseen other-CPU events under rely/guarantee conditions, not a prophetic runtime component or unrestricted assumption. Mover proofs justify rearranging queries, then aggregating local events; right/left/none classifications must be established against permitted environment actions. §4.2/§5.2: Relaxed-memory result is relative to VRM extended Promising Arm model and proved permutation conditions. Decomposition separates DRF code from non-DRF parts. Non-DRF conditions must both hold for allowed hardware reorderings and imply SC-equivalent behavior; arbitrary proposed conditions do not automatically establish arbitrary racy programs correct. §4.3: C/assembly accounting assumes AAPCS64-conforming compilation and the stated C integer/pointer calling shape (≤8 parameters, scalar/pointer return). Tracks unknown caller-saved registers conservatively and requires assembly independence from them. It does not verify an optimizing Arm compiler or establish correctness of every possible C ABI/language feature. §4.3 Figure6: Inline assembly translated to logical input/output registers; supports r,Q,m constraints, prohibits explicit GPR names/goto labels, and requires multi-instruction outputs constrained & or + to avoid unintended overlap. Paper prose says final read by set_pr, whereas code and preceding definition use get_pr; record uses code-consistent get_pr. These are concrete supported cases, not unrestricted inline assembly. §4.4/§5.4: Ideal model gives each Realm private memory and each REC exclusive registers, with six explicit declassification rules. Simulation preserves memory/register observations despite allocation control. This intentionally weaker availability-sensitive integrity property differs from standard noninterference; failure to apply a particular standard formulation does not prove that every generalized noninterference formalism is impossible. §5: Proof covers early prototype RMM/EL3M runtime C/assembly, excluding assembly initialization (.1K RMM/.5K EL3M) and external cryptographic library. Simulation assumes correct initial relation at boot. Later production firmware and current CCA architectures are not automatically verified by this historical result. Roughly .2K Coq ideal specification is trusted security policy, not the total trusted computing base: hardware/model, Coq, compiler/ABI, initialization and crypto remain relevant. §1/§5: Introduction says43refinement layers; §5 says45total layers and gives machine-model, spinlock, three EL3M,39RMM, ideal-model breakdown. Preserve this accounting distinction rather than reporting a single count without context. RTT atomicity takes nine layers; REC.Run takes five. §4.4 Table3 versus §5.4: Table specifies seven hypercall GPRs r0–r6 and four RMM-call GPRs r0–r3, plus system/timer/emulation disclosure. §5.4 concluding prose calls them eight hypercall GPRs. This source inconsistency is retained; no inference that all registers are protected from every intended disclosure. §6: Fast Model has RME functional behavior but is not cycle accurate and too slow for full application performance. N1SDP performance port lacks GPT/Realm hardware and cannot enforce security. Two NS contexts mimic world switching; GPT memory writes occur but register control/check costs are absent. Expectations that GPT cost cancels, future interrupts/passthrough improve costs are predictions, not measured results. §6: N1SDP GIC writes make some userspace exits about800ns more expensive; prototype lacks direct virtual interrupt injection. Thus measurements neither establish actual CCA-hardware performance nor a strict lower/upper bound. Modified KVM/QEMU/guest integration demonstrates functionality without proving the full application/device stack. §6.2: Fifty runs report average/best/worst, not confidence intervals. Mostly<8% overhead and18% MongoDB are author prose claims; plot bars are approximate and some ratios (notably Memcached) do not exactly reproduce that prose. Native baseline normalizes lower-is-better cost; source does not give raw per-workload timings/throughput for every bar. §§7–8: Research relevance is concurrent low-level refinement, specification trust, weak-memory proof and evaluation limits. No direct distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation. Originality/first-proof claims are authors’ historical claims, not an independent literature proof. No artifact appendix/repository pointer in saved PDF; scripts and external claims unexecuted.
use_for_goal: Concurrent low-level proof case extending mover patterns with local rely/guarantee, proving racy code under weak-memory conditions, and linking C/assembly confidentiality. Useful for evaluating agent-written proofs: independently stated ideal policy, explicit declassification and trusted boot/tool/compiler boundaries, proof-found bugs, and performance on a non-enforcing platform must stay separate. No direct Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM/distributed-failure result.

title: Learning Semantic Representations to Verify Hardware Designs
what: Introduces Design2Vec, a GNN representation of Verilog RTL control/data-flow graphs that predicts coverage and generates tests from simulation data, targeting scalable industrial hardware verification. Design2Vec embeds RTL token sequences and node attributes with an LSTM/word2vec plus GCN, and adds RTL IPA-GNN propagation for concurrent, non-terminating semantics. A differentiable gradient search over test parameters targets individual cover points. The paper defines cover-point/test data generation, compares semantic GNNs to black-box MLP and random/Vizier baselines, and tests transfer/generalization across IBEX v1, security-enhanced IBEX v2, and Google's TPU.

up to 88 fewer simulator calls for TPU and 40 fewer for IBEX versus random/black-box search

assumptions_limits: The approach learns from simulation labels rather than proving reachability or functional correctness; designs are restricted to synthesizable behavioral RTL and considered graphs without loops. Test parameters define input distributions and coverage is branch-oriented. TPU code/data are proprietary, so only open IBEX designs are reproducible; medians over random seeds are reported without error bars. The authors position the learned abstraction as a proxy and acknowledge it inherits best-effort simulation limits.
use_for_goal: Connects learned program abstractions to verification workflows: useful evidence for where ML-assisted verification can accelerate test exploration while remaining simulation-based and non-proof-producing.

title: Deterministic Client: Enforcing Determinism on Untrusted Machine Code
what: Deterministic Client (DeCl) accepts an adversarial x86-64 or Arm64 binary only when its instructions, control flow and configured sandbox rules establish deterministic execution within that ISA. A trusted native-code verifier replaces trust in a compiler/JIT for this property. It handles undefined instruction results/flags, instruction bundling, deterministic metering and load-address independence, and integrates with Groundhog. Evaluation measures selected SPEC integer benchmarks, payment-contract scalability, startup and Rust zero-knowledge proof-verification code. No machine-checked correctness proof of DeCl is reported. Preserves precise runtime/hardware trust assumptions, ISA differences and undefined-input/flag guards, the full conservative two-pass dataflow algorithm, CPU-fuzzer coverage limit, gas accounting/overcharging and timer observability condition, position-oblivious register/pointer/flag handling, verifier passes and padding treatment. Includes all five tables, fixed-resource/compiler/runtime benchmark qualifications, startup aliasing and cryptography comparisons, portability and hardware bug limits.
assumptions_limits: §2.1: Threat is an adversarial binary, not just output of a benign compiler. Verifier may conservatively reject deterministic programs. Guarantee covers valid microarchitectures within one chosen ISA, not agreement between separately compiled x86 and Arm programs. Hardware must implement accepted ISA correctly; required extensions such as BMI2 restrict deployment. Deterministic runtime call API, no shared-memory multiprocessing and deterministic sandbox initialization are assumed. Runtime API implementation, input state and memory protection remain trusted. §§2.1/2.2: Memory isolation is necessary to prevent reading external nondeterministic data; hardware or software isolation can provide it. Sandbox code cannot be writable and executable by untrusted code. title: Developing Bug-Free Machine Learning Systems With Formal Mathematics
what: Presents Certigrad, an implementation of stochastic computation graphs in Lean, with a reported machine-checkable proof that stochastic backpropagation produces unbiased estimates of the mathematical gradient of expected cost. It demonstrates a workflow in which formal specifications and attempted proofs guide implementation and expose both code errors and missing assumptions. It also reports verified Gaussian integration/reparameterization optimizations and an MNIST variational-autoencoder experiment with performance comparable to TensorFlow. Separates an executable stochastic program from its mathematical expectation semantics using Dist n, built by primitive sampling, deterministic returns and composition. The paper gives expectation and RNG-threading equations for each constructor. The initial all-graphs unbiasedness specification is strengthened with WellFormed, GradsExist, IntegralsExist and CanDiffUnderInts preconditions. A simple single-parameter, nonmemoizing implementation is proved first; a multi-parameter memoizing implementation is then proved equivalent. A heuristic tactic proves model-specific preconditions for the transformed AEVB graph. The verified optimization sequence integrates Gaussian KL terms and replaces parameter-dependent Gaussian sampling with standard-normal sampling followed by scale/shift, preserving the objective while changing the gradient estimator.
assumptions_limits: Correctness is relative to the stated mathematical specification and adopted axioms. The authors assume real numbers, integration and primitive mathematical laws rather than constructing their foundations. They report repairing initially unsound axioms by restoring integrability conditions, but this reading does not independently audit that axiom set. The final displayed scalar theorem requires unique node identifiers and scalar leaves (WellFormed), appropriate differentiability for all relevant stochastic choices (GradsExist), existence of integrals (IntegralsExist), and conditions allowing gradients through integrals (CanDiffUnderInts). The implementation is reported to handle arbitrary tensor shapes and multiple parameters; the displayed specification deliberately simplifies these. Proving the generic algorithm is insufficient for an arbitrary client graph: each graph must meet the preconditions. Some are undecidable in general, so the theorem-proving tactic is heuristic rather than a complete decision procedure. The proof concerns ideal infinite-precision real arithmetic. The authors explicitly say replacing reals with floating-point numbers technically invalidates the specification and may cause numerical instability; no floating-point error bound is established here. The running system trusts optimized Eigen tensor operations and a small C++ wrapper to match the formally reasoned operations, and relies on Lean VM/runtime and primitive pseudo-random sampling. The paper describes corresponding mathematical/procedural distribution interpretations but does not establish a checked correctness theorem for the concrete RNG, Eigen, C++ wrapper or execution platform. Unbiased stochastic gradients do not establish convergence of ADAM, bounded gradient variance, statistical validity, good generalization or model fit. The empirical AEVB training comparison addresses one example, not those general guarantees. The source repeatedly says proving exposes all implementation errors. The supported guarantee is absence of violations of the modeled specification under its assumptions; specification errors, inconsistent axioms and implementation layers outside the model remain material, as the paper itself discusses. Claims of reduced cognitive burden and finding all bugs early are the authors’ development experience, not a controlled developer study or complete empirical bug census. The paper reports increased overall workload but supplies no person-hour or proof-size measurements.
use_for_goal: Relevant precedent for proof agents implementing verified systems: separate algorithm specifications, mathematical assumptions, implementation refinement and client preconditions, and let proof obligations guide construction and debugging. It supplies a concrete trust-boundary lesson for Verus/Rust/TLA+ evaluations: a checked mathematical algorithm can still run through unverified numerical libraries and runtime layers. Transfer to LLM agents or distributed systems is a reader inference; neither is evaluated.

title: Formal Verification of Safety Architectures for Automated Driving
what: Extends differential Floyd–Hoare logic (dFHL) with assume-guarantee Hoare quintuples and interruption/fallback constructs to prove safety envelopes and graceful degradation in automated-driving controllers. The layered simplex combines a goal-aware RSS controller with a collision-avoiding RSS fallback around a black-box advanced controller. The paper gives trace semantics for nondeterministic hybrid programs with continuous physical dynamics and environment variables, defines α↓A interruption, fallback α on β, and a two-way simplex that switches back to α. Hoare quintuples split a global assumption from a guarantee; strong and weak as-long-as/fallback rules are proved sound, and an interruption-extension discharges the weak case when an assumption fails. In the pull-over model, GA-RSS can stop at the shoulder under constant-speed POV assumptions, while CA-RSS preserves collision avoidance if POV speeds change. Margined switching conditions, counters, or timers prevent infinite controller oscillation. Simulations with a sampling-based planner answer safety, strong goal, and best-effort goal questions, including POV2 braking that interrupts and later returns control to GA-RSS.

assumptions_limits: Proofs are conditional on explicit physical/environment assumptions (RSS distance, bounded accelerations, legal speeds, and no rear-end collision responsibility). Strong goal achievement assumes all POVs keep constant speed; when that assumption fails, the weak guarantee preserves safety but may lose the stopping goal. The advanced controller is modeled as a black box constrained only by the switching contract. Termination of a simplex requires a finite switch counter or timer construction. The case study is one pull-over geometry and a prototype planner, so it does not establish broad automated-driving coverage.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for compositional, assume-guarantee verification of a safety envelope around an unverified controller. The explicit weak/strong guarantees and switching-termination mechanisms are useful analogues for distributed systems that degrade under violated assumptions, while the narrow physical case and conditional assumptions limit generalization.

title: Characterizing Algebraic Invariants by Differential Radical Invariants
what: Characterizes invariant algebraic varieties of polynomial vector fields using a finite chain of successive Lie derivatives of one polynomial. The resulting differential-radical invariant rule is sound and complete for checking invariance over real-closed fields, and generation reduces to maximizing the kernel dimension (equivalently minimizing rank) of a symbolic matrix. Defines the Zariski closure of an ODE orbit as the smallest algebraic overapproximation, proves its soundness and differential-ideal property, and establishes the differential radical characterization theorem: h vanishes on an orbit iff finitely many Lie derivatives vanish initially. Theorem 2 gives a decidable invariant-variety check and a sound/complete proof rule; Theorem 3 says every invariant variety is a differential-radical ideal of one polynomial. Homogenization converts generation to biaffine symbolic linear algebra; Gaussian elimination searches parameter assignments and Proposition 3 gives a sound orbit overapproximation condition. Case studies recover trigonometric identities, airplane collision invariants, and three longitudinal-aircraft energy functions.

Generation is at least NP-hard and PSPACE under stated no-parameter assumptions; de-homogenization may fail for projective candidates. Results target algebraic equalities, not general semialgebraic safety regions; upper bounds on differential-radical order and hybrid-system use remain future work.

title: Diffy: Inductive Reasoning of Array Programs Using Difference Invariants

Distinguishes QN-1 (only loop bounds truncated, with data-dependency repairs) from PN-1 (all N replaced), explains required precondition splitting and cross-program coverage, records conditional peel simplification and failed loop propagation, and retains the strengthen-transfer obligation rather than treating arbitrary quantifier elimination as sufficient. title: Distributed Model Checking on Graphs of Bounded Treedepth
what: Proves distributed decision of every fixed monadic second-order graph formula in a constant number of CONGEST rounds on bounded-treedepth networks. Constructs an elimination tree as a network subgraph, converts it to an ancestor-bag tree decomposition, and distributes finite-state dynamic programming for regular predicates. Decision uses all-nodes-accept semantics: legal iff every node accepts; the final root may be the only rejecting node. This differs from requiring all nodes learn a global Boolean answer. title: Distributional Probabilistic Model Checking
kind: probabilistic model checking method and empirical evaluation
what: Extends probabilistic model checking from expected rewards to full reward distributions for DTMCs and MDPs, supporting variance, quantiles, value-at-risk and CVaR for rewards accumulated until co-safe LTL goals. The paper defines categorical and quantile distribution representations, distributional queries and optimization semantics, and reduces co-safe LTL goals to reachability with a DFA product. Algorithm 1 computes a DTMC distribution by forward propagation while separating non-target BSCCs that yield infinite reward, with a provable per-atom error bound and truncation mass ε. Risk-neutral distributional value iteration (DVI) chooses actions by expected value; risk-sensitive DVI uses the CVaR dual slack variable, a discretized product MDP and a convergence result whose error is O(stride). A PRISM prototype evaluates betting, Deep Sea Treasure, obstacle, UAV and energy models, with risk-sensitive products up to 2.3e6 states and runtime up to 15,051 s; distributions converge toward ground truth as atom counts increase. DTMC forward computation is often faster than DVI on large PRISM benchmarks, but DVI can be faster when Vmax is high.

what: Presents DiVinE 3.0, a parallel/distributed LTL model checker that directly explores closed multithreaded C/C++ through an LLVM bitcode interpreter, supports untimed LTL over Uppaal timed automata, and exposes the CESMI plug-in interface for external model languages. Core reductions include partial-order/path/heap-symmetry methods, disk queues and optional hash compaction. The paper explains how closed programs substitute unsupported I/O with nondeterministic choices and how DiVinE explores all thread interleavings at individual bitcode instructions. It reports LLVM reduction counts for Peterson under compiler optimization, fair-run LTL for DVE, zone-abstraction timed-automata interpretation and deadlock checks, and CESMI modules for DVE, Murϕ and MATLAB Simulink. title: DiVM: Model Checking with LLVM and Graph Memory
what: Presents DiVM, an LLVM-IR virtual machine with graph-organized memory and verification hypercalls, plus DiOS, a verification-oriented OS that supports POSIX-like C/C++ programs in explicit-state and abstraction-driven model checking. The VM represents heap objects as graph nodes linked by pointer edges, tracks pointer/definedness types in shadow memory, uses object-level allocation/free and stable object identifiers, and stores stacks as graph-linked activation frames. A small hypercall interface exposes nondeterministic choice, interrupt points, tracing, shared-object marking and machine control to a virtualized OS. This separation lets the verifier keep a simple initial/successor interface while the OS implements scheduling, threads, syscalls, monitors and faults. The paper explains τ and symmetry reductions, abstraction compatibility, and evaluates DIVINE 4 against DIVINE 3 and ESBMC.

title: Djinnlang: Higher-Level Programming by Unambiguous Specification with an LLM in the Compiler
what: Proposes Djinnlang, a specification-only language whose translator emits Dafny relations and proof/implementation obligations, then uses an LLM to fill implementations and proofs checked by Dafny. Its central unambiguity constraint requires the specification relation to be deterministic, eliminating semantic freedom for the generated implementation; procedures add ordered effects through generated step machines. The paper formalizes unambiguity as pre(x) ∧ q(x,o1) ∧ q(x,o2) ⇒ o1=o2 plus an existence obligation, and distinguishes deterministic funcs, nondeterministic rels, and effectful procs. The translator pins regenerated declarations, scans solutions for Dafny escape hatches, and re-translates the source before verification. Examples show sorting via a permutation relation, string parsing as a preimage, Sudoku and optimal LZ77 specifications, and a step-function compilation of procedures. Bootstrapping djinnc itself required 2,106 obligations and found four genuine specification bugs before synthesis succeeded. Two LLM implementers discharged all benchmark obligations, but generated performance differed by hundreds-fold.

title: DL-PA and DCL-PC: model checking and satisfiability problem are indeed in PSPACE
what: Corrects prior complexity claims and gives a deterministic polynomial-space model-checking procedure for Dynamic Logic of Propositional Assignments and Coalition Logic of Propositional Control and Delegation. The paper exhibits a concrete PEEK-G5 counterexample to the prior EXPTIME-hardness reduction, and explains why an earlier DCL-PC evaluator was alternating rather than nondeterministic. Its DL-PA algorithm represents valuations and iteration counters as k-bit strings, and uses mutually recursive deterministic Boolean procedures REL, MOD, and ITE. Divide-and-conquer evaluates α* by splitting iteration counts, while a well-founded order and induction establish soundness and completeness. Recursive depth is linear in formula/program size and k, yielding polynomial space. Polynomial reductions transfer the upper bound to DCL-PC; QSAT reductions make both logics PSPACE-complete.

title: Don’t Sweat Interaction Trees: Proof-Guided Local Variable Lifting for Interaction Trees
what: Implements semi-automatic local variable lifting for interaction trees in Rocq: replace effectful local-memory reads/writes with typed Rocq values while preserving observational equivalence and leaving global effects uninterpreted. Constructive proofs instantiate an existential simplified program,using Derive and Ltac; equivalence and program arise together. A read-only handler freezes variables satisfying NoWrites; WriteFirst allows dropping bindings dead for a continuation; WriteWithin constrains every local write to a named set and its typing context. A heterogeneous list carries typed surviving variables,with extract_hlist/reconstruct_memory mediating the memory representation. Lemmas1–3 justify these components. Theorem4 combines them for a head and continuation with equivalence modulo discarded bindings;Theorem5 additionally lifts both loop backedges and loop exit. Reconstructing memory from a universally quantified typed list makes subsequent reads reduce without repeatedly proving presence/type. Users choose variable sets and proof tactics; an arbitrary equivalence proof need not produce simpler code.

Integers are unbounded Z,so C overflow behavior is excluded;AutoCorres2 bounded-integer guards removed for displayed comparison. Theorems require NoWrites,WriteFirst,WriteWithin and an initial memory obeying surviving-variable typing context. Final relation allows differences on dropped dead variables;not equality of all memory bindings. Loop rule conservatively requires dropped variables dead at loop continuation as well as each iteration;supporting post-loop reads of overwritten iteration locals is future work. Variable-set inference/liveness analysis and other AutoCorres simplifications are future work. Three small qualitative examples;no measured proof-time,speedup,line-count,industrial scaling or concurrent-system correctness evaluation. Only bump_counter worked in paper;other examples are in uninspected artifact. Authors report Rocq formalization and linked source artifact;reader did not rebuild it. title: Formal Specification and Verification of Dynamic Parametrized Architectures
what: Defines Dynamic Parametrized Architectures (DPAs), where indexed component sets, connections, initial configurations, invariants and reconfiguration transitions are first-order formulas over unbounded index sets. It translates information-flow reachability into array-based transition systems and checks the resulting safety problem with MCMT/Yices. The formal language separates parametrized architecture guards from dynamic formulas, restricts transition syntax so index sets and parameter arrays can be rewritten into array updates, and translates component presence plus taint propagation into an array-based safety system. The paper proves that the translation stays in the array-based fragment and that information-flow witnesses correspond exactly to unsafe traces. A C/GNU-Bison extended-AADL translator and five scalable benchmark families expose transition-count, quantifier and solver-call bottlenecks.

title: Merge-width and First-Order Model Checking
what: Introduces radius-r merge-width via construction sequences that merge vertex parts and resolve default edges/nonedges. It unifies structural graph parameters and proves first-order model checking is fixed-parameter tractable on classes of bounded merge-width when a witnessing construction sequence is supplied. The paper defines construction/merge sequences, radius-r width, and translations from twin-width, degeneracy, bounded expansion, clique-width, generalized coloring numbers, and flip-width. It proves bounded twin-width and bounded expansion imply bounded merge-width, bounded merge-width implies bounded flip-width, and gives almost-bounded results for nowhere-dense classes. The model-checking algorithm maintains local first-order types through merge and resolve operations; distance-FO locality and scatter types yield Theorem 5.4, with O_{σ,q,w}(|V|²m) for a sequence of length m and O_{q,w}(|V|³) for graphs. Closure under first-order interpretations/transductions is proved. Examples and case arguments include bounded-degree/degenerate graphs, planar/minor-excluding classes, ordered structures, graph squares, and the relationship to twin-width and clique-width.

title: DRPBench: Evaluating LLMs in Concurrent Code Comprehension via Fine-Grained Data Race Prediction
what: Introduces DRPBench, a static fine-grained data-race prediction benchmark for concurrent-code comprehension: 1,003 SV-Benchmarks C/C++ programs, 226 racing and 777 race-free, with 557 manually annotated variable/line-level races. Evaluates six LLM families in standard/reasoning/agentic configurations (15 LLM configurations) on a balanced 200-program DRPBench-Lite subset, plus Deagle and UGemCutter. Gemini-3-thinking reaches F1 74.89%; Llama 3 70B reaches 8.80%. Defines a race as a variable and exact conflicting access-line pair, parses JSON predictions as sets, and reports precision/recall/F1. Annotation combines three human annotators, o3-mini, GPT-4o and Deagle, two senior meta-reviewers, and consensus. DRPBench-Lite stratifies 100 racing and 100 race-free programs. Prompts provide definitions of mutexes, semaphores, atomics, condition variables and thread lifecycle. Ablations compare domain-knowledge prompts; tables compare reasoning and OpenHands agentic scaffolds against standard models. Qualitative cases identify shared-variable distraction and synchronization-logic myopia.
assumptions_limits: The corpus is isolated pthread-based C/C++ and assumes sequential consistency; races only under weak memory models are excluded. Ground truth is an expert/LLM-assisted annotation process, not a machine-checked universal oracle. The reported LLM evaluation and error analysis use DRPBench-Lite (100 unique racing plus 100 race-free programs), not all 1,003 programs. The full corpus statistics and 557 race annotations should not be read as the test-set size. A true positive requires exact shared-variable name and exact pair of conflicting line numbers; this strict score measures localization under the supplied race definition, not general concurrent-code correctness, bug severity, or absence-of-race proof. Six base LLMs yield 15 standard/reasoning/agentic configurations; Deagle and UGemCutter are separate symbolic baselines. OpenHands agentic runs are only for Gemini, Claude and DeepSeek, with default decoding/agent configurations; other models lack agentic results. Annotation uses LLM tools (o3-mini and GPT-4o) alongside humans and Deagle, then two expert meta-reviewers; source SV-COMP labels and the paper's manual review are not independently reproduced by reader. The benchmark authors report >500 person-hours. No quantitative uncertainty bars or statistical tests are reported for the main F1 comparisons; no external artifact execution or independent annotation was performed by reader. LLM outputs remain candidates and cannot prove race absence. Appendix says this version covers isolated pthread C/C++ and SC only; real multi-component software, Java/Go, and weak-memory-only races are future scope. Symbolic-tool limitations and timeout/heuristic effects complicate direct superiority comparisons.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM evaluation for concurrent-code comprehension and agentic debugging. Reader inference: use race predictions as triage candidates before a sound analyzer/model checker or human review; high recall with low precision is unsafe as a verdict. The paper does not evaluate Verus, Rust, TLA+, distributed protocols, proof generation, or machine-checked absence of races.
