title: DryVR: Data-Driven Verification and Compositional Reasoning for Automotive Systems.
what: Combines black-box continuous simulators with white-box acyclic timed switching graphs. Learns exponential sensitivity bounds from sampled trajectory pairs, bloats simulations into reachable-state enclosures and refines initial/switching intervals. Provides trace-containment and sequential-composition arguments for extending selected bounded analyses. Reports five safe/three unsafe automotive benchmark configurations and two composition/containment illustrations. Correctness is conditional on learned functions actually being universal discrepancy bounds; sampled validation does not establish that premise. Defines graph/trajectory/hybrid semantics, sample-to-linear-program sensitivity learning, topological enclosure propagation and conditional safety. Separates polynomial sufficient graph simulation from general timed trace inclusion and gives an inductive repeated-composition closure theorem. Complete learning protocol/table/resource details expose the gap between empirical point coverage and universal verification. Reader counterexample refutes the printed generic separator sample bound and identifies formula/pseudocode defects without inferring implementation bugs.
assumptions_limits: Finite modes and a directed acyclic transition graph with nonnegative closed bounded dwell-time intervals. Repeated modes are permitted at different vertices; cycles require bounded unfolding. Thus a graph describes finitely many switches within bounded time, not arbitrary unconstrained switching. Intervals are durations in current mode, not absolute global timestamps. Continuous trajectory sets are deterministic and prefix-closed, with connected compact initial domains and existence over every finite horizon. At a mode switch the next trajectory starts at the preceding final state: no reset map is modeled. Mode-local time constraints support settling requirements measured since last transition. Physical fidelity of the Simulink model and mode/initial/unsafe specification remains assumed. Execution ends with a terminal mode label and no terminal-mode trajectory. It does not analyze arbitrary evolution after arrival at that label. Reachability formula allows i=k although tau_k is absent, so terminal reach needs an endpoint convention; composition prose uses final arrival states. The terminal case and final-state projection are presentation assumptions rather than an inspected implementation semantics. Definition4 assumes perfect simulation values equal true trajectory samples; validated simulations are proposed as an alternative. MATLAB numerical solver use in experiments is not by itself proof of that assumption or a validated enclosure for every inter-sample point. Imported reach-bloating machinery and numerical error treatment were not independently audited. A discrepancy beta must bound all same-mode trajectory-pair distances and vanish as initial states coalesce. GED is norm(x1−x2)*K*exp(gamma*t). Logdistance/time samples give linear inequalities in gamma,lnK; LP minimizes gamma*T+lnK. Identical initial points or zero later distance require limiting/exclusion conventions for logarithms. Neither finite pairs nor sampled times establish the universal continuous-time premise without additional assumptions. Proposition4 prints k>=epsilon^(-1)*ln(delta^(-1)) for any feasible sampled separator. Its proof treats the bad set B of the data-selected separator as fixed. Reader counterexample: Gamma={(y²,y):0<=y<=1}, uniform y, true separator x<=1. With k=2 choose sampled chord a=y1+y2,b=−y1*y2, feasible on both samples. Its error is1−abs(y1−y2). For epsilon=.5,delta=.4,k2 satisfies the printed bound, yet probability(error>.5)=.75>.4. This refutes the stated generic feasible-learner guarantee/proof, not PAC learning generally and not necessarily a separately analyzed specific LP selection. Even a valid distributional PAC bound would constrain probability mass of missed pairs/time points rather than prove every trajectory satisfies beta. Correlated pairs/times, multiple learned modes, refined initial distributions, repeated calls and continuous-time interpolation need separate sampling/union/error arguments; these budgets are absent. Theorem1 explicitly assumes every returned beta is a valid discrepancy, and therefore cannot turn the reported test fraction into universal soundness. PED partitions time adaptively to keep gamma_i<2. Printed local condition uses exp(gamma_i*t) rather than elapsed local time, and displayed chained bound has only one K. Multiplying separate local bounds with K would normally introduce K^i as well as appropriate shifted times; global normalization/K=1 or another derivation is needed. The printed norm expression also has equality instead of subtraction in places. These are presentation/derivation issues; actual code not inspected. GraphReach topologically processes initial enclosures, learns beta per vertex/enclosure, bloats finite simulations and restricts the reach tube to each outgoing dwell interval as a successor initial enclosure. Multiple incoming sets can coexist. All states/times must be enclosed for safe-disjointness. Algorithm1 computes max over outgoing labels even for a terminal vertex, where that set is empty; terminal skipping/zero-time handling is unstated. VerifySafety partitions initial sets and refines initial/switching intervals on ambiguous overlap. Printed line3 calls GraphReach(H) after popping S without setting H.initial=S, although prose clearly intends analysis from S. Line6 types a tuple as a subset of U; a valid unsafe certificate requires an actual witness, or a slice guaranteed to contain a reachable state whose entire enclosure lies inside U; mere nonempty overapproximation overlap is insufficient. Visible line1 is nonempty-worklist inequality; raw extraction drops the slash and is not an actual printed defect. Theorem1 gives conditional SAFE/UNSAFE soundness if every learned beta is a true mode discrepancy; relative completeness is stated with proof following thesis[13], not established for inaccurate learned functions. No machine-checked proof or independently inspected imported proof is supplied. Robust separation/refinement and simulator assumptions matter for termination; table success does not establish a general total decision procedure. Definition2(c)(i) visibly uses (v,u_j) in R, not successor(v_prime,u_j). Along with label preservation this prevents the intended matching of a differently labeled successor. The expected successor-pair repair is reader inference. No implementation comparison was made; simulation/subsequent theorem claims are interpreted with intended successor matching rather than silently accepting the printed relation. Graph simulation checks a sufficient condition for prefix trace containment; not a complete containment procedure. The paper describes polynomial greatest-fixpoint removal and contrasts non-elementary general one-clock timed-language containment. Transferring safety also requires compatible initial sets, trajectory inclusion and interpretation of mode map/unsafe predicates; arbitrary relabeling alone does not preserve an unchanged physical unsafe set. Sequential composition identifies matching unique terminal/initial labels. Theorem2: if the terminal reach after one G cycle is contained in initial Theta, then every finite G^i reach is contained in one-cycle reach. It is an inductive closure result for generated compositions, not every arbitrary mode sequence. A sound enclosing terminal set B must be re-used as initial B and prove its own image subset B; checking unrelated component ranges alone is insufficient for correlated-set containment. Learning experiments use independently sampled initial states for10–20training traces,100–10000time points/trace, then1000test traces and all test pairs/times. Authors report96percent point coverage beyond10training and>99.9percent beyond20. These are empirical fractions of correlated test points across unspecified mode/seed distributions, not universal trajectory coverage or a per-mode confidence guarantee. Full per-mode results/repetitions/error bars are absent. Table1 has eight selected configurations: five Safe,three Unsafe, using GED. TH is explicitly shortest-path duration, not a maximum horizon. All times include simulation, learning, tubes, safety and refinements. i7-6600U/16GB laptop; no OS/solver versions, repeats, raw trace datasets or uncertainty estimates reported. PED claimed more precise on Powertrn and otherwise comparable, without quantitative ablation. Random simulation precheck can return Unsafe before VerifySafety; dash refinement counts are preserved as unspecified rather than changed to zero or assigned a cause. Figure2 AutoPassing initial sets differ from Table1; its farther-forward B interval[30,40] is unsafe while[15,17] is safe because fixed maneuver timing matters. This does not support a monotonic distance rule. Powertrain composition uses lambda terminal enclosure[14.68,14.71], next terminal[14.69,14.70], with containment of other variables asserted but not tabulated. GA composed with GB and with GB³ are reported safe with zero refinements; extending to all finite GB repetitions is conditional on actual full-state enclosure closure. This is not an unconditional arbitrary-time physical safety guarantee. Models/remaining initial coordinates and ATS details are deferred to arXiv:1702.06902 appendix; that version was not read here. Python implementation uses MATLAB Python API/Simulink,PyGLPK andZ3. GitHub https://github.com/qibolun/DryVR and a Python benchmark port are cited, uninspected/unrun. No LLM-agent,Verus/verified-Rust,TLA+or distributed-protocol proof is provided. Independent reviewer identified another literal pseudocode omission: Algorithm2 line10 offers graph refinement as an alternative to requeueing Partition(S) at line9, but does not explicitly requeue or recheck the popped ambiguous S. If taken as a standalone alternative on the last work item, the worklist can empty and line11 return SAFE without rechecking it. Intended refinement must retain the pending obligation; no implementation bug is inferred. Independent review: GraphReach initializes only one initial vertex v_init, while Definition1 allows multiple initial vertices and the explicit singleton assumption is introduced for sequential composition. Applying the algorithm to the general graph definition requires initializing every initial vertex or an additional unique-initial-vertex assumption.

title: Dsolve: Safety Verification via Liquid Types
what: Introduces Dsolve, which infers Liquid refinement types for OCaml by generating subtyping constraints and solving predicate abstractions with Z3. It verifies array bounds, arithmetic safety, sorting and tree invariants with low annotation overhead and reports inferred types useful for debugging. The weighted_avg example shows higher-order foldn inference: Dsolve infers index bounds for callback f, proves equal positive array lengths, discharges an unreachable assertion and proves nonzero division. Errors are mapped to source lines. The tool found and guided repair of a real vec balancing bug by inferring a balance-factor bound of 4 before the fix.

title: Detectable Sequential Specifications for Recoverable Shared Objects
what: Defines detectability by transforming an ordinary sequential object specification into a detectable sequential specification (DSS). Per-process abstract state remembers a prepared operation and its response. prep-op announces the operation, exec-op performs it, and resolve reports whether it took effect and its response; ordinary operations remain available without detection. Section 2 gives the state transformation and four operation axioms. prep-op and resolve are total and idempotent, while exec-op requires the matching prepared operation with no recorded response. An auxiliary parity bit can distinguish repeated identical operations. DSS is combined with a separate concurrency correctness condition and leaves nesting recovery to the application. Section 3 derives a queue from the Michael–Scott/durable queue: tagged per-thread pointers record operation preparation and completion, CAS and helping maintain the linked list, and Appendix A supplies a centralized recovery scan. A variation replaces centralized recovery with individual recovery. Theorem 1 states lock-freedom and strict linearizability, but the article omits the analysis and detailed model. Section 4 measures failure-free queue throughput on real Optane memory.

DSS specifies sequential behavior and requires a separate concurrent correctness condition. The queue uses asynchronous shared memory, persistent memory, volatile caches, explicit flushes and system-wide crashes. Correct nesting is an application responsibility. The correctness theorem is stated rather than proved in this article. Experiments cover failure-free runs, use debug compilation at O0 and sequentially consistent atomics, and do not measure crash recovery latency. The log queue comparator is the authors’ implementation and could be optimized further.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to crash-recovery specifications for concurrent systems. The useful distinction is detecting whether an operation took effect versus forcing its completion. A Verus implementation would need to connect the abstract prepare/execute/resolve state to persistence and recovery invariants; the failure-free measurements do not establish recovery behavior.

title: Recursive Variable-Length State Compression for Multi-Core Software Model Checking
what: Introduces dtree, a concurrent chain-of-balanced-trees storage structure for variable-length model-checker states, supporting partial reconstruction and incremental delta updates; integrates it into the DMC multi-core checker. The paper contrasts dtree with TreeDBS and Compact Tree, explains why fixed alignment fails under dynamic allocation, and defines a StateID combining root index and length. Its API supports insert, delta, full/partial get and nested sub-states, enabling models to update heap regions without reconstructing complete states. Dtree experiments model Michael-Scott queues, sorted linked lists and concurrent hash maps, then compare 118 BEEM fixed-length models against LTSmin/TreeDBS, Compact Tree and SPIN Collapse. Results expose the trade-off: dtree wins on variable-length variance but loses compression on fixed-length vectors because its chain can be less balanced.

title: DuoAI: Fast, Automated Inference of Inductive Invariants for Verifying Distributed Protocols
what: Infers inductive safety invariants for Ivy distributed-protocol models by filtering formulas on reachable simulation states and refining candidates with Ivy/Z3. A finite directed implication graph organizes formula weakening. Runs top-down weakening, bottom-up universal-core strengthening and a universal-only search in parallel. Reports26of27protocols solved, including five Paxos variants; vertical Paxos exhausts memory. Completeness is relative to an adequate finite decidable formula space and graph/optimization correctness, with a reader counterexample to the printed arbitrary-alternation decomposition extension. Supplies exact/approximate implication graphs, sample-preserving coverage theorem, monotonic-refinement proof, counterexample-pruned powerset search proof, quantified-variable/type ordering, mutual-implication optimizations and all benchmark outcomes. Explains which refinement wins per protocol, why hundreds of existential candidates can stall SMT, what human choices baselines require, and how specification/retrofitting differences affect claims of automation. Reader checks distinguish sufficient invariant inference from implemented-system verification and identify a quantifier-dependency flaw in a printed optimization lemma.

Trusted Ivy/Z3 checks initialization and transition preservation of the conjunction and safety implication for all modeled instances, rather than bounded simulation being the certificate. Scope is safety; no liveness, crash-recovery implementation refinement, verified Rust/Verus proof or LLM-agent evaluation. Sampled states are assumed genuinely reachable; incorrect simulation could discard needed true invariants and compromise completeness, though final sound SMT checks still guard returned results. Finite formula search space uses prenex DNF, relational predicates/equality; extension to uninterpreted functions referred to DistAI. Bounds are quantified variables per sort, max_exists, max_literal, max_and and max_or. Tautologies/contradictions excluded. Nonempty sorts are implicit in universal-to-existential implication. Quantifier alternation must follow a fixed sort order, inferred partly from axioms or supplied by user; absent user choice multiple orders are tried in parallel. The actual full verification condition, including protocol axioms/transitions, must remain in the intended decidable fragment. Exact graph is transitive reduction of strict implication over finite formulas; syntactic implementation instead uses five sound weakening shapes and may connect equivalent formulas. Lemmas1–5 establish claimed acyclicity, implication and coverage of nontrivial formulas from selected roots. No theorem says every semantic implication is an edge/path in the approximate graph; coverage plus sound directed weakening is what enumeration/refinement need. A candidate is retained if it holds on all sampled states; descendants can be skipped if dominated by an existing candidate. Retained candidates can still be false on unseen reachable states; simulation removes candidates, not proof obligations. Top-down refinement checks conjunction plus safety, replaces a failed candidate by noninvalidated immediate successors not already dominated by a reachable ancestor, and returns NotProvable if safety fails. title: Duper: A Proof-Producing Superposition Theorem Prover for Dependent Type Theory
what: Implements Duper, a Lean proof-producing saturation prover adapting higher-order superposition to dependent types, potentially empty types and universe polymorphism. Generates classical Lean proof expressions; uses LeanAuto preprocessing for type classes/monomorphization. Benchmarks compare raw search and re-proving minimized ATP problems, showing near-Metis reconstruction performance on these suites, not a full Lean hammer or evaluated Mathlib-dependent-type capability. A DISCOUNT-style active/passive given-clause loop combines simplification and generation with higher-order KBO and unification. Proof reconstruction retains quantified variables unless unification supplies witnesses, eagerly records substitutions and passes transfer expressions for new variables. Empty types require Skolem functions with a dummy argument, separate Nonempty clauses and restrictions on vacuous-clause simplification; discovered inhabitation reactivates clauses for simplification. Dependent unification extends forall transitions/imitation; universe instantiations propagate backwards through the proof DAG. LeanAuto abstracts dependent parameters into essentially higher-order problems, heuristically instantiates type classes and identifies some definitional equalities. These are implemented algorithms and explanatory soundness arguments; no whole-calculus dependent-type completeness theorem is established here.
assumptions_limits: Input lemmas must be supplied manually; no relevance filter. Full hammer integration and Mathlib evaluation are future work at publication. The assertion that no Lean hammer exists is historical to this2024 paper. Proof search and reconstruction use classical logic, including double-negation elimination, even for constructively provable goals. Producing a Lean term supports checking within Lean's axiomatic foundation; reader did not execute artifact or independently certify implementation. Author completeness statement in §4.1 concerns the higher-order fragment of the unification procedure, not completeness of Duper over all dependent type theory. Native unification/preprocessing extensions and illustrative examples do not constitute exhaustive dependent-type benchmark validation. If inhabitationReasoning is disabled, search temporarily assumes nonpropositional types inhabited and errors at reconstruction if unsound inference results. Enabled mode reasons about Nonempty throughout saturation; vacuous clauses must not eliminate nonvacuous facts. LeanAuto monomorphization is heuristic and only sketched here. Its same-head representative mechanism cannot recognize all definitional equalities; preprocessing does not eliminate every universe-polymorphism issue. Benchmarks are TPTP FOF/THF translations of Seventeen and GRUNGE. They do not measure verified Rust/Verus/TLA+,distributed execution or LLM specification accuracy. GRUNGE formats differ in encoding difficulty. All runs externally terminated after30s wall time on a3.8GHz Mac,16GB RAM. Zipperposition portfolio forced to one core because Python multicore code was not Mac-compatible; Vampire portfolio ran unaltered. No statistical uncertainty reported.
use_for_goal: Provides a possible checked-proof backend for agents: separate premise selection,proof search and Lean-term reconstruction. Reader inference: report end-to-end success separately from success conditional on external proof discovery/minimization. The vacuous-type handling shows why transplanting first-order algorithms into dependent foundations requires extra logical obligations. Relevance is to proof automation and evaluating generated proofs;paper contains no LLM agent,Verus/Rust/TLA+ implementation or distributed-system verification.

what: Defines a five-step model-checking approach for formalizing dynamic architecture patterns and their guarantees, and applies it to Singleton, Model-View-Controller and Broker patterns. title: Extending a High-Performance Prover to Higher-Order Logic
what: Extends the first-order E prover with native full higher-order logic support (λE), adding lambda-term representation, beta/eta normalization, higher-order unification and indexing, pragmatic lambda-superposition, Boolean/extensionality handling and preprocessing. title: Editable Proof Sketch for Automated Theorem Proving
what: Introduces EditableSketch, a dependency-explicit editable proof representation, and SketchRefine, a Lean 4 ATP agent alternating verified subgoal proofs with local repair/decomposition while retaining unaffected proofs. Evaluates MiniF2F-test (244 statements) and FormalMath-Lite (425). Reported 99.6% and 76.0% solved rates count either proofs or certified refutations, not only proofs of the original theorem. Table 2 FormalMath-Lite proof-only rate is 69.2%. Four node types: Deduction produces a term, Construction produces witnesses satisfying a predicate, Assumption opens a local scope, Conclusion discharges it. Distinguishes syntactic dependencies from proof premises; compiler adds indirect syntactic dependencies. Scopes must nest without crossing. DSL supports NEW/UPDATE/DELETE and ADJUST of logical premises. Compilation produces per-node subtheorems and a Lean fragment composing them. Lean checks structure/types with temporary sorry; all subproofs must subsequently verify and final script is checked. Direct prover first samples eight proofs; unsolved subgoals get eight attempts. LLM plausibility judgment directs error repair versus decomposition; modified subgoals invalidate cached proofs. LeanExplore supplies up to three candidates for each of five queries, then selects up to five lemmas and inherits parent selections. Refutation strategy restarts with original theorem assumed and False as goal; can switch back when that attempt appears invalid.
assumptions_limits: Lean 4/Mathlib v4.19.0 and Kimina Lean Server are the checking environment. Structural/type acceptance using sorry is an intermediate condition, not a completed proof. Correctness of completed certificates depends on Lean and the formalized assumptions; there is no separate mechanized correctness theorem for the EditableSketch compiler in the supplied paper. The solved metric combines theorem proofs with certified refutations. FormalMath-Lite 76.0% with refutation versus 69.2% without; MiniF2F Table 1 gives DeepSeek 97.5% versus 96.7% and Gemini 99.6% versus 98.8%. These are different outcomes and cannot all be described as proofs of the original statement. MiniF2F uses the Goedel-Prover-V2 repository version; two statements are false under those formalizations. Hilbert uses slightly different corrected statements, so headline comparison is not identical-input proof generation. The 99.6% Gemini result includes upgrading from Gemini 2.5 Pro (99.2% in prose) to Gemini 3.0 Pro Preview on imo_2001_p6. Output budget is 10M general-purpose-model tokens per MiniF2F problem and 2M DeepSeek-V3.2 tokens per FormalMath-Lite problem. Cost plots and Table 3 concern the general-purpose LLM; they exclude specialized prover tokens, total wall time and other system costs. Table 3 averages condition on problems not solved in pre-proving, rather than all problems. Baseline pass@ and models/budgets differ; many baseline figures are imported from other papers. Figure 4 reports a matched general-purpose-output-token Hilbert reproduction, but that is not a full-system compute comparison. No repeated-run confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied. LLM correctness/plausibility and dependency annotations are heuristic search guidance, not sound semantic oracles; acceptance requires formal verification. Authors identify compiler-based extraction of syntactic dependencies as future work. The supplied description of an irrelevant-premise experiment gives a qualitative trend without a corresponding quantitative table/plot. Figure 7 is captioned as a retrieval ablation and describes parallel versus sequential decomposition, while its visible legend lists In-Place, Build and Hilbert. This source inconsistency prevents assigning those curves to retrieval variants confidently. Appendix A gives informal false-statement constructions; full Lean refutations are deferred to supplementary material not included here. No artifact or generated certificate was independently rerun. Evaluation is formal mathematics, not software refinement, concurrency or distributed protocols.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM proof agents, dependency-aware incremental repair, caching verified obligations and detecting false specifications through checked refutations. Reader inference: a similar proof-obligation graph could guide Verus or TLA+ workflows, but that transfer is untested here. No Rust/Verus/TLA+ or distributed-system case study; no inference from mathematical benchmark scores to production specification correctness.

title: Efficient Exact Verification of Binarized Neural Networks
what: Presents EEV, an exact (sound and complete) verifier for binarized neural networks. BNN layers compile to reified cardinality constraints; MiniSatCS adds native propagation for these constraints. BinMask induces balanced layer-wise sparsity, Cardinality Bound Decay (CBD) shrinks threshold bounds, and adaptive gradient cancelling trains networks whose exact robustness is tractable. The SAT encoding uses {0,1} activations, sparse {-1,0,1} weights, quantized inputs, thermometer-encoded perturbation intervals, and cached network clauses. The paper explains why balanced sparsity matters more than total sparsity and why lower cardinality bounds reduce sequential-counter encoding size, improve propagation, and make outputs predictable. Standard hard-tanh straight-through adversarial training can produce high PGD but low exact robustness; tanh/adaptive gradients and verifier-generated adversaries narrow this gap. EEV also encodes ensemble reject queries requiring all models to agree on the same wrong class.
numbers: MiniSatCS >100x over unmodified SAT
EEV total speedup 338.28–2440.65x vs real-valued exact verifier
BinMask solve 756.288→0.002s MNIST and 0.267→0.003s CIFAR10
CBD mean bound 148.3→2.7 MNIST; 123.8→2.1 CIFAR10
ensemble mean solve 0.003s, attack success 17.21%
assumptions_limits: Exactness applies to the quantized BNN and encoded infinity-norm perturbation domain, not arbitrary floating-point inference. Inputs are quantized (s=1/255 or 2epsilon), final batch normalization is restricted to scalar statistics, and verification remains NP-hard with timeouts for harder settings. Robustness/accuracy tradeoffs are severe on CIFAR10 at large epsilon; CBD can reduce natural accuracy. Results use MNIST/CIFAR10 architectures and do not prove properties of real-valued or distributed systems.
use_for_goal: Strong direct evidence that restricting model arithmetic and co-designing training with a complete solver can make exact robustness verification practical. The SAT/cardinality encoding pattern is relevant to verified components and proof obligations, while quantization and benchmark scope delimit what can be claimed for Verus or distributed protocols.

title: Efficient Synthesis for Concurrency by Semantics-Preserving Transformations
what: Synthesizes assertion-safe concurrent libraries from sequentially correct libraries using sequential-semantics-preserving instruction reorderings and atomic sections. Generalizes a failing linear trace into a partial order representing many failing schedules, then eliminates all its linearizations with constraints obtained from a minimal cycle in a weighted elimination graph. §3 models deterministic instructions/CFG methods, arbitrary concurrent method invocations and sequential input/output behavior. §4 computes allowed within-block statement reorderings by commutativity checks, combines ordering and atomicity constraints, and motivates idempotent duplication without formally incorporating it. §5 defines error invariants that overapproximate states reachable along the trace and underapproximate states from which the error is forced. A complete generalization check is expensive; two sufficient rules exploit conditional commutativity or an error-preserving common postcondition, while checking intervening instructions preserve supporting invariants. Previously relaxed edges are rechecked. §6 encodes essential happens-before relations, available reorderings and atomicity additions as weighted graph edges; creating a cycle makes every represented trace infeasible. A large atomicity weight prefers reorderings; shortest paths find an elimination cycle in polynomial time. Constraints monotonically accumulate. The minimality result concerns the constraint eliminating the current partial-order counterexample, not a globally optimal repaired program.

assumptions_limits: Sequentially correct deterministic methods with reducible CFGs; formal semantics permits an unbounded number of concurrent threads, each making one method execution, but the experiment uses a supplied seven-thread environment model. Reordering is restricted to a straight-line basic block. Safety/assertion specifications are central; deadlocks in experiments are manually translated into assertions because Poirot does not detect them. The prototype handles a restricted C subset excluding pointer arithmetic, aliasing and bitwise arithmetic. It uses bounded model checking, and no benchmark bounds are specified here; therefore experimental verification should not be relabeled an unbounded machine-checked library proof. The implementation does not compute error invariants even though they motivate the generalization theory. Weak memory and required fences remain future work; enforcing a source-level order assumes sequential consistency. Repair may introduce other bugs and further counterexamples; there is no guarantee of intermediate regression freedom.
use_for_goal: Concrete comparison point for automated concurrent-program repair and LLM proof assistants: partial orders explain a failure class rather than one schedule, and sequential semantics constrain allowable patches. The real-driver skeleton demonstrates why model extraction, environment assumptions, verification bounds, synthesis time and final checking time must remain separate. The source-level ordering/fence distinction matters when applying any generated repair to Rust atomics. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM evaluation is reported.

what: Generalizes Epistemic Halpern-Shoham logic by labeling whole intervals with regular expressions over their state histories. title: Formal Verification of the Empty Hexagon Number
what: Formalizes in Lean the geometric-to-SAT reduction behind h(6)=30: every set of 30 planar points in general position contains an empty convex hexagon. The development defines convexity/emptiness in mathlib, proves a triangle characterization, reduces geometry to triple-orientation Boolean assignments, proves canonical-position symmetry breaking, and verifies the optimized Heule–Scheucher CNF encoding. A distributed CaDiCaL/cake_lpr computation supplies the n=30 unsatisfiability certificate. Sections 3–4 connect Lean convex-hull predicates to triangle emptiness and determinant-based orientations; σPtInTriangle_iff under four-point general position closes an implicit gap in prior work, and OrientationProperty proves that holes depend only on triple orientations. Section 5 constructs a six-step canonical-position transformation (rotation, translation, projective map, sorting, reflection and return from infinity) and proves existence of a σ-equivalent canonical set. Section 6 defines orientation, triangle, cap/cup and hole variables plus 16 clause families; variable-defining and orientation clauses are proved, while forbidden configurations imply six-holes. The n=30 CNF is partitioned into 312,418 subproblems, solved by CaDiCaL 1.9.5 with LRAT proofs checked on the fly by cake_lpr in 25,876.5 CPU hours (~3 CPU years). The Lean encoder emits CNF below 1 s on a laptop; a comparison g(6) corollary takes 28 s to solve versus Marić's 787 s and uses O(n⁴) rather than O(n⁶) clauses. The formalization required ~300 hours/3 months and ~4.7k Lean lines, and corrected an orientation-map error and a lex-order/code mismatch in prior work.

title: Enhancing Interactive Theorem Prover Error Messages with Hints
what: Heuristic enhancements to three Agda v2.8.0 error messages, evaluated with novice-Agda programmers in a university course. Measures successful repairs, time among retained successful submissions and perceived helpfulness. Confusable hints improve measured success and speed; correct whitespace hints improve retained-success timing; correct hints consistently improve perception. Incorrect hints show no statistically significant performance effect in this study, which is not an equivalence or harmlessness theorem. Documents exactly when each hint is shown, false-positive/false-negative limits, counterbalanced error-message variants on distinct snippets, timing-data exclusions and uneven participation. Results separate objective repair outcomes from subjective ratings. Conditional timing, repeated observations per participant and unsupported no-practical-danger language materially limit generalization to proof-development or agent workflows.
assumptions_limits: Participants are final-year bachelor CS students in one elective functional-programming course: experienced programmers, new to Agda/ITPs after four Agda lectures, not general programming novices. Recruitment during lecture limits population to that course and language/demographic setting. Two survey variants swap original/enhanced error messages (OEM/EEM) across distinct A/B or C/D tasks. Every participant may see both conditions across different snippets, without seeing the same snippet twice. Per-snippet comparisons are between participants; pooled observations reuse participants. This is not a simple all-hints versus no-hints participant split. Ten one-error snippets represent three correct hint types and two incorrect ones, with two snippets per type/intention. No incorrect Confusable task was included because authors found no sufficiently realistic scenario. Incorrect hints are therefore a selected set, not all possible harmful hints. Whitespace heuristic splits an unknown name into in-scope names, without proving resulting application typechecks. Confusable compares unknown names only against in-scope names using generic Unicode spoof data. TooFewArgs triggers at function application sites with inferred function result type, not bare references with zero supplied arguments. Heuristics do not rerun a repair and certify its correctness. Compiler stops at the first error, making interpretation of a subsequent failure ambiguous. No semantic-correctness proof of suggested edits or trust theorem for modified Agda is presented. After removing 17 single-open/no-rating participants, analysis has 56 participants (32/24 variants), 412 submissions (228/184), average about 7 tasks and median 10; task response count 37–55. Random task ordering activated only after first TooFewArgs#A, so all users saw that task first. Timing analysis removes 136 failures, nine successful submissions interleaved with other tasks and 25 with >2-minute compilation gaps. Thus 242 retained successful observations inform timing, not all attempts. Successful-case conditioning and missingness can change group composition; results do not measure time-to-success including failures. Single-tailed Mann–Whitney U tests use directional hypotheses chosen by correct/incorrect intention, p<0.05. Table 3 has 21 p-values across five type/intention groups plus two pooled summaries and three outcomes. No multiplicity correction or participant-cluster model is described; pooled independence and multiple testing are reader concerns, not rerun statistical results. Online environment uses Haskell highlighting, no Agda Unicode-entry support or cursor-column display, and snippets use visible small libraries rather than standard Agda library. This differs from normal local Agda editing. Eleven-day access and 1–2-minute advice do not impose a strict per-task time limit. Subjective ratings range very misleading through very helpful, plus did-not-read option; Table 3 labels epsilon no rating. Exclusion of disengaged participants and differing availability of ratings affect denominators. No long-term learning/retention, error fatigue or realistic multi-error proof-development study is performed. Non-significant incorrect-hint performance tests do not establish zero harm or an acceptable bounded harm. No equivalence margin, confidence interval or statistical-power calculation is reported. The authors recommendation is broader than the exact study sample evidence. Only stated GenAI use is activated GitHub Copilot in PyCharm during data analysis. Hints themselves are designed heuristics, not evaluated LLM-generated hints or proof attempts. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed protocol result is supplied. Authors report that cleaning gaps above two versus five minutes made no statistically significant difference (§3.4), without presenting a detailed comparison. Uneven task topics and recency across hint types constrain comparisons between types; Confusable material was more recent than TooFewArgs material (§5).
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful evidence for designing and evaluating compiler/prover feedback in human or LLM-assisted verification workflows. It supplies a controlled comparison of specific heuristic hints and shows why repair success, conditional time and perceived helpfulness need separate metrics. Its sample/analysis limits caution against treating plausible hints as reliable proof guidance. No LLM proof agent, distributed-system theorem, Verus/Rust verifier or TLA+ tool was tested.

what: Presents PSR,data selection for Isabelle theorem proving: score approximately200,000 theorem-proof pairs by proof complexity,semantic coverage and reasoning diversity,then select≈4,200 examples. Fine-tuning DeepSeek-Math-7B-Base on the selected set reaches84.8% Pass@64 on the Isabelle miniF2F test;history-aware Isabelle verifier feedback and dynamic temperature scheduling reach90.6%. Complexity combines log proof/theorem lengths and structural marker counts;semantic clusters use TF-IDF plus K-Means;strategy diversity uses tactic-label entropy with fixed priority matching. Selection removes lower/upper complexity tails,allocates cluster quotas with entropy penalty and suppresses one-shot templates. Inference generates8 candidates per round,verifies in parallel with PISA,retains summarized error history,raises temperature after failures and early-stops solved theorems. Ablations compare no tuning,raw≈200k SFT,random/complexity/clustering selection,fixed temperature and dynamic feedback. Appendix robustness randomizes strategy-label priority (entropy r=.70,quota r=.997,Jaccard=.94);AppendixC reports 10-run means/std/95% CI;AppendixE tests exact and character-level theorem contamination. Explicit selection equations:ci=.6log(1+prooflen)+.3log(1+theoremlen)+.1structuralcount;retain middle50%;K=50,60k TF-IDF features,minDF5. Quotas floor(weight/sumweights×M),rounding remainder by weight;non-one-shot samples first,12%cluster/8%global one-shot caps,then non-one-shot backfill from high-entropy clusters.
assumptions_limits: All correctness is relative to Isabelle2025,PISA,DeepSeek-Math-7B-Base,LoRA hyperparameters and the supplied miniF2F Isabelle formalizations. The reader did not run Isabelle,PISA or released code. PSR strategy labels assign one tactic by exact keyword matching under a fixed priority;entropy therefore depends on the label inventory/order. Robustness changes priority but not label set,and clustering sensitivity is discussed rather than fully quantified. Main benchmark is mathematical miniF2F,not project-scale software or distributed verification. Authors explicitly leave Lean/Coq and project-level verification for future work. Transfer to Verus/TLA+ is an inference,not measured. All reported results average10 decoding runs;AppendixC gives full-framework90.6±3.3% and95%CI[88.2,93.0],versus PSR84.8±1.0,[84.1,85.5]. These quantify run variation on fixed formal statements,not uncertainty over all theorem populations. Full-framework attempts are feedback-dependent,so this is success within64 adaptive attempts rather than independent-sample pass@64. Raw corpus and selected subset may differ in theorem domains,proof style and contamination despite AppendixE statement-level matching. Training samples are from Isabelle/HOL and AFP;the test has no reference proofs as input. Only two7B backbones and one benchmark family are evaluated. Prior-system headline scores are imported with different models,budgets/prompts and possibly Isabelle setups;no matched end-to-end compute/cost comparison or human assessment of proof readability is supplied. Raw theorem-proof validity is inherited from source corpus. The supplied paper does not specify checks excluding admissions,sorry or theorem-statement changes in generated output;verifier acceptance is reported,not independently audited here. Finite accepted proofs establish only their exact statements. Semantic coverage is a textual proxy:TF-IDF over concatenated theorem/proof withKMeans,not a formal semantics distance. Complexity is likewise log textual lengths plus keyword count,not measured proof difficulty. Tactic-label entropy measures cluster distributions,not the internal reasoning diversity of one proof.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to verified proof agents: curate training data by formal proof structure and use checker diagnostics as adaptive generation signals. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ agents,the transferable hypothesis is that diverse moderate-complexity verified traces and history-aware counterexamples can improve search;the paper does not evaluate code refinement,concurrency or distributed systems.

Separates batch final-state verification from update-trajectory correctness and parallel centralized computation from distributed on-device verification.

A rule is match/from/to/priority; hit is match minus higher-priority matches. Correctness depends on complete accurate controller inputs and faithful FIB semantics. Packet drops/valid terminal nodes need explicit interpretation; multicast, stateful transformations and hardware behavior are not modeled here. §§2/3/5.3: Update storm is a batch of insert/delete operations; verifier updates its model and then checks affected packets on the resulting graph. It does not prove all intermediate device-installation states, asynchronous rollout orders or packet histories are safe. Snapshot freshness and eventual installation correspondence are inputs, not established by speed measurements. Whole-network invariant maintenance additionally needs an initially valid state or separate initial check, since unchanged packet classes are not newly checked. §4.1 Figure3: EC labels are global forwarding-behavior classes, so local rule changes can split class labels on unchanged switches. EPs denote local packet sets per directed edge and change only edges outgoing from affected switch; this is representation locality, not a theorem that a local update has only local end-to-end consequences. Global path checks remain necessary. §§4.2/5.1 Algorithm1: Partition occurs after storm arrival. Greedily place the currently most-updated unassigned switch into least-loaded region. Whole switch remains indivisible; one hot switch can dominate and equal update counts need not mean equal BDD cost. No optimal-balance/complexity or runtime-bound proof. §5.1 recommends region count smaller than cores, but §6.2 uses8regions on8cores. §5.1: Separate BDD manager per switch avoids cross-thread manager sharing during local model updates. BDD operations across switches require common variables/manager, motivating shared B0/M′. Parallel local maintenance is not on-device distributed verification; §7 leaves that design for future work. Global transfer/traversal can remain bottlenecks. §5.2 Algorithms2/3: Compute actual hit by subtracting higher-priority hit regions; insertion adds new hit to selected next hop and removes overlap from lower-priority alternatives. Trie-based overlap optimization is described but omitted from listing. Preserving manager variables and original per-switch update order matters when grouping; no executable-refinement argument supplied. §5.2 Algorithm3 printed deletion lines14–21 appear incorrect; this is a source-pseudocode finding, not an executed implementation failure. Example: high-priority rule A→B matches nonemptyP, lower-priority A→B also matchesP and currently has emptyhit. Deleting high-priority rule removesP from edgeB atline14; branchline18 skips re-adding it because both destinationsB match, leavingB empty though lower rule should forwardP. Correct code/proof must resolve these cases. §5.3 Algorithm4: Transfer old-minus-new and new-minus-old formulae from local manager into sharedB0, accumulate union of changed packet sets. Enumerating formulas can be much larger than BDD representation; paper explicitly admits worst-case all formulas affected. Empirical >97%one/two formulas does not bound worst-case cost. §5.3 Algorithm5 printed traversal subtracts edge predicate fromp atline8 before passing edge∧p atline10; under sequential assignments that intersection is empty. It also adds child tohistory before entering child, so a nonempty recursivecall would immediately satisfy loopguard; outerloop uses s but call uses undefinedn. It tests globalmatch instead of recursivep for termination and records entirematch at reached waypoint/destination, even if only a subset arrived. No cycle/history guard is shown. As printed it cannot substantiate all-matched-packets reachability. Reach-set aggregation does not explicitly encode ordered waypoint traversal; desired waypoint semantics must be specified before formal proof. Link failure overwritesM′[l] and requires restoration/copy for independent queries. §5.3: Network invariants include loops and blackholes via DFS from each node; optional tuple(match,source,waypoints,dst) checks all requested packets and can disable a link. title: Equilibria-Based Probabilistic Model Checking for Concurrent Stochastic Games.
what: Extends rPATL with Nash formulae for two coalitions pursuing distinct probabilistic or reward objectives in concurrent stochastic games, and implements model checking/strategy synthesis in PRISM-games. Defines coalition games and subgame-perfect (epsilon-)Nash/social-welfare-optimal equilibria, extends syntax/semantics with summed probability or reward objectives, and gives algorithms: labelled-polytope enumeration for bimatrix SWNEs; backwards induction for finite-horizon objectives; value iteration for infinite-horizon objectives; and MDP solving when one target is reached. Assumption 1 excludes non-terminal end components for infinite-horizon probabilities and requires almost-sure target reachability for infinite-horizon rewards. Strategies may require randomization and memory; infinite-horizon synthesis is approximate, although case studies found NE profiles. PRISM-games uses Z3 SMT to enumerate equilibria and filters dominated strategies. Case studies cover robot coordination, Aloha, medium access control, and cellular power control.
numbers: Implementation handles models over 2 million states and 20 million transitions in under two hours; highly branching models only tens of thousands of states fit that limit. Robot, Aloha, MAC, and power-control studies show SWNE strategies collectively improve summed objectives versus zero-sum baselines. Example table includes Aloha 17,057 states/42,654 transitions and power-control up to 32,812 states/260,924 transitions.
assumptions_limits: Two coalitions are complements in the coalition game; finite-horizon values are exact, while infinite-horizon properties rely on convergence under Assumption 1 and produce epsilon-SWNEs. Nash existence for infinite objectives is open in general. Complexity includes EXPTIME Nash solving for reachability and repeated LCP solving; convergence gives no precision guarantee. Experiments use finite CSG models and chosen parameters, not deployment traces.
use_for_goal: Provides formal algorithms and measured scalability for verifying/synthesizing strategies in probabilistic distributed interactions with non-zero-sum objectives. It complements TLA+/Verus by handling stochastic strategic behavior, while exposing assumptions around equilibrium existence and convergence.

title: A New Era in Software Security: Towards Self-Healing Software via Large Language Models and Formal Verification
what: Presents ESBMC-AI, a counterexample-guided repair loop in which ESBMC finds a bounded C vulnerability and emits a trace/stack trace, an LLM proposes a patch, and ESBMC verifies the patch again. The paper evaluates GPT-4o-based repair on FormAI vulnerability samples and measures both verification outcomes and manual semantic correctness. The framework has User Chat and Fix Code modes, converts ESBMC counterexamples into a human-readable prompt, and uses a 10-second ESBMC timeout with overflow, memory-leak, stack-trace, one-unwind and multi-property options. Because program equivalence is undecidable, the authors manually inspect 1,337 samples from common categories and use lines-of-code and cyclomatic-complexity changes as additional patch-impact indicators. Table III separates verified-safe, verified-failed and unknown outcomes for eight vulnerability classes; examples show that adding one to an upper bound can leave the same violation, while arithmetic-overflow repairs may require a second iteration. A misleading MD5/password example demonstrates that LLM-only diagnosis follows names and semantics poorly, whereas the BMC trace identifies the actual multiplication overflow.
numbers: Table III samples: lower-bound array 182, fscanf 241, scanf 175, division by zero 133, NULL dereference 229, arithmetic add overflow 73, forgotten memory 187, upper-bound array 117

single-iteration accuracy: 95.60% lower-bound array, 91.29% fscanf, 90.40% scanf, 86.47% division by zero, 80.35% NULL dereference, 70.27% add overflow, 48.66% forgotten memory, 41.03% upper-bound array
second-iteration arithmetic example reaches 88% on the same samples
FormAI corpus described as 50,000 randomly selected C programs; manual subset 1,337
ESBMC invocation timeout 10 seconds, --unwind 1
assumptions_limits: BMC only checks bounded executions and depends on ESBMC modeling and timeout; a successful verification is not a proof of whole-program semantic equivalence. LLM patches can compile yet preserve or introduce bugs, and the off-the-shelf model is nondeterministic and not explainable. The study manually verifies a subset rather than all 30,000 candidate samples, uses human-designed prompts and GPT-4o, and notes that forgotten-memory failures may require external headers/files absent from the prompt. Results therefore measure one model, one prompt workflow and selected FormAI categories, not general self-healing correctness.
use_for_goal: Concrete evidence for an LLM-agent verification workflow: an external formal checker supplies machine-generated counterexamples, the model proposes a repair, and the checker gates acceptance. The failure categories and boundedness limits are useful when evaluating agents that write distributed specifications or proofs.

title: ESBMC-Arduino: Closing the Deployment Gap for Formal Verification of Open-Hardware PLCs
what: Introduces a hardware-faithful verification method for IEC 61131-3 programs on open-hardware PLCs and instantiates it as ESBMC-Arduino. A declarative HAL fixes MCU word width, ADC/PWM resolutions and I/O bindings; the lowering injects realizable input bounds and bit-precise arithmetic before ESBMC BMC/k-induction. The paper formalizes the deployment gap as disagreement between an abstract model with unbounded integers/free inputs and a device model with finite-width arithmetic and hardware domains. It defines HAL H=<w,badc,bpwm,mu>, gives four lowering transformations (width, input assumes, quantization/PWM clamp, nondeterministic nonlinear abstraction), and proves Reach_device subset Reach_model under a faithful descriptor, with every reported counterexample physically realizable. The motivating adc*100 alarm flips at AVR adc=898. Controlled variants isolate vulnerable scaling versus safe offsets/comparisons. The 123-program corpus finds 54/123 naive false alarms, all unphysical IN-5 underflows; HAL bounds reduce 54 to 0 while retaining 32 proofs. CBMC and Frama-C mirrors reproduce the phantom and genuine width defect.

HAL annotated: 0 unsafe, 91 unknown, 32 safe; all 54 false alarms removed
Controlled median solve time 168 ms, maximum 412 ms; real runs under 1 s
CBMC reproduces 54/54 naive overflows and bounds remove 54/54
AVR model int_bits=16, ADC=10 bits, PWM=8 bits
assumptions_limits: Scope is integer/Boolean IEC logic and model-level verification, not hardware-in-loop. Scan-cycle sampling ignores plant dynamics, sensor noise and actuator latency. Soundness depends on correct HAL word width and per-input ranges; uniform 10-bit AVR treatment can be wrong for wider ADC, network or digital-word inputs. Nonlinear blocks are sound but imprecise nondeterministic ranges, and k-induction leaves 91 real programs unknown. Binding and quantization mechanisms are future work.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for target-faithful formal verification: abstract proof can be unsound when machine arithmetic and physical input domains are omitted, while a small declarative model restores realizable counterexamples. The explicit assumptions and unknown verdicts are useful when assessing Verus or other verification pipelines deployed on real hardware, though this is PLC/ESBMC rather than Rust/Verus.

title: Model Checking C++ Programs
what: Presents an SMT-based bounded model checker for C++ in ESBMC with operational models for templates, inheritance, polymorphism, STL containers, and exception handling. It encodes bounded executions into decidable first-order SMT constraints and compares ESBMC with LLBMC and DIVINE. Details type checking and template instantiation, inheritance/polymorphism encodings, a C++ operational model replacing STL with contract-like assertions, and exception-to-control-flow encodings. The study evaluates 1,513 C++03 programs and includes a commercial telecommunications Sniffer application.

assumptions_limits: Verification is bounded by loop-unwinding/call bounds and depends on the correctness of the simplified C++ operational model (COM) for STL semantics. Coverage targets C++03 and lacks several C++11 features; template/SFINAE support remains incomplete. CBMC comparison is limited because CBMC aborts or lacks STL support on this benchmark set.
use_for_goal: Demonstrates an end-to-end SMT/BMC pipeline for realistic C++ features and memory-safety checking, with stronger benchmark coverage than compared tools. Bounded search, model fidelity, and legacy C++ scope limit claims about arbitrary modern C++ programs.

title: Using Model Checking to Generate Test Cases for Android Applications
short_name: Espada et al. Android model-based testing
what: Defines modular view and device state machines for realistic user/system interactions across Android applications, composes them with back-stack and inter-device communication semantics, and uses SPIN exhaustive exploration to emit each bounded execution trace as an executable UiAutomator test. The generated tests can feed runtime monitors such as DRAGONFLY. Formal definitions distinguish deterministic view machines, user versus system events, connection/return states, view reuse and automatic return, and device configurations containing active state plus histories. Composition rules R1–R7 model calls, returns, reuse, inter-device message production/consumption, and partial-order reduction. Because histories make the composed machine infinite, the implementation bounds trace depth MAX_TR. A tool chain extracts UI controls with UIAutomatorViewer, stores state-machine/XML models, generates PROMELA inlines and backstacks, runs SPIN, translates traces to UiAutomatorTestCase classes, compiles a .dex file, and executes via adb. The Facebook/YouTube case demonstrates cross-app behavior rather than random event fuzzing.

assumptions_limits: Models encode intended/realistic behavior supplied by an expert; exhaustive traces cover only modeled views, controls, events, and depth. Device histories and matching make the unbounded semantics non-finite, so termination depends on a fixed maximum depth. Runtime tests can still fail from UI selector drift, unmodeled Android/OS behavior, timing, or environment; model checking traces are test generation, not a correctness proof of the app. Quantitative evaluation is small (three-run averages) and reports generation cost rather than defect detection or monitor findings.
use_for_goal: A concrete example of model checking used as an exhaustive test generator for event-driven distributed interactions, with explicit state/history bounds and a runtime-monitoring boundary. It informs how TLA+/Verus specifications can drive executable tests while preserving the distinction between bounded trace coverage and proof of implementation correctness.

title: Euclean: Automated Geometry Problem Formalization with Unified Verification in Lean
what: Euclean translates informal geometry into native Lean 4/MATHLIB statements through four stages: constraint explication, prove-first configuration anchoring, retrieval-based mapping to canonical MATHLIB primitives, and compiler-feedback iterative repair. It uses Plane = EuclideanSpace R (Fin 2), injects affine-independence, distinctness, positive-radius and strict-betweenness hypotheses, and contrasts this kernel-checked analytic foundation with custom-axiom geometry DSLs. OMNI-Geometry and Numina-Geometry are generated with DeepSeek-V3; examples show mapping ‘D, A, B collinear in that order’ to Sbtw and triangle non-degeneracy to AffineIndependent. Downstream Goedel v2 training tests whether the corpus transfers to unified theorem proving.
numbers: OMNI starts with 780 problems; 768 compile (98.5%). Numina starts with 183,796; 177,597 compile (96.6%). On 30 ablation problems with 32 generations/configuration (960 each), compiling candidates rise Basic 125 (13.0%), +concept mapping 254 (26.5%), +repair 465 (48.4%), +constraint mapping 500 (52.1%), +anchoring 480 (50.0%). Human evaluation on 180 OMNI problems (difficulty ≥4) gives TOP1 48.89% and TOP5 73.33%; 8.0+ problems score 20.00%/60.00%. Goedel v2 Numina Pass@1 is 13.6% base, 15.1% after SFT and 15.0% after DPO. Aristotle proves 25/100 sampled cases after filtering, with 19 unresolved but unrebutted.
assumptions_limits: The method is text-only and assumes problem statements fully specify relevant geometry; it does not parse diagrams. Semantic validation at corpus scale is difficult, so Numina-Geometry is a candidate corpus needing expert review and prover filtering. LLMs may omit necessary constraints or add redundant/over-strong hypotheses, reducing generality. Coverage is limited by current MATHLIB geometry APIs. Compilation is only a proxy for semantic faithfulness. The pipeline relies on LLM-generated prove-first reasoning and iterative repair; no guarantee ensures the formal statement preserves the exact intended theorem.
use_for_goal: Shows a practical route from natural-language geometry to a single kernel-checked Lean ecosystem, with explicit treatment of hidden diagram assumptions. Dataset scale, compilation/semantic gaps, human accuracy and downstream proof gains are useful evidence for evaluating LLM formalization pipelines and deciding where verifier feedback helps or fails.

title: Contextuality in distributed systems
what: Defines a lattice of distributed-program specifications as subpresheaves of relative execution traces paired with maximal covers of a finite topological variable space. The lattice order captures refinement and parallelism; associated information algebras define local and global consistency, with global consistency related to sequential consistency. The paper constructs relative traces from nondegenerate simplicial cells of products of variable prosets, proves the trace presheaf is flasque and a tuple system, and derives an ordered adjoint information algebra of relations. It characterizes local consistency by flasqueness and global consistency by an inference/join test. A dining-philosophers specification is locally consistent but globally inconsistent: three singleton traces induce a causal loop in chopstick acquisitions. title: Tailoring Stateless Model Checking for Event-Driven Multi-Threaded Programs
what: Introduces Event-DPOR, a dynamic partial-order-reduction algorithm for stateless model checking event-driven multithreaded programs whose handlers process mailbox messages in arbitrary order. The paper defines a finite-thread/shared-variable model with handler mailboxes, happens-before traces and trace equivalence. Event-DPOR extends Optimal-DPOR using happens-before prefixes, weak initials, wakeup trees, parked wakeup sequences and race reversal that can reorder serialized messages. Weak-initial redundancy checking is proved NP-hard; the implementation uses a sequence of inexpensive incomplete tests and a final decision procedure. Correctness proves at least one maximal execution per equivalence class; optimality proves exactly one for non-branching programs. The Nidhugg implementation stores vector clocks and handles first-conflict reversals. Benchmarks compare Event-DPOR with Optimal-DPOR, GenMC DPOR and LAPOR on posters, buyers, ping-pong, consensus, prolific, sparse-mat and plb programs.

title: Compositional Verification of Interacting Systems Using Event Monads
kind: mechanized compositional verification framework and case studies
what: Defines event monads, event systems and Hoare rules in Isabelle/HOL, then composes independently verified handlers into correctness results for distributed summation, a German cache-coherence model and real-time partition scheduling. An event monad returns a set of value/state/output-trace triples and a failure flag, supporting nondeterminism, state updates, signal, bind and while loops. Preconditions and postconditions can depend on traces; an append-only trace frame rule preserves prior output, unlike simply treating traces as arbitrary state. Event systems map events to handlers; unhandled events become environment output, while emitted handled events execute recursively in sequence. Separate inductive reachability and guaranteed-termination predicates support partial/total Hoare rules. Pair and indexed-array lifting rules preserve untouched subsystem properties. The MapReduce model proves that alldone implies the accumulated sum is correct. Cache-coherence proves an invariant ensuring exclusive access for arbitrary N clients. The scheduler case proves watchdog representation refinement, scheduler refinement, their product composition and a final tick-level specification. Both no-switch and next-tick/next-window/next-frame switching cases reuse the watchdog proof.

example major frame 160 ticks, windows 40/60/40/20
assumptions_limits: Interactions send events without waiting for immediate replies; all output events may be placed at function end. Handlers and the recursive event-dispatch semantics execute sequentially, so this is not a general concurrent interleaving or network-failure model. Unhandled events are delegated to the environment. Termination must be proved for recursive event chains and loops; MapReduce permits a server to skip progress forever and proves correctness conditional on alldone, not eventual completion. RTOS verification is at design level: parts resemble C, but AutoCorres C translation is not used; the concrete doubly-linked watchdog is abstracted to a list/array of relative deadlines. Case studies demonstrate functional correctness/refinement, not measured end-to-end implementation performance, schedulability for arbitrary workloads, or spatial separation of an entire OS.
use_for_goal: Contributes a mechanized composition pattern for state-and-trace specifications, useful when designing Verus or agent-generated distributed proofs around independent components and explicit environment events. The cases show how to state output traces and refinement relations and reuse a difficult subsystem proof. Evaluation should distinguish these sequential design models from verified C/Rust implementations or arbitrary asynchronous network interleavings. No TLA+, Verus or LLM-agent evaluation is present.

title: Exact Verification of ReLU Neural Control Barrier Functions
what: Derives necessary and sufficient safety conditions for feedforward ReLU neural control barrier functions and an exact verifier for continuous-time nonlinear systems. Because ReLU NCBFs are nondifferentiable at activation boundaries, the paper uses a generalized Nagumo theorem and Clarke tangent cones. Lemma 2 gives sign-consistency constraints for each activation set; Proposition 1 combines boundary/intersection conditions with safe-set containment. The verifier discretizes state space, uses LiRPA and IBP to enumerate boundary activation sets, prunes impossible sets, and solves nonlinear programs for interiors and intersections. The resulting theorem is sound and complete for the stated model. Experiments cover Darboux, obstacle avoidance, spacecraft rendezvous, and an eight-dimensional system, comparing runtime with dReal and Z3.

title: Parameterized Verification of Round-Based Distributed Algorithms via Extended Threshold Automata.
what: Extends threshold automata (TA) with shared-variable increments, decrements, and resets, including cycles, and develops parameterized coverability and reachability checking. Threshold values are interval-abstracted into abstract counter systems (ACS); a well-structured transition-system backward algorithm computes predecessor bases, builds an error graph, and uses SMT constraints to reject spurious abstract counterexamples. A (0,1)-abstraction handles reachability. Soundness and completeness hold for the abstractions; termination requires restricted updates, while the general extension is a semi-decision procedure. The concrete TA model includes process-location counters, shared variables, parameter vectors and linear resilience conditions. Algorithm 1 computes upward-closed predecessor bases and retains visited transitions so all paths can be checked for non-spuriousness; Lemma 5 gives completeness and Corollary 2 soundness. Theorem 1 proves termination when all update vectors are nonnegative and no resets occur. PRA uses symbolic BDDs; examples include reliable broadcast, Byzantine/crash consensus, commit, phase king and multi-round Red Belly Blockchain. The reachability abstraction preserves only location occupancy and is exact for reachability/coverability specifications.

title: EXVERUS: Verus Proof Repair via Counterexample Reasoning
what: An LLM proof-repair pipeline for Verus synthesizes source-level Z3Py queries, generates concrete candidate counterexamples, diagnoses wrong versus weak annotations, proposes mutations and chooses repairs with verifier feedback. Final proofs are checked by Verus. Counterexample validation is implemented for loop-invariant failures only; other examples are heuristic reasoning aids. Avoids decoding lowered solver models by asking the LLM to encode the failing source obligation directly, with finite vector concretization, namespaced element variables and model blocking. The validation module extracts one loop body, translates invariants into start/end assertions and injects candidate assignments; expected assertion-error patterns distinguish establishment from preservation failures. Error triage chooses replace/relax versus strengthen, five candidate mutations are ranked by blocked validated examples for invariant errors or verified subgoals otherwise. Appendices supply all prompts, construction/filtering policies, toolchain sensitivity and failure cases. A separate qualitative Copilot/Sonnet temporal proof rerun illustrates lifting state invariants to execution-trace entailment in an Anvil Kubernetes controller.

assumptions_limits: A successful final Verus check certifies the supplied formal specifications under the verifier/SMT/toolchain trust assumptions; semantic fidelity to intended requirements and preservation of code/specifications remain separate obligations. Printed prompts forbid changing executable code and requires/ensures. No independent artifact replay was performed. LLM-generated queries can simplify or mistranslate obligations and concretize arrays. Finding no candidate proves neither absence of violating states nor correctness. Validation for non-invariant errors is explicitly future work; the loop module classifies verifier error symptoms rather than supplying a general independently checked concrete execution witness. An inductiveness counterexample may satisfy current invariants but be unreachable from program initialization. LLM reachability triage is heuristic, not a reachability proof. Blocking finitely many states is a search score, not proof that the repaired annotation is inductive; final verification is essential. Results use Verus0.2025.07.12.0b6f3cb/Z3Py4.15.1.0, temperature1.0, at most10 repair iterations and5 mutation responses. Model providers and stochastic generation limit exact reproducibility; AppendixC notes token costs and provider-side changes. No repeated-run uncertainty intervals or significance tests are supplied. Main tasks are146 VerusBench,67 Dafny2Verus,28 Leetcode-Verus and68 HumanEval-Verus. Four original VerusBench tasks were excluded because they no longer verify. Dafny filtering uses five LLM judgments with majority vote, not formal certification that retained specifications express meaningful intended behavior. ObfsBench has266 LLM-transformed tasks with verified versions repaired as needed. Verification of each transformed specification does not establish semantic equivalence to the original program, and obfuscation is not a guarantee that training contamination has been removed. InvariantInjectBench retains187 of426 mutations from142 seeds, with exactly one invariant different from a reference proof. Its one-repair experiment measures near-correct invariant repair, not arbitrary proof synthesis. Blocking/success associations are observational and the reported subsets do not account for all187 tasks. The system-level AppendixA.3 is one qualitative counterexample-augmented Hands-Off rerun, separate from the core query/validation pipeline. The cited81% over800+ VeruSAGE tasks/eight projects is prior work, not a new ExVerus suite result. Six supplied temporal axiom lemmas remain part of its trust/context boundary.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for Verus/verified-Rust proof agents: source-level candidate generation, verifier-guided repair, specification-preservation prompts, version-sensitive evaluation and finite-counterexample limitations. The Anvil case directly touches distributed-controller temporal proofs in TLA+-style logic and shows a state-to-trace entailment gap. It provides one qualitative success, not a new distributed liveness benchmark result. No new Rust semantics, verifier soundness theorem or general proof of algorithm convergence is established.

title: FACT: A Probabilistic Model Checker for Formal Verification with Confidence Intervals
what: Introduces FACT, which computes statistically valid confidence intervals for PCTL and reward properties of parametric discrete-time Markov chains whose unknown transition probabilities are estimated from transition counts. It combines PRISM symbolic verification, simultaneous parameter confidence intervals, convex optimization, and optional hill-climbing allocation of confidence levels. Defines an extended PRISM PMC language with param declarations carrying observed transition counts and independent parameter sets. The verification pipeline first derives a rational function for the property, then computes simultaneous intervals at α^(1/m) per parameter set, solves a convex optimization for the property interval, and optionally reallocates α_i to narrow it. The modular Java architecture wraps PRISM, Kwong–Iglewicz intervals, YALMIP, and hill climbing. Supported formulas are non-nested PCTL P=? [Ψ] plus all PCTL reward forms; case studies cover web, tele-assistance, low-power wireless bus, bounded retransmission, and Zeroconf protocols.

The α^(1/m) allocation is conservative and may be widened; hill-climbing can reduce width by up to 14% but is time-consuming and off by default. Confidence intervals quantify sampling uncertainty, not model-structure or observation bias; implementation depends on external PRISM/MATLAB/YALMIP components.

title: Verification of Eventual Consensus in Synod Using a Failure-Aware Actor Model
what: Introduces a predicate-fair failure-aware actor model (FAM) and mechanically verifies sufficient asynchronous conditions for eventual progress of the basic Synod protocol without a unique leader. The report formalizes proposers, acceptors, quorum predicates, message transitions and actor availability/failure in an asynchronous actor semantics. It states fairness axioms for send/receive, nonfaulty-agent assumptions, and P1/P2 proposal-number conditions preventing higher-numbered interruption. Lemmas show eventual promises and votes from a nonfaulty quorum; Theorem 1 derives that some proposal is eventually learned as chosen. Athena and SPASS mechanically check the proof sketches in roughly 6000 lines. The appendices include the actor-language operational rules and code correspondence discussion.

assumptions_limits: Safety is inherited from Synod; the result is eventual progress, with no time bound. The sufficient condition CND assumes a nonfaulty proposer eventually ready to send a P1/P2 proposal to a quorum of nonfaulty acceptors. FAM assumes stable storage, uncorrupted but asynchronous messages, and fairness axioms; failures can be temporary or permanent, but progress requires the relevant actors eventually available. The proof does not use generic predicate fairness directly, instead relying on a system-specific uninterrupted-proposal property. Applicability to UAM timing requires additional bounds not proved here.

title: Fairness Modulo Theory: A New Approach to LTL Software Model Checking
what: Introduces Fairness Modulo Theory, reducing LTL software verification to absence of feasible fair paths in a Büchi program and prioritizing finite-prefix infeasibility proofs before expensive infinite-path ranking proofs. Ultimate LTLAutomizer implements the CEGAR loop with SMT trace abstraction and termination analysis. The paper defines Büchi programs/products and proves that P satisfies φ iff the product with A¬φ has no trace both fair and feasible. The algorithm maintains an automaton of known infeasible fair traces, checks stem/loop/concatenated finite prefixes, then invokes ranking synthesis only when needed; refineF and refineω generalize proofs. Implementation uses ACSL C parsing, LTL2BA, trace abstraction, ranking synthesis and Büchi automata operations. It reports benchmark behavior on Windows/PostgreSQL/Apache, RERS and coolant sets, including product-size and refinement observations.

title: Fast, Verified Computation for Candle
what: Adds a verified fast computation primitive to the Candle HOL prover kernel. Translates a restricted HOL term to a computation-specific representation,interprets it with native arbitrary-precision arithmetic,and returns a HOL equality theorem. HOL4 proofs show every successful result has a derivation from HOL inference rules;Version4 is integrated into Candle’s existing end-to-end soundness proof. Develops four implemented stages from verified numeral addition to a first-order recursive code-equation interpreter,then compiles its IR to de Bruijn local variables,indexed code vectors and environment-based execution. Establishes soundness through inverse translations to HOL,checked characteristic equations and user-supplied theorem objects,rather than replaying millions of primitive kernel rewrites at runtime. Benchmarks both arithmetic and structural workloads against in-logic evaluators.
assumptions_limits: Soundness theorem assumes the current Candle theory supplies the characteristic equations for arithmetic and compute primitives. Kernel checks user-supplied theorem objects on each call;names alone are insufficient because the user could define constants differently. Context-relative derivability is the guarantee,not unrestricted truth of arbitrary code equations. Code equations must be Candle theorems for fully applied user constants,with cval arguments/results and RHS free variables among formal parameters;every RHS user-defined constant needs an equation. Translation sanity checks reject unsupported input. No arbitrary higher-order HOL/datatype evaluation is supported. Compute values are Lisp-like trees Pairc/Numc.
