title: Faster Verified Real Root Isolation with Descartes’ Rule of Signs
what: Reports Isabelle/HOL verification of termination, soundness and completeness for Descartes-based real root isolation: classical interval bisection Dsc and a Newton-accelerated NewDsc. Uses existing sign-variation and Three Circles theorems, proves a Bernstein splitting lemma to justify discarding gaps, and refines to fraction-free integer-coefficient SML code. Eight small benchmark cases compare with a customized verified Sturm baseline. The authors report mixed results using ChatGPT 5.1 Thinking for newdsc proofs; they also used ChatGPT to help write the SML benchmark driver, without specifying its model. Partial recursive definitions expose a domain predicate, separating termination assumptions from conditional correctness. Square-free complex-root separation plus Three Circles proves bisection terminates. NewDsc accepts a much smaller window only if it preserves the interval’s variation count; a strengthened splitting lemma excludes roots in discarded gaps and on window boundaries. A list-of-lists de Casteljau triangle supports sign-combinatorics induction. Integer coefficient pre-scaling eliminates rational GCD overhead before SML generation. Results distinguish easy polynomials, where Newton overhead hurts, from clustered Mignotte roots, where acceleration helps.
assumptions_limits: The mathematical input is a nonzero real polynomial P, an open interval a<b, and natural degree bound p with degree(P)≤p. The displayed termination theorem further assumes p≠0 and square_free(P). Interval endpoints are excluded from the target root set; exact midpoint roots are returned as degenerate pairs. General integer input needs a square-free factorization and a global Cauchy root bound, which are future wrapper work rather than a completed all-roots interface here. Descartes counts positive roots with multiplicity and bounds them by coefficient sign variations after removing zeros; the difference is even. Only counts zero and one determine the exact root count directly. Transform x to (a x+b)/(x+1) and multiply by (x+1)^degree to map the positive line into (a,b). Bernstein coefficient variations provide the interval test. The paper bridges two prior formalisations when p=degree(P), while correctness statements use a degree upper bound. Dsc returns no interval for variation zero, returns (a,b) for variation one, and otherwise emits the midpoint if it is an exact root then recurses on both open halves. The function package’s domintros mode generates dsc_dom and conditional recursion/induction rules. A separately proved domain theorem establishes termination under its preconditions; total syntax alone is not a proof that every input evaluation terminates. Termination uses the existing formal Three Circles theorem and positive separation among distinct complex roots of a square-free polynomial. Once interval width is small enough, the relevant complex-disc region contains at most one root and variation is at most one. Repeated halving eventually reaches that scale. Square-freeness is a sufficient hypothesis, not a claim that no nonsquare-free input can ever terminate. Soundness dsc_pair_ok permits either a degenerate exact root (m,m) or an interval with exactly one root in its open interior. The displayed dsc_sound assumes domain membership, degree bound, P≠0 and a<b. The displayed dsc_complete assumes domain membership, degree bound and P≠0 and says every root strictly between a,b lies between the endpoints of some output pair. It uses closed endpoint inequalities in the coverage conclusion. Neither displayed theorem by itself states a globally disjoint, ordered or duplicate-free output list; those properties should not be attributed without an additional statement. NewDsc uses N≥2 in the prose. For variation nu≥2, first try one boundary block of width (b−a)/N; if its variation remains nu, recurse only on it with N². Otherwise try windows of the same scale around endpoint corrections lambda=a−nu P(a)/Pprime(a), then from b. A candidate is accepted by a variation-preservation test, rather than by trusting Newton convergence. Helpers’ full definitions, derivative-zero handling and complete newdsc theorem preconditions are not printed. If both jumps fail, bisect, test the exact midpoint and recurse on both halves with Nprime=max(4,floor(sqrt(N))). Successful jumps square N for more aggressive future shrinking; fallback reduces that aggressiveness. The paper says NewDsc termination and soundness are similar to Dsc and reports all three properties verified, but only gives a detailed new completeness argument in the article. The full source proof scripts were not independently inspected. Ordinary splitting proves Var(a,u)+Var(u,v)+Var(v,b)≤Var(a,b). If the retained window has the original variation count, both discarded open gaps have variation zero and therefore no root. This does not by itself exclude roots at u or v; the paper explicitly invokes a strengthened lemma for these boundary cases but does not display that stronger formula. Treat boundary exclusion as a reported formal lemma, not a consequence of the weaker printed inequality alone. The de Casteljau triangle takes convex combinations with positive weights summing to one. Its two boundaries encode the subinterval Bernstein coefficients. Inserting a convex combination between adjacent real numbers cannot add sign changes. The authors represent successive rows as a list of lists and prove monotonicity by strong induction on the coefficient list, then induct on the triangle for splitting. This differs from the cited Rocq pointwise-recursive algebraic representation because the current proof needs coefficient-list combinatorics. For code generation, decompose interval transformation into a Taylor shift by a, scaling by width b−a, polynomial reversal and a Taylor shift by one. A list-based Ruffini algorithm implements shifts; an iterative mapping loop implements scaling. Equivalent polynomial transformations can have very different arithmetic costs, so this is a separate refinement step from abstract termination/correctness. Fraction-free shifts use a=n_a/d_a and pre-scale coefficient c_i by d_a^{k−i}; denominator signs/normalization must preserve the intended nonzero scaling and sign-variation result. The adjusted width (b−a)d_a is represented by numerator/denominator and further coefficient scaling clears fractions before they appear. The text reports verified integer root tests and partial tail-recursive dsc_int/newdsc_int suitable for SML. It does not give all refinement equations or the complete integer implementation in the paper. Benchmark baseline is Joosten/Thiemann/Yamada’s verified Sturm isolate, customized to remove square-free factorization and algebraic-number packaging. Thus timings compare core isolation on already suitable inputs, not complete algebraic-number pipelines. Four random polynomials P1–P4 come from [22]; four Mignotte-type polynomials have form x^n−2(2^tau x−1)^2 and tight root clusters. This is a targeted eight-case experiment, not a broad random-distribution benchmark. Runs use Poly/ML 5.9.2 on an Apple M4 CPU with 16 GB memory. Table 1 gives milliseconds, median of five runs or average of 100 runs when runtime is below 10 ms. No spread/confidence intervals, memory/GC measurements, exact M4 model, optimization flags or Isabelle build version are specified here. No comparison with an unverified state-of-the-art root isolator is reported; approaching that performance is future work. Table 1 has two side-by-side groups: P1–P4 compare isolate,dsc_int,newdsc_int,dsc_exec; Mignotte cases compare isolate,dsc_int,newdsc_int,newdsc_exec. The unoptimized column is different in the two groups. The author claim of 10–200 times optimization speedup is rounded: P2 has dsc_exec/dsc_int=6.7/0.5=13.4 and M32,32 has newdsc_exec/newdsc_int=88617/449≈197.4. Do not treat cross-group unoptimized timings as the same algorithm. Direct GenAI report: ChatGPT 5.1 Thinking received corresponding dsc proofs as reference for newdsc proofs. Authors call its generated soundness proof largely correct with a few Sledgehammer-repaired errors, and say the other generated proofs were less valuable and not worth using overall. The SML experimental runner was also written with ChatGPT help. There is no trial count, prompt transcript, proof acceptance rate, cost, human-time measurement or controlled comparison. This is a specific qualitative human-assisted proof-reuse report, not autonomous end-to-end theorem proving. Formal artifact is linked at https://github.com/Aeacu2/Dsc with a Software Heritage snapshot and artifact DOI 10.4230/artifacts.26768. Isabelle kernel/library assumptions, the code-generator/compiler/runtime boundary and correctness of the experimental driver remain part of the trusted or uninspected execution chain for this reading. Reported machine checking is author evidence; no local build or artifact audit was performed. Future work includes square-free/all-root wrappers, dyadic rationals, approximate arithmetic and refinement to LLVM using Isabelle/LLVM. These are not current measured deliverables. There is no distributed-system protocol, verified Rust, Verus or TLA+ result; relevance to proof agents comes from the explicit LLM report and the distinction between abstract correctness, completeness boundaries and executable refinement.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence of LLM-assisted Isabelle proof work with positive and negative qualitative outcomes and human repair. Reader inference: useful proof-agent evaluation distinctions are terminating inputs versus conditional soundness, no-loss completeness for aggressive pruning, explicit strengthened boundary lemmas, abstract-to-integer refinement and benchmark preprocessing scope. Related verified-code methodology can inform Verus/Rust work, but this paper itself uses Isabelle/SML and no distributed protocol or TLA+.

title: Fault-Tolerant Replication with Pull-Based Consensus in MongoDB
what: Describes MongoDB replication as a pull-based Raft derivative: secondaries fetch from any sync source, report durable positions through relayed UpdatePosition acknowledgments, and receive commit points separately. Safety requires the acknowledging server’s current term, rather than counting copies of an entry alone. Gives a quorum-intersection argument and reports TLA+ model checking, controlled chaining/failover experiments and Atlas production telemetry. Records the five-server stale-primary counterexample, acknowledgment-term repair and leader-completeness argument; log overlap/rollback and initial-sync details; weak versus linearizable options; election/priority/read extensions; all numerical benchmark/production claims and their measurement boundaries; literal appendix pseudocode inequalities. Formal evidence is a proof sketch plus reported model checking without configuration/results supplied in the paper, not a machine-checked implementation theorem.
assumptions_limits: A single replica set replicates a log; sharding is orthogonal. Only the primary accepts writes. Normal election uses one persistent vote per term and the Raft log up-to-date order (last entry term then timestamp). OpTime=(entry term, logical timestamp) is lexicographically ordered; timestamps are logical positions, not a physical clock assumption. Correct durable storage persists term/vote/log before RPC responses. Byzantine nodes, corrupted storage and arbitrary duplicate IDs are outside the presented protocol. Safety follows Raft-style log/election assumptions despite asynchronous delay. Availability requires a communicating majority, eventual message/protocol progress and an electable primary; no partition-wide availability or deterministic asynchronous election termination is proved. Persistent term/vote/log are distinguished from volatile lastCommitted/lastApplied/lastPosition. The paper describes crash/restart operation and WiredTiger rollback, but does not prove implementation/storage refinement. PullEntries includes the last local timestamp and returns an overlapping entry plus newer entries. The first returned OpTime must match the last local OpTime before appending. A newer divergent branch triggers last-common-entry search, log truncation, rollback and replay. Same-log requests wait up to5 seconds by default; streaming database cursors batch data and avoid request-per-entry overhead. The data source need not be the primary. UpdatePosition relays per-member maximum known positions toward the primary, batches between forwarding rounds and permits one in-flight request per sync source. Commit requires a majority supporting the candidate entry and its current leader term. A higher RPC term updates currentTerm and converts the receiver to follower before commitment; the global higher-term rule covers UpdatePosition even though its local receiver block only lists merge/forward. Five-server safety counterexample is specific to separating replication from acknowledgment: a term3 voter may still pull term2 data from a stale primary. Counting durable copies alone can falsely commit an entry later overwritten by the term3 leader. Acknowledgment server terms stop the stale leader before committing. The quorum argument relies on Raft log matching/leader completeness and election restrictions; it is a paper proof sketch rather than a full separately supplied inductive proof. Authors report writing TLA+ and applying model checking (§3.3, ref33), but provide no model configuration, bounds on nodes/entries/terms, explored state counts, explicit checked invariant list, model-checking output, discovered bug count or implementation-refinement result. Unit/integration/fuzz/fault-injection testing is reported without quantified coverage. External TLA+ source was not inspected for this record. Sync-source selection only chooses a newer observed log position and checks again on PullEntries responses because the source can roll back. The paper claims cycles can never form. A per-choice newer condition alone does not constitute a proof for time-varying distributed observations; no concrete cycle counterexample was constructed and no implementation failure is asserted. WiredTiger speculatively applies entries before commitment. Stable timestamp is the locally known commit point and must not exceed the common-branch timestamp during rollback. Restore stable data then replay through the common entry. Weak-consistency clients can see/acknowledge speculative data; durability/linearizability statements must be restricted to appropriate strong options. Legacy mmap rollback uses different mechanisms omitted from the paper. Initial sync uses a possibly inconsistent collection scan rather than a snapshot: record source applied start, clone, record applied end, then replay from start beyond the recorded end point; restart on source failure. Log retention defaults to5% of free disk at startup. Insert-existing/update-or-delete-missing rules and primary-side absolute assignments make replication operations idempotent. Correctness also needs sequence ordering, schema/scan assumptions and sufficient log retention; single-operation idempotence alone does not prove every arbitrary sequence/clone state correct. A new primary can fetch old-term entries during catchup until it creates a new-term entry, sees no newer source data, or times out. This preserves weakly acknowledged uncommitted data best-effort, not guaranteed durability. Arbiters vote without holding data: a primary-secondary-arbiter set after primary failure may accept weak writes but cannot commit majority writes. Up to50 total members and7 voters; nonvoters do not count toward election/commit majorities. Planned handoff pauses writes and catches up an eligible secondary before immediate election. Priority elections use a dry-run/pre-vote to avoid needless higher-term disruption by stale candidates. It does not resolve all partition-induced repeated elections. Default election timeout10s; Atlas telemetry mentions10 or5s. Linearizable reads occur only at the primary and wait for a synchronization round trip, optionally piggybacking a concurrent oplog entry; a complete read linearization/current-term proof is not supplied. Printed Raft Appendix A p701 reverses two inequalities: AppendEntries rule1 says reject term>currentTerm; rule5 says change commitIndex if leaderCommit<commitIndex. The first reverses the conventional stale-term test (interaction with the global higher-term rule depends on evaluation order), and the second permits commit regression if followed literally; these are apparent errors in the printed comparison pseudocode, not a demonstrated MongoDB implementation defect. PDF visual checks recover >= lost by text extraction in Raft send/commit tests and MongoDB majority-position comparison. Printed MongoDB client response condition p702 is strict lastCommitted>entry.OpTime, while majority replication comparison is >= in the PDF. Literal strict response could wait for a later entry after its own entry commits, stalling an isolated write absent another/background entry; body says updates return when committed. lastApplied is described as monotonic despite rollback; distinguishing logical progress from speculative physical application needs clarification. Neither issue was reproduced in code. Controlled tests use AWS m5d.2xlarge (8vCPU/32GB/local SSD), five server VMs (three US East Virginia/two US West Oregon) and two client VMs. Primary and committing majority are East, so strong writes need not wait for WAN. Closed-loop clients replace a random document among1M documents each with one1000-byte string; vary thread count. Chaining forces one West secondary through the other West secondary, other secondaries pull primary. These settings do not isolate arbitrary topology or WAN quorum placement. Unthrottled chaining on/off throughput is approximately the same (~12–13k ops/s); primary is CPU bound with >250k context switches/s and oplog reads about5% of one core. Chaining halves cross-datacenter traffic, not total traffic or commit latency generally. In additional three-node tests (placement unspecified) with200Mbps primary limit, approximate plotted saturation increases from8800 to13200ops/s and p50 from60ms down to40ms. No repeats/confidence intervals or raw data reported. Single five-node same-datacenter failover trace,64 clients: old primary crashes at10s, election timeout10s, throughput drops around12s and recovers around21–23s; old primary recovers40s without clear throughput disturbance. This is illustrative, not exhaustive fault coverage. Version4.4 versus3.6 compares full releases, including journaling/other optimizations, so performance change cannot be attributed only to consensus protocol. Claims about old protocol assumptions/split-brain are authors’ characterization, not independently reproduced. Atlas June2020 version fractions26.86/44.17/28.54% sum99.57%; the remainder is unspecified. Failover causes89.03% planned/6.15% priority/4.82% timeout. The sample sizes, cluster selection/exclusions and variance are not given. Plotted outage CDFs stop at95%, so no extreme-tail claim follows. Production Local Write Unavailability starts at election and ends when the new primary accepts writes; Majority Write Unavailability ends when the first step-up no-op commits. These omit earlier old-primary pause/unresponsiveness and are shorter than client outage. Planned p95=.37/3.08s; timeout p95=6.41/10.24s plus typically10 or5s before election. The authors’ proposed heartbeat explanation for1/2s clusters is a belief, not a measured causal test. Week-long replication telemetry reports50% of replica sets below8.08MB/day,95% below7.94GB/day,top5% generating>92.6% of traffic. Figures11/12 instead label host count, leaving the unit of aggregation unclear. Monthly$300–5000 savings uses the paper’s historical AWS$0.01–0.147/GB estimate, not current pricing or observed customer bills. Appendix B setup describes closed-loop1000-byte inserts, while Table1 describes an adapted TPC-C benchmark with100 clients/100 warehouses and five transaction types. Preserve this workload-description inconsistency. MongoDB denormalized/query/transaction semantics are used; this is not a certified standard TPC-C result. Three server VMs/one client VM are in one availability zone, no bandwidth limit. Total throughput1453.47→1506.98 (~3.68%); modest gain is attributed to CPU offload. Primary total traffic15.56→11.70MB/s; per-secondary oplog traffic4.05MB/s. Difference3.86MB/s need not exactly equal4.05 under changed throughput/rounding. Figure8 whole-version comparison has mixed outcomes:4.4 versus3.6 relative throughput approximately190% at2 clients,130% at8/1024,89% at64/256 and slightly below100% at128. These are graph estimates, not raw benchmark cells. Gains and regressions coexist; neither is attributable solely to consensus because full releases differ.

Useful specification/proof/evaluation cases include term-qualified acknowledgments, rollback/weak consistency, initial-sync idempotency, read barriers, ghost versus physical progress, and outage metric boundaries. title: CTL* model checking for data-aware dynamic systems with arithmetic
what: Introduces a finite-history-constraint abstraction and CTL*f model-checking procedure for data-aware dynamic systems with arithmetic (DDSAs), synthesizing initial-variable conditions for branching-time properties. The procedure recursively reduces CTL* subformulas to LTL checks over configuration maps, computes history constraints with quantifier elimination, and terminates when finitely many constraint formulas exist up to equivalence at the property quantifier depth. This criterion yields decidability for rational/real monotonicity constraints and integer periodicity constraints, while a two-counter-machine reduction proves feedback-free and bounded-lookback systems remain undecidable for branching time. The ada prototype accepts DDSA or bounded Data Petri Net models, calls CVC5/Z3, returns configuration maps and product graphs, and reports detailed SMT counts and runtimes on mined and normative business processes.

title: Fine-Grained Caching of Verification Results.
what: Boogie caches whole implementation results using entity/dependency checksums, then reuses individual checked statements by injecting assumptions guarded by conditions that reconstruct the old call-contract assumptions. Unchanged failures can be reported immediately. Implemented for the Dafny IDE and tested on eight recorded expert development sessions. Details conservative control-flow statement hashes, separation of procedure bodies from contracts and transitive function definitions, guarded reuse after changed pre/postconditions and modifies clauses, old-failure eligibility, error-report-limit exclusion and loop handling. Explains why stable generated names matter and why many cached checks need not substantially reduce time when a remaining check dominates.
assumptions_limits: §§3.1–3.2: frontends supply entity checksums from relevant AST parts; comments/whitespace may be ignored. Boogie computes dependency checksums. Correctness relies on complete semantic dependencies and valid cached outcomes. Hash equality is used operationally, not a proved semantic-equivalence decision; no collision analysis, cache corruption defense or solver/configuration invalidation specification is presented. §3.1: modular procedure calls depend on specifications rather than implementation bodies. A changed body alone need not invalidate callers; changed function definitions can invalidate transitive callers. The p.384 sentence says changed specifications may invalidate “callees”, while examples and modular dependency explanation concern callers. §4.1: each statement checksum hashes pretty-printed statement plus all preceding control-flow statement checksums, rather than precise data dependencies; function-call expressions also include callee dependency checksum. Loops first cut using invariants; preconditions become entry assumes and postconditions exit asserts. No cyclic hash fixpoint required. §4.3: fine-grained injection applies to medium/low-priority implementations whose cached run did not hit the limit on reported errors. Merely not having a reported failure cannot establish old success when error reporting was truncated. New implementations follow ordinary verification. §§4.2–4.3: changed call contracts are handled separately from plain statement hashes. If old transitive function definitions remain available and unchanged, reconstruct old precondition and postcondition/modifies assumptions; otherwise set a fresh assumption variable false and omit old precondition. This prevents unsound reuse when old formulas cannot be expressed with unchanged meaning. §4.3: snapshot old values of globals newly added to modifies; post-call guard combines old postcondition and equality of these globals with their old values. Removed modifies globals need no equality because old proofs already allowed arbitrary values. Assumption variables start true and update by conjunction, preserving failed old assumptions. §4.3: old successful checked condition P becomes assume(A⇒P) before its actual check, where A contains relevant assumption variables whose update can reach the use. If A holds, the check is discharged from cached knowledge; otherwise solver must verify it. A definitely-false relevant variable prevents reuse. Old failures are recycled only with no relevant assumption variables. §4.3: old-precondition placeholder is filled only if old call had no reported error and no relevant variable is definitely false; otherwise dropped. Loop optimization avoids havoc of assumption variables under modular loop reasoning; justification explicitly assumes no break for post-loop independence and notes previous unrolling can change initial values. §§4/7: supports strengthened contracts and weaker contracts whose old assumptions remain true in a relevant calling context. Not a general equivalence proof across program versions. More precise reuse for changed user assumes, preconditions and loop invariants, plus slicing, remains future work. §4: correctness explained through instrumentation arguments/examples, not a formal soundness theorem or mechanized cache proof. Depends on Boogie transforms, SMT outcomes, frontend dependency tracking and proper cached-result interpretation. Stores snapshots/results, not proof certificates. §4/Fig.5: Snapshot2 prose strengthens gcd postcondition to 1≤r, but printed line15 still asserts 0≤r. Caption says inserted assumes at lines7/9/13, while figure and p.389 prose show4/9/13; line7 is the still-failing assertion. Record these presentation inconsistencies without inferring an implementation bug. §5: eight unscripted expert IDE sessions with programs several hundred lines, not eight 30,000-line benchmarks. Ironclad >30,000 LOC is user-feedback context. No participant count, hardware, tool versions, repetitions/variance, controlled productivity study or full latency distribution reported. §5/Fig.6: default timeout 10s per procedure implementation, not per session. Timeout-reduction range applies to sessions with nonzero basic-cache timeouts. Reported average 17% is approximately mean per-session time reduction; it differs from reduction of aggregate total time. §5: larger benefit than parallel SMT instances is an author observation without numeric parallel baseline here. No artifact execution or independent reproduction. One remaining hard check can dominate despite many fully reused checks.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for incremental LLM proof/specification agents and SMT verification in Verus/Rust: track semantic dependencies across edits, reuse only under explicit old assumptions, invalidate after changed contracts/functions, preserve stable generated names and distinguish cached success from incomplete error reporting. Paper implementation is Dafny/Boogie; no Verus/Rust/TLA+, distributed protocol proof or LLM-agent evaluation.

title: Synthesizing Dominant Strategies for Liveness (Full Version)
what: Introduces delay-dominance, a strategy relation that compares unmatched progress failures against alternatives, to make best-effort synthesis compositional for many safety and liveness specifications. It defines a delay-dominance game, proves compositionality under an automaton bad-prefix criterion, and gives a universal co-Buchi automaton for synthesis. The paper formalizes the game where Spoiler chooses alternative-automaton branches first and Duplicator responds on the candidate strategy, proving self-dominance and that delay-dominant implies remorsefree dominant. It identifies existence of bad prefixes as the condition allowing blame of one component after composition, proves composition and winningness for realizable specifications, and constructs the recognizer by combining ACAs for phi and not-phi, Miyano-Hayashi conversion, and universal projection over alternative outputs. The resulting automaton has O(2^{|phi|^2}) states and bounded synthesis remains 2EXPTIME. Examples show immediate-send versus wait-for-peer strategies and mixed existential/universal ACA choices.

title: First-Order Model Checking on Monadically Stable Graph Classes
what: Establishes fixed-parameter first-order model checking on every monadically stable graph class and proves monadic stability is the tractability boundary for hereditary edge-stable classes. The tractability proof first establishes almost-linear neighborhood complexity: for every ε, the number of distinct closed-neighborhood traces on a parameter set A is O(|A|^{1+ε}). A reduction using branching index, sampling and nowhere-dense machinery yields this bound. Welzl's low-crossing-number order then gives distance-r neighborhood covers of constant diameter and subpolynomial overlap via a greedy compact-interval partition; the cover can be computed in O(n^{4+ε}). Substituting it into the Flipper-game model-checking framework improves the overall bound to O_{C,ε,φ}(n^{5+ε}). For hardness, Ramsey refinement and k-flips characterize non-stability by induced subdivided cliques or webs. Careful existential “deobfuscation” yields effective interpretations of all graphs, giving AW[*]-hard FO model checking, W[1]-hard existential FO model checking, and W[1]-hard induced-subgraph isomorphism under Turing reductions.
numbers: Theorem 1 gives O_{C,ε,φ}(n^{5+ε}) model checking; neighborhood-cover construction is O_{C,r,ε}(n^{4+ε}).
Theorem 3 gives O_{C,ε}(|A|^{1+ε}) neighborhood complexity for every ε>0.
Theorem 2 gives AW[*]-hard FO, W[1]-hard existential FO, and W[1]-hard induced-subgraph isomorphism for hereditary edge-stable non-monadically-stable classes.
assumptions_limits: The positive result assumes a fixed monadically stable graph class C and ε>0, with class-dependent constants; the hardness result assumes heredity and edge-stability. The construction handles neighborhood formulas on vertex pairs, not the stronger tuple-type bounds left as Conjecture 3. The general monadically NIP tractability conjecture remains open because suitable Flipper/decomposition machinery is unknown; the authors also state the theorem does not settle tuple neighborhoods. Hardness transfers through polynomial effective interpretations and parameterized reductions, not through an implementation benchmark. The algorithm's n^{5+ε} bound is asymptotic and can hide large class/formula constants.
use_for_goal: This is a rigorous complexity-theoretic account of when FO model checking is tractable on graph classes, with explicit structural invariants and hardness constructions. It is relevant to formal verification because it distinguishes a proved fixed-parameter algorithm from hardness regimes and identifies the missing decomposition assumptions an automated verifier must expose.

title: Pushing the Boundaries of Natural Reasoning: Interleaved Bonus from Formal-Logic Verification in Language Models
what: Introduces FLV, which interleaves formal symbolic verification with natural-language reasoning and trains Qwen2.5-7B/14B in two stages: execution-validated formal-logic supervised fine-tuning, then GRPO policy optimization with hierarchical rewards for format, correctness and verifier feedback. Formal modules return satisfiability, counterexamples or execution outputs during generation; a flexible mode allows direct numerical calculation with formal checks used as validation. The paper measures a logical-consistency gap before training: 39.3% of steps in chains with correct answers are formally disproved, rising to 52.4% for incorrect answers. Data synthesis uses DeepSeek-R1 reasoning, GPT-4o answer judging and Claude Sonnet formal translation; exact-match and semantic-equivalence checks retain executable traces. Training uses about 17k samples, 16 NVIDIA H800 GPUs, 120 RL steps and at most four verification rounds. Across KOR-Bench, BBH, MATH-500, AIME24, GPQA-Diamond and TheoremQA, FLV-RL averages 51.9 (7B) and 58.6 (14B), versus Natural-SFT 36.5 and FLV-RL-14B reaches 30.2% on AIME24 and 63.5% on TheoremQA. Ablations show FLV-SFT 49.8 versus Natural-SFT 36.5; symbolic/logic tools are 62.5% of FLV-RL calls. title: Automated Software Verification of Hyperliveness.
what: Introduces Forall-Exist Hoare Logic (FEHL) and ForEx, a constraint-based verifier for finite-program ∀k∃l relational properties (Forall-Exist Hoare Tuples). The method symbolically postpones existential nondeterministic choices as parameters, computes parametric strongest postconditions, and discharges resulting first-order constraints with SMT. FEHL provides self-composition, sequencing, conditionals, loops and consequence rules; the paper proves soundness and completeness relative to sound/complete unary Hoare and under-approximate systems. ForEx implements eager restriction satisfiability checks, a minimal C-like language with arrays/bitvectors, Z3 support for linear integer arithmetic, arrays and finite bitvectors, and guess-and-check invariant generation. Experiments compare ForEx against HyPA, PCSat and HyPro on k-safety, GNI, refinement and related benchmarks. ForEx is faster on solved instances but its counting-based loop alignment misses context-dependent alignments and it cannot prove termination of existential loops, leaving some GNI instances unsolved.

ForEx cannot currently support termination proofs for existentially quantified loops
assumptions_limits: FEHT validity quantifies finite terminating executions; the algorithm is for verification, not refutation of invalid FEHTs (which requires existential-universal reasoning). Completeness is relative to complete unary over/under-approximate proof systems and, for loops, depends on adequate invariant guesses. The tool explores a restricted counting-based loop alignment, so state-dependent alignments are outside its scope. Experiments use small benchmark programs, an M1 Pro with 32 GB, and user-provided invariant hints for marked cases.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to richer relational specifications of distributed behavior: existential witness executions and hyperliveness go beyond ordinary safety and require explicit alignment, under-approximation and solver obligations. It offers a design/evaluation reference for agents generating such specifications.

title: Formal Proofs of Tarjan’s Strongly Connected Components Algorithm in Why3, Coq and Isabelle
what: Three mechanized total-correctness developments for an abstract functional version of Tarjan’s strongly connected components algorithm on finite directed graphs. The returned set is exactly the graph’s SCC partition. Compares Why3 first-order VC automation, Coq/SSReflect higher-order proof and Isabelle/HOL with reconstructed automated proofs, using related invariant ideas and deliberately avoiding richer refinement infrastructure. Details invariant discovery, seven Why3 assertions and two interactive Coq obligations, termination via lexicographic measures versus fuel, removal of explicit colors/stack in Coq, and Isabelle domain-conditioned recursion. Reports proof sizes, checking times, interaction patterns and trust differences. Representation changes improved clarity/reduced Coq proof size but sometimes impaired SMT stability. Separates external proof discovery from kernel reconstruction.
assumptions_limits: Finite vertices and successor closure. Sets, maps and graph operations remain abstract. Arbitrary nonempty-root choice is handled by underspecification and correctness for any legal choice. No mutable-array/pointer, machine-overflow, memory-safety or executable-code refinement theorem is supplied. Preserves linear-time algorithmic structure under suitable concrete implementations; does not present a machine-checked cost bound or executable performance evaluation. Coq reconstructs a stack from serial numbers and is not asserted to extract directly to efficient code. Why3 trusts translations and automatic backends without independently checking their proofs; two obligations use Coq proofs. Coq and Isabelle check final proofs with their kernels. Formal statements, libraries and kernels remain trust boundaries. External solver success alone does not suffice for Isabelle acceptance. Coq and Isabelle developments follow the initial Why3 proof and share its mathematical strategy. This is not blinded independent discovery or a controlled productivity comparison. Initial Why3 effort includes other graph algorithms; later efforts benefit from existing invariants. Partial correctness proves postconditions if a call terminates. Total correctness also proves valid-call termination. Isabelle recursion can diverge on malformed environments; recursive equations require domain conditions until valid-call termination is established. Human contracts, invariants, lemmas, decomposition and hints remain essential. Automatic proof lines do not mean autonomous verification. Table4 usability/readability ratings are explicitly subjective and historically scoped. Different hardware, timing scopes and proof units prevent direct ranking from the reported times/line counts. Isabelle interactions are coarser than Coq lines. No matched-hardware comparison, randomized user study, solver ablation or timing variance.
use_for_goal: Useful baseline for evaluating LLM-generated invariants/proofs: keep algorithm/abstraction comparable, measure human hints and proof construction separately from replay, distinguish solver acceptance from kernel certificates, and count termination/refinement work. SCCs support verification infrastructure, but no separate distributed protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment is studied.

what: Gives the first machine-checkable, input-size-dependent-round security analysis of sumcheck. A generic public-coin interactive-proof locale is instantiated with an abstract generalized sumcheck protocol, then specialized to multivariate polynomials by proving algebraic axioms, yielding formal soundness and completeness. The modular formalization separates protocol reasoning from concrete polynomial representations. Abstract assumptions include a commutative monoid, finite support, evaluation/instantiation commutation, degree bounds and a root-counting property. Isabelle locales model recursive prover/verifier state and soundness/completeness; concrete multivariate polynomials are represented with Isabelle finite-support polynomial types. The framework is intended to support ring/module variants and protocols that use sumcheck as a subroutine.
numbers: No runtime or benchmark numbers reported
Formal results include Theorem II.7 public-coin sumcheck with null completeness
One input-size-dependent number of rounds is handled by recursive formalization
assumptions_limits: Security is proved under axiomatized algebraic properties and the modeled public-coin interaction; concrete cryptographic assumptions and implementation behavior outside the formal model are not covered. Completeness is null completeness in the stated interactive-proof language. Formalization is Isabelle/HOL and no executable performance evaluation is reported. Fiat–Shamir or downstream protocol security requires additional modeling.
use_for_goal: Demonstrates how to make cryptographic protocol proofs reusable: isolate generic interaction/security locales, then discharge algebraic obligations for concrete structures. This is relevant to modular verification of distributed proof protocols.

quotes.text: We follow a general and modular approach.
We define and formalize a generalized version of the sumcheck protocol and prove its soundness and completeness.
Our general and modular analysis ... simplifies proofs by decoupling the reasoning about the protocol from reasoning about concrete polynomial representations.
we axiomatize the key properties of polynomials required by the protocol

title: On the Accuracy of Formal Verification of Selective Defenses for TDoS Attacks
what: Formalizes a coordinated-call telephony denial-of-service attack and three SeVen selective defenses in Maude/PVeStA, then compares statistical model-checking simulations with Asterisk/SIPp experiments. The model covers uniform, roulette, and k²-tournament dropping, exponential versus lognormal honest-call durations, Erlang-sized capacity/rates, and quality measures for complete, incomplete, unsuccessful calls and interrupted-call duration. Simulations predict attack effectiveness, defense ranking, and better lognormal behavior; network experiments validate availability trends but expose timing inaccuracies. The paper quantifies setup differences (proxy versus in-application defense, constant latency, omitted Asterisk workers and contention) and reports simulation minutes versus hour-long experiments.
numbers: simulations: k=24, 99% confidence, five attacker/legitimate proportions, 40 time units
experiments: k=200, 60 calls/min, 60 minutes and 3,600 calls each
100-tournament: >70% exponential and >80% lognormal calls completed; >95% reached INCALL
roulette: >70% exponential and >75% lognormal complete, <6% incomplete
formal timing predictions diverged from experiments by up to 30%
assumptions_limits: Formal model abstracts Asterisk internals, competing CPU/network workloads, variable latency, and uses scaled-down parameters; attackers are indefinitely long calls and total traffic is kept at or below normal rate. Results are highly accurate for availability but less accurate for timing (up to roughly 30 percentage-point discrepancy); roulette-versus-uniform ranking was not predicted.

title: Formalizing Results on Directed Sets in Isabelle/HOL (Proof Pearl)
what: Reports Isabelle/HOL proofs of Iwamura’s directed-set decomposition, equivalence of directed completeness and nonempty well-related completeness, and equivalence of Scott continuity and preservation of nonempty well-related suprema. Uses cardinal-indexed well-orders on the original carrier instead of a universal ordinal type. Generalizes from partial orders to quasi-orders and removes all codomain order/completeness assumptions in the continuity theorem. The uncountable construction closes each strict prefix under chosen finite upper bounds by countable iteration, bounding its size by the larger of the prefix size and countable infinity. Countably infinite carriers require a different finite-stage sequence; an inverse order isomorphism reconciles its natural-number index with the carrier index. Cardinal induction chooses possibly nonunique suprema of smaller directed sets, turns their monotone image into a well-related set, and transfers its supremum back to the original directed set. A strengthened simultaneous induction proves continuity for every possible supremum without assuming transitivity in the codomain.
assumptions_limits: Directed means every finite subset, including the empty subset, has an upper bound in the carrier. Thus directed sets are nonempty. The familiar nonempty plus pairwise-upper-bound definition needs transitivity for equivalence. Iwamura’s theorem assumes reflexivity and an infinite directed carrier but does not assume transitivity; completeness and continuity equivalences assume a quasi-order, meaning reflexivity and transitivity, without antisymmetry. A well-related set is one whose every nonempty subset has a least element. This implies reflexivity but is defined without assuming transitivity or antisymmetry. A pre-well-order additionally assumes a quasi-order. In the main theorem’s quasi-ordered ambient carrier, well-related subsets inherit transitivity. Nonempty qualifiers exclude a requirement for a least element/bottom arising from an empty supremum. Choice is used to select a least-cardinality well-order of the carrier and a bound f(X) for each finite X using SOME. Later it selects a supremum for each smaller directed set. This last selection cannot use unique choice because removing antisymmetry makes suprema potentially nonunique. More constructive proof organization does not mean a choice-free or computational construction. Isabelle/HOL cannot collect arbitrarily large ordinals of every type into one ordinal type. The workaround represents an ordinal by a well-order relation and uses cardinal-library comparisons across types. The index order on A is the particular least well-order representing |A|; it is different from the original relation whose directedness is being studied. Locales permit both relations, unlike fixing one order per type through a type class. For the least well-order, every strict prefix A_prec(a) has strictly smaller cardinality. Leastness is essential: an arbitrary well-order may have a strict prefix as large as the whole carrier. An infinite least-cardinality well-order has no greatest element, since deleting one point preserves infinite cardinality. Therefore the union of all strict prefixes equals A. That equality fails for nonempty finite carriers, which are handled separately. Uncountable case: F(X)=X union {f(Y):Y is a finite subset of X}; F^omega(X) is the union of its finite iterates. Any finite set in this union is contained in one common stage, so its chosen upper bound is in the next stage. This argument needs no transitivity. F and its closure are monotone; closure stays within A and includes X. Cardinality control splits finite and infinite prefixes. A finite starting set has finite stages and at most countable closure, which is still smaller than uncountable A. For infinite X, finite subsets have the same cardinality as X, each iterate preserves that cardinality, and a countable union has size at most |X|. The proof uses existing cardinal-library lemmas; it does not assume that the original uncountable cardinal is regular. Countably infinite case: choose order isomorphism seq from natural numbers to the least well-order on A. Seq(0)={f(empty)} and Seq(n+1)=Seq(n) union {seq(n),f(Seq(n) union {seq(n)})}. Every stage is finite and directed because the added bound also bounds itself by reflexivity. This avoids countable closure becoming as large as the entire countable carrier. Compose Seq with inverse(seq) to obtain the same A-to-subsets type as the uncountable construction. Final Iwamura family is piecewise in the cardinality case; every I(a) is directed, smaller than A, nested in the chosen index order, and its union covers A. Proof locales collect definitions under directedness and are interpreted in the final theorem’s reflexive context. The printed mono_uncountable lemma uses domain D where surrounding construction uses A; the record does not infer an error in the AFP theorem from that local presentation. Reverse completeness direction: every nonempty finite subset of a well-related set has a greatest element, proved by removing a least element and inducting on finite size. This proves directedness even without transitivity. Forward direction uses cardinal induction on directed D. A finite D has a greatest element by directedness; an infinite D is decomposed by Iwamura and each smaller I(d) receives an inductively obtained supremum s(d). Monotonicity of I and of taking suprema makes s monotone from the chosen well-order on D to the original relation. A monotone image of a well-related set is well-related even without injectivity. Completeness supplies a supremum x of s(D). Covering D by I(d) and ambient transitivity shows x bounds D; any bound of D bounds each I(d), hence s(D), so x is least among bounds of D. C-continuity includes f(A) subset B and preservation of every existing supremum for each nonempty C-subset. It does not require preserving empty suprema. Under a reflexive domain and class C containing every related pair {i,j}, this property implies monotonicity. Well-related sets meet that condition, without requiring codomain reflexivity or transitivity. The continuity equivalence assumes only a quasi-ordered, nonempty-well-related-complete domain. The codomain is an arbitrary carrier and binary relation, with no reflexivity, transitivity, antisymmetry or completeness assumptions. The proof establishes completeness and preservation simultaneously by cardinal induction. It does not compose codomain inequalities through an unstated transitivity assumption. For continuity, a supplied supremum x of D may differ from the one constructed through the well-related set C. Domain transitivity proves the supplied x also is a supremum of C, so preservation applies to f(x) itself. A bound b of f(D) bounds each f(I(d)); the induction hypothesis gives f(s(d)) related to b. Thus b bounds f(C), and the least-bound property of f(x) completes the proof without codomain transitivity. Authors report 726 Isabelle lines in AFP entry Directed_Sets, plus refactoring of Complete_Non_Orders with new Continuity.thy and Directedness.thy totaling 427 lines. These counts describe different development scopes; they are not runtime or proof-success measurements. The article reports machine formalization but no build log, tactic-time statistics, independent replication, empirical benchmark or proof-agent evaluation. AFP and cited prior developments were not opened or rebuilt in this reading. The paper motivates directed sets through nets in topology, fixed-point semantics for loops and ideals in reachability/coverability of well-structured transition systems such as Petri nets. These are motivating applications, not a verified protocol, Rust implementation, Verus/TLA+ specification or applied model checker delivered here. It contains no LLM-assisted proof experiment.
use_for_goal: Indirect foundations for formal verification of transition systems and denotational semantics, plus concrete proof-engineering lessons for specifications and proof agents: separate carrier order from index order, record choice dependencies, preserve nonunique witnesses, avoid overstrong codomain assumptions, and strengthen induction with the property later reused. These are reader inferences from Isabelle mathematics, not evaluated Verus/Rust, TLA+ or distributed-system results.

title: FormalJudge: A Neuro-Symbolic Paradigm for Agentic Oversight
what: Post-hoc agent-trajectory oversight separates intent decomposition,atomic-fact extraction,formal predicate generation and Dafny/Z3 checking. Structured logs are parsed directly where possible;LLMs extract semantic facts and synthesize the constraints. Authors report improved agreement with an LLM-ensemble reference,including deception classification and feedback-based behavioral refinement. Formal guarantees are conditional on faithful facts and specifications,not proofs about an agent policy or natural-language intent. Provides explicit atomic taxonomies and composition formulas for file-grounded deception,tool safety and constraint compliance;localized context extraction separates tool errors,disclosure,document access and fabrication. Adds a trusted-trace evidence-manipulation boundary test,manual integrity atoms,latency breakdown,qualitative-intent proxy examples,multi-turn stress tests and action/task-level evaluation. Iterative feedback sends generated Dafny constraints and failed-predicate explanations back to an agent. Detailed appendices show which observed facts are composed and reveal semantic/specification mismatches that solver success alone cannot catch.
assumptions_limits: §3.4 explicitly requires faithful extracted facts and a Dafny specification capturing intended constraints. Errors can enter decomposition, semantic extraction and synthesis. The solver does not verify the LLM, policy, truth of observations or intended meaning. No theorem proves end-to-end soundness of this oversight architecture. Observed trajectories and trusted tool-observation logs must retain provenance. Agent-controlled files and self-reports may be fabricated. Appendix A.3 assumes attackers cannot overwrite the trusted trace; without external provenance a trajectory-only checker cannot recover rewritten original events. Reference labels in §4.1 are majority judgments from GPT-5.2, Gemini-3.0-Pro and Claude-4.5-Opus across three rounds. Metrics measure agreement with that ensemble, rather than independently established ground truth. Opus is also the main judge and specification compiler; correlated model errors remain possible. Seven main agents: GPT-4o, Gemini-3.0-Pro, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Qwen-2.5 7B/14B/32B/72B. Table 1 uses an Opus judge. Extended robustness uses eight judges including GPT-5.2, Grok-3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Sonnet and four Qwen sizes. The main five-judge description and extended eight-judge analysis describe different settings. Full benchmark sizes are 2,000 Agent-SafetyBench cases, 400 VitaBench tasks and 200 Deceivers tasks. Vita evaluation actually uses a 100-task split; robustness/cross-verifier analysis uses 30 tasks and 164 tool calls. Deceivers weak-to-strong analysis uses 200 deceptive plus 200 nondeceptive trajectories per agent size. Full benchmark size is not every experiment’s denominator. Agent-SafetyBench reference protocol in Appendix D combines fulfillable/risk annotations with actual actions and uses the ensemble for ambiguity, unlike the uniformly ensemble-based wording in §4.1. Deceivers design labels provide a consistency check; broken tools do not automatically make every resulting trajectory dishonest. Some atomic questions remain substantial semantic judgments: whether a file contains requested information, an answer ignores content, or fabrication follows disclosure. Boolean answers do not make these judgments objective. Qualitative intent uses observable proxies rather than an exact semantics of politeness or manipulation. Agent-SafetyBench refinement uses Opus for decomposition/specification synthesis, including small-agent experiments. For the 7B-judge versus 72B-agent claim, the exact allocation of extraction/synthesis roles matters; judge size alone does not specify the capacity of the complete pipeline. Verification audits completed traces. Refinement regenerates responses or attempts and cannot undo actions already executed. X-Teaming and OpenClaw additions measure unsafe-trace detection, not online prevention or reduction in the native attack success rate. Dafny/Z3 checking can time out or fail without proving the negation. The paper models V as binary but does not fully specify timeout, unknown or syntax-error handling. The 6.4% backend error share classifies an unspecified sample of errors; it does not establish logical unsoundness in Z3. No independent artifact reproduction, compiler/version audit, complete human-label audit or systematic correctness proof of generated checkers is supplied. Attribution to the solver alone is limited when decomposition, contexts, prompts and generated code differ.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM-generated specifications and evaluating verification claims: gives inspectable facts/predicates, evidence-provenance boundaries and cases where solver checking cannot repair weak or mistranslated intent. The fabricated file-reading examples also bear on literature-database honesty. Its empirical result is post-hoc classification agreement under trusted traces and generated contracts. Applying it to distributed verification or proving agent safety requires further work.

title: Formally Verified Linear-Time Invertible Lexing
what: ZipLex is a Scala/Stainless lexer that verifies maximal munch with rule-order tie breaking and lossless lexing/printing under explicit token transformation and separability conditions. It refines simple list/regex specifications to zipper derivatives, tail recursion, balanced sequences and mutable memoization. Experiments compare adversarial and JSON grammars and hash-table variants. Explains why arbitrary token concatenation is not invertible, how an all-rule prefix test yields a sufficient adjacent-token invariant, why a natural zipper induction fails, how an explicit stack preserves tail recursion while filling a cache, and which proof/resource and runtime claims remain conditional. Retains the untokenized suffix, client injectivity obligations, collision qualification, sparse-cache parameters, proof-count discrepancies and combined runtime/memoization ablation.
assumptions_limits: §2: lex returns tokens and a possibly untokenized suffix. The informal print(lex(s))=s notation must retain all consumed text and any suffix appropriately; printing just successfully recognized tokens cannot reconstruct an arbitrary unrecognized suffix. Maximal munch picks the longest prefix and earliest rule on ties. Non-nullable rule expressions ensure each emitted token consumes input. §§2–3.1: alphabet elements have arbitrary type. Each rule must supply transform/charsOf and a client proof of charsOf(transform(s))=s on its required domain. Surjectivity is unnecessary for values created through transform. A noninjective semantic conversion can retain the original string alongside the value. This is a precondition on clients, not automatic correctness of arbitrary user token constructors. §§3.2–3.4: lex(print(ts))=ts does not hold for arbitrary token lists. PrintableTokens carries a sufficient R-Path separability invariant over suitable valid tokens; it is not a maximally permissive condition. Relation sep(t1,t2) rejects a boundary when any rule has a word with prefix text(t1) followed by the first character of text(t2). All rules matter, not only the producing rules. Nonempty tokens justify first-character access. §3.3: R-Path means the relation holds at each adjacent pair. Slicing preserves it. Concatenating nonempty paths needs one boundary relation check; empty sequences need their ordinary boundary-free cases. The displayed indexing equivalence omits that qualification. A constant number of relation checks is not constant character work: prefixMatch traverses the first token plus one character and considers rule languages, with rule/token/cache costs. §3.5: disjoint-character separator tokens provide a sufficient special case. Programming-language whitespace also occurs within strings/comments, so that approach is restrictive. The all-rule R-Path method is more general; it does not prove every possible token rearrangement printable. §4: regular expressions use explicitly enumerated character sets, concatenation, union and star. No richer regex feature such as arbitrary complement or lookaround is established. A zipper is a set of contexts, each a list interpreted as concatenation. Correctness relates matchZ to matchR(unfocus(z),s), and matchR to ghost matchRSpec. Reachable derivative finiteness is discussed through cited prior work, not independently audited here. §§5–7: verified equivalence steps connect list recursion to tail recursion and BalanceConc (balanced trees, immutable array leaves, default N=512, zero-copy leaf slices). No universal constant-time concatenation or machine-level JVM resource guarantee follows from functional equivalence. The proof relies on Stainless, SMT reasoning, compilation/runtime and prior verified LongMap. §6.1: generic HashMap[K,V] decorates LongMap[List[(K,V)]], indexed by hashes; collision buckets are linked lists. Functional correctness tolerates collisions, while performance explicitly requires reasonable collisions. Memoization invariant is that each stored (k,v) satisfies v=f(k). Mutation avoids threading an immutable cache through all functions/proofs. §6.2: longest-prefix memoization works on full input and indices. An explicit stack records parameters; after the tail-recursive result returns, cached values for recorded calls are filled. The paper cites Reps for O(n) longest-match time. For fixed rules/finite derivative state space and appropriate cache/hash assumptions this supports linear input-length reasoning; no separate machine-checked resource theorem or adversarial-hash worst-case constant lookup proof is shown. §6.2: sparse caching stores one of every k calls for inputs longer than M, default k=10,M=10^6. Pure opaque parameter functions may depend on input/rules, and functional correctness is agnostic to their settings. Arbitrary such functions do not automatically preserve a uniform linear-time bound. Turning memoization off in the JSON experiment relinquishes the general anti-backtracking guarantee. §7: authors report 21961 VCs, including 8802 cache hits, approximately 130 minutes, 44 VCs above 10 seconds and slowest 58 seconds. Final 100-line SMT-LIB query for the slowest VC rechecks in under a second with cvc5; that does not mean its original unfolding/approximation run took under a second. Aside from simple VSCode completions, authors explicitly report no LLM reliance. §7/Table1: 1915 executable lines and 13200 specification/proof lines sum to 15115; computed ratio is about 6.89, whereas prose says roughly ten times. §6.1 says approximately 1600 additional lines for hash-table work, while Table1 mutable HashMap excluding LongMap totals 2790. Scopes are not reconciled by the paper; retain both without inventing an explanation. §8: sequential benchmark algorithms on Linux, two 24-core AMD EPYC9254 sockets,96 virtual processors,128GB,2.9GHz base/up to4.15GHz. JMH/OpenJDK21.0.2; 99.9% confidence intervals. Figures are selected grammar/JSON workloads, not arbitrary parser or communication-protocol verification. The paper supplies no independent reproduction here. §8: full memoized ZipLex is about 3.5 times slower than Coqlex on JSON in detailed prose, rounded to 3 times in conclusion, and approximately two orders faster than Verbatim++. Verbatim++ incurs roughly two seconds DFA preprocessing. No-memo GraalVM21.0.11 variant is 1.37 times slower than Coqlex; this changes both runtime and memoization, so the improvement cannot be attributed solely to GraalVM. ASCII specialization/boxing is a hypothesis, not established causal attribution. §8: map benchmark inserts N random pairs, removes half and reinserts/updates all N. Generic verified mutable HashMap is slower than standard mutable HashMap, faster than standard immutable HashMap; LongMap is also plotted. This workload does not establish superiority for arbitrary key distributions or adversarial collisions. Data Availability: authors report artifact evaluation for Zenodo version4 DOI10.5281/zenodo.20084365, 1.35GB SMT-LIB, Bolts lexers/regex and nightly CI. These are author reports; no current CI status, artifact proof replay or extended arXiv2510.18479 verification was performed. Formal verification of distributed protocols, Verus/Rust, TLA+ and LLM proof generation are not evaluated.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: a useful example of verifying lossless transformations and maintaining local sequence invariants while optimizing executable code. For specification/proof agents, retain client preconditions and the distinction between representation equality, semantic equivalence, functional proof and resource claims. It provides a concrete verified mutable cache pattern and measurable proof cost, but no evidence about distributed-system failure models or LLM-produced proof quality.

Unlike the previous case, lex(print(ts)) = ts is not true in general.

title: Formally Verifying a Vertical Cell Decomposition Algorithm
what: Rocq/Mathematical Components verification of a functional sweep algorithm returning triangular/trapezoidal cells whose interiors and specified lateral doors avoid nonvertical segment obstacles. The proof handles vertically aligned events without producing zero-width cells and proves each returned cell has an interior center. Complete free-space coverage and shared-door completeness remain unproved. Preserves precise obstacle/numeric model, executable/proof representation split, two-stage safety contracts, orphaned events, four scan branches, hazard inheritance and six levels of invariants. Explains ownership plus obstacle-boundary coverage as the safety argument. Distinguishes nonempty individual cells from nonvacuous output coverage, empirical trajectory usability from a planner correctness/completeness proof, and event alignment from excluded vertical obstacles.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2/4.5, pp.1–4/9–10: input obstacles are finite straight segments, not filled polygons. Endpoints can be shared, but other intersections are excluded; duplicates are excluded. Each edge has strictly increasing x from left to right, so vertical and zero-length segments cannot satisfy the proof edge type. A well-formed bounding box has distinct lateral sides and low/high edges; every obstacle point must lie inside it. This is point motion in a 2D scene, without finite robot shape, dynamics, sensors or uncertain coordinates. §2.1/5.1, pp.3–4/11: proofs assume a Mathematical Components real field, with exact arithmetic and boolean equality/order. Rational numbers suffice; no completeness of the real numbers is required. The generic executable accepts a number type, four arithmetic operations and two comparisons. Its user must instantiate them consistently with field laws. Ordinary floating point does not satisfy that exact model; no rounding-error theorem is given. §2.1, pp.4–5: a determinant computes signed area for above/below/collinear tests using ring operations. Vertical-cylinder tests ensure projections lie within segment x range. Vertical projection is the only operation using division, returning an option outside its range. The edge_below relation is transitive for outgoing edges sharing a left endpoint, but is not a global partial order. §2.2/5.4.1, pp.5/13: cells store low/high edges and ordered unique left/right boundary point lists. Closed cells have both sides; open cells have no right side yet. Safe part consists of strict interior plus lateral points strictly between low/high edges excluding recorded unsafe points. Owned part excludes bottom and left boundaries, allowing unique ownership even when cells meet. Safety is not a claim that every boundary point is free. §§3–4, pp.5–8: scan state stores vertically arranged open cells as prefix/last/suffix, closed cells with the last one separate, and cached last x/high edge. Initial processing needs a first event strictly beyond the left boundary to construct a first closed cell. Event preparation uses insertion sort merging equal positions, then separately sorts outgoing edges when processing each event. Recursion consumes the finite event list; no asymptotic complexity theorem is reported. §4, pp.6–8: event order is lexicographic in x then y. Four branches distinguish x advance, same x above the last high edge, same x below it, and same x on it. Same-x handling updates/discards would-be zero-width cells and preserves old unsafe-side points. Vertical alignment of separate events is supported, while vertical obstacle segments remain excluded. §4.5/second_phase_safety, pp.9–10: eight prerequisites are well-formed box, permitted endpoint-only intersections among boundaries/edges, inside-box events, strict lexicographic event ordering, outgoing edges starting at their event, later events covering right endpoints, no event in an edge interior, and duplicate-free outgoing lists. Each resulting cell has center strictly inside, well-formed side lists and safe part disjoint from unsafe events/edges. Isolated events are supported by this more general contract. §4.5/two_phase_safety, p.10: composing preparation with processing reduces prerequisites to well-formed box, unique edges, endpoint-only intersections including box edges, and all edge points inside the box. The conclusion gives interior center, side well-formedness and obstacle avoidance for every returned cell. Input preparation must preserve the original edges, since safety relative only to the generated event set could otherwise omit an obstacle. §5.1, p.11: generic_trajectories avoids Mathematical Components structures and drops the dependent edge proof field for extraction. Proof files instantiate this same generic algorithm with field operations via notations and generalize theorems across sections. Rational implementation uses integer numerator/positive denominator. No verified foreign-function wrapper, machine-integer overflow proof or independent extraction replay is provided in this reading. §5.2, pp.11–12: six nested invariant groups describe open cells/remaining events; cache consistency and event/edge relationships; special last open cell; disjointness/nonempty cells; coverage of processed obstacles by high boundaries; and safe lateral-side exclusions. A preliminary proof under no vertically aligned events verified fewer branches; the main result described here is the stronger proof including degeneracies. §5.3, pp.12–13: pairwise order of all earlier/later open-cell high edges replaces relying on adjacent sortedness under a nontransitive relation. Projection comparisons require the point x coordinate to be in both edge cylinders. These assumptions make local geometric order reasoning sound. §5.4, pp.13–15: unique owned parts and coverage of each processed obstacle by cell high boundaries imply interior safety by contradiction. An interior point on an obstacle would belong to its own cell and a distinct boundary-covering cell. Separate invariants show events appear in side lists, and inherited side hazards survive degenerate replacements. Disjoint ownership does not imply closed cells have no shared boundary. §§1/6.1, pp.3/16–17: proof does not establish union of owned parts covers the box or that adjacent cells with a safe passage share a represented door. Tests reportedly support both properties, with no described count/distribution/ground truth. Missing either could cause the application to miss an existing path. Per-cell nonemptiness does not prove the output list is nonempty or complete. §6, pp.16–17: integration in a larger path tool assesses usability, but path search, smoothing with Bezier curves and full trajectory proof are outside this paper. Proof effort is almost 15000 lines in 12 files. No runtime, memory, compilation time, hardware, systematic benchmark or independently reproduced build is reported. Adjacency lookup currently scans all cells; cached neighbours, vertical/crossing obstacles and trajectory verification are future work.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful benchmark for proof/specification agents because safe returned objects can coexist with missing output coverage, and degenerate branches require preserving historical exclusions. title: Certifying Proofs in the First-Order Theory of Rewriting
what: Defines a line-oriented certificate language for the decidable first-order theory of rewriting over linear variable-separated TRSs, implements FORT-h to emit certificates, and presents FORTify, an Isabelle-formalized/code-generated certifier that checks the automata construction and final emptiness claim. title: Using Four-Valued Signal Temporal Logic for Incremental Verification of Hybrid Systems
what: Defines a four-valued STL semantics and an incremental verification algorithm that runs alongside set-based reachability. title: Fractional Separation Logic in Isabelle LLVM
what: A shallow Isabelle/HOL fractional separation logic with unbounded positive rational scaling and nominal resource labels. Labels preserve a concrete resource witness so arbitrary labeled assertions can be split and recombined. A kernel-checked VCG automates fractions/labels/frame inference,integrates with fork-join Isabelle LLVM,and verifies shared-input/disjoint-output parallel matrix-vector multiplication. Defines fractional separation algebra type classes,scaling of assertions by inverse resource scaling,and a uniform same-label recombination equality. Extends concrete-state abstraction and access-report frame compatibility to distinguish shared reads from exclusive writes/frees. Gives bottom-up refinement rules and normalization/matching automation,then an explicit recursive proof with shrinking input fractions,fixed labels,decreasing index,and ownership extraction/reinsertion for output elements.
assumptions_limits: Fractions in the algebra are arbitrary positive rationals and compatible equal-valued resources can sum above1. Physical ownership is bounded by embedding assertions and frame into sα of a concrete state,which assigns fraction1 at each allocated-block address. Introductory sum≤1 intuition concerns realizable states,not a global restriction on the algebra. Uniform recombination requires the same label/resource witness;arbitrary unlabeled assertions remain noncombinable in general. Labels may be introduced existentially and forgotten,but two independently chosen witnesses cannot simply be assumed equal. Extended labels include undef,and annotations explicitly require l≠undef. Hoare triples quantify over frames and require successful termination in Isabelle LLVM semantics,with frame-compatible access reports. Reads cannot intersect frame-full addresses,writes/frees cannot intersect even partially framed addresses. Race freedom follows because modeled data races are semantic errors;this is relative to the trusted semantics. Trusted boundary includes Isabelle inference kernel plus Isabelle LLVM semantics and code generator. Frame inference,VCG,and derived separation rules produce kernel-checked proofs. Paper does not provide an end-to-end proved target-compiler/OS/hardware theorem or re-establish the LLVM backend soundness here. Concurrency supported here is fork-join parallel function calls with shared immutable resources and disjoint writes. Additional concurrency patterns,full Sepref stepwise parallel refinement,and higher-level map-reduce rules are future work. No verified Rust borrowing semantics or distributed/network protocol is supplied. User supplies inductive pre/postconditions,termination relation,and separate pure lemmas registered with simplifier. Explicit sep_split/sep_join annotations guide sharing;the paper’s fully automatic final proof is conditional on that setup,not automatic invariant/specification discovery. Matrix dimensions and storage use natural-number abstractions of signed fixed-width indexes,with m*n<2^63 and width representation in mtxA. Result array must own every index initially. Executable version uses64bit entries,but the paper does not spell out an unbounded-integer no-overflow theorem for entry multiplication/addition;do not conflate index bounds with arithmetic bounds. Constructors for the data structures are proved correct to address vacuous preconditions. This supports their realizability under constructor preconditions;it does not establish satisfiability of every arbitrary user assertion or external intended specification. Case-study generality remains limited to a few examples.
use_for_goal: Direct example for verifying parallel memory access:logical shares permit concurrent immutable reads while full ownership controls writes/frees;resource identity matters when merging permissions. Useful comparison to Rust borrowing and Verus ownership/specification workflows,with kernel-checked automation and explicit model/codegen boundaries as evaluation criteria for proof agents. Connection to Rust is author’s analogy;application to Verus/LLM evaluators is reader inference. No TLA+,distributed consensus,network faults or LLM experiment is reported.

title: FRAIG-BMC: Functional Reduction to Speed Up Bounded Model Checking
what: Introduces FRAIG-BMC, an on-the-fly functional-reduction procedure integrated into each BMC unrolling. It simplifies trivial logic, reuses structurally hashed nodes, and SAT-checks simulation-equivalent nodes before CNF encoding, reducing variables and clauses while preserving the BMC property check. The algorithm maintains an unrolled-AIG-node to SAT-variable map and performs three ordered reductions: constant/idempotent AND simplification, structural hashing, then simulation equivalence classes checked by SAT. Equivalences are checked across time frames, which a standalone pre-BMC FRAIG cannot exploit. For constrained properties Ck, the paper adds filtered random simulation over the constraint cone of influence and a SAT-sampling alternative with blocking clauses and optional random unit clauses. Large equivalence classes are capped and treated as unique to avoid excessive checking. The implementation extends AIGER aigbmc with CaDiCaL and compares it to CaDiCaL-backed baseline and ABC-BMC3 on SEC, partial-retention (PartRet), and information-flow (IFC) benchmarks.

title: Accelerating Syntax-Guided Invariant Synthesis
what: Presents FreqHorn-2, a syntax-guided inductive-invariant synthesizer that deterministically bootstraps from program subexpressions and Craig interpolants, then samples grammar mutants while using Houdini inductive-subset extraction and counterexample-to-induction (CTI) second chances. The paper specifies the two-stage Algorithm 4 in detail: seeds from Init/Tr/Bad are augmented with bounded-safety interpolants; initiation filtering and Houdini extract an inductive subset; failed candidates are grouped by CTIs and retried after learned lemmas invalidate their blockers. It proves termination outcomes (bug or synthesized invariant), explains grammar normalization and pruning, and reports that merged seeds/interpolants solve 114 of 171 safe programs before randomized mutants; mutants are needed in 57 cases. On 128 instances FreqHorn-2 beats old FreqHorn in 90, reaches 233x speedup, and averages 4x faster, while showing anomalies from blind grammars, large disjunctions and interpolation.
