title: From LLM-Generated Conjectures to Lean Formalizations: Automated Polynomial Inequality Proving via Sum-of-Squares Certificates
what: NSPI learns approximate polynomial sum-of-squares structures with Qwen3-8B, refines their coefficients numerically, recovers exact rational certificates, and generates Lean identity/nonnegativity proofs from templates. PolyIneqBench has 522 goals with 3–10 variables: 102 literature/competition examples and 420 synthetic ones. Reported final success is 44/102=43.14% on literature examples and 109/420=25.95% on synthetic examples, totaling 153/522≈29.3%. It has the best reported higher-variable success, while Maple/Z3 and LIPS outperform it on relevant low-dimensional/literature subsets. Exact final checking can protect accepted proofs from faulty heuristic discovery; several supplied theoretical/benchmark listings contain errors that require qualification. Training synthesizes polynomial–certificate pairs through eigenvalue shifting, factorized PSD matrices, LMI shifting and diagonally dominant/scaled diagonally dominant matrices. Over one million pairs support supervised cold start, followed by GRPO on unsolved samples in 3–5,6–8,9–10 variable curricula. Rewards combine coefficient error, format and missing/spurious-monomial penalties. At inference, 32 conjectures are ranked by residual; Gauss–Newton refinement is followed by full-rank projection/rationalization or rank-deficient LDLᵀ/Diophantine reconstruction. A final exact identity and positive weighted squares, rather than an LLM judgment or numerical tolerance, support the claimed Lean result. Appendices supply all stages, source examples, training costs, budget curves, complete Lean scripts, failure analysis and proposed extensions.
assumptions_limits: A polynomial SOS certificate is sufficient for global nonnegativity, not necessary. Nonnegative polynomials outside polynomial SOS, inappropriate monomial support, rank constraints or failed rational recovery can remain unproved. Real-coefficient SOS existence does not itself establish a rational certificate in the chosen basis. The task is global nonnegativity over real variables, not general constrained inequalities, optimization algorithms, floating-point implementations or distributed protocols. Converting a constrained/informal problem to this target requires a separate faithful reduction, which Lean acceptance of the resulting polynomial alone does not certify. The final claimed trust boundary is Lean checking polynomial identity and nonnegativity using linear_combination and positivity. Heuristic generation, floating-point refinement and rational recovery need not be trusted if their concrete outputs are fully checked against the intended target. The reader did not run Lean or audit imports, bypass prevention, source conversion or repository implementation. Numerical YALMIP/SDP infeasibility or failure to produce an SOS is not a certified proof of non-SOS without an exact infeasibility witness. The source switches between numerical-certificate failure and categorical non-SOS claims; preserve the weaker measured evidence. Appendix D.2 explicitly states training is disjoint from evaluation. Both synthetic sets share the proposed construction families; no detailed deduplication, near-duplicate search, pretraining audit or independent distribution test is provided. Manual sampling of 50 examples per variable setting is not exhaustive semantic validation. One-hour cap and candidate budget 32 are reported. Mean runtimes are conditional on each method’s solved instances, which differ; reported speedups are not paired-instance or total-throughput comparisons. Baseline default prompts/configurations and API systems differ; no statistical uncertainty or repeated-seed variance is reported. Success at up to ten variables is empirical within the supplied datasets and certificate class. It does not prove asymptotic scalability, complete SOS discovery, human readability, neural novelty, convergence of numerical recovery or superiority on all polynomial inequalities. Future applications to global optimization and Lyapunov stability are proposals. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed-systems experiment appears. Transfer to generating invariant certificates would require an appropriate semantics, target reduction and checker.
use_for_goal: For proof-writing agents, this is a concrete separation of learned certificate discovery, untrusted numerical repair and exact final checking. It illustrates why evaluation should separately check target fidelity, certificate existence, acceptance artifacts and search cost. The certificate-producing design may inform invariant or arithmetic proof automation for verified systems, but it supplies no measured transfer to Verus, Rust, TLA+ or distributed verification.

title: Verification of the CVM Algorithm with a Functional Probabilistic Invariant
what: Introduces functional probabilistic invariants—inequalities of the form E[h] ≤ h(c) over distributions of program states—to verify tail bounds directly for the randomized CVM distinct-elements streaming algorithm, and mechanizes both the original and a new total unbiased variant in Isabelle/HOL. The invariant proof tracks each stream element's indicator X_s for membership in the sampled buffer and establishes E[p^{-1}X_s]=1 inductively across insertion/removal and subsampling steps. The approach uses Isabelle's Giry-monad semantics and expectation bind equation to reason despite state-dependent Bernoulli parameters and dependent buffer elements, avoiding the original paper's transformation sequence. A modified variant samples a fixed-size random m-subset when the buffer is full; it is total (never returns ⊥) and unbiased, and its proof uses a newly formalized library of negatively associated random variables. The authors also mechanize the transformation-based original proof for comparison.
numbers: The mechanized functional-invariant proof uses 1,003 lines of Isabelle code versus 2,634 lines for the transformation-based proof (counts exclude empty/comment/presentation lines). CVM's stated space complexity is O(ε^{-2} b ln(δ^{-1} l)) mutable-state bits when each element uses b bits; no proof-runtime numbers are given.
assumptions_limits: The CVM algorithm receives a finite stream a1,…,al and accuracy parameters ε,δ; the buffer size n is chosen from these parameters and the analysis assumes element equality. The extracted text analyzes Algorithm 1 with the failure check (Line 11) removed; the original proof bounds total-variation distance between this modified algorithm and the failing version by 2δ, so transfer requires that correction. Functional invariants are shown on the presented algorithm and rely on Isabelle probability/expectation libraries; no runtime or memory measurements of the mechanization are reported. The available extraction ends in §3.1, so later theorem statements and full evaluation details are not present.
use_for_goal: Provides a concrete pattern for verifying randomized algorithms in a proof assistant without assuming independence: state-distribution invariants plus expectation laws can yield concentration bounds and expose specification variants (totality/unbiasedness). The line-count comparison is useful evidence for proof engineering; omitted later sections and no timing data limit claims about scalability.

title: Variability Abstraction and Refinement for Game-based Lifted Model Checking of full CTL (Extended Version)
what: Introduces Verify, the first variability-specific abstraction-refinement procedure for full CTL over featured transition systems. It abstracts feature configurations into modal transition systems, solves three-valued CTL through game graphs, and refines only indefinite/failure regions by splitting configurations on the may-transition responsible for the tie. Definitions formalize TS/FTS/MTS projections, may/must semantics, and full CTL three-valued evaluation. A preservation theorem shows the join abstraction conservatively preserves true and false CTL results. Game nodes encode state/subformula positions; failure nodes identify a may-edge whose feature condition is split into ψ and ¬ψ. title: A Formal Verification Approach to Safeguard Controller Variables from Single Event Upset
what: Defines conditionally relevant variables (CRVs): variables whose single-event-upset bit flip can change a controller safety-property result. It combines static slicing with CBMC bounded model checking, instrumenting a shadow program and one nondeterministic bit flip per candidate variable; a counterexample establishes relevance while no violation establishes irrelevance within the bound. The paper gives a two-case formal CRV definition covering both upset-induced violation and upset-masked violation, a concrete instrumentation algorithm that duplicates the program and asserts XOR disagreement of safety outcomes, and a compiler-facing selective-hardening workflow. In three C benchmarks, slicing retained 4 relevant variables in each case; CBMC removed 1, 2, and 1 false positives for motivating, temperature-control, and fan-speed programs respectively, with reported efficiencies of 25%, 50%, and 25%.

title: Some approximations in Model Checking and Testing

what: Surveys approximation methods connecting model checking, black-box checking, model-based testing, and probabilistic model checking, with complexity and quality guarantees. title: Gauntlet: Finding Bugs in Compilers for Programmable Packet Processing
what: Gauntlet finds P4 compiler crashes with well-formed random programs, semantic mistakes in accessible compiler passes through SMT equivalence checking, and backend miscompilations through model-derived input/output packet tests. Its symbolic P4 interpreter supplies both oracles. The authors report96confirmed distinct bugs across P4C,BMv2 and Tofino over eight months,54fixed, and six specification changes. This is compiler bug finding with conditional translation validation of tested transformations, not verification of every compiler execution or correctness of the user network program. Captures generator probability/size controls, independent block semantics, symbolic table encoding and parameter directions, undefined-behavior taint and unstable-code distinction, parser/ToP4 dependencies, per-pass reparse/check workflow, constrained backend test generation and dropped-test limits. Preserves all bug status/location counts, timing rows, six concrete bug families, specification ambiguities, recent-merge count inconsistency, manual reduction and unmeasured coverage.
assumptions_limits: §1–2: P4_16 finite bit-vector state and bounded/forbidden loops make equivalence decidable in principle. Control-flow loops are forbidden; parser loops are bounded by packet processing, so headline “no loops” should not be generalized to absence of every parser cycle. Efficient practical checks still depend on small programs and limited branching. This restriction distinguishes the method from unrestricted C; it is not an equivalence decision procedure for arbitrary Rust or distributed programs. §2.1/Table1: Crash bug means abnormal compiler termination without usable output/error, including assertion failure, segmentation fault,incomplete error and out-of-memory. Semantic bug means compiled behavior differs from input-program semantics, including packet outputs. Taxonomy levels1–7 are ASCII,words,syntax,type,static,dynamic,model conformity. Focus is static and higher-level failures rather than lexer/parser fuzzing alone. Some concrete failures reveal valid input incorrectly rejected; legality/specification uncertainty is resolved with developers. §2.2–2.3: Goal is many bugs, not completeness or a verified compiler. Differential testing across P4 targets cannot assume identical target semantics; independent same-target compilers were unavailable. Gauntlet tests mature P4C,BMv2,Tofino, excluding preliminary eBPF/uBPF/PSA toolchains. Its principal tests deliberately avoid target-specific extern calls. This is not a proof a particular P4 application satisfies network safety properties. §3/§5.2: Package parameters define input/output observables. Each programmable block is encoded separately; BMv2 v1model has Parser,VerifyChecksum,Ingress,Egress,ComputeChecksum,Deparser. out/inout form outputs; in/inout are symbolic inputs. Paths yield nested if-then-else expressions containing resulting parameter tuples. Copy-in is left-to-right; out values start uninitialized, and out/inout copy back on return. Correct interpretation of these effects is part of the trusted semantics. §4: Random generation grows a P4C IR AST probabilistically and emits P4 with ToP4. Node probabilities steer language coverage and keep programs small in lines/paths. A skeleton captures each target package/restrictions; two generator backends correspond to BMv2 and Tofino. A correctly rejected ill-typed/generated input is a generator bug, not a compiler bug. P4Fuzz comparison is qualitative; no matched-budget bug-yield experiment is reported. §4/§5.2: Unlike Csmith, generator permits undefined behavior and interpreter tracks affected expressions, so suspicious legal refinements are distinguishable from true miscompilation. Undefined-variable taint propagates through affected values. Replacing tainted expressions only in the before-pass formula classifies legal reductions of undefinedness as unstable code; changing a previously defined expression into undefined behavior remains a bug. Such warnings are not counted automatically as semantic bugs. §5.2: Interpreter took five months to become reliable enough for finding compiler semantic bugs. Developed with >600 P4C tests and >100 custom tests, generator co-evolved to expose interpreter mistakes, authors consulted compiler/specification maintainers. Their belief that discrepancies on audited regression tests probably indicate interpreter bugs is a debugging heuristic, not proof of the oracle. title: Generalised Bit-Vector Abstractions for Formal Verification of Quantum Error-Detection and Entanglement Circuits over {H, X, C-NOT}: CSS Constructions, Soundness, and Mutation-Based Validation
what: Extends a two-bit-vector abstraction for H, X, and C-NOT quantum circuits to parametrized repetition/concatenated codes, arbitrary CSS syndrome extraction, a formally characterized sound fragment, mutation validation, and large GHZ circuits. The abstraction separates superposition tags from basis-state XOR behavior and reduces verification to bit-vector SMT constraints. The paper defines fragment F conditions under which the abstraction is sound, proves an explicit invariant theorem, gives necessity counterexamples, and differentially tests against exact state-vector simulation. Properties cover arbitrary error patterns, detection limits, and classical-decoder recovery; tested codes include Steane, [[15,7,3]], [[15,1,3]], and rotated surface codes. Direct Z3 encoding uses bit-vectors, XOR code-word constraints, and cardinality-bounded error variables. Evaluation finds all 12,000 in-fragment random circuits agree with state-vector simulation, while unrestricted circuits agree only about 55%; all 622 non-equivalent single mutants are detected. GHZ verification reaches 262,144 qubits, but random dense parity networks become very hard as depth/support grows.

At 32 qubits, depth 4 solve 0.033 s versus depth 7 27.5 s; depth 8 had timeouts

assumptions_limits: Soundness is only for fragment F: no non-phase gate between Hadamards and no Hadamard after a qubit has interacted; S/Z gates, genuine Y stabilizers, entangled-qubit Hadamards, and general stabilizer circuits are outside scope. Logical circuit faults are modeled, not hardware noise, decoherence, measurement errors, or fault propagation/hook errors. Code-word preconditions and error-location assumptions are explicit. Mutation coverage is single-modification classes only; the 100% rate is not complete fault coverage. GHZ scale is family/solver-specific; Python term construction and memory dominate at large sizes, and comparison with prior work is observational.
use_for_goal: A strong recent example of formal verification combining a soundness theorem, SMT encoding, counterexamples, differential testing, and mutation evaluation. Its explicit scope and threats-to-validity provide useful evidence for judging automated verification claims, though the subject is quantum circuits rather than distributed Rust systems.

title: Generating Verified LLVM from Isabelle/HOL
what: Isabelle-LLVM shallowly embeds a structured subset of LLVM in Isabelle/HOL, generates LLVM text, supplies a total-correctness separation logic and kernel-checked verification-condition generator, and retargets Sepref to synthesize imperative programs with explicit memory deallocation. Binary search and KMP refine mathematical specifications to fixed-width arrays/words. Details the executable state-error monad and structured memory semantics, proof-producing normalization to monomorphic instructions/recursive equations, separation ownership including allocation-size tags, framed total-correctness triples, and synthesis rules that insert deallocators when variables leave scope. Connects abstract algorithm proofs to overflow-safe64bit implementations while explicitly identifying the unverified text translation and ABI/runtime boundary.
assumptions_limits: Total correctness is established for the shallow Isabelle-LLVM semantics through successful SUCC results, excluding FAIL and NTERM under the proved preconditions. Translation from shallow logical constants to actual LLVM text remains trusted; no proved correspondence to a deep LLVM semantics, optimizer, assembler, physical machine or OS is supplied. Memory is a finite list of allocation blocks with an unbounded supply of new blocks with structured pairs, pointers and fixed-width integers, rather than byte-level target memory. Pointer addresses have no finite bit width in the model. Floating point, poison values and structures beyond nested pairs are outside the supported fragment. Generated allocation calls use C calloc/free with architecture-dependent size_t; generator refuses potentially lossy size downcasts. Allocation-failure code exits1 after an error. Thus the claimed actual-program behavior permits out-of-memory termination rather than guaranteeing the modeled successful result under all finite resources. Recursive calls implicitly have unbounded stack in the semantics. Stack probing/split-stack protection is future work; likely guard-page termination is an informal engineering argument, not a proved resource bound or implemented universal protection. Application binary interface and correct C header are user responsibilities; C/LLVM ABIs only partially match. Correct callers, library behavior and target configuration therefore matter beyond proved Hoare triples. Refinement assertions impose representability and arithmetic bounds. Binary search requires sorted list, valid array/length representation and signed64bit elements; KMP requires |s|+|t|<2^63 and its arrays/word representations. Correctness is relative to these formal specifications, not arbitrary external input encodings. Kernel-checked preprocessing/VCG/Sepref proofs rely on Isabelle inference kernel and modeled logic. Incomplete preprocessing can fail or produce rejected shapes without supplying an unchecked proof. Trusted shallow semantics/text generation remains separate from these checked transformations. Only medium-complexity binary search/KMP case studies are demonstrated. Existing Imperative HOL basic data structures cannot simply be reused because of words/pairs; nested imperative containers currently need ad-hoc separation proofs. Large model-checker/SAT-solver ports and general overflow-refinement automation are future work.
use_for_goal: Useful infrastructure comparison for Verus/verified Rust and LLM proof-agent evaluation:distinguishes kernel-checked transformations,formal operational semantics,word overflow obligations,memory ownership/deallocation,code generation trust and ABI fidelity. Supplies a concrete example where accepted proofs need explicit specification/precondition and compilation-boundary audits. It does not evaluate distributed protocols,TLA+,Rust,Verus or LLM agents;application to those topics is reader inference.

title: Liveness Properties in Geometric Logic for Domain-Theoretic Streams
what: Defines LTL over the algebraic cpo of partially defined streams JStrAK and studies formula denotations through Scott topology, sobriety, frames and geometric logic. Negation-free LTL formulas translate inductively to geometric theories whose models are exactly the denotations; the paper applies the translation to prove a liveness specification for the non-productive stream filter function. The stream domain is DCPO[N,JAK] with a pointwise flat order, so finite-support streams are compact approximants and total streams are their directed suprema. The authors prove negation-free denotations are upward-closed and induce sober subspaces, while negation can destroy sobriety (e.g., J¬□aK excludes aω). They stratify negation-free LTL into G, Gδ and full fragments, define geometric-formula operators for next/until/weak-until, and prove model equivalence (Theorem 3). A frame/deduction treatment establishes spatiality for countable theories and gives complete deduction for Gδ formulas. For filter, ordinary fixpoint induction fails because the bottom function does not satisfy total-output liveness; finite-occurrence formulas ψn,k and output approximants φk yield Lemma 13 and prove that infinitely many predicate-satisfying input elements imply a total filtered stream.

assumptions_limits: The semantic development assumes a set A (finite for the filter theorem), flat Bool and a Scott-continuous predicate p that is defined on every a∈A. Results concern denotational stream semantics, not an implemented language or distributed protocol. Negation-free formulas are the main tractable fragment; arbitrary negation and Fσ cases may lack a geometric-theory model presentation. Decidability and refinement-type automation are left open, and the filter proof handles a single recursively defined function/specification.
use_for_goal: Provides a rigorous semantic template for specifying liveness over infinite traces and recursive stream computations. Its explicit compact approximants, fixpoint obligations and failure of negation under sobriety are useful when designing TLA+/Verus liveness specifications, although no distributed implementation or empirical tool evaluation is given.

title: Stateless Code Model Checking of Information Flow Security
what: Proposes complete stateless code model checking (CSMC) for observational determinism in concurrent programs. title: Constraint-Driven Modeling Enabling Dual Model Checking and Simulation for Discrete Event Systems
what: Introduces Constraint-DEVS, a bounded variant of Parallel DEVS, and extends DEVS-Suite so the same component models support simulation and exhaustive reachability/model checking. A state-exploration protocol wraps one-cycle simulation, with bounded state variables, bounded ports, discrete-time events, selective state exploration, and transducer-based trace/property analysis. NoC and circular-buffer models demonstrate the framework. The paper gives concrete finiteness conditions and an algorithm: state and port values are specified by regular expressions, input events include an explicit null value, and a Q/V/U exploration loop injects every possible input into each reachable state, using simulation for one cycle. It defines explorable versus unexplorable variables to reduce state space without changing simulation behavior, and reuses an experimental-frame generator/transducer for state, path, and QoS-like checks. The circular buffer verification catches a simultaneous-event bug; NoC experiments compare round-robin and adaptive task distribution and quantify the severe state-explosion tradeoff. An appendix details VerifiableAtomic, StateVar/PortState, VerificationEngine, and integration with existing simulator classes.

assumptions_limits: Exhaustive checking requires finite bounded state variables, bounded port values, discrete external-event times, finite time-advance values, and no converging time-advance sequences. Selective state exploration can omit information needed by a property, and complex Java data/trace processing raises cost. Results are reachability checks, not automatic proof of an unbounded DEVS model. NoC models simplify packet/data behavior and rely on abstraction; the framework does not remove state explosion: a 4x4 network was not completed, and authors propose partial verification and multiresolution modeling. title: Semi-Automated Modular Formal Verification of Critical Software: Liveness and Completeness Thresholds
what: Develops (1) ghost-signal separation logic for modular termination proofs of busy-waiting concurrent programs under fair scheduling and (2) completeness thresholds reducing unbounded memory-safety proofs for array-traversing programs to bounded checks. Ghost signals are verification-only resources with obligations to set signals, well-founded levels preventing cyclic wait dependencies, and shared-state invariants connecting signal state to arbitrary data structures. The logic is modular over threads/functions and extends to race freedom, deadlock freedom, arbitrary conditions, signal erasure, higher-order features and fine-grained concurrency; appendices prove soundness. A bounded FIFO producer-consumer example and CLH lock were verified with tool support. Completeness-threshold chapters define thresholds over input sizes, derive verification-condition based approximations, prove modular/transitive/elimination rules, and characterize simple unconditional array accesses.

assumptions_limits: Liveness requires fair scheduling and proof obligations that every signal is eventually discharged; levels must be well-founded and correctly encode dependencies. Ghost signals are not runtime state, so invariants linking them to concrete conditions are mandatory. Completeness thresholds target heap programs traversing arrays without allocation/freeing and can yield sound bounded guarantees only when verification conditions are precise; broader data structures remain future work. The dissertation reports no broad benchmark runtime study.
use_for_goal: Provides proof obligations and well-founded dependency structure for liveness in concurrent systems, plus a principled account of when bounded checking can be complete. These ideas map directly to distributed protocol termination and bounded state reasoning.

title: Ghost Signals: Verifying Termination of Busy Waiting
what: Develops a modular Hoare/separation-logic approach to termination of busy-waiting programs under fair scheduling. Ghost signals represent conditions other threads must establish; linear obligations require setting them. A well-founded partial order forbids waiting on a signal at or above any obligation held by the waiter. Data-structure invariants tie signals to real conditions, allowing resource-local proof of waiting over arbitrary shared structures. §2 derives the logic through thread-safe physical signals, non-thread-safe signals guarded by mutexes, arbitrary heap cells, then erasure into ghost state. An augmented operational semantics makes a thread get stuck if it exits with outstanding obligations; fork transfers obligations rather than discarding them. A program-order graph tracks the path carrying each obligation. A minimal infinitely-waited signal would have an infinite obligation path that can wait only on finitely-waited lower signals, yielding contradiction under fairness. Points-to/signal ownership prevents races. Mutex acquisition creates a release obligation and also obeys the level order. §3 splits signal-ID allocation from initialization so a fixed finite collection of signal IDs can be named early without creating premature obligations. Loop iterations may select from a finite signal set, and outer productive loops use ordinary decreasing counters. §5 explains call/wait permissions and thread phases; permission consumption only in descendant phases prevents a self-fueling busy loop. §6 describes a possible reduction of termination to instrumentation safety for higher-order step-indexed logics.

The proceedings presentation restricts busy loops to with-mutex-await syntax and ultimately to a finite fixed set of signals per loop; the external report generalizes looping/recursion. Physical machine memory models are not analyzed; claims use the presented language semantics. Higher-order assertions are not supported by this logic itself; Iris integration is proposed, not demonstrated as a mechanized embedding here. Abstract specifications for CLH require a suitable level universe supporting bounded infinite level sets. No automated signal/invariant/level inference or LLM experiment is reported. Potential evaluation tasks include generating the invariant linking real state to signals and finding a valid level order. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM-system result is established.

title: Gillian, Part II: Real-World Verification for JavaScript and C.
what: Introduces separation-logic verification in the multi-language Gillian symbolic-execution platform. A language instantiation supplies a trusted compiler to GIL and a compositional memory model; core predicates with consumer/producer actions describe memory resources, including negative information such as absent properties, freed C blocks, and out-of-bounds cells. The same language-independent AWS message-header predicates are connected to JavaScript and C implementations. title: Monotonic Prefix Consistency in Distributed Systems
what: Defines Monotonic Prefix Consistency (MPC) for replicated lists, gives a centralized toy implementation whose traces satisfy MPC, and proves that no convergent distributed implementation under asynchronous message delivery, availability, and the paper’s observability can be strictly stronger than MPC. title: Specification of the Giskard Consensus Protocol
what: The paper gives a rigorous executable-style specification of the Giskard consensus protocol used by PlatON, defining nodes, epochs/views, message formats, local/global block stages, state transitions, and fault behavior. It proves three safety properties: same-height prepare blocks in one view are identical; same-height precommit blocks across views are identical; and same-height committed blocks are identical. The proofs reduce quorum intersections and view-change height relationships to contradictions under the one-third Byzantine bound. The specification is intended as an implementation and formal-verification reference, while liveness is left open.
assumptions_limits: The network is partially synchronous and nodes communicate by authenticated broadcast; at most one third of participating nodes are Byzantine. Epoch/view changes can be asynchronous across nodes, and Byzantine behavior includes proposing multiple same-height blocks or voting without required messages. Safety reasoning focuses on message/block stages and does not establish liveness, performance, implementation correctness, or cryptographic assumptions beyond authenticated signatures and quorum behavior. The protocol has ten-block views and VRF-selected epoch participants as modeled in the specification.

It exposes the assumptions (partial synchrony, authenticated messages, ≤1/3 Byzantine nodes) and the gap between proved safety and unproved liveness.

title: Verifying Strong Eventual Consistency in Distributed Systems
what: Builds a reusable Isabelle/HOL framework that formalizes strong eventual consistency (SEC), an asynchronous unreliable causal-broadcast network, and three operation-based CRDTs: Replicated Growable Array, Observed-Remove Set, and increment-decrement Counter. The abstract convergence theorem proves that distinct happens-before-consistent operation lists with the same set of operations yield the same state when concurrent operations commute, while a separate no-failure condition gives progress. The network locale has six axioms covering unique node histories, delivery cause, local delivery, globally unique message IDs, causal delivery, and valid broadcast operations; messages may be delayed, reordered, dropped, or nodes may crash permanently. RGA proof models immutable element IDs, tombstones, insertion ordering, causal validity, and proves concurrent operations commute and application never fails. ORSet uses add IDs and remove sets of observed IDs; Add/Remove commute only under a proved independence condition. Counter operations commute unconditionally. title: Graph2Tac: Online Representation Learning of Formal Math Concepts
what: Studies online representation learning for Coq proof search. The online k-nearest-neighbor solver learns from recent tactic scripts; Graph2Tac is a graph neural network whose definition task computes hierarchical embeddings for new definitions. On a package-disjoint benchmark of unseen Coq developments, online k-NN improves from 15.0% to 25.8% solved, Graph2Tac with online definition updates from 17.4% to 26.1%, and a time-scaled combination solves 33.2%. The paper argues that online information matters most when test theorems have many dependencies unseen during training. Represents Coq's kernel environment as one reversible, hash-shared graph; proof-state and definition subgraphs stop expansion at global definition nodes and are topologically ordered. Graph2Tac prunes each graph to 1024 nodes, uses an eight-hop message-passing GNN with 128-dimensional embeddings, predicts base tactics and local/global definition or hypothesis arguments, and computes new definition embeddings from their graphs in dependency order. The definition loss is one minus cosine similarity and the tactic/argument loss is cross-entropy, combined as 1000 Ldef + Ltactic. Inference uses beam width 256. Three variants separate anonymous/name-aware embeddings and no-definition-task controls. Tactician turns single-tactic predictions into whole proofs with iterative-deepening Dijkstra-style search. Online k-NN searches the 1000 most recent tactic steps; offline k-NN searches training proofs with LSH forests. The artifact includes code, models, benchmark data, commits and analysis notebooks.
assumptions_limits: Evaluation uses 120 jointly installable Opam packages selected by a SAT solver for Coq v8.11, covering mathematics, compiler/programming-language formalization, separation logic and HoTT. Package-version compatibility does not imply logical consistency. The paper does not specifically evaluate transfer to Verus/Rust/TLA+ agents or distributed-protocol specification tasks. The reported main results exclude hott and tlc. The paper found inconsistent axioms in three packages; G2T-Anon-Update used tlc's skip_axiom (False) for 192/500 five-minute theorems (38.4%), so including them would distort pass rates. Comparisons with CoqGym and prior neural systems are explicitly informal and non-conclusive because projects, Coq versions, theorem counts, time limits, hardware, parallelism and solver implementations differ. The paper states that ‘more work is needed to compare’ its methods fairly. The one-model, one-package-split evaluation is variable; the authors say excluding hott and tlc heavily influences final results and that the split and training instability increase variability. No multiple-seed confidence intervals are reported. Graph2Tac cannot predict arbitrary term arguments and uses a fixed tactic vocabulary after excluding tactics occurring fewer than six times; the transformer can generate arbitrary term arguments but has no online learning. The graph is pruned to 1024 nodes, so claims about representations concern the retained closure, not the entire 250-million-node universe. Definition embeddings are trained with manually tuned settings, and training had periodic instability and checkpoint restarts. The online k-NN's advantage depends on recency and same-file proof availability; the ablation calls it ‘slightly brittle’ because proof ordering outside the current file is arbitrary. Model-called pass rates are affected by how many tactic suggestions each call returns and by search speed; aggregate solvers time-share one CPU and are simulations, not concurrent runs with extra compute. The paper reports the artifact as fully reproducible, but this reading did not execute the code, Coq benchmark or provided models.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal proof agents: retaining verifier-visible definitions and recent proof scripts online can help on unseen domains, and hierarchical graph representations provide a route to adapting to new symbols without retraining. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ agents this suggests online environment encoding and recent-proof retrieval, but transfer is an inference because the evaluation uses Coq libraries and software formalizations.

what: Introduces SMC4PEP, which converts pool-based or event-based BPMN product-engineering processes into PRISM Markov Decision Processes, removing redundant processes and replacing cross-abstraction message flows with events to reduce model size while preserving stochastic, timing and reward analyses. The architecture has differentiator, converter and generator stages. The converter eliminates exactly identical processes, removes pools/message flows and inserts events; the generator builds one PRISM module list per diagram and adds timeline rewards. Two automotive OEM cases compare pBPMN and eBPMN models: event-based models reduce states/transitions substantially, including orders-of-magnitude reduction in the four-level case, though one build time increases. PRISM checks A-SPICE properties for deadlock freedom, objective fulfillment and conformance, plus minimum duration and expected cost. The authors explicitly acknowledge state-space explosion and rely on model minimization as future mitigation.

title: Quantitative Safety and Liveness
short_name: Henzinger Mazzocchi Sarac quantitative safety liveness
what: Generalizes safety, liveness, the safety-progress hierarchy, and safety-liveness decomposition from Boolean properties to quantitative trace properties over complete lattices. It defines quantitative safety/liveness by finite-prefix rejection of threshold hypotheses, proves closure/decomposition theorems, and derives finite-state approximate monitors for properties that are approximately safe and co-safe. The paper introduces quantitative properties Φ:Σ^ω→D over complete lattices, quantitative safety via finite witnesses for wrong lower-bound hypotheses, and the safety closure Φ*(f)=inf_{s≺f} sup_g Φ(sg). It proves safety iff upper semicontinuity iff equality with safety closure, safety iff inf-property, co-safety iff sup-property, and characterizes lim-inf/lim-sup levels. New liveness and co-liveness definitions are shown to generalize Boolean liveness; every property decomposes as min(Φ*,Ψ) with Ψ live, and as the minimum of two live properties. Approximate α-safety/β-co-safety are characterized by closure gaps; for real-valued limit properties these imply suffix influence eventually falls below any δ>α+β, yielding a finite-state (δ,δ)-monitor. Examples include minimal/maximal/average response times and discounted safety.
numbers: complete-lattice value domain
safety/liveness decomposition for every property
approximation threshold δ>α+β
monitor with at most 2|Sδ| equivalence classes
assumptions_limits: The core definitions assume a nontrivial complete lattice; finite-state monitoring Theorem 59 additionally assumes a limit property with finite real values, finite observation alphabet, and finite α/β error bounds. Quantitative liveness is intentionally stricter than prior multi-live or verdict-live notions, and the paper proves strict separations. The results are semantic and monitor-construction theorems rather than implementation benchmarks; applications to distributed systems require choosing an appropriate trace domain and quantitative metric. Limit-property converse results are left as conjectural/partial in places (e.g., the full converse of the countable-supremum characterization for lim-inf properties).
use_for_goal: Supplies rigorous quantitative safety/liveness semantics and monitorability criteria that can be instantiated for distributed protocol costs, latency, or resource bounds. The closure/decomposition results clarify which finite-prefix checks can certify thresholds, complementing TLA+/Verus safety proofs and liveness assumptions.

title: Globally reasoning about localised security policies in distributed systems
what: Defines AspectKBL, a process-algebra language for distributed networks with security policies attached to locations, Belnap four-valued policy composition, labelled-transition semantics, and ACTL-like global safety obligations. It proposes checking each syntactic action directly instead of constructing the full LTS, yielding a safe over-approximation for finite systems. AspectKBL models parallel locations, tuple data, out/in/read actions, nondeterministic choice, and replicated processes; local aspects have pointcuts, applicability conditions, and four-valued recommendations. Policy-guarded transitions induce a pruned LTS. ACTLv obligations quantify over all paths and transitions matching a cut, checking predicates before/after interactions. The alternative checker unifies each action with an obligation cut, identifies source/target policies, collects recommendations as constraints, and certifies an action if policies deny it or their constraints imply the obligation predicate. It forbids replication to guarantee finite paths and avoid undecidable general model checking. Healthcare role/private-note examples and third-party-cookie models show both unsafe and policy-protected behavior. An Appendix gives a partial Haskell prototype; constraint solving, parser support, and a correctness proof remain incomplete.

assumptions_limits: Soundness is claimed as a goal but not proved in the report. The finite-network restriction excludes replication; obligation cuts require constant target locations; direct action inspection may over-approximate impossible paths and return inconclusive false. Current tool handles only simple constraints by substitutions, lacks a parser and complete constraint solver, and uses a conservative liberal Belnap combination. The language is Turing-complete without restrictions, global logic covers safety rather than liveness, and examples are small abstractions.
use_for_goal: A direct precedent for local policy composition and global safety verification in distributed systems. Its action-level over-approximation, explicit inconclusive outcomes, and unfinished soundness proof are useful cautionary comparisons for TLA+/Verus specifications and automated proof agents.

title: Higher-Order Bounded Model Checking
what: Defines a bounded model-checking translation for HORef, a higher-order call-by-value language with higher-order references, using SMT formulas, SSA return variables and nominal method names; adds a local points-to analysis and evaluates prototype BMC-2. The translation maps a valid configuration and call-depth bound to a formula whose satisfying assignments correspond (up to fresh-name permutations) to bounded outcomes. It propagates fail/nil through a guard, joins conditional and method-application branches with SSA store maps, and handles unknown higher-order references by branching over repository methods of the matching type. A soundness theorem covers closed terms and ground-typed free variables. The points-to pass computes finite method-name sets for references, variables and returned terms, lock-steps with translation, and cuts factorial method choices to linear growth in a recursive triangular-number example. BMC-2 parses an OCaml-like syntax and emits SMT-LIB for Z3.
numbers: 20 MoCHi benchmark programs, three runs per program and bound, Intel i7-6700/16GB, 10-second timeout and maximum k=10.
Points-to analysis reduced mean execution time 55.8% and reached a maximum 96.8% decrease at k=3; k=1's maximum increase was 2.4%.
hrec timed out at k=3 without points-to and k=9 with it; hors timed out before but did not time out with it and could be checked beyond k=200.
All benchmark bugs were found within k=2.
assumptions_limits: HORef has global references (no fresh-reference construct), integer arithmetic and dynamically named methods; the bound limits nested calls, so unsatisfiable formulas only establish bounded behavior unless bounds are complete. Open higher-order free variables are unsound because unknown code is not modeled; the authors suggest making such checks unsatisfiable. The basic translation can explore all matching methods, and SSA joins/repository duplication add clauses; points-to is an over-approximation. Experiments use 20 MoCHi-derived examples, k≤10 and 10-second timeouts; MoCHi comparison was unreliable.
use_for_goal: A formal, solver-backed treatment of higher-order state shows how method identity, SSA stores and bounded recursion can make functional programs amenable to BMC while preserving a clear soundness boundary. Its points-to optimization and empirical shallow-bug limits are useful when assessing automated proof generation for higher-order or Rust-like code.

title: Hitching a Ride to a Lasso: Massively Parallel On-The-Fly LTL Model Checking
what: Introduces Hitchhiking, a massively parallel on-the-fly LTL emptiness algorithm for GPUs. It tracks interrupted accepting-state searches with a restart set, proving that the algorithm finds an accepting lasso iff one exists and terminates otherwise. Hitchhiking adapts the Map accepting-predecessor algorithm to exploration-time GPU execution. It maintains open, active, and interrupted sets plus a monotone maximal-predecessor function; detailed lemmas establish finite rounds, propagation invariants, cycle detection, and no-cycle termination, and a thread-safety argument explains atomic maxima and barriers. GPUexplore 3.0 integrates the algorithm with a compressed tree hash table, work claiming, generated CUDA successor functions, and Spot NBA construction. The evaluation compares Hitchhiking with Map, Spin NDFS, and 1/32-core LTSmin over 96 BEEM instances spanning 150,000–1.2 billion states.

title: Propositional Dynamic Logic for Higher-Order Functional Programs
what: Introduces HOT-PDL, a dynamic logic over higher-order traces (HOTs) with call/return (CR), caller-to-callee (CC) and returned-function-to-caller (RC) pointers. It specifies temporal control flow of call-by-value higher-order functional programs, including stack-based access control and dependent refinement-type properties, and proves model checking decidable for bounded integers by reduction to modal μ-calculus checking of higher-order recursion schemes. HOTs are labeled DAGs whose events are linearly ordered by next-event edges and whose pointer conditions enforce unique call/return and higher-order links. The paper gives trace semantics for a simply typed ML-like language with recursion and bounded integers, translates dependent refinement types into HOT-PDL, and refines stack inspection so function origin is tracked through higher-order passing (rejecting unsafe partial-application examples that ordinary stack paths miss). Decidability expands each HOT DAG into a HORS-generated tree and translates path expressions to μ-calculus fixpoints; an event monitor/handler simulates pointer traversal, assuming CPS (without loss of generality via transformation).

title: Model Checking for Fragments of Halpern and Shoham’s Interval Temporal Logic Based on Track Representatives
short_name: HS interval model checking track representatives
what: Develops model checking for Halpern–Shoham interval-temporal-logic fragments over finite Kripke structures. For AABBE (and symmetrically AAEBE), it introduces finite track descriptors and bounded track representatives, yielding an EXPSPACE procedure and PSPACE-hardness; AABE/AB are PSPACE-complete and universal ∀AABE/Prop are coNP-complete. The paper maps every finite Kripke track to a homogeneous abstract interval model and defines B_k-descriptors encoding prefixes up to B-nesting depth k. Descriptor-element types, clusters, and k-indistinguishability identify repeated prefixes with identical descriptors; contraction replaces them while preserving the descriptor. The bound τ(|W|,k)=min(1+(1+|W|)^(2k+4)+|W|, 1+(k+3)|W|^(|W|²+1)+|W|) limits representative length. An unravelling algorithm explores forward/backward tracks with this bound, and recursive Check/ModCheck procedures are proved sound and complete. Examples encode scheduler mutual exclusion, reachability, and starvation; hardness reductions establish PSPACE-hard AABE/AB and coNP-hard propositional fragments.

title: Hybrid Spatiotemporal Logic for Automotive Applications: Modeling and Model-Checking
what: Defines Hybrid Spatiotemporal Logic (HSTL), combining temporal next/until, grid-neighbor spatial modalities, and hybrid nominals/binders that name vehicle positions over time. title: Distributed Bounded Model Checking
what: Presents HYDRA, an adaptive distributed BMC algorithm that dynamically unfolds call graphs and splits path sets into disjoint verification partitions farmed to cluster clients. It modifies Microsoft CORRAL, uses solver complexity to choose split points, and adapts split intervals to idle workers. what: Introduces a Rust push-button bounded model checker for synchronous HyperLTL and asynchronous A-HLTL over NuSMV and Verilog, using SMT or QBF encodings and returning counterexamples or existential witnesses. It offers pessimistic/optimistic and halting bounded semantics, three interfaces, asynchronous trajectory-position quantification, synthesis of existential traces, and explicit/implicit simulation encodings for ∀∃ and ∃∀ loops. Case studies cover information flow, linearizability, robotics, fairness, co-termination, deniability, cache attacks and hardware constant-time properties.

title: Model Checking Time Window Temporal Logic for Hyperproperties
what: Defines HyperTWTL, a trace-quantifying extension of Time Window Temporal Logic with synchronous and asynchronous semantics, and reduces decidable alternation-free and one-alternation model checking to ordinary TWTL checking via self-composition and trace synchronisation. The syntax adds universal/existential trace quantifiers and, for asynchronous formulas, trajectory quantifiers that choose which traces advance or stutter. A timed Kripke structure supplies finite states, nonnegative transition durations and labels. The algorithm first converts asynchronous formulas to synchronous ones by invariant trace generation with silent events, translates HyperTWTL to plain TWTL over an n-fold self-composed model, then invokes PyTWTL. The paper formalises security/concurrency examples—non-interference, opacity, side-channel timing, mutation testing, linearizability—and path synthesis objectives on grids.

title: Visual Analysis of Hyperproperties for Understanding Model Checking Results
what: Presents HYPERVIS, a web tool with coordinated formula, graph, trace, timeline, and explanation views for analyzing counterexamples to HyperLTL hyperproperties. It links model, formula, multiple executions, and causal explanations, with editing and rechecking support. Formalizes Moore-machine traces and HyperLTL counterexamples as sets of executions, then derives design goals for recognizing cross-trace relations, linking components, guiding violation diagnosis, and editing specifications/models. The tool uses causal analysis to extract a minimal set of top-level subformulas and atomic propositions contributing to a violation; linked highlighting maps them across five views. Binary filled/hollow encodings, timeline compression, state-transition highlighting, filtering, and step-through interactions support diagnosis. Editing currently supports HyperLTL formula editing and DOT graph editing; graph edits do not trigger re-model-checking. Case studies use an OpenCores I2C circuit (254 latches, 86 I/O variables) and symmetric mutual-exclusion arbiters. Six domain experts analyzed three examples in think-aloud sessions; all identified violations, while participants reported missing scalability/graph and editor features.
numbers: Six participants (mean age 27.5, SD 3.33; model-checking expertise 4.5/5, hyperproperty expertise 4.0/5) all correctly identified violations in provided examples. I2C trace had 680 columns; filtering isolated the relevant output divergence at T6. Tool evaluations are case studies and qualitative sessions, not statistical benchmark comparisons.
assumptions_limits: Counterexamples come from MCHYPER/ABC on finite hardware circuits encoded as AIGER and HyperLTL; visual causal explanations cover top two formula levels and recognized equivalence/consistency patterns, so arbitrary nested relations may not be verbalized. User study has six knowledgeable participants, qualitative feedback rather than controlled accuracy/time comparison. I2C graph can be too large to generate; current DOT editing cannot initiate updated model checking.
use_for_goal: Shows how model-checking counterexamples and hyperproperty violations can be made auditable to humans through causal explanations and linked views. It informs verification workflow and explainability, but offers no proof automation or distributed-system runtime measurements.

title: IBFT 2.0: A Safe and Live Variation of the IBFT Blockchain Consensus Protocol for Eventually Synchronous Networks
what: Defines the IBFT 2.0 proof-of-authority BFT protocol with immediate finality, dynamic validator sets, and eventual-synchrony robustness. It gives pseudocode and a high-level lemma-based proof of optimal safety, persistence, weak liveness, and (with a fair-network probability assumption) liveness for up to floor((n−1)/3) Byzantine validators. The protocol removes IBFT locking and relies on prepared certificates, round-change certificates, and quorum commit seals. Height-tagged messages make lagging nodes request missing finalized blocks, addressing persistence. Safety derives from quorum intersections and induction over rounds (Lemmas 1–7); weak liveness derives from exponential round timers and eventual synchrony (Lemmas 8–17). Full liveness additionally assumes every sent message has positive probability of delivery within one-third of the initial timeout, then uses round-robin proposer selection and stable validator windows (Lemmas 18–23). The paper proposes ten concrete improvements, including fair proposer selection to remove the probabilistic assumption, two-phase fast path, quorum-triggered round advancement, hash certificates, reduced signatures, and aggregate signatures.

title: ICE: A Robust Framework for Learning Invariants
what: Introduces ICE learning, in which a black-box invariant learner receives positive examples, negative counterexamples, and implication pairs generated by a white-box teacher. It formalizes honest teachers and strong convergence, then gives learners for Boolean combinations of numerical constraints and universally quantified array/list properties. Defines ICE samples (E,C,I), target descriptions, iterative rounds, honesty/progress, and strong convergence under arbitrary teacher choices. For scalar programs, the learner enumerates Boolean templates of octagonal constraints with bounded constants and solves a quantifier-free linear integer arithmetic encoding using incremental Z3; dovetailing guarantees simplest-template search and strong convergence. For quantified invariants, it lifts learning to sets of valuation words and adapts RPNI state merging to elastic quantified data automata (EQDAs), yielding polynomial work per round and strong convergence for fixed alphabets. Boogie/SMACK and a QDA teacher connect the abstractions to C and array programs.

assumptions_limits: Scalar learning is complete only relative to the enumerated template class and bounded constants, though dovetailing eventually explores all finite templates. The teacher must soundly generate examples, counterexamples, and inductiveness implications using verification conditions. EQDA strong convergence relies on a fixed finite set of pointer and quantified variables; no polynomial-time iterative learner exists for unbounded alphabets. Array experiments use decidable array-property-fragment translations; list support is described but not evaluated because no Strand decision procedure was available. Learners synthesize invariants expressible in their concept classes and do not remove underlying theorem-proving costs.
use_for_goal: Provides a principled interface for LLM or black-box agents proposing invariants: teachers expose inductiveness failures as implication constraints, while convergence and concept-class assumptions make success claims auditable.

title: ICE-Based Refinement Type Discovery for Higher-Order Functional Programs
what: Extends the ICE invariant-learning framework to infer refinement types for recursive higher-order OCaml programs. It generalizes implication constraints from (x,y) to ({x1,…,xk},y) for nonlinear Horn clauses, learns multiple mutually dependent predicates, verifies candidates with SMT, and iterates counterexamples. Formalizes a simply typed call-by-value higher-order language with recursion and a refinement type system whose typability implies main never fails. Verification conditions become Horn clauses; the teacher extracts positive, negative and generalized implication samples from falsified clauses, while a decision-tree learner synthesizes predicates. Effect analysis and Horn-clause reduction shrink predicate sets. RType (OCaml frontend) plus HoIce (Rust solver using Z3) was evaluated on 162 safe programs; 63/164 OCaml programs generated nonlinear Horn clauses, and failures exposed missing qualifiers or type-system incompleteness.

title: Systematic API Testing Through Model Checking and Executable Contracts
what: Introduces ICEPICK, a black-box REST API testing framework that models API state in TLA+, exhaustively explores the TLC state-space graph, extracts call sequences, and checks execution with GLACIER first-order contracts. The paper specifies a two-phase pipeline: CRUD/OAS contract generation, manual semantic predicates, a conservative TLA+ abstraction, TLC state-space preprocessing, coverage-guided BFS path selection, and execution with an emulator that evaluates preconditions, postconditions and invariants. PUT updates are inserted into post/delete paths; results are classified OK, WARN, ERR or NOT_TESTED. State coverage is complete for generated paths, while transition coverage can miss parallel transitions represented by the same abstract state pair. In the evaluation, Tournaments, Petstore and Features-Service expose distinct scalability and compliance behavior; injected delete and referential-integrity faults are detected, but non-REST APIs block useful inference.

title: Igloo: Soundly Linking Compositional Refinement and Separation Logic for Distributed System Verification
what: Introduces Igloo, an Isabelle/HOL framework connecting compositional event-based distributed-system refinement to code verification in expressive separation logics. Sound refinement and trace inclusion let protocol proofs transfer to heterogeneous Java/Python implementations verified by VeriFast and Nagini. The framework proves composition and translation theorems for event systems, I/O specifications and process implementations. Case studies cover leader election, primary-backup replication and two-party authentication, including fail-stop servers, TCP, UDP, cryptography and unbounded component instances. Isabelle formalizes all definitions/results; code-level abstraction functions connect model states to locked heaps and message bytes.

title: A Certified Proof Checker for Deep Neural Network Verification in Imandra
what: Implements and formally proves a checker for Marabou UNSAT certificate trees in the Imandra functional language and interactive theorem prover. DNN queries are represented as affine tableau equations, bounds and ReLU constraints. The checker parses inductive proof trees with ReLU or single-variable splits, updates child bounds, and checks Farkas contradiction vectors at leaves. A polynomial Farkas lemma and its DNN specialization connect negative linear combinations to UNSAT; covering lemmas show every satisfying assignment falls into one split child, enabling functional induction over the tree. The formalization includes 2,113 lines and 267 auxiliary lemmas. SAT assignments remain directly checkable; this work certifies UNSAT trees.

title: Improving the SMT Proof Reconstruction Pipeline in Isabelle/HOL
what: Adds cvc5 to Isabelle/HOL’s SMT proof reconstruction through Alethe, refactors reconstruction modules, extends the format and supported rules, registers generated rewrite lemmas, and adds standalone certificate checking and proof slicing for testing. Evaluates proof generation, reconstruction, rewrite-step checking and Sledgehammer portfolio gains. Explains concrete CPC-to-Alethe translation mismatches, incompatible fresh-term steps, typed numeral changes, previously veriT-specific parser/replayer behavior, checked assertion matching, and debugging slices that intentionally trust boundary steps. Separates solver success from kernel reconstruction and short-budget portfolio benefit. Tables expose a contradiction between the rewrite-lemma comparison’s prose conclusion and most reported rows.
assumptions_limits: Reconstruction uses Isabelle/HOL’s logic and kernel plus the existing theory context and original goal encoding. Successful external solving alone does not establish an Isabelle theorem: assertions must match and proof steps must be reconstructed. Solver, translator and unverified Carcara need not be trusted for an ordinary completely reconstructed result. This paper does not formally verify the whole translation pipeline. Alethe here targets quantified linear real/integer arithmetic with uninterpreted functions. cvc5’s broader bit-vector, string/regular-expression and finite-set capabilities are future reconstruction targets, not supported successes of this work. CPC rules introducing unjustified fresh terms cannot be translated and leave holes. The paper calls this rare without enumerating a failure taxonomy/count. Alethe hole and lia_generic steps can be expensive; reconstruction can fail or time out. No completeness guarantee follows. The Carcara slice tool’s basic configuration inserts hole steps with argument "trust" at cut boundaries and for the final empty clause; these are deliberately skipped during Isabelle testing. Passing such a sliced unit test validates the targeted step in this test setup, not the original whole refutation. The alternative premise/negated-conclusion configuration supports many steps outside subproofs; general subproof slicing remains future work. The direct reconstruction-function testing method excludes rules introducing subproofs because of nontrivial context dependencies. Registered IsaRARE or handwritten lemmas must already be proved in Isabelle; lemma generation/registration is not permission to accept arbitrary rewrite axioms. Benchmarks originate from the same 5000 AFP goals with seven fact budgets, so the 35000 configurations are not independent goals. Tests intentionally do not sample the general SMT-LIB library, whose structural profile differs. No distributed-system, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment is reported. Proof sizes are average line counts on the common solved subset, not bytes, node counts or step complexity. Generation totals and reconstruction averages are conditioned on common solved problems, and cannot establish unconditional end-to-end speedup. Reconstruction has a much larger budget than the final Mirabelle experiment. The supplied paper gives hardware and selected veriT release context, but no complete exact revision/configuration manifest, raw-data artifact link, repeated-run dispersion or significance test. The author expectation that optimized cvc5 would surpass veriT at short budgets is prospective.
use_for_goal: Useful evidence for proof-producing agents and verification infrastructure: count kernel-reconstructed results separately from solver reports, check premise identity, isolate testing trust holes, and measure both checker budgets and complementary portfolio coverage. The rewrite-table discrepancy motivates auditing reported evaluation claims against data. Application to distributed verification, Verus/Rust or LLM proof workflows is reader inference; none is directly evaluated.

title: Incremental Bounded Model Checking of Artificial Neural Networks in CUDA
what: Extends ESBMC-GPU with CUDA operational models and incremental BMC to verify ANN coverage properties and generate adversarial inputs for MLP implementations. Builds manually conformance-tested operational models for cuBLAS/cuDNN and symbolically analyzes actual CUDA implementations. Four MC/DC-inspired neuron coverage properties (sign-sign, distance-sign, sign-value, distance-value) are encoded as assertions over pairs of images. The checkNN procedure constrains a nondeterministic image to an Euclidean radius around a dataset image and asserts that the ANN output retains the desired classification. Incremental unwinding separates bug search, using unwinding assumptions, from completeness checks of unwinding assertions; CUDA interleavings are explored up to a context bound with partial-order reduction.
numbers: All four coverage methods were verified; on 200 images average coverage checking was about 20 minutes and 80% coverage failed for the benchmark dataset. assumptions_limits: The framework reasons about MLPs using sigmoid activation and CUDA cuBLAS/cuDNN primitives; layer changes require adapting fixed operational models. BMC guarantees are bounded unless all loops are fully unwound, and bit-vector/array QF_AUFBV encoding is expensive. Sigmoid uses a lookup table that can create false adversarial cases; the 5×5 vocalic dataset has only 200 images and may be unusually easy. Experiments use CPU time despite GPU-targeted code and lack a direct comparison on the same ANN with DLV.
use_for_goal: A concrete symbolic-verification implementation with bounded guarantees, counterexample generation, and explicit threats to validity. It is relevant to verified systems and automated proof tooling, but concerns neural-network CUDA code rather than distributed protocols or Verus/TLA+.

title: Inductive Predicates via Least Fixpoints in Higher-Order Separation Logic
what: Explains least/greatest predicate fixpoints encoded internally in higher-order separation logic using persistent premises and magic wand. Applies least fixpoints to heap predicates not aligned with mathematical structural recursion and to Iris total weakest preconditions. Provides a Rocq-Elpi prototype generating fixpoints, constructor/induction lemmas and an induction tactic from inductive-looking specifications, with kernel validation of generated declarations. Records exact fixedpoint/iteration/induction laws, persistent monotonicity and ordinary-conjunction resource sharing, deleted-list/search-tree/nested-rose cases, total-WP adequacy and scheduler/timeless-invariant restrictions, elaboration pipeline, extensible variadic signatures, tactic-port trust boundary and full size evidence. Identifies a concrete cons-tail typo in printed generated definition and limits prototype/performance claims.
assumptions_limits: §2, pp.4–6: framework is higher-order predicate separation logic with persistence modality, abstracted as Modal BI. iProp describes owned resources and is embedded within Rocq rather than native Prop. Impredicative quantification over iProp predicates is essential. Iris’s affine presentation identifies separating unit with True; general Modal BI distinguishes Emp/True and its persistence/intuitionistic modalities, as footnote1 notes. Theorem1, pp.5–6: F:(A->iProp)->A->iProp must satisfy persistent internal monotonicity: box(forall x,Phi1 x wand Phi2 x) wand forall x,F Phi1 x wand F Phi2 x. Persistence allows reuse for multiple recursive children. Least fixedpoint mu F x=forall Phi,box(forall y,F Phi y wand Phi y) wand Phi x. Gives both unfold/fold entailments and iteration. These are logical equivalences, not definitional reductions of a native inductive datatype. §2, p.6: strengthened induction supplies Phi y AND mu F y for each recursive occurrence. Ordinary conjunction shares the same resource evidence; separating conjunction would wrongly require duplicate disjoint ownership. There is no dependent elimination/computation principle for iProp predicates. Greatest fixpoint dual is existential predicate plus persistent post-fixedpoint proof and separating witness; coinductive command generation remains future work. §3, pp.6–8: representation predicates may recurse through deleted nodes without shortening abstract list, or partition finite sets into tree children without syntactic structural decrease. Least fixpoints need monotonicity rather than a visible mathematical-size argument. Parameters (tail pointer, element relation, type) stay fixed during induction; indices change. Nested predicate uses require explicit Proper monotonicity instances in prototype. §4, pp.8–9: total wp(e,Phi) means all operational executions terminate safely and return values satisfying Phi. Safety excludes stuck expressions and invalid accesses. Hoare triple is persistent precondition wand wp. Nonvalue case combines reducibility and universally quantified one-step preservation using state interpretation and ghost update modality. Least fixpoint handles recursion without emitting later modality or requiring explicit numerical step bound. Theorem2, p.9: a closed triple [True] e [Phi] implies strong normalization of(e,h) for any heap h. This is a meta-level adequacy result under the Iris logic/language setup, not arbitrary scheduler fairness or universal correctness of every concurrent program. Strong normalization does not by itself state one uniform numeric bound or asymptotic runtime, especially for general nondeterministic branching. §4, p.10: ordinary partial WP puts recursive continuation under later; guarded Banach fixpoint requires contractiveness rather than positivity. Löb induction may prove partial wp of a diverging program with false postcondition because it never returns. Removing later and using least fixpoint changes termination obligations; total implies partial, reverse does not follow. §4, p.10: invariant-opening for total correctness is limited to timeless assertions; general nested invariants/WP-containing assertions cannot be opened unrestrictedly without later. Landin’s knot demonstrates why the restriction matters. Logic supports limited ghost state/invariants/concurrency, not full usual Iris reasoning power for total correctness. §4, p.10: concurrent total WP requires termination for every scheduler. Busy waiting that terminates only under fair scheduling cannot be verified. Paper explicitly leaves fair scheduler integration for future work; no distributed-protocol liveness or eventual network-delivery assumption is supplied. §5.1, pp.11–12: command parses familiar Inductive syntax as raw bound-variable-aware terms, turns top-level constructor wands into separating conjuncts, binders into existentials, cases into disjunctions, abstracts parameters/recursion/indices, replaces recursive calls with rec, turns the constructor conclusion into index-equality constraints, and simplifies trivial equalities. Higher-order abstract syntax helps binder substitution. Rocq elaborates holes and type-checks resulting declarations. §§5.1–5.2, pp.12–13: generated curried fixpoints avoid tuple plumbing and recognize required nonexpansive OFE morphisms for higher-order predicate arguments. Signature relations live in iProp; combinators express equality, wand, persistent relation, contravariance flip and respectful function relation. Proper instances in Rocq typeclasses make monotonicity extensible beyond a fixed syntactic positivity checker. §5.2, p.13: solver normalizes quantifiers/wands/modalities, then closes equal terms, applies hypotheses or searches signature/Proper rule and recurses. It is goal-directed proof generation, not complete decision procedure for monotonicity. New nested predicates may need manual instances; improved automation/errors are future work. §5.3, pp.13–14: IPM separates persistent and spatial named hypotheses. Proving object-logic wand is not a Rocq lambda introduction; tactics apply derived context-manipulation lemmas. Elpi port manages typed holes, controls typeclass resolution, reduces context functions and checks fresh names. It reimplements selected Ltac wrappers because bridge changes contexts inefficiently; declarations remain subject to Rocq validation. §§5.4–5.5/7, pp.15/17: Elpi database records generated induction theorem, parameter/constructor counts; iInduction queries it and opens case hypotheses. Prototype2106LOC=345Rocq+1761Elpi. Evaluation redefines totalWP and derives its existing proof rules without changing user signatures; no runtime timings, proof-speed comparison, broad benchmark suite or user study. Production integration unresolved due partial duplicated IPM wrappers. §§6–7, pp.16–17: native Rocq Inductive can target unfolded heap->Prop predicates but not Iris’s Sigma-bundled iProp arity; this is not a universal impossibility for all separation logic embeddings. Mere semantic positivity/monotonicity is more general than syntactic strict positivity, with no real-life strictness-gap case claimed. Source code is archived but not built here; no Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof-generation evaluation.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly useful for concurrent/distributed verification foundations and LLM proof-agent evaluation. Shows how representation invariants, induction principles and generated lemmas can be derived with explicit resource/monotonicity contracts and kernel checking. Every-scheduler termination versus fair-scheduler liveness is a key distinction for distributed systems. Timeless-invariant restrictions and deleted-node induction are concrete proof obligations agents must respect. Prototype is Rocq/Iris metaprogramming, not Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ code; no LLM experiment or complete distributed-protocol liveness proof is provided.

A fundamental challenge for intent formalization is that there is no oracle for specification correctness other than the user.
Soundness: the specification is consistent with correct behavior—it does not reject valid implementations.
Completeness: the specification is discriminating—it rejects incorrect implementations.

The central bottleneck is validating specifications: since there is no oracle for specification correctness other than the user, we need semi-automated metrics that can assess specification quality with or without code, through lightweight user interaction and proxy artifacts such as tests.

title: Inferring Invariants with Quantifier Alternations: Taming the Search Space Explosion
what: Presents a PDR/IC3 invariant-inference algorithm that learns first-order invariants with quantifier alternations. It lifts quantifier-prefix choice to the inductive-generalization level for parallel breadth-first search, introduces k-term pseudo-DNF (k-pDNF) matrices, and combines EPR restrictions, incremental SMT, multi-block generalization and heuristic may-proof-obligations. The IG procedure partitions prefix space into categories/workers, orders prefixes by quantifier depth/alternations/universals/existentials, shares constraints only from immediate sub-prefixes, and interleaves separation with SMT checks of Init and relative inductiveness. k-pDNF represents a negated cube followed by up to k−1 cubes, expressing implication-shaped Paxos lemmas more compactly than CNF/DNF. The complete P-Fol-Ic3 algorithm has learning and heuristic tasks, optional EPR edge restrictions, and solver robustness via restarts, parallel Z3/CVC5, and incremental assertions. Evaluation covers 30 safe distributed-protocol problems, including Paxos variants, with ablations for pDNF, EPR, incremental SMT and multi-block generalization.

title: Learning Markov Decision Processes for Model Checking
what: Introduces IOALERGIA, an adaptation of Alergia that learns deterministic labeled Markov decision processes from alternating input/output traces. It builds an IO frequency prefix tree, merges states using recursive Hoeffding compatibility including disabled-action errors, chooses epsilon by BIC, and produces a DLMDP suitable for PLTL and scheduler analysis. The paper gives formal LMDP/DLMDP and scheduler semantics, a fair-scheduler observation model with unbounded independent sequence lengths, explicit IOFPTA/merge algorithms, convergence to the true structure up to bisimulation and parameter convergence with probability one, and the limitation that analogous convergence does not carry to PCTL. title: Compositional Model Checking of Consensus Protocols Specified in TLA+ via Interaction-Preserving Abstraction
what: Introduces Interaction-Preserving Abstraction (IPA) for compositional checking of TLA+ consensus specifications. Actions are partitioned into modules, dependency/interaction variables are identified, internal actions are abstracted, and each module is checked in a context formed from abstractions of the others. Strong refinement proves that passing all compositional checks implies refinement of the original specification to the abstract one. IPA defines recursive dependency and interaction-variable sets and four abstraction constraints: abstract dependencies cannot use other modules’ locals; interaction updates depend only on interaction/dependency variables; abstract locals avoid other-module locals; and every externally visible action has a mapped abstract action preserving effects. A strong action mapping is used because ordinary refinement does not record correspondence of omitted actions. Case studies identify polling, centralized control-flow and brute-force replacement of performance optimizations as practical patterns. Raft is split into PreVote, Vote and Replication; ParallelRaft merges Replication into LeaderRecovery when it offers little abstraction. The theorem composes per-module refinements into S⇒A.
