title: Distributed Parallel Build for the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs
what: Introduces Isabelle/Scala technology for distributed AFP builds without shared memory or shared file systems. A master analyzes session dependencies, synchronizes workers with SSH/rsync, stores coordination state and compressed ML heaps in PostgreSQL, and workers execute sessions independently. A runtime predictor scales historical timings across hosts/threads; a heuristic solves the multi-mode resource-constrained scheduling problem quickly and reschedules as measurements change. The implementation sets concrete infrastructure assumptions (same platform, local SSDs, SSH/bash, PostgreSQL, repository clones) and explains why Slurm was rejected for cross-platform, low-privilege academic clusters. Build phases include dependency extraction, worker initialization, optional benchmark sessions, queue execution and HTML/LaTeX finalization. The scheduler uses Amdahl-law interpolation, conservative overestimation, host/thread modes and a parallel serial-generation scheme; experiments compare classic, heuristic and CPLEX schedules on preliminary, heterogeneous and Isabelle2024 release data. Three datasets contain 19,263, 30,510 and 30,203 session data points. On release hardware the heuristic finishes AFP in 35:40 (40:50 with slow sessions, 1:59:13 full), while distribution classic mode takes 8:10; full AFP CPU/elapsed speedup exceeds 100.

Results use small 8–14-machine clusters and AFP/Isabelle workloads, so scaling to other provers or much larger clusters is not established. The heuristic assumes plentiful slower hardware; solution quality drops when only the four fastest hosts are used. Timing bootstrapping stabilizes after 7–8 runs, so the classic scheduler is recommended for one-shot builds.
use_for_goal: Reliable proof-library CI is infrastructure for verified Rust/Verus and Isabelle/TLA+ projects. The paper gives a concrete model for scaling regression checks while exposing environment, dependency-tree and timing-prediction assumptions that affect evidence of verification.

title: Verifying pCTL Model Checking

title: Complexity of Polyadic Boolean Modal Logics: Model Checking and Satisfiability
what: Studies complexity of satisfiability and combined model checking for polyadic modal logic with relation permutations and Boolean operators (negation, intersection). It proves ExpTime-completeness for PML(¬), ExpTime-completeness for PML^c(p,s,¬,∩) when the accessibility vocabulary is bounded by a constant c, and PTime-completeness for combined model checking of PML(p,s,¬,∩). The paper defines k-ary relation terms, cyclic/swap permutations, Boolean operations, k-tables, and their Kripke semantics. For PML(¬), it gives a polynomial reduction replacing R and ¬R by fresh relations R1,R2 plus a coverage formula η, then reconstructs a model with a two-copy domain. For bounded-vocabulary full Boolean polyadic logic, Lemma 11 first converts modalities to table terms; formulas ξ1–ξ3 force table coverage and closure under permutations, after which a layered domain W×{2,…,m}×N reconstructs a model. The PTime model-checking proof normalizes negations to leading form, evaluates relation terms as polynomial-size sets, and uses a subformula-labeling algorithm with pointer enumeration for complemented relations.

The reductions rely on finite formula subformula sets and table expansion, so the polynomial translation depends on the constant vocabulary (a bound on arity alone is insufficient). PML+global-diamond ExpTime-completeness is imported through a guarded-forward-fragment translation. The model-checking result concerns explicit finite relational structures and formulas, not distributed protocols or infinite-state verification.

title: Justness: A Completeness Criterion for Capturing Liveness Properties
what: Defines justness as a completeness criterion for transition-system paths: once a non-blocking transition enabled by parallel components is not interfered with, some component must eventually act. The paper gives an LTSC framework with blocking actions, concurrency relation, and B-just paths; defines dynamic and static synchron/component relations and proves they induce the same justness. It proves feasibility by constructing extensions of finite paths when countably many enabled non-blocking transitions (or equivalence classes) exist, relates justness to fairness, and proves agreement with coinductive definitions for CCS extensions and abstract paths. It also treats indicators/signals, infinitary choice, and gives inductive/coinductive characterizations.

title: Verifying Asynchronous Interactions via Communicating Session Automata.
what: Introduces k-multiparty compatibility (k-mc) for deterministic communicating session automata. k-mc combines k-safety (eventual reception and progress within channel bound k) with k-exhaustivity (all k-reachable sends can fire within the bound), strictly broadening synchronous multiparty compatibility. The paper proves soundness, local bound-agnosticity characterizations and pspace-completeness, then implements bounded checks with partial-order reduction. Sections 2–4 define FIFO configurations, k-reachability, stable property, output/input bound independence (k-obi/k-ibi), k-exhaustivity and k-mc. Theorem 1 gives safety for k-obi/ibi systems; Theorem 3 characterizes k-exhaustivity by local bound-agnosticity; Theorems 4–7 relate existential boundedness and synchronisability. The client-server-logger example accepts fire-and-forget sends rejected by synchronous criteria. The full benchmark table includes buggy/fixed gen_server, elevator, cloud, SMTP, HTTP, Fibonacci and industrial protocols. Section 5 reports reduced transition systems and generated worst-case chains, including the largest 12,222-state/22,220-transition run.

what: Introduces k-synchronous bounded analysis for finite-state processes communicating through unbounded FIFO buffers. Each phase has at most k sends followed by corresponding receives. The paper decides k-synchronizability, proves reachability over k-synchronous executions complete when synchronizability holds, and establishes PSPACE-completeness. Defines traces with program-order and send-receive edges, k-synchronous semantics and happens-before equivalence. A conflict-graph characterization detects bad cycles or cycles larger than k; monitor processes reduce invariant checking to reachability. The paper handles unbounded buffers, gives examples where small k suffices or fails, and proves the decision procedures and complexity bounds.

assumptions_limits: Finite-state processes and FIFO channels are assumed. Completeness is conditional on a finite k-synchronizability result; general asynchronous programs may fail it. Preserved equivalence is happens-before trace equivalence, and the method targets reachability/invariants rather than liveness. PSPACE procedures can still be costly.
use_for_goal: A precise completeness contract for bounded distributed verification: finite exploration is justified only after proving synchronizability. This is relevant to agents generating message-passing specifications and to TLA+/Verus claims about bounded executions.

When this holds, we say that the program is k-synchronizable1 . Knowing that a program is k-synchronizable allows to conclude that an invariant holds for all computations of the program if no invariant violations have been found by its k-bounded exchange analysis. Notice that k-synchronizability of a pro- gram does not imply that all its behaviours use bounded buﬀers. Consider for instance a program with two processes, a producer that consists of a loop of sends, and a consumer that consists of a loop of receives. Although there are computations where the entry buﬀer of the consumer is arbitrarily large, the program is 1-synchronizable because all its computations are equivalent to com- putations where each message sent by the producer is immediately received by the consumer. Importantly, we show that checking k-synchronizability of a program, with possibly inﬁnite-state processes, can be reduced in linear time to checking state reachability under the k-synchronous semantics (i.e., without considering all the program computations). Therefore, for ﬁnite-state processes, checking k- synchronizability is PSPACE and it is possible to decide invariant properties without dealing with unbounded message buﬀers when the programs are k- synchronizable (the overall complexity being PSPACE). Then, a method for verifying asynchronous message passing programs can be deﬁned, based on iterating k-bounded analyses with increasing value of k, starting from k = 1. If for some k, a violation (i.e., reachability of an error state) is detected, then the iteration stops and the conclusion is that the program is not correct. On the other hand, if for some k, the program is shown to be k-synchronizable and no violations have been found, then again the iteration terminates and the conclusion is that the program is correct. title: Kalas: A Verified, End-To-End Compiler for a Choreographic Language
what: Mechanizes a five-phase compiler from global asynchronous Kalas choreographies to endpoint code and CakeML, composing with CakeML compiler correctness to obtain machine-code guarantees. Proves operational correspondence and network-level deadlock freedom, and deploys a generated producer/filter/consumer system through seL4/CAmkES. Sections 2–3 define asynchronous swapping/deferred-action semantics and endpoint projection, requiring immediate branch notifications when another endpoint’s behavior differs; orphan recursion and divergence introduced at uninvolved endpoints are excluded. Sections 4–6 encode choice as boolean messages, split arbitrary strings into fixed payload chunks with a bookkeeping byte, and convert substitution-based fixpoints into letrec closures, passing variables modified by the body. Section 7 proves weak operational correspondence up to strong bisimilarity with catch-up transitions, then network-level deadlock freedom; local confluence and inert reductions control the interleaving explosion. Section 8 compiles Payload endpoints to CakeML using FFI models, proves FFI irrelevance and forward correctness, and uses proof-producing HOL-function synthesis to discharge each deployment’s environment assumptions. The infinite-execution liveness limitation is discussed explicitly.
numbers: 5 compilation phases and 2 intermediate languages
3 generated producer/filter/consumer endpoints
fixed payload σ>0; transmitted chunks σ+1 bytes
assumptions_limits: Theorems assume projectable choreographies, all free variables initially bound, well-formed/uniquely named endpoint networks and totally correct CakeML implementations of local HOL functions. Values are byte strings; functions compiled at selected endpoints must be sufficiently executable (no arbitrary Hilbert choice/sets/quantifiers). Communication assumes a live backend, lossless delivery and unbounded queues; payload size σ is positive, chunks are σ+1 bytes. Machine-code liveness is subject to out-of-memory behavior in CakeML. The deployment uses C send/receive glue and seL4/CAmkES IPC, but its proofs are not formally connected to the kernel/platform proofs. Section 8.1 says the current compiler theorem guarantees global progress but does not exclude endpoint livelock for choreographies with only infinite paths; stronger fairness/receive-matching transfer remains unproved. No Internet/TCP deployment or bounded-queue result is supplied.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to verified distributed implementation generation: it links global protocol descriptions, asynchronous local endpoints, communication serialization and compiler preservation down to machine code. For specification/proof agents it offers projectability and backend assumptions as concrete obligations and demonstrates why global progress is weaker than each endpoint making progress. It uses HOL4/CakeML, not Verus/Rust/TLA+, and contains no LLM experiment.

title: First-Order Model Checking on Generalisations of Pushdown Graphs
short_name: Kartzow dissertation on pushdown model checking
venue: Doctoral dissertation, Technische Universität Darmstadt; arXiv:1202.0137v1
what: Develops decidability and complexity results for first-order (FO) model checking on infinite structures arising from higher-order software models. It proves tree-automatic representations for level-2 collapsible pushdown graphs with regular reachability and L-mu predicates, FO decidability for nested pushdown trees, a new higher-order nested-pushdown-tree hierarchy with a level-2 algorithm, and decidability of FO extended with counting, infinity, and Ramsey quantifiers on automatic structures. The thesis supplies the constructions behind each theorem: encodings of level-2 stacks into trees; regular reachable configurations, stack operations and reachability predicates; product constructions combining automata and L-mu predicates; locality/Ehrenfeucht-Fraisse and pumping arguments for nested pushdown trees; relevant-ancestor equivalences and small-witness algorithms for higher-order nested trees; and tree-comb/Ramsey reductions. It proves a nonelementary lower bound for FO on level-2 collapsible pushdown graphs, gives 2-EXPSPACE bounds for nested trees, and includes an appendix reducing the Turing-machine halting problem to L-mu model checking on a bidirectional half-grid. The work is mathematical proof and automata construction, not an empirical tool evaluation.
numbers: Theorem 3.0.1: the FO theory of level-2 collapsible pushdown graphs expanded by regular reachability and Lµ-definable predicates is decidable; the following paragraph extends the logic to infinity, modular counting and Ramsey quantifiers
Theorem 3.0.2: FO(REACH) model checking on nested pushdown trees is decidable; plain FO has structure complexity EXPSPACE and expression/combined complexity 2-EXPSPACE
Theorem 3.0.3: FO model checking on level-2 nested pushdown trees is decidable; the preceding EXPSPACE/2-EXPSPACE bounds do not apply to this theorem
Theorem 3.0.4: FO(∃∞, ∃mod, (Ram_n)n∈N) theory of tree-automatic structures is decidable
Theorem 3.1.1: level-2 collapsible pushdown graph expansions are tree-automatic; §3.1.6 proves a nonelementary lower bound and reviews Broadbent’s level-3 FO undecidability result
assumptions_limits: Structures are finitely represented transition/configuration graphs or trees of pushdown systems; the main positive automaticity result is for level 2 collapsible pushdown graphs and stated regular/L-mu expansions. Level 3 collapsible pushdown FO model checking is undecidable, so the technique does not extend generally. Nested-tree complexity bounds are upper bounds, and the automatic FO procedure has nonelementary complexity. Ramsey results assume tree-automatic presentations. The appendix explicitly uses deterministic Turing machines and standard undecidability assumptions.
use_for_goal: Provides foundational formal-verification evidence for infinite-state software abstractions. It complements TLA+ state-machine specifications and Verus verified Rust by proving decidability/complexity of model checking classes rather than verifying one implementation. It also supplies sharp scope limits that an LLM agent must preserve when writing specifications or claiming proofs.

title: Formally Verified Liveness with Multiparty Session Types in Rocq
what: Mechanizes a synchronous multiparty session-type system in Rocq and proves safety, deadlock freedom, and liveness for sessions whose local type environments are associated with balanced global type trees. The formalization uses coinductive local/global type trees, coinductive subtyping and projection, parameterized coinduction (Paco), and explicit fair traces. The paper introduces an explicit association relation between local type environments and global types and proves soundness and completeness of their labelled transitions, allowing a path-level liveness transfer from direct projections to subtyped environments. Balancedness supplies a finite grafting context for the coinductive proof. A reactive semantics makes session transitions correspond one-for-one with type transitions, avoiding weak-simulation machinery. The mechanized liveness theorem is lock-freedom under full fairness; it also exposes a counterexample showing why an unbalanced protocol can be associated yet not live, and gives a precise liveness definition that avoids a stuck recursive process falsely satisfying an earlier formulation.

title: Kratos – A Software Model Checker for SystemC
what: Kratos verifies SystemC safety assertions through two paths: sequentializing the design into C and applying lazy predicate abstraction, or retaining threaded C and using ESST, which explicitly explores scheduler states while symbolically abstracting threads. title: Verifying an HTTP Key-Value Server with Interaction Trees and VST
what: Verifies memory safety and termination-insensitive functional correctness of a hand-written C key-value server against an interaction-tree implementation specification. Proves user-level VST socket specifications refine CertiKOS kernel specifications, and supplies a reusable verified C string library. Section 3 decomposes the event-driven server into String, Buffer, Socket, Parse, KeyValue, Hashtable, Connection and Server APIs. The C HTTP parser refines an executable Gallina parser; the C hash table refines a Gallina model; top-level main relates the event loop to ITree.iter run_server. Section 4 translates higher-order VST assertions through first-order dry specifications on CompCert memory and external state, then connects those to CertiKOS socket/log state. Each successful ITree event matches a kernel log event; failed calls leave the permission tree unchanged. Refinement exposed a missing bind port-range precondition. Section 5 defines permission-aware C-string predicates and indexed strstr/strchr/strcasestr wrappers that discharge pointer-subtraction obligations once. Sections 6–7 precisely identify the absent high-level request/response refinement and describe a specification-derived test client finding a liveness bug.

title: Lazy Proof Automation for Separation Logic
what: Yolo separates a fast unverified heap-entailment simplifier from later Lean proof reconstruction. Mixed native-expression/list syntax and extensible operator tags retain host-language terms and permit operator-specific simplification and proofs. Integrates with Iris-Lean and relational LGTM; evaluates interactive and reconstructed runtimes against several separation-logic automation systems. Details how CFML-style six-component symbolic simplification becomes list manipulation with a recorded tacticScript, followed by replay of list-based soundness lemmas. Extensible plain-tag trees avoid positivity restrictions of recursively parameterized functor encodings. No full formal correctness theorem for all metaprogramming code is presented in the paper. Generic integration requires MoSeL BIBase/BI instances and the algebraic/soundness lemmas used by handlers. Adding an operator’s unverified Eval/equality/parsing instances is insufficient for foundational certification; each simplification handler needs its proof justification. The implementation only automates supported core operators and registered extensions. Unknown connectives remain unchanged. Iris-specific modalities in the example still require IPM tactics. Generic extensibility does not establish automatic proof search or completeness for arbitrary separation logics. Native Lean Expr and isDefEq retain polymorphic/dependent host terms, but definitional matching is heuristic and does not establish arbitrary semantic equivalence. The positivity-safe opT tree carries a plain operator tag and arbitrary argument list; its type alone does not enforce an operator’s arity. Checked reconstruction is the relevant boundary. Table1 baseline is Splean’s Lean port of CFML-style xsimpl, not a direct Rocq CFML execution comparison. Timings instrument tactic work inside selected proofs, not full project build time or user productivity. The small selected set is not a representative corpus claim. Synthetic competitors share only shuffled conjunction cancellation. HTT uses equality of disjoint heap unions, while other frameworks prove entailments. Different logics, host languages, tactic interfaces and measurement methods limit ranking beyond those tasks. Pulse comparison is against Yolo’s unverified phase; Bedrock/iFrame figures explicitly include reconstruction. Machine: Dell Ubuntu workstation,5.4GHz Intel i7-14700. No repetition counts, confidence intervals, random seeds, complete software revisions, memory results or controlled ablation of each design change are reported. Zenodo software link and GitHub are provided but were not inspected or executed by reader. The paper does not evaluate verified C/Rust execution, distributed protocols, TLA+, liveness, LLM agents or generated specifications. Iris is a concurrency-capable framework, but integration and entailment benchmarks do not by themselves prove a concurrent application correct.
use_for_goal: A candidate architecture for proof agents: explore with fast unchecked simplification, then require reconstructed proof and faithful assumptions before acceptance. Gives concrete extensibility costs, trace/checking boundaries and runtime measurement distinctions relevant to evaluating generated verification proofs. Transfer to Verus/Rust/distributed systems is reader inference, with no direct evaluation here.

title: Lazy Self-composition for Security Verification.
what: Combines symbolic path-sensitive taint analysis of one program copy with precise two-copy safety verification to avoid eager full self-composition. Ifc-CEGAR validates candidate taint leaks, transfers relational invariant information and refines taint updates. Ifc-BMC duplicates only possibly tainted computations while unrolling, and can prove safety early when all live initial taint disappears. SeaHorn prototypes are compared to eager composition on small security benchmarks. Details observability/declassification predicates, the one-sided meaning of taint, proof-trace rewriting versus strengthening and the model refinement needed to restore induction. Keeps conditional completeness separate from prototype support; preserves no-fresh-secret condition for BMC termination, unknown handling, bitvector/struct limitations, all benchmark values and the narrow evidence behind scalability/constant-time claims.
assumptions_limits: §§3–4: transition-system variables and quantifier-free first-order theory formulas describe Init, Tr and Bad. Tr is assumed reflexive so either program copy may stutter. H identifies initially secret variables and L is its complement. Security is defined relative to the chosen operational model and observation predicates, not every possible timing/cache/network observation. §4: Obs_x specifies when a low variable is adversary-observable. The terminal-output policy, concurrently executing observers and selected declassification contexts are modeled by these predicates. Setting Obs false or explicitly marking a value untainted changes the permitted policy and must be justified externally; it is not a derived no-leak theorem. §4.1: taint marks high variables true and low variables false initially. Theta(expression) disjoins taint of its variables; conditional update taint includes condition taint and the chosen branch expression. It tracks explicit and implicit flows but overapproximates value dependence, e.g. different expressions with the same result. The final prose reverses x1/x2 dependency direction; the displayed update gives the intended meaning. §4.2: self-composition starts low variables equal and leaves high values independent. Bad requires one low value unequal while both copies satisfy its observation predicate. Results concern this paired-execution definition under the chosen stuttering model; termination behavior or microarchitectural leakage is not automatically covered. §5 Corollaries1–2: real self-composition leaks imply possible taint leaks; no taint leak proves no modeled leak. A tainted output alone does not prove insecurity. Untainted implies equality across the related copies, whereas equality need not imply untainted in the original abstraction. §5.1 Algorithm1: taint solver SAFE ends the check; a taint counterexample triggers a constrained self-composed problem. One described Constraint choice bounds all self-composed executions by the counterexample length k rather than merely replaying one control path. An actual paired witness gives UNSAFE; a spurious one supplies relational facts for refinement. §5.1: ReWrite adds single-copy facts and entailed equalities/disequalities while preserving claimed inductive traces, without itself improving the taint abstraction. Strengthening additionally uses proved equalities to require no taint, which can destroy induction. Refine changes selected next-taint functions under the strengthened frame condition to restore induction; it is not merely adding an unproved invariant to the original model. §5.1 Theorem1 assumes a sound and complete first-order-theory model checker maintaining inductive traces. It states Ifc-CEGAR soundness/completeness under that assumption and gives a proof sketch, not unconditional decidability or termination for arbitrary C/CHCs or a proof that Spacer always terminates. Lemma claims/trace transformations are not mechanically verified here. §5.1 printed formula issues, visually confirmed: equations10/12 initialize a trace over Y=X∪Xt using Init_d, which is defined over X∪Xd; displayed component-preservation implications on p.145 use frame i on both sides instead of i+1; equation13 switches superscript d to s. The record follows the stated algorithmic intent without silently treating the typeset formulas as a complete executable correctness proof. §5.2 Algorithms2–3: an UNSAT taint query permits the duplicate value to reuse the original computation. SAT or UNKNOWN conservatively duplicates it. At BND without a conclusive result return UNKNOWN; failure to find a bounded counterexample alone is not safety. The simplified bad formula omits Obs only for exposition. §§1,5.2: early safety requires no live variable tainted and no leak found in the checked prefix. Initial secret taint must be exhausted and no new secret input introduced later; the introduction explicitly states this assumption and says later tainted inputs need a modified check. Does not provide a general finite completeness bound for ongoing distributed services. Algorithm notation issues: Algorithm2 calls LazySC(M,Mt), whereas Algorithm3 header orders(Mt,M); Algorithm1 advertises UNKNOWN but main loop has no solver-UNKNOWN branch, and its UNKNOWN return follows until-infinity. These are high-level sketches; practical resource/solver-unknown handling is not completely specified. Algorithm2 also does not explicitly distinguish an unknown composed-property query before its early-safety check. §§6–6.2: prototype initially described as not bit-precise and not supporting complex lists. More specifically CEGAR uses LLVM instrumentation plus Spacer and cannot handle benchmark structs or bitvector operations; BMC works over CHCs with Z3 and handles all evaluated programs. Do not generalize CEGAR restrictions to the list/BV BMC rows or infer full C bit-precise semantics from them. §§6.2–6.4: Intel Core i7-4578U,8GB RAM;300s timeout. Eager comparisons use the same backend on two copies. All seven CEGAR rows are safe, only pwdcheck2 needs one refinement; the other six are discharged by taint analysis with no self-composition refinement. Eight BMC rows include two unsafe variants. These selected small/microbenchmarks are not a large deployed-code security audit. §6.4: Table3 runtime at array size64 is85.44s, supporting under2min on that instance. Author statement of exponential runtime growth is a qualitative characterization of eight observations, not a proved asymptotic bound or scaling to unbounded arrays. Exact BND values, program sizes, solver versions, repetition variance and memory consumption are not supplied. §§7–8: security-type, dynamic-taint and product-program comparisons are discussion claims without separate head-to-head benchmark data here. General k-safety and quantified relational invariants for unbounded data structures are future work. No verified implementation, certificate validation, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM evaluation is reported. Frontend, instrumentation, policy and solvers remain trusted.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for agents specifying noninterference or secret-dependent iteration counts in distributed service components. Treat single-copy taint as a sound preliminary abstraction, validate alarms relationally and retain three outcomes. Invariant reuse can reduce duplicated proof state, but any taint-clearing refinement needs the relational justification. Preserve observer/declassification assumptions and fresh-input restrictions; bounded service executions and exhausted initial taint do not establish confidentiality for an indefinitely running system.

title: Leaderless State-Machine Replication: Specification, Properties, Limits
what: The paper gives a framework for leaderless state-machine replication (SMR), modeling dependency graphs, command phases, dependency discovery, consensus objects, and execution batches. It defines reliability, optimal latency, and load balancing (ROLL) properties and proves a trade-off: with n processes, fast-path quorum size n−F and failure tolerance f, ROLL protocols must satisfy 2F+f−1≤n. It further proves a lower bound on message delay for ROLL-optimal protocols, explaining the chaining effect seen in EPaxos. Generic SMR is shown to reduce to the leaderless abstraction, while cycles mean leaderless protocols need mutual dependency visibility rather than a total order.
assumptions_limits: The model is wait-free asynchronous message passing with fail-stop failures, unbounded logs/commands, deterministic state machines, and a conflict relation that safely over-approximates non-commutativity. Correctness is expressed by validity, stability, and consistency of dependency graphs; liveness and implementation details are abstracted. The supplied text contains the framework and introductory definitions but not the later full proof pages, so numerical lower-bound derivations beyond the stated inequality and the complete §4–§8 argument cannot be independently quoted from this extraction.
use_for_goal: Provides a formal abstraction and performance limit for leaderless consensus protocols such as EPaxos. Its explicit conflict/dependency invariants and quorum trade-off are useful when specifying or verifying distributed logs and when checking whether a protocol's claimed latency and fault tolerance can coexist.

quotes.text: We first propose a framework that captures the essence of leaderless state-machine replication (Leaderless SMR). Then, we introduce a set of desirable properties for these protocols: (R)eliability, (O)ptimal (L)atency and (L)oad Balancing.

More precisely, in a system of n processes, the ROLL theorem (§4) states that Leaderless SMR protocols are subject to the inequality 2F + f − 1 ≤ n, where n − F is the size of the fast path quorum and f is the maximal number of tolerated failures.
In a leaderless state-machine replication (Leaderless SMR) protocol, there is no primary process to arbitrate upon the ordering of commands.
Stability: For each command c, there exists D such that if c is stable then deps(c) = D. Consistency: If a and b are both committed and conflicting, then a ∈ deps(b) or b ∈ deps(a).
I Theorem 1. Generic SMR reduces to Leaderless SMR.
This lower bound explains the persistent chaining effect observed in experimental results.

title: Lean Formalization of Completeness Proof for Coalition Logic with Common Knowledge
what: Reports a Lean 4 formalization of soundness, completeness and the finite model property for coalition logic with individual/common knowledge. Uses reusable syntax and proof-system typeclasses across CL, CLK and CLC, canonical coalition models and finite filtration. Main contribution is mechanized logical metatheory and proof engineering, not an implemented distributed-system case study. Records exact semantic/frame assumptions, positive-length common-knowledge paths, canonical effectivity cases, closure changes needed for deep embedding, finite-state construction, staged Set/Finset/List proofs and the concrete N-maximality derivation. Identifies a printed semantic discrepancy for empty-group common knowledge between the usual reflexive-transitive interpretation of starred notation and the shown Lean path constructors. Separates reported sorry-free artifact from abridged paper snippets; no independent replay.
assumptions_limits: §§3–5, pp.3–7: finite nonempty agent set for stated logic, nonempty state space, atomic propositions encoded by naturals. Syntax is an inductive deep embedding with bottom, variables, conjunction, implication, coalition effectivity, individual knowledge and common knowledge. Syntax itself accepts arbitrary agent types; Fintype and Nonempty hypotheses are introduced where needed. Semantics uses classical reasoning and noncomputable finite-set conversions within Lean/Mathlib. §4, p.4: effectivity E(s,G) is a family of outcome sets a coalition can force, abstracting away explicit actions and strategies. True playability requires six conditions: empty outcome never forceable, universal outcome forceable, grand-coalition maximality relative to empty-coalition complements, outcome monotonicity, superadditivity for disjoint coalitions and a least empty-coalition outcome set. These are model assumptions, not distributed runtime liveness or memory-safety claims. §4/5, pp.4–7: each individual knowledge relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive (S5-style equivalence). Coalition effectivity means the satisfying-state set belongs to E(s,G). Individual knowledge quantifies over indistinguishable states. Printed mathematical common knowledge uses a starred union relation, whereas Lean snippets use paths with at least one edge. For a nonempty coalition reflexivity bridges these conventions; empty coalition requires a different convention and exposes a discrepancy. §6/Table 1, pp.5/7: reported soundness Theorem 4 is theoremhood implies validity in the defined class of models, proved by induction on derivations. Axioms for coalition operators correspond to playability conditions; knowledge axioms use equivalence relations. Common-knowledge axiom C and induction rule RC use path-constructor arguments. This is not correctness of any specific program or natural-language requirement. §7, pp.8–9: Pformula gives constructors, Pformula_ax adds propositional derivability, CLformula adds effectivity and laws, Kformula individual knowledge, Cformula common knowledge with finite agent type. Typeclasses state minimum operations/laws; they are not generic inductive syntax. Generic semantics is omitted, so some proofs by induction remain tied to particular formula datatypes. §8.1, p.9: canonical coalition states are maximal consistent sets. For proper coalitions, X is effective iff some formula has its truth set inside X and its effectivity formula in the state. The grand-coalition case uses complements and absence of empty-coalition effectivity. Generic construction assumes nonempty agents and propositional bottom is not derivable. Initial canonical model has only five playability conditions and no epistemic relations. §8.2, pp.9–11: finite closure contains every subformula of every closure member, single negations, Ki CG ψ for members of common-knowledge groups and CG[G]ψ for effectivity formulas. Finiteness of agent groups enables finite expansion. Filtered states are canonical-state intersections with closure, represented by a filtered powerset and attached membership proof. There are at most 2^|cl(φ)| possible filtered states; this is a reader counting bound, not a paper runtime measurement. §8.2/8.3, pp.10–14: filtered effectivity treats grand coalition existentially and proper coalitions universally over canonical representatives. Finite models make empty-coalition principality follow from playability. Proofs use pairwise incompatibility of distinct filtered states and provability of the universal state disjunction. Set-to-Finset-to-List conversions require preserving disjointness, membership and absence of duplicates. §8.4/8.5, pp.14–15: Truth Lemma 5 equates filtered-state membership and satisfaction for formulas inside the finite closure. Common-knowledge proof inducts on positive-length paths from the front. Completeness Theorem 6 is validity implies theoremhood, using a maximal consistent extension of {¬φ} and a finite filtered countermodel. This establishes formula completeness/finite countermodels under the chosen semantics, not strong completeness for arbitrary infinite theories or a measured decision algorithm. §§1/3/9, pp.2–3/15–17: authors report all artifact proofs sorry-free, Lean 4.4.0-rc1 and Mathlib 98fe17fd, after completing an original Lean 3 proof and porting it. Paper snippets omit proof steps and even show an explicitly explained sorry. Code size about 6,000 lines: 300 CL, 700 CLK, 1,100 CLC and almost 4,000 shared. No exact build timings, proof-search benchmark, independent axiom audit or implementation replay provided in this reading. §9, pp.16–17: main engineering burden is finiteness/datatype conversion and long routine inductions. Native quantified representations and more generic semantics/inductive structures are proposed improvements, not implemented evaluations. IoT and metro systems motivate the introduction but are not verified cases. No Rust, Verus, TLA+, LLM agent or deployed distributed protocol experiment.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: supplies foundational semantics for strategic ability and knowledge in interacting agents, and a reusable metatheory formalization useful for assessing generated logic specifications. Most relevant lessons are explicit frame assumptions, local finiteness hypotheses, syntax/closure dependence and matching an intended meaning to its formal encoding, especially empty-group common knowledge. Completeness of a logic and a successful proof check do not establish that a distributed-system requirement has been modeled appropriately. No end-to-end distributed implementation, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-generated proof evaluation.

title: A Graphical User Interface Framework for Formal Verification
what: Designs and implements ProofWidgets, a Lean metaprogramming framework for declarative web UIs inside an interactive theorem prover. Components use functional reactive state and a virtual DOM; server-side Lean handlers retain tactic context while the editor renders HTML and forwards events. The framework exposes Html and Component with init/view/update; component state can contain the complete tactic state. A JSON client/server protocol annotates source positions with VDOMs, reconciles trees while preserving component state, dispatches event-handler identifiers and returns editor effects. Structured eformat tags pretty-printed subexpressions with expression addresses, enabling semantic highlighting, nested tooltips, go-to-definition and rewrite tooling. The Lean 3 implementation supports VSCode and remote sessions, has been adopted in mathlib with hundreds of contributors, and demonstrates interactive expressions, plots and community widgets. A 1000-node goal widget measured under 80 ms pointer-to-pixels on a 2012 Intel i7 laptop. Long-running tactics currently block rendering; concurrency and Lean 4 support are future work.

title: Lean4Agent: Formal Modeling and Verification for Agent Workflow and Trajectory
what: Presents Lean4Agent, a Lean4 dependent-type framework with FormalAgentLib for structural, semantic and execution-trajectory verification of LLM-agent workflows, plus LeanEvolve for verification-guided workflow refinement. Workflows are typed heterogeneous graphs of read/write variables, natural-language instructions and execution types; trajectories record pre/post states and reasoning/tool traces. Layer 1 checks node reachability, edge validity and read/write consistency. Layer 2 translates explicit and implicit variables into decidable predicates and graph-level information-flow/context predicates, proving precondition entailment under an LLMExec local-correctness assumption. Layer 3 checks concrete trajectories using Lean propositions, Python validators and LLM-as-judge, localizing failed steps. LeanEvolve feeds diagnostics and optional test feedback to an LLM for targeted workflow edits, with a pure-LLM exploratory mode. Experiments generate 40 workflows, compare verification-passing/failing workflows across five LLMs on 50 hard SWE-Bench-Verified tasks and 100 ELAIP-Bench questions, and study graph-predicate and pure-LLM ablations.

title: LeanLTL: A Unifying Framework for Linear Temporal Logics in Lean
what: Presents a Lean 4 temporal-logic library with a shared semantic representation for finite and infinite nonempty traces, arbitrary Lean propositions/data expressions, LTL-like macro notation, and preliminary simplification-based automation. Gives machine-checked embeddings of LTL and LTLf and a traffic-light safety/liveness example. Trace uses an Option-valued sequence N→Option σ, extended natural length, nonemptiness proof, and a proof that values are defined exactly before length. TraceSet is a predicate on traces; TraceFun maps a trace to Option α, with strong/weak get interpreting undefined values as False/True. The LLTL macro recursively rewrites host connectives, pushes next into trace-function arrows, binds strong gets before weak gets, and coerces remaining propositions/predicates into trace sets. The push_ltl simp set translates satisfaction into first-order semantics so existing Lean tactics can finish arithmetic obligations; Figure 1 proves an invariant of the recurrence n=5 initially and n_next=n² by globally_induction and nlinarith. LTL/LTLf embeddings use inductive syntax, evaluation, translation, and a satisfaction-equivalence theorem. The traffic-light example includes queue arithmetic and environment assumptions, proving exactly one light green globally and both lights green infinitely often for traces satisfying those assumptions.

The traffic-light system behavior is assumed from external specifications; complete example/embedding proofs are in the cited software repository rather than fully printed in the short paper. title: Timed Automata Verification and Synthesis via Finite Automata Learning.
kind: conference verification and synthesis algorithm paper
what: Decomposes a timed-automaton system into a large finite-state machine A and smaller timed component T, learns DFAs approximating T, then applies finite-state model checking or game solving. Model checking is sound via an overapproximation; synthesis alternates over- and under-approximations and is sound but incomplete under a Controller-silent restriction. For model checking, L* or TTT learning uses membership and inclusion oracles answered by TChecker; once L(T)⊆L(H), finite-state checking of A×H yields assume-guarantee safety. For synthesis, learners maintain H_under⊆L(T)⊆H_over, with Abssynthe solving finite games and NuSMV checking strategy containment. Controller-silent means controller transitions are silent and controller locations urgent, enabling transfer of winning strategies from G×H to G×T. The Scala prototype integrates TChecker, NuSMV, LearnLib/AutomataLib, Yosys/berkeley-abc and Abssynthe.

title: Learning dynamic polynomial proofs
what: DQN selects elementary polynomial inference steps, building a small set of nonnegative lemmas. A linear program combines those lemmas into an upper-bound certificate. A permutation-invariant polynomial embedding supports transfer across graph sizes. On dense random maximum-stable-set instances, reports tighter bounds with much smaller final LPs than tested static hierarchy levels. Learned search proposes steps; algebraic rules and final identities justify the certificates. Explains the distinction between a feasible stable set (existential lower bound) and a nonnegativity proof (universal upper bound). Gives strict-positivity completeness for hypercube certificates, a complete-graph dynamic degree-two derivation, and a supplementary n/l lower bound for the specified static LP. Constructs trilinear monomial-orbit features invariant to variable renaming plus max pooling over memories/equalities. Supplies dense LP-based rewards, cached action scoring, full DQN settings, a symmetry ablation and explicit rational graph certificates.
assumptions_limits: Inference rules multiply an established nonnegative polynomial by x_i or 1−x_i and take nonnegative linear combinations. Their soundness requires x in [0,1]^n and correct initial axioms. Stable-set experiments also reduce modulo x_i^2=x_i and x_ix_j=0 for graph edges. Polynomial simplification and coefficient equality must preserve that quotient semantics. The main completeness theorem is quoted from Krivine: strictly positive polynomials on the compact hypercube have a finite nonnegative sum of x^alpha(1−x)^beta generators. The footnote restricts the completeness claim to strict positivity/refutation. It does not prove every merely nonnegative polynomial has such a certificate, nor that bounded-degree learned search is complete. Training uses random graphs with25 vertices and edge probability p in[0.5,1]. Generated memories start with2n inequality axioms and graph/Boolean equalities. Search is capped at100 additions and degree2 intermediate lemmas. Results do not establish performance on arbitrary polynomial optimization, sparse graphs, distributed programs or natural-language statements. No human proofs or optimal α(G) labels train the agent, but the dense reward depends on solving a mathematical LP after each addition. “Unsupervised” here means absence of supplied target proofs/optimum labels; it does not mean learning without an exact optimization environment. The orbit-based embedding and symmetric pooling establish architectural invariance under set enumeration and joint variable relabeling. Invariance is not injectivity or a proof of successful generalization. Fixed degree bounds the orbit feature dimension independently of sufficiently large n, while enumerating polynomials/actions still grows with n. Bounds are certified only if nonnegative coefficients and polynomial identities are checked accurately. Printed rational examples admit exact arithmetic; the paper does not provide a verified LP implementation or a systematic numerical-to-rational certificate-reconstruction/error protocol for every aggregate experiment. Supplementary theorem γ_l≥n/l concerns the precise product-generator hierarchy in Eq.10 with only Boolean and edge equalities. It is not a lower bound for every static method or for formulations strengthened by extra valid inequalities. Dynamic advantage is demonstrated against tested levels2–5 and random legal actions, not every proof search strategy. Only one training seed(0) and one NVIDIA V100 are specified. Test means cover100 random graph instances for each reported size. No intervals, multi-seed variability, end-to-end wall-clock comparison, total GPU training time or ground-truth optimality-gap table is supplied.
use_for_goal: An early concrete example of learned proof search with a small trusted mathematical core: neural choices guide lemmas, while certificates can be checked without trusting the neural model. Useful for evaluating LLM proof pipelines through certificate validity, search budget, representation assumptions and actual compute rather than aggregate success alone. Polynomial invariants could support verification in future integrations, but distributed-system/Verus/TLA+ applications are not demonstrated.

title: Infinite Time Horizon Safety of Bayesian Neural Networks
short_name: Lechner et al. Infinite Time Horizon Safety
what: Defines sure infinite-time-horizon safety for Bayesian neural-network policies in closed-loop discrete-time systems and computes a safe subset of the weight posterior. The method learns a neural-network positive-invariant certificate and uses a constraint-solving verifier; unsafe posterior samples are rejected, with an adaptation to safe-exploration reinforcement learning. The paper turns a product of intervals W_epsilon around posterior means into a verifiable weight set. For feed-forward ReLU BNNs, it encodes existence of an unsafe input/output and all weight choices as Phi constraints, proving safety iff Phi is unsatisfiable (Theorem 1), with MILP, Reluplex, or NRA-SMT options. For feedback systems it defines W_epsilon-safe positive invariants, proves they imply safety of every trajectory (Theorem 2), and gives a counterexample-guided learner/verifier: a classifier g_Inv is retrained on violating transitions and the verifier checks closedness, initial non-negativity, and unsafe-state negativity. Epsilon is enlarged iteratively from a previously successful certificate; rejection sampling and projected updates support safe exploration.

title: Lessons for Interactive Theorem Proving Researchers from a Survey of Coq Users
what: Analyzes the Coq Community Survey 2022, an online survey with 466 submitted responses, using descriptive comparisons and multiple-variable regressions. Regressions restrict to 390 recent users, then remove 18 without age, leaving 372 (367 for IDE satisfaction). It reports associations between experience, learner status, software-verification use, location and Coq tools, interfaces, satisfaction and requested improvements. Experience is associated with tool/library/CI/extraction use; software-verification respondents report more ecosystem-tool use and extraction. Results concern associations and a non-random respondent sample, not causal effects or all Coq users. Regressions first restrict to 390 respondents who used Coq in the last year, then exclude 18 without age, leaving 372 (367 for IDE satisfaction), Romano-Wolf adjusted p-values and a 0.1 threshold. Controls include age, gender, operating system, research area, employment and PhD. Robust examples include more than two years associated with CoqIDE use, North America with Emacs use, more than five years with lower favorite-IDE satisfaction and a larger excess of essential technical over community improvements, and software-verification use with new extraction-target requests. The paper explains why raw responses are withheld for privacy while code, generated plots and aggregated/open-text data are supplied. Figure 3 (p.12:13) ranks “Fixing bugs” and “Documentation” first by majority judgment: 62% of 299 answers and 56% of 342 answers, respectively, mark them “Essential”; question-specific denominators differ. These are respondents’ priorities, not measurements of improvement effectiveness.

title: Stochastic Games with Lexicographic Reachability-Safety Objectives
what: Studies finite turn-based zero-sum stochastic games whose ordered objectives are reachability or safety, and computes the lexicographic value and optimal strategies. For absorbing targets, removes locally suboptimal actions and characterizes optimality as local lex-optimality plus almost-sure reachability of a final set. It reduces safety objectives to quantified reachability, then handles non-absorbing targets by recursively solving stages for visited target sets (up to 2^n−1), composing stage strategies with n-bit memory. It proves determinacy, deterministic strategies with at most 2^n−1 memory classes, PSPACE-hardness and an NEXPTIME∩coNEXPTIME upper bound (NP∩coNP for constant n or absorbing objectives).
numbers: Dice[50]: 96,295 states, 3 s lex solve; Hallway 10x10: 400,000 states, 548 s; Avoid Observer 20x20: 1,436,404 states, 281 s; stages used 1/3 for Dice and 4/7 for AV; all instances solved within minutes on 2.4 GHz quad-core i5 with 4 GB Java VM
assumptions_limits: Finite state, turn-based stochastic games with Borel reachability/safety objectives; values use lexicographic sup-inf and the algorithm relies on a single-objective solver (experiments use approximate PRISM-games value iteration, so exact lex-values are not measured). General-case complexity leaves a PSPACE-vs-NEXPTIME gap; only reachability/safety are treated, and parity or richer quantitative objectives are future work.
use_for_goal: Relevant formal baseline for multi-objective distributed/reactive verification: explicit strategy memory, determinacy and staged decomposition inform protocol synthesis, although it is not Rust/Verus and assumes finite game models.

quotes.text: To the best of our knowledge, stochastic games with lexicographic objectives have not been studied before.

We estab- lish determinacy of such games and present strategy and computational complexity results.

title: LLM-Guided Loop Bound Generation for Program Termination Verification
what: Introduces LIFT, a guess-and-check termination framework in which LLMs generate conjunctive or lexicographic loop bounds and a formal validator proves them or refutes them. A candidate bound b(V) is converted to a safety query by adding a counter initialized with b and asserting cnt>0 at each loop head. Constant bounds use bounded unrolling; symbolic bounds use ICE-DT or LLM invariant learners plus Boogie/SMT. If invariant proving fails, bounded violation analysis searches for a reachable counterexample state and feeds it back, while timeout and syntax diagnostics steer later prompts. Progressive generation starts with simple conjunctive bounds and escalates to lexicographic tuples; constant-offset correction and k-induction are included.

Nineteen of 171 benchmarks remain unsolved: ten lacked precise bounds and nine exceeded validator capability.

title: Limit-Deterministic Büchi Automata for Linear Temporal Logic
what: Gives a direct compositional translation from full LTL to limit-deterministic Büchi automata (LDBA). A nondeterministic initial component tracks after-formulas and guesses eventually true G-subformulas; a deterministic accepting component uses breakpoint G-monitors and auxiliary monitors to check the guess. The construction supports the standard quantitative MDP model-checking algorithm by encoding jumps as product actions. The construction defines Reach(ϕ) via the after-function modulo propositional equivalence, then builds one deterministic G-monitor for each guessed G-subformula and a product of monitors, plus an auxiliary monitor for the G-free residual. Stable sets characterize which G-subformulas eventually hold; Lemmas 4–8 establish monitor/product correctness and Theorem 1 proves language equivalence. Theorem 2 gives a double-exponential lower bound. Theorem 3 proves that the LDBA can be used directly in quantitative MDP checking by delaying the jump until a BSCC determines the eventual G-set. Optimizations remove sinks/transient jumps and simplify monitor states.

title: Model-Checking Parameterized Concurrent Programs Using Linear Interfaces.
short_name: Linear interfaces for parameterized model checking
what: The paper introduces linear interfaces that summarize the effect of an arbitrary block of threads during k-round schedules of Boolean parameterized programs. A compositional fixed-point algorithm computes k-round reachability without enumerating all threads, and a two-player adequacy game checks whether states reachable at k+1 rounds are already reachable at k; if Adam wins, the program is proved correct for any thread count and schedule. The implementation uses symbolic BDDs/Getafix and evaluates predicate abstractions of Linux device drivers interacting with an OS kernel.
assumptions_limits: Programs have Boolean data, finitely many process templates, shared variables, arbitrary finite thread counts, interleaving semantics, and no true dynamic thread creation (dormant threads can model it but creation incurs a context switch). General reachability is undecidable; k-round exploration is an under-approximation. The adequacy game is sound but incomplete because Eve's one-thread-at-a-time declaration can give her spurious power. Detailed proofs are omitted from the conference paper and supplied in a cited full version.
use_for_goal: Offers a concrete compositional method for verifying unboundedly many concurrent threads and a stopping certificate for bounded-round exploration. Linear interfaces and adequacy games are relevant to distributed-system verification where exhaustive state-space search is impossible and to assessing whether a generated invariant proves all thread counts.

quotes.text: We propose that such programs can be model-checked by iteratively considering the program under k-round schedules, for increasing values of k, using a novel compositional construct called linear interfaces that summarize the effect of a block of threads in a k-round schedule.
If Adam has a winning strategy (and hence Eve has none), then this proves that every global state reachable in the (k + 1)-th round is already reachable in the k-th round.

Our implementation ... [reports] experiments performed on about 8000 programs and properties, and show that our tool can effectively find reachable error-states, and furthermore prove that more than 80% of them are entirely correct, using the adequacy check.
Since two threads communicating through a finite shared memory suffice to simulate a Turing machine, this problem is clearly undecidable.
the model-checking problem in our setting is Pspace-complete.

title: LISA – A Modern Proof System
what: Initial proof assistant and kernel for single-sorted schematic first-order logic with equality and axiomatic set theory. Kernel uses ortholattice-based formula comparison, explicit DAG proof steps and theory-specific sealed theorem values. Scala DSL constructs checked proofs/tactics; demonstrations include a propositional solver, unique/underspecified definitions and Cantor’s theorem. Explains which propositional equivalences and limited quantifier rules the efficient kernel handles, why automatic quantifier instantiation is excluded from F(OL)^2 comparison while explicit instantiation proof steps remain kernel-checkable, how standalone proof imports differ from justified theory theorems, and why schematic axiom schemas make existence-only definition unsound as a conservative extension. Underspecified definitions use a unique concrete witness while exposing only a weaker property.
assumptions_limits: Logical foundation is classical first-order sequent calculus with schematic function/predicate/connector instantiation, equality and chosen axioms. Schematic symbols are not bound higher-order quantifiers; authors argue they do not increase expressive power because instantiation can be simulated. No proof of consistency of ZFC/Tarski-Grothendieck axioms is supplied. Kernel implementation is about 1607 Scala lines of code, with about 300 for the ortholattice algorithm. Polynomial/quadratic complexity claims concern checking explicit proof data and formula comparisons, not general proof search. No machine-checked verification of the whole Scala kernel/compiler/runtime or empirical complexity benchmark is reported. Ortholattice equivalence is a restricted propositional theory excluding Boolean distributivity. F(OL)^2 extends it with equality symmetry/reflexivity, universal monotonicity and congruence for schematic connectors. It is not a complete validity or equivalence decision procedure for first-order logic. Standalone proof checking establishes derivability from explicitly listed imports; it does not prove imported axioms/theorems themselves. Theory validates imports against its own stored axioms/theorems/definitions, and a theorem remains relative to that theory’s assumptions. Calling the result unconditionally true in the paper does not establish consistency of arbitrary user axioms. Theorem type depends on a specific Theory instance; host language path-dependent types prevent ordinary mixing of facts from distinct theories. Scala type checking is a usability/encapsulation mechanism, while kernel proof checking remains the proof-validity boundary. Function definitions require fresh symbol and proof of unique existence. Existence alone could yield a global pick function and Choice when new symbols are usable in replacement schemas. Underspecification weakens the exposed fact after checking a unique construction; it does not discard the existence/uniqueness obligation. Tautology is a non-clausal DPLL-like propositional proof search with worst-case exponential atom branching, most-frequent-atom heuristic and ortholattice simplification. Its stated completeness is for propositional reasoning, not quantified mathematical proof or all first-order validity. Quantifier automation/external ATP integrations are future work. Interaction model at publication uses Scala IDE, rerunning projects and incremental compilation; live interactive proof state and serialized theories are not established features. Future usability/interoperability/verification benefits are design goals, not measured comparative outcomes. Set-theory library is early: basic sets, relations, functions and Cantor. Orders/ordinals/induction ongoing; category theory/Coq embedding via Grothendieck universes future. No distributed-system proof, Verus/Rust implementation verification, LLM experiment or TLA+ proof integration is presented.
use_for_goal: Suggests proof-agent infrastructure with explicit import checking, bounded-cost certificate verification, theory separation and controlled definition interfaces. Distinguishes proof search cost from checking and intentional underspecification from arbitrary missing assumptions. Relevance to distributed/TLA+/Verus workflows is reader inference from proof architecture; no such application is evaluated.

title: Towards LLM-based Generation of Human-Readable Proofs in Polynomial Formal Verification
what: Argues for using LLMs to draft human-readable explanations of polynomial formal-verification proofs, illustrated with induction and BDD size examples, while insisting that a formal reasoning engine must validate every generated claim. The paper places PFV in a resource-bounded setting for adders/multipliers and describes induction prompts for two-variable and three-variable monomial sums and totally symmetric Boolean functions, where BDD size is linear or quadratic under stated structures. It deliberately probes a multiplication-function answer: ChatGPT first gives a misleading variable-ordering claim, then the author identifies the complexity error, showing why LLM prose cannot be trusted as proof. Proposed future directions include retrieval-augmented proof context, chain-of-thought and feedback from formal tools, and application to modern data structures.

Examples concern well-studied Boolean functions and do not establish general proof synthesis, scalability, or correctness of generated text. title: Bridging LLM Planning Agents and Formal Methods: A Case Study in Plan Verification
what: Introduces an LLM pipeline that translates natural-language plans into NuSMV Kripke structures and LTL properties, then uses model checking to classify plan validity on a simplified PlanBench task. NuSMV bounded model checking labels generated models valid (SAT), invalid (UNSAT) or unknown (parse/model failure). what: Introduces LLMLIFT, an LLM-based verified-lifting workflow that generates a DSL program summary and loop invariants in Python IR, verifies equivalence to side-effect-free source code with SMT, then rewrites the verified IR into concrete DSL syntax. title: Unbounded Software Model Checking with Incremental SAT-Solving
what: Presents LLUMC, translating optimized LLVM IR from sequential C into four DimSpec CNF formulas for unbounded reachability, solved by incremental SAT (IncPlan) or IC3 (MinireachIC3). It targets assertion failures and undefined signed arithmetic overflows. title: Local Verification of Global Proofs
what: Compares local labels, one shared global proof, and mixed proofs for constant-radius distributed verification, quantifying the cost of distributing global evidence. Defines local, global and mixed certificate sizes s_l, s_g and s_m and proves s_l≤s_m≤s_g, s_m≤n s_l and s_g≤n s_l+O(n log n). The price of locality is n s_l/s_m. Uniform local proofs yield Θ(n) price; At-most-one-selected (Amos) has O(log n) uniform labels and Θ(n) price. Minimum Spanning Tree has O(log²n) local proofs and O(n log n) global proof, giving Θ(log n). At-least-one-selected requires Ω(n log n) mixed proof, and reversing decision therefore needs Ω(log n) local or Ω(n log n) global evidence. A block-neighborhood counting argument supplies the lower bound and is lifted to leader election, spanning tree and odd-cycle. Bipartite global proofs are conjectured Θ(n log n), with bounds depending on identifier range. The paper connects local/global nondeterministic hierarchies to communication-complexity hierarchies.

title: Local Reasoning About the Presence of Bugs: Incorrectness Separation Logic
what: Incorrectness separation logic combines under-approximate reachability triples with separation logic’s frame rule. Owning an invalidated location as a negative heap resource prevents unsound framing after deallocation. The paper states logic soundness, a footprint characterization covering successful and erroneous executions, and soundness of a begin-anywhere symbolic execution calculus. Pulse illustrates bounded path pruning and inferred heap assumptions; its practical call-skipping mode has weaker guarantees than the calculus. Distinguishes a satisfiable error result reachable from some inferred local state from whole-program reachability, all-path correctness, or a failed proof. Explains the negative-heap counterexample, domain monotonicity, reversed consequence/bi-abduction entailments, error reporting without assuming the error, optional allocation-reuse pruning, and the explicit gap between sound intra-procedural rules and heuristic treatment of calls. Preserves all reported experimental counts and the limits of fixes as evidence.
assumptions_limits: §§2–4: [p] C [epsilon:q] means every q state is reached from some p state via a finite C execution with that exit. It does not say every p state reaches q or that every run terminates. A false q makes any such triple vacuous; an erroneous triple establishes bug existence only with a satisfiable result. Inferred p is a local environment assumption, not a proof that main or any real caller reaches it. §1 p227: no-false-positive logic guarantee is conditional on the model assumptions; the authors explicitly separate these from whether running code satisfies them. This is a semantic theorem, not a machine-checked implementation guarantee or universal empirical zero-false-positive claim for all Pulse configurations. §3/Fig4: language has infinite values, finitely many variables, standard interpreted expressions, nondeterministic choice/havoc/finite iteration, assume, local variables, labeled explicit errors and heap allocation/free/load/store. Labels are unique. No concurrency, network, message passing, fairness or infinite-trace liveness semantics is supplied. Procedure calls are not a primitive in this calculus; examples use given models/inlining. §§3–4/Figs5–6: heap is a finite partial map from locations to values or a distinguished deallocated marker bottom. A missing location is unknown, while a bottom-marked location is owned and known deallocated. Neither may be silently equated with the other. Two separated resources cannot own the same location, including two negative resources. Deallocation retains its domain entry; allocation may use an absent or deallocated location. §3/Fig5 and §4/Fig6: FreeNull treats free(null) as an error. Reader comparison with ordinary C semantics: C free(NULL) is a no-op, so this toy-language rule needs a matching translation/model before using its error result as a claim about C code. The paper’s C/C++ motivation is not a complete source-language semantics; pointer arithmetic, undefined behavior, allocation layout, integers and library contracts are not fully formalized. §3: frame requires mod(C) disjoint from free variables of the frame. Consequence weakens the presumption and strengthens the result, reversing Hoare implication directions. Choice may select one branch; loop rules describe finite paths, and early errors short-circuit sequential composition. Standard backward SL rules are generally invalid here. Store/Free rules quantify over an arbitrary old value, rather than merely an existentially unknown old value, to retain usable under-approximate specifications. §4/Theorem1: derivable ISL triples are semantically valid. The chapter states this theorem but refers full proofs of all theorems to separate technical appendix [38]. No proof-assistant checking or verified Pulse implementation is reported here. §4.1/Theorem2: the entire denotational relation equals framing the footprint relation; footprint pairs include only memory accessed along that particular successful or erroneous execution. The result follows from heap-domain monotonicity with negative resources, is a property of the model rather than under-approximate syntax, and could also benefit over-approximate logic using that model. Full footprint function appears only in the separate appendix. §4.2: a naive over-approximate post inclusion alone does not justify the standard frame rule; fault avoidance or explicit frame preservation is needed. ISL instead uses simple under-approximate post inclusion and includes unsafe-state footprints. This comparison concerns the stated semantic models; it is not a claim that existing sound SL tools lack frame reasoning. §5/Fig8: symbolic heaps omit inductive predicates; loops are bounded by Nloops and paths at each program point by Ndisjuncts. Pruning preserves under-approximate soundness but can miss bugs. No joins or widening are needed for this bounded exploration; no completeness beyond these explored/modelled paths is established. Bounded decidability is described as likely under decidable Boolean conditions, not a proved theorem. §5/SymbExec: with previously valid [p0] C0 [ok:q0] and primitive [p] C [epsilon:q], find missing M and frame F satisfying p*F entails q0*M. Frame M through C0 (mod(C0) disjoint fv(M)), frame F through C (mod(C) disjoint fv(F)), then compose. This reverses the ordinary SL bi-abduction direction. It can extend inferred initial assumptions along a chosen branch without a second all-path re-execution. §5 p243: practical error rules require no missing M and require current state to force the fault, using entailment in both directions with an appropriate frame. They do not invent a dangling/null assumption solely to report an error on a bare dereference. This is a chosen reporting policy in addition to logical under-approximation, not a complete bug detector. §5 p244: formalized analysis is intra-procedural; function-call summaries remain future work. Practical call skipping assumes no effect except fresh nondeterministic return/reference-parameter values and may introduce both false positives and false negatives. Hence theorem3 must not be applied unqualified to this deployed mode, or to arbitrary library models. §5 p245: Pulse omits Alloc2 (reuse), assumes distinct memory unless known aliases, bounds paths/loops, and uses selected under-approximate library models (vector push_back always reallocates). These prune feasible modeled behaviors; their soundness assumes the selected behavior really is possible under relevant library/input conditions. They do not prove every push_back invalidates existing pointers. §5 evaluation: OpenSSL1.0.2d has8681 functions and yields zero reports in6s on24 Linux cores. Proprietary C++ corpus has hundreds of thousands of procedures and17 reports, without per-report validation or a ground-truth bug denominator. Separate four-month CI deployment reports20 issues/15 fixed; fixes are not an independently audited precision measure and the paper does not label the other five false positives. No modern Pulse reproduction or comparison benchmark was run. §6: concurrency/RacerD connection is explicit speculation about a future incorrectness CSL; no such logic or distributed verification result is proved here. RustBelt grant support is acknowledged but is not a Rust/Verus theorem. No TLA+, LLM agents, automated proof-generation evaluation, or verified Rust implementation result appears.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful for proof-agent evaluation because a failed correctness proof is not a proven bug, and a local error witness is conditional on input/environment/library semantics and nonempty output. Can guide memory-error evidence for unsafe Rust or generated C/C++ and principled path-budget reporting. It supplies no direct distributed/TLA+/Verus method, concurrency theorem, protocol liveness argument or LLM experiment. A translation and validated primitive/library models would be needed to apply the theory to those systems.

quotes.text: Interestingly, this semantic feature is needed in ISL for logical (and not merely pragmatic) reasons, in that it yields a sound logic for proving the presence of bugs: when ISL identiﬁes a bug, then there is indeed a bug (no false positives), given the assumptions of the underlying ISL model.

(That is, as usual, soundness is a relationship between assumptions and conclusions, and whether those assumptions match reality (i.e., running code) is a separate concern, outside the purview of logic.)
The under-approximate triples can be equivalently interpreted as: every state in result can be obtained by executing C on a starting state in presumption.
Observe that unlike in SL where one needs to reason about all branches, in ISL it sufﬁces to pick and reason about a single branch, and the remaining branches are ignored.

In particular, whilst the heap domain grows via allocation, all other base cases (including deallocation) leave the domain of the heap (i.e., the heap size) unchanged – deallocation merely updates the value of the given location in the heap to ⊥ and thus does not alter the heap domain.
We note that our footprint theorem is a positive by-product of the ISL model and not the ISL logic.

title: Lock Removal for Concurrent Trace Programs
what: Removes redundant lock statements from concrete concurrent trace programs while preserving shared-memory-access partial orders. This reduces constraints for later SMT-based predictive bug analysis. The method goes beyond removing purely thread-local locks by checking which locks maintain impossible control-state transitions. §2 shows a lock around only local operations can still restrict the order of surrounding shared accesses; naive removal introduces an assertion failure. §3 defines visible successors of global control states and a conservative static successor relation ignoring data. Theorem 1 says equality of these static successor sets before and after removal preserves partial orders of global operations. §4 summarizes each local path between adjacent shared accesses/lock acquisitions (pairs of interest) by a lock access pattern: initial/final held sets, backward/forward acquisition histories, continuously held locks and acquired locks. Inconsistent pattern pairs expose reachability barriers. Retaining at least one blocking lockset per barrier preserves impossible transitions; remaining locks can become nops. Pattern equivalence classes avoid enumerating all program-counter tuples. §5 iterates removal in the running example: B is first removed, then A becomes removable. Other synchronization can be ignored conservatively or incorporated through a universal causality graph.

assumptions_limits: Input is a finite trace program with a fixed finite thread/lock set: branch choices already made, calls inlined, loops and recursion unrolled, actual accessed addresses known. Preservation concerns alternative interleavings of those fixed local paths, not all paths or whole-program source optimization. Static reachability overapproximates by ignoring shared-data consistency; extra synchronization can only reduce executions. The decomposition assumes nested locks and is incomplete beyond two threads. Experiments assume sequential consistency and use Yices. No proof for relaxed memory, fences, dynamic whole-program lock sets, general liveness, or arbitrary executions. The claimed linear worst-case local analysis should be read with the fixed-pattern/thread/lock assumptions; the algorithm explicitly compares inconsistent pattern combinations. Most measured acquisition-history depths are zero, some one, so benchmarks do not establish behavior with deep nesting.
use_for_goal: Relevant to distributed/concurrent proof and LLM-repair evaluation because removing apparently redundant synchronization must preserve happens-before behavior, including dependencies spanning local-only critical sections. Trace reduction can accelerate model-checking counterexample exploration, but the finite-trace guarantee must remain separate from a Verus implementation proof or unbounded TLA+ invariant. No Rust, Verus, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment is reported.

title: Binary-Compatible Verification of Filesystems with ACL2
kind: mechanized filesystem refinement and co-simulation paper
what: Builds executable FAT32 model LoFAT and directory-tree specification HiFAT, proves their transformations/refinement in ACL2, and tests correspondence with existing Linux FAT32 and mtools implementations through disk-image co-simulation. HiFAT contains directory entries and complete file strings; LoFAT uses a single-threaded object close to the on-disk FAT32 layout. §4 proves termination, inverse transformations modulo equivalence, correct error behavior, and composition of image/LoFAT/HiFAT transformations. Clusterchain recursion is bounded by maximum file length; directory traversal uses a bound on total directory entries derivable from the data region, rather than an arbitrary nesting-depth limit. EqFAT ignores file order, allocation choices, deleted and dot entries, redundant FAT copies and metadata that does not remove data. Most POSIX operations execute by converting to HiFAT, operating there and converting back; equivalence justifies eliding repeated conversions. Direct open/pread/lstat versions are proved equivalent. Guard verification, stobjs, string representations and mbe proofs support efficient execution. Proofs found incorrect FAT bounds and an off-by-one directory attribute bug; Linux co-simulation exposed a missing one-cluster directory constraint and also found an ACL2 I/O bug.

assumptions_limits: The theorem is refinement of the authors’ FAT32 model/specification; Linux and mtools correspondence is finite co-simulation evidence. LoFAT validity uses a deliberately minimal subset of the official FAT32 constraints. HiFAT excludes duplicate entries and imposes FAT32 size limits; malformed images/LoFAT states share an equivalence class. EqFAT sets aside creation/access/write times and long filenames, restricting claims about programs such as Make. statfs exposes metadata that EqFAT abstracts, limiting its co-simulation use. The subject is single-process filesystem behavior rather than distributed protocol proof, and no TLA+ or LLM agent is evaluated.
