what: LORIS iteratively synthesizes C loop invariants: an LLM proposes an invariant, writes a natural-language proof of failed verification conditions, another LLM translates local steps into first-order implications, and Z3 checks those implications to produce targeted feedback. title: Synthesis of Self-Stabilising and Byzantine-Resilient Distributed Systems
what: Synthesizes synchronous fault-tolerant distributed algorithms from LTL specifications, covering strong self-stabilization and Byzantine faults. Fixed-size bounded synthesis is complete for realizable specifications and optimizes implementation size and stabilization time. Defines universal transition systems, local transition systems and a bounded-synthesis SMT encoding. Byzantine synthesis uses an incremental CEGIS-like loop with error traces. The paper proves completeness for fixed network size, presents sufficient classes for arbitrary network-size correctness, and reproduces Dolev two-counting while extending to n-counting. Colorless specifications and majority-based abstraction support parameterized reasoning.

assumptions_limits: Synchronous reactive processes with finite local state and a specified communication/failure model. Fixed-size completeness does not imply arbitrary-size correctness; the two arbitrary-size classes require stated structural hypotheses. Byzantine synthesis can be expensive; experiments use sequential solver runs and finite bounds. LTL specifications capture the modeled behavior, not physical network timing or implementation bugs.

This is in contrast to a posteriori methods like veriﬁcation, which are being studied very actively [35,45,46].  c Springer International Publishing Switzerland 2016 S. Chaudhuri and A. Farzan (Eds.): CAV 2016, Part I, LNCS 9779, pp. 157–176, 2016. DOI: 10.1007/978-3-319-41528-4 9 158 R. Bloem et al. One reason for this is that the underlying computational problems in syn- thesis are even harder than in veriﬁcation. However, research on synthesis has picked up again in recent years [1,8,24,36,52], pushed forward by advances in theorem proving [26,42] and model checking algorithms [10,40] that can be used as building blocks for eﬃcient synthesis algorithms. In particular, also the synthesis of concurrent and distributed systems has received more attention lately. However, research in this area is to a large extent still restricted to basic theoretical problems [23,24] or to simpler sub-problems, such as synthesis of synchronisation for existing programs [12,54]. Failure resilience is critical in this setting, for two reasons: ﬁrstly, it enables use in safety-critical applications with weaker assumptions on the environment and the component itself. Secondly, it is needed to ensure scalability in practice, since in large networks it is unrealistic to assume that all components work without failure. In this work, we consider two kinds of failures: transient failures, as exempliﬁed by self-stabilising systems [16,53], where the whole system can be transported to an arbitrary state; and permanent failures, as exempliﬁed by Byzantine failures [38], where some processes can deviate arbitrarily from the algorithm they should be executing. Previous approaches for the synthesis of failure-resilient systems are either restricted in the systems that are considered [14], or in the kinds of failures that are supported [21].1 For systems that support both self-stabilisation and Byzantine failures, the only result known to us is a problem-speciﬁc and semi- automatic approach by Dolev et al. [15], explained in the following. Motivating Example [15]. Consider the problem of automatically constructing a distributed counter, ranging over m possible values. Processes in the system are arranged in a fully informed clique with synchronous timing, and should satisfy the following properties under self-stabilisation and Byzantine failures: (a) agreement: at every turn, all processes output the same value; (b) increment: the value is incremented in each step (mod m). Since increment is an easy-to-implement local property, the main problem is agreement on the value. Dolev et al. [15] have recently shown a semi-automatic approach to obtain solutions for this problem. For a ﬁxed number f of Byzantine nodes, they construct the distributed algorithm in two steps: 1. synthesis for a clique of suﬃcient size n; 2. extension to arbitrarily many processes. The ﬁrst step is based on a problem-speciﬁc encoding of the synthesis problem into a SAT problem. For a ﬁxed number n of processes, the approach ﬁnds a solution – if one exists – by searching for implementations of increasing size and with increasing stabilisation time. The suﬃcient size of the clique is n = 3 · f + 1, since this guarantees that (after stabilisation) the Byzantine nodes 1 Related to this are also approaches for the synthesis of robust systems [6], essentially modelling failures in the environment of a single process. Synthesis of Self-Stabilising and Byzantine-Resilient Distributed Systems 159 cannot change the majority value [43]. Therefore, processes that are added to a correct system will be correct if they simply replicate the majority output of the existing processes. The results of Dolev et al. [15] are impressive, since their solutions for the 2-counting problem extend to systems of arbitrary size, and have smaller state space and stabilisation time than any hand-crafted solution before. However, application of their approach to other problems requires signiﬁcant eﬀort for the development of a problem-speciﬁc encoding, and for proving its correctness. In contrast, we introduce a general-purpose method for synthesis of failure- resilient systems that is fully automatic, can easily be proven correct, and is applicable to a wide range of problems. In particular, our preliminary imple- mentation can replicate the results of Dolev et al. [15] and extend them to n-counting (with n > 2). Contributions. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for the automatic synthesis of Byzantine-tolerant self-stabilising systems, in the form of distributed labelled transition systems. Our synthesis method takes as input a description of the network of processes and a speciﬁcation in linear-time temporal logic, as well as a bound on the number of Byzantine processes in the network. It encodes the existence of a solution into a problem in satisﬁability modulo theories (SMT), and synthesises correct implementations for all processes, if they exist. We show that our method is correct and complete, and will terminate if a bound on the size of process implementations is given. The ﬁrst-order problems that result from our encoding critically need quan- tiﬁcation over ﬁnite, but possibly large, sets. We provide a dedicated approach to solve those problems incrementally. On a prototype implementation of the approach, we show that this makes our examples tractable. Finally, we give new results for extending our synthesis method from networks of ﬁxed size to families of networks of unbounded size, based on the notion of cutoﬀs and the Parameterised Synthesis approach [30]. In particular, we deﬁne colourless speciﬁcations (or tasks) for non-terminating systems in cliques and similar network topologies, as well as a class of local speciﬁcations for networks with a ﬁxed degree. For colourless speciﬁcations, we obtain cutoﬀs that depend on the number of Byzantine nodes, while for local speciﬁcations we obtain cutoﬀs that depend on the stabilisation time. Structure. We introduce our system model and class of speciﬁcations in Sect. 2, and the basic synthesis approach in Sect. 3. We present the incremental approach for solving our synthesis problem in Sect. 4, the extension to parametric networks in Sect. 5, and experimental results in Sect. 6. 2 System and Failure Model, Specifications We consider distributed systems that are deﬁned by a ﬁxed network of ﬁnite-state processes, in a synchronous composition: in every global step of the system, each process observes the outputs (possibly the complete state) of neighbouring com- ponents, and makes a transition. Our composition models atomic snapshot, the 160 R. Bloem et al. classical communication model for self-stabilising systems [13]. Furthermore, syn- chronous timing (possibly as an abstraction of the system behaviour) is a stan- dard assumption when reasoning about consensus problems, as these problems are undecidable in asynchronous networks in the presence of faults [25,39,47]. To support asynchronous systems, one option is to use an abstraction to an eﬀectively synchronous system, like for example in the model based on “commu- nication rounds” by Dragoi et al. [18]. In the following, we formalise these notions for the case of ﬁxed-size networks. We will consider networks of parametric size in Sect. 5. 2.1 System Model Labelled Transition Systems. For given ﬁnite sets Σ of inputs and Υ of labels – or outputs – a Υ -labelled Σ-transition system (or short: a (Υ, Σ)-LTS) T is a tuple (T, T0 , τ, o) of a set T of states, a set T0 ⊆ T of initial states, a transition function τ : T × Σ → T and a labelling (or output) function o : T → Υ . T is called ﬁnite if T is ﬁnite. We consider Υ = 2O and Σ = 2I , representing valuations of a set of Boolean output variables O (controlled by the system) and a set of Boolean input vari- ables I (not controlled by the system). A communication graph C is a tuple (V, X, I, O), where V is a ﬁnite set of nodes, X is a set of system variables, and I : V → P(X), O : V → P(X) assign sets of input and output variables to the nodes, with O(v) ∩ O(v  ) = ∅ for all v = v  ∈ V . We model these failures as self-stabilisation and Byzantine failures, respectively. The conjunction of both kinds of failures is called Byzantine tolerant self-stabilisation [17]. Self-Stabilisation. Self-stabilisation is the strongest model for transient fail- ures, introduced by Dijkstra [13,16,53]; it assumes that the system as a whole fails – once – and is put in an arbitrary state. When the failure is over, processes resume their execution from this state. In transition systems, it is thus easily modelled by making all global states of the system initial. Since an arbitrary state of the system will in general not satisfy strict safety requirements, in self-stabilisation one usually requires that a speciﬁcation will eventually be satisﬁed, i.e., after a (either ﬁxed or unknown) stabilisation time. Byzantine Failures. Byzantine failure is a model of permanent failure where some processes do not execute the protocol, but are under the control of a Byzantine adversary. Our assumptions on the adversary are: – non-adaptiveness: the adversary picks the set of faulty nodes before the algo- rithm is run; – full information: the adversary can read the global state of the system; – computational power : the adversary has unbounded computational power. In our setting, the non-adaptiveness does not remove any power from the adversary [11].2 Therefore, it is equivalent to the strong Byzantine adversary, which subsumes most models of permanent failure. title: MA-LoT: Model-Collaboration Lean-based Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning enhances Formal Theorem Proving
what: Presents MA-LoT, a Lean4 proof-generation and verifier-guided correction framework, and LoT-Transfer Learning (LoT-TL), a three-stage SFT procedure intended to transfer general long natural-language reasoning to Lean without annotated Lean long-reasoning traces. A LoT-Solver model serves prover and corrector roles under different prompts, generating whole proofs, checking them with Lean, and repairing failures. The Goedel-based system reports 61.07% MiniF2F-test success with 16 initial attempts plus two rounds of 8 repairs, versus 55.33% baseline at 32 samples; the cumulative 63.93% result pools outputs across experimental models/settings. Builds LoT-ProveData: 54,465 formal statements/proofs with generated natural-language statements and proof comments, using DeepSeek-Prover-v1 and LeanWorkbook proofs plus Qwen2.5-72B annotation. LoT-CorrectionData has 64,912 incorrect/correct proof pairs and error messages. Train on 126K OpenO1-SFT-Pro general reasoning examples, then LoT-PD with a WITHOUT Long CoT system prompt and placeholder thought, then correction pairs. At inference, switch the prompt to WITH Long CoT and seed a header requiring mathematical analysis, tactics and final Lean code. Correction embeds the failed proof and real Lean diagnostics into the thought context before requesting analysis and revision. Appendix F clarifies correction training suppresses error analysis but retains a WITH Long CoT header containing the failed draft/messages; this differs from the main text’s simpler description. No reinforcement learning is part of this training pipeline.
assumptions_limits: Success is reported Lean verification of supplied mathematical formal statements, not verification of the generated natural-language reasoning or statement faithfulness. Prompts prohibit sorry, but the PDF does not give a full admissions/axiom/statement-integrity audit or exact Lean/Mathlib versions. The name model collaboration refers to separated proof-writing and correction roles. §2.3 explicitly uses LoT-Solver as the base model for both; the paper does not establish that different model weights or multiple independent epistemic agents are necessary. The WITHOUT/WITH prompt change is trained on general long-reasoning SFT and domain code/comment data. No specially annotated Lean long-reasoning dataset is needed, but substantial synthetic Lean data and Qwen annotations are still used; this is not a data-free method. Main benchmark is MiniF2F-valid/test,244 statements per split. Imports are manually configured. DeepSeek-Prover-v1.5 used the valid split for training according to the paper’s footnote, so valid results are not held-out comparisons for that baseline. Baselines differ in model size, sampling method, context and search budgets. Whole-proof runs generally use4096 context and128 samples, Goedel and Table1 DeepSeek-V3 use32; tree-search figures use other budgets. The authors exclude DeepSeek RMaxTS because its smallest disclosed3200 budget is incomparable. The authors could not use vLLM and report that baseline results differ from original papers. Training is about1 GPU-day and evaluation11 GPU-days on a4×H100-96G cluster as stated, without a detailed wall-clock/batch breakdown. The reported corrector advantage combines feedback placement, learned correction behavior and explicit thought prompts. Prover-as-corrector ablation puts draft/errors in code comments; it does not isolate weights or prove that role separation itself causes the gains. No repeated-run variation, confidence intervals or training-data contamination audit is supplied. Scores and illustrative cases do not establish general long-reasoning scaling laws or transfer to systems verification. ProofNet adds only a small Goedel-versus-MA-LoT comparison,15.47% at16+16 versus12.15% at32 independent samples, with no broader model or project study. The paper claims more insightful/structured proofs and emergent self-reflection. Success rates and selected traces supply evidence of task performance; there is no formal or blinded human metric validating insight, cognitive mechanism or truthfulness of thoughts.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for proof agents that alternate whole-proof planning with checker diagnostics and repair, and for transferring a general reasoning model to a formal language through synthetic training. Potential relevance to Verus/Rust/TLA+ agents is the staged training and checker-feedback loop; no code, specification generation, refinement, concurrency or distributed-system benchmark is evaluated.

title: MALICE: Memory-aware Loop Invariants Generation on Symbolic Execution Traces
what: A proposal-and-check framework generates separation-logic loop invariants for C memory-manipulating programs from bounded symbolic execution traces. Three prediction stages choose heap predicates, abstract spatial memory regions and infer pure constraints; a two-step explanation/correction refinement loop uses QCP feedback. Authors report82.69% ICL and86.15% SFT pass@8 on260 LIG-MM+ programs. Separates read/write-permission and region planning from heap abstraction and scalar constraints. Two alternative spatial strategies either fold one deeper unrolled assertion or align multiple states to infer a common predicate shape; the reported solved set is their union. QCP supplies detailed pre-failure states, error locations and symbolic histories. A postorder loop-dependency traversal resolves sequential loops in order and inner loops before outer ones. Successful refinement trajectories yield9698 explanation/correction examples for an8B LoRA refiner with program-grouped fivefold cross-validation. A long array_max example reveals the exact memory-safety specification and both useful trace information and limits of automated diagnosis.
assumptions_limits: Correctness relies on QCP semantics, symbolic execution, entailment checking and supplied predicate/specification definitions. The paper invokes standard partial-correctness Hoare rules; no new soundness/completeness theorem, termination proof or successful-generation guarantee is supplied. Unrolling depth4 provides examples for proposing invariants, not a proof of induction over unbounded executions. Pure properties retained after all observed branch-specific states must still pass full QCP initialization, preservation and exit obligations. The method assumes annotated C tasks, pre/postconditions and a supplied library of separation-logic predicates such as data_at,listrep,lseg,array shapes. It selects/folds these predicates; it does not generally synthesize arbitrary recursive predicate definitions or discover intended requirements. LIG-MM+ has133 doubly-linked-list,96 singly-linked-list,8 array and23 other(tree/hash-table) programs,260 total,reported average35 lines. At least one loop and data structure per task; authors mention several two-loop cases but give no count or broad nested-loop stress test. Main pass@8 result takes the union of solved sets from two spatial strategies, with three prediction interactions and up to10 refinement iterations per run. The relationship between strategy union and the stated call budget is not fully specified; token/cost/latency equivalence across methods is not established. SFT changes the refiner to Llama3.1-8B but retains DeepSeek-V3.2 for prediction. Full-8B uses Qwen3-8B prediction plus distilled Llama refiner; inference uses only8B models, while training-data generation still used the large teacher. Fivefold splitting groups all trajectories from each program, preventing direct trajectory sharing across train/test folds. The paper does not establish project/family-level disjointness, deduplication of near-identical programs or absence of base-model contamination. AutoSpec is a numerical tool and obtains0 here; LIG-SE/SLING lack array support. The comparison measures tool applicability plus invariant generation on this benchmark; it does not isolate framework effects under identical models/predicate coverage. Same-backbone Vanilla and Full-8B/budget comparisons add narrower controls. No repeated-run confidence intervals, significance tests, total API costs, full per-category results or independent artifact replay are supplied. Broad deployment to larger C systems, concurrency, distributed protocols, Verus/Rust and temporal liveness is untested.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to proof agents for memory ownership and invariants: exposes heap-state evolution, separates spatial and pure reasoning, uses checkable final annotations and distills verifier-error repair. Transfer to verified Rust/Verus is a plausible reader hypothesis; it evaluates sequential C/QCP separation logic only. The memory-only array contract is a concrete warning that successful formal verification must be interpreted through the supplied specification rather than a function name. No distributed-system or TLA+ result is established.

title: The Impact of Strategies and Information in Model Checking for Multi-Agent Systems
short_name: Malvone strategies and information in MAS model checking
what: Reviews model-checking complexity for Alternating-time Temporal Logic (ATL/ATL*) and Strategy Logic under memoryless, memoryful, bounded/natural strategies and perfect or imperfect information, then identifies open research directions. The paper fixes a concurrent-game-structure model with finite states/actions, protocols respecting indistinguishability, and temporal/strategic semantics. It defines memoryless and history-dependent uniform strategies and natural guarded-action strategies, including epistemic conditions and regular-expression recall. Tables give concrete complexity classifications: ATL is PTIME-complete with perfect information but undecidable with imperfect information and memoryful strategies; ATL* is PSPACE-complete memoryless and 2EXPTIME-complete perfect-information memoryful, while imperfect-information memoryful is undecidable; SL is PSPACE-complete imperfect-information memoryless and non-elementary perfect-information memoryful. NatATL/NatSL regain PSPACE or DeltaP2 bounds. The review argues memoryless strategies are weak, memoryful strategies are costly, and natural-strategy complexity and imperfect-information taxonomies remain open.

assumptions_limits: Models are finite concurrent game structures with finite action sets and equivalence-based observation; uniformity is required for indistinguishable states/histories. title: MathlibLemma: Folklore Lemma Generation and Benchmark for Formal Mathematics
what: Introduces MATHLIBLEMMA, a four-stage LLM pipeline for mining reusable folklore lemmas missing from Mathlib. Discovery proposes statements from Mathlib seed files; an LLM judge filters mathematical plausibility; a Lean-connected formalizer repairs syntax and type errors; a prover generates proofs with Lean checking and a proof-bypass screen. The resulting benchmark contains 4,028 non-trivial type-checked statements, and the released repository contains 1,506 Lean-checked generated proofs. Across seven model/settings configurations, union Success@2 is37.39% while the best individual GPT-Reasoning model reaches19.39%; a small pilot curated six outputs for Mathlib, with three merged. Formalizes each target as a pair(S,P) in seed context C⊂L with semantic novelty, mathematical plausibility and syntactic validity requirements. Discovery is prompted to generate at least 100 candidate lemmas per seed with sorry; Judge ignores Lean syntax and returns correct/wrong; Formalizer uses Kimina Lean server diagnostics for up to10 syntax-repair trials; Prover allows an initial attempt plus two repair rounds and rejects sorry/admit/sorryAx and model-added axiom/constant/opaque declarations. Benchmark seeds 109 Mathlib source files, manually stratified into Foundational, Applied and Abstract domains; aesop-immediate instances are excluded. Main evaluation is closed-book, sequential Success@2, with full context C supplied but no retrieval. Appendix D audits 138 model-unsolved statements (107 human-proved,78%); held-out audit proves79/94 (84.0%). Appendix E documents three merged lemmas: Gronwall-bound monotonicity, restriction of a constant kernel, and almost-everywhere congruence of central moments.
assumptions_limits: LLM Judge filtering is imperfect: in a 53-rejected-candidate audit,54% were false and46% valid false negatives. Judge acceptance is not a proof of truth; kernel checking establishes well-formedness, and proof checking establishes the supplied theorem, not preservation of the intended informal idea. The benchmark is generated by GPT-5.1 discovery/judging/repair and is explicitly a versioned pipeline distribution, not a model-independent census. Discovery is seed-file local and one-shot, with no repository-wide retrieval, dependency traversal or proof-attempt-driven gap discovery. The 78% residual audit samples model-unsolved instances and lets human experts use full Mathlib, AI assistance and external search. It estimates provability of that stratified sample, not the full 4,028 benchmark. The 84.0% held-out audit uses a different five-seed design and is not pooled. Closed-book Success@2 measures internalized library knowledge plus reasoning under a serial two-repair budget. It is not directly comparable to parallel Pass@k; the 8B Pass@16 appendix is explicitly a separate stress test. The proof-bypass screen excludes common incomplete or assumption-injection artifacts but does not by itself establish that a lemma is novel, well named, minimally stated or suitable for Mathlib. Authors state novelty filters are mainly syntactic and semantically equivalent restatements may remain. All Lean checks use Lean v4.25.0-rc2 and a fixed Mathlib revision through a stateless server; results may change as APIs and typeclass elaboration evolve. The reader did not rerun this environment. Union performance is an oracle union over model outputs, not one executable ensemble with a stated orchestration cost. Model comparisons use different architectures and inference settings; domain interpretations are author claims. Three of six curated submissions merged, one was rejected as redundant and two were not pursued. This is a small selection signal, not a 1,506-proof upstream acceptance rate. Costs exclude curation, local open-model serving and maintainer review. Human audits can prove statements with open-book tools, while models receive no retrieval; the human/model gap therefore mixes proof ability with access to library search and assistance.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal-verification agents that need reusable intermediate lemmas: it turns checker-validated LLM outputs into a versioned auxiliary library and exposes missing-hypothesis and library-recall failure modes. For Verus/Rust/TLA+, the transferable pattern is staged candidate generation, semantic filtering, syntax repair and proof checking; the benchmark itself covers Lean/Mathlib mathematics only.

title: McScM: A General Framework for the Verification of Communicating Machines
what: Introduces McScM, an OCaml platform for safety verification and controller synthesis of finite-state processes communicating over reliable unbounded FIFO channels. It unifies abstract interpretation, abstract regular model checking, CEGAR and lazy abstraction behind a common verify front end and symbolic queue-content representation. The paper specifies the CM input and bad-state representation, explains verify outputs (safe certificate, counterexample or resource-bounded abort), and details four algorithms sharing FCID/QDD infrastructure and path-invariant generators. It describes compile-time interface guarantees from OCaml modules/functors and on-the-fly validation of path invariants and inductive certificates. The control tool computes a safe restriction using distributed control. Benchmark analysis finds algorithm-dependent strengths: absint terminates but may be inconclusive, cegar is good when precision is local, and armc often handles global refinement better; no method dominates.

what: Presents MET, a two-layer workflow that model-checks CRDT designs in TLA+ and turns model-checking traces into deterministic implementation tests. A test manager controls message order through intercepted RPCs and compares code-level state traces with model-level oracles, targeting transcription and assumption bugs that design verification alone misses. The framework specifies CRDT operations and strong eventual consistency in TLA+, then coarsens the model by binding receive/do/send events while preserving conflict-resolution interleavings. Test inputs are extracted event schedules; test oracles are model state traces. A central manager hacks inter-replica RPCs for controllability and adds state-inspection APIs for observability. Practical CRDT-Redis Rwf-RPQ and Rwf-List studies expose a re-add/dummy-position transcription bug, a RemoveWin causal-delivery assumption mismatch, and a position-ID generator bug. The paper reports exact TLC trace counts, disk/time costs, model configurations up to three replicas, and argues from the small-scope hypothesis that three replicas expose most deep conflict bugs.

title: Metha: Network Verifiers Need To Be Correct Too!
what: Metha generates network configurations, runs them on network analyzers and real-router images, and compares converged routing tables to expose model discrepancies. Semantic constraints activate meaningful protocol computations; minimum/middle/maximum parameter reduction and PICT pairwise tests cover selected feature interactions. Iterative delta debugging isolates all inclusion-minimal failure-inducing feature sets under explicit monotonicity/outcome assumptions. Records grammar versus semantic constraints, finite topology/parameter/test domain, exact coverage definition, iterative delta-debugging proof/complexity/masking limits, practical convergence oracle, eight detailed model-mismatch examples, complete bug/ablation/localization counts and commits, baseline parser exception and simulation-only NV boundary.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3,7: Differential oracle is actual Cisco/Juniper router software, including vendor quirks and bugs. A discrepancy establishes disagreement with the selected implementation/version, not protocol-standard truth or independent proof that the analyzer is at fault. Developers confirmed 59/62 reports. Oracle fidelity, routing-table extraction, grammar/semantic constraints and comparison code remain trusted. §7: Convergence means ten unchanged routing-table snapshots sampled 10s apart (~100s), a heuristic rather than proof that the protocol has stabilized forever. Transients or oscillations slower than sampling, hidden state, timing/hardware differences and output normalization may affect comparisons. Paper gives no exact Cisco/Juniper image versions or host CPU/RAM. Batfish/NV source commits are cited. §§4–5: Search uses fixed physical/logical topology and provided features, finite recursive grammar, predefined strings, numeric minimum/maximum/one interior value. Pairwise coverage is over selected router×feature/value combinations, not all configurations, numeric values, protocol states, failures, traffic or code paths. Supporting prefix/community lists are not independently fuzzed. §5.1: Full t-wise coverage finds every bug only if each is exposed by at most t interactions of selected value dimensions and test behavior meets the premise. Empirical one/two-feature causes do not prove larger or unseen-boundary bugs absent. PICT yields a covering suite; no proof of globally minimum test count provided. §6/Appendix A: Theorem 1 concerns all inclusion-minimal failing subsets, not globally smallest cardinality or every underlying code bug. Iterative extension lifts the unique-minimal-fault assumption, retaining monotone failure and definite consistent outcomes; proof explicitly invokes monotonicity. No proof every real configuration discrepancy satisfies these assumptions. §6.2: Bugs whose triggers strictly contain an already failing subset cannot be identified separately until the smaller bug is fixed. Different minimal triggers can share a source-code cause; the black-box method cannot deduplicate by code or pinpoint erroneous code. Counts represent developer-assessed/configuration-trigger evidence, not automatically proved distinct code defects. §6.2: Uncached worst case is O(|Q|!); caching unique queued feature sets gives stated O(2^|Q|) bound. Router/tool calls and minimization also cost time. Algorithm 1 prints head(queue) without explicit dequeue; narrative describes consuming the queue until empty. This listing omission is not evidence of implementation nontermination. §§7–8: Routing-table comparison catches crashes and silent control-plane model bugs, but does not directly check packet forwarding, data-plane execution, every proof procedure, solver soundness or live production networks. Only NV simulation was tested; authors infer likely verification impact from its shared model. Table 3 marks confirmation of C-BGP’s three reports as unknown (?). Batfish’s 29 and NV’s 30 reports were confirmed. §8.1: Each of four approaches runs 1794 tests with the same four-router Cisco star features. Semantic baseline finds 16 bugs versus random’s 3; boundary values add one, pairwise adds three. Original Metha misses a random parser bug because OSPF area numbers are fixed; adding that dimension finds it. Discussion’s claim that all random bugs are found with fewer tests needs this augmented input space. §8.1/Figure 5: Coverage measures pairs of feature values, with continuous random numeric values bucketed into minimum/maximum/middle. It is not code coverage or proof soundness. Semantic and random approaches have similar coverage but different bug counts, illustrating semantic activation. No repeated random seeds, confidence intervals or sample variance reported. §8.2: Mean 14.1 extra tests per discrepancy, range 7–58, not per bug; 58 localizes five bugs. Complete testing takes several days; single test averages two minutes, PICT generation six minutes. Full cost includes fault localization; no precisely timed total or resource scaling study. §§9–11: Testing supplements unit/system testing. No universal absence-of-bugs proof or Verus/verified Rust/TLA+/LLM-written proof result. Testing configuration synthesizers is future work. Version and confirmation claims refer to source publication time.
use_for_goal: Directly addresses trust in verification models and independent test oracles. For agent-generated TLA+/Verus specifications and proofs, a checked proof can describe the wrong model; comparing model and real implementation and minimizing semantic counterexamples provides additional evidence. Preserve finite input coverage, oracle/convergence/monotonicity limits and different confirmation statuses. This paper itself reports no LLM, Verus or Rust results.

title: Policy Monitoring in First-Order Temporal Logic.
what: Defines an effectively monitorable safety fragment of metric first-order temporal logic (MFOTL): formulas Ψ = □Ψ′ with bounded future temporal operators, arbitrary nesting of metric past and bounded future operators, quantifier alternation, and finite or automatic structures. An incremental monitor rewrites violations into a finite-relation fragment, maintains auxiliary relations for temporal subformulas, queues future obligations, and emits violating assignments online. The algorithm handles events and duration-like states by encoding starts/finishes, supports point-based metric timestamps, and incrementally updates past-since and bounded-future relations rather than recomputing windows. Four concrete policies formalize report approval and anti-money-laundering requirements (threshold reporting, authorization windows, and repeat-suspicious customers). The implementation’s steady-state analysis separates incremental time, mean/max auxiliary-relation space, and relevant active-domain size, exposing formula-structure effects (future operators can delay checks and inflate max space). Automatic structures are available in the broader work, while this paper evaluates finite relations.

assumptions_limits: This paper restricts experiments to finite relations and formulas whose negated violation can be rewritten into a syntactic finite-intermediate-relation fragment; domain independence is required for unrestricted infinite domains. Temporal structures use constant domains, rigid constants and monotonically increasing timestamps. It monitors safety properties, not arbitrary liveness; aggregation such as summing a trader’s transactions is outside MFOTL fragment. Synthetic singleton-relations streams and a 1.4 GHz dual-core/3 GB machine limit ecological validity. Formula syntax strongly affects memory/time, and policy enforcement/distributed control are future work.
use_for_goal: Useful design for runtime policy checks over structured events: retain first-order data relations while bounding temporal lookahead and memory through auxiliary relations. It offers concrete latency/space baselines and clearly states where domain independence, finite relations, and non-aggregating safety requirements constrain deployment.

title: Formal Verification of Obstacle Avoidance and Navigation of Ground Robots
what: Builds hybrid-system models of dynamic-window-style ground-robot controllers and proves safety and liveness in differential dynamic logic (dL). The series covers static, passive, passive-friendly, and passive-orientation safety, then adds actual acceleration, sharp turns, location/actuator/velocity uncertainty, asynchronous obstacle control, and arbitrarily many obstacles via quantified dL. KeYmaera X proofs are converted into ModelPlex runtime monitors. The models make control-loop delay ε, robot acceleration/braking, obstacle speed, and circular motion symbolic. Theorems 1–4 prove collision properties using loop and differential invariants; Theorem 3 additionally proves an obstacle has an execution that can brake safely, and Theorem 4 limits responsibility to visible orientation sectors. Refinements prove safety with actual acceleration (Theorem 5), trajectory-distance sharp turns (Theorem 6), location uncertainty (7), actuator damping (8), velocity uncertainty (9), asynchronous obstacle decisions (10), and quantified arbitrary obstacles (11). Liveness proofs establish waypoint reachability (12), intersection crossing (13), and deadline variants (14–15). Concrete instantiations analyze indoor doors/corridors, and synthesized ModelPlex conditions check sensor/actuator samples against the verified model and trigger fail-safe stopping on deviations. Proof statistics show automation but nontrivial QE cost.

assumptions_limits: Guarantees are conditional on the hybrid model: forward planar motion, bounded acceleration/braking, bounded control delay, obstacle velocity bounds, and (for passive-friendly safety) obstacle braking/reaction bounds. Robot shape is abstracted to a point by inflating obstacles; infinity-norm distance overapproximates Euclidean distance. Liveness requires explicit fairness/nonblocking assumptions (e.g., obstacle minimum speed at intersections) and suitable goal/deadline conditions. Formal proof establishes correctness of the model, not realism; probabilistic bounds are only safe when converted to guaranteed intervals. title: Model Checking Matrix Product States against Linear Chain Logic
what: Introduces Linear Chain Logic (LCL) for spatial, size-indexed properties of periodic matrix product states and approximate model-checking algorithms based on completely positive transfer maps, irreducible decomposition and semilinear evidence sets. LCL has interval-valued atomic predicates over MPS observables and spatial X/E/G operators; evidence sets are sets of chain lengths. Algorithm 1 recursively propagates over/under evidence approximations, while Algorithm 2 splits residue classes, projects peripheral modes, checks second spectral radii and computes finite thresholds. Second, it factors Multi-Paxos optimizations into protocol-aware network-semantics transformations (out-of-thin-air, duplication, reordering, bunching) and proves behavior preservation, allowing the single-decree proof to be reused for a register-provider Multi-Paxos implementation. title: Modular Verification of Intrusive List and Tree Data Structures in Separation Logic
what: A modular separation-logic method for intrusive data structures, where clients embed link nodes inside data objects. The representation separates node topology from attached data. Coq/Iris proofs in HeapLang reuse node-level specifications to verify cyclic/doubly linked lists, deques, and unbalanced binary-search-tree maps, including internal pointers and insertion. Shows that singly linked intrusive sequences compose into cycles, two oppositely directed cycles compose into a dcycle, and data fields framed alongside dcycles give a deque. For search trees, separates shape, key ordering and attached values; uses functional one-hole contexts and separating implication to retain the traversed tree while returning a pointer to an interior link. Locate is proved once and its contract makes insertion a modular, non-inductive client proof.
assumptions_limits: Object programs are in unmodified Iris HeapLang, a simplified language with dynamic allocation, arrays and location arithmetic. The paper deliberately omits C fixed-width integers, byte representation and alignment. It does not verify actual Linux/Boost C/C++ code, C container_of provenance rules, a compiler, or machine execution. Hoare triples guarantee no crash under their ownership preconditions, and the stated result if execution finishes. This is partial correctness, not a proved termination/cost bound. The illustrated operations are sequential; the use of the concurrent Iris framework does not establish concurrent linearizability or thread-safe list mutation. Node APIs require ownership of supplied link cells and return detached ownership after removal. Clients allocate/deallocate enclosing objects. Data-layout predicates require separate ownership of topology and payload fields; arbitrary aliasing between those fields is not admitted. Concrete BST API uses natural-number keys and ordinary comparisons. Generic functional discussion uses a Boolean comparison p, but the printed assumptions/as-stated lemmas have apparent gaps detailed below. No balanced-tree invariant, rotations, deletion API or logarithmic complexity theorem is provided. Partial-tree reconstruction requires a valid one-hole context and a subtree whose insertion preserves the whole-tree BST invariant. A magic wand does not allow plugging an arbitrary key arrangement into the hole. Functional correctness lemmas and context generalization are part of the proof effort. Formal checking depends on Coq, Iris reasoning about HeapLang, and the declared definitions/specifications. Diaframe assists proof search and small pointer-arithmetic support is added in Setup.v. The paper supplies a Zenodo mechanization, but this reader has not replayed it or compared printed inconsistencies to source. The deque proof-size claim is less than30Coq proof lines for the deque API after underlying dcycle specifications, Iris lemmas and Diaframe support exist. It is not the size or cost of the full library or tree development. Scaling to more graph-like shared structures remains open.
use_for_goal: Concrete ownership-specification patterns for low-level mutable structures relevant to verified Rust and Verus: separate topology/payload, preserve ownership when returning interior pointers, and specify reconstruction after mutation. Useful tasks for LLM proof agents would test faithful layout/alias assumptions and modular reuse, but this paper does not evaluate agents or Verus/Rust code. Its verified objects are sequential HeapLang structures, not distributed protocols or TLA+ models. Rust connection is related work on intrusive types; transfer to Verus is reader inference.

title: Model Checking: the Interval Way
what: Develops model checking for Halpern–Shoham interval temporal logic (HS) over finite Kripke structures and timeline-based system models. It proves decidability and EXPSPACE hardness for full homogeneous HS, classifies many fragments, compares interval and point logics, studies regular-expression extensions, and derives timed-automata procedures for timeline planning and MITL model checking. The thesis builds BEk descriptors for a nonelementary decidability procedure, reductions proving EXPSPACE hardness, and fragment-specific small-model/oracle/automata algorithms ranging through PSPACE and bounded-query polynomial hierarchy classes. It compares HS variants with LTL, CTL, and CTL* under homogeneous semantics, then relaxes homogeneity using regular expressions while preserving or increasing fragment complexity. For dense-time timelines, unrestricted planning is undecidable; simple future trigger rules are decidable via timed automata, with EXPSPACE completeness for non-singular intervals and PSPACE completeness for intervals in Intv(0,∞). MITL model checking reduces inclusion to timed-automata emptiness.
numbers: Full homogeneous HS MC decidable with nonelementary upper bound and EXPSPACE-hard
Simple-trigger future timeline planning decidable; EXPSPACE for non-singular intervals and PSPACE for Intv(0,∞)
MITL-over-timelines MC in EXPSPACE or PSPACE under corresponding interval restrictions
Low-level HS fragments classified into PSPACE, co-NP, and bounded-query polynomial-hierarchy classes
assumptions_limits: Homogeneity is a major semantic assumption when evaluating HS on point-based Kripke structures and limits expressiveness. Complexity varies sharply by fragment; full HS exact complexity remains open (the thesis conjectures elementary/possibly EXPSPACE-complete). title: Fault-Tolerant Design and Multi-Objective Model Checking for Real-Time Deep Reinforcement Learning Systems
what: Introduces a formal design pipeline for real-time deep-reinforcement-learning controller switches: timed automata model switching and clocks, incremental synchronized composition adds counters/metric recorders, syntactic conversion produces an MDP, and a convex-query algorithm synthesizes schedulers balancing hard safety and soft cost/reward objectives. MOPMC implements CPU/GPU policy/value iteration and exports schedulers. The TA-to-MDP conversion separates mutually exclusive branching guards (probabilistic underdetermination) from equivalent-guard choice states (design nondeterminism), estimates guard probabilities from distributions or simulation, and encodes controller cost, lane departure, TTC and headway as total rewards. The HighwayEnv case trains DDPG without delay, then injects fixed/random observation-action delays; at 0.30 s average random delay, no-switch lane departure is 0.2849. A four-configuration switch and convex query find a minimum-MSE point (ExpCTL 1.9, PRTTC .0377, PRHW .2189, ProbLD .1720), and exported schedules improve TTC/headway while increasing lateral departure risk. Perturbing transition probabilities ±1.5–15% gives stable median outputs. Runtime experiments vary switch size, objective count to 100, and the Team Formulation Protocol, showing GPU gains on large models but mixed results on small ones.

title: MORA - Automatic Generation of Moment-Based Invariants
what: Presents MORA, a Python tool that automatically derives expected values and higher-order moment invariants for Prob-solvable probabilistic loops. It rewrites random polynomial updates into monomial expectation equations, solves resulting constant-coefficient recurrences, and emits text or LaTeX invariants. what: Defines Minimal Proof Search (MPS), a best-first effort-number algorithm for model checking multi-agent modal logic K over game automata, and proves termination, correctness, minimal-cost proofs/disproofs, and optimality among purely exploratory algorithms. what: Extends ESBMC SMT-based bounded model checking with OpenMP-launched independent instances that search different hardware-cost bounds, applying it to NP-hard hardware/software partitioning and comparing against ILP and a genetic algorithm. title: Multi-Objective Statistical Model Checking using Lightweight Strategy Sampling
what: Introduces the first statistical model-checking approach for multi-objective Pareto queries. It samples deterministic strategies with lightweight strategy sampling (LSS), estimates all objective values by Monte Carlo confidence intervals, and constructs convex-hull underapproximations and incremental overapproximations of the achievable/Pareto set. The paper formalizes simultaneous confidence boxes across strategies and objectives using Bonferroni/union-bound error allocation. Its incremental algorithm assigns geometrically shrinking error budgets to batches and almost surely converges, under ideal LSS on finite contracting MDPs, to a confidence band of precision sqrt(2d) epsilon. Three fixed-budget algorithms (weight-vector refinement, fixed-iteration budget, fixed-strategy budget) combine strategy-discarding heuristics with an independent evaluation phase to retain sound lower bounds. The modes implementation evaluates 40 instances from quantitative-verification and reinforcement-learning benchmarks, and reports when SMC remains usable while Storm PMC times out.

The theory assumes ideal LSS eventually samples every deterministic strategy, while implementation uses 32-bit identifiers and can miss strategies. Finite-time sampling cannot soundly overapproximate the Pareto front because an optimal strategy may never be sampled; only underapproximations have finite-time statistical guarantees. Results use three seeds, 40 instances, fixed confidence alpha=0.1, and arbitrary hypervolume reference points, so cross-model comparisons are not meaningful.

title: Multi-Threaded Software Model Checking via Parallel Trace Abstraction Refinement
what: Parallelizes trace-abstraction CEGAR in Ultimate Automizer by assigning distinct counterexample traces to worker threads while a coordinator serially applies interpolant-automaton refinements and uses diverse trace selection. The paper formalizes sequential trace abstraction over automata of syntactic error paths, then observes that feasibility checking and interpolant generation are independent and sound with stale abstractions. A coordinator tracks assigned traces, workers perform SMT checks and interpolant automata, and a recursive selector prioritizes paths that diverge early from previously selected traces. The Java implementation uses fixed thread pools and CompletionService. Evaluation on 14,560 SV-COMP 2025 unreach-call C tasks compares 1/2/4/6 workers, the competition sequential configuration and DSS, reporting correctness, solved tasks, speedups and validity threats.
numbers: 14,560 tasks: 11,158 property-satisfying and 3,402 violating; each run is capped at 8 cores, 15 minutes and 30 GB.
PAR-2 is faster on 49% (2,369/4,787) commonly solved tasks, PAR-4 on 43% (2,002/4,760), and PAR-6 on 34% (1,619/4,735); speedups >3, >5 and >7 occur for 67, 42 and 31 tasks.
Against DSS on 1,395 jointly correct tasks, DSS is faster on 66% by a median 7.1 s, largely due to Ultimate startup overhead; the paper reports its approach as more effective.
assumptions_limits: Soundness relies on the trace feasibility/interpolant machinery; stale abstractions may waste work but are argued sound. Parallel workers require memory-expensive copies and can analyze redundant traces; one incorrect PAR-6-UA alarm was observed and attributed tentatively to reused Ultimate functionality. Results cover only sequential C, unreach-call safety tasks under 8 cores, 15 minutes and 30 GB; generalization to other languages/properties/resources is uncertain. PAR-6 can lose proofs due to overhead when PAR-1 solves a task with fewer traces.
use_for_goal: This paper evaluates a practical way to parallelize a proof-producing CEGAR loop while retaining a serial abstraction invariant. It supplies concrete evidence about worker-count trade-offs, stale-state soundness, false-result risk and benchmark coverage relevant to automated formal verification systems and agent-generated proofs.

title: Multilevel Monte Carlo Method for Statistical Model Checking of Hybrid Systems
what: Develops statistical model checking for continuous-time stochastic hybrid systems that cannot be exactly simulated. It discretizes SDE executions, estimates first-exit/reachability distributions, and uses coupled multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) estimators with a tunable polynomial smoothing of the discontinuous indicator. The paper defines the ct-SHS model with mode invariants, Lipschitz bounded drift/diffusion and boundary-triggered switching; reduces safety to a first-exit distribution; derives standard-MC and MLMC mean-square error/cost rates; introduces a cubic smoothing function, decomposes error into smoothing, bias and variance, and gives an adaptive algorithm selecting smoothing level, maximal discretization level and sample counts. A thermostatically controlled load (TCL) case instantiates Euler discretization and reports variance/mean decay and cost gains.
numbers: TCL horizon is 1 hour with residential-air-conditioner parameters in Table 1
target accuracies epsilon=2^-k for k=3,...,8, 10^6 runs for decay plots and 100 runs for cost comparison
adaptive MLMC shows increasing computational gain as epsilon decreases; non-monotonicity remains from re-evaluating functionals when smoothing changes
assumptions_limits: Drift and diffusion are bounded and Lipschitz; the exposition restricts to forced boundary jumps and continuous state at mode switches, though modifications are claimed for spontaneous jumps. The MLMC rates require exponential bias/cost and variance assumptions; adaptive estimates presume near-exact empirical means/variances. Smoothing changes the target and requires simulation through s+delta; experiments use one TCL and compare costs while assuming the SMC rate parameter known, favoring SMC.
use_for_goal: Relevant to formal verification of stochastic/hybrid distributed controllers as a principled statistical alternative when exact trajectories are unavailable; it quantifies approximation and confidence errors but does not prove implementation invariants or distributed protocol correctness.

title: Nanopass Back-Translation of Call-Return Trees for Mechanized Secure Compilation Proofs
what: Rocq-verified back-translation from a finite well-formed collection of finite call/return trace prefixes into generated source whole programs sharing a context. Organizes the construction as initialization plus four small compiler passes over call-return trees, using identifiers, ghost call stacks and flattened rules before code generation. Proves each requested prefix can be produced by the back-translated source program. Handles stateful, arbitrarily reentrant callbacks and returns separated from their calls by nested interactions. Private loc, is_call and res distinguish external callbacks from internal recursion and recover the correct branch after a return. Separates determinacy and stack invariants across intermediate semantics, then relates ghost locations/stacks to concrete memory/frames. Gives an informal path to stronger finite-relational security, while explicitly leaving integration into a complete compilation-chain security theorem unmechanized.
assumptions_limits: Inputs are finite sets/lists of finite prefixes satisfying well-formedness, including deterministic context behavior: after the same visible history, a context in control cannot choose two different outgoing events. The exact well-formedness predicate is not reproduced. Arbitrary incompatible trace collections are not covered. Compartment interaction uses well-bracketed calls/returns with integer payloads, private state and procedures/interfaces. The exposition assumes one procedure per compartment; the actual development supports multiple procedures and records procedure identifiers in call events. Fine-grained sharing of secure data/code pointers is future work. Theorem3 establishes inclusion of each requested finite prefix in generated-program behavior. It neither states equality of all trace sets nor forbids extra generated behavior, and it does not establish infinite-trace/liveness properties. Finite-prefix witness preservation must not be inflated to arbitrary hyperproperty preservation. The proven artifact is the back-translation and its pass simulations, not a new full RFrSP theorem for the existing compiler or compartmentalized CompCert. Figure1 describes an adaptation requiring forward/backward compiler correctness, separate compilation and recomposition. §1 explicitly says mechanization of that integration is not yet done; §8 makes realistic SECOMP integration future work. RFrSP quantifies finite families of possibly different programs under one target context, requiring one shared source context for the corresponding prefixes. RSP has only one program/prefix. Pointwise independent source contexts would not meet the stronger quantifier order. The informal implication to full abstraction is qualified in §3.1 as a variant of the security-relevant direction, not an unconditional complete fully abstract compiler theorem. It relies on the chosen trace/context/source-target models and the remaining compilation-chain proof. Back-translation constructs whole source programs: a common context depends on the entire trace family, while each generated program depends on its own trace. It does not directly translate the syntax of an arbitrary low-level adversary or prove that every original source program already behaves like the generated replacement. Adding ghost-state conditions to intermediate semantics is justified by forward simulations, not by simply assuming invariants in the final source semantics. Proof obligations include initialization and invariant-preserving matching steps; finite-prefix simulations permit stuttering without establishing divergence preservation. Reuse across languages and proof-effort improvements are author expectations/experience reports. No controlled comparison of developer time, proof checking time, memory, runtime of generated contexts, scale benchmark or LLM-agent result is reported. Prover/library axioms were not audited by this reader.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful compositional-proof method for agents generating systems specifications and simulation proofs: explicit intermediate invariants make a hard stateful proof divisible, and each stage has a semantic obligation. Finite trace inclusion, quantifier order of shared contexts and missing end-to-end composition are important evaluation boundaries. Compartment adversaries and reentrant calls concern systems security; this is not a distributed-protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent implementation/evaluation.

title: NaturalProver: Grounded Mathematical Proof Generation with Language Models
what: Fine-tunes GPT-3 to generate natural-language mathematical proofs conditioned on theorem/definition reference titles, using reference reconstruction and optional stepwise constrained decoding. Reference titles alone enter the context; a separate reconstruction objective teaches their content. Stepwise++ samples multiple temperatures and keeps clusters with different likelihood/reference-coverage weights; this does not check logical validity. Retrieval uses top-20 titles and avoids constrained decoding because irrelevant references would create noisy constraints. Human evaluation marks reference deployment/justification/hallucination/self-loop, equation/derivation, reasoning/repetition/skipped steps, language and symbolic errors; overall 0–5 correctness uses ≥4, usefulness ≥3. ProofWiki gold proofs can themselves contain mistakes (Figure 1).
assumptions_limits: ProofWiki proofs are community-contributed natural language/LaTeX; core evaluation selects 100 validation and 100 test theorems chosen for human comprehensibility, an easier slice. Correctness/usefulness are university-student judgments, not machine-checked; references and constraints are lexical. External code/data URL is stated, but no external supplement was read; no Verus/Rust/TLA+ artifact. Human-provided references are titles from the gold proof and serve as privileged assistance/upper bound; retrieved-reference full proof correctness is 24%, vanilla fine-tuned GPT-3 13%. Annotators see theorem and gold proof before generated proof, can skip unfamiliar theorems, and evaluate model text stepwise; claims are human ratings, not formal theorem proving. Supplied PDF ends after p.15 checklist. It cites Appendices C–G, Table 24 annotation schema and Tables 10–23 examples/ablations, but these external supplemental pages are absent and were not read. Do not describe their details as inspected.
use_for_goal: Direct caution for LLM-generated Verus/TLA+ explanations: human-rated natural proof quality does not establish kernel validity. Reference grounding and stepwise interfaces could assist specification review, but distributed safety needs machine checking.

quotes.text: We adopt these splits of roughly 12.5k training, 1k validation, and 1k test examples, and sampled core evaluation sets with 100 dev and 100 test theorems that are used for human evaluation.

The retrieval setting simulates a fully automated proof assistant, while the second simulates a human specifying a plan for an assistant that writes a proof, and acts as an upper bound for a retrieval system optimized to predict references in a ground-truth proof.
A rating of 4 or 5 is needed to be considered as correct, and a rating of 3 or above is needed to be considered as useful.

These theorems were selected by the authors such that by looking at the theorem title each author could recall its content and sketch a proof. While this may shift the evaluation towards an easier slice of the dataset, it was necessary to make human evaluation at a meaningful scale feasible.

title: NDD: A Decision Diagram for Network Verification
what: A network-specific decision-diagram library factors Boolean network state by fields. Each NDD node branches on a whole field and each edge labels allowed field values with a BDD; reduced ordered NDDs merge equal residual functions. Per-field atomization replaces label BDD operations with atom-set operations, and an incremental update API splits affected atoms. A paper induction proves intended canonicity for fixed field grouping/order; Java integration into five verifiers measures time/memory, including packet rewriting and link-failure models. Benefits rely on field locality and are not uniform across workloads. Records three reduction rules, exclusive/exhaustive edge semantics, field/bit-order assumptions and full canonicity construction, atom minimality and update precondition, complete apply/exist/atomize/update algorithms and qualified listing concerns, hash/GC/cache/implicit-false details, all eight tables and complete scope of empirical results. Separates representation canonicity from implementation correctness and end-to-end network verification, and identifies workload, baseline and source-count discrepancies.
assumptions_limits: §§3.1/6.6: Field locality means rules usually match few of many fields and different rules match different fields; values are sufficiently independent to create cross-product redundancy in monolithic BDDs. It is a performance assumption, not a logical restriction needed to represent correlated packet sets. Networks matching all fields can reverse advantage. NDDs can still grow exponentially and a node can have up to2^n outgoing edges for an n-bit field; pairwise apply may compare m×n successors. §3.3/AppendixC: Fixed grouping of consecutive bit variables into fields and fixed field order, plus canonical BDD labels with fixed internal bit order, underpin canonicity. Ordered nodes, uniqueness, removal of a sole true-labeled edge and merging edges with same successor are essential. Equivalent Boolean functions yield one reduced graph under these conventions; claim does not establish minimum graph size across groupings/orders or efficient construction in worst case. AppendixC proof: Generalize Shannon expansion by partitioning first-field assignments according to equal residual functions, recursively represent residuals, label each equivalence class with its BDD and merge equal successors. For uniqueness, compare an assignment shared by matching edges, invoke induction for successors, then no-duplicate-successor rule forces equal labels. Constants and unused fields reduce away. This is handwritten mathematical proof, not mechanized code refinement. §3.3 Definition1/AppendixC qualification: Formal edge conditions require disjoint/exhaustive labels but do not explicitly forbid false (empty) labels. Uniqueness argument chooses B1∈label(eu), implicitly requiring every retained edge nonempty. Without that convention, add an empty-labeled edge to an unused distinct later-field successor: represented function is unchanged while edge map differs and listed no-duplicate-successor rule still holds. Algorithm1 line7 does discard false intersections. Record this as a formal-statement convention to make explicit, not an implementation bug established by execution. §3.4: Atoms per field are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, exhaustive and minimum in number such that every relevant edge label is a union of atoms. Sum of per-field atoms is compared with number of whole-header equivalence classes; these counts represent different objects, so count reduction alone is not total-memory reduction. NDD graph stores inter-field correlations. Table3 measures actual JVM delta separately. §4.1/AppendixB Algorithm1: apply intersects labels of every successor pair, recursively combines successors and merges labels for equal output successors. Atomized mode uses set intersection/union. Pseudocode covers explicit false edges; source says or/diff need modifications with false-node removal. Trivial cases and mk reduction/unique-table behavior are delegated. These helpers are trusted unless separately verified. AppendixB Algorithm1 printed swap atlines11–12 is valid for commutative and/or but reverses operands for noncommutative diff when var(a)>var(b), unless direction is tracked elsewhere. Example fields f<g, a=(g=1), b=(f=1): intended a minus b is g1∧f0, swapping yields f1∧g0. No direction adjustment is shown. This is a visually confirmed pseudocode issue, not an executed-library failure. Literal translation into a proof/spec requires preserving operand order. §4.1/AppendixB Algorithm4: update(δ,a) requires δ⇒a, where a is already atomized. Traverse corresponding intersecting paths, split old atoms by new label BDDs, globally replace old IDs with new atoms, repeat until no split remains. Updates can overwrite split[ap] during one traversal; repetition can discover further subdivisions, so one pass alone is insufficient. Finite Boolean domains permit eventual refinement, but no practical complexity bound supplied. AppendixB Algorithm4 printed updateRec has cases δ=true, equal variables, and var(δ)<var(a), but no var(δ)>var(a) case. Precondition δ⇒a alone does not rule that case out: let f<g, with g a two-bit field, a=(f=0)∨(g∈{0,1}), δ=(g=0). Then δ⇒a, a starts atf andδ atg; g0 requires splitting existing g-atom{0,1}, yet listing has no branch. Terminal false/a=true behavior and initialization of atomized δ are also implicit. This is a source-listing completeness question, not a claim observed code is unsound. §4.2: Per-field BDDs are logically isolated namespaces but share the same underlying BDD node table, unlike separate-manager parallel EPVerifier design. title: A Domain Specific Language for Testing Consensus Implementations
what: Presents Netrix, a central networking server plus DSL for programmer-guided exploration of consensus implementations. Instrumentation shims intercept RPC/message APIs; filters and key-value context encode semantic waypoints. Case studies cover Tendermint, Raft and BFTSmart across Go and Java, including regression tests and protocol-coverage measures. Filter-distance analysis predicts when PCTCP alone can find reorderings.

title: NetSMC: A Custom Symbolic Model Checker for Stateful Network Verification
what: NetSMC checks temporal policies on models of stateful network functions with persistent tables and one packet traversing the network at a time. It translates a restricted LTL language into CTL and represents sets of network states as existential first-order formulas. Backward preimages and a containment algorithm adapted from database query containment avoid general solver costs. A packet-order argument gives equivalence to interleaved executions for selected policies under an order-preservation condition. Benchmarks compare VMN, a Z3 containment variant, NuSMV and Cubicle; author-run exercises inject configuration mistakes into real network functions. Records exact NF/packet transition semantics, commutation and order-preservation conditions, restricted temporal operators and full appendix proofs, EFO preimage and containment construction, proof/implementation boundaries, printed listing/formula concerns, every Table2 timing and the narrow scopes of speedup, planted faults and model fidelity.
assumptions_limits: §§4/8: A fixed topology and NF rule set; packets contain modeled header/application fields, not arbitrary payload processing. State is a collection of finite key-value maps; tests use specified finite domains, updates assign modeled expressions or increment/decrement by constants, expressions may choose nondeterministically from a domain. No multicast/broadcast, averages, generic computations, clocks/timeouts or direct network failures. Failures require separate enumerated scenarios. Integer/counter bounds and overflow semantics are not developed into an implementation-level finite-state proof. §§4.1/4.3/AppendixA: Exactly one matching NF rule; sequential commands are atomic at NF network-step granularity. A link preserves packet and tables. Drop/Exit permits an arbitrary next packet at arbitrary ingress, retaining all tables. Correct rules/topology/initial tables/model extraction are trusted; sequential packets do not mean tables reset between packets. Nondeterministic backend choice abstracts a concrete policy rather than verifies its implementation. §4.3/AppendixC: Every packet eventually leaves or drops; transient loops allowed, indefinite loops excluded. Unique immutable IDs distinguish packets. Interleaved model buffers unordered sets, not FIFO queues, and proof considers finite closed traces with no unfinished nonterminal packets. No general liveness/fairness or live controller-update verification. AppendixC/Definitions4–5/Lemma1: Non-conflict means swapping two same-NF processing steps preserves both output packets and final table valuation for every relevant initial valuation. A strict total packet order must be respected wherever packets conflict. Adjacent inversion swaps decrease an out-of-order index until packets can be serialized with identical per-packet located-packet traces. Conditions are assumptions on networks; no checker that establishes them for arbitrary input models is evaluated. §5/AppendicesB/D: Policies universally quantify outer variables; basic predicates inspect fields/location/tables. Permitted temporal forms are basic, F basic, within-packet eventual f basic, X(guard→formula), G(guard→formula), and within-packet g(guard→formula). f/g expand to restricted strong-until formulas terminated by Drop/Exit. General until, arbitrary quantifier alternation, generic temporal nesting/past properties excluded. A positive answer for arbitrary policies under serialization does not establish concurrent correctness. §5/AppendixD/Theorem7/Corollaries2,8: Conditional equivalence explicitly covers isolation, tag preservation and tag-based isolation on order-preserving networks. Other policies such as flow affinity/NAT consistency/service chaining are checked under the one-packet model and may miss interleaving bugs. Do not read Table1 sound/conditionally-complete labels as unconditional verification of all concurrent deployments. AppendixD qualified proof-scope concern: Theorem7 syntactically uses basic guards without explicitly excluding table predicates, although Lemma1 preserves only located-packet input/output traces, not every intermediate table valuation while a packet waits. Reordered unrelated processing can alter such valuations. The printed transfer argument therefore needs a restriction to predicates determined by those traces or an additional preservation proof; isolation/tag examples avoid this issue. This is a reading concern, not an executed counterexample against the tool. §6.2: EFO state formulas are disjunctions of conjunctive clauses with membership, inequality, location/field equality and table lookup. Variables are existential and outermost; denotation is a set of concrete packet/table valuations. This is a symbolic representation, not sampling of packet histories. §6.3/Algorithms1–2: Preimage unions NF-rule, link and new-packet predecessors. Commands processed in reverse order; tests conjoined. New-packet transition drops successor field/location constraints but preserves their variable/table relationships, restricts successor ingress and predecessor Drop/Exit. Table updates split equal-index overwritten entry versus an unequal index retaining old value. Helper expression translation F and link routine are omitted; precise implementation behavior is not reconstructed from pseudocode alone. §6.4/Algorithm3: Interpret clauses as conjunctive queries; homomorphism maps variables of candidate containing clause into contained clause. Inequalities require splitting equality patterns into atomic clauses; finite domains need emptiness checks (e.g., singleton variables forcing incompatible table values). Every nonempty atomic clause must map to some disjunct of target. This avoids a naive implication query to Z3, while still potentially expanding many clauses. §6.4/Theorem3 and AppendixE: Authors state exact True iff satisfaction under one-packet semantics. Appendices provide detailed semantics, trace reordering, policy transfer and structural LTL→CTL arguments (Theorem9/Lemmas10–12); no separate complete proof of Algorithm1/2 preimages, Algorithm3 domain splitting/emptiness, or Python refinement appears. Theorem3 is not a machine-checked verified implementation. Algorithm2/p188 printed-listing concerns: loop binds β_j on line14 but line15 passes β_i, and line21 recursive COMPUTECLS call omits expression-environment arguments present in its signature. Figure11/p196 sequence rule leaves c2 as a pending command without giving the corresponding continuation rule in the displayed semantics. Treat as incomplete/inconsistent presentation; no artifact tested. AppendixF/p200 printed-policy concerns: NAT consistency formula contains p without the displayed outer binder (only ∀i), despite closed-formula requirement. Flow affinity shown for S1 needs analogous instances for other servers. Conditional reachability uses G(loc=B→f(loc=A)) from the same arrival state at B, so without distinguishing request arrival from new reply injection it can demand that the current packet return to A; the prose speaks of packets sent afterwards. Qualified formula/specification boundary, not a measured tool failure. §7: Python prototype,20core2.8GHz/128GB server. CPU model/OS/Python/solver versions, source LOC, repeated-run statistics, confidence intervals and memory usage not reported. Alembic-generated NF models and manual POX translation used; authors assert high fidelity, but no formal extraction/refinement theorem or measured model-fidelity error rate is provided. §7.1/Figures6–8: Synthetic host/rule scaling and extended fattree/Ai3/Sprint topology isolation checks; flow-space sliced for both tools. Specific speedups depend on policy/model and baseline. VMN lacks service-chain policy support, so policy-complexity comparison uses only NetSMC/Z3. NuSMV fixed16-entry table and NetSMC without that size constraint are different encodings; Cubicle750× lacks detailed absolute timing/setup in text. §7.2: Red team authors2/3 inject secret deleted/modified rules; blue team author1 diagnoses with NetSMC, then rechecks fixed model. Four described real-NF exercises and nine modeled Table2 scenarios all succeed as reported; no production-discovered fault count, exhaustive fault set, detection rate, false-positive rate or independent user study. All benchmark/tool outcomes here are authors reports, not reproduced.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for specification/model-checking evaluation of stateful distributed network components: serialization assumptions determine what a proof covers, symbolically exact model checking differs from implementation verification, and injected-fault success differs from concurrent completeness. Useful for auditing LLM-written temporal specifications and checking theorem-to-implementation transfer. No Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ implementation, or LLM-agent experiment.

title: Partial Model Checking Using Networks of Labelled Transition Systems and Boolean Equation Systems
what: Generalizes partial model checking from binary CCS-style composition to networks of labelled transition systems, represents quotient formulas as formula graphs, simplifies them with bisimulation/reduction and Boolean-equation solving, and supports an alternation-2 fairness operator. The network model subsumes m-among-n synchronization, synchronization interfaces, hiding, cutting and renaming. Quotienting is implemented as a synchronous product of a formula graph and one process; graph encoding/decoding preserves closed formulas, while simplification rules eliminate disjunction transitions, unguarded variables, double negations, fixpoint transitions and constant subformulas. For Pdl-∆ fairness, marked variables and A4cyc detect modality-free cycles containing marked variables in linear time. A Cadp prototype integrates Exp.Open, Evaluator, Reductor/Bcg Min and a 1,000-line solver extension. Two case studies compare against on-the-fly checking for TFTP/UDP and SCSI-2 bus arbitration, exposing both major memory savings and combinatorial blow-ups.

TFTP product sizes range from 1,963×10³ to 35,024×10³ states across scenarios
SCSI-2 configuration B with six disks: product LTS 708,174,559 states; partial checking 24,276 seconds and 16,239 MB versus on-the-fly 47,532 seconds and 39,236 MB
On the SCSI-2 three-disk configuration, on-the-fly took 1.12–1.67 s while partial checking took 19.16 s or 4 minutes depending on property truth
assumptions_limits: The main efficient solver specialization targets alternation-free modal µ-calculus plus ∆R; arbitrary alternation depth would need a corresponding BES solver. Formula quotient order uses a heuristic and reductions can still explode, especially for existential regular-path formulas. Experiments use finite LTS models and Cadp on a 148-GB machine; results are case-study dependent and partial checking complements rather than dominates on-the-fly exploration.
use_for_goal: This paper supplies a mature compositional verification pattern for distributed processes: quotient a temporal property through one component, simplify the residual graph, and solve it with BES algorithms. Its fairness treatment and explicit trade-offs between memory, time and graph explosion are useful when designing scalable verification of distributed protocols.
