title: Towards Reliable Neural Specifications
what: Proposes neural representation as specification: mine partial neural activation patterns (NAPs) shared by most examples of a class, then verify classification and robustness for the whole input region following that pattern. A relaxation factor δ controls precision/recall. NAPs can be encoded directly in Marabou, support non-ambiguity checks between labels, and augment input norm-balls to verify larger regions. The method’s mining algorithm counts neuron activation frequencies on class training data, selecting activated/deactivated neurons above δ and below 1−δ. The paper distinguishes NAP robustness (all inputs following a pattern are classified as the label) from NAP-augmented robustness (norm-ball intersected with the pattern region). Controlled 2-D visualization explains why activation regions are flexible and larger than boxes. VNNCOMP-21 MNIST and CIFAR10 experiments quantify precision/recall, timeouts, coverage and robustness bounds; δ=0.99 yields an MNIST digit-1 NAP covering 84% of test images and verifies ε=0.3 for six of seven previously non-robust inputs. CIFAR10 verifies some examples at ε=0.12 (10× the prior bound) when δ=0.9.
numbers: MNIST δ=0.99 digit-1 NAP recalls 959/1135=84% test images; δ=1.0 recalls 1124/1135=99% but admits 8 wrong-label images

assumptions_limits: Targets feed-forward ReLU classifiers and uses Marabou; extension to other activations/architectures is conjectural. Mining is approximate, requires δ>0.5 and trades recall for precision; lower δ can cover fewer inputs. NAP guarantees concern the network’s classifier, not semantic correctness of labels or distribution shift. Noisy/mislabeled data can violate ideal same-label patterns. Marabou has timeouts and complete verification remains expensive; abstract verifiers can be inconclusive. Experiments use MNIST/CIFAR10 VNNCOMP models, not deployed systems.
use_for_goal: Strongly relevant to verifier-oriented specification mining: it shows how internal neural predicates can define larger, machine-checkable regions and exposes precision/recall and timeout limits. For Verus/distributed systems the transferable idea is invariant mining from implementation states, while the concrete guarantees are only for ReLU network classification.

title: Automated and Formal Synthesis of Neural Barrier Certificates for Dynamical Models.
what: Presents a counterexample-guided inductive synthesis loop in which a neural network is trained as a barrier certificate and an SMT verifier proves its safety conditions or returns counterexamples. The paper states the barrier conditions (initial set non-positive, unsafe set positive, negative Lie derivative on the zero level set), translates trained networks symbolically, and adds bespoke losses, polynomial/tanh/sigmoid/ReLU architectures, prioritized and multiple counterexample generation, and numerical-robustness measures. It handles polynomial and transcendental ODEs, a piecewise hybrid model, and 4/6/8-dimensional ODEs. The CEGIS loop is sound when SMT returns unsat, but not complete; it retains weights and augments samples after each counterexample. SOS candidates are often numerically ill-conditioned and fail SMT verification.

title: Let a Neural Network Be Your Invariant
what: For hardware designs, one small neural network is trained to be both an inductive invariant (a set of states that contains all reachable states and is closed under steps; this proves safety) and a ranking function (a number that drops each time something bad could recur; this proves liveness). A solver then checks the network exactly, so a yes answer is a real proof. Training uses a constraint solver (MILP) rather than gradient descent.

what: Proposes NFV: an AI agent translates mainstream-language source, property and environment assumptions into staged formal artifacts, then uses Dafny or CBMC to produce machine-checked proofs/refutations. title: Nickel: A Framework for Design and Verification of Information Flow Control Systems
what: Nickel verifies that deterministic sequential system interfaces and their C implementations satisfy information-flow policies. A state-dependent action-domain function and possibly intransitive flow relation define permitted influence. Noninterference compares observations after original and optionally purged action histories. Coq-proved unwinding and restricted-refinement theorems reduce system proofs to Z3 checks over individual operations. Demonstrations cover the NiStar DIFC kernel, NiKOS process isolation and a repaired ARINC 653 interface specification. Records exact purge and seven unwinding obligations, lockstep data/policy refinement, trusted policy/checker/initialization boundaries, deterministic/uniprocessor/static-policy restrictions, manual observational equivalence, all object/label/quota/scheduler mechanisms, concrete covert channels and interface redesigns, complete LOC cells, verification/effort times and the logical-time experiment. Separates mechanized metatheory from trusted SMT implementation and ARINC specification analysis from kernel implementation verification.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3.1,3.5,6.3: Only sequential deterministic state machines, with system-call/trap handlers atomic on a uniprocessor. NiStar disables timer interrupts in kernel space and all other interrupts, using polling drivers. This does not establish security under multicore/shared-memory concurrency, weak memory or interleaved kernel handlers. §3.1 Definition1: Policy P=(D,flow,dom); domains represent exercised authority, flow is a fixed relation on domain pairs, and dom(action,state) may depend on the current thread/labels. Intransitive flow can allow p1→scheduler→p2 while forbidding direct p1→p2. A state-dependent dom does not make the can-flow-to relation dynamic; changing that relation is unsupported. §3.2 Definition2/Figures4–5: sources recursively tracks permitted direct or intermediate influence along a trace. purge is a SET of subtraces: it always permits retaining an action and permits dropping it only when its domain is outside sources, recomputing later state on the removed branch. Noninterference quantifies over every action, original trace and permitted purged trace and requires equal next-action output from the two resulting states. This is a relational security property over histories, not only memory isolation or functional refinement. §3.2: Authors establish reduction to classical noninterference for state-independent dom and monotonicity when flow is relaxed while domains/dom stay fixed. The PDF states these sanity checks but does not print their detailed proofs. Do not generalize monotonicity to changes of all policy components. §3.3 Theorem1/Figure6: Developers supply an inductive state invariant and per-domain observational equivalence. Seven universally quantified obligations cover invariant initialization/preservation, equivalence, consistency with dom, consistency with flow, output consistency, local respect and weak step consistency. Accepted invariants/equivalences are checked proof inputs, not trusted axioms; inventing an unsuitable relation can fail the checks. They remain substantial human work. §3.4 Theorem2: General refinement may introduce leaks. Supported data refinement requires same actions/outputs, related initial states, one-step preservation and equal output for related states satisfying the implementation invariant. Policy refinement additionally preserves dom for the same action/history and uses the same domain set/flow relation. No arbitrary stuttering, action splitting or nondeterministic refinement is claimed. §§3.5,6.2: Guarantees cover modeled interface observations, including logical scheduling time. Physical timing, sound, energy and microarchitectural channels outside the model are excluded. No distributed network fault, crash-recovery, availability, termination or fairness guarantee is supplied. The scheduler description assumes an infinite stream of timer interrupts rather than proving hardware progress. §4: Coq mechanizes the two general theorems. Python specifications/proof inputs and symbolic execution of C-derived LLVM IR produce Z3 obligations. Paper explicitly trusts information-flow policy, unwinding checker and Z3; implementation verification adds refinement checker and unverified initialization/glue. This is not an independently checked proof certificate for each SMT result or fully verified checker/compiler/hardware chain. §4: The intended policy is the trusted top-level requirement and needs auditing. Automated verification cannot show that an overly permissive policy matches the user’s security intention. A failed condition may reflect a genuine interface/implementation channel or insufficient invariant/observational equivalence; every solver counterexample is not automatically an exploit. §5: Determinism is obtained by exposing allocation choices as arguments, specifying allocation behavior precisely (NiStar), or hiding choices below the interface (NiKOS virtual addresses). Encrypted sequential names technically violate exact noninterference despite a claimed negligible practical leak; Nickel avoids them rather than proving probabilistic security. §§6.1–6.2: DIFC safe-flow relation combines sender and receiver ownership for controlled declassification/endorsement. Alice’s tty daemon is trusted to release secrets only to her terminal; a label proof does not verify that daemon’s declassification logic. Only threads/gates may have nonempty ownership. Fixed-size pages and finite interfaces aid SMT automation. §6.3: NiStar uses a kernel identity mapping and separate user/kernel page tables. The incomplete POSIX emulation, musl, lwIP, file-system wrapper and applications demonstrate usability; their existence does not extend the kernel proof to full application correctness, network security or durable filesystem semantics. §7: NiKOS mirrors a particular mCertiKOS interface after changing executable loading to make quotas agree. It is not a proof of every mCertiKOS variant. ARINC 653 result verifies a Python-modeled 14-operation communication interface after fixing three previously known channels; no ARINC kernel implementation/refinement proof or new bug discovery is reported. §8: Counterexamples for injected §2 examples and the round-robin workload demonstrate detection within these models. The logical-time plot supports its stated scenario, not absence of unmodeled physical channels. No Linux performance comparison, end-to-end application throughput benchmark, repeated-run confidence interval, or quantitative covert-channel capacity study is provided. §8 Figure11: LOC for interface implementation excludes shared C/x86 infrastructure; user-space LOC excludes third-party musl/lwIP. Effort figures are authors’ experience, not a controlled productivity comparison: one author six/two/one weeks for specification+verification, several researchers about six months implementing NiStar, and two months exploring framework definitions. §§9–10: Related work includes seL4/CertiKOS/Ironclad/Komodo and Covern, plus DIFC policy-synthesis tools; those citations do not mean Nickel supports concurrency or automatically synthesizes the complete policy/observational equivalence. No direct Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment. Public source pointer saved; artifact/proofs not run.
use_for_goal: A concrete security-property case for evaluating generated specifications and proofs: trusted policy correctness, relational observations, manually discovered equivalence, checked proof inputs, restricted security-preserving refinement and trusted tool gaps. Mechanized metatheory plus SMT automation contrasts with paper-only proofs. Kernel-local sequential guarantee; adapting it to distributed concurrent failures requires additional semantics and proof. No direct Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLM evaluation.

title: Stateless Model Checking for TSO and PSO
what: Introduces chronological traces for executions under TSO and PSO. The traces induce an acyclic happens-before partial order that is in one-to-one correspondence with Shasha-Snir traces, enabling Source-DPOR and Optimal-DPOR to explore complete equivalence-class representatives without redundant relaxed-memory executions. The paper formalizes TSO store buffers, loads, fences and auxiliary update threads, defines six chronological edge relations and proves equivalence with Shasha-Snir traces for completed executions. It proves DPOR coverage (at least one execution per class) and Optimal-DPOR minimality (exactly one), then implements Source-DPOR in Nidhugg over LLVM IR/pthreads, with spin-loop replacement by load/assume. Experiments cover racy mutual-exclusion benchmarks, robust mutex code, Apache Portable Runtime (~8000 lines), and comparisons with CBMC/goto-instrument; PSO slowdown is linked to one buffer per memory location.

title: Data-driven Numerical Invariant Synthesis with Automatic Generation of Attributes.
what: Extends ICE-DT invariant learning with data-driven generation of linear attributes: positive/negative/implication samples are covered by join-maximal separators represented in interval, octagon or polyhedral abstract domains. The paper defines inductive safety conditions and ICE samples, explains decision-tree learning with implication closure, and introduces separator construction that joins convex abstract objects covering positive states while excluding negatives. Algorithm 4 computes a join-maximal separator; Algorithms 5–6 incrementally reuse separator stacks and parent indices when counterexamples arrive. Examples show the learned invariants evolve from simple equalities to disjunctive loop invariants. The C++ NIS prototype uses Z3 and APRON and solves 154/164 SyGuS-Comp LIA programs with polyhedra and 160/164 using a virtual best across intervals/octagons/polyhedra, outperforming enumerative ICE-DT/LoopInvGen in many cases while remaining complementary across domains.

title: Interpolation and Model Checking for Nonlinear Arithmetic

title: OCTAL: Graph Representation Learning for LTL Model Checking
what: Introduces OCTAL, a graph-representation-learning approach that classifies whether a Büchi automaton satisfies an LTL formula. It represents the automaton as a bipartite graph, the formula as an expression tree, joins matching variables, and trains GNNs to avoid explicit negated-formula automaton and product construction. Section 3 specifies graph construction, NNF formula normalization, shared variable/negation node encoding, and a unified graph C. A 3-layer GIN performs message passing and mean pooling for binary classification. Section 4 builds Short (9,424), Diverse (6,107), and RERS19 (1,798) datasets, compares OCTAL GIN/GCN against MLP, LinkPredictor and LTL3BA, tests domain shift and one-vs-many ranking, and drops graph edges to assess robustness. title: On Temporal Verification of Stateful P4 Programs
what: Defines P4LTL temporal properties over completed packet processings while retaining register state between packets. Models arbitrary input packets and changing table actions, optionally constrained by symbolic control-plane assumptions. Constructs a Büchi transaction product in which the specification automaton advances only at packet return, reducing violations to fair feasible traces. A proof sketch establishes the abstract correspondence; p4tv implements P4-to-Boogie translation, ghost instrumentation and an Ultimate Automizer extension. Evaluation checks19 temporal tasks on nine programs plus assertion checks/scaling, identifying two naturally occurring property failures and three injected defects. Records exact packet-boundary/old/free-variable semantics, register initialization and control-plane scope, product transitions/acceptance and proof-sketch qualifications, refinement algorithm and implementation trust, all Table2/3 cells, actual versus injected bug distinction, p4v approximation and assertion instrumentation, rapid scaling growth, and source specification/prose inconsistencies including vacuous liveness formula. Separates local P4xos checks from whole Paxos consensus verification.
assumptions_limits: §3: Environment is a serial infinite loop of complete packet processings, persistent registers outside loop, nondeterministic packet fields each iteration and metadata initialized per P4-16. Table applications are nondeterministic action choices. This abstracts a single programmed switch; no proof of interleaved pipeline concurrency, simultaneous register read/modify/write races, multiple switches, queue dynamics or actual hardware refinement is supplied. Packet time is not wall-clock time. §§2/3/7/8: Register initialization is part of each verification configuration. P4NIS failing task9 leaves count unconstrained; successful invariant/assertion examples assume valid/zero initialization or add recovery logic. Persistent arbitrary initial values differ from independently re-randomizing registers every packet. Results under initialization assumptions do not show a real deployment meets those assumptions. §§3.2/4: CPI constrains table keys/actions/parameters, allows symbolic sets of entries and changes between packets. Empty CPI permits every modeled rule. Property checked is assumption implies desired property; it can hold if assumption is impossible. Authors do not report systematic assumption satisfiability/vacuity checks or prove a real controller always enforces CPI. Table2 needs CPI for tasks6,7,8,16 only. §4.1: Predicates are evaluated at packet boundaries: terms normally after processing; old(t) at ingress start after parsing; valid(h) records validity after parsing, hit/apply record occurrence during processing. old(key) and old(para) expressly arbitrary. fwd(t) is egress_spec==t syntactic sugar, so packet-output/architecture correspondence matters. Free variables describe nondeterministic values intended to cover all names; scope/stability must be preserved when translating specifications. §§4/6/7.2: Boundary-only temporal properties can miss transient within-packet violations. Assertion checks use a shadow variable initialized true per packet and capture the assertion at its program point, then check its boundary value. This is an explicit instrumentation workaround; the native P4LTL language still cannot directly observe arbitrary internal events. Correct instrumentation and all relevant visits are part of the trust boundary. §5.1: Product keeps program/specification location pairs, updates specification only on TR(s), uses assume true on other statements, and accepting locations require spec acceptance plus TE/TR boundary. Fair means Büchi acceptance (infinitely recurring accepting states), not automatic network-delivery, scheduler or adversary fairness. Liveness assumptions about infinitely many particular packets are written explicitly in the property. Infinite repeated packet processing is the base execution model. §5.1/Appendix A: Theorem5.1/A.1 is an abstract correspondence with an informal proof sketch, not a mechanized proof of P4 semantics, Boogie translation, instrumenter or executable checker. Projection deletes only true steps imposed by non-return transitions; a return transition labelled true must remain. Appendix switches the named if/only-if directions, and reverse construction retains TE(s)∨TR(s) while operational product advances spec on TR(s) only. A rigorous proof should distinguish statement/boundary indexing and establish infinitely many returns; no concrete tool-unsoundness counterexample claimed. §5.2/6: Algorithm1 reuses counterexample-guided refinement from cited fairness-modulo-theory work: select accepting trace, test feasibility, return genuine trace or remove a generalized set of infeasible traces, finish when none remain. No universal termination/runtime bound or translation correctness theorem provided. Trust includes P4/Boogie modeling, ghost instrumentation, LTL conversion, automata/refinement/feasibility engine and underlying reasoning tools. Code/proofs not run in this reading. §6: Prototype fully supports V1Model but limited TNA/PSA. Authors claim model transferable with more detailed P4 processing; future architecture support is not demonstrated full support. State explosion remains. About10000C++/JavaLOC and selected small benchmark programs do not establish production-scale coverage. §8 pp.228–229: Printed P4NIS liveness consequence is conjunction over ports i of GF(phi_sp -> fwd(i)), under GF(phi_sp). This is weaker than GF(phi_sp AND fwd(i)): infinitely many non-specific packets satisfy every implication regardless of forwarding. Alternating specific/non-specific packets with no fwd(i) satisfies the displayed formula while violating the natural-language goal. This is a semantic observation about the printed specification, not a run of artifact specifications. §4’s earlier liveness example has a different stronger shape. §8: NDN weak-until formula is activated only after a data packet was forwarded; it then forbids repeated data forwarding until a matching forwarded interest. It does not by itself forbid the first unsolicited data forward before that trigger, nor require eventual forwarding because W permits no future interest. Task6’s separate property covers interest-before-data. Universal free hash variable is not a proof of hash collision freedom or data-name authentication. §5.1 Figure5/§7.2 Table3: Figure5 prose says status becomes0 when hdr.cnt<0, while listing/automaton tests>0; record follows code when describing example. Table3 says acceptor stored round strictly less than current round, while adjoining prose uses≤ under zero initialization. Strict< would fail on equal zeros; cannot silently interchange these properties. Printed description/code discrepancies do not establish implementation bugs. §7: Dataset has nine manually selected programs and manually authored properties; artificial bugs inserted in CPI/task8 and code/tasks15,18. Natural failures tasks9,13 are author-reported findings without external maintainer confirmation/production exploit in paper. 14 verified tasks and five counterexamples are outcomes for specified models, not whole programs certified correct. §7.2: Temporal comparison with four prior tools is a support limitation discussion; measured assertion comparison runs bf4 and an approximate p4v implementation from bf4 work because original p4v unavailable. Vera limited user assertions and Aquila unavailable. Spurious counterexamples are relative to chosen persistent-register configuration, not evidence prior tools unsound for their broader nondeterministic model. p4tv is much slower but more precise for these stateful examples. §7.3: Program and specification scaling varied separately on P4NIS ports and acceptor index clauses. Curves grow rapidly; Figure8 about8600s near64ports and Figure9 about24000s near32clauses, approximate visual readings only. Reported trace receives interest then drops data. A dropped data packet alone cannot violate this only-if safety condition. title: On Verifying Secret Control Flow Elimination
what: CompCert extension implementing and verifying a partial control-flow linearization transformation for an acyclic, call-free, initially memory-free subset of C/RTL. Intermediate PredRTL keeps original and transformed program counters to prove semantic preservation via postdominance. A taint analysis and new influence-region proof establish secret-independent control-flow traces at PredRTL. Separates semantic preservation, operation-definedness and two-execution control-flow security. Uses detour postdominance to align live states; instructions on dummy detours execute but discard effects, requiring safe defined operands. Taint includes both explicit data dependence and writes in secret-controlled regions. Chain invariants prove uniform vertices cannot be dummy. Security transfer to lower IRs/assembly remains unproved, while a proposed memory relaxation has an explicit axiom and inconsistent location wording.
assumptions_limits: Current transformation requires a finite acyclic CFG, fixed topological vertex permutation and unique entry/exit, with no calls or memory instructions in the principal safe-operation account. Unique exit may be obtained by gotos to a shared return. Semantics is simplified in the exposition; paper does not claim production C coverage. PCFL assumes a secret_cond labeling and guarantees a topological transformed graph, one successor at each secret condition, and detour_spec: each original edge v→w maps to v→detour(v,w), with w postdominating the new target. Postdominance alone needs progress/definedness and acyclicity to justify reaching the original target. Dummy PredRTL states preserve architectural register values but still evaluate operations/conditions, which must succeed. Safe operations on typed defined arguments must return a defined value; all registers are initialized to typed defaults. Safety/condition/progress lemmas have only been proved for x86, according to §3.3. CompCert semantic preservation permits improvement of source undefined behavior; it is not exact equivalence for every undefined source execution. Taint selection is irrelevant to preservation provided PCFL/operation premises hold; security additionally needs correct secret labeling and taint invariants. Control-flow security compares runs of the same transformed function with equal public parameters and arbitrary secret parameters, preserving equal public registers and equal program-point traces at equal trace lengths. It addresses control decisions, not constant runtime of individual operations, cache/data-access behavior, microarchitecture or leakage from output values. PredRTL security is proved; §4.2 explicitly says the cube simulation carrying security to SelRTL/RTL is not written. §7 says integration through downstream CompCert assembly passes is future work. Semantic simulation alone does not establish preservation of this two-run security property. Predication implements live/dummy state in a fresh v_orig_reg plus scratch registers, updating with select. Selects are assumed constant-time in the motivating account; x86 builtins are used. Bit-mask lowering is a suggested alternative with 0/1 conditions, not a machine-level constant-time proof. Security transfer would need to treat introduced registers as secret. §5 critical-register relaxation is neither implemented nor proved. Its proof-of-concept Iload extension explicitly assumes axiomatically that any successful load returns a value other than Vundef. This qualification must accompany claims about memory support; no sound arbitrary-memory guarantee is established. §7 proposals for shadow memory, safe division, function calls, global taint and uniform-exit loops are future work. Secret-exit loops may diverge after linearization even when source terminates; authors say existing PCFL variants cannot generally satisfy their preservation goal without extra guarantees or weaker simulation. No execution-time overhead measurements, leakage attacks/tests, benchmark cases, production programs or proof-check run are reported here. ~9000addedlines is an author development-size report including four transformations and graph theory, not performance data. Reader did not audit Coq assumptions or execute artifacts.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful verification/agent-evaluation case for distinguishing single-run semantic preservation from relational leakage properties, tracking proof transfer between IRs, and testing unsupported-operation assumptions with concrete counterexamples. Global graph invariants supply reusable proof structure. Direct subject is secure compilation, not distributed protocol correctness, Verus/Rust,TLA+ or LLM proof generation.

title: OptProver: Bridging Olympiad and Optimization through Continual Training in Formal Theorem Proving
what: OptProver adapts BFS-Prover-V2-7B from Olympiad mathematics to Lean optimization via successful-search expert iteration and preference training. OptBench contains 400 Optlib-derived goals. Reported full-method success rises from base 13.25/32.00% to 37.75/55.25% under step prover Pass@1/32. The evidence is finite proof-search evaluation and ablations, not a theorem guaranteeing domain transfer or absence of forgetting. Separates tactic validity from budget-conditioned usefulness. Successful proof-path actions win over sibling actions that error or consume the search budget without closing a proof; locally valid but unresolved actions are not labeled mathematically invalid. Perplexity-weighted DPO replaces sequence log scores with clipped inverse-reference-perplexity weighted token averages; PW-UAPO combines this with utility-aware pairs. Expert iteration mixes Mathlib self-play, LLM-formalized Convex Analysis/Real Analysis and nearly 7k DeepTheorem analysis/linear-algebra problems. Detailed cases show optimization definitions unfolded before arithmetic, reuse of existing library lemmas, an ADMM inequality proof and extended-real edge cases.
assumptions_limits: Lean acceptance establishes the formal goal relative to imported definitions, axioms and implementation. It does not establish faithful autoformalization of textbook/DeepTheorem prose or optimization software correctness. No statement-faithfulness audit, axiom audit or explicit sorry/admission bypass filter is documented in the supplied paper; the reader did not run the artifact. Utility labels depend on the current policy, sibling sampling, search allocation and stopping budget. Unresolved branches may be provable and may become useful under another policy. No theorem establishes the pairwise preference as optimal or a state-value oracle. OptBench has 121 basic, 135 convex and 144 algorithm-analysis goals; algorithmic goals are extracted partial proof obligations, not independent end-to-end algorithm or implementation verification. The benchmark is optimization mathematics in a fixed Lean 4.10.0/LeanDojo 2.1.3 environment. Whole-proof baselines use 32/256 generated proofs; step provers use accumulative 1/32 search budgets. These labels are not equal tactic counts, wall time or compute. No absolute node/time/token budget, hardware cost comparison, per-problem timeout or statistical intervals are supplied. Training includes large-scale Mathlib and Optlib-related mathematical material. No explicit theorem/dependency deduplication, benchmark exclusion rule, base-pretraining contamination audit or held-out construction protocol is reported; do not infer a leakage-free novel-theorem result. MiniF2F parity and ProofNet gains are finite evidence on two benchmarks. They do not establish universal retention, robustness or domain-transfer ability. No repeated-seed uncertainty or causal mechanism study is provided. Perplexity is a model-likelihood statistic, not semantic correctness. Poorer naive-SFT performance supports a failure case for the tested training recipe; it does not establish that textbook data or perplexity filtering generally harms proving. PW-DPO uses normalized weighted token log scores; these need not define a normalized sequence probability distribution. Its numerical-stability and anti-forgetting explanations are author interpretations, without a convergence, gradient-variance or stability proof. No distributed protocols, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or temporal/concurrent semantics are evaluated. Search-budget labels and domain-adaptation methods may inform proof-agent design; transfer to software verification remains a reader hypothesis.
use_for_goal: For specification/proof agents, the useful distinction is between a checker-valid step and a step that helps close the target under available search compute. Domain-specific data can alter tactic priorities; successful self-play and budget-aware preferences offer an evaluated adaptation recipe. The record preserves different budget semantics and formal-statement trust boundaries. It supplies no direct verification result for distributed systems, Verus, Rust or TLA+.

title: Efficient Verification of Network Fault Tolerance via Counterexample-Guided Refinement
what: Introduces Origami, which compresses symmetric routing networks and uses CEGAR to refine abstractions until bounded-fault reachability is proved or a real counterexample is exposed. Its soundness uses label approximation: concrete routes need only be at least as good as abstract routes under well-formed routing policies. The paper defines Stable Path Problems with Faults (SPPFs), including topology, attributes, preference order, transfer function, destination and failure bound. It gives local effective-approximation conditions (forall-exists topology, rank-equivalence and transfer-equivalence) and proves every concrete solution has a label-approximating abstract solution. The refinement loop uses min-cut plausibility, policy-aware unusable edges learned from counterexamples, candidate breadth and counterexample minimization. Models cover RIP and simplified BGP; Section 7 distinguishes pure shortest-path SP40 from policy-rich FT20/FT40/FbFT and explains actual failures when min cuts are below k+1.

title: Parallel Explicit Model Checking for Generalized Büchi Automata
what: Develops parallel Tarjan- and Dijkstra-style SCC emptiness checks for transition-based generalized Büchi automata. Threads swarm DFS traversals while sharing only stable SCC/dead-state structure through a lock-free union-find augmented with acceptance marks; a mixed portfolio combines both strategies. The generic canvas defines shared stop/union-find state and local DFS, LIVE, livenum, and pstack structures. Tarjan propagates lowlinks on backtracking; Dijkstra merges partial SCCs on closing edges and detects acceptance earlier. Proof sketches establish safety of shared information and acceptance detection, while complexity analysis identifies union-find contention in large SCCs. Experiments with Spot and DiVinE compare 1–12 threads on BEEM products, separating empty (satisfied) and nonempty (violated) formulas and analyzing topology-dependent scaling.

10 benchmark models per plot group

Products average 0.5–101.6 million states, 3.2–349.9 million transitions and up to 22.7 million SCCs (Table 1). 3268 formulas were selected so sequential cndfs took 15 s–30 min on 4×Xeon X7460; 24-core machine used for parallel runs. Within one-hour limit, proposed algorithms solved all 3268 products; owcty failed 11 and cndfs 784. Dijkstra was 25% faster than cndfs on adding.4 with 12 threads (though 2× slower with one thread). Speedups were quasi-linear for adding.4/bridge.3/exit.3/leader-election.3, modest for six large-SCC models; Mixed lay between Tarjan and Dijkstra. Violated products can exceed thread-count speedups due to search-order effects.
assumptions_limits: The automaton is finite and transitions carry generalized acceptance marks; correctness relies on lock-free compare-and-swap union-find and stable SCC/DEAD facts. Local traversals may redo work when another thread marks a state DEAD. Speedups depend strongly on SCC shape and union-find contention; prototype absolute times lag sequential CNDFS, and one comparison precomputes products for LTSmin due to a bug. The approach is explicit-state and does not address symbolic or unbounded systems.
use_for_goal: A foundational parallel explicit-checking design with stable shared invariants, lock-free union-find, and empirical contention analysis; directly relevant to distributed verification algorithms and their proof/evaluation tradeoffs.

title: An Abstraction Technique for Parameterized Model Checking of Leader Election Protocols: Application to FTSP
what: Develops a simulation-preserving abstraction for parameterized timed leader-election protocols with unique identifiers and arbitrary topologies. It abstracts non-leader nodes and network edges around a shortest path to the future leader, approximates clock drift with finite schedulers, and incrementally checks FTSP root election for all graphs bounded by leader distance K. The method first maps identifiers/messages to future-root versus non-root values and relaxes irrelevant sequence/entry variables, then completes the graph outside a chosen shortest path and merges those nodes into an environment process. Simulation lemmas establish that checking the finite abstract model implies LTL properties on every topology in G_K. Approximate-synchrony scheduler S_a(Δ) over-approximates real clocks for a finite horizon derived from σ_l,σ_u,Δ. An incremental proof initializes already-converged path nodes and uses a non-interference guard to remove spurious environment messages. A NuSMV semi-algorithm finds optimal FG bounds without storing all reachable states.
numbers: synchronous K=7: N=107 in 13 minutes; includes 13×13 (169-node) and 13×13×13 (2197-node) grids

assumptions_limits: FTSP broadcasts are assumed to complete before the next send event; nodes start in arbitrary configurations and no faults occur during the recovery window. Clock periods lie in [σ_l,σ_u], and finite approximate-synchrony simulation only covers a bounded execution horizon. The abstraction over-approximates behavior, so spurious traces require guard strengthening and proof of the non-interference lemma. Results concern FTSP root convergence, not full time synchronization or failures during the checked interval; asynchronous K=5 timed out beyond that range.
use_for_goal: A concrete parameterized-verification pattern for distributed protocols: abstraction by topology distance, simulation/refinement, clock-drift modeling and incremental model checking. It gives strong finite bounds while making explicit the assumptions that prevent direct claims about unrestricted distributed executions.

title: Parameterised Complexity of Model Checking and Satisfiability in Propositional Dependence Logic
what: Classifies parameterized complexity of model checking (MC), satisfiability (SAT), and exact-team-size satisfiability (m-SAT) for propositional dependence logic (PDL). It proves a dichotomy: most listed parameters yield fixed-parameter tractability, while team-size, dependence-atom arity, or split count can make problems paraNP-complete. The paper defines team semantics and syntax-circuit treewidth, then gives explicit reductions and algorithms. MC parameterized by team-size is solved by bottom-up enumeration of subteams in time polynomial in formula size and O*(2^(2k)); MC by split count is paraNP-complete via a 3-coloring reduction with three team splits. SAT reduces to singleton assignments because PDL is downward closed, making dependence atoms true and split disjunction classical; SAT by split count is solved by partial assignments with conflict markers and at most 2^k candidates. m-SAT adds a unary requested team size and is FPT for number of variables, formula size, or depth but paraNP-complete for team-size or dep-arity. The table leaves m-SAT under formula-treewidth and split count unresolved.

MC team-size algorithm runs |Phi|·O*(2^(2k))
SAT split-count algorithm runs O(2^#splits(Phi)·|Phi|^O(1))

SAT formula-treewidth, variables, size, depth are FPT; team-size and dep-arity paraNP-complete
assumptions_limits: The logic uses atomic negation only and lax split-junction semantics, though the authors state complexity is unchanged under strict semantics and proofs work for both. Inputs are already binary-encoded, so database-value encoding blowup is not included in parameters. Hardness/FPT claims are parameterized-complexity results, not implementations or empirical benchmarks; open cases remain. Downward closure makes ordinary SAT equivalent to singleton-team satisfiability, which does not apply to m-SAT.
use_for_goal: Provides formal complexity evidence for verification logics with team semantics and explicit reductions/algorithms. It informs how structural parameters can make model checking tractable or leave NP-hardness, useful context for specification and verification complexity, but it does not verify distributed implementations or use Verus/TLA+.

title: Parametric Schedulability Analysis of Fixed Priority Real-Time Distributed Systems
short_name: Parametric schedulability of distributed real-time systems
what: Compares an analytic parametric schedulability method with model checking of parametric timed automata (PTAs) for fixed-priority distributed real-time pipelines on CPUs and CAN buses. The analytic extension represents schedulability as a disjunction of polyhedra over computation times, deadlines and jitters; the PTA approach uses IMITATOR’s Inverse Method and is necessary-and-sufficient for the modeled periodic system. The analytic method extends Seto/Bini sensitivity tests to preemptive processors, non-preemptive networks, precedence pipelines, unconstrained deadlines and jitters by enumerating scheduling-point vectors and linear inequalities. The PTA model explicitly encodes pipeline activation, preemptive/non-preemptive processors, deadline-failure states and parameter valuations; tiles returned by the Inverse Method have uniform discrete behavior. Two test cases compare RTSCAN, MAST holistic analysis and IMITATOR: PTA regions contain the sufficient regions from analytic/holistic methods because they explore all synchronous periodic traces, while MAST can outperform RTSCAN when offset-based interference reductions apply.

IMITATOR’s current model supports only strictly periodic, zero-offset pipelines with end-to-end deadlines no larger than periods, and exhaustive region exploration is slow. MAST uses sampled parameter searches/slack computation and can miss exact regions or depend on step size. Scheduling support is preemptive fixed priority for CPUs and non-preemptive fixed priority for CAN networks; other protocols and multiprocessors are future work.

title: Parsimonious, Simulation Based Verification of Linear Systems
kind: validated simulation-based reachability for linear continuous systems
what: Computes reachable sets for affine linear, possibly time-varying ODEs from n+1 validated simulations for n-dimensional state space. Generalized star sets retain an arbitrary coefficient predicate while advancing a center and basis vectors, allowing nonconvex and unbounded initial sets, sound safety proofs, and sound unsafety witnesses. Superposition makes the exact time-t image a basis transformation with the coefficient predicate unchanged (Algorithm 1, Theorem 1). Algorithm 2 uses synchronized convex enclosures of center/basis trajectories; existential formulas overapproximate the union of reachable states across a time interval, while universally quantified enclosures with existential coefficients underapproximate even the intersection across that interval (Theorem 2 proof). Only m+1 simulations are needed for m basis vectors. For normalized bounded polyhedral/ellipsoid coefficients, Theorem 3 gives a 3ε bloating bound enabling efficient LP checks. General predicates need bilinear reasoning and quantified real formulas. The hybrid extension applies guards, invariants and linear resets through a mode queue. Simulations can be reused for multiple initial predicates sharing the same center/basis. The implementation combines ODEINT fourth-order Runge-Kutta with separate rigorous error bounds, GLPK for polyhedra and Z3 quantifier elimination for general initial sets.
numbers: insulin: 9 simulations; safe 0.206 s versus SpaceEx 8.07 s; unsafe 0.2 s versus 7.89 s
platoon: 11 simulations; 0.356 s safe and 0.342 s unsafe; SpaceEx times out
helicopter: 29 simulations, 4.826 s versus SpaceEx 121.66 s
LTV tank 2–10 dimensions: 0.132–0.484 s versus Flow* 1.56–33.67 s
nonconvex/unbounded ACC/tank: 1.01–2.717 s
assumptions_limits: Core results assume linear affine dynamics, valid numerical trajectory enclosures, synchronized time intervals and convex simulation regions; integration width tends to zero as step size tends to zero. n+1 bounds simulation count, not overall computational complexity. General OA/UA formulas contain NP-hard bilinear constraints and UA has alternating quantifiers. The hybrid-system queue may not terminate and all reported experiments are purely continuous. Nonconvex/unbounded examples are small and quantifier elimination is more expensive than polyhedral LP checks. Table 1 tank rows show roughly 4.6–5.5× speedups, so the prose claim of at least an order-of-magnitude SpaceEx improvement is stronger than those rows support.
use_for_goal: Provides a continuous-system proof component that could be composed with distributed agent/controller proofs. The evidence distinguishes rigorous simulation enclosures from sampled testing and exposes the solver and numerical assumptions that an agent-generated certificate must preserve. No Verus/Rust, TLA+ or learned proof generation is implemented.

title: PASS: Abstraction Refinement for Infinite Probabilistic Models
what: Presents PASS, a tool for concurrent probabilistic guarded-command programs whose semantics may be infinite MDPs. It maintains finite predicate abstractions as stochastic games, computes sound probability intervals, and iteratively refines predicates using probabilistic counterexamples, interpolation or game-strategy diagnostics. title: Passport: Improving Automated Formal Verification Using Identifiers
what: Enhances Coq proof-synthesis models with identifier information through category vocabularies, subword sequence modeling and fully qualified path elaboration. title: Lifted Model Checking for Relational MDPs
kind: formal verification method and empirical evaluation
what: Introduces pCTL-REBEL, a lifted probabilistic model checker for relational Markov decision processes that reasons over first-order abstract states instead of grounding all objects, and proves decidability for state-bounded infinite domains via finite abstract RMDPs and probabilistic bisimulation. The paper defines OI-subsumption relational states, grounding semantics, relational pCTL including next and bounded/unbounded until, and a relational Bellman operator whose V and Q rules store probabilities rather than rewards. Logical regression, Q-rule combination, V-rule maximization and three mutually recursive Check/CheckUntil/CheckNext algorithms implement lifted checking, including absorbing goals and state-bound filtering. Theorem 1 proves that an abstract RMDP for a state-bounded infinite model is probabilistically bisimilar for a formula, so checking the finite abstraction is equivalent to checking the infinite MDP. Worked blocks-world regressions and nested formulas expose rule construction. The unoptimized SWI-Prolog prototype checks infinite blocks/box worlds and compares against PRISM/STORM; pCTL-REBEL handles 15 blocks (6.6e13 ground states) under 1800 seconds while PRISM explicit handles 8 and STORM sparse 9, but indefinite-horizon checking grows exponentially and road-map constraints cause runtime explosions.

Finite-domain soundness applies to step-bounded pCTL; the naive epsilon convergence criterion is not sound for unbounded until, though intended as an approximation. Infinite-domain decidability requires a state-bounded MDP and finite formula-relevant constants; an optimal deterministic stationary policy is assumed for infinite abstractions. use_for_goal: A formal pattern for scaling temporal-probabilistic verification through relational abstraction, with an explicit soundness boundary for finite horizons and a bisimulation theorem for state-bounded infinite domains. The regression/rule machinery and measured grounding limits are relevant to TLA+/Verus abstraction design and to reporting where convergence is only approximate.

title: Property-Directed Inference of Universal Invariants or Proving Their Absence
what: Extends IC3/PDR to universal first-order invariants using finite-model diagrams. On termination returns an inductive universal safety invariant, a concrete counterexample, or a proof that no such invariant exists over the chosen vocabulary. Implements the algorithm for linked structures and evaluates verification, deliberate bugs and invariant-expressibility failures. Finite-state models are generalized to existential diagrams specifying every relation/constant and distinct element, so their negations provide universal strengthening clauses. Lemma 1 shows that a diagram implies every closed existential formula true of its model. This makes diagram blocking precise relative to universal inductive invariants. Frames overapproximate bounded reachable states; recursive predecessor blocking, clause propagation and unsatisfiable-core generalization seek a fixed point. If blocking reaches initial states, bounded model checking distinguishes a genuine trace from a spurious diagram trace; Proposition 1 proves the latter excludes every universal safety invariant in the vocabulary. The shared-tail/traverseTwo example demonstrates the universal-submodel preservation obstruction: removing the shared tail from a reachable model creates a bad submodel. Implementation uses EAR reachability logic reduced to EPR, Z3 finite models and auxiliary allocation/input-membership/order predicates for rich specifications. Table 1 compares memory safety to prior human-template PDR shape analysis and also reports stronger functional verification.
numbers: 22 verified correct-program rows (11 singly-linked, 4 sorted singly-linked, 3 doubly-linked, 4 composite structures)
full verification: split 206 s, 8 frames, 1,143 Z3 calls, 36 clauses (19 universal)
full verification: sorted-merge 655 s; insertion-sort 1,934 s, 14 frames, 4,783 calls, 41 clauses (18 universal)
no universal invariant: shared-tail 3.6 s, 2 frames, 42 Z3 calls; comb 2 s, 3 frames, 52 calls
four deliberate bugs: 0.4 / 3 / 5 / 7.5 s; maximum model size 4 in every reported counterexample
prior memory-safety baseline: abstraction failure on concat/merge/sorted-merge/nested-flatten/nested-split and >1-hour timeout on uf-union/insertion-sort/overlaid-delete
assumptions_limits: No termination guarantee. Init, transition and Bad must be representable in the chosen first-order logic; satisfiable queries need finite models. The presentation assumes SAT/model procedures; implementation uses decidable EAR (relational ∃*∀* with restricted deterministic transitive closure, no function symbols), reduced to EPR. More complex control flow is encoded via a program counter. Absence result is limited to universal inductive invariants over the fixed vocabulary, not program incorrectness or impossibility of richer proofs. Auxiliary predicates are used despite no user-supplied abstraction templates. EAR has limited ability to express list segments not pointed to by variables. Benchmarks are small list/data-structure algorithms; four bugs are deliberate. No liveness, distributed-protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+, or LLM evaluation. Timing comparisons to [32] concern memory safety; that baseline’s functional specifications are stated to be weaker, so full-correctness columns are not directly like-for-like.
use_for_goal: Foundational quantified-invariant source for automation in unbounded-state/distributed verification; the explicit no-universal-invariant outcome can distinguish insufficient proof vocabulary from a program bug (reader inference). Actual evaluation is sequential heap analysis. It supplies no verified Rust/Verus, TLA+ model, LLM agent or distributed protocol case; network-program verification is future work.

We require that every satisﬁable formula in L has a ﬁnite model, and assume to have a decision pro- cedure SAT (ψ), which checks if a formula ψ in L is satisﬁable, and a function model (ψ), which returns a finite model σ of ψ if such a model exists and None otherwise.
In this sense, the abstraction based on diagrams is precise for programs with universal invariants.

title: Peregrine: A Tool for the Analysis of Population Protocols.
what: Introduces Peregrine, a web tool for designing, simulating, statistically sampling and parameterized-verifying population protocols. It verifies silent protocols over all infinitely many initial populations using layered termination and Presburger overapproximations, with LoLA confirmation and counterexample replay. The paper defines protocol/configuration/fairness semantics and illustrates majority voting. The UI supports graphical or script descriptions, manual/random simulation with rewind, convergence-speed statistics and JSON export. Verification first proves layered termination (a sufficient condition for silence), then searches an iteratively strengthened Presburger overapproximation for bad initial-to-terminal executions; candidate counterexamples are checked for concrete reachability by LoLA and replayed/exported. It distinguishes ordinary and increased-accuracy consensus classification, where LoLA checks whether a nonterminal consensus can later be broken.

Reachability is approximated, so satisfiable bad formulas require LoLA confirmation and unsatisfiable formulas prove correctness only under the approximation theorem. Fairness abstracts random interactions. Constraint-system size limits current verification to roughly 100 states and a few thousand transitions; arbitrary non-silent protocols and finite-state tools' scalability are outside scope.
use_for_goal: A distributed-computing verification tool with parameterized, fairness-based semantics and explicit counterexample checking; useful precedent for scalable verification beyond fixed population sizes.

title: A Formal Framework for Predicting Distributed System Performance under Faults (Extended Version)
what: Introduces PerF, a Maude framework that composes a distributed-system model with a reusable actor-based fault injector and uses statistical model checking to predict throughput, latency and other metrics under configurable single or combined faults. The paper defines seven fault types (message loss, duplication, delay, tampering, equivocation, node crash, partition) as message-manipulating actors. A scheduler samples normal latency and orders in-flight messages; a priority-aware controller selects eligible behaviors; handlers can modify, duplicate, delay, drop or trigger environment changes. Composition preserves system rules and proves absence of nondeterminism (AND), enabling PVeStA/QuaTEx analysis. Preprocessing labels message-producing rules; transformation adds event monitors for throughput/abort metrics. The six-system study spans 2PC+CTP, Raft, PowerDNS, Cassandra, RAMP/OPW and Fast-HotStuff, and explicitly evaluates mixed equivocation+partition faults.
numbers: Six case studies; model/implementation LoC: 2PC 314/354, Raft 536/1400, PowerDNS 2200/4887, Cassandra 465/1402, RAMP 2523/7977, Fast-HotStuff 304/4247. PVeStA uses 95% confidence and 0.01 error margin on 2.4-GHz quad-core Xeon Emulab machines. Model curves for throughput/latency align closely with deployment evaluations; RAMP shows markedly higher latency than OPW as loss increases; Fast-HotStuff throughput declines with more equivocators and only moderately with combined partition.

assumptions_limits: Maude probabilistic rewrite semantics and absence-of-nondeterminism are required for SMC. Delays come from user-chosen distributions (lognormal, Weibull, exponential), and fault rates/times/targets are configured abstractions. Accuracy is judged by curve trends up to an unknown deployment/model time-scale factor, not absolute values. The framework models faults as message interception, so faults outside message effects or inaccurate distributions are not covered. Experiments use six systems, one deployment per system and 95% confidence/0.01 error; deployment implementations and models differ in size and platform. Dynamic actor/message populations challenge automata-based alternatives but are not claimed solved generally.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for evaluating formal distributed designs quantitatively under faults: modular fault semantics, explicit assumptions about delays/fault priorities, AND preservation for SMC, and deployment-correlated throughput/latency results. Useful for Verus distributed work when distinguishing safety proofs from performance prediction and when specifying fault models.

title: Petri Games: Synthesis of Distributed Systems with Causal Memory
what: Introduces Petri games in which tokens are system/environment players and causal synchronization reveals history; strategies are subprocesses of net unfoldings. Proves decidability and synthesis complexity for bounded games with one environment token. Defines global unfolded strategies: system places must be deterministic while environment places retain all local choices; plays are concurrent runs and strategies must be deadlock-avoiding. For concurrency-preserving nets every global strategy is distributable over one-token local controllers. Introduces mcuts, which maximally progress system places relative to an environment place, and ecuts after environment moves; these summarize knowledge in the unfolding. Reduces deadlock-avoiding synthesis to a finite graph game over decision sets and proves EXPTIME-completeness for bounded one-environment-token games, with exponential strategy construction. Shows unbounded Petri-game synthesis is undecidable.
numbers: Theorem 6.3: bounded Petri games with one environment player and bounded system players are EXPTIME-complete; winning strategy can be constructed in exponential time. Theorem 6.4: unbounded Petri-game winner problem is undecidable. Distribution theorem applies to bounded concurrency-preserving games. No empirical benchmark.
assumptions_limits: Underlying net is a bounded P/T net with an arbitrary bounded number of system tokens and exactly one environment token for the decidability theorem; concurrency-preserving is required for finite distributable strategies. Communication is abstract maximal causal-history exchange rather than concrete message contents. Safety objective is avoidance of designated bad places, and deadlock avoidance rules out vacuous doing-nothing strategies. title: On Invariant Synthesis for Parametric Systems
what: Develops goal-oriented invariant synthesis for transition systems over local theory extensions. Starting from a universal safety formula, Algorithm 2 repeatedly checks inductiveness and strengthens the candidate by eliminating primed and non-parameter symbols with symbol elimination; the paper proves partial correctness and derives termination conditions. title: Plankton: Scalable network configuration verification through model checking
what: Network configuration verifier combining trie-derived packet equivalence classes (PECs), dependency-aware analysis and SPIN exploration of a reduced path-vector protocol (RPVP). RPVP replaces asynchronous message buffers by shared best paths while preserving converged outcomes under stated assumptions. Domain-specific partial-order reduction, policy pruning, failure symmetry and route-entry interning make model checking much faster on evaluated OSPF/BGP/static-routing configurations. Records precise converged-state-only abstraction theorem, consistency-based pruning theorem and proof structure; full fixed-filter/ranking/message assumptions; PEC dependency and correlated-choice limitations; distinction between exact route-entry interning and lossy bitstate hashing; all evaluation setups, full numerical tables and adverse resiliency/memory/ablation cases. Establishes finite configuration/model checking rather than implementation correctness or protocol convergence.

State model/config parser/policy callback/SPIN implementation are trusted. Checks only converged data-plane states, not transient loops, update safety during convergence, absence of oscillation, guaranteed eventual convergence or recovery latency. A configuration with no converged outcome can satisfy a universal converged-state property vacuously. SPVP may diverge on some/all schedules; RPVP deliberately discards divergent/transient behavior. BGP multipath is unsupported; OSPF has a special multipath extension whose theorem details are omitted. Extended SPVP has reliable FIFO buffers per peer, atomic advertisement handling, rib-in per peer and best-path. Origins start with empty path, others no route; ranking is a partial order permitting time-based tie persistence and may change over time for IGP cost. Fixed import/export filters reject with bottom; imports reject forwarding loops and otherwise preserve path; export appends local node and otherwise preserves path. Bottom ranks lowest. Failed sessions discard buffers and deliver route withdrawal. No link-recovery/changing-filter correctness theorem is supplied. Choose node, reset invalid route to bottom, choose best acceptable update nondeterministically among tied best peers. All investigated failures occur before execution and ranking uses its final version. title: SAT Based Bounded Model Checking with Partial Order Semantics for Timed Automata
what: Extends SAT-based bounded reachability checking for timed automata with multisteps that execute pairwise-independent transitions together. It defines synchronous, semi-synchronous and relaxed time-progress semantics, proves all are equivalent to ordinary timed runs, and implements the encodings in POEM with PicoSAT. The paper formalizes read/write independence, Mazurkiewicz equivalence and timed multisteps, proving via bubble-sort and extraction arguments that relaxed sequences can be reordered to normal-time runs and that all three multistep semantics preserve reachability. It gives SAT clauses for transition effects, dependency conflicts, value maintenance and timestamps, and explains how state invariants require local, reset-induced global and final-state checks. Experiments quantify clause/path-length tradeoffs: synchronous is compact, semi-synchronous often shortens paths, and relaxed can shorten paths further at encoding cost.

Independence is syntactic reader-writer nonconflict, so hidden semantic dependencies are outside the model. The method is bounded reachability SAT, not unbounded verification; relaxed invariant coding is complex. POEM experiments use one CPU core and small synthetic protocols; the authors report no observed runtime advantage for relaxed semantics and leave SMT and realistic case studies for future work.

title: POPACheck: A Model Checker for Probabilistic Pushdown Automata
what: POPACheck translates finite-data recursive probabilistic MiniProb programs to probabilistic operator precedence automata and checks LTL plus a stack-aware POTL fragment. A support-chain semi-algorithm distinguishes positive nontermination from positively almost-sure termination using numerical upper bounds and expected-runtime certificates. Separated formula automata avoid determinization; experiments cover nested conditioning, games, branching populations and finite-array randomized search. Explains why numerical approximations alone cannot decide exact probability one, how finite expected time is stronger than almost-sure termination, why conditioned support-chain edges need probability ratios, and how stack-aware properties differ from ordinary trace order. Preserves finite data versus unbounded stack, incomplete decisions, all measured rows, two quantitative timeouts, approximate probabilities, formula/code mismatches and absent cross-tool comparison.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2,4: pOPA is a subclass of probabilistic pushdown automata with finite control states and label-driven stack actions, while its induced Markov chain has unbounded stack configurations. MiniProb integers have a chosen finite bit width and arrays fixed size. Arbitrary chosen width does not mean unbounded integer values in a single model. Recursion/nested query depth can be unbounded; this is not arbitrary unbounded array or concurrent distributed-state verification. §2.1/Definition1: precedence matrix is total over labels; bottom symbol # yields to all program labels, so first move pushes. Push records current state/label, shift changes the top label, pop depends on current and saved state. The extra pop-label condition preserves precedence compatibility. Precedence relations are not assumed reflexive/transitive orders. These restrictions enable synchronized stack-aware formula products; do not replace the model by unrestricted pPDA and assume identical algorithms. §§1–2: observe failure rejects and restarts the current query. obs unwinds only to nearest qry boundary, preserving outer queries, so nested posterior sampling is modeled. A conditioning event of zero probability gives an ill-defined query, not an ordinary normalized posterior. Markov probabilities model specified sampling distributions; no adversarial scheduler or Markov decision-process strategy synthesis is evaluated. §2.2: supported logic is LTL and POTL_fχ, not all POTL. Atomic propositions include program events/function names and finite-variable arithmetic tests. Directional next and chain-future/until operators move through procedure frames. Call-return/postcondition matching can be context-free and beyond LTL. Full formal semantics/proofs are referred to [10,40], not fully redeveloped or mechanized here. §3.1: termination triple probabilities are least nonnegative fixed-point solutions of a monotone nonlinear polynomial system. Nontermination at node c is 1 minus the sum of termination outcomes. Support-chain states include only c with strictly positive nontermination; division by that positive quantity conditions push/shift/support probabilities. Support edges summarize finite nested runs. This chain captures limit behavior with the intended probabilistic construction, not a claim that all time-indexed observations can be erased without the formula-aware machinery. §3.1: upper bounds on termination give lower bounds on nontermination. A positive lower bound includes the node. Otherwise the algorithm tries a stronger certificate: stack symbol popped with probability one in finite expected time (PAST). A valid linear expected-time solution implies almost-sure termination (AST), excluding the node. Failure to prove PAST is inconclusive, not nontermination. AST with infinite expected time can fail this stronger test; no total decision procedure is claimed. §3.1: zero variables are removed through value iteration; decomposed Newton computes lower bounds. Upper bounds either satisfy lower<=v<=lower+epsilon and v>=f(v) in Z3, or come from optimistic value iteration initialized at the lower bound. SCC decomposition solves bottom-up. Exact epsilon, stopping tolerance, rational/floating implementation details and independent certificate validation protocol are not supplied in this tool paper, so printed approximate probabilities are not exact certified decimal values. §3.2: separated Büchi/omega-operator-precedence automata have disjoint languages from distinct starting states, allowing synchronized products without determinization. Qualitative checks analyze product SCCs; quantitative checks solve additional support-probability equations with OVI. Theoretical claims: singly exponential time in formula size, polynomial space in pOPA size for qualitative theory, and EXPSPACE for quantitative model checking, citing [40]. These are not guarantees that the implemented semi-algorithm terminates on every valid input. §4: function parameters pass by value or value-result; actual value-result arguments must be variable identifiers. Boolean operators treat zero as false. Bernoulli(e1,e2) has success probability e1/e2; Uniform(e1,e2) is stated half-open [e1,e2). Distributions need valid parameters; general C/Rust overflow, pointer aliasing and undefined behavior are not analyzed. Fig6 supports while, recursion, query and observe, not arbitrary source-language execution. §5: benchmark has three nested-query programs and 16 distinct Q formulas, yielding 20 program/formula rows, plus Sherwood with four S formulas and varied finite sizes. This is a demonstration suite, not a random production corpus. AMD 8-core 4.5GHz,64GB,Ubuntu24.04; one-hour timeout. No timing variance, independent replay or directly measured PRISM/Storm/PReMo/Pray comparison. PReMo/Pray are excluded because they only compute termination probabilities, which OVI handles below one second here. §5/Table3: all three OVI upper-bound runs are below one second, but Z3 times out on Schelling/Virus. Thus the blanket below-one-second prose concerns the chosen successful method, not every attempted solver. NT equation counts are those with circular dependency after SCC propagation, not all raw equations. Maximum SCC size, total equations and program control-state count measure different costs. §5/Table4: all 20 qualitative queries finish: nine hold almost surely and 11 do not. Of those 11, nine obtain approximate probabilities and Virus Q6/Q7 time out quantitatively; non-AS qualitative result does not give an exact probability or concrete counterexample probability by itself. A probability-one property may still admit measure-zero violating runs; do not equate AS with all-run deterministic correctness. §5/Schelling: two agents cannot communicate but know each other’s preferences perfectly. p controls recursion and its distribution is fixed to make the model AST. This is a sequential probabilistic model of recursive reasoning, not measured LLM behavior or a distributed protocol with message failures. Printed prose misidentifies Q13 as first Bob rejection even though Table1 Q13 mentions Alice and negated rejection; it also calls Q14 first Alice acceptance, while Table1 Q14 is a tic-tac-toe return-coordinate formula. Retain exact table/formula identifiers rather than adopting these prose descriptions. §5/Sherwood: K element bits in1..4 and M array size in1..7 are investigated; Figure10 has timeouts as state space grows, so range is not a universal completed result. Table2 gives seven selected quantitative S3 instances. Uniform divergence is assumed when left>right. Fig1 calls Uniform(left,right), whereas the language definition states exclusive upper endpoint; endpoint semantics must be checked before reusing this as a conventional inclusive-pivot algorithm. No universal all-K/M correctness theorem is proved by these finite experiments. §5/Table1: S1/S2 assert sorted-array partial return correctness for value present/absent. S3/S4 guard left<right and require a downward-compatible next step followed by ordinary eventuality of a recursive call, as ○ᵈ◇(call ∧ B). Prose p116 instead writes left<=right. Table2 probability one when M1 for S3 is consistent with its false strict guard. This is vacuous implication satisfaction, not proof that a singleton input recurses. The reported S1/S2/S4 AS behavior remains model/finite-instance scoped. §6: suggestion that determinization-based methods would not work follows from predicted formula blowup; no direct determinization experiment is reported. Lower-expressivity subclasses and more efficient algorithms are future work. Reusable/Available artifact badges appear on the PDF, but no artifact evaluation report, current build or repository commit was independently checked. No implementation proof, Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM-generated specification/proof experiment.

It illustrates why proof-agent evaluation must distinguish AS, finite expected time, numerical bounds, inconclusive output and timeout. MiniProb’s agents are specified probabilistic procedures, not LLM agents; linking this method to distributed protocols, TLA+ or verified Rust would require an explicit translation and correctness argument.

title: Partial Order Aware Concurrency Sampling
what: Presents POS, a randomized concurrency scheduler that samples partial orders rather than redundant total interleavings.
