title: PoWER Never Corrupts: Tool-Agnostic Verification of Crash Consistency and Corruption Detection
what: PoWER encodes crash consistency as a precondition on each storage write: every durable state introduced by a partial write must be permitted by a ghost permission. Prophecy-based storage views and recovery-equivalent writes simplify proofs. A bounded-bit corruption model and an eight-byte corruption-detecting Boolean support atomic data/checksum updates. CapybaraKV in Verus and CapybaraNS in Dafny demonstrate the method, with coarse concurrent KV variants and performance comparisons. Records exact permission quantification, prophecy flush semantics, state versus transition and blanket versus single-use permissions, all four write strategies and concurrency restrictions. Includes correspondence-proof trust boundaries, CRC corruption bounds, Tick-Tock counterexample and CDB protocol, full type/LOC/startup/resource tables, all workload setups and adverse performance cases. Separates conditional detection from arbitrary-media-error recovery and reported proofs from independent proof replay.
numbers: CapybaraKV 5,531 executable / 14,255 spec+proof / 5,244 trusted lines; CapybaraNS 278 / 673 / 414
verification 54 s single-thread, 23 s eight-thread for KV, 12 s for NS
Table 2 KV total: 5244 trusted, 14255 spec/proof, 5531 implementation lines; notary 414/673/278
assumptions_limits: Core technique requires Hoare pre/postconditions, ghost variables and quantification over crash states. Each asynchronous write requires all chunk-wise old/new durable outcomes to satisfy its permission; executable annotations erase. Soundness depends on every actual storage mutation using the controlled API, correctness of the storage model and a meaningful allowed-recovery predicate. A permission that allows all states proves no useful crash property. Natural storage semantics distinguish readable last-written bytes from outstanding writes. Atomic persistence chunks can survive independently until flush. The prophecy model instead stores read_state and one prophesized durable_state; write updates all readable bytes and chooses a subset of chunk subwrites for durable state. Flush constrains these two states to agree without changing either in the ghost model. This is a logical modeling device, not a runtime ability to predict crash outcomes. The authors report a Verus proof implementing the prophecy model over a natural model using prophecy variables. The PoWER-to-Crash-Hoare-logic proof in Rocq/Perennial is metalogical and trusts a translation of PoWER semantics, since PoWER was not implemented in Rocq. The Verus correspondence to crash invariants is entirely machine-checked within Verus. Formal theorem bodies are in artifacts; this reading examined paper explanations only. Crash states can be specified through rec(bytes), commonly allowing pre-operation or post-operation abstract state. Transition permissions instead authorize pairs of durable states. Blanket permissions cover arbitrary recovery-equivalent transitions; single-use permissions authorize a mutating transition once and are consumed or invalidated. A blanket permission can manufacture single-use permissions only for its allowed transitions. Initial recoverability and all permission constructions remain proof obligations. Tentative writes change only addresses irrelevant to rec and need no value-specific proof. Committing writes are a single aligned atomic chunk, typically after flushing tentative data, so only old/new durable states matter. Recovery writes rely on idempotent recovery that overwrites all possibly torn bytes on retry. In-place writes can use weaker specifications with many allowed outcomes, but the authors have no verified examples or helper-library support for that category. Atomic PoWER adds durable ghost resources owned by atomic invariants, proof callbacks and completion objects for consumed transition permissions. Completions witness an issued/applied operation even if another thread later changes its key. This extension needs concurrency facilities beyond the minimal core features; a tool-agnostic core does not imply arbitrary concurrent proofs in plain sequential Dafny. Concurrency allows multiple readers, or disjoint statically allocated storage regions with exclusive access during writes. It excludes read/write or write/write overlap within one region because callers must know its current logical state. Sharded wrappers establish linearizable individual create/read/update/delete/list operations, not cross-shard transactions. The reusable inner implementation still supplies a transactional API to wrappers. Corruption is modeled by a fixed device bitmask with at most c potentially faulty physical bits. A zero mask bit reads correctly; a marked bit can return either value independently on each read. The trusted CRC axiom distinguishes byte strings at Hamming distance 1 through c. Current ECMA CRC-64 implementation uses c=1 for arbitrary lengths; the cited c=3 for data shorter than about1 GiB is not exploited. Detection is conditional on that device-wide bound, not a guarantee against arbitrary bursts, malicious rewrites, rollback or unbounded media failure. Reader qualification: integrity proofs must cover corrupted data and checksum bytes, repeated/noncontiguous address mappings, and the chosen CDB codeword distance under the same physical-bit bound. The paper reports verified checking and a trusted CRC library; it does not derive an unrestricted cryptographic collision-resistance guarantee. Detecting a mismatch permits reporting corruption, not necessarily repairing damage or preserving availability. Tick-Tock’s old-checksum/new-data mismatch after a crash is not a small-bit corruption event relative to the old data. CRC(D0) can collide with CRC(D1-prime) even if D1-prime differs by only bounded media corruption from D1, because D0 versus D1-prime may differ arbitrarily. The paper gives a logical counterexample to the algorithm in its model, not an independently reproduced NOVA-Fortis artifact exploit. CDB stores one of two known eight-byte values CRC(0) and CRC(1), with aligned crash atomicity and sufficient corruption separation assumed/proved for the primitive. Two data/CRC slots accompany it. Write the inactive slot and checksum, flush, atomically switch CDB, flush. The selector identifies the committed slot independently of potentially matching stale checksums. This costs extra storage and flushes; it does not remove hardware atomicity assumptions. CapybaraKV values contain a fixed-size item and a list of fixed-size elements, with fixed-size keys. The abstract state has on-abort and on-commit maps. Ordinary operations affect the latter; abort restores it from the former; commit publishes it to the former. A crash during commit may commit or abort, while other uncommitted operations abort. Reads within a transaction see tentative operations, so visible results need not already be durable. Implementation uses main/item/list tables, per-field CRCs, validity CDBs, copy-on-write updates and a physical redo journal. Journal commit writes a CRC of pending entries then flips a CDB; replay installs operations and clears the journal. Volatile key index and free lists rebuild on startup. Correctness depends on recovery traversal, bounds, allocation and CRC checks, not merely the commit selector. Capacity is statically allocated at initialization with maximum key/item/list counts and sizes. No dynamic resizing, partial-value updates or range queries. All keys reside in a volatile Rust HashMap and must be indexed again at startup. Designed target is small records on tens of GiB of dedicated PM in a cloud-storage service. Prototype integration into an Azure Rust system is reported, not evidence of production deployment of all verified variants. Trusted pmcopy bridges Verus and compiler-generated representations. It requires repr(C) and derive(PmCopy), implements PmSafe/PmSized/Clone/PartialEq, generates specifications and static layout assertions checked by Rust. PmSafe includes numeric types, bool and char; composites require safe fields. Casts still require correct layout, valid discriminants/values and prior corruption checks. Compiler assertions caught a u128/i128 layout change; this is a concrete consistency check, not a proof of the macro or compiler. CapybaraNS stores a 64-bit logical timestamp and last hash. Advance increments and atomically persists them using CDB; Sign signs their binding. A trusted C# wrapper supplies CRCs, cryptography and serialization. This paper does not supply a complete distributed-notary protocol, a cryptographic implementation proof, remote attestation argument or availability theorem. Counter overflow handling and full security assumptions require the external specification. PM model permits independent eight-byte chunk reorderings until flush; backend write uses PMDK non-temporal stores or mov followed by clflushopt/clwb, and flush uses sfence. It deliberately overapproximates strongly ordered clflush and same-cache-line hardware ordering, including potential compiler reorderings. Eight-byte alignment/atomicity, backend calls and hardware behavior remain trusted. PoWER can use other models; current model is not a universal storage-device specification. Table 2 counts unverified pmcopy source but not its generated code. KV trusted count includes mock byte-vector PM plus Windows/Linux backends, concurrency and sharding wrappers. Trusted versus proved LOC therefore should not be interpreted as executable core size alone. Reported proof/code ratios are2.6 KV and2.4 NS; LOC is not a measure of specification adequacy. KV design, implementation and verification took about1.5 years by a team of experts and newcomers; headcount and person-time are unspecified. After that experience, porting the PM spec to Dafny took under an hour, porting helper lemmas about an hour, and implementing/verifying NS about nine hours after its spec and C# wrapper were already written. This is author experience, not a controlled productivity comparison. On Linux6.9.3 with i7-11850H eight physical cores and32 GB RAM, KV verifies in54s with one thread or23s with eight; NS takes12s with one. Appendix expects KV1–2min serial or15–40s parallel on other hardware. Paper gives no independent proof replay in this reading and no controlled comparison against alternative verification approaches. Performance setup is a two-socket32-core machine with128 GB RAM and one128 GB Optane DC PMM, Debian Trixie/Linux6.12.10. All KV runs use the sharded variant with one shard per thread. Redis client/server run together but retain communication overhead; RocksDB uses memory-mapped files and non-temporal log appends; Viper preallocates enough capacity except in utilization measurement. Different supported features and durability architectures affect comparison. Microbenchmarks use25M records,64-byte keys,1 KiB values and8-byte list elements. Append adds16 elements per record in random order; read-list returns the entire list; trim removes it. Other operations run once per record. Figure2 uses logarithmic latency axes and95% confidence intervals. KV matches or beats RocksDB but Viper is faster on several operations, including most writes; Redis is slowest. Windows/Azure20 GiB battery-backed DRAM tests run only KV, with up to2× improvement; other systems lack Windows support. YCSB uses15M keys,24-byte keys,1140-byte values and five executions per system. RunE range queries are omitted and RunA/RunB partial updates become full-value updates. X is uniform75% updates,5% read-modify-write and20% reads; Y/Z use50/50 or5/95 read/update with90% accesses to10% records. LoadE is omitted only from Figure4 as similar to LoadA. These modified workloads must not be called an unmodified full YCSB suite. At one thread KV is broadly comparable to Viper and often slightly slower. At16 threads it substantially leads Viper on update/read-heavy run phases but not every load phase; the broad prose claim of outperforming other systems needs this figure-level qualification. Viper is tested on one non-interleaved NVDIMM despite optimizations for interleaved PM. Authors attribute scaling issues partly to CCEH semaphore costs nearly doubling1→16 threads. Hash sharding distributes hot keys across shards, so this does not demonstrate performance under all accesses contending on one shard. Full-instance startup fills each store to its own out-of-space point with64-byte keys/1 KiB values; capacities and record counts can therefore differ. title: Context-Bounded Model Checking for POWER
venue: Logical Methods in Computer Science (preprint arXiv:1702.01655)
what: Defines a POWER-specific context bound and a polynomial code-to-code translation from K-bounded POWER executions to K-bounded sequential-consistency executions, then implements the reduction in Power2SC over CBMC. The paper gives an operational POWER semantics with fetch, initialize, commit and propagation events, dependency and coherence predicates, and extensions for address operators plus sync/lwsync/isync. The translation uses nondeterministically guessed initialization/commit/propagation contexts and timestamps, per-process/variable summaries, and a verifier process that checks summaries at context boundaries. Theorem 6.1 establishes a reachability equivalence for complete K-bounded runs; examples show POWER outcomes impossible under SC, including message passing and sync/lwsync behavior. Experiments cover 913 litmus tests and 24 C/Pthreads benchmarks, plus scaling with loop and context bounds.

assumptions_limits: Analysis is an under-approximation parameterized by K contexts; it does not bound context length or storage size, so a missed bug remains possible when K is too small. The finite-data decidability consequence relies on finite data, and the backend must support nondeterministic data choices. The grammar initially omits load-reserve/store-conditional (CAS) instructions; ARM and C11 extensions are future work. CBMC experiments unroll loops and use 1800-second timeouts, and safe results mean safety only within the chosen context bound.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal verification of concurrent/distributed behavior: it reduces weak-memory executions to an SC checker while making the finite context bound and under-approximation explicit. The guessed summaries and exact reachability theorem are useful design precedents for verifying low-level distributed implementations, but POWER-specific assumptions and bounded coverage limit transfer.

title: Probabilistic Model Checking on Propositional Projection Temporal Logic
what: Defines a probabilistic model-checking procedure for infinite linear-time Propositional Projection Temporal Logic (PPTL) over discrete-time Markov chains by constructing an infinite-path normal-form graph, adding Rabin acceptance, determinizing it, and taking a product with the chain. The paper gives PPTL syntax and interval semantics, distinguishes finite and infinite normal-form paths, and removes finite paths to form NFG_inf. Its construction algorithm records self-loops and paired Rabin sets to exclude infinite repetition of strong chop; a Safra-style tree algorithm determinizes NFG_inf while merging equivalent PPTL formulas. The product construction labels accepting bottom strongly connected components and reduces formula probability to reachability of accepting BSCCs. A worked p;q chain yields an almost-sure result, illustrating the complete pipeline.

title: A Practical Verification Framework for Preemptive OS Kernels
short_name: Practical verification framework for preemptive OS kernels
what: Presents a Coq-mechanized framework that models preemptive-kernel API correctness as contextual refinement from a practical C subset, with abstract specifications, concrete interrupt-aware semantics, a relational concurrent separation logic, and proof tactics. It verifies scheduler, timer interrupt, synchronization APIs and priority-inversion freedom in commercial μC/OS-II. The framework separates application state from kernel state, gives small-step sequentially consistent semantics for task continuations and x86-8259A interrupt state, and uses a high-level language with nondeterministic/configurable scheduler relation. Relational assertions connect concrete memory, abstract state and remaining abstract command; ownership-transfer invariants account for nested interrupt levels. A soundness theorem is proved by compositional simulation. PIF is stated using original task priorities and proved for a simplified μC/OS-II mutex under no nested mutex use; verification required minor defensive changes because contextual refinement quantifies over arbitrary clients.

title: Practical verification of decision-making in agent-based autonomous systems
kind: compositional program model checking of autonomous-agent decision code
what: Verifies actual Gwendolen belief-desire-intention decision code with AJPF, while abstracting continuous control and the external world into nondeterministic percepts and messages. Properties describe beliefs, goals, intentions and actions. Separate environmental hypotheses and control theorems can be combined deductively with these local results to obtain conditional whole-system claims. The property specification language gives temporal operators over belief, goal, action, intention and percept modalities. The method derives possible incoming shared beliefs by inspecting the abstraction-engine code, then explores their combinations instead of simulating a particular physical environment. Search-and-rescue examples distinguish finding a human from believing one was found, and prove a searcher/lifter result under explicit sensor, motion and message-delivery hypotheses using Logics Workbench. The satellite implementation separates reasoning R, abstraction A, continuous planning Ω and physical control Π; the authors verify R and report extra failure/abort plans discovered necessary during verification. Cruise-control agents add speed-limit goals and UK lane rules while retaining the discrete safety constraints previously proved in KeYmaera. Appendices explain abstraction and reasoning code, leader position assignment, cruise-control sensor translation and the propositional encoding used for deduction.

title: PRALINE: A Tool for Computing Nash Equilibria in Concurrent Games.
what: Presents PRALINE, a prototype synthesizing pure Nash-equilibrium strategy profiles for finite concurrent graph games with state-based integer limsup payoffs. Reduces unilateral-deviation prevention to winning a two-player suspect game with a co-Buchi objective, outputs on-equilibrium shapes and full strategy automata, and lets users challenge the solution interactively. Seven wireless medium-access/power-control instances report equilibrium counts and runtimes, exposing limited explicit-state scaling. Explains how hidden actions require sets of possible deviators, how suspects are retained/eliminated following a successor chosen against a recommended joint action, and why a finite on-path shape is insufficient to specify punishment after deviations. Gives a concrete profitable-looking deviation defeated by a later action, a125-edge strategy for a nine-state arena, a payoff-dominance coverage guarantee, and all benchmark rows. Distinguishes construction from interactive illustration and prior theoretical correctness.
assumptions_limits: Finite concurrent arena: at each step each player independently chooses a legal action and the joint move deterministically selects a successor. Players observe the complete sequence of states, not other players’ actions. Strategies can depend on observed history; no memoryless-only restriction is stated. Any number of players is allowed by the model, but explicit graph size may already encode exponentially many joint actions. Each player has an integer payoff per state and maximizes limsup along an infinite play. On a finite arena this is the largest payoff recurring infinitely often; finite transient rewards do not determine the outcome. Boolean0/1 state payoffs recover Buchi objectives. This is not general mean-payoff, discounted reward, stochastic game synthesis or a fairness/service guarantee. Synthesizes pure strategies. Nash equilibrium excludes profitable unilateral deviations while all other complete strategies stay fixed, including their reactions after a changed history. It does not ensure coalition resistance, subgame perfection or credible punishments at every off-path history. Paper states resistance to randomized deviations, but construction does not synthesize randomized equilibrium profiles. Paper states that randomized-equilibrium existence with a specified payoff is undecidable and cites[12], titled The complexity of Nash equilibria in limit-average games. The chapter does not supply the reduction or precise scope needed to transfer that statement to its integer-limsup setting; cited work was not read here. Preserve this as an attributed statement, not an independently verified limsup theorem. Guarantee stated: for every attainable pure-equilibrium payoff vector v, at least one returned equilibrium has componentwise payoff>=v. This does not mean every strategy profile is enumerated, every exact payoff vector is returned, or all returned profiles are Pareto-undominated. The meaning of Solutions in Table1 is reported tool outputs, not a count of all mathematical equilibria. Suspect game positions track original state and remaining possible unilateral deviators. Eve recommends a legal joint move; Adam chooses a successor. If the prescribed successor occurs, suspects remain; otherwise retain only players able to induce it by changing their own action alone. Ultimately suspected players must obtain at most their target payoffs. Empty suspects make unilateral-deviation checking vacuous; arbitrary coalition deviations are not checked. For target vector v, cited equivalence requires both an Eve winning strategy preventing any ultimate suspect improving and an obedient outcome with exactly v. Prevention alone does not establish that a chosen target is realized. The chapter gives no formal pseudocode, full correctness proof, payoff search procedure, or transformation-size bound; those are imported from[2,3]. Polynomial-time result is explicitly attributed to the specialized algorithm for these preferences and a co-Buchi game. Generic suspect subsets suggest a potentially exponential construction in player count; the chapter does not explain the specialization resolving this. Do not infer polynomiality in a succinct source program, arbitrary objective, or unbounded numerical state domain. Benchmark discussion says up to quadratically many subgames with quadratic winning-region computation, but gives no precise overall asymptotic formula including all representation parameters. Input programs generate explicit arenas from variable valuations, legal-action clauses and updates. Fig.1 is only part of medium_access.game: declarations, initial values, payoff clauses and general multiuser model are not supplied in full. Finite state bounds are essential to finite graph solving; arbitrary programs with unbounded variables are outside the described finite implementation. Power-control payoff R/pow_i * (1-exp(-0.5*gamma_i))^L is real-valued, while tool model requires integer state payoffs. The paper does not state numerical R,L, the precise interference/noise model for gamma_i, integer rounding, or the convention at pow_i=0 where the displayed expression divides by zero. Numerical payoffs110/131/94 illustrate a supplied instance rather than a reproducible model derived solely from chapter parameters. Interactive playing against Eve can explain a deterrent, but finite sampled interactions do not independently prove all-history equilibrium. Full returned automata contain off-path actions absent from the equilibrium shape. No verified compiler, machine-checked correctness certificate, independent equilibrium checker, or artifact replay is reported in the chapter. Timing machine is Intel Core2 Duo2.8GHz with4GB RAM. Seven rows vary players, emission levels or initial energy; no repetitions/error bars, timeouts, software versions, operating system, memory profile, baseline, or end-to-end wireless implementation measurement. Prototype is described as effective to about100states, but table contains completed216/729/1360state instances at much larger runtimes. That prose is not a hard supported-size limit. 2013 novelty and comparison claims are historical author claims: PRISM-games is said to check a given equilibrium and handle random games but not generate equilibria. Current PRISM-games capabilities were not checked. Original artifact URL http://www.lsv.ens-cachan.fr/Software/praline/ is supplied but not fetched or run. Relevance is rational-agent distributed protocol modeling and verifying synthesized history-dependent strategies against unilateral deviations. Wireless/network cases are finite abstractions, not verified distributed implementations. No Verus/verified Rust, TLA+, LLM specification/proof agents, or automated proof-agent evaluation. Symbolic implementation is proposed future work.
use_for_goal: Provides a concrete finite-game model for selfish distributed participants and a history-dependent synthesis/checking distinction. Suspect sets account for hidden actions; limsup semantics require checking infinite punishment behavior rather than finite transient reward. No direct Verus/Rust/TLA+ or LLM proof contribution.

title: Checking Qualitative Liveness Properties of Replicated Systems with Stochastic Scheduling.
what: Develops Presburger stage graphs for sound and complete verification of stable-termination/liveness properties of replicated systems with an unknown number of indistinguishable agents and stochastic scheduling. A stage graph is a finite DAG of inductive Presburger configuration sets with ranking certificates. The authors give a decidability/completeness result, an incomplete practical constructor using Z3, well-quasi-order and Petri-net techniques, and evaluate it on population protocols, leader election and mutual exclusion. The paper formalizes replicated systems as 1-conservative Petri/VAS-style multiset rewriting and assumes a scheduler whose transition probabilities depend only on the current configuration and are nonzero for every enabled transition. Proposition 2 characterizes fair-run progress by ranking certificates; Proposition 3 and Theorem 2 establish stage-graph soundness/completeness, while Theorem 3 reduces candidate checking to Presburger satisfiability. Algorithm 1 starts from a potential-reachability overapproximation, computes eventually dead transitions (linear ranking or layer functions), and splits stages when needed. Exact dead-state sets are computable via backward reachability but can be doubly exponential; the practical procedure is incomplete. Z3 experiments build mostly chains of at most three stages (five for approximate majority), verify infinite families of protocols, and produce independently checkable invariant/ranking certificates.

title: PRESTO: Predicting System-level Disruptions through Parametric Model Checking
what: Introduces PRESTO, a MAPE-K analysis workflow that forecasts trends in monitored system/environment parameters and evaluates predicted requirement violations by re-evaluating parametric model-checking expressions for a pDTMC. title: PRISM-games 3.0: Stochastic Game Verification with Concurrency, Equilibria and Time.
what: Describes PRISM-games 3.0, adding concurrent stochastic games (CSGs), social-welfare-optimal Nash-equilibrium properties and turn-based probabilistic timed games. The release extends model/property languages, value-iteration and game-solving engines, and strategy synthesis, with security, networking, robot and scheduling case studies. CSG models associate players with modules whose actions are chosen simultaneously; joint labels and joint probability distributions express interference and rewards. rPATL gains instantaneous rewards and coalition syntax for zero-sum and equilibria objectives. what: Introduces proof-based coverage: translate a C program with an assertion to SSA and an SMT formula, extract an unsatisfiable core proving the assertion, and map core constraints back to source statements. Defines Trace(P) and Proof(P), line coverage LC(P)=|Trace(P)|/|N(P)| and proof line coverage PrLC(P,T)=|Proof(P)|/|N(P)|. The prototype translates a restricted loop-free C subset to SSA/SMT and marks a minimal unsat core. The paper adds non-trace conditions using undefined-variable metadata, states Lemma 1 and Theorem 1 that proof statements share one execution trace, and derives PrLC≤LC. A Siemens TCAS experiment found lines repeatedly execution-covered but never proof-covered; replacing the relevant if with result=0 left all tests outputs unchanged.

title: Proof Pearl: Playing with the Tower of Hanoi Formally
what: Coq/SSReflect formalization of Hanoi variants, including uniqueness and optimality for three-peg regular perfect-state transfers, optimal arbitrary-state strategies for three pegs, and Frame–Stewart optimality between perfect states for four-peg regular and outer-to-outer star puzzles. Four-peg proofs reconstruct technical mathematical lower bounds rather than merely verify a recursive solution. Records finite-function state encoding, peg-relation-parametric legal moves, projection with adjacent-repeat deletion, equality-sensitive minimality induction, greedy counterexample and linear variant, triangular-number valuation for four regular pegs, 2^i3^j sequence and alternating multi-state penalty invariant for four-star pegs. Distinguishes puzzle variant and endpoint scopes, stated optimality from generated legal paths, proof effort and printed formula/side-condition errors.
assumptions_limits: §2, pp.3–6: n differently sized disks are finite ordinals 0..n−1, smaller number means smaller disk; k pegs are finite ordinals. A configuration is a finite function from each disk to its peg, uniquely inducing sorted stacks. Thus every encoded state is stack-legal; on_top checks no smaller disk on that peg. Finite-function equality/extensionality comes from the finite representation, not an assumed axiom for arbitrary Coq functions. §2, pp.3–7: auxiliary-peg selector is symmetric but guaranteed different from both pegs only for at least three pegs. General move requires one chosen disk on top before and after, an allowed peg relation and all other disks unchanged. If the relation is reflexive, unchanged states may qualify; regular/linear/star relations are irreflexive. This is a discrete sequential graph, with no simultaneous moves. §2, pp.6–7: regular relation allows every distinct pair; linear relation allows consecutive ordinal pegs; star relation requires distinct pegs and at least one equal zero, so zero is center. Three-peg linear/star graphs are isomorphic after relabelling, not equal under the displayed labels (linear center 1 versus star center 0). Endpoint role matters for distances. §2–2.1, pp.5–8: transforms remove/add largest disks, split/merge size ranges, or restrict arbitrary disks/pegs. Projecting a legal path can produce identical adjacent states when a removed disk moves, so rm_rep deletes adjacent repetitions before applying the smaller-puzzle path theorem. It need not delete all repeated states or establish shortestness. §2.1, pp.7–8: distance is least length of a connecting path in a finite state graph; gpath combines path legality, endpoint and size equal to distance. Paper does not spell out its convention for disconnected arbitrary relations. Uses in the Hanoi results have connected move graphs; an unconditional metric theorem for every arbitrary peg relation should not be inferred. §3.1, pp.8–9: recursive perfect-state transfer has 2^n−1 configurations after the starting state, and is a legal path when source differs from destination. Equality-sensitive comparison proves every such transfer path is at least this length and equals it iff it is the generated path. Double induction on disks and path length handles the largest disk moving once, twice or returning. Uniqueness applies to these regular perfect endpoints, not all shortest paths in all variants. §3.1, p.10: in regular three-peg arbitrary-state transfer, a greedy largest-disk destination move may be suboptimal. Greedy is optimal if one endpoint is perfect; for two arbitrary endpoints compare one- and two-jump strategies for the largest disk whose location differs, leaving larger disks fixed. The paper describes these formalized results but does not print all algorithm/optimality proofs. §3.2, pp.10–11: for linear three pegs, greedy is optimal. Distinct adjacent perfect pegs have distance (3^n−1)/2; the two outer pegs have 3^n−1; identical endpoints have zero. With 3^n states, a shortest outer transfer visits every configuration exactly once. This is a state-graph result, not a measured search benchmark. §4.1, pp.11–12: Frame–Stewart parks top m<n disks using four pegs, transfers remaining n−m using three while avoiding the occupied peg, then retrieves m. Choose m minimizing 2T4(m)+T3(n−m). The generic k-peg recurrence yields an algorithm; its optimality for arbitrary k is stated open at publication. This paper proves four-peg regular and four-peg star scopes only. §4.2, pp.12–13: regular four-peg optimal perfect-transfer cost Phi(n) is the prefix sum of 2^(triangular_root i), and satisfies the Frame–Stewart recurrence with 2^(n−m)−1. The proof uses a valuation Psi of an arbitrary disk set E, defined through a max over L with capped triangular-root exponents. If v uses only two pegs avoiding p0, then Psi of disks on p0 in u bounds d(u,v) below. Distinct p0,p2,p3 and the codomain restriction are essential. §4.2, p.13: strong induction follows first/last visits of the largest disk and a selected disk T through a geodesic, splits at critical configurations and modifies/project paths to fit the induction hypothesis. Combined with the generated upper bound, this yields exact Phi(n) for distinct perfect endpoints. The 1000-line proof formalizes a six-page main argument, with most details referred to Bousch rather than reproduced. §5, pp.13–15: star theorem concerns two different outer pegs. Transfer parks small disks on the third outer peg, uses a three-peg outer-to-outer linear transfer for the rest, then retrieves. Cost is 2S1(n), where S1 sums increasing distinct numbers 2^i3^j starting at 1. Its recurrence contains (3^(n−m)−1)/2; doubled cost satisfies the star Frame–Stewart recurrence. §5, p.14: lower bound generalizes from two endpoints to l+1 configurations, with intermediate codomains alternating between pairs of outer pegs. Sl(n) and its differences alpha_l plus endpoint penalty beta support induction on n and splitting into alternating subpaths. Convexity in n and concavity in l combine lower bounds. At l=1 and perfect outer endpoints penalties vanish, matching the algorithm upper bound. §5–6, pp.15–16: star main argument spans about 3500 Coq script lines versus 15 informal pages, organized into three sublemmas and a without-loss-of-generality step. Proofs use little automation and natural numbers. Replacing subtraction inequalities with addition needs the source proof’s bounds; truncated natural subtraction is not ordinary integer subtraction. §6, pp.15–16: evaluation is formal theorem reconstruction, counterexamples and proof-size descriptions. No implementation runtime, hardware, proof-check time, total LOC, finite test campaign or independent artifact replay is reported. Claimed mechanical checking and historical flawed general proof are author reports; the cited original papers/source were not independently read here.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: suitable proof-agent evaluation for legal versus optimal traces, invariants stronger than the final theorem, finite-state encodings with intrinsic legality, projection that removes stuttering, and variant-dependent shortest paths. Natural arithmetic and printed missing guards give concrete specification checks. Technical four-peg lower bounds test inductive reasoning beyond elementary recursion. Sequential Coq puzzles, without a distributed protocol, Verus/Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment.

title: Proof Pearl: Purely Functional, Simple and Efficient Priority Search Trees and Applications to Prim and Dijkstra
what: Verifies a purely functional priority map with decrease-key by augmenting balanced search-tree nodes with subtree minimum bindings. Uses it to refine Prim’s minimum-spanning-tree algorithm and Dijkstra’s distance algorithm down to executable red-black-tree implementations in Isabelle/HOL. Main contribution is functional data-structure simplicity plus end-to-end abstract-to-concrete correctness, rather than a new distributed protocol or measured benchmark. Records getmin’s nonempty-map contract, annotation membership/minimality invariant, hybrid undirected-edge model, adjacency/parser contracts, root-component MST semantics, exceptional first-iteration refinement, update-before-removal proof choice, five queue/predecessor invariant clauses, deterministic ADT instantiation and Dijkstra distance-only coupling. Separates informal asymptotic efficiency from verified functional correctness and supplies concrete boundary/pseudocode/precondition cases.
assumptions_limits: §§3.1–3.2, pp.2–3: priorities and keys are linearly ordered. Priority map is keyed uniquely, with update replacing a binding and subsuming decrease-key. getmin only promises a present binding of minimal priority when representation invariant holds and map is nonempty; ties can be arbitrary and implementation-specific. It returns the minimum pair; removal is a separate delete operation. §3.2, p.3: augmented node stores ordinary key/priority binding, balancing information and a cached minimum pair. invpst requires cached pair belong to that subtree and have minimum priority, recursively. Smart constructor recomputes min from node binding and child caches. Transform every constructor occurrence, including balancing rotations; carrying stale annotations through a structural change is not enough. §3.2, p.3: replacing each constructor with constant-size comparison work preserves underlying search-tree asymptotic operation costs under usual unit-cost comparison/constructor assumptions. Balanced red-black update/delete/lookup are described as logarithmic; root cached getmin is constant time. No mechanized cost semantics, whole-algorithm complexity theorem, benchmark timings or code/proof line counts are supplied. §4, pp.4–5: undirected graph type contains finite vertex set, symmetric irreflexive relation, and endpoints in vertex set. This models simple graphs, not parallel edges. Directed pairs support existing relation/path lemmas; doubleton {u,v} identifies opposite orientations for edge equality/weight summation. Natural-number weights are nonnegative and unbounded mathematically; claimed generalization beyond naturals is not proved in paper. §4, pp.4–5: constructor takes symmetric closure, drops self-loops and adds endpoint nodes; empty path allows u=v even outside explicit node set. Connectedness quantifies graph nodes, and tree is connected/cycle-free. Their simple path forbids repeated undirected edges, a trail convention rather than necessarily distinct vertices. Weight counts each undirected edge once via the doubleton image. §4.2, p.6: graph ADT gives adjacency list, empty and insertion of a fresh nonloop edge; adjacency order and duplicate occurrences are unspecified, but set of entries must match graph edges and weights. Non-node adjacency is empty. Empty weight function is fixed zero for determinism. Graph invariant and abstraction functions mediate every operation, avoiding direct data-structure inspection. §4.3, p.7: foldr parser accepts only lists with no loops and no repeated undirected edge, including opposite-direction duplicates. It then preserves exactly endpoints, symmetric edges and weights. Edge-list input cannot name unrelated isolated vertices; the selected root/reachable-component construction is separate. No hostile text parser or machine-integer conversion is verified here. §§5.1–5.2, pp.7–9: fix root r in graph for the main development and work on its reachable component rg, avoiding whole-input connectedness precondition. Generic safe-edge argument maintains A as subset of an MST. Prim additionally maintains paths from every selected edge endpoint back to root; adding a minimum cut edge preserves invariant and decreases number of unreached component vertices. §5.3/Definition1, pp.9–11: abstract queue maps vertices to enat, with infinity meaning absent. Predecessor edges whose source has infinite queue value encode the completed tree. Queue stores frontier vertices only after special initialization. Continued invariant states MST subset/root reachability, root has no predecessor and is absent, every cut’s outside endpoint is queued, every predecessor is a real component edge into selected vertices, and every queued finite weight matches its predecessor and is minimum among its crossing edges. §5.3, p.10: initial queue contains only root at zero, so it does not refine the abstract already-rooted tree state through the usual continued invariant. Disjunctive initial/continued invariant plus piecewise variant handles this first iteration. Updating neighbors before deleting chosen vertex lets inner proof use original loop invariant; reversing order would need an intermediate-state assertion. §5.4, p.11: foreach is foldr over adjacency entries. Update checks vertex not root, not already finished via queue/predecessor status, and strictly improved weight. Partial-list generalization enables induction; repeat adjacency entries are harmless under valid invariant. Displayed equality omits an explicit invariant antecedent and is not sound for arbitrary malformed Q/pi states; concrete case below. §§5.5–5.6, pp.12–14: abstract choices intentionally remain relational proof obligations rather than deterministic HOL code; tie breaking/order is fixed only by concrete ADTs. Locale-parametric implementation assumes graph/map/priority-map contracts, then instantiates all maps as red-black trees and graph as node-to-adjacency-list tree. While correctness uses invariant plus well-founded decreasing variant. Isabelle code generator targets SML/OCaml/Haskell/Scala; generated compiler/runtime behavior was not independently validated here. §§6.1–6.2, pp.15–16: directed graph is weight function V×V→enat, edge iff finite weight; finiteness is a separate assumption, not in graph type. Dijkstra returns distances, not paths or predecessors. Abstract D gives upper bounds, exact values on finished S, and relaxation bounds via finished vertices. Refined disjoint maps Q(frontier)/V(finished) combine into D, with S=dom V; nonnegative natural weights justify finalizing minimum estimate. §5.7/§7, pp.14/17: authors claim first verified executable Prim with efficient data structures; earlier work comparisons and novelty are author assessments, not independently surveyed here. They explicitly expect manual obligation generation against informal abstract sketches to scale poorly and point to Isabelle Refinement Framework. AFP artifacts are linked but unbuilt; no distributed communication/failure model or LLM-generated proof evaluation.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: useful template for verifying reusable maps/priority queues and sequential graph kernels inside distributed software. It shows explicit representation invariants, interface boundaries, root-component specifications, nondeterministic-to-deterministic refinement, termination and executable-code endpoints. Concrete initialization/update/precondition cases are valuable when evaluating LLM-generated specifications/proofs: a proof about an abstract sketch must be linked to actual data structures and intended evaluation order. This verifies sequential functional algorithms, not a distributed MST protocol, Verus/verified Rust or TLA+ system; functional correctness and runtime complexity evidence remain separate.

title: ProofAug: Efficient Neural Theorem Proving via Fine-grained Proof Structure Analysis
what: Postprocesses whole-proof LLM proposals by retaining a compatible hierarchy of proof blocks, replacing failures with temporary admissions, filling holes with Isabelle automation, and collapsing enclosing blocks when automation fails. Optional efficient recursive proving requests completions at failed original conjectures. Reports miniF2F improvements with fixed deepseek-math-7b-base, multiple prompting strategies and changed benchmark statements, plus a small Lean implementation. Exact printed pseudocode omits proof-replacement and rollback-state updates; implementation results remain author reports. Records observable-state equality, maximal compatible semi-proof procedure, finite-time ATP fallback, original-conjecture-only ERP tree, query-versus-verifier accounting, prompt and context details, all mixed-strategy rows, benchmark subtraction/typo curation and author rechecking limitations. Concrete printed Algorithm2 trace exposes retained sorry admissions and uninitialized rollback states; distinguishes these presentation findings from the unchecked code/results.
assumptions_limits: §§2.1–2.2, pp3–5: ITP modeled by parsed transitions and state; completion initially defined by finish=True. Actual equality compares only displayed proof-state string, mode, available facts, error and finish. Equality of these observations is not proved equivalent to full kernel/proof-object equality. An admission-free final check is needed because sorry closes a goal without constructing its proof. §3.1 Algorithm1,p5: maximal compatible semi-proof preserves exact original steps outside replaced by/proof...qed blocks. Execute proposal; on error in proof(prove), replace step by sorry and retry; otherwise collapse innermost block, restore recorded pre-block state; error outside any block returns Null. Blocks and parsing depend on Isar syntax; no correctness, uniqueness or completeness theorem for MCSP is proved. §3.2 Algorithm2,p6: try builtin heuristics/Sledgehammer at holes. Failure collapses enclosing block and retries at coarser granularity, eventually the theorem alone. This searches retained structural choices without retraining the model. Finite-time failure of these particular tactics does not establish that the intermediate goal is mathematically unprovable or that no compatible proof exists. §3.3,pp6–7: optional ERP requests completion with theorem/informal draft, already accepted prefix and goal state when ATP first fails. If raw completion fails, replace failed tactics by ATP and retry; compare resulting observable state with the sorry-generated next state. Only failed conjectures of original MCSP generate new nodes; descendants precede ancestors, otherwise earlier blocks first. This is a restricted completion search, not an unrestricted recursive repair of all new subgoals. §4.1/AppendixH,pp7/16/18: Isabelle DSP-version miniF2F-test has244 statements and accompanying informal drafts. Authors identify wrong statements and later use curated variant with typo changes and nat-to-int changes for subtraction. Different formal propositions can produce different success rates; curated66.0% cannot be read as improvement on identical original statements. Only still-unproved cases are rerun on curated data. Existing FAIR upstream also fixes some errors; paper points to PR18. §4.2,pp7–8: Isabelle2022/PISA; model deepseek-math-7b-base on RTX3090/vLLM;12PISAinstances on XeonGold6326@2.90GHz; proof-step timeout10s/Sledgehammer120s. Temperature0.6,top-p0.95,response cap2048 or4096−prompt tokens if prompt>2048. Few-shot examples randomly sampled; authors write full proofs matching informal demonstrations, default1shot. Zero-shot means no demonstrations and can still include informal statement/draft. §4.2/AppendixD,pp7/14: heuristic list plus Sledgehammer; paper calls it8methods but displayed list repeats auto and has more entries. Added mod_simps; remove force,presburger,linarith versus DSP. Sledgehammer candidatesCVC4,vampire,verit,e,spass,z3,zipperposition;30seach/120stotal. Author reports DSP code usedcvc5 and about35stotal, and fixes this. No AFP/AoFcompiled library due to disk space for12instances, so no Symmetric_Polynomials.Vieta import. These changes affect baseline comparisons. §4.2/AppendixD,pp8/14: checked semi-proofs cached across samples to avoid re-verifying; authors acknowledge caching can reduce success because ATP outcomes vary. CPU and timeout nondeterminism affect reproducibility. Authors say obtained proofs reverified and supplied, while some reconstructed smt/metis proofs time out. No independent replay, admission/axiom audit, or per-proof replay-success count was performed for this record. §§4.3–4.5,pp8–9: same-setting DSP baseline is strongest local comparison, but prompting content also changes from sketches to full proofs. Query budget counts model requests; it does not measure tokens, ATP calls, repeated proof checking, elapsed CPU/GPUtime or total cost. Cross-paper16384versus1400comparisons also change models, training and environments; they do not isolate an efficiency factor. Figure3 also compares augmentation on/off within DSP,full-proof and zero-shot prompting families and shows gains in each, providing controlled evidence beyond the combined prompt-and-method headline comparison. §4.5/AppendicesE–F,pp9/15/17: authors explore multiple prompt recipes and report union of successes. Three few-shot sets and two zero-shot instructions differ; draft-off excludes both informal statement and proof. A mixed cumulative rate is a portfolio outcome, not performance of one fixed recipe selected without seeing test outcomes. No confidence intervals or controlled total-compute comparison reported. AppendixC,pp13–14: Lean version uses block indentation/context inference with Aesop,omega and hand heuristic try norm_num[*];try field_simp[*]at*;try ring_nf at*;try nlinarith. Kimina-Prover-Preview-Distill-1.5B pass@1reported44.3→50.4%onminiF2F-test. Detailed Lean version/hardware/sampling controls are not supplied in this appendix. Extension to other procedural systems via declarative wrappers/training is a proposal, not evaluated across all ITPs. AppendixA/§5,pp9/12–13: related-work distinctions include bottom-up structural repair versus top-down POETRY/LEGO, Coq PALM backtracking, retrieval/premise automation and expert iteration. Claims that top-down prompting hurts intrinsic model ability are author explanations rather than a separately controlled causal experiment. Informal mathematics/software-engineering applications and online/expert-iteration integration remain future work.

title: Neural Theorem Proving: Generating and Structuring Proofs for Formal Verification
what: Presents a three-module framework that turns natural-language statements into formal Isabelle proofs: statement generation, LLM proof generation and heuristic proof structuring. SFT teaches syntactic Isabelle, RL rewards proofs checked by PISA, and recursive proof search uses ATPs, ERP and backtracking. The proof representation is a state-transition system; each generated step is checked by ATPs, with ERP repairing failures and heuristic tactics/backtracking reorganizing proof trees. The framework targets both miniF2F-test mathematics and AWS S3 bucket policy verification, and curates an FVELER-derived training dataset. The authors emphasize whole-proof generation plus structured subproof reuse.

Framework validated on miniF2F-test and Isabelle
AWS S3 policy used as application case; detailed success tables are in §4 of extraction
assumptions_limits: Formal correctness is relative to Isabelle/PISA/ATP checking and the formalized statement; natural-language translation can misrepresent program intent. RL and heuristic search depend on finite budgets and solver availability. The supplied experiments report benchmark results but do not establish coverage of arbitrary software policies.
use_for_goal: Relevant to LLM proof-generation pipelines that combine model proposals with trusted proof checking and search. Statement formalization remains a trust boundary, and benchmark evidence may not transfer to systems code.

title: ProofWala: A Framework for Multilingual Proof Data Synthesis and Theorem-Proving
what: Provides itp-interface and ProofWala, a shared infrastructure for extracting and executing Lean/Rocq tactics, training proof-step models, and searching cloned proof environments in parallel. Controlled 220M-parameter model experiments find significant multilingual gains on Mathlib and CategoryTheory adaptation, with smaller nonsignificant pass@5 gains on CompCert, MathComp and GeoCoq. Sections 2–3 formulate proving as transitions between finite sets of obligations, implement Lean instrumentation inside the elaborator, export declaration/dependency graphs to SQLite, and retain reusable environment pools keyed by current proof state. Beam-search pseudocode generates, concurrently executes, and prunes tactic candidates; annotated trees contain only assistant-accepted transitions. Sections 4–5 document theorem-level corpus splits, identical prompt serialization without assistant/repository labels, fixed-step CodeT5 training, pass@1–5 and paired bootstrap tests, analogous Lean/Rocq category-theory examples, search-tree size/degree and tactic-length/runtime tables, MiniF2F transfer and CPU scaling. Section 3.1 explains why preliminary Isabelle/PISA integration is too expensive to scale.

220M parameters; 34,000 max updates; batch 128
CategoryTheory pass@5 45.54→53.47%, p=.008

assumptions_limits: Empirical scope is tactic-based Lean and Rocq with CodeT5-Base (220M), not a frontier-LLM or specification-generation benchmark. Lean support is reported as 4.15.0–4.24.0 with a compatibility layer; detailed Rocq backend support is 8.10–8.18. CompCert/Mathlib reuse prior splits; other corpora use theorem splits, so structurally analogous theorems across languages can remain in training (explicitly analyzed in Table 4). No stronger contamination audit is demonstrated. Search uses 600-second timeouts, 1200 seconds for GeoCoq. Isabelle support is preliminary and requires tens of gigabytes per PISA instance. Gains outside Lean and adapted CategoryTheory are not statistically significant; multilingual MathComp and GeoCoq pass@1 are lower than monolingual. Proof acceptance inherits assistant correctness; this paper does not prove a distributed program or generate Verus/TLA+ specifications.

CompCert provides software-verification cases, but the study does not test distributed-system invariants, Rust/Verus or TLA+. Reusing its pool/data API for those settings is a research direction, not an evaluated result.

title: PropertyGPT: LLM-driven Formal Verification of Smart Contracts through Retrieval-Augmented Property Generation
what: PropertyGPT retrieves human-written Certora properties by embedding their associated code, prompts GPT-4-turbo to generate Solidity-like PSL properties for new contracts, repairs candidates with compiler/static feedback, ranks them by code/property similarity, and verifies them with source-level symbolic execution, modular verification and bounded model checking. The PSL intermediate language expresses invariants, function pre/postconditions and scenario rules in Solidity-like syntax. A conservative code-similarity threshold retrieves roughly 10–20 references; generated properties are iteratively repaired (up to nine attempts in the implementation), checked for inclusion of the target function, then ranked using four raw/summary embedding similarities with learned weights α=.134, β=.556, γ=.141, η=.168. The prover uses strongest-postcondition symbolic execution and Z3, over-approximates unknown on-chain calls, and bounds model checking to depth three (five loop iterations). The dataset contains 623 properties from 23 Certora projects; tests include 90 held-out properties, 13 CVEs, 24 attack incidents and four bounty projects.

title: Propositional Proof Skeletons.
what: Introduces semantic proof skeletons: selected learned clauses that summarize an unsatisfiability proof and allow later reconstruction of a complete DRUP/DRAT proof by incremental SAT solving. Online glue/reason-clause filters and offline LRAT-activity filters are implemented in CaDiCaL and DRAT-trim, with independent chunks enabling parallel reconstruction. The paper formalizes the reconstruction invariant: each skeleton clause is proved as a RUP under preceding clauses, then chunk proofs are stitched into a complete proof; variables in skeleton clauses are frozen to prevent unsound incremental inprocessing. It gives online Glue, Glue+Trail and Dynamic filters, offline activity-based Offline/Offline+Units/Offline-Opt filters, UNSAT-core restriction, and post-reconstruction shrinking. It also adapts DRAT-trim to concatenate chunk LRAT proofs and explains when deletions must be removed.
numbers: 65 unsatisfiable formulas
500–5,000 s original solving range and 5,000 s timeout
100–5,000× skeleton compression
24-core reconstruction around 5× faster for the majority
AWS m5d.metal: 96 vCPUs, 500 GB RAM
assumptions_limits: The method targets unsatisfiable CNF instances with clausal DRUP-style proofs; a skeleton alone is not a proof and needs a sound SAT solver/checker to fill each gap. Independent reconstruction must remove deletions that could invalidate later gaps; incremental reconstruction requires freezing variables occurring in skeleton clauses. Runtime and compression depend on heuristic clause selection and chunk balance; the study uses CaDiCaL/DRAT-trim and does not establish comparable gains for satisfiable cases or other proof systems.
use_for_goal: Provides a concrete, independently checkable proof artifact design: store a compact semantic summary, reconstruct complete proofs with solver calls, and parallelize verification. The soundness constraints around deletions, frozen variables and checker trust are useful when evaluating generated proofs for distributed systems.

title: Prover agent: An agent-based framework for formal mathematical proofs
what: A loop around three parts: a general reasoning LLM that writes an informal proof, a small prover model that turns it into Lean code, and Lean that checks it and returns errors. If the direct attempt fails, the reasoner proposes helper lemmas (special cases, facts from the assumptions), each is proved separately, and the proved lemmas are fed back for a final proof. No training; it is a prompt-and-control pipeline.

title: Proving Safety with Trace Automata and Bounded Model Checking.
what: Combines loop acceleration with trace automata to remove redundant accelerated executions before bounded model checking. Trace subsumption preserves reachable states while lowering the transformed program diameter, enabling safety proofs and faster bug finding. Defines under-approximating accelerators, trace subsumption and regular restriction languages. Theorems show every original trace is represented or subsumed and that restricted accelerated traces preserve safety reasoning. A source-to-source implementation instruments CFAs, and experiments compare CBMC, acceleration and acceleration plus trace automata on SV-COMP14 and crafted deep-loop bugs.

crafted bug time 12.31 s to 1.85 s
~15% average binary-size increase
assumptions_limits: Accelerators must under-approximate loops; trace elimination is sound only under the subsumption conditions proved. BMC proves safety only past the transformed reachability diameter. Nested loops and unsupported operations remain incomplete. Results depend on CBMC/Z3 timeouts and selected benchmarks; acceleration may increase binary size.
use_for_goal: Shows how a machine-checkable transformation can make bounded verification complete on selected programs, with explicit trace-preservation theorems. It informs evaluation of generated loop proofs but is C/BMC rather than Rust/Verus or distributed systems.

title: A Model Checker for Hierarchical Probabilistic Real-Time Systems
what: Presents a PAT plug-in model checker for Probabilistic Real-time Systems (PRTS), a CSP extension with hierarchical composition, shared data, dense-time constructs, and probabilistic choice. Automatic zone abstraction produces a finite MDP while preserving probabilities for supported reachability and LTL analyses. Defines PRTS constructors Wait, timeout, interrupt, deadline, within, and pcase; supports integer/boolean/array/user-defined data and fully hierarchical processes. The concrete semantics are MDPs with finite reachable data/process valuations but dense-time transitions. A proof sketch establishes time-abstract bisimilarity between scheduler-induced concrete and abstract DTMCs. Verification includes max/min reachability, reward, SE-LTL without next, refinement checking, counter abstraction, and safety-via-refinement detection. The PAT implementation provides Visual Studio editing, simulation, and verification.

assumptions_limits: Requires finite valuations of variables and reachable process structures; dense time is the only source of infinite states. Probability preservation is claimed for the supported properties under the zone abstraction and scheduler correspondence. LTL is restricted to LTL-X because next is hard to define after abstraction; counter abstraction applies only when process identities are irrelevant. Future work lists zeno checking, digitization, and richer real-time properties; experiments are small case studies rather than exhaustive scalability evidence.
use_for_goal: Shows how hierarchical process structure, dense time, probability, and max/min temporal properties can be combined in a practical model checker; relevant to distributed-system verification when protocol timing and stochastic choices coexist.

title: Propose, Solve, Verify: Self-Play Through Formal Verification
what: Introduces PSV, an iterative proposer/solver loop for verified Rust/Verus code. At each iteration the solver samples k_trn candidates per specification, Verus supplies binary correctness outcomes, rejection fine-tuning trains on at most one verified solution per problem, and a proposer generates B new specifications conditioned on solver-estimated difficulty classes. Specifications are parsed, deduplicated and body-ignored checked before solving. The paper explains why RFT is preferred to advantage-weighted RL when Verus is sound but incomplete, and evaluates transfer learning and test-time training on Dafny2Verus, MBPP-Verified and HumanEval-Verified. Ablations isolate solution verification, difficulty-aware proposal and prompt diversity; scaling studies vary question budget and iterations.
numbers: Main Table 1 (mean over 5 seeds): test-time Dafny2Verus pass@1 65.63% vs AlphaVerus 24.06% and RFT 34.46%; MBPP 36.78% vs 6.48% and 3.83%; HumanEval 19.07% vs 7.24% and 5.56%. Transfer pass@1 is MBPP 25.25% and HumanEval 16.18%. PSV averages 48.12% across benchmarks/metrics vs 25.43% RFT and 25.55% AlphaVerus. Scaling from 4k to 32k questions raises Dafny pass@1 59.5→74.3%; MBPP 1k→32k raises 22.3→44.3%; HumanEval 13.9→26.3%. Fixed-budget iteration increases Dafny pass@1 21.0→42.3% at 1k. Removing verification drops pass@1 by 51.5% Dafny, 55.2% MBPP and 52.1% HumanEval relative; -Difficulty averages −5.6%, -Diversity −10.6%. Only 47.7% of generated specs are valid on average without spec verification, causing 2.1× inference compute.
assumptions_limits: The key guarantee is conditional on Verus soundness: accepted code satisfies the formal specification. Verus is incomplete, so rejected correct solutions can be mislabeled and advantage-weighted RL is avoided. Formal specifications may themselves be invalid or underspecified; spec filtering is syntactic/body-ignored and generated questions need not match human intent. Benchmarks are translated/verified datasets, use a 3B Qwen model, five random seeds and roughly 24 hours on one 8×L40 machine; human-written solutions are not trained. Difficulty prompting only partially controls difficulty (target means 0.55 easy, 0.45 medium, 0.36 hard with substantial overlap). Generalization beyond Verus or sound verifiers remains future work.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence that verifier-accepted Rust/Verus programs can provide a scalable self-play reward signal. The benchmark gains, budget/iteration scaling and ablation failures quantify the value of sound verification, while incompleteness, invalid specs and partial difficulty control define practical limits for automated verification datasets and training loops.

title: PSyHCoS: Parameter Synthesis for Hierarchical Concurrent Real-Time Systems
what: Presents a C#/.NET toolkit for timing-parameter synthesis and model checking of hierarchical concurrent systems specified in Parametric Stateful Timed CSP (PSTCSP). The inverse method starts from a reference parameter valuation and synthesizes a convex region with the same time-abstract action behavior. Evaluates full reachability, inverse synthesis and equivalent-state reductions on eight timing examples; Fischer mutual exclusion yields Delta<Epsilon from reference (3,4). The reference-valuation contract preserves time-abstract linear-time behavior, rather than finding all safe valuations or proving all timed properties. PSTCSP creates clocks implicitly as execution proceeds, supports nested processes and shared/programmatic data, and stores states as process/constraint identifiers. The paper exposes nontermination and memory limits, overhead of equivalent-state merging, and confounds in cross-tool comparisons caused by manual translation. Complete table includes negative performance cases as well as a Fischer instance enabled by reduction.
assumptions_limits: PSTCSP is a process algebra with shared variables, data structures, user-defined programs, several choice/concurrency constructs and timing operators Wait[d], timeout[d], within[d], deadline[d]. Parameters are unknown constants representing timing delays, not the number of processes. The displayed Fischer model fixes N=3; benchmark Fischer4/5/6 separately fix those process counts. No theorem quantifies correctness over arbitrary N. Clocks are implicit and dynamically introduced, unlike an explicitly fixed timed-automaton clock set. Footnote 1 identifies PSTCSP with parametric closed timed epsilon-automata; expressiveness is stated incomparable with parametric timed automata. Formal semantics, inverse-method soundness, undecidability and equivalent-state reduction are imported from [3]/[4], not reproved in this six-page tool paper. IM takes a model and reference valuation pi and returns a convex constraint K guaranteeing the same time-abstract sequences of actions as pi. A known correct reference transfers the relevant linear-time properties to all valuations in K. Synthesis itself is not a test that the reference is correct, not necessarily a maximal safe region, and not a guarantee that all safe parameter choices are found. Clock-sensitive or bounded-time specifications require their own semantic encoding; equal untimed action traces alone do not establish identical event times. Parameter synthesis is undecidable; authors deliberately constructed examples where IM fails to terminate. They report termination on their practical cases, not on all models. Full parametric reachability can have an infinite reachable state set even where IM terminates. A finite evaluation timeout or memory-out does not establish mathematical nontermination, and the table itself marks M.O. rather than an infinite-time execution proof. Fischer model uses shared turn (initial Idle=-1) and counter (initial zero), with two parameters Delta and Epsilon. Processes read Idle, update turn within Delta, wait Epsilon, and enter iff turn still equals their ID. Entry increments counter, exit decrements it and resets turn. Reference Delta=3,Epsilon=4 gives Delta<Epsilon, which authors call the weakest known mutual-exclusion constraint. The record preserves that as their model-specific claim, not a proof of necessity for every Fischer variant. The toolkit reports LTL, deadlock and refinement checking, simulation/trace playback and full state graph generation. It also permits C# functions/data in models. The paper supplies no machine-checked implementation proof, proof-producing interface or verified semantics for arbitrary host functions. Correctness of tool implementation, parsing, polyhedral operations, host code and input model remains outside the article’s demonstrated formal guarantees. Implementation uses C#/.NET and Parma Polyhedra Library for constraints. Architecture has separate parser, internal representation, algorithms, simulator and GUI. Each semantic rule and algorithm is a separate class; authors propose reusing algorithms on labeled transition systems. Internal states pair string-coded process and constraint IDs. A string equality test is reported for constraint identity; exact normalization/interning correctness and cost are not specified here. Optimized reachAll+ and IM+ merge equivalent PSTCSP states. The technique can reduce state counts exponentially in the best case but requires costly operations. Both original and optimized variants are exposed to users. The article does not provide a new proof of equivalence preservation or a formal refinement relation to deployed concurrent-system code. Table 1 contains eight fixed examples: Bridge (four persons/17 time units), Fischer4/5/6, Jobshop scheduling, railway control RCS5/6, and TrAHV train. It reports parameters, state/transition counts, maximum clocks and seconds. IM groups omit transition counts. State counts with k are rounded; M.O. denotes memory-out in context, not an unsafe answer. Full numeric rows are stored separately in benchmark_table. Environment is Windows XP 32-bit, Intel Quad Core 2.4 GHz, 4 GB memory. No tool/compiler/PPL versions, run repetitions, variability, CPU utilization, exact memory peaks or common time limit are stated. Model sizes and chosen reference valuations depend on each benchmark; references for non-Fischer cases are standard valuations, and Fischer uses values satisfying known good-behavior constraints. IM+ can help sharply: Fischer5 states 133k→13k and seconds1176→84.5; Fischer6 IM is M.O. while IM+ reaches86k states in1144s. It also costs time: Bridge253→455s with identical2.8k states; RCS5 7.83→16.7s with identical5.6k states. These measured cases do not prove general speedup or guaranteed termination. Reader table check: the prose says state reduction makes IM+ faster whenever it reduces states, yet Jobshop has1112→877 states and17.1→22.8s. Also the stated up-to80% slowdown for Bridge is not the largest table slowdown: RCS5 has about113% overhead. These are discrepancies in the performance summary, not counterexamples to the inverse method’s correctness. The article reports deadlock checking when full reachability terminates and identifies Jobshop’s terminal deadlock as expected because every task runs once. A completed acyclic schedule is a counterexample to a naive deadlock-free requirement, not necessarily a scheduling failure. Exact checked LTL formulas and full per-model verification outputs are not tabulated. Authors say a synthesized True region for railway models allows timing constructs to be removed and claim this for all parameter valuations. The formal abstraction/refinement argument and full parameter-domain restrictions are not presented here. Record this as an author application claim; it does not by itself prove real-world railway safety or eliminate implementation timing requirements. IMITATOR comparison used the same hardware under Ubuntu11.10 64-bit, unlike the Windows32-bit main table. Authors explicitly call comparison inaccurate due to manual PSTCSP/PTA translation: each tool favors native models. IMITATOR Jobshop8.96s andTrAHV0.097s are reported; Fischer translations fail to terminate, Bridge/RCS are too large for manual translation. No fair overall cross-tool ranking follows; automated efficient translation remains future work. Sources, binaries, manual and models were linked at the historical PSyHCoS page http://lipn.univ-paris13.fr/~andre/software/PSyHCoS/. This reading used the saved paper only and did not fetch or run the artifact or import cited proofs. No verified Rust, Verus, TLA+, LLM-agent result or deployment-level distributed implementation is supplied.
use_for_goal: Concrete formal-model analysis of concurrent timing behavior, with useful evidence distinctions for evaluating generated specifications: fix process count separately from delay parameters, validate the reference valuation, state which trace properties transfer, retain nontermination/memory-out results, and account for model-translation confounds. These are reader inferences; this tool paper does not evaluate LLM specification/proof agents or verify Rust/distributed-system implementation code.

title: Formal Verification of Termination Criteria for First-Order Recursive Functions
what: Formalizes semantic and syntactic termination criteria for first-order recursive functions in PVS, using an embedded language PVS0 and proving equivalence among semantic termination, Turing-style bounded evaluation, size-change principles, calling-context graphs and matrix-weighted graphs. PVS0 embeds univariate first-order recursive functions [Val→Val] using constants, one variable, unary/binary operators, recursive calls and conditionals. The paper defines a relational semantics ε and bounded-step functional semantics χ returning a distinguished ♢ when the recursion bound is insufficient, then proves determinism, equivalence of ε/χ determination, and equivalence of ε- and χ-termination. The minimum recursion depth μ is formalized. Ackermann serves as a nontrivial encoding example, with an automated proof strategy relating PVS and PVS0 definitions. The introduction states that the NASA PVS Library also includes formalized size-change, calling-context and matrix-weighted criteria plus mechanizable automation for user-defined recursive functions.
numbers: No empirical benchmarks or runtime measurements appear in the extracted text. The paper reports a NASA PVS Library formalization and automated proof strategy for PVS/PVS0 equivalence; quantitative proof-size data are not given.
assumptions_limits: PVS0 has a single input variable; multi-argument functions such as Ackermann are encoded into tuples. Built-in operators are treated atomically, so their internal termination/correctness is outside PVS0's model. Termination remains undecidable in general; the criteria and automation target the embedded first-order fragment. The available extraction ends in §2.3 after semantic termination definitions, before the paper's later criteria, equivalence proofs, experiments and automation details; therefore no benchmark or runtime claims can be made from this file.
use_for_goal: Relevant to verified recursive Rust/Verus libraries because it separates executable bounded semantics from logical termination and shows how calling-context/size-change criteria can be mechanized in an interactive prover. title: $\mathbf{{\textsc {PyCaliper}}}$: Python-Embedded Infrastructure for RTL Verification and Specification Synthesis.
what: Introduces PyCaliper, a Python-embedded DSL and infrastructure for writing RTL specifications close to the design, connecting commercial Jasper FPV and custom BTOR2 symbolic execution backends, and synthesizing missing invariants/specification holes. PyCaliper represents RTL modules with SpecModule, Struct, Group, Logic and LogicArray elements that mirror hierarchy. Inductive specifications separate input assumptions, state invariants and output assertions; single-trace and two-trace miter invariants support security properties such as no-stale-data leakage. Two synthesis-hole templates are provided: ceqhole selects signals equal across miter traces under a condition, while ctrlhole synthesizes a LUT relation between control and dependent signals. Synthesis engines use verifier oracles for SyGuS/CEGIS and incremental invariant synthesis. Python classes enable parameterized widths and reusable libraries; SVA and BTOR2 backends make the framework compatible with proprietary and open tooling.
numbers: No quantitative case-study numbers appear in the extracted 216-line text; the architecture names two backends (Jasper FPV and BTOR2) and two synthesis-hole templates.
assumptions_limits: The extracted text ends during Section 2.1, so implementation details and quantitative case-study results from later sections are unavailable here. PyCaliper itself is infrastructure rather than a standalone verifier; soundness/performance depend on Jasper or BTOR2 engines and synthesis methods. Inductive proofs require adequate input assumptions and candidate invariants; two-trace hyperproperties rely on self-composition. The paper presents FIFO/no-stale-data and invariant-synthesis examples, but no numerical benchmark results are present in the available extraction.
use_for_goal: Shows a practical way to keep hardware specifications close to RTL while integrating verifier-guided invariant synthesis. The separation of assumptions/state/output and explicit synthesis holes may inform Verus specification-generation workflows, while backend dependence and missing quantitative data caution against treating the framework as an evaluated verifier.

title: Learning Universally Quantified Invariants of Linear Data Structures
what: Introduces quantified data automata (QDAs) for universally quantified properties of linear data structures and reduces active QDA learning to Moore-machine learning; elastic QDAs support decidable verification conditions. Theorem 1 establishes a unique minimal QDA for valuation-word languages; Theorem 2 gives a polynomial active learner assuming membership/equivalence teachers, with complexity also depending on longest counterexample. Theorem 3 constructs the most precise elastic over-approximation using blank-symbol closure, powerset states and formula-lattice joins. Section 6 translates EQDAs to Strand exactly and to the array property fragment by a sound one-way abstraction. The implementation uses libALF and a passive sample teacher over bounded executions, learns QDAs, elastifies and converts them to formulas, then validates adequate invariants with an SMT solver. Table 1 contains 25 invariant/postcondition rows and 3 precondition rows, including sorting, cachePage, Glib, Linux/driver routines and GNU sortlines.
