title: Formal Verification of Quantum Algorithms Using Quantum Hoare Logic.
what: Formalizes quantum Hoare logic syntax, denotational semantics and partial-correctness proof rules in Isabelle/HOL, proves soundness and relative completeness, and verifies Grover search correctness. The formalized language has skip, unitary assignment, measurement branches and while loops over finite-dimensional quantum variables represented as partial density matrices. Semantics uses superoperators and the Löwner order; partial correctness accounts for nontermination via trace loss. The qPD calculus includes Skip, unitary, sequential, measurement, loop and order rules. The Isabelle development extends complex linear algebra with Hermitian/unitary matrices, positivity, Schur decomposition, Löwner order and tensor products, plus automation for matrix identities. Grover is proved correct for an infinite class of inputs whose expected success probability is 1. The available extraction ends in §3.1, so implementation-cost and §4–§7 benchmark details are not present.
numbers: No runtime or proof-size numbers are available in the extracted text. Contributions are mechanized theorems (soundness and relative completeness of qPD) and one nontrivial Grover verification; an AFP entry QHLProver is linked.
assumptions_limits: Only partial correctness is formalized (total-correctness rules are omitted). Variables have finite dimensions and initialization is removed relative to full QHL. The approach reasons mathematically in Isabelle rather than executing large state spaces; quantum-state simulation/model checking remains exponentially bounded (roughly 25–30 qubits for model checking, 50–60 for simulation as context). Completeness is relative, relying on underlying predicate reasoning. Source extraction is incomplete after linear-algebra preliminaries, limiting quantitative cost claims.
use_for_goal: Illustrates end-to-end mechanization of a domain-specific Hoare logic and nontrivial algorithm correctness in an interactive prover. The finite-dimensional, partial-correctness scope and incomplete extracted sections caution against assuming coverage of practical quantum languages or total correctness; the tensor/matrix formalization pattern may inform verified numeric libraries.

title: Model Checking the Quantitative µ-Calculus on Linear Hybrid Systems
venue: Logical Methods in Computer Science 8(3:21); arXiv:1209.1738
what: Proves arbitrary-precision decidability for quantitative µ-calculus model checking on initialised linear hybrid systems by reducing interval games to discrete counter-reset games. Defines linear hybrid systems with locations, real-valued variables, interval-constrained transitions, resets, and location rates; initialisation requires resetting a variable whenever its rate changes. Gives quantitative µ-calculus semantics over the infinite state graph and constructs interval parity model-checking games whose values equal formula values. Initialised games are flattened by rescaling constraints/payoffs, rational games converted to integer games, and epsilon-discrete strategies are shown sufficient up to the largest payoff multiplier. A state-equivalence relation preserves integer intervals and fractional ordering; discrete moves are encoded by counter-reset games, then solved through counter-parity algorithms.
numbers: Theorem 2.7: given K, formula φ, and n>0, decide ±∞ or return rational r with |JφK−r|<1/n; combined complexity is 8EXPTIME. Counter-parity solving contributes 6EXPTIME in general and 4EXPTIME for a fixed number of counters, but the game construction is doubly exponential.
assumptions_limits: The main theorem assumes initialised linear hybrid systems; non-initialised stopwatches are outside the flattening argument. Variables and rates may be real/rational initially, but reduction uses finite games over Z∞ and integer initial states. The result approximates finite or infinite values to 1/n and decides ±∞, with an 8EXPTIME upper bound; exact values and tight complexity remain open. Practical scalability is not evaluated and a solver implementation is left as future work.

title: Quantitative Synthesis for Concurrent Programs.
what: The paper synthesizes a deterministic finite-state concurrent program by resolving nondeterministic synchronization choices in a partial program. A weighted-automaton performance model assigns architecture-sensitive costs to locking, context switches, memory/cache operations; a possibly probabilistic scheduler induces worst- or average-case limit-average objectives. Correctness is specification-free safety such as race or deadlock freedom. The synthesis problem reduces to imperfect-information stochastic graph games and is Nexp-complete; practical solving uses static strategy pruning, MDP strategy improvement, Gaussian elimination for Markov chains, and value-preserving data abstraction. A prototype handles producer-consumer, optimistic concurrency, and two other finite-state patterns. For two producers/two consumers and four cells, fine-grained locking is 19% better when copying costs 100x locking, while coarse locking is 25% better when costs are equal; measured optimistic-concurrency runtime peaks then declines as batch size n grows.

Results depend on chosen weighted automata and scheduler, so they do not claim universally optimal synchronization; desktop measurements are a sanity check against synthesis trends.

title: QWIRE Practice: Formal Verification of Quantum Circuits in Coq
what: Embeds the QWIRE quantum circuit language in Coq with higher-order abstract syntax, a linear-wire type checker, and denotational semantics as superoperators on density matrices. It proves correctness properties for concrete circuits and parameterized circuit families. The development gives both flat and HOAS circuit representations, uses Coq dependent types and a Linearity Monad to enforce disjoint wire contexts, and defines composition/unboxing without explicit substitution. Matrix, complex-number and density-matrix libraries support unitary, measurement, discard and dynamic-lifting semantics. Verified examples include a quantum coin flip (12-line proof), induction for Deutsch–Jozsa families, unitary followed by transpose for arbitrary input width (<20 lines), and equivalence of lift-based and gate-based measurement. The paper also documents missing foundational proofs and matrix scalability limits.
numbers: 3 authors

assumptions_limits: The gate set is finite and wire types have finite interpretations; matrix dimensions are annotations on function-based matrices and rely on functional extensionality. Several matrix-library lemmas, preservation of well-formed superoperators, and compositional denotation equality were still unproved. Density matrices scale exponentially, and the authors struggled with circuits beyond a few qubits. Results verify selected examples, not a complete QWIRE metatheory or fault-tolerant implementation.
use_for_goal: A concrete example of machine-checked semantics plus linear typing for a domain-specific circuit language. Its HOAS, compositional proofs and explicit scalability gaps inform verified-language design, although it is quantum rather than distributed systems.

title: RAHFT: A Tool for Verifying Horn Clauses Using Abstract Interpretation and Finite Tree Automata
what: Introduces RAHFT, a modular CHC safety verifier combining constraint specialization, convex-polyhedra abstract interpretation, finite-tree-automata trace abstraction refinement and SMT feasibility checks. It returns safe, unsafe or an abstract counterexample and can be reconfigured to use each component separately. The abstraction module specializes clauses without unfolding, computes a convex-polyhedra fixed point containing at most one constrained fact per predicate, and records derivation traces as an FTA. A verifier accepts an inductive model or selects an abstract false trace; infeasible traces are generalized by interpolant automata. The refinement module computes FTA difference via optimized determinization, then generates equisatisfiable refined clauses that split predicates, so previous refinements need not be retained. Ciao Prolog integrates Yices, Parma Polyhedra and FTA libraries.

reported comparisons favor Rahft in runtime and instances solved (details in cited papers)
uses Yices SMT, Parma Polyhedra Library and optimized FTA determinization
assumptions_limits: The current implementation targets CLP constrained Horn clauses over linear arithmetic; arrays, maps, sets and richer theories are unsupported. Convex polyhedra can bottleneck large programs; library arity limits and interpolant generation do not scale well. Counterexample/model reconstruction in the original program is difficult after transformations and external-library use. The paper reports comparative evaluation by reference to prior studies rather than a full new benchmark table.
use_for_goal: Relevant as an example of modular automated verification that combines abstract state invariants with trace-level refinement. Its explicit domain/theory limitations and witness-reconstruction issues are useful when assessing automated proof pipelines and LLM-generated Horn specifications.

title: Liveness of Randomised Parameterised Systems under Arbitrary Schedulers (Technical Report)
what: Reduces almost-sure liveness of randomized parameterized systems under arbitrary schedulers to two-player reachability games and synthesizes regular progress relations with CEGAR, SAT solving and Angluin-style L* learning. The method ignores nonzero probability values because finite MDP liveness depends on graph topology, then represents length-preserving arenas as letter-to-letter transducers. Advice bits comprise an inductive reachable over-approximation, a winning set and a well-founded progress preorder; VERIFY checks four conditions and SYNTHESISE searches bounded automata via SAT, refining with counterexamples. Incremental proofs split progress into disjunctive advice bits, L* precomputes inductive invariants, and ring symmetries close winning sets. SLRP evaluates randomized and deterministic protocols plus infinite-graph games, with Lehmann–Rabin requiring incremental invariant+rotation symmetry.
numbers: four randomized protocol examples
length-preserving transducer arenas
Lehmann-Rabin 10 min with invariant+symmetry
23-state invariant, 25 win calls, 4,324 refinements
20 GB heap and 2 h timeout
assumptions_limits: The core presentation assumes strictly alternating arenas, initial/final states controlled by Scheduler, no non-final dead ends, finite alphabets and length-preserving transducers; probability-zero transitions are removed. The reduction proves almost-sure liveness through a game strategy but does not retain quantitative probabilities. Termination/completeness of the learning loop depends on regular advice bits and minimum-size hypotheses; fairness is not modeled and is listed as future work. Experiments use a proof-of-concept Java tool, fixed resource limits, and protocol encodings that may not cover arbitrary data-bearing systems.
use_for_goal: Direct evidence for automated liveness proofs of parameterized distributed protocols: game reductions, regular invariants, well-founded progress, CEGAR and symmetry. It clarifies what Verus/TLA+ liveness specifications must assume (scheduler/fairness, topology and regularity) and gives concrete scalability data.

title: Fast Ramsey Quantifier Elimination in LIRA (with applications to liveness checking)
what: Presents REAL (Ramsey Elimination for Arithmetic Logic), a solver-agnostic implementation eliminating Ramsey quantifiers from existential LIA, LRA, and LIRA formulas, with SMT-LIB extension and Alchemist translation from FASTer/Armoise reachability relations. The resulting existential formulas can be solved by standard SMT solvers to check liveness/termination. The paper defines the infinite-clique semantics and gives a worked arithmetic elimination argument using arithmetic progression witnesses. REAL adds SMT-LIB parsing/export, formula sharing and normalization, and compact Boolean/theory encodings. The FASTer pipeline verifies McCarthy91 termination and checks liveness of sliding-window, Lamport bakery, and cache-coherence protocols (SYNAPSE, Berkeley, Dragon, futurbus, MOESI). On eight pipeline benchmarks, REAL elimination/solving times and formula sizes are reported; parameterized integer/real families scale near-linearly in elimination, with solving dominating, and comparison to the prototype shows orders-of-magnitude speedups.

dimensions 10, 100, 1000

futurbus FAST 125.95s and REAL 28.570s
prototype speedups of several magnitudes
assumptions_limits: Ramsey elimination applies to existential linear arithmetic; liveness claims depend on FASTer computing a sound reachability relation and on the encoded fairness/model assumptions. The Lamport bakery starvation check fails without fairness assumptions. Mixed LIRA has substantial overhead because integer and real variables are separated; large benchmark solving times reach hundreds of seconds. The paper does not provide completeness beyond the supported arithmetic fragment or direct comparison on identical prototype benchmarks.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal liveness verification of parameterized distributed protocols: it turns reachability relations into decidable Ramsey-quantifier queries and reports concrete protocol checks. It complements safety-oriented SMT/inductive methods with an infinite-clique termination criterion.

title: Reasoning over Permissions Regions in Concurrent Separation Logic
what: Introduces SLLP, an extension of concurrent separation logic for fractional permissions over arbitrary shared regions. It combines strong and weak separating conjunctions with nominal labels and a jump modality to recover permission distribution and recombination principles without precision side conditions. The paper diagnoses failures of weak separation on imprecise predicates, formalizes a permissions algebra and p-heap semantics, proves algebraic entailments for the two separating connectives and labels, and gives three worked CSL proofs: parallel read, recursive tree processing, and channel-based cross-thread transfer. The transfer proof shows how labels and magic wands recover full ownership after a subtree is sent and modified.

assumptions_limits: Uses a fixed permissions algebra satisfying associativity, commutativity, cancellativity, non-zero, top, divisibility and distributivity axioms; p-heaps are finite and predicate interpretations are supplied externally. Examples use binary-tree predicates and simplified channel rules. The strong frame rule requires a syntactic condition that commands do not receive resources; automation and tractable fragments remain future work.

title: SMT-based Model Checking for Recursive Programs
what: Presents RecMC, an SMT symbolic model checker that analyzes procedures modularly using both over-approximating summary facts and under-approximating reachability facts. It is guaranteed to find a counterexample over decidable theories if one exists and is polynomial in the number of states for Boolean Programs. RecMC avoids inlining by using reachability facts, blocks spurious counterexamples with summaries, and advances a call-stack bound. Model-Based Projection (MBP) supplies lazy under-approximations of quantifier elimination for linear rational/integer arithmetic, while interpolation supplies over-approximations. The implementation is in Spacer/Z3 and evaluated on SV-COMP.
numbers: Evaluated on 799 SV-COMP benchmarks (§1)
RecMC/Spacer significantly outperformed Z3 GPDR implementation (§1, §8)
Boolean-Program decision procedure is polynomial in number of states (§Abstract, §8)
assumptions_limits: The guarantee is co-semidecision over decidable theories and depends on SMT and quantifier-elimination/projection procedures; efficiency can degrade when QE is expensive. The paper assumes procedures are not passed as parameters. Boolean polynomial complexity does not imply polynomial behavior for richer arithmetic theories.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to recursive protocol and program verification: combining under- and over-approximations avoids repeated expansion and preserves counterexample guarantees. Theory-specific QE costs and undecidability remain practical limits.

title: Holistic Verification of Blockchain Consensus
what: Parameterized model checking verifies binary Byzantine consensus associated with Red Belly Blockchain under n>3t and0≤f≤t. First verifies binary-value broadcast, then substitutes a smaller specification-based automaton into the outer consensus and checks safety and progress properties with ByMC. Agreement and validity do not require the added good-round fairness; termination does. The verified algorithm is the coordinator/timeout-free pseudocode variant under that fairness, rather than a proof of the deployed implementation or its partial-synchrony mechanism. Makes the decomposition concrete: global sent-message counters replace local receive counts; Byzantine effects lower enabling thresholds by f; four temporal broadcast properties support a replacement gadget; round communication closure reduces selected all-round LTL obligations to one-round checking. Manual meta-arguments connect per-superround invariants to global agreement/validity and good-round existence to eventual decision. Gives a fair-round definition, a nonterminating4-process trace, detailed automaton rules, explicit liveness preconditions and measured schema counts.
numbers: n>3t and t≥f≥0
Table 2 broadcast properties: 5.61, 6.87, 27.64, 6.75 s
simplified-consensus properties: 4.13–4.68 s
complete compositional verification <70 s
Table 2 naive properties >24 h; introduction reports 64-core safety run >3 days
assumptions_limits: Fixed n sequential processes communicate through reliable fully connected asynchronous point-to-point links; delays are finite but unbounded, steps interleave, each receive is atomic and sender identities distinguish quorum members. Up to t<n/3 are Byzantine; f≤t is the actual fault count. The threshold abstraction assumes faulty senders cannot impersonate arbitrarily many distinct processes. Communication closure is essential: each process uses only messages for its current round, discards earlier tags and buffers later tags. Monotone send counters and threshold guards admit the prior ByMC reduction. Guarantees do not automatically extend to arbitrary protocols with cross-round data dependencies, timing constraints or changing membership. Reliable communication is encoded by progress assumptions on enabled rules and source-location emptiness. This excludes scheduler executions that indefinitely withhold enabled productive actions. Added consensus fairness is different: some round r has every correct process first deliver r mod2 in that round’s binary-value broadcast. Neither fairness follows from asynchronous reliability alone. Algorithm1 is the DBFT variant without coordinator/timeouts. The second DBFT variant uses partial synchrony, but this paper replaces that mechanism with a good-round assumption. It does not prove a synchronizer, coordinator rotation, timeout correctness or that the deployed environment enforces the assumption. Threshold models describe correct processes and abstract Byzantine influence with f-offset guards; global send counters abstract possible local receipt histories. Parameterized checking ranges over symbolic parameters satisfying n>3t≥3f, rather than testing a list of network sizes. Soundness still depends on faithful manual abstraction and ByMC’s reductions/SMT checks. Inner broadcast verification establishes justification,obligation,uniformity and termination. Replacement must preserve all behaviors relevant to the outer consumer because contestants is shared and the outer algorithm can proceed before the broadcast finishes. The paper argues this and supplies encoded preconditions; it is not a machine-checked source-to-source refinement of production code. ByMC handles a restricted LTL fragment and one-round systems. Cross-superround agreement,initial validity and existential good-round termination require manually chosen intermediate formulas and mathematical composition arguments. The model checker does not directly discharge each final quantified formula as written. The proof covers binary agreement,validity and eventual decision for the displayed algorithm. It does not prove blockchain transaction semantics,multi-value reduction,ledger consistency across all block heights,network/cryptographic code,resource bounds or end-to-end behavior of the deployed Red Belly software. Processes continue participating after deciding so others can finish; only the first decision matters. Text states safe exit after two later rounds but does not supply a verified executable stopping implementation. A process that halts immediately on first decision would change progress assumptions.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal distributed-system verification: a concrete arbitrary-size Byzantine consensus case with both safety and conditional liveness,explicit fairness and communication assumptions,and a composition method that reduces model-checking cost. Useful for comparing TLA+models or Verus proofs through property scope,abstraction boundaries and termination assumptions. For LLM assistance it offers precise obligations—faithful quorum models,correct progress conditions and valid local-to-global reasoning—without testing any LLM pipeline.

title: Refinement of Parallel Algorithms down to LLVM
what: Adds parallel execution to the Isabelle Refinement Framework and generates verified LLVM. A state-nondeterminism-error monad reports reads, writes, allocation and frees; parallel composition assumes feasible allocation pairs and fails on races. Concurrent separation logic and a VCG prove low-level commands; Sepref refines pure list algorithms to in-place arrays, tracks pointer equalities and splits arrays for disjoint parallel updates. A parallel introsort/pdqsort-style algorithm is proved total-correct and benchmarked against C++. The memory model uses never-reused blocks, so use-after-free and allocation conflicts are detectable. The M-monad invariant requires consistency and an execution avoiding every finite forbidden block set. The disjoint concurrency rule composes Hoare triples; with_split and npar refine independent list subcomputations to same-array disjoint slices. Parallel psort partitions, falls back when depth/size is small or partition is unbalanced, and uses median-of-64 sampling. The final theorem states in-place return of the original pointer and sorted-permutation contents. Generated LLVM is instantiated for uint64 and strings. Figure 2 compares verified, std::sort(par-unseq), and Boost sample_sort over many distributions on laptop/server; Figure 3 shows speedup versus core count. Results are comparable on laptop integers, slower for server strings and highly parallel speedup. The semantics and generated LLVM text remain within an explicit trust boundary: Isabelle’s kernel, the shallow LLVM embedding and the code generator are trusted, and parallel execution uses an external C++ TBB primitive.
numbers: {'printed_pages': 18, 'server_cores': 22, 'server_ram_GiB': 128, 'laptop_threads': 12, 'laptop_ram_GiB': 32, 'pivot_samples': 64, 'code_width_bits': 64}
assumptions_limits: Parallel strands must have disjoint or race-free access reports; potential races cause semantic failure. Memory blocks are never reused; each execution allocates finitely many blocks and the model assumes an unbounded supply of fresh blocks (actual OOM is separately defined termination). The framework targets a small LLVM fragment, multicore CPUs and a parallel combinator; locks, atomics, read-only fractional ownership and GPUs are future work. Sorting correctness assumes a weak ordering and array length represented by a fixed-width word; code generation fixes widths to 64 bits and uses an int64 size signature. Benchmark evidence is runtime comparison, not a proof of speed or broad hardware scalability; no distributed network model, Rust/Verus, TLA+ or LLM agent is evaluated. The trusted code base includes Isabelle’s inference kernel, the shallow embedding of a small LLVM fragment and the text code generator. The parallel primitive calls an external C++ implementation using tbb::parallel_invoke. Correctness is proved against the embedded semantics; the paper does not prove the LLVM compiler, TBB runtime or complete LLVM-to-binary toolchain correct.
use_for_goal: This supplies a concrete proof-to-LLVM pipeline for parallel algorithms and race freedom, useful as a systems-level comparator for Verus’s verified Rust and for assessing generated distributed implementations. Its access-report race model is shared-memory and synchronous; it does not address network faults, TLA+ temporal specs, or LLM-written proofs. Evaluation demonstrates both theorem-backed correctness and performance measurement, a useful standard for agent-generated verification claims.

title: Refinement with Time – Refining the Run-Time of Algorithms in Isabelle/HOL
what: Extends the Isabelle Refinement Framework with NREST, a nondeterminism monad carrying per-result worst-case time bounds, and adapts Sepref synthesis into timed Imperative/HOL. Relates abstract operation costs to concrete heap/time-credit assertions, hiding amortized potential within data-structure representations. Reports formal correctness and cost developments for dynamic-array append, duplicate removal, Kruskal minimum spanning forest and Edmonds–Karp maximum flow. The evidence is formal theory, rules and case developments, not elapsed-time benchmark measurements. Records lattice/failure/infinity semantics, latest-starting-time calculus, orthogonality of data refinement, exact HNR resource accounting, limited automation and operation-rule requirements, explicit dynamic-array constants and potential, duplicate-removal cost specification, label-dependent Kruskal complexity, reused versus newly difficult BFS arguments, and limitations of the cost model and target backend. Preserves printed mismatches separately from verified-artifact claims.
assumptions_limits: §2.1, pp.2–3: α NREST = RES(α→enat option) | FAIL, with enat=N∪{infinity}. A map entry gives the upper cost allowed for that result, None excludes it. None is bottom, lifted pointwise; FAIL is top, empty result map bottom. Refinement reduces allowed results and cost upper bounds. FAIL permits everything as a specification and models failed assertions/nontermination; finite total-correctness claims require an appropriate nonfailing specification. An arbitrary infinite-cost NREST value is not a finite runtime guarantee. §2.1, p.3: return costs0; consume adds cost; bind takes supremum over all reachable intermediate results and adds costs. Any reachable failure makes the compound FAIL, so nondeterministic alternatives are treated conservatively. Per-result bounds can become infinite even when each separate path has finite cost. NREST is stated to form a complete lattice and monad with monotone bind/consume. §2.2, p.4: recursion RECT uses greatest fixed point in a separate flat ordering with FAIL top; F must be monotone in both flat and refinement order (mono2), otherwise RECT returns FAIL. This is not simply greatest fixed point in the cost-refinement lattice. Framework derives while/foreach/fold and monotonicity rules. Folding a finite list requires no extra termination argument; general recursive proofs still need suitable invariants/cost arguments. §§2.3–2.4, pp.5–7: latest starting time lst c Q is an infimum of per-result specification-minus-program slack, or None for failure, forbidden results or excessive cost; unreachable results contribute top. c≤RES Q iff Some0≤lst c Q. Composition lst(bind m f) Q = lst m (λy.lst(f y)Q) enables syntax-directed rules for return/consume/SPEC/bind/recursion/loops. Fold rule uses processed/remaining-list invariant and uniform body cost; VCG creates obligations, not all proofs automatically. §§2.5–2.6, pp.7–8: concretization maps an abstract result/time map through a relation, taking supremum of costs for related abstract values. Data refinement changes map domains, not time values. Refinement VCG simulates structurally similar abstract algorithms in lock step, reducing to local refinement and cost inequalities; valid relation and data invariants remain user proof obligations. §3.1, pp.8–9: concrete Heap procedure maps heap to optional(result,heap,natural-cost). Separation algebra uses abstracted heap plus time credits, allowing heap ownership and potential to split. Total-correctness Hoare triple requires termination and t≤n credits, leaves n−t credits and permits garbage collection via separating true. Basic array/reference operations cost one model step; whole-array operations cost length+1. These are semantic operation counts, not measured CPU instructions, wall time, allocator overhead or arbitrary-precision arithmetic bit costs. §§3.2–3.3, pp.9–11: Sepref symbolically executes NREST, synthesizing structurally similar timed Imperative/HOL and refinement assertions. HNR is conditional on abstract m≠FAIL; concrete execution uses heap credits n plus ta reserved for a related abstract result, preserves Γ′ and result relation R with leftover n+ta−t≥0. Hidden credits support amortized implementations. Result-dependent bounds are needed for compositional bind; constant final SPEC P (λ_.t) gives an equivalent ordinary time-credit Hoare triple. §4, pp.11–12: abstraction separates algorithmic cost proof from concrete data operations; generic BFS and greedy minimum matroid basis can be reused. Automatic steps include generating specification VCs, lock-step algorithm refinement and Sepref synthesis using available HNR leaf rules. Side-condition automation is limited; assertions carry size/precondition facts. Concrete operation proofs use timed separation logic/sep_auto with time-credit frame inference, sometimes interactive proofs. §4.1 Table1, p.12: matrix array create O(n²), lookup/update O(1); red-black set/map create O(1), operations O(log n); array set/map create O(n), operations O(1); dynamic-array list create/append amortized O(1), lookup/update O(1); union-find initialization O(n), union/find O(log n). Those representation-specific bounds are not claimed for all abstract sets or arbitrary unbounded labels. §5.1, pp.13–15: dynamic-array append worst-case raw budget5n+9 and amortized19 with potential10n−5capacity. Advertised HNR append budget19; client reserves23. Potential proof requires unfolding implementation, not merely applying coarse raw triple. Duplicate-removal client uses red-black sets and dynamic output arrays, reserves membership/insertion cost in input length rather than actual set size, and uses assertions to prove this overestimate sufficient. §5.2, pp.15–16: Kruskal development starts from minimum weight basis in a matroid, instantiates cycle matroid, replaces independence with disjoint-set comparison, then fixes natural-number vertex labels and union-find domain0..M where M is maximal label. Final minimum weight spanning forest bound O(E log E + M + E log M) assumes linear edge-list extraction, O(n log n) sorting and logarithmic union/find. This bound depends on numeric label range, not merely number of vertices. Only logarithmic union-find proof is supplied; inverse-Ackermann bound cited from a separate Coq development. §5.3, p.16: Edmonds–Karp refinement reuses abstract BFS, shortest augmenting paths and residual-graph operations. Outer augmentation bound O(VE) already prepared in earlier correctness development; final timed Imperative/HOL cost O(VE(E+V)). Tight BFS O(E+V) needs an additional amortized argument beyond its earlier lexicographic termination proof. Residual matrices implemented with arrays; source says linear initialization, while Table1 gives O(n²) matrix creation, so the unit of size matters. §§5.2–5.3, pp.16–17: authors report functional proof obligations reusable unchanged after adding time, but extra size assertions and runtime VCs needed. No lines-of-proof/reuse percentage, check-time table, machine timings, dataset or head-to-head empirical speed benchmark is supplied. The working hypothesis that old termination proofs transfer cheaply holds only for coarse bounds; fine bounds can demand substantial new work. §6, p.17: timing-function parameters remain inconvenient; abstract operation currencies and exchanges are proposed future design. Only runtime upper bounds studied; lower bounds, stack, energy, generalized source/target Sepref, timed LLVM semantics and stronger automation left future work. Mention of existing untimed LLVM generation does not establish this paper’s time guarantees for native LLVM code. No distributed-system,TLA+,Verus,Rust or LLM-agent experiment.

title: Regression-Free Synthesis for Concurrency.
what: Defines concurrency repair that preserves sequential behavior and, when initially correct, complete preemption-free behavior, while eliminating assertion errors. Adds constraints learned from good traces to the constraints learned from counterexamples, aiming to prevent a repair from breaking previously good behavior. Names the generic positive-and-counterexample extension to CEGIS PACES. §2 precisely relates traces before and after adjacent within-basic-block instruction swaps or atomic-section insertion. A regression must preserve reads-from relationships into assume/await conditions and must originate from a good trace that could not already become bad by scheduler choices alone. §3 uses trace-analysis graphs with intra-thread, reads-from-conditional/assertion and non-free write-order edges. A cover proves the necessary happens-before edge; additional noninterference edges place other writes before the source write or after the read. Conjoining/disjoining cover constraints yields a polynomial-time sufficient regression-prevention algorithm; when no cover exists, the theoretical fallback fixes every current intra-thread order. Exact sound-and-complete constraints can be computed exponentially. Bad-trace elimination reuses partial-order generalization and cycle constraints from the 2013 predecessor. §4 maintains cumulative constraints and good-trace images as the program changes, formalizing correspondence more carefully than scheduler input reuse. Wait/notify repair is discussed for inputs outside the standard sequential-correctness precondition.

assumptions_limits: Fixed number of threads in Cwhile; await is the only blocking operation and defines preemption points. All complete sequential traces must be good; preservation of preemption-free traces is conditional on their original correctness. Bugs are assumed data-independent: changing valuations without changing instruction-location sequence cannot change whether the trace is bad. Regressions are a restricted class requiring identical conditional reads-from, so newly enabled conditionals from different writes can evade the definition. Good-trace constraints cover seen traces, not all unobserved behavior; final correctness depends on Verify. The implementation uses CBMC and the evaluated finite/simplified driver models; no full Linux driver proof or weak-memory guarantee. Fair termination refers to choosing bad traces in the synthesis loop, not scheduler fairness for an executing repaired program. An unsound learner can still be followed by verification, but it lacks the stated intermediate-regression theorem.
use_for_goal: Useful as a baseline and warning for LLM-driven Verus/TLA+ repair: preserving successful examples can steer edits away from known correct behavior, but the guarantee must specify a trace correspondence and its blind spots. The paper cleanly separates a sound theoretical learner from its unsound practical implementation. An agent-evaluation database should preserve final verification, intermediate regressions, front-loaded analysis cost and unnecessary synchronization as distinct outcomes. No distributed protocol, Rust/Verus or LLM experiment appears.

title: Regular Model Checking with Regular Relations
what: Extends regular model checking from rational transition relations to MSO-definable regular relations over infinite strings, introducing nondeterministic streaming string transducers on infinite strings (ω-NSSTs). Proves ω-NSST and ω-NMSOT express exactly the same relations; gives a PSPACE type-checking procedure by automata products and summary maps; uses closure under composition to obtain decidable bounded model checking even when a regular relation's post-image is not regular. Formalizes activation/outcome protocols and pending memory, explains how Fair-Outcome assumptions can be falsified by system-controlled retry bookkeeping, and introduces a post-synthesis explicit-state auditor. title: Robustness in the Presence of Liveness
what: Defines robustness for liveness specifications by requiring a minimum number of system guarantees to remain true as environment assumptions fail. It reduces single and multiple counting requirements to Generalized Reactivity (GR) objectives and gives verification and synthesis algorithms for robust systems. The paper develops concrete robustness measures using dining philosophers, formalizes them as ordered sets of GR(1)-like implications, and shows that disjunctions of conjunctions of Büchi objectives can be exponentially simplified to generalized Büchi objectives. It proves DCB game solving co-NP-complete via a 3SAT reduction, then gives a counter-based construction reducing GR(1) games to one-pair Streett games. The construction preserves winning strategies, extends to GR(k), and yields verification and synthesis complexity bounds; synthesized strategies trade lower runtime for larger memory than Zielonka’s method.

GR(k) synthesis O(|S|^k|E|(mn)^{k(k+1)}k!)

dining-philosopher examples n=5 and n=7
assumptions_limits: Specifications are finite products of deterministic Büchi automata over input/output signals and robustness is measured by counts of assumptions and guarantees, with a user-supplied total order. The model is reactive infinite-play games; liveness violations cannot be detected finitely, so safety guarantees cannot generally be sacrificed in response to a fairness-assumption violation. DCB-to-generalized-Büchi simplification is exponential and DCB game solving is co-NP-complete. The proposed GR(1) algorithm uses O(|S||E|(mn)^2) time but stores (m+1)(n+1) memory states (or n with an extra strategy computation); GR(k) incurs factorial/exponential factors. No implementation benchmark is reported beyond the worked examples and asymptotic analysis.
use_for_goal: Provides a formal game-theoretic way to specify graceful degradation when distributed-system environment assumptions fail, with explicit complexity and memory tradeoffs useful for robust protocol synthesis and verification.

title: Formal Verification of an Out-of-Order Multiprocessor against an In-Order Weak-Memory ISA
what: Mechanizes an unbounded refinement proof that a multicore out-of-order RISC-V implementation with weak-memory behavior refines an in-order ISA, using a clean core specification to eliminate excess executions and then serializing memory/inter-core behavior. The proof decomposes n·Coreᵢ+ShMem⊆ISA into core refinement Coreᵢ⊑Coreₛ and system inclusion n·Coreₛ+ShMem⊆ISA. Coreₛ stores instructions in a single program-order list, allowing invalid excess instructions to be dropped; lightweight option-lifting encodes pure method preconditions without changing the refinement metatheory. Rocq mechanizes module refinements, arbitrary traces, and arbitrary design parameters.

title: Stateless Model Checking for POWER
what: Derives an operational execution model from axiomatic POWER semantics and introduces Relaxed Stateless Model Checking (RSMC), which explores inequivalent Shasha-Snir traces exactly once for threadwise-deterministic bounded programs. States combine fetched and committed events with program order, coherence and read-from relations; a commit-before function constrains commits while preserving POWER-allowed speculative effects. Validity and deadlock-freedom conditions yield equivalence between axiomatic and operational semantics. RSMC detects read-write races, constructs generalized sub-runs and queues branches so that all complete traces are covered without duplicate complete traces. Theorems establish soundness under valid/deadlock-free models and optimality for POWER with cbpower. Nidhugg validates 8,070 POWER litmus tests, compares C/pthreads benchmarks with goto-instrument, and shows blocked runs are usually absent or at most 10%; fences can reduce a Dekker-style test from 184,759 to 3 traces.

title: Certifying Safety when Implementing Consensus
what: Designs distributed certification agents that repeatedly check agreement and validity predicates supplied by a running consensus implementation. Agreement compares each local decision with child decisions on a certified spanning tree. Validity combines Boolean certificates that a local proposal equals the agreed value, and depends on concurrent agreement checking. Tree certification checks root consistency, acyclic distances, and an aggregate node count. Unique IDs are checked by comparing the multiset of IDs with their ordered successors using polynomial evaluation at n+1 points; this initialization is more expensive than normal certification. After failures the tree is rebuilt and soundness/completeness are weakened to inputs from non-faulty nodes. These are runtime checks of existing code rather than proofs of its implementation.
numbers: one combined agreement/validity message per node per check
O(n log n) bits per node for deterministic unique-ID initialization
n−1 fail-stop failures with properties restricted to non-faulty-visible inputs
up to O(n) communication rounds from tree height
assumptions_limits: Nodes communicate over a partially synchronous network; certification agents share fate with implementation processes and only see local implementation inputs, not internal protocol messages. Failures are fail-stop, not Byzantine, because the implementation is assumed buggy but non-malicious. At least one agent must signal a violation, and operators must monitor agents. General predicates, automatic certificate synthesis, and automatic recovery after errors remain future work. IDs must remain stable across failures; variable-length decisions use cryptographic hashing and then have probabilistic soundness. Tree height can require O(n) communication rounds.
use_for_goal: Shows a practical runtime-certification alternative for distributed implementations, with strong fail-stop resilience but weaker trust and observability than Byzantine-proof verification.

title: RustyDL: A Program Logic for Rust
kind: source-level dynamic logic and sequent calculus for Rust
what: Presents RustyDL, a source-level dynamic logic and sequent calculus for a safe Rust subset, plus a Rusty KeY prototype. The logic models ownership moves, shared and mutable references, arrays, integer overflow, loops and non-standard control flow directly over Rust compiler HIR, aiming to support inspectable human-in-the-loop proofs instead of translating to an intermediate language. RustyDL maps Rust primitive, array and reference types to logical sorts, uses mutating updates for mutable borrows, and treats moved values with fresh constants. Dynamic-logic box/diamond modalities express partial/total correctness; updates decompose deterministic state changes. Symbolic-execution rules split conditionals, model moves and borrow/deref/mutation operations, branch on debug-mode overflow versus panic, and check array bounds. Loop-scope rules record break/continue/return exits and permit invariants for Rust loops that compile to unconditional loops. The prototype implements taclets in KeY and demonstrates borrowing, loops, arrays, tuples and enums; a binary-search proof is reported.
numbers: 4,260 rule applications for binary-search proof in 2.1 s
safe-Rust subset; lifetimes, traits, iterators, pattern matching and generic functions deferred

assumptions_limits: The logic focuses on safe Rust and assumes unsafe code is encapsulated and separately verified. It covers primitive values, shared/mutable references and arrays; structs/enums are analogous, while unions, smart pointers, traits, lifetimes and a fuller specification language remain future work. Rust programs are assumed deterministic; the Rust transition function is left abstract and rule soundness is described as relative to ongoing formal semantics. Integer rules target debug semantics and must prove absence of overflow. The KeY proof system is not foundational and relies on integer/sequence theories. Verification is a proof of concept with limited automation, not a mature benchmarked verifier.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to Rust verification and proof-generating agents: source-level rules expose ownership and borrow reasoning to human or LLM interaction, while the explicit trust boundary contrasts with Verus translation/SMT workflows. It does not verify distributed protocols or implement TLA+.

title: SACO: Static Analyzer for Concurrent Objects.
what: Presents SACO, a static analyzer for actor/concurrent-object programs that infers termination, resource bounds and deadlock freedom. title: SATMC: A SAT-Based Model Checker for Security-Critical Systems
what: Describes SATMC 3.0, which combines planning-graph encodings with reactive-system bounded model checking to reduce bounded security-goal violations to SAT. ASLan models rewrite rules, Horn clauses, first-order LTL constraints and goals, with NuSMV generating LTL encodings and MiniSAT solving them. The formal framework defines states as facts closed under Horn clauses, rewrite-rule paths, closed-world semantics and first-order temporal satisfaction. Security systems compose a system model with a Dolev–Yao intruder and optional custom intruder; examples encode SAML messages, RBAC and PKCS#11 operations. SATMC specializes intruder rules, builds a monotone planning graph, grounds first-order LTL using only matching facts, and creates Φk whose satisfying assignments correspond exactly to length-k counterexamples. Iterative deepening is sound for each bound but can be semi-decision when kmax is infinite.

assumptions_limits: Bounded model checking only proves absence of attacks up to kmax; setting kmax to infinity may not terminate. Planning graphs over-approximate reachable states and quantifier grounding can be expensive or infeasible for unbounded domains, although SAT encoding avoids false positives. Models rely on symbolic Dolev–Yao cryptography and user-specified constraints; the paper does not establish completeness for arbitrary unbounded security systems.
use_for_goal: Relevant to automated verification of security-critical distributed systems: it shows how first-order protocol/intruder models and temporal security policies can be reduced to SAT, while making boundedness and grounding limits explicit.

title: SAW: A Tool for Safety Analysis of Weakly-Hard Systems
what: Presents SAW, a tool for infinite-time safety verification of general nonlinear weakly-hard systems under (m,K) deadline constraints. It partitions the safe state region into grids, builds Flow*-based one-step reachability graphs, uses dynamic programming to enforce local safety for all K-step paths with at most m misses, then reverse-searches for the largest inductive safe set. Algorithm 2 labels edges by deadline meet/miss and discards grids whose Flow* overapproximation intersects the unsafe set. Algorithm 3 computes DP(v,n,k) over miss counts and horizon K; Algorithm 4 removes states that can reach the unsafe complement in the K-step graph. The method avoids prior exponential-stability/Lipschitz assumptions and handles nonlinear benchmarks #5/#6. Example 1 and Table 2 show every benchmark initial set contained in SAW safe set while one-dimensional abstraction often returns none or an insufficient set; granularity and Flow* step size materially change conservatism.

Complexity is quadratic or worse in number of grids, and the authors note grid granularity tradeoffs and no probabilistic uncertainty model.

title: Model Checking Techniques for Verification of an Encryption Scheme for Wireless Sensor Networks
what: Presents a framework that models a hierarchical wireless-sensor-network encryption transmission as a Petri net, translates the net to Promela, and checks LTL correctness properties with SPIN. The example combines elliptic-curve encryption/decryption, LDPC encoding/decoding, modulation, fading/noise, and channel-parameter restoration. The paper gives a concrete Petri-net-to-Promela encoding: place and transition markings are integer arrays, firing macros atomically remove input tokens, add output tokens, and increment transition counts, and a BNF skeleton generates one init process with a do-loop of atomic firings. It explains SPIN never-claim generation from negated LTL, then defines deadlock-freeness as eventual firing of every transition and safeness as always keeping every place at ≤1 token. The communication model has 25 places and 14 transitions, including elliptic-curve/LDPC operations and a noisy fading channel. SPIN reports zero errors for the modeled liveness and safeness checks; the authors identify integrity/security properties as future work.

title: SceneChecker: Boosting Scenario Verification Using Symmetry Abstractions.
what: Introduces SceneChecker, which abstracts vehicle-plan hybrid automata by symmetry, delegates reachability to Flow*/DryVR and refines modes when the abstraction is inconclusive or unsafe. Safe abstraction results imply concrete scenario safety; unknown remains possible. A scenario is a directed graph of waypoint segments, uncertain initial set, guards, time bounds and polytope obstacles. User maps must be differentiable, invertible and commute with trajectories. Abstract modes aggregate symmetric segments, map guards and unsafe sets, and use nondeterministic resets. A DFS verifier caches per-mode initial sets, and split refinement separates modes until safety is shown or the concrete automaton is reached. The paper proves soundness and losslessness relative to the subroutine and map assumptions, but does not produce counterexamples.

Unmodeled dynamics can break exact symmetry. Guard and reachability over-approximation can produce unknown. Unsafe cases lack counterexamples. Experiments use hyperrectangular initial/guard sets, polytopic obstacles and selected vehicle controllers/scenarios.

title: Model Checking Disjoint-Paths Logic on Topological-Minor-Free Graph Classes
what: Proves an algorithmic meta-theorem: model checking first-order logic extended with vertex-disjoint-path predicates is fixed-parameter tractable on graph classes excluding a fixed graph as a topological minor, with runtime f(H,phi)*n^3 and a witness tuple when the formula is true. Proof strategy decomposes graphs into strongly unbreakable tree decompositions, collapses FO+dp predicates to FO on unbreakable regions containing large clique minors, computes bounded-size folio/type-preserving representatives for boundaried subgraphs, proves compositionality under gluing, and runs a bottom-up dynamic program. The collapse uses generic folio and partition-linkedness lemmas; replacement preserves topological-minor exclusion, unbreakability, and annotated types. The result improves the earlier minor-free theorem and yields O(f(k)n^3) applications such as F-Topological Minor Deletion when a large clique certifies a no-instance.

It handles subgraph-closed topological-minor-free classes; dense non-subgraph-closed classes and constant-time postprocessing queries remain open. The dynamic program relies on deep decomposition, irrelevant-vertex, folio, and bounded-treewidth machinery; no implementation benchmark is reported.

title: Formal Verification of a Fail-Operational Automotive Driving System

what: Defines and model-checks a distributed arbitration logic for a redundant, fail-operational highly automated driving system. The NuSMV model encodes state machines, buses, power supply, failures, and LTL/CTL safety requirements; the verification scope and tool qualification are aligned with ISO 26262. The architecture has nominal and fall-back channels with distributed state machines for driving strategy, vehicle control, braking, steering, sensors, communication, and power. In the BMW case, seven coupled state machines have 30 states, over 6000 potential combinations, 48 single failures and 2256 double faults; single failures took 3.5 hours and double-fault checking seven days. title: S CHWARZ: Solver-Aware Agentic Program Verification
what: Presents S CHWARZ, a trusted harness that turns coarse SMT verification failures into obligation-local repair using snapshots, checked SMT-local lemmas and theory-aware solver policies, evaluated on C and Rust/Verus tasks. The harness separates an untrusted agent that proposes specifications, decompositions and counterexamples from a checker that regenerates obligations, invokes configured solvers and validates unsafe witnesses by concrete replay. Program-point snapshots expose checked facts; local lemmas must themselves be entailed before use; theory policies select numeric, quantified, memory and floating-point encodings. The paper reports detailed ablations: removing local lemmas drops aggregate pass rate from 92.7% to 77.7%, removing policies to 88.2%, and removing both to 73.3%. Capability analysis identifies strong integer/recursion/control-flow performance and weaker floating-point, library semantics, layout and long proof routes.

title: Analyzing Behavioural Scenarios over Tabular Specifications Using Model Checking
what: Introduces a free tool for specifying and checking families of behavioral scenarios over SCR tabular requirements. Scenario programs combine guarded state changes, tests, sequencing, and iteration; the tool translates SCR tables and scenario programs to Promela and checks an end-state safety assertion with SPIN. A pacemaker specification is the running case. The paper defines the scenario grammar (stateChange, guarded stateChange[f], tests [f], sequencing, and Kleene iteration) and compiles each sentence with a program counter; unrestricted changes rely on SCR table transitions, guards filter traces, and the final property becomes assert(pc==n+1 → PROP). In the pacemaker study, SPIN finds two counterexamples: POR can return to Normal while battery voltage remains low, and magnet release can fail when the bradycardia program is off. title: Protocols to Code: Formal Verification of a Next-Generation Internet Router
what: Presents end-to-end verification of a production SCION border router: Isabelle/HOL refinement proves path authorization, valley freedom and loop freedom under a strong adversary; Gobra verifies optimized concurrent Go code for memory safety, crash/race freedom, finite processing and protocol conformance. title: Efficient Synthesis of Symbolic Distributed Protocols by Sketching
what: Introduces SCYTHE, a syntax-guided and counterexample-guided synthesizer for completing TLA+ sketches of parameterized distributed protocols. It enumerates typed expressions with cache/equivalence reduction and short-circuiting, uses TLC to check finite instances, and generalizes counterexamples into pruning constraints for safety, deadlock, liveness, and stuttering. The tool synthesizes protocols including consensus, 2PC, locks, sharded stores, and Raft reconfiguration. The paper formalizes protocol instances, fairness, sketches with pre/post holes and regular-tree grammars, and distinguishes finite-instance synthesis (Problem 1) from all-parameter-instance synthesis (Problem 2). Candidate generation uses cache-based size enumeration and semantic normal forms for Boolean/set/equality expressions; pruning constraints are disjunctions of hole interpretations. Safety constraints are optimal, while deadlock/liveness/stuttering encodings are sub-optimal but non-over-pruning; fairness and explicit implementability/environment constraints prevent vacuous solutions. TLC exhaustive checks each finite instance. In 22 benchmark rows, equivalence reduction cuts generated expressions by orders of magnitude; final TLAPS proofs establish safety for arbitrary instances in all but the two-process-only Peterson cases. Extra-checks expose finite-size overfitting: two Raft variants initially correct up to 3 nodes failed at 4+ and required larger-instance checks.

Grammar restrictions, typed symbols, opaque domains, finite-state verifier instances, fairness constraints, and manually specified implementability/environment separation shape results. Liveness pruning is sub-optimal; weak-fairness handling may under-prune. TLC calls dominate many runs, and the final all-instance verification remains a difficult/undecidable step. title: The SeaHorn Verification Framework
what: Presents SeaHorn, an LLVM-based automated safety verifier whose modular layers separate source syntax, LLVM operational semantics and verification semantics. LLVM bitcode is transformed into Constrained Horn Clauses (CHCs); configurable small-step or large-block encodings and varying register/pointer/heap abstractions feed interchangeable Horn engines, including Spacer/GPDR PDR/IC3 and IKOS abstract interpretation. The paper gives concrete front-end transformations (SSA, CFG simplification, function internalization, switch lowering and mixed-semantics assertion lifting), CHC encodings for loops and procedure summaries, error propagation across calls, model-based projection (including arrays), and DSA heap-to-array modeling. It distinguishes register-only, register+pointer and register+pointer+memory semantics. In SV-COMP 2015, SeaHorn won one gold and two silver medals; on 215 hard benchmarks with 30-minute/15GB limits, Spacer verified 21 safe and 74 unsafe cases normally, 76 unsafe in compositional BMC mode, while Z3-PDR verified 3 safe and 7 unsafe. The avionics case study checks buffer over/underflows in 160K-LOC mnav and 20K-LOC paparazzi, proving absence of overflows for both; inter-procedural encoding and IKOS invariants improve performance.

title: SecCSL: Security Concurrent Separation Logic.
what: SecCSL extends concurrent separation logic with relational assertions for data-dependent value sensitivity and location sensitivity. Assertions can express pointers, arrays, shared invariants, and security labels; lock invariants combine functional heap facts with policies for attacker-observable sinks. The logic's compositional noninterference property is timing-sensitive, so branches on secret values are forbidden. The authors mechanize soundness in Isabelle/HOL and implement SecC, a symbolic-execution verifier for a C subset. The central case study is a lock-protected record whose classified flag controls data sensitivity and whose public OUTPUT_REG sink must never receive secret data; a variant of Covern's CDDC case study and known benchmark problems are reported as verified within milliseconds in the abstract/overview.

title: Securing the Foundations of an Intermediate Language for Probabilistic Program Verification
what: Formalizes in Lean/mathlib a chain from probability spaces for discrete-time Markov chains through optimal expected costs of MDPs and sound expectation calculi to correctness of HeyVL encodings for probabilistic programs. Covers unbounded loops,nondeterminism,resource ticks and failed observations. Adds a fault-tolerant calculus to establish liberal-preexpectation soundness with conditioning,and idle k-(co)induction that preserves values of variables unmodified by the loop. Provides a deep embedded verification-condition generator and a small interactive proof case. This is foundational encoding/logic verification,not end-to-end verification of the production Caesar implementation or a new distributed-protocol case study. Theorem3 constructs a probability measure over infinite valid paths with cylinder probabilities equal to finite transition products; reconciles textbook path cylinders with mathlib measure cylinders via successor-of-finite-path spaces,Ionescu-Tulcea and pushforward. History-dependent deterministic schedulers induce Markov chains whose states are paths. Expected nonnegative extended-real cost is a supremum of finite-horizon path sums. Theorem12 gives angelic/maximizing Bellman least-fixed-point equality generally; Theorem19 gives demonic/minimizing equality for finitely branching MDPs by constructing an optimal memoryless scheduler,avoiding an unjustified interchange of infimum and supremum. pGCL has dependent typed states and shallow function-valued expressions inside a deep program syntax; small-step rules lead to a sink-extended operational MDP. The soundness recipe sandwiches an expectation transformer against a higher-order Bellman least fixed point. wp includes tick costs and a least loop fixed point; wlp uses one-bounded expectations,a greatest loop fixed point and ignores ticks. wfp uses least loop fixed points and counts failed observations; complementing expectations and swapping the nondeterminism optimization relates it to wlp. Conditional expectation is defined as wp/wlp(1),rather than a compositional transformer. Idle induction checks states agreeing with the initial values of all unmodified variables. HeyLo is deeply embedded with Nat,ENNReal,Bool variable types; HeyVL is loop-free and its computable vp produces formulas. Syntax-level spGCL loops carry invariants. Encoded wp overapproximates wp; encoded wlp underapproximates wlp. Assuming a candidate bound,encoding the program and asserting the postexpectation yields a sound bound when the VC is valid. Loop encodings use modified-variable havoc and validate,with dual operations for upper bounds.

assumptions_limits: MDP transitions are PMFs: discrete probabilities,not arbitrary continuous-distribution kernels. Every state has an enabled action. Costs are nonnegative extended reals; state space may be infinite. General angelic Bellman theorem and finitely-branching demonic theorem have different assumptions. Finitely branching means both successor states and enabled actions are finite at each state; the pGCL operational model satisfies finite-step branching. Memoryless optimal scheduler construction is for the demonic cost problem,not a universal optimality theorem for all objectives. wlp and wfp operate on expectations bounded by1; wlp loop invariants and wlp postexpectations must respect this bound. Failed observations are distinguished from nontermination and successful termination. Conditional rescaling is defined via wp/wlp,not given an independently compositional rule. wp soundness for expected cost does not by itself prove that every program terminates: unbounded loops/nontermination remain represented by the semantics. Almost-sure termination and finite expected runtime are distinct,as the introduction explicitly warns. HeyLo embedding limits variable types to Nat,extended nonnegative reals and Bool for expression reification,while underlying pGCL state types are more general. HeyVL has no loops/recursion; loop reasoning depends on encoded invariant rules. Authors report formalization on Lean/mathlib and provide a Zenodo DOI and linked Paper.lean theorem index. This reading did not inspect source axioms/admissions,recheck Lean,run Caesar or audit correspondence with the actual Caesar implementation. The proved embedding/encodings do not establish SMT/model-checker implementation correctness. Related almost-sure termination verification for randomized distributed algorithms is cited as a prior Caesar application,not verified as a concrete case in this paper. GenAI declaration limits LLM use to formatting code snippets; no LLM proof-agent experiment.
use_for_goal: Provides a concrete trust-chain pattern for evaluating automated specifications/proofs: prove the intermediate assertion language and VC encoding sound against operational semantics and foundational probability,retain bounding/invariant/finiteness premises,and distinguish a checked VC from validation of the encoding and implementation. Supports future probabilistic distributed-protocol verification; the paper cites such applications but verifies the framework and a toy cost example. No Verus,Rust,TLA+ or LLM agent benchmark. Connections to those workflows are reader inference.

title: SEEV: Synthesis with Efficient Exact Verification for ReLU Neural Barrier Functions
what: Introduces SEEV, a synthesis-and-verification loop for ReLU neural control barrier functions (NCBFs) on continuous nonlinear control-affine systems. It regularizes activation patterns along the barrier boundary and exactly checks correctness, hyperplane, and hinge conditions required by a nonsmooth Nagumo-style safety theorem. The model is xdot=f(x)+g(x)u with safe set C={h>=0} and inner set D={bθ>=0}. Proposition 1 requires feasible controls on every boundary activation set and D⊆C. Training combines correctness, derivative/feasibility, and a boundary activation regularizer; outer CEGIS adds verifier counterexamples. The verifier finds an initial boundary activation set by a line segment and LP, enumerates all boundary hyperplanes with neural breadth-first search, enumerates boundary hinges by LP, then applies cheap sufficient checks before nonlinear exact checks (dReal where needed). Theorem 2 gives a valid NCBF when all checks pass. Experiments on Darboux, obstacle avoidance, hi-ord8 and spacecraft rendezvous show major speedups; SR 6D L4/M8 falls from 298.7s baseline to 60.1s, while dReal/Z3 are unavailable or time out in many cases. Regularization cuts SR boundary hyperplanes from 6218 to 627 at equal coverage in one configuration.

title: ShieldAgent: Shielding Agents via Verifiable Safety Policy Reasoning
what: An LLM guardrail converts natural-language policies into logical rules, refines their predicates, clusters relevant rules by action, assigns observed predicate values through tools and generated code, then thresholds a learned probabilistic rule model. Reports improved classification and conditional online policy compliance for web agents. The paper calls its probability comparison a dynamic safety guarantee, but supplies no invariant theorem establishing it. Separates action constraints from background state rules; uses GPT-4o policy extraction, verifiability refinement and redundancy pruning; learns soft Markov-logic weights rather than requiring every rule to hold. Gives a hybrid history/workflow memory, specialized search/check tools, an action-circuit training algorithm, attack-generated data and a fully worked Reddit bio example. Appendices expose translation, predicate-binding and probability inconsistencies that formal checking alone does not repair.
assumptions_limits: Logical checking is conditional on correct policy extraction, refinement, merging, action retrieval and assignment of observed facts. GPT-4o performs policy translation and optional human experts may correct rules. No equivalence proof establishes fidelity to original policies or completeness of retrieved constraints. Rules have finite learned weights, explicitly allowing tradeoffs to reduce false positives. A positive likelihood margin is not a requirement that every policy holds. Negative rule weights are not explicitly excluded. Classification accuracy is an empirical property of the learned rule model, not a universal enforcement guarantee. Equation 5 compares probabilities with one action bit flipped and state predicates fixed. The source supplies neither environment transition dynamics nor a proved inductive invariant/control-barrier condition linking that comparison to safe future trajectories. Current-state likelihood improvement does not by itself prove temporal safety. Predicates are grounded by learned search/binary-check models, moderation APIs, external sources and generated code. Observability and truthful, complete interaction history are required. Specialized operations use fine-tuned InternVL2-2B; formal tools include Stormpy in the main text and Prover9/Mace4 in the worked appendix. LTL over finite traces is defined in Appendix C.3, but most displayed rules and the worked code are propositional. The paper does not specify an end-to-end implementation or correctness argument for temporal monitoring, finite-trace termination, solver unknowns, missing observations or an inability to assign every predicate. The training recipe allows real labels or simulated pseudo-labels but does not give sufficient actual training/test splits, model hyperparameters, number of optimization steps, specialized-tool training data or random seeds to independently reproduce all reported scores. Algorithm 1 loops until all predicates are assigned without an explicit fallback budget. Human annotators manually label safety and violated policies. Annotator count, disagreement resolution, agreement rates and a detailed labeling protocol are absent. Policies include empirically constructed constraints as well as platform documents. Benchmark attacks are targeted to extracted policy violations. Existing benchmarks are augmented with policies and safe/unsafe trajectories. Scores concern those augmented guardrail tasks, not the original benchmarks unchanged. AWM is the protected web agent; results do not establish safety of arbitrary agents or environments.
use_for_goal: Relevant to LLM-written specifications and evaluation: concrete policy-translation prompts, grounding/tool boundaries, semantic counterexamples and soft-versus-hard constraint tradeoffs. Useful comparison for agent-assisted verification pipelines, where solver success must be separated from faithful requirements and empirical scores. Distributed-system or Verus safety would require independently justified specifications, program links, environment assumptions and hard proof obligations.

title: Should We Learn Probabilistic Models for Model Checking? A New Approach and An Empirical Study
what: Many automated system analysis techniques (e.g., model checking, model-based testing) rely on first obtaining a model of the system under anal- ysis. System modeling is often done manually, which is often considered as a hindrance to adopt model-based system analysis and development techniques. To overcome this problem, researchers have proposed to automatically “learn” models based on sample system executions and shown that the learned models can be useful sometimes.

title: Show Me The Money: An Exercise in Proof-Driven Software Understanding
what: Retrospective human-led analysis of Stellar SDEX exchangeV10 uses LLM-generated PVS abstractions, interactive theorem proving and SeaBMC symbolic C++ harnesses to recover rounding invariants and test a supposedly unreachable exception. Authors report 37 of 38 lemmas/typechecker obligations proved, establishing P1–P3 in their model. The remaining P4 obligation leads to an executable local exception witness; reachability through upstream production callers is left unresolved. Records the actual human/LLM/prover division of work, the distinction between generating and discharging type obligations, the asymmetry of the one-percent bound, exact harness assumptions and concrete exception inputs. Separates PVS model proofs and parallel code-property checks from a general abstraction-to-C++ refinement theorem. Preserves unresolved caller assumptions, schematic figure issues and the absence of a measured maintenance or controlled LLM experiment.
assumptions_limits: §§1–3: the target is a mostly functional arithmetic function in deployed blockchain infrastructure, not consensus, network behavior, smart contracts or the entire order book. Source has 1344 C/C++ lines plus 758 comment lines; abstraction has 260 PVS lines plus 84 comment lines. Code structure and substantial informal invariants are important favorable inputs. §3.1: humans copied full source to ChatGPT 5 Pro, fed PVS errors back and repeated with Claude Opus 4 with qualitatively similar results. Invalid DIV, misplaced IMPORTING and invented libraries needed repairs. Models originally represented exceptions as unused booleans. Humans split theories into three files and supplied interface preconditions. This is not autonomous proof generation. §3.1 footnote4: passing the initial typechecker phase means name resolution and sound generation of type-correctness conditions (TCCs), not their discharge. TCC generation itself is distinct from a complete checked proof. §3.2: the introduction says 16 generated lemmas and 22 generated proof obligations were proved, but the detailed account reports 37/38 and one failed P4 obligation. Retain the detailed denominator; do not claim all 38 obligations or absence of exceptions were established. §§2–3/Figs3–4: P1 favors the offer remaining in the book. P2 bounds relative rounding error by 1% for a single matched offer. P3 permits path-payment asymmetry: error favoring the wheat seller can be unbounded, whereas the sheep-favoring case remains bounded; non-path exchanges exceeding the bound are rejected. These claims depend on input bounds and formalized preconditions. §3.2/Fig5: PVS assert/grind use Shostak reasoning; Yices2 handles nonlinear arithmetic. Type subranges and explicit bounds matter. The displayed Price uses uint32 fields although the source comment says int32_t; uint32 includes zero while the shown posint64 obligations require 100*n>0 and 100*d>0. The schematic includes ellipses and does not show all premises, so it alone neither proves positivity nor establishes unsoundness of the full artifact. §3.3: C++ unit proofs encode PVS type constraints as assumptions, call the implementation and assert corresponding properties; SeaHorn lowers harness and source to LLVM for SeaBMC. These are parallel property checks and a sanity check on relevance. The paper supplies no general relational refinement/equivalence theorem covering the PVS abstraction and all C++ operational semantics. §3.3/Fig6: price n,d are nondeterministic signed 32-bit integers with n>0,d>0. Four maxima are signed 64-bit; assumptions constrain maxWheatSend>=0, maxSheepSend>0 and maxWheatReceive>0. No positivity assumption is shown for maxSheepReceive. The postcondition is !res.wheatStays || (res.numSheepSend>0 && res.numWheatReceived>=0). §3.3/Fig7: a counterexample confirms local exception behavior for the stated harness domain. Developers believe upstream code excludes it; that caller claim is not proved. A failed PVS proof alone would not establish a code bug, and the witness does not establish an exploitable end-to-end production vulnerability. Algorithm2: graphical line14 asserts round=PPS_SEND implies Ss≠0; extracted text loses the negation. Prose p.237 calls it line15, but printed line15 zeroes amounts. The function declaration omits several variables used by its body, so the pseudocode is schematic rather than a complete executable specification. §4/Fig8: revised prompt asks for total mathematical functions, explicit bounds and exceptions converted to preconditions/subtypes. It explicitly excludes full C++ semantics and asks only to state lemmas. Reader inference: strengthening a precondition can remove the failing behavior from the model; callers must separately establish it. No memory, exception or arithmetic semantic correspondence follows from well-typed PVS alone. §4: claims of low manual effort, transfer to larger codebases and useful continuous integration are qualitative. No attempt counts, token costs, elapsed human/prover/model-checker times, resource limits, unroll bounds, solver configurations, controlled comparison or repeated-run variance are reported. §4: exchangeV10 did not change during the exercise. Maintenance/evolution benefits and automatic harness/proof updates are proposed opportunities, not measured longitudinal outcomes. Conclusion still says specification finalization and broader coverage are ongoing. Trusted components include human interpretation, abstraction/precondition selection, PVS and its proof/solver integration, source-to-LLVM compilation, SeaBMC and harness construction. No independent artifact execution, proof replay or upstream-call analysis was performed for this record. No Verus, Rust or TLA+ result is reported.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: directly relevant to evaluating LLM-generated specifications and proofs for distributed-system components. Keep candidate generation, accepted typing, discharged proofs, concrete code checks and reachable production errors as separate evidence. Recover informal invariants from comments, preserve exact caller assumptions, and test allegedly unreachable branches with symbolic harnesses. The arithmetic case supports this workflow but does not establish distributed protocol correctness, automatic code/model equivalence or a measured advantage for an LLM model.

title: Multi-agent Safety Verification Using Symmetry Transformations.
what: Develops symmetry-based reachability caching for parameterized hybrid/dynamical agents. Equivariant dynamics map modes and initial sets into a common virtual system; cached virtual reachtubes are transformed back instead of recomputed. CacheReach implements tube and safety caches, supports multi-agent collision checks, and derives finite-cache proofs of unbounded-time/agent safety under scenario-coverage assumptions. Theorem 2 proves transformed over-approximated reachtubes remain sound for parameterized systems; Theorem 3 constructs a virtual parameter pv and inverse transformations for every mode. symComputeReachtube covers an initial set with cached tubes, extends/truncates horizons, computes uncovered regions, and unions results (Theorem 4). symSafetyVerif reuses monotone cache results; unsafe answers can be false positives because over-approximation and cache cells may include extra states, while safe answers are sound (Theorem 5). Theorem 6 lifts one safe virtual scenario to infinitely many transformed scenarios, and symMultiVerif time-aligns guard-triggered mode tubes for pairwise collision checks.

3-D linear and 4-D nonlinear aircraft models

assumptions_limits: Agent vector fields must be Lipschitz and Γ-equivariant with invertible transformations; virtual-system coverage requires every mode to map to a fixed pv. Reachtubes are over-approximations, so unsafe reports may be spurious; cache cells and grid quantization trade savings for conservatism. CacheReach assumes agents share dynamics and do not interact, and unbounded safety requires proving no new virtual scenarios appear. Experiments cover only 3-D linear and 4-D fixed-wing models.
