title: Evaluating Model Testing and Model Checking for Finding Requirements Violations in Simulink Models
short_name: Simulink model testing versus model checking
what: Compares search-based model testing with SMT-based model checking for requirements violations in eleven industrial Simulink CPS models, formalizing requirements in Signal Temporal Logic and measuring faults found, proofs, inconclusive outcomes, and runtime. The study categorizes benchmark models as open/feedback-loop and by state-machine, continuous, nonlinear/non-algebraic, matrix, and machine-learning features; translates 92 natural-language requirements into STL and robustness fitness functions; and runs Hill-Climbing testing against QVTrace SMT checking and bounded model checking. Across the benchmark, testing found 40 violations (including 17 that checking could not find), checking proved 41 requirements and found 23 violations, and the combination resolved 81/92. Twelve violations appeared beyond BMC bounds (for example, Two Tanks failures around 500–1000 steps despite bounds below 270). The paper turns these observations into five lessons about applicability, bounds, speed, scalability, and heuristic choice.

assumptions_limits: The benchmark has eleven models and seeded faults from one aerospace/defense company under NDA; results may not generalize to other CPS domains or tools. Model testing is stochastic/search-guided and only demonstrates failures, so repeated runs and heuristic choices affect coverage. QVTrace/SMT cannot handle some continuous dynamics, non-algebraic functions, machine-learning components, or large translations; simplification/discretization can alter behavior. BMC proofs are bounded and may miss late failures. The study compares one Hill-Climbing tester and QVTrace, not all possible implementations, and no absence-of-fault guarantee follows from testing.

Its STL-to-robustness translation, bounded-search failures, and model-feature taxonomy inform how Verus/TLA+ users should separate exhaustive proof from bug-finding and report inconclusive analyses.

title: Skipping Refinement
what: Introduces skipping refinement for optimized reactive systems whose concrete implementation can perform several abstract specification steps in one step. It defines skipping simulation by finite path partitions, defines refinement using a relation and refinement map, and gives well-founded and reduced well-founded skipping relations. Theorems 2 and 3 establish soundness and completeness of the reduced proof rule; Theorem 1 shows equivalence of the two local formulations. Three case studies cover a JVM-inspired buffered stack machine, an optimized memory controller, and scalar-to-vector SIMD compiler transformation. The proof rule handles four local cases: direct matching, left stuttering with a well-founded rank, right stuttering with a natural rank, and bounded-or-general reachability for skipping. Completeness constructs ordinal ranks from computation trees, and the authors argue refinement maps always exist. In experiments, BSTK/STK and OptMEMC/MEMC models ranged from 24K gates/500 latches to 2M gates/23K latches; four model checkers (TIP, IIMC, BLIMC, SUPER PROVE) were run with a 900-second timeout on a Xeon X5677, 16 cores, 3.4GHz, 96GB. Most I/O-equivalence configurations timed out while all except TIP solved all configurations with skipping refinement, with several-orders-of-magnitude improvement. ACL2s proved the infinite-state SIMD case; the authors report less manual effort than I/O-equivalence proofs.
numbers: {'printed_pages': 17, 'model_checker_count': 4, 'timeout_seconds': 900, 'gate_range': '24K–2M', 'latch_range': '500–23K', 'hardware_cases': 2, 'compiler_cases': 1}
assumptions_limits: Transition systems have left-total relations and possibly infinite state spaces. The local reachability argument relies on a constant bound on the number of abstract steps a concrete step can skip for the optimized systems considered; unrestricted reachability is otherwise nonlocal. The SIMD case simplifies states to instruction sequence, program counter and store, assumes that a SIMD instruction operates on two sets of data operands simultaneously and basic-block parallelism, and excludes control flow. The paper says existing correctness notions do not allow skipping; its model-checking comparison uses I/O equivalence as a straightforward baseline, not an equivalent proof obligation. Experiments use relatively simple configurations and public artifacts were recorded but not rerun here. The paper leaves characterizing which temporal properties are preserved by skipping refinement to future work; it does not establish arbitrary temporal-property transfer.
use_for_goal: Directly informs formal verification of optimized distributed/concurrent implementations: it separates stuttering from skipping and offers local proof obligations that can be automated. The paper predates Verus and does not evaluate Rust, TLA+, distributed protocols, or LLM agents.

title: SL-VC: A Benchmark and Automated Framework for Separation Logic Verification Condition Proving
what: Introduces SL-VC, 289 separation-logic verification conditions from textbook data structures and real C system code, and SPLIT, an LLM-friendly Rocq tactic library plus two-stage spatial/pure proof workflow. SPLIT decomposes mixed entailments into spatial elimination and independent pure goals, using explicit tactics such as split_pure_spatial, cancel, sep_apply and pure_solve with verifier-driven repair. The benchmark includes linked lists, merge sort, trees, LiteOS circular lists and mini-gmp; the full 288-VC evaluation and 207-VC core subset separate benchmark construction from prover comparisons. CoqHammer is evaluated as an alternative pure-stage solver, and failures concentrate in arithmetic-heavy mini-gmp and recurrence-like goals.

title: Prototyping the Semantics of a DSL using ASF+SDF: Link to Formal Verification of DSL Models
what: Prototypes operational semantics for the Simple Language of Communicating Objects (SLCO), a concurrent communicating-object DSL, by translating SLCO models through an intermediate CS representation into labeled transition systems. The LTS output connects the DSL to Dot, mCRL2, CADP and other existing visualization and verification tools. SLCO models classes, objects, state machines, typed channels, synchronous/asynchronous lossless/lossy communication, guards, effects, signal reception and delay triggers. ASF conditional rewrite rules implement SLCO2CS execution steps; CS2LTS maps configurations to states and steps to labeled edges. Reduced LTSs can compare transformed models for observable-behavior preservation, while larger LTSs can be checked by CADP or mCRL2.

title: Model Checking Spatial Logics for Closure Spaces
venue: Logical Methods in Computer Science 12(4:2), arXiv:1609.06513
what: Extends Spatial Logic for Closure Spaces (SLCS) with propagation and path-based surrounded operators, introduces collective SLCS (CSLCS) for sets of points, and supplies model-checking algorithms and an OCaml proof-of-concept tool for finite quasi-discrete closure models. The paper formalizes closure spaces as a generalization covering topological and graph structures, distinguishes Euclidean and directed quasi-discrete paths, and proves that its path-based surrounded operator coincides with the earlier boundary-based until on quasi-discrete models. CSLCS adds share and group operators; group satisfaction reduces to finding a path-connected superset, and derived operators express collective surrounding, partitioning and reachability. For finite quasi-discrete models, the SLCS checker uses recursive satisfaction plus breadth-first propagation, while CSLCS uses Tarjan-style strongly connected component search. Correctness and O(k·(|X|+|R|)) worst-case bounds are proved for formula size k.

title: Liveness of Randomised Parameterised Systems under Arbitrary Schedulers
what: Presents a fully automatic CEGAR method for liveness of randomised parameterised systems under arbitrary schedulers by reducing probabilistic protocols to two-player reachability games and synthesising regular progress relations with L*-learning and SAT. The method ignores nonzero probability values, retaining transition topology, and represents configurations as words with length-preserving transducers. Regular advice bits consist of an inductive reachable over-approximation and a well-founded progress relation; VERIFY checks four conditions while SYNTHESISE searches deterministic automata via SAT and eliminates counterexamples. An incremental variant composes disjunctive advice, refines reachable/winning sets, learns inductive invariants, and exploits automorphisms such as ring rotation. Soundness follows from the advice conditions; a completeness claim is given under existence of regular advice, minimum-length selection and minimum automata.

assumptions_limits: Each finite instance is treated as an MDP whose liveness depends only on transition topology, so actual nonzero probabilities are abstracted away; this proves almost-sure reachability only under the chosen scheduler/game interpretation. Systems are encoded by finite-state letter-to-letter transducers, excluding non-length-preserving/data-rich protocols; fairness is not handled and is future work. Results are proof-of-concept on finite benchmark encodings, with hard-coded invariant precision n=5 and substantial SAT/refinement cost for complex cases.

title: Model Checking Linear Temporal Logic with Standpoint Modalities
what: Extends standpoint linear temporal logic (SLTL) with four history-information semantics in addition to step semantics: pure observation, public-history, decremental, and incremental. It supplies one history-DFA/model-checking construction that handles all five semantics, translates pure-observation SLTL to perfect-recall LTLK, and derives complexity bounds separating semantics and standpoint alternation depth. The formal semantics use separate finite transition systems Ta whose labels expose subsets Pa of propositions and define future-history satisfaction. Decremental nesting observes Pa intersections, while incremental nesting unions coalition observations; Example 3.5 gives explicit formulas and systems separating all five semantics. The algorithm computes bottom-up history DFAs using powerset constructions and products with subordinate DFAs, then applies standard LTL model checking. The paper proves PSPACE-completeness for full step/public SLTL and depth-1 pure-observation/decremental/incremental fragments, single-exponential time for step/public/decremental (and disjoint-observation pure observation), N-fold exponential time and (N-1)-EXPSPACE upper bound for incremental, and (d-1)-EXPSPACE membership for pure observation at alternation depth d.

assumptions_limits: Transition systems are finite, total, and have unique initial states; agent systems label only Pa subsets and agents may guess unobserved propositions. Complexity results rely on finite-state automata and alternation depth; pure-observation translation assumes perfect-recall LTLK and the improved time bound requires pairwise-disjoint Pa. No implementation or empirical benchmark is reported; the conclusion explicitly leaves experimental evaluation, stronger lower bounds, and analogous decremental space improvements as future work.

title: Model Checking of Workflow Nets with Tables and Constraints
what: Redefines workflow nets with tables as WFTC-nets by adding guard-constraint sets, generates a constraint-aware state reachability graph (SRGC) that removes pseudo states, and defines database-oriented CTL (DCTL) to express table-data design requirements and data-flow properties. A C++ WFTCMC tool implements SRGC generation and DCTL model checking. The paper formalizes data refinement of abstract data items, table records, and three-valued guards; firing rules require both Petri enablement and guard constraints. Algorithm 1 explores reachable configurations while refining only data needed by reads/writes/selects/inserts/deletes/updates. DCTL extends CTL with quantification over table records and attribute comparisons; Algorithms 2–7 compute satisfaction sets bottom-up and fixed points with stated O((n+r)|φ|) complexity for verification. The motivating vehicle-management model shows how guard relationships eliminate impossible combinations and reveal a license-consistency defect invisible to soundness alone.

title: Spatiotemporal Robustness of Temporal Logic Tasks Using Multi-Objective Reasoning
what: Defines spatiotemporal robustness (STR) for discrete-time temporal-logic tasks as the Pareto-maximal set of jointly admissible spatial and temporal perturbation magnitudes. It gives sound under-approximating robust semantics with min/max operations over Pareto sets, predicate-level algorithms and case studies for fighter-jet and robotaxi trajectories. STR treats spatial noise and asynchronous per-signal time shifts as separate objectives; a scalar pair of independent robustness values can be unsound. For STL in positive-normal form, robust semantics recursively combine predicate STR using downward-closure min/max. Theorem 1 proves every robust-semantic point is dominated by a true STR point, yielding sound task satisfaction but conservative margins. Predicate STR is reformulated as a monotone worst-case-margin constraint; Algorithm 1 scans temporal shells and solves robust spatial optimization, with a signed-distance shortcut from 1-Lipschitzness. Algorithm 2 propagates Pareto envelopes through parse trees.

The robust semantics require STL positive-normal syntax and can under-approximate true STR. title: Specifying Message Formats with Contiguity Types
what: Introduces contiguity types, a formal-language layer for self-describing binary messages with records, arrays and guarded alternatives. Defines semantics over byte strings and a matcher computing field slices. Proves termination, substitution reconstruction and soundness in HOL4; completeness is not proved. Extends the matcher and proofs with empty languages and tagged lists. Applies filters/parsers to OpenUxAS LMCP messages. The formalism treats a base contiguity type as a set of strings of fixed width rather than a set of program values. Array lengths and alternatives can read earlier message fields through L-values; partial expression evaluation yields an empty language. The matcher returns an assignment from L-values to byte slices, enabling filters and test generation. Recursive list encodings handle finite nested structures but recursive first-order terms require mutual recursive constructions. The UxAS application adds semantic assertions for GPS ranges, bounded optional arrays and enumerations; filters and parsers were instantiated and tested with the UxAS simulator. The HOL4 model is supplied as supplementary material. Assertions should precede arrays so limits are checked before allocation. First-order terms with nested recursive term lists are a challenge needing more elaborate mutual recursion, rather than an already verified general construction.
numbers: {'application': 'LMCP messages in OpenUxAS; payload and key-value arrays bounded at 8 and 32 in shown example'}
assumptions_limits: Messages are contiguous byte arrays/strings; interpretation functions map leaf byte strings to numbers/booleans. Expression evaluation can fail when a referenced L-value is absent; the presentation omits error-handling details but HOL4 formalization models option failure. Current matcher is interpreted and copies or indexes slices; compilation to CakeML and a correctness proof are future work. Application testing reports successful simulator tests, but no size, speed or fault-detection measurements are given. Matcher soundness and reconstruction are proved; completeness has not been tackled. Tagged-list extension verified, generalized nested-recursive term handling needs further work.
use_for_goal: Useful verified-message-format layer for distributed systems: it can generate parsers/filters from specifications and enforce semantic constraints before Verus/TLA+ protocol logic consumes messages. The HOL4 proof and explicit failure semantics suggest reusable proof obligations for Rust serializers. No LLM component.

quotes.text: The matcher has been used to enforce semantic well-formedness conditions on complex message formats for an autonomous unmanned avionics system.
Our assumption is that a message is the result of a map from structured data and we will rely on a basic collection of programming language types to capture that structure.
If an expression evaluation fails, the language being constructed will be ∅.

For our purposes, namely decoding datastructures in binary format, the central decoding algorithm is a matcher: given a contiguity type τ and a string s, the matcher will either fail, or succeed with an assignment θ : lval 7→ string mapping each L-value in τ to its corresponding slice of s.
The filters and parsers have been added to an existing UxAS design and successfully tested with the UxAS simulator.

We have designed, formalized, proved correct, implemented, and applied a specification language for message formats, based on formal languages and the venerable notion of L- and R-values from imperative programming.

title: SpecSyn: LLM-based Synthesis and Refinement of Formal Specifications for Real-world Program Verification
what: SpecSyn combines top-down AST/dependency decomposition and sketch planning with bottom-up ACSL generation, verifier-guided repair, and variant-discrimination refinement. Semantic-non-equivalent mutations test whether candidate specifications reject changed programs; undistinguished variants are fed back for stronger specifications. Tarjan SCCs produce dependency-respecting segments, and depth-first postorder handles nested POIs such as loop invariants and function postconditions. At each POI, Frama-C/WP verifies generated candidates, returns errors for repair, and deduplicates accepted specifications. Variant discriminative rate measures the fraction of 188 mutation operators (35 equivalent operators removed; GCC -O2 TCE filters equivalents) rejected by the specification set. Experiments use 50 real-world C programs, seven verification benchmarks totaling 1,421 targets, three LLMs, and 17 trained reviewers.

title: A Composable Specification Language for Reinforcement Learning Tasks
what: Introduces SPECTRL, a language with achieve, ensuring, sequencing (;), and disjunction (or) over state predicates. A compiler builds a task monitor (an automaton with registers), augments state and action spaces, and generates quantitative plus subtask-progress reward shaping. Any RL optimizer can then learn a policy for the compiled MDP; the projected policy carries monitor memory. The monitor resolves non-Markovian sequencing by recording completed subtasks and exposes nondeterministic transition choices as actions. Quantitative semantics use max/min over trajectory segments; shaped rewards preserve rollout ordering under explicit lower/upper bounds on final and progress rewards. Theorem 3.1 links Boolean satisfaction to existence of a positive-reward augmented run; Theorem 3.2 proves ordering properties of the shaped reward. SPECTRL is implemented with ARS and modular neural networks, and is tested on seven waypoint/obstacle/fuel tasks plus continuous-action CartPole.

assumptions_limits: Policy guarantees are probabilistic optimization objectives, not formal synthesis guarantees for stochastic dynamics. Reward shaping’s policy-order preservation assumes deterministic MDPs for the stated guarantee and requires known bounds C_l and C_u. The language has finite-horizon rollout semantics and user-supplied quantitative predicate functions whose sign must match Boolean truth. Experiments use a 2-D noisy point robot, horizon 40, hand-designed tasks and ARS; scalability beyond the tested nested sequencing depth and other RL algorithms is not established.

This is relevant to designing temporal contracts for distributed agents, but empirical policy success should not be read as formal correctness under stochastic or unmodeled environments.

title: Simplifying Loop Invariant Generation Using Splitter Predicates
what: Defines splitter and phase-splitter predicates that decompose multi-phase loops into semantically equivalent sequences of single-phase loops. Weakest-precondition and SMT checks find phase transitions, allowing ordinary conjunctive invariant generators to prove assertions requiring disjunctions. A Hoare-triple theorem proves splitter equivalence; a second theorem adds conditions ensuring the branch predicate is constant in each phase. The recursive inside-out algorithm computes a weakest precondition, validates the remaining conditions with an SMT solver, splits and recursively simplifies each loop. A SAIL/Mistral prototype uses SSA and quantifier elimination. Experiments compare Interproc polyhedra and InvGen on literature and real-code benchmarks, including stronger assertion variants.

first nine benchmark comparison
6 Interproc and 4 InvGen previously failing cases repaired
90 ms maximum splitter computation
assumptions_limits: The formal language is integer-valued and restricts holes from occurring inside nested loops; weakest-precondition approximations for nested loops rely on an invariant generator. The method targets conditionals with a fixed number of phase transitions and can miss loops alternating behavior. SMT quantifier elimination and path constraints may be expensive; mergesort demonstrates incomparable/non-improving widening results.
use_for_goal: Shows a lightweight SMT transformation that turns disjunctive loop reasoning into compositional conjunctive obligations, a useful pattern for proof automation in systems code.

title: Spoq: Scaling Machine-Checkable Systems Verification in Coq
what: Spoq translates Clang-generated LLVM IR and Armv8 assembly into structured Coq programs, then automates layered specifications and refinement proofs using CCALs. Low-level functional specifications aggregate instruction semantics; high-level specifications unfold/simplify lower interfaces into self-contained transitions. Coq checks generated proofs including Z3-suggested transformations. Evaluates translation coverage on five codebases and verifies updated SeKVM trusted core, followed by a separately written confidentiality/integrity refinement to an ideal machine. Records every CFG rewrite and specification transformation, loop ranking/branch/manual-data-abstraction limits, SC/Arm-memory bridge, security declassification model and full trust chain. Saves translation numerators/denominators, all manual-effort table cells, generated sizes and application/platform details. Distinguishes generated behavioral equivalence from desired correctness, translating Linux from verifying Linux, and changed-version/security-method comparison from a controlled labor experiment.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2,8: LLVM-to-Coq translator/CFG restructuring is unverified and trusted. TCB explicitly includes Clang/LLVM toolchains, translator, LLVM/assembly semantic definitions and ultimately proof checker/model adequacy. Earlier wording only part unverified needs trust is restricted to Spoq internals, not whole stack. Coq checking does not establish the correctness of trusted translation, compilation, runtime/hardware semantics or intended property. §§2,7.2: Automatically generated specifications intentionally preserve code behavior, including bugs; behavioral refinement alone does not prove desired functionality. User must prove an independent high-level property, or supply an independently justified top-level specification. The SeKVM security proof trusts approximately200LOC ideal machine/declassification policy, not the much larger generated real-system specification as an axiom. §§4,8: Broad full-C claims mean using Clang to accept unmodified GNU-C constructs rather than verifying all C semantics/programs. Prototype supports only a subset of LLVM IR and Arm assembly; advanced callbr/invoke/resume unsupported. Only Armv8 assembly currently parsed; automatic assembly specification/proof synthesis handles no-jump procedures. All translated functions in broad-codebase experiment are representation successes, not correctness proofs. §§2–3: User supplies layer configuration, bottom machine model completion, ranking function per loop, and manual data abstractions/refinements. A layer calls only lower layers, so A→B→C requires three layers. Generated global memory/getters/setters omit concurrency event/oracle structures; these must be added manually. Cyclic function dependencies/general recursion support is not demonstrated. §4: CPU-local concurrency partitions memory into CPU-private, lock-protected and lock-free objects. Lock access requires local CPU ownership; lock-free access emits global events with environmental oracle steps. Model assumes sequential consistency. Propagation to Arm relaxed memory additionally requires six weak-data-race-free conditions as in VRM; SeKVM authors report doing this but omit details. No blanket proof for arbitrary relaxed-memory C programs follows. §§3,5: Loop ranking must be nonnegative/decrease, supplied by user and checked with xlia/induction. Fixed-point recursion has fuel and break/return flags; after flags set it preserves state through remaining recursive steps. Rank0 must not silently truncate a live loop. Loops within conditional branches need manual copied/adjusted induction templates in current implementation. No generic automatic termination/invariant discovery theorem. §5: Assembly-C linking follows AAPCS64; caller-saved registers become UNKNOWN after calls and cannot be read before write. Inline assembly may use declared C input/output operands, system registers/constants; direct general-purpose-register access disallowed. These restrictions constrain supported code despite broad inline-assembly headline. Assembly branches require user-written specification/proof. §§3,6: Automatic lifting applies to identity/no-data-abstraction layers. Mapping arrays/page tables/locks/ownership to abstract maps requires user relations, operations and proofs. Self-contained means no calls to other layers except bottom machine model, not an independently meaningful security specification or absence of all low-level detail. §6: Z3 proposes branch/rely/math simplifications; annotations guide Coq hrefine reconstruction and are removed by a final refinement. Z3/spec/proof generators are outside soundness TCB when all required proofs check. Coq tactic failure still requires manual completion. Half-second Z3 timeout reduces simplification opportunities rather than permitting unproved solver facts; large functions can take>30min. §7.1 Figure8: C translation experiment uses default source build configurations; Linux v5.15 specifically allnoconfig. Makefiles may be changed to emit LLVM .ll and ClightGen unsupported flags filtered. Reported functions are those in tested builds, not every possible kernel configuration/source path. Broad translation does not verify Linux/OpenSSL/Redis/Memcached/mbedtls properties or assembly compatibility of every function. §7.2: Verified SeKVM is already retrofitted KVM/Arm trusted core, not the entire unmodified vanilla Linux/KVM codebase. Updated RaspberryPi4 support is a modest code change with same34layers. Spoq avoids additional parser-driven source alterations to that core; verified3.8KLOC C/assembly matches compiled source, conditional on trusted compiler/toolchain. Source proof is not an independently verified binary compiler chain. §7.2 Table1: Proof cost is manually written Coq LOC, not elapsed developer time, person-months or a randomized same-version comparison. Baseline is previous SeKVM version, machine model differs, security proof changes from noninterference/data-oracles to ideal/real. Security LOC38% reduction explicitly unrelated to Spoq; functional79% reduction and total74% should not be causally conflated. §7.2: Trusted-core all3.8KLOC translation and checked proof claims are authors’ results, not replayed here. One security use case and five translation codebases do not show general automatic proof of arbitrary concurrent systems. Article gives proof strategies/examples, not complete machine-checked metatheorems of translator soundness or every reconstruction algorithm. §7.2 Table1: Original functional categories add33.5K and security38.3K. Spoq rounded component cells plus26rankinglines add≈7.026K/10.026K versus printed7.0K/10.0K; compatible with rounding. Summary ratios1/3specLOC and1.4proofLOC use approximate categories, not exact timed effort. Preserve printed percentages and units. §7.2 Figure 10: Benchmarks compare source-verified SeKVM, vanilla KVM and native on Raspberry Pi 4B, with resources matched to two CPUs and 4GB RAM. SeKVM guest uses a modified virtio driver; the other guest uses vanilla Linux 5.4; host is 5.4.55. Guest changes and one platform constrain comparison. Bars normalize native to one; lower is better. The below-15% overhead claim uses vanilla KVM as baseline. §§7.2,8: No benchmark run counts/confidence intervals/random variation are reported. Code-generation runtime2h on8core2.3GHzXeonE5-2686v4/32GB differs from execution benchmark platform; Coq-check time is not separately isolated. Timing/labor adjectives are author assessment. No concrete newly discovered vulnerability list or proof failure corpus is supplied. §9: Related-work broad impossibility/completeness claims are authors’ comparisons, not independent findings about all versions of those frameworks. No distributed-consensus theorem, Verus/Rust proof, TLA+ model or LLM experiment. Paper demonstrates proof-producing automation relevant to agents, not evaluation of model-generated specifications/proofs.
use_for_goal: Proof-producing automation baseline for systems and agents: translate real source, generate intermediate specifications, reconstruct solver suggestions in a trusted checker, and expose manual abstraction/termination obligations. Generated specifications can copy bugs until independently checked against intended properties. The concurrent VM-isolation proof establishes more than translation coverage. No Verus, Rust, TLA+, LLM experiment or distributed-protocol theorem.

title: Sprout: A Verifier for Symbolic Multiparty Protocols.
what: Presents Sprout, a sound and complete implementability checker for symbolic multiparty protocols with dependent refinements, loop memory and generalized sender-driven choice. It reduces symbolic coherence conditions to µCLP and solves them with MuVal. Defines symbolic protocols with finite control plus dependent registers and refinement predicates. Sprout checks GCLTS eligibility, determinism, send/receive coherence, approximate simultaneous reachability and causal consistency before generating least/greatest fixpoint constraints. The two-bidder protocol illustrates dependent ISBN and increasing-bid refinements. Benchmarks include implementable/non-implementable protocols and custom properties; OCaml implementation compares with the prior naive checker.
numbers: ~3,500 lines OCaml
MuVal µCLP backend
two-bidder and calculator examples
benchmark times from seconds to minutes
assumptions_limits: Soundness/completeness apply to the symbolic protocol semantics and µCLP reduction. Implementability does not prove application-level functional correctness. Expressivity depends on supported first-order theories and GCLTS eligibility; multiplication and some receiver-choice patterns are outside competing/local-type syntax. Runtime is benchmark-dependent.
use_for_goal: Provides a clean protocol-level precondition before proving distributed application invariants. The explicit reduction and solver-backed completeness are useful for evaluating agents that generate multiparty specifications.

title: Improve Model Testing by Integrating Bounded Model Checking and Coverage Guided Fuzzing
what: Presents SPsCGF, a two-stage test-generation workflow for Simulink/Ptolemy control models: CBMC bounded symbolic execution supplies initial seeds, then coverage-guided fuzzing mutates signal inputs using signal-pattern operators. The implementation translates models through an intermediate representation to C/C++ drivers and measures coverage. The paper explains why indirect time-series effects defeat symbolic execution (an ONDLC shutdown model can yield 2^n combinations while only one signal pattern reaches the target), and why ordinary fuzzing creates irregular signals. SPsCGF combines CBMC branch/MC/DC seeds, an efficient dynamic-programming n-wise generator for constant ports, seed selection based on half-flipped conditions, and time/signal mutation operators. It supports nonlinear elements by executing generated raw code and directly embeds complex Simulink code in the IR. Experiments compare SPsCGF, raw coverage-guided fuzzing, SimCoTest, and Simulink Design Verifier across benchmark and industrial vehicle-control models.
numbers: 12 experiments
8–38% higher coverage
3–10× time efficiency
NLGuidance MC/DC: 20% SPsCGF, 0% SPsCGF-BMC, 0% SLDV
assumptions_limits: Bounded model checking explores only a finite loop expansion and can fail on nonlinear arithmetic, floating point, long horizons, or complex loops; n-wise testing is restricted to constant ports because it is expensive. Fuzzing inputs are byte buffers decoded by generated drivers, so legal signal semantics depend on mutation operators. Coverage is a proxy for testing effectiveness, not a proof of safety; the paper is an arXiv evaluation with limited benchmark disclosure.
use_for_goal: Evidence for combining bounded formal exploration with fuzzing when full model checking does not scale. It informs verification engineering tradeoffs: generated tests improve coverage and speed but remain bounded, input-model dependent, and not equivalent to a correctness proof.

title: SquirrelFS: using the Rust compiler to check file-system crash consistency
what: A 7500-line Rust persistent-memory file system uses typestate to enforce ordering constraints of synchronous soft updates (SSU). Persistence and operational types restrict legal update sequences; recovery rename pointers provide metadata rename atomicity. A separately authored Alloy model checks bounded concurrent/crash traces, while tests exercise unmodeled code. Evaluation compares runtime latency/throughput and compilation against Ext4-DAX, NOVA and WineFS, and reports SquirrelFS mount/recovery costs and index-memory sizes. Reconstructs six-stage rename/recovery, dirty/in-flight/clean typestate and ownership requirements, mkdir dependencies, backpointer layout and range-type trust. Records all empirical checks/bugs, model bounds, frame-condition failures, compile/mount tables and benchmark baseline numbers. Qualifies complete-checking language as conditional ordering enforcement rather than end-to-end crash consistency, and saves adverse recovery/memory/performance cases.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3.5: Authors explicitly state SquirrelFS is not fully verified. Successful compilation checks ordering encoded in types, assuming those rules, transition bodies, unsafe/FFI/ownership interfaces and Rust compiler are correct. It does not prove data values, inode contents, arbitrary functional behavior or the sufficiency of the rules for crash consistency. Table 1 marks this work Complete, but the later explicit trust/coverage qualifications constrain that label. §§3.1,3.4: x86 PM model assumes aligned writes of at most eight bytes are crash atomic. Cache-line writeback and store fence must make/order writes durable; non-temporal stores still require a fence. No proof of hardware/flush primitive correctness is supplied. Every system call is synchronous and fsync is a no-op; metadata operations are crash atomic, file-data updates are not. §3.1: SSU enforces initialize-before-link, clear-old-pointers-before-reuse and new-link-before-removing-old-link. Synchronous calls and fine-grained updates on byte-addressable storage avoid traditional cross-operation pending-dependency graphs/cycles. This simplification does not prohibit concurrent calls; VFS locking must serialize conflicting resource access. A future asynchronous implementation requires more complex rules. §3.2 Listings 1–2: Persistence types Dirty→InFlight via flush→Clean via fence are independent of operational types such as Free/Init/Alloc/Committed. Transition functions consume old wrapper ownership and return a new type. Compiler can reject inappropriate ordering or redundant persistence calls through this API, but cannot confirm the instruction flushes the right address or a body initializes every required field. §§3.2,3.4: Rust ownership plus VFS resource locking must ensure each durable resource has one owner/type at a time; indexes/allocators have internal locks. Reader qualification: Rust permits shared references, so the paper’s one-owner statement is about the exclusive mutable typestate wrapper discipline, not a claim that Rust forbids every alias. No concurrent implementation-refinement theorem or liveness proof is provided. §3.4: Persistent allocation means any object byte nonzero; validity of dentries/page descriptors is set inode number, validity of inodes is root reachability. Deallocation clears links before zeroing every byte. Volatile allocators/indexes are reconstructed by scanning. Backpointers in page descriptors simplify dependencies at the cost of mount scans/DRAM indexes; per-CPU page allocators and one global inode allocator affect scalability. §§3.4,5.7: Alloy model has roughly one-to-one transition correspondence with Rust typestate transitions, separately authored and not mechanically linked to code. Checks are bounded to two possibly concurrent operations, ten persistent objects and at most thirty steps. Bounded model success is not a proof of every-size/every-length implementation execution. §§4.1–4.3: General initialization typestate combines many field writes, deliberately trading bug coverage for simpler interfaces. Unbounded collections cannot be checked element by element with the chosen Rust types, so one typestate represents a page range and trusted transition loops update every page. This moves the universal obligation into unchecked bodies; it does not prove all range elements were updated correctly. §4.3 reader qualification: The broad claim that universally quantified formulas are undecidable must be read as general unrestricted checking, not a claim that every universally quantified property is undecidable. The concrete limitation is this unmodified Rust/typestate encoding cannot prove all objects in dynamically sized collections meet a property. Richer theorem provers or other encodings may establish particular quantified properties. §4.3: Alloy checking can take days/weeks. Missing frame conditions permit unconstrained state changes and yield false positives; custom syntactic checker demands each transition mention all mutable structures but explicitly cannot detect every issue. Parallel independent checks and split invariants improve turnaround without proving model intent or implementation correspondence. §4.4: No equivalent verified/unverified system exists for controlled development-effort comparison. Authors’ lower-effort/faster-debugging statements are experience and belief. Footnote durable-log three months is one author’s separate experience, not a measured SquirrelFS development duration. Staying synchronized through types applies to encoded API rules, not automatically to omitted requirements or incorrect transition bodies. §5.1: Measurements use two-socket 32-core machine,128GB DRAM,128GB Intel Optane DC PM,Debian Bookworm/Linux6.3. Baselines configured for metadata consistency without data atomicity to match prototype. SoupFS unavailable as closed source; ArckFS excluded for time. Means of multiple trials with plotted min/max; microbenchmarks specify ten trials. No per-system equal-functionality or production-maturity claim follows. §§5.2–5.4: Microbenchmarks do not call fsync, but SquirrelFS already makes each call durable. Filebench defaults; RocksDB/YCSB uses25GB/25M records/25M operations/eight threads and normal syscall interfaces. LMDB100M keys uses mmap, reducing metadata/syscall differences. Figure5 prints Ext4 absolute baselines and plots normalized throughputs; unprinted bar values in record are approximate visual estimates, not exact source cells. §5.5 Table2: Recovery timing is forced recovery scans of cleanly unmounted images, not measured worst-case recovery from interrupted operations. Full means100% data/inode utilization. True crashed layouts may differ; no general recovery upper bound proved. Future parallel rebuild/CXL claims are prospective, not evaluated. §5.6 Table3: Ten-second compile includes typestate checks, compared with other kernel modules of different sizes/features. Historical FSCQ11h/VeriBetrKV1.8h(10min parallel) verification references are cross-project comparisons, not controlled measurements or equal proof strength. Ext4 LOC includes DAX/non-DAX. No background threads started by operations is not zero CPU overhead or absence of concurrent caller threads. §5.7: Passes67 supported generic xfstests; others use unsupported arguments/syscalls. Chipmunk generators omit unsupported syscalls, then systematic tests plus about24h fuzzing found no ordering-related bugs but did find four crash-consistency bugs in unchecked code. This is finite evidence supporting encoded ordering checks, not absence of all crash bugs. §§3.6,6–7: CXL PM suitability is an extrapolation conditional on comparable byte-addressable persistence semantics; larger devices worsen scan/memory costs. No Verus proof, TLA+ experiment, distributed protocol implementation, LLM-agent experiment, artifact build or crash-test replay is included in this reading.
use_for_goal: Direct Rust evidence for encoding persistence/update order through ownership and typestate, with explicit limits contrasting compiler checks and full functional verification. Bounded Alloy modeling, frame-condition omissions and four unchecked crash bugs are concrete evaluation targets for agents writing specifications/proofs. Relevant to verified-storage foundations of distributed systems, but uses no Verus/TLA+ or LLM-agent experiment and proves no distributed protocol theorem.

title: Starling: Lightweight Concurrency Verification with Views
what: Introduces Starling, a lightweight proof-outline logic and tool for concurrent algorithms. Views are linear invariant units held by threads; constraints define their shared-state meaning and interactions. Starling translates outlines through the sound Views metatheory into finite verification conditions discharged by Z3 for shared variables or GRASShopper for heaps. ARC specifications use arc() tokens, countCopy constraints and iterated views to express reference ownership and prevent use-after-free; both shared-variable and heap implementations are verified. The Views rule preserves frames and parallel interference; defining functions and downclosure reduce arbitrary context quantification to finite proof terms, with a core rule over weakest contexts. Examples include Rust ARC, spin/ticket/reader-writer locks, Peterson, CLH queue-lock and lock-coupling list (memory safety, not linearizability).

title: Static Race Detection and Mutex Safety and Liveness for Go Programs (extended version)
what: The paper develops GoL, a process-calculus model for shared memory, locks, read-write locks, and later channels, with behavioural types that encode happens-before synchronization. Type soundness and progress connect processes to µ-calculus types; model checking these types detects data races, lock safety/liveness, and mixed channel/shared-memory errors. The migoinfer+ extractor and Godel2/mCRL2 backend form a static toolchain. Beyond the abstract, the authors define race and lock properties over GoL, prove subject reduction, process safety/data-race transfer, and conditional equivalence of type and process liveness for terminating, may-converging, and finite-branching programs. The channel extension models channel-as-lock and pointer-through-channel errors. Evaluation includes mutex/channel variants, producer-consumer, and five-philosopher programs with explicit false-positive caveats for approximated cyclic analyses.

title: STLmc: Robust STL Model Checking of Hybrid Systems Using SMT
what: Introduces a Python tool for bounded quantitative STL checking of hybrid automata by threshold-shifting formulas and invoking an existing Boolean STL SMT encoding. Supports exact algebraic trajectory encodings through Yices/Z3 and approximate Lipschitz ODE reasoning through dReal. Adds minimized Boolean-scenario enumeration with parallel ODE refinement and counterexample plots. Thirty reported benchmark tasks favor direct solving for linear/polynomial flows and25-core two-step solving for ODEs. Published strict-threshold and atomic-sign presentation issues require explicit qualification. Makes three bounds explicit: time horizon tau, truth-change/mode-change count N, and robustness epsilon. Its actual no-counterexample theorem supplies rho>=epsilon, hence strict satisfaction at every smaller positive threshold, rather than at epsilon itself. Describes abstraction/implicant minimization/refinement/blocking and its solver interfaces. Complete results preserve encoding sizes, counterexample bounds, scenario counts and algorithm failures. Reader checks identify reversed atomic shift signs in Definition3 and a misleading paraphrase of the nested thermostat property; neither establishes an artifact bug.
assumptions_limits: Hybrid automata have discrete modes, real states, initial/invariant/jump/flow conditions and finite-horizon signals on[0,tau). STL uses state propositions, negation, conjunction and interval until; other connectives are derived. Quantitative semantics use signed atomic scores, negation, minimum and supremum/infimum over time intervals truncated by the finite horizon. Results are bounded finite-signal claims, not arbitrary infinite-run temporal verification. Definition2 requires rho(phi,sigma,t)>epsilon for every trajectory. Theorem1(2) only concludes rho>=epsilon after no Boolean counterexample. Therefore the authors explicitly guarantee strict robustness for each0<epsilon_prime<epsilon and warn epsilon itself may fail. Abstract/conclusion descriptions saying greater than the specified threshold overstate this boundary if read literally; record preserves the theorem and caveat. Visually confirmed source defect: Definition3 prints p_minus(s)=p(s)−epsilon as weakening and p_plus(s)=p(s)+epsilon as strengthening. For atomic truth p(s)>=0, adding epsilon weakens the requirement. These signs conflict with the intended reduction/Theorem1(2). Reader check p=x>=0, constantx=0,epsilon=1: printed p_plus=x+1 is true everywhere, so no Boolean counterexample exists, yet claimed rho=x>=1 fails. Swapping atomic signs is a natural presentation repair, not confirmed implementation behavior. Theorem1 proof details are deferred to technical report42; Theorem2 encoding correctness is imported from refs3/29. No proof assistant development, machine-checked end-to-end compiler/solver theorem or certified implementation is reported. The printed-sign issue must not be described as evidence of a kernel accepting a false proof or an observed tool unsoundness. N bounds mode changes and variable points where any relevant STL subformula changes truth. It is not merely a jump bound or a consequence of elapsed time. The paper uses y(t)=sin(pi*n*t/tau) to exhibit n−1 interior truth changes with no mode change. Restricting N can exclude continuous oscillation behavior even when a hybrid trace has no jumps. Time intervals are truncated at tau and may be open/closed, bounded/unbounded. Empty-time-window conventions and boundary equality affect Boolean/quantitative correspondence; the paper explicitly takes only inequality implications with a threshold gap. No unbounded-time or all-discrete-bound guarantee follows from a True result at a fixed N,tau. Linear/polynomial model categories refer to explicit trajectory solutions expressible as linear functions/polynomials, not arbitrary polynomial-vector-field ODEs. Yices/Z3 handle algebraic encodings; dReal approximately handles Lipschitz ODEs. The latter are generally undecidable in exact form. Experiments use dReal precision delta=.001, distinct from property robustness epsilon; the paper supplies no detailed error-budget theorem translating delta-sat to an exact original-model witness. A generic SMT-LIB wrapper and automatic solver selection improve interoperability but do not prove parser, encoding implementation or solver correctness. Two-step abstraction replaces flow/invariant constraints by Booleans, producing a weaker propositional problem. A scenario pi is a conjunction of literals implying that abstraction; its ODE/invariant refinement must be checked. UNSAT refinement permits blocking pi; SAT ends search and cancels jobs. After every scenario at each bound is excluded the algorithm returns True. Correctness needs complete coverage and sound refinement/blocking; the abstract Boolean scenario alone is not a real counterexample. Z3 unsat cores of pi and not-Psi are used for dual-propagation scenario reduction. A core supplies a sufficient implicant, while strict subset-minimality requires minimization beyond arbitrary core extraction. The text calls scenarios minimal but does not specify all core-minimization details. No concurrent scheduling correctness proof or distributed fault model is provided for parallel jobs. title: Stochastic Omega-Regular Verification and Control with Supermartingales
what: Introduces nonnegative Streett supermartingale certificates for probability-one omega-regular properties of general discrete-time stochastic processes. Uniform expected decrease on A minus B, bounded increase on B and no increase elsewhere certify each Streett pair. For Markov models, combines deterministic Streett automata, inductive invariants and parametric policies into polynomial-real constraints. Gives template-relative synthesis reductions to quantified NRA, existential NRA, QCP or LP, and eleven small example timings. Completeness for every satisfying stochastic process is explicitly open. Uses Robbins–Siegmund to certify disjunction of finite A-visits or infinite B-visits without proving either disjunct individually almost surely. Derives product-state post-expectations and six classes of universally quantified constraints, preserving invariant and policy synthesis jointly. Explains parametric versus known guards, Farkas infeasibility disjunct, external shielding and finite-memory encoding. Complete table/control parameters support checking exact model/property consistency; reader calculations identify printed automaton boundary and controller discrepancies, not inspected tool defects.
assumptions_limits: General theorem uses a filtered probability space, measurable/adapted processes, nonnegative real V and fixed positive epsilon,M. It certifies probability1, permitting measure-zero exceptional runs, not every possible trajectory or a quantitative failure probability/time bound. Conditional expectations must be well-defined with the stated nonnegative drift inequality. Any connection to implementation numeric/physical behavior remains outside the mathematical theorem. A Streett pair(A,B) means finitely many visits to A OR infinitely many visits to B. Drift is E[V_next|history]<=V−epsilon*1_(AminusB)+M*1_B. Uniform epsilon matters; arbitrary strictly positive but summable decreases would not exclude infinite A-visits. B may recharge the certificate, so V need not be an ordinary supermartingale globally. Reader derivation of Theorem2 from Theorem1:take U_t=epsilon*1_(AminusB),W_t=M*1_B. On finite B-visits,sumW finite; Robbins–Siegmund implies sumU finite almost surely, hence finite AminusB and finiteA. Finite conjunction of probability1 pair-events preserves probability1. The paper gives theorem statements/intuitive examples rather than a machine-checked derivation. Theorem3 restricts Markov drift conditions to a measurable supporting invariant I containing the initial state and preserved with probability1. This can exclude unreachable regions where no global certificate exists. V must remain nonnegative onI; disregarding invariant initiation/consecution would break the proof. Common epsilon,M across finitely many pairs can be obtained by min/max if separate finite constants exist. title: STP: Self-play LLM Theorem Provers with Iterative Conjecturing and Proving
what: STP trains one LLM as both conjecturer and whole-proof prover. The conjecturer proposes related statements conditioned on a proved seed and either an extracted lemma or a fixed trivial lemma; the prover attempts new conjectures and remaining dataset statements. Verified, barely provable and heuristically elegant conjectures train the conjecturer, while correct nontrivial proofs train the prover. This supplies denser training signals than repeatedly attempting hard unproved statements. Lean training reaches 28.5% cumulative LeanWorkbook coverage, and the final model reports 65.0% miniF2F-test and 23.9% ProofNet-test pass@3200, plus 8/644 PutnamBench solves. Three stages: supervised initialization from proof libraries, iterative self-play, then final retraining from the base model on SFT data and selected generated proofs. Conjecturer SFT uses ordered shared-lemma/theoremX/theoremY tuples; self-play selects verified seed proofs, deduplicates statement–lemma pairs, caps frequent lemmas at 0.1 n and sometimes inserts a trivial lemma. K=32 proof samples estimate conjecture difficulty; keep empirical success in(0,1/4], require the seed lemma in a successful proof, deduplicate conjectures, and discard the bottom 20% of minimum-proof-length/statement-length elegance scores. Reweight conjectures toward unproved statements using mean-last-layer embeddings and negative cosine transport cost. Prover training keeps correct proofs from tasks with success below 1/2, uses a three-iteration replay buffer, inverse proof-count weights, length discount and Lean verification-time discount. Periodic refresh and final retraining counter forgetting/distribution shift; final data keeps at most 16 distinct proofs per task with empirical success≤1/4.
assumptions_limits: Correctness is relative to the formal statements, loaded libraries and verifier configuration. Generated conjecture proofs are reported checker-accepted, but semantic equivalence to a natural-language problem and mathematical usefulness are separate. No artifact/checker execution or admissions/axiom audit was performed here. The barely-provable criterion uses 32 sampled proofs, not exact underlying success probabilities. Elegance is a textual length ratio; relevance/diversity uses shared lemmas and embedding proximity. These are heuristics, not guarantees of novelty, difficulty or scientific value. Lean uses DeepSeek-Prover-V 1.5-SFT already trained on public/proprietary proof data including LeanWorkbook, miniF2F-valid and ProofNet-valid. The 24-iteration ablation without valid-set STP training still inherits those base-model exposures; its stronger out-of-domain interpretation is qualified by footnote 7. Main Lean self-play also explicitly includes miniF2F-valid/ProofNet-valid. After 24 iterations their matching weights increase from 1 to 128. Held-out test results should be distinguished from this validation-targeted curriculum and from cumulative training-dataset coverage. Isabelle starts from Llemma-7 b, translates LeanWorkbook using DeepSeek-V 2.5, uses PISA and disables heavy tactics. This is a separate restricted-verifier experiment rather than an equal-strength cross-language comparison. The source argues expert iteration cannot improve indefinitely from a fixed difficulty dataset and motivates indefinite self-improvement. Finite 48-Lean/58-Isabelle-iteration experiments do not prove either an impossibility bound for expert iteration or unbounded STP progress. Training plots count generated proofs, not equal end-to-end wall time, tokens, CPU verification or retraining FLOPs. Conjectures are comparatively few; Lean verification time nevertheless became a bottleneck without an explicit time penalty. The 20-item audit samples only unproved LeanWorkbook statements:16 are labeled faithful formalizations and 7 labeled provable. This conditional small sample cannot estimate the whole-corpus falsehood rate or a numerical global maximum pass rate; the human labels themselves are not formal certificates. Whole-proof pass@k uses independent sampled outputs per statement. Tree-search budgets count steps or complete-proof generations and have different state/value-model costs; Table 1 explicitly says they are not fully comparable. The paper gives uncertainties for several benchmark rates but does not specify repeat counts or whether ± denotes standard deviation, standard error or another interval in the supplied text. Training-curve uncertainty and controlled multi-seed self-play runs are absent.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM proof-agent training: checker-accepted generated tasks can provide a curriculum when proofs of remaining target tasks are rare. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ and distributed verification, the transferable hypothesis is to generate related specifications or lemmas and train on verified solutions while controlling task relevance and diversity. This is reader inference; STP evaluates mathematical Lean/Isabelle proofs, not executable systems or specification fidelity.

title: Slow Down, Move Over: A Case Study in Formal Verification, Refinement, and Testing of the Responsibility-Sensitive Safety Model for Self-Driving Cars
what: Formalizes longitudinal Responsibility-Sensitive Safety (RSS) as hybrid programs in differential dynamic logic, proves collision safety and minimal safe distances in KeYmaera X, proves deterministic controller refinement and verified compilation to Python, then uses formally derived ModelPlex monitors for testing and debugging. The model template makes acceleration, reaction-time, orientation, safe-distance and evolution-domain assumptions explicit. The same-direction proof uses an inductive stopping-distance invariant; opposite-direction safety uses a shared-responsibility invariant. Optimality is established constructively by choosing worst-case accelerations and showing any epsilon-smaller initial separation reaches collision. A deterministic det-HP controller is proved a refinement of the nondeterministic envelope, and structural induction proves Python compilation preserves reachable states. ModelPlex monitors connect runtime states to formal paths: faulty controllers trigger alarms, and collisions without alarms expose modeling flaws. Simulations explore reaction-time parameter effects after proof.

title: Strong Extension-Free Proof Systems
what: We introduce proof systems for propositional logic that admit short proofs of hard formulas as well as the succinct expression of most techniques used by modern SAT solvers. Our proof systems allow the derivation of clauses that are not necessarily implied, but which are redundant in the sense that their addition preserves satisfiability. To guarantee that these added clauses are redundant, we consider various efficiently decidable redundancy criteria which we obtain by first characterizing clause redundancy in terms of a semantic implication relationship and then restricting this relationship so that it becomes decidable in polynomial time.

title: Putting Strong Linearizability in Context: Preserving Hyperproperties in Programs That Use Concurrent Objects
what: The paper places strong linearizability in a general observational-refinement framework. It defines strong observational refinement for concurrent-object labeled transition systems and proves it equivalent to forward simulation; strong linearizability is shown as a special case/generalization when the abstract object is atomic. This establishes compositionality both horizontally (local object composition) and vertically (instantiation). When no efficient strongly linearizable implementation exists, the paper advocates simpler non-atomic abstract objects that strongly refine the concrete one, preserving enough hyperproperty behavior for reasoning about randomized and security-sensitive clients.

Strong refinement is defined against deterministic schedulers/strong adversaries, and forward simulations are parameterized by observable alphabets. The supplied extraction contains §§1–3 and the motivating stack example but not the later formal theorem sections, so detailed proof statements, Section 4–6 constructions, and quantitative experiments are absent. The framework targets hyperproperties expressible over sets of projected program traces.

title: Structural Liveness of Conservative Petri Nets
what: Proves EXPSPACE-completeness of structural liveness for conservative and structurally bounded Petri nets, with doubly-exponential bounds on minimal live markings. The paper models Petri nets as action vectors and develops a proof chain: reversible virtual reachability is represented by bounded linear systems; conservative, structurally bounded and live-bottom-SCC properties are related; dead markings are represented by disjunctions of bounded restricted markings; quasi-dead markings and extractor cases reduce non-liveness to linear-system constraints. Small-solution theorems then yield a 2-exp bound on a live marking, enabling an exponential-space nondeterministic algorithm. A strengthened EXPSPACE lower bound completes hardness for conservative nets and transfers it to structurally bounded nets. The proof extends integer-solution bounds with divisibility constraints.
numbers: The complexity result is theorem-based; no runtime data or benchmark suite.
Linear-system dimension in the construction is d·2^d; solution norms are bounded by (2+||A||)^{2^{poly(d)}}.
The upper-bound algorithm guesses a binary-encoded live marking and checks liveness in polynomial space in that encoding.
assumptions_limits: Results concern standard finite-dimensional Petri nets with nonnegative markings and conservative/structurally bounded subclasses; general structural liveness complexity remains open. Bounds are doubly exponential and not practical algorithms. Several technical ingredients are cited from prior work (Rackoff/Leroux), and the proof uses virtual reachability, reversibility and large-component extractors. No implementation or experimental evaluation is reported.
use_for_goal: This is a rigorous complexity and small-witness result for Petri-net liveness, a foundational distributed-systems model. It supplies explicit assumptions and proof structure that matter when formal verification tools claim liveness coverage, but its nonconstructive huge bounds and reliance on prior lemmas limit direct automation or performance conclusions.

title: Subgoal-based Demonstration Learning for Formal Theorem Proving
what: Introduces subgoal-based demonstration learning for LLM formal theorem proving. It iteratively turns informal proofs into subgoal sequences that are checked and repaired against Isabelle, then trains a discrete graph diffusion model to select and order in-context demonstrations. On miniF2F with Isabelle, the full method reports 48.0% cumulative validation pass rate and 45.5% test pass rate; without diffusion it reports 44.1% test, and without subgoals 40.6%. The method reaches 38.5% test pass rate with 20 LLM calls, versus 100 calls used for the comparable DSP reference setting. A valid subgoal sequence must be reachable from the theorem statement and able to reach a passing proof state. Iterative refinement starts from manually written subgoals, asks an LLM to produce them, recursively calls an Isabelle-backed Verify-and-Correct routine for each segment, and retains only verified or fallback pairs. Demonstration reorganization treats selection and ordering as a Hamiltonian-path-like graph problem; successful randomized organizations supervise a discrete diffusion model. A GNN denoiser encodes Ada embeddings of the target and each demonstration, and inference samples 200 candidate organizations, scores them, picks the highest-scoring candidate, and appends examples until the context limit. The paper supplies recursive algorithms, prompt templates, failure/success traces, ordering and count ablations, leakage checks and Sledgehammer-cost analysis.
assumptions_limits: Formal-sketch validity is defined as no “sorry”/“oops” cheating keyword and Isabelle authentication of the generated proof. The reported cumulative validation rate includes organizations discovered during the diffusion training-data collection, so it is not a held-out estimate in the same sense as the test rate. The training data has no separate miniF2F training split: successful randomized organizations from miniF2F-valid are used to train the diffusion model. Test statements are separate, but examples, prompts and problem names can be web-visible; the paper reports a leakage audit and randomized-name experiment rather than proving no contamination. Subgoal reachability is operational: an LLM fills or repairs the formal sketch and Isabelle accepts or rejects it. A failed verification can trigger a correction/decomposition, but after the finite call budget the algorithm returns the original pair, so not every retained demonstration is guaranteed to contain a newly repaired valid subgoal in that path. Algorithm3 describes a10-call budget for Verify-and-Correct,counting one call for verification and one for correction. Reader observation:the pseudocode can spend a correction call after a failed verification has exhausted the last remaining unit,so a strict10-call bound is not established by the shown loop. No budget-exhaustion frequency or full recursive-cost distribution is reported. The main LLM is GPT-3.5-turbo-0301 at temperature 0 and 1024 max tokens. The diffusion model uses 137 collected successful organization contexts from 116 statements, split 81 for training and 56 for validation, with three repeated experiments. Small data and model/version choices constrain generality. miniF2F contains high-school mathematics in Isabelle, HOL-Light and Lean, but this study evaluates Isabelle only. No Verus, Rust, TLA+, concurrency, distributed systems or software specifications are tested. Ordering and selection results are benchmark-specific. Shuffling an organization drops solved problems from 94 to 39 in a 20-attempt test, but this is not a causal decomposition of all prompt effects; the model also changes selected examples, order, and uses a finite context. Figures 16–18 show malformed or failed Isabelle outputs from reordered demonstrations, including an incorrect use of mod_mult_self2, an unsuitable conjecture, and an unresolved factorial equation. The paper reports them as qualitative cases, not formal error rates. The authors’ statement that the approach can extend to software verification is future-work motivation; the experiments establish only mathematical theorem-proving behavior.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM theorem-proving agents: align natural-language subgoals with verifier states, recursively repair them, and treat demonstration order as an explicit search problem. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ systems, the transferable idea is verifier-checked decomposition and context organization; the paper does not evaluate software or distributed specifications, and its 2024 Isabelle/GPT-3.5 results do not establish modern LLM or Verus performance.

title: On the size of data structures used in symbolic model checking
what: Analyzes whether preprocessing the model or temporal formula can make model checking tractable and proves conditional lower bounds on symbolic state representations. The paper models systems as synchronous or interleaved compositions of finite transition systems, reduces from planning, and uses compilability theory. The reductions establish k-arrow-PSPACE hardness/completeness even when one input part is preprocessed into polynomial space: interleaved model checking remains complete for full LTL and hard for the F fragment, while synchronous variants are hard. A separate state-membership problem shows that a polynomial-size BDD for legal initial states would collapse compilability classes; the argument extends to arbitrary decision diagrams whose evaluation lies in a polynomial-hierarchy level. Thus the worst-case blow-up is representation-independent under standard separation assumptions.

kind: symbolic runtime monitoring and parameter synthesis
what: Introduces parametric timed data automata (PTDA) and an online monitoring algorithm that symbolically returns the complete validity domain of both timing and data parameters for a finite timed event log. The automata include unbounded data variables, memory, aggregation and unobservable transitions, allowing parameter inference and timed pattern matching in one formalism. Defines typed data guards and updates separately from clocks: rational data support linear arithmetic; strings support equality/disequality and assignments. Timing parameters are positive rationals. Observable and unobservable symbolic configurations propagate clock/parameter and data constraints; accepting configurations project to parameter valuations, and a final unobservable closure catches matches after the last observed event. Theorem 1 establishes termination when symbolic restriction/update, emptiness and projection terminate, under the global no-unobservable-cycle assumption. Convex polyhedra and finite string-constraint representations provide concrete terminating instances. SyMon implements strings and integers in C++ with PPL and merges adjacent polyhedra. Experiments explain bounded configuration counts in the selected automata rather than asserting a general linear complexity result.

title: Functional Reasoning for Distributed Systems with Failures
what: Defines twin Rocq-embedded languages Sync and Async to make high-level functional reasoning about asynchronous distributed protocols precise, then proves that compiled Async executions are included in Sync denotations. The authors mechanize the framework and safety proofs for Bosco and Sequential Paxos. Sync is a choreography language whose typed programs are ordered communication steps over role-indexed vectors; its power-set denotation explicitly enumerates message loss, reordering, truncation and arbitrary Byzantine injections. The configuration model separates good, crash-prone and Byzantine nodes and uses a Netwk relation as an executable over-approximation. Finite loop unwinding supports safety proofs for nonterminating protocols. Bosco proofs derive a strong one-step theorem for n>7f and an inductive univalence/agreement invariant for n>3f. SeqPaxos proofs use a weakest precondition UC_D to show once a value is decided, later iterations decide it or abstain when n>2f; the condition is weaker than the protocol’s strongest postcondition and exposes optimization opportunities. Async is a monadic node LTS plus single-use channel LTS; alignment permutes arbitrary interleavings into channel order, and adequacy (Theorem 5.1) follows through aligned traces, big-step semantics and channel-erasure lemmas. The Rocq development is about 2.5k lines and includes endpoint projection/executable extraction.

Network messages are authenticated, nonduplicated, eventually delivered between correct nodes, and well typed; signatures and parsing are assumed rather than modeled. title: Verifying Safety of Synchronous Fault-Tolerant Algorithms by Bounded Model Checking
what: Introduces synchronous threshold automata (STA) for round-based fault-tolerant algorithms, proves parameterized reachability undecidable in general, and uses SMT to infer parameter-independent diameters as completeness bounds for bounded model checking safety. For monotonic 1-cyclic STAs, schedules can be shortened to O(|Ψ|c), where Ψ is guard-atom count and c longest automaton path; trapped guards imply monotonicity. Python tooling with Z3/CVC4 evaluates reliable broadcast, FloodMin/Floodset, k-set agreement, phase king/queen and other fault models; it found a published phase-king threshold bug.
