title: Synthetic Programming Elicitation for Text-to-Code in Very Low-Resource Programming and Formal Languages
what: SPEAC makes an LLM generate a familiar intermediate language, repairs that output with compiler checks and weighted MAX-SMT, then translates it into a language poorly represented in training data. Eudoxus instantiates this with a subset of Python that describes UCLID5 transition systems. It prunes unsupported syntax, replaces inconsistent syntax-tree nodes with holes, infers repairs from a satisfying model and asks the LLM to fill remaining holes. The evaluation measures compiler acceptance and a single author’s manual semantic scores on 33 textbook tasks. Preserves how the intermediate language was manually designed, exact pruning/constraint/repair contracts and minimality conditions, the traffic-light input ownership mistake, type and timer concerns, every result-table cell and denominator, three dataset roles, baseline and call settings, manual scoring, timing components and limits of the semantic claim. Distinguishes satisfying static constraints from preserving intended behavior or proving the generated transition system.
assumptions_limits: §3–§5: Requires a target language T, familiar parent P, child subset C and compiler f:C→T. Here T is UCLID5, P Python and C an abstract Module subclass with declaration/init/next methods. The language design and syntax-directed translator are supplied by people; the paper does not prove compiler semantic preservation or automatically derive a correct modeling language. §5.1: Synthetic elicitation is a manual lightweight grounded-theory analysis of LLM outputs, not a human-subject study. People label output fragments, group codes into concepts/categories and design C. The object-oriented category is chosen for ease of translation; no experiment establishes universal LLM naturalness or superiority over every alternative child language. §5.1, p.6: GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 and GPT-4-turbo-2024-04-09 each generate ten samples on each of 33 curated regression tasks: 660 direct-UCLID5 attempts, none parses. This is a result for those models/tasks, not a universal inability theorem. Imaginary FormalVerificationLibrary prompts elicit from-scratch Z3, procedural API and object-oriented subclass styles. §5.2/Figure 4: Initial prompt specifies parent, task, unique code block and child description, ending with an affirmative assistant prefix. Repair prompt asks to replace every ?? and repeats the task. The templates are partial; the PDF does not include every concrete benchmark prompt or the complete child grammar. §5.3: Error-tolerant parsing first builds a parent-language AST, then removes constructs outside C. This initial pruning may lose program intent. Static checks are encoded as soft clauses per node; MAX-SMT keeps a satisfiable weighted subset and rejected clauses identify nodes to replace with holes. Hard clauses and algebraic data types constrain legal structure. §5.3, p.7: Minimum node-edit guarantee is conditional on uniform weights and exactly one clause per node. Actual depth-proportional weights favor edits near leaves and explicitly break syntactic minimality guarantees. Largest consistent subtree therefore does not imply globally fewest edits in the implementation or smallest semantic change. §5.4: A satisfying model can infer a hole’s type, e.g. integer from integer-literal assignment; unresolved holes return to the LLM. Satisfying static constraints establishes a well-formed intermediate program, not equivalence to its original candidate, natural-language task satisfaction or a verified safety/liveness property. §3/Figure 1: Compiler-accepted traffic-light output declares pedestrian with var and initializes it false, although the task requires a nondeterministic input from another subsystem. Authors explicitly identify var→input as a semantic correction. Inference for distributed modeling: changing an environment input into locally controlled state can remove executions and make a property misleadingly easy to satisfy. Figure 1 lines 13–15 and Figure 5: The shown state-zero branch resets count to zero immediately before checking count<60 and incrementing it. Under the sequential step semantics suggested by the excerpt, that prevents this branch reaching 60. This is an apparent concern in a partial excerpt, not a confirmed full-model counterexample; the complete generated model and execution were not inspected. Authors discuss the pedestrian mistake, not this timer concern. Figures 5–6: Repairs replace BitVector declarations with int to match integer literal use, and replace Boolean()/False values in declarations with bool. Changing a bounded bitvector to integer changes wraparound/range behavior; static consistency alone does not preserve a bounded-state interpretation. Final snippets also show declarations/init separately and contain ellipses. §3/Figure 5: Figure 5 caption identifies (a) initial output and (b) repair; overview prose reverses these references. Figure 6 likewise contains partial outputs. Preserve the caption/code reading rather than treating the displayed snippets as a complete executable proof artifact. §6: Python implementation uses tree-sitter and Z3 MAX-SMT; local solver machine is a 2.3 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7 with 32 GB RAM, LLMs through OpenAI Python API. Repository is https://github.com/FedericoAureliano/eudoxus. This read covers the PDF, not repository code or a reproduced run. §6/Table 1: Text says allow repair loop five times; caption says limited to five LLM calls per benchmark. Self-repair baseline uses five iterations starting from zero-shot. Exact initial-call versus repair-count convention is not reconciled in the PDF; use the caption’s reported cap without silently adding an initial sixth call. §6: Three datasets have distinct roles: 33 curated developer regression tests with hand-written descriptions for language design; 317 repository regression tests self-summarized by the LLM for fine-tuning; 33 textbook exercises/examples for end-to-end evaluation. Textbooks are Baier/Katoen 2008, Lee/Seshia 2016 and Huth/Ryan 2004. No explicit split-overlap/contamination audit is given. §6: Fine-tunes GPT3t for 284 steps with learning-rate multiplier .16; no GPT4t fine-tune is reported. Baselines include one/three examples, with/without chain of thought, each on two models; two compiler-feedback self-repair variants; and fine-tuning. That is eleven baseline variants plus two Eudoxus variants, thirteen Table 1 rows; prose saying all eleven approaches is a counting slip. Abstract/§6: Abstract mentions retrieval baselines, but the specified baseline is repository few-shot prompting; no operational retrieval pipeline, retriever-quality measurement or retrieval ablation is described. Do not infer a separate implemented RAG system from that phrase. §6.1: Parse is shorthand for passing all compiler checks, including static typing, rather than grammar alone. Semantic assessment is one author’s manual reasoning plus hand-written specifications, performed only for compiled outputs. Scores run from 1 entirely wrong to 5 fully correct; ≥4 means authors believe useful, allowing minor errors. This is not an independently machine-checked end-to-end correctness result. Table 1: GPT3t Eudoxus parses 28/33=84.8%; GPT4t 24/33=72.7%. Combined 52/66=78.8% explains approximately 78% prose. Fine-tuning Table 1 is 2/33=6.1%, inconsistent with introduction 9.1%; preserve the discrepancy. Best GPT4t few-shot parses 4/33=12.1%. Percentages here are derived from printed counts. Table 1: Fully correct score-5 outputs are GPT4t 11/33 and GPT3t 9/33, not 24/33 or 28/33. Useful score≥4 outputs are 19/33 and 14/33 respectively. These derived unconditional denominators differ from the table’s conditional semantic denominators of 24 and 28 compiled outputs. §6.1: Across both Eudoxus variants, 30/33 unique tasks have at least one compiled output; across all eleven baseline variants, only 6/33 do. Eudoxus has 33/52 compiled outputs scoring ≥4, covering 24 unique tasks. Four unique baseline-useful tasks are also useful under Eudoxus. These unions are not a single model’s success rate or 33 verified specifications. §6.1: Four benchmarks hit iteration cap and three suffer implementation syntax/output-extraction/printing bugs. Their scope across model variants is unclear: the two table rows together have fourteen non-compiling outputs. Do not assign the seven reported cases independently to both models or invent an overlap explanation. §6.1, p.10: Reported GPT3t mean repair time .9 s (SD .6), LLM time 7.2 s (SD 4.6); GPT4t repair 1.8 s (SD 2.0), LLM 35.1 s (SD 24.7). These components support that LLM calls dominate reported local repair time. They are not total project compute, API dollars, token counts or a precisely specified aggregate wall-clock distribution. §6.1–§6.2: Authors explicitly caution that few baseline outputs compile, making conclusions about semantic performance difficult. No ablation separates child-language design, pruning, model-based repairs and repeated LLM calls; no broad budget-matched repeated-sampling comparison is reported. §6.2/Checklist: Only one target language, two LLMs and one semantic rater. No inter-rater agreement, semantic-score confidence intervals or statistical-significance claim; checklist item 7 explicitly calls this a case study. Generalization to other languages/models remains open. Checklist items 3–8: No theoretical results claimed. Code/data are said to be in supplemental material/GitHub; not executed here. Checklist says temperature settings are reported, but no numerical temperature is supplied in the PDF’s experimental description. Solver/compiler versions, exact seeds, repeated-run counts and solver timeouts are not disclosed there. Checklist items 10–15: Broader impacts answer No because work targets compiler checks; existing UCLID5 license stated as 3-clause BSD, textbook examples cited, new code/documentation claimed public. Human-subject and IRB questions marked NA. These are disclosure statements, not independent license or artifact verification. Whole paper: No generated distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust proof, TLA+ specification, termination argument, concurrency refinement proof or validated natural-language specification oracle is evaluated. Formal tools repair syntax/types; UCLID5’s verification capabilities do not by themselves make generated models faithful to the task.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to LLM agents writing formal models: use a familiar interface and solver-assisted static repair, then evaluate model meaning separately. The external-input mistake concretely shows why specification fidelity and environment ownership need review even when compilation succeeds. Evidence supports syntax/type repair in UCLID5; it does not establish automatic distributed-system verification or proof correctness in Verus, Rust or TLA+.

title: T2: Temporal Property Verification
what: Presents the open-source T2 framework, translating C/LLVM or native integer transition systems into safety, termination and temporal-logic proofs for CTL, Fair-CTL, CTL* and LTL reductions. T2 front-end builds location/transition graphs and uses LLVM simplifications. Safety proving uses Impact, Z3 GPDR or Spacer via linear Horn clauses. Termination alternates safety checks with lexicographic ranking-function synthesis and counterexample refinement; preprocessing removes directly provable loops (about 80%). Nontermination searches recurrent sets. CTL uses bottom-up precondition synthesis; Fair-CTL uses prophecy variables to reduce fairness; CTL* uses explicit future-outcome variables and is incomplete. Machine integer overflow is handled by normalization in the C front-end.

Heap, recursion and concurrency are future work. Fair-CTL is relatively complete only relative to safety/termination procedures; CTL* is incomplete. Temporal experiments exclude Fair-CTL/CTL* due to lack of competing tools.

The Horn-clause, ranking-function and recurrent-set decomposition suggests components for extending Verus workflows beyond safety.

title: Improved Bounded Model Checking of Timed Automata
what: Presents TA2SMT, a direct BitVector/real-arithmetic SMT encoding of timed-automata networks for bounded model checking, preserving TACK’s MITL property encoding while removing the intermediate CLTLoc representation and adding semantic and implementation fixes. TA2SMT encodes active transitions as BitVector identifiers, adds one location-specific null transition per location, derives location aliases from transition sources, represents bounded integer variables in two’s complement, and encodes clock guards with elapsed-time terms before resets. The complete formula combines initialization, transition, synchronization and lasso constraints; an argument relates its soundness/completeness to the prior TACK CLTLoc encoding. It supports non-equality integer guards, broadcast synchronization and all left/right-closed interval combinations that the old implementation lacked. Experiments compare TA2SMT with TA2CLTLOC and MITL0,∞ BMC on Fischer mutual exclusion, Gearbox, Token Ring, Philips Audio and modified CSMA/CD models, showing scalability gains and new model coverage.

title: TACO: A Toolsuite for the Verification of Threshold Automata
what: Introduces Taco, a modular toolsuite for developing and verifying threshold-based distributed algorithms modeled as monotonic or extended threshold automata, with SMT, ZCS/BDD, and ACS/WSTS model checkers plus semi-decision support for reset/decrement extensions. The paper specifies TA configurations, resilience conditions, guards and updates, and ELTL_FT safety specifications, then details a preprocessor and three algorithms. TACO accepts ByMC .ta/.eta and a TLA+ fragment, emits traces, uses safe Rust crates and interchangeable SMT/BDD backends, and reports about 97% line coverage.

title: Taming an Authoritative Armv8 ISA Specification: L3 Validation and CakeML Compiler Verification
kind: conference mechanized ISA-validation and compiler-verification paper
what: Connects a compact L3 Armv8 specification to a HOL4 model extracted from Arm’s authoritative Armv8.6 A-class ASL specification via Sail and Lem. Instruction simulation lemmas then support a CakeML compiler correctness theorem with respect to the ASL-derived machine semantics. Sections 3–4 explain the extraction pipeline, manual patches and proof engineering needed for a 488 kLOC HOL4 specification. The authors replace set-valued nondeterminism with Hilbert choice, replace address translation by an identity map and widen physical-address types. The state relation aligns common registers and memory under system-register and well-formedness constraints; l3_models_asl requires allocated decoding and successful exception-free L3 execution. Symbolic evaluation bypasses monolithic ASL decoding before interactive proofs for arithmetic, logical, branch, address and load/store instruction classes. The simulation takes 7.5 kLOC proof plus 0.5 kLOC automation. Section 5 reuses CakeML’s L3 encoder and runs Asm, L3 and ASL state machines together to establish instruction and whole-program results. The final theorem permits resource-limit failures. The work reproduces a known cbnz/cbz error and validates its correction; CakeML does not emit cbnz.

assumptions_limits: The theorem covers the supported general-purpose instruction subset under explicit system-register constraints, a well-formed state, encodeability and appropriate compiler/machine configurations. Address translation is stubbed, and the machine stepping model omits interrupts and devices. The proof does not cover all Arm features, exception behavior or hardware concurrency. Official ASL is the root of trust; ASL→Sail→Lem→HOL4 extraction is unverified and includes manual changes. The paper suggests testing generated HOL4 against Arm tests or hardware as future validation. Whole-program machine behaviors refine source behaviors extended with out-of-memory errors.
use_for_goal: Useful for locating the machine-semantics trust boundary beneath verified systems code. The concrete technique is to retain a tractable compact ISA model and prove that its supported instructions simulate an authoritative model. It illustrates why a proof at one specification layer needs explicit extraction, state and hardware assumptions before being treated as an end-to-end systems guarantee.

The latter extends source behaviours with out-of-memory errors: unlike source semantics, machine semantics is bounded by finite memory.
Our root of trust is the extensive Arm-internal evaluation of the ASL specification, but extraction via Sail could introduce unintended semantic changes.

title: Taming Large Bounds in Synthesis from Bounded-Liveness Specifications (Full Version)
what: The paper synthesizes reactive systems from Safety LTL extended with bounded next/eventually/until operators. It translates formulas to countdown-timer games, representing large numeric bounds symbolically rather than expanding them into nested next operators. The construction defines timer ordering and closure invariants, expansion/tree/timeout/squeeze operations, and a safety-game reduction whose locations encode current obligations. The full evaluation compares the prototype to ebr-ltl-synth and Strix on LTLEBR, SYNTCOMP, discretized real-time, railroad, conveyor-belt, robot-camera, and office-robot benchmarks, including bounds up to 21,600.

title: Data-Driven Verification of Procedural Programs with Integer Arrays
what: Introduces Tapis, a data-driven Horn-ICE decision-tree learner for procedural C-like programs with parametric-size integer/boolean arrays. It learns universally quantified loop invariants and procedure pre/postconditions by diagramizing array states into scalar samples, learning a quantifier-free decision tree, and lifting the classifier back to quantified array formulas; Z3 is the teacher that supplies counterexamples and inductiveness implications. The paper specifies finite-size array semantics (out-of-bounds reads return 0/false and writes have no effect), CHC encoding and Horn implications, then states the diagramization/lifting correctness results (proofs are deferred to the cited full version): Theorem 1 lifts a classifier of a consistent diagram sample; Theorem 2 guarantees consistency once each array has enough quantified indices. Attribute generation combines interval/octagon templates with patterns extracted from program assignments/guards. Bubble sort illustrates learned invariants; permutation preservation is explicitly outside that example. The implementation uses Clang frontend, C++ Tapis and Z3, tunes the teacher toward small arrays, and compares 215 programs: 121 SV-COMP array programs (84 safe, 37 unsafe) plus TAPIS-Bench (49 iterative, 37 recursive, 8 mutually recursive). Under 300-second runs on an 8-core 3.2GHz/16GB machine, Tapis solves 159/215 (95 safe iterative and 45 recursive safe plus 19 unsafe), versus Spacer 132 and Prophic3 118; it handles recursive procedures that several competitors cannot. Tapis uses at most two quantified variables per array/predicate in these sets and solves array-argmax for arbitrary N in 0.47 s where UAutomizer exceeds 36 minutes at N=5.

Its learner/teacher loop separates candidate synthesis from Z3 checking and exposes concrete failure conditions, while recursive array support broadens the cases beyond simple loops. It remains a C/CHC method whose formulas, solver model and attribute choices must be trusted and whose benchmarks are not distributed protocols.

title: Temporal-Logic Based Runtime Observer Pairs for System Health Management of Real-Time Systems
short_name: Temporal-logic runtime observer pairs for SHM
what: Defines and proves correct paired runtime observers for mission-time LTL/MTL specifications: an asynchronous observer emits exact verdicts once future information is available, while a synchronous observer emits an immediate three-valued abstraction (true/false/maybe). The rt-R2U2 architecture maps both observers to static FPGA blocks with configurable interconnections and feeds verdicts to Bayesian health reasoning. The paper formalizes discrete-time MTL, execution sequences and mission-time LTL projection, then gives algorithms for negation, bounded invariants/eventuality, conjunction with FIFO synchronization queues, and bounded until with lockstep input. It proves observer space/time bounds and synchronous circuit bounds (11 two-input gates per AST observer; depth 4d). Configuration synthesis parses an AST, allocates paired blocks and computes queue sizes from worst-case delay. A Swift UAS case uses flight-rule and sensor-fusion specifications; FPGA simulation and Bayesian posteriors detect a laser-altimeter outage without instrumenting flight software.

assumptions_limits: Time is discrete and event verdicts are sampled from a real-time clock; mission-time bounds make future operators finite. Hardware observers avoid recursion/dynamic memory and use finite-width timestamp registers/queues, so queue sizing depends on worst-case delay and formula depth. Synchronous outputs are an over-approximate three-valued abstraction and may be maybe; exact asynchronous outputs can be delayed. The evaluation is a proof-of-concept on one UAS trace/FPGA design, not a broad statistical flight campaign, and Bayesian model quality is external to observer correctness.
use_for_goal: Shows a complete specification-to-monitor pipeline with proofs, bounded real-time semantics, hardware resource bounds and field data. The paired exact/abstract observers and Bayesian interface are useful precedents for runtime checking of distributed-system assumptions, though the paper targets UAS hardware rather than distributed protocols.

title: Termination Analysis with Compositional Transition Invariants
what: Introduces Compositional Termination Analysis (CTA), replacing repeated expensive whole-program safety checks in Binary Reachability Analysis with ranking of loop-free unwindings and a transitivity check on a disjunctively well-founded candidate transition invariant. Increasing unwinding depth and removing already-ranked transitions permits short terminating fragments to yield a global termination argument. §2 defines transition invariants as supersets of transitive reachable transition closure, and disjunctive well-foundedness as finite unions of well-founded relations. §3 observes a transitive disjunctively well-founded relation is well-founded. Lemmas 1/2 accumulate rankings of increasingly deep, not-yet-covered unwindings and allow skipped intermediate depths; the implementation uses powers of two. Algorithm 1 tracks an overapproximation X of reachable states. A failed ranking produces a candidate nontermination precondition C: reachable C establishes nontermination; unreachable C is removed from X. Thus reachability checking remains where ranking fails rather than in every refinement. §4 slices each loop independently, havocs other loops and assignments depending on five or more variables, and uses CBMC symbolic execution to discover paths in loop-free fragments instead of enumerating all of them.

assumptions_limits: Soundness depends on the rank subprocedure returning a disjunctively well-founded superset or a genuine nontermination precondition, and on valid reachability checks. Finite-state nontermination completeness requires a complete rank procedure, unlike the implemented incomplete engine. Per-loop slicing/havoc overapproximates behavior and can lose termination proofs; practical heuristics replace assignments depending on at least five variables. Evaluations compare identical abstracted slices, not untouched drivers. Baseline is selected from BRA-successfully-analyzed, nontrivial loops, so speedup figures are conditional on that subset. Fast variants skip path-precondition checking or all reachability checking, potentially reporting false nontermination outside these benchmarks; the paper reports no precision loss on its measured examples. No scheduler fairness or busy-waiting progress argument is supplied for concurrent programs.
use_for_goal: Useful for generated Verus termination arguments and specification/proof-agent benchmarks: a local ranking argument must cover reachable multi-step behavior, and transitivity can avoid repeated global checks. This paper provides a clear example where an introductory completeness claim needs qualification from the technical theorem. It is systems-code termination analysis rather than a concurrent or distributed protocol liveness proof. No Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment is reported.

title: The Formalization of Decision-Free Petri Net
what: Reports a Mizar-library formalization of decision-free Petri nets, alternating directed paths and simple circuits, natural-valued markings, enabled transitions and totalized firing. Proves that each circuit’s sum of place tokens is preserved by a transition and by every finite sequence under that firing operation. Separates genuinely firable sequences from total evaluation, where disabled transition attempts leave the marking unchanged. The decision-free condition requires exactly one incoming and one outgoing transition per place, not one input/output per transition. A key structural lemma shows that any transition incident to a circular path’s place must occur on that path. Alternating-position and almost-injective-sequence lemmas support the one-step circuit invariant, which extends to finite sequences through the firing composition law. Firing is explicitly a no-op when disabled, so the final theorem needs no enabled-sequence premise; this strengthens the total-function equality without establishing legal execution or liveness.
assumptions_limits: Markings map places to natural numbers. Arcs are unweighted relations in the displayed definitions: a successful firing subtracts one at input-only places, adds one at output-only places, and leaves both/neither places unchanged. No timed transitions, capacities, inhibitor arcs, arc weights, failure model or scheduling fairness appear in this formalization, despite reference [19] being a timed-Petri-net textbook. Decision-free-like (Definition 7) says every place has exactly one predecessor transition and exactly one successor transition. A transition may have multiple input or output places. The final decision-free-net mode also assumes Petri-like and existence of a directed circuit. Underlying Petri-like/basic-net definitions are imported and not expanded in the article; this reading does not independently audit those MML definitions. Directed paths have odd length at least three, alternate place-to-transition and transition-to-place arcs, and end at a place. Circuits additionally are circular and almost one-to-one: they close at the first place without internal repetitions. The repeated endpoint is not counted twice, since token sums use the finite set of places in the sequence, not the sequence with multiplicities. Preliminaries define an enumeration of marking values on a finite place subset and sum it to obtain the token number. Empty subsets use the empty sequence. The paper also establishes finite-sequence uniqueness facts and a smallest example PN0 with place 0, transition 1 and both connecting arcs. It does not provide a new algorithm for finding every circuit in a large net. Propositions 5–10 locate initial/final arcs and show places occur at odd indices and transitions at even indices, with neighboring arcs around each internal occurrence. Proposition 15 uses unique per-place predecessors/successors to show that a transition incident to any place of a circular path is a transition of that path. Without that closure, a transition outside the circuit could inject or remove a circuit token. A transition is firable exactly when all its input places have positive token counts (Definition 11). Definition 12 makes firing total: if firable, update by incidence; otherwise return the original marking. Input-output self-loops still require a positive token even though their net update is zero. Disabled attempts are stuttering evaluations, not enabled transitions. Definition 13 separately defines a firable finite sequence using a chain of intermediate markings and an enabledness obligation at every position; the empty sequence qualifies. Definition 14 evaluates any finite transition list using the total one-step Firing function and returns the initial marking for an empty list. Its absence of enabledness conditions is deliberate in the displayed definition and determines the scope of Proposition 17. Propositions 11/12 connect a transition with its singleton list and their firability. Proposition 13 gives Firing(Q concatenated Q1,M)=Firing(Q1,Firing(Q,M)) without a firability premise. Proposition 14 derives prefix firability and suffix firability at the prefix result from firability of the concatenation; no converse is stated in the printed proposition. Proposition 16 quantifies over a decision-free net, one circuit, any natural marking and any transition. It preserves the sum over exactly that circuit’s place set. Proposition 17 extends this equality to any finite transition sequence, with no assumption that the sequence is firable. It does not establish global conservation of all places, boundedness of every place in an arbitrary net, liveness, deadlock freedom, fairness, reachability completeness or infinite-trace properties. Reader proof explanation: a disabled transition stutters. A transition disjoint from the circuit changes no circuit place. If it touches the circuit, Proposition 15 puts it on the circuit; almost injectivity and unique place incidence leave one circuit input and one circuit output (possibly the same place). Thus the one-step sum change is zero, and finite-sequence iteration preserves it. The article gives dependency lists rather than a complete displayed Mizar proof script for the final two propositions. The article identifies MML entry PETRI_DF, version 8.1.02 5.22.1199, and supplies formal theorem statements with short proofs/dependency references. This is evidence of a published formalized development, not an independent local check. No MML files, proof checker, executable simulator, benchmark, empirical protocol case study, proof-time measurements or artifact build was run or inspected here. The paper has no Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent result. Its relevance is reusable transition-system invariants and precise enabledness semantics. Applying its invariant to a distributed protocol would require a proved model relation from protocol states/steps to this restricted net class. A claim that a resource count is preserved in deployed code would need that extra refinement argument.
use_for_goal: Concrete finite-step invariant model for distributed/concurrent resource reasoning. Reader inference: proof-agent benchmarks should separate enabled execution from totalized no-op semantics, conserve the specified place set rather than a larger global quantity, and retain assumptions needed for transition closure. The finite-step invariant can motivate a TLA+ invariant or Verus proof, but no such translation, distributed implementation or agent evaluation is supplied.

title: The Marabou Framework for Verification and Analysis of Deep Neural Networks.
what: Presents a modular SMT-style satisfiability engine for piecewise-linear neural-network queries. Custom revised simplex repairs linear constraints; activation objects repair or case-split nonlinear constraints; topology-aware bound tightening simplifies them; timeout-driven input partitioning supports parallel solving. Reports comparisons on 180 ACAS Xu, 500 CollisionDetection and 81 TwinStream queries. Soundness/completeness is asserted through an extension of the cited Reluplex proof, not proved in this tool paper or machine-checked here. Specifies contracts for activation satisfaction, local fixes, equivalent exhaustive linear case splits and entailed bounds. Describes an ordered engine loop and queue-based D&C timeout escalation, plus symbolic input-dependent neuron bounds. At four cores Marabou generally beats Planet but not ReluVal; at 64 cores the authors report better average ACAS runtime, with ReluVal crashes qualified and their treatment in averages unspecified. Arithmetic trust, imported proof details and exact solved counts and per-query timing data remain outside the presentation.
assumptions_limits: Query variables represent neurons; weighted sums are linear equations and activations are piecewise-linear constraints. Supports fully connected and convolutional feed-forward DNNs, with built-in ReLU and Max. Modularity does not establish support for arbitrary smooth activations, recurrence or every TensorFlow operator. Activations are restricted to guarantee termination. The solver checks satisfiability of network plus property constraints. To verify safety, encode a violating behavior: UNSAT excludes violations, while SAT supplies a satisfying assignment/counterexample relative to that encoding. The text mentions nonlinear property constraints, but no decision procedure for arbitrary nonlinear input/output relations is specified. Soundness, completeness and eventual termination are author claims said to follow from a straightforward extension of Reluplex. No full proof, machine-checked development, proof certificate checker or rounding analysis appears here. Imported proof assumptions and correspondence to actual C++ execution are not independently established. State includes the current assignment, variable bounds and constraints. Custom revised simplex uses implicit matrices, steepest-edge selection and Harris ratio tests. Replacing GLPK avoids repeated translation and supports deductions tailored to activations. No ablation isolates these choices or validates numerical behavior. Activation objects implement satisfied, getPossibleFixes, getCaseSplits and getEntailedTightenings. A local fix can violate other constraints; SAT requires all constraints. Splits must be equivalent and exhaustive; bounds must be entailed. New classes must meet these obligations, which extensibility alone does not prove. Repeatedly violated activations are case-split to ensure progress. For Max, cases select either maximal input and permit overlap at ties. The paper provides examples/contracts, not an implementation-level proof for all branches and pivot heuristics. Constraint deduction uses activation notifications and row equations. Network deduction expresses neuron bounds as linear functions of inputs; tighter inputs can force activation phases. Bounds must enclose every feasible value. Reader observation: an uncertain ReLU cannot be replaced by one chosen phase without a valid bound or case split. Ordered engine rules: split after repeated fixes; backtrack or UNSAT on inconsistency; repair linear violations; repair activation violations; otherwise SAT. Deduction uses heuristics. Stack management, cycling avoidance, thresholds, tolerances and implementation invariants are not fully specified. D&C queues query/timeout pairs starting at (phi,T). UNSAT removes a subquery; SAT ends search; timeout partitions into k queries with timeout m*t. UNSAT aggregation requires complete input coverage; any SAT branch suffices. Partition heuristics and parallel coordination are not formally verified. This is not a distributed-protocol correctness result. Smaller input regions may improve sequential deductions, but no controlled single-core D&C ablation appears. Partition overhead and imbalance prevent inferring linear speedup. Core theoretical termination does not guarantee completion within experimental timeouts. Interfaces accept compiled C++ queries, NNet/text files and Python/TensorFlow protobuf. Parser correctness, operator translation and correspondence to deployed floating-point inference are unproved here; results concern the encoded query. Four-core comparisons use 180 ACAS Xu queries with Marabou D&C T=5,k=4,m=1.5 and one-hour timeout. ReluVal/Planet comparisons explicitly use four cores; Reluplex parallelism is unstated. The additional Planet comparison uses 500 CollisionDetection and 81 TwinStream queries: 761 total named queries by reader arithmetic. ReluVal could not run CollisionDetection/TwinStream due to technical difficulties. At four cores Marabou generally beats Planet, not ReluVal; Figure3 also shows many gains over Reluplex and outliers. No solved-count table, SAT/UNSAT split, medians, repeats, machine configuration or exact revision hash appears. TO/ERR bins are not finite runtime measurements. Figure2 plots average ACAS runtime for P1–P4 at 2,4,8,16,32,64 CPUs. Authors claim better overall average at64 cores and completion within two hours, except a few ReluVal segfaults. ReluVal remains faster on P4, so this is not superiority on every property. Exact means, crash counts, censoring treatment and raw data are absent; no plot values were digitized. Figure3 has logarithmic axes, Marabou vertical, comparator horizontal, equal-time diagonal and TO/ERR categories. Bottom-right legend calls the prose CollisionDetection family CollisionAvoidance; no extra distinct dataset is inferred. Overlapping points prevent exact solved-count recovery. Front page bears a CAV/AEC Artifact Evaluated badge. Reference14 links https://github.com/guykatzz/Marabou/tree/cav_artifact; modified BSD license is reported. Published evaluation is distinct from this reader’s execution/replication. Source, imported proof and benchmark artifact were not opened or run. Future work includes abstract interpretation, heuristics and tighter integration of linear/nonlinear solving; current parts remain relatively separate. No LLM proof-agent, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or verified distributed implementation result appears.
use_for_goal: Reusable verification-tool and proof-agent evaluation ideas: distinguish search from deduction; require equivalent case splits and entailed bounds; preserve witness versus UNSAT trust and parser/number-domain boundaries; compare explicit resource budgets with timeout/crash treatment. Parallel query execution does not prove a distributed protocol. No LLM specification/proof, Verus/Rust or TLA+ result.

title: The Rewster: Type Preserving Rewrite Rules for the Coq Proof Assistant
what: Extends Coq definitional reduction with user rewrite rules and presents a bidirectional type-preservation criterion for PCUIC with universe cumulativity and SProp proof irrelevance. Pattern types and metavariable types are inferred generally; right sides are checked against those types, optionally using equality constraints safely forced by a well-typed match. Coq implementation is reported, while confluence checking and justified conservative rules remain future work. Explains why checking a propositional equality at some common type is unsound under cumulativity and why ordinary unification can infer unjustified symbol injectivity. Gives higher-order metavariable substitution, restricted symbol-headed patterns, triangle/confluence restrictions, a matching antisubstitution proof and a constraint-extraction relation robust under later environment extensions. Separates type preservation from consistency, confluence and termination; implementation status is explicitly dated to publication.
assumptions_limits: Underlying setting is annotated PCUIC with metavariables plus universe/sort-quality variables. Typing depends on a well-formed environment, local/metavariable contexts, structural guard conditions for fixpoint consistency and usual positivity for inductives. Virtual sort annotations matter to principal pattern types but do not carry observable matching content. Pattern matching is restricted: head of main elimination branch must be a declared symbol, not an arbitrary metavariable; variables may occur in argument holes. Patterns are left-linear, contain no β/ι-redexes, and cannot inspect syntactically irrelevant/SProp terms. Holes at irrelevant positions are allowed. These restrictions support the confluence/postponement argument. Subject reduction is conditional on appropriate confluence/triangle and pattern restrictions as well as the type-preservation criterion. Implementation of arbitrary rewrite declarations alone does not establish these global conditions. §8 says porting the Agda confluence checker is an immediate future goal. Definition4 requires a pattern-inference derivation at Tp with exactly its pattern metavariables Θ, and ordinary typing of the right side at Tp. Definition5 permits typing the right side under equalities E extracted soundly from pattern typing; it does not permit arbitrary assumptions selected to make the right side typecheck. Constraint extraction relies on rigidity/injectivity stable under environment extension. Symbols may receive future rules, so eliminations headed by symbols do not justify injective decomposition. Bare metavariable equality can be retained; equalities under higher elimination contexts are discarded, and if several equalities are extracted for one pattern variable, all but one are discarded. The full relation returning no equalities is sound but less useful. Type preservation is not consistency: symbols and rewrite principles may already be inconsistent propositionally. Consistency transfer is attributed to prior extensional-type-theory interpretation when proposed rules are admissible as propositional equalities. Justified-rules support proving this connection is future work, not required/checked automatically for every declaration. Termination is not assumed for subject reduction. The paper states a checker can be correct when it answers while potentially diverging. Its repeated decidable-criterion wording must therefore not be read as a proved total decision procedure for unrestricted user-supplied nonterminating rewrite systems. Article formally presents metatheory in the PCUIC framework and reports implementation. It does not provide a demonstrated machine-checked end-to-end proof that the modified Coq kernel implements this metatheory. No proof-checking session, kernel audit or artifact run was performed by the reader. At publication, rewrite PR18038 was integrated in development, expected for Coq8.20; type-preservation PR19290 was implemented but not yet integrated. These are historical paper statements, not checked current Coq/Rocq release status. Implementation extends presented syntax to primitive projections, universe/sort polymorphism and unfold_fix symbols. Exceptions example has acknowledged potential universe-inconsistency warnings on the if/match rules. No claim that all examples/rules are automatically safe, terminating or conservative. No runtime benchmark, corpus acceptance/rejection rate, proof-size comparison or user-study evaluation. Evidence consists of formal rules/proof arguments, counterexamples and implementation examples. Abstract formally-expressed wording is not interchangeable with fully mechanized verification.
use_for_goal: Reader inference: important for evaluation of LLM proof/extension agents because accepted rewrite declarations may change kernel conversion and require distinct checks for typing,confluence,termination and consistency. Provides concrete adversarial examples for universe constraints,dependent holes and unsafe injectivity. Direct subject is proof-assistant metatheory; no distributed protocol,Verus/Rust,TLA+ or agent benchmark is reported.

title: The Rocq-NN-Roll Prover: Soundly Verifying Hyperproperties of Neural Networks in Rocq
what: Reports a Rocq implementation and soundness/completeness proof for checking rational piecewise-affine feed-forward neural networks against finite-arity universal relational specifications. Reduces a network plus hyperproperty to a joint piecewise-affine function, enumerates affine segments and searches each segment for a negative satisfaction value by a verified mixed-strictness Fourier–Motzkin solver. Provides monotonicity/robustness examples and a small nine-network runtime experiment. Printed solver theorem and robustness example contain concrete inconsistencies, which this record separates from uninspected artifact correctness. A computational real-subset interface and reduced-rational dependent type support evaluation while retaining embeddings into reals. Total piecewise-affine functions prevent partial-domain gaps from vacuously proving network properties. The formal specification restricts input preconditions to a convex polyhedron and both generator/satisfaction maps to total piecewise-affine functions. A specification-equivalence proof guards manual encoding, then verified decomposition, segment splitting and strict-negative feasibility compose into the final boolean iff theorem. Prototype limits and differing GitHub/evaluated-artifact content are explicit.
assumptions_limits: Targets feed-forward, finite piecewise-affine networks with rational arithmetic, exemplified by affine Linear and elementwise ReLU layers. It does not support arbitrary sigmoid/nonlinear activations, recurrent cycles, training correctness or deployed floating-point/parallel semantics. The formal interface generalizes to ordered real subsets with suitable operations; its computable exact solver requires division. Exact mathematical soundness does not remove a mismatch with finite-precision inference. RealSubsetOAM packages an embedding into real numbers preserving order, addition and multiplication; Coquelicot algebra/matrix support is extended around it. QDEP is the dependent subtype of rationals fixed by rational reduction, removing multiple representatives. The authors explicitly assume proof irrelevance to identify equal reduced-rational values under standard Rocq equality. Rationals with division support FME; merely being an integer subset is not enough for the solver’s division interface. AffineSegment pairs a convex polyhedron with an affine map. Segments can be partial and domain membership is tested. Total piecewise-affine functions (TPWAFs) have composition/concatenation preserving totality. Neural-network affine decomposition returns a total function. Segments can overlap at activation boundaries; a function representation must agree there, not count each segment as a distinct execution. The supported hyperproperties quantify universally over finitely many executions of the same deterministic network. Arity r is fixed in the specification. This is a finite-input/output relational class, not arbitrary temporal hyperlogic, probabilistic fairness or infinite-trace properties. The paper uses monotonicity, robustness and individual fairness as examples of this class; only monotonicity and one-dimensional robustness receive worked formal encodings. Informal NNDH uses input tuples X generated from W by netIn and output acceptance netSat>=0. Formal NNHyperproperty narrows W to a convex polyhedron, netIn to a total piecewise-affine generator and netSat to a scalar total piecewise-affine map over the restricted real subset. Thus not every mathematical relation or arbitrary precondition is accepted. Rational instances quantify through the chosen representation/embedding; no theorem about floating-point inputs is supplied. Specifications are manually translated into the framework. The recommended method first writes a natural predicate and proves equivalence to the encoded hyperproperty. Monotonicity1d uses r=w=2, precondition x1<=x2, identity generator and affine netSat=y2−y1; the paper displays monotonicity_1d_correct. This protects the property encoding when the equivalence is proved, but the prover does not infer the human’s intended specification. joint_pwaf composes netSat with concatenated netIn and r copies of the network composed with netIn. Because concatenation takes separate inputs, evaluation duplicates x as colvec_concat x x, explaining the 2w segment input dimensions. The network-to-piecewise semantics theorem asd_preserves_satisfiability connects this construction to natural network satisfaction. Partial pwaf_eval None is treated as True; using total network/generator/satisfaction components is essential to avoid certifying an undefined input. Segment splitting universally requires satisfaction on each segment under W. Linear constraints combine W, segment domain and strict violation of the required nonnegative scalar output. Feasibility gives a counterexample; infeasibility for every segment proves the universal property. A zero satisfaction value is allowed, so the negated output condition is strictly<0 rather than<=0. Mixed strict/non-strict inequality support is therefore a correctness requirement. Fourier–Motzkin solver returns Some assignment when feasible and None when infeasible according to the intended algorithm and subsequent equivalence theorem. Reader visually confirmed that displayed fme_correct on p.494 instead says None => exists sol,is_linear_system_solution sys sol, missing negation. Both printed branches assert feasibility. This cannot be the claimed correct theorem for an inconsistent system such as0<0; record it as a printed theorem defect. Artifact proof may differ and was not inspected. The final verify_hyperporperty_correct states boolean true iff nn_satisfies_nndh, composing decomposition, split and linear-system correctness. The counterexample interface returns a solver assignment on first failing segment; None across the finite list yields boolean true. Correctness is author-reported machine formalization, not established here by executing the shown code. Some displayed type parameters/dimensions and theorem names are abbreviated or inconsistent; this record does not treat the printed snippets as a compilable standalone artifact. Robustness predicate on p.496 has parameter order (epsilon,delta), and requires |x1−x2|<=delta implies |N(x1)−N(x2)|<=epsilon. For fixed epsilon, robustness is downward closed in delta. The prose on p.497 claims robust for delta=.096,epsilon=.1 but not for smaller delta=.0959,epsilon=.1, which contradicts that order property. The theorem calls actually supply first arguments .096/.0959 and second .1, so they instead vary epsilon with delta=.1; the prose swaps meanings. The displayed example_not_robust2 statement on p.498 also omits negation before is_robust_1d, while its proof starts by introducing the positive property and deriving contradiction. That script shape proves a negated proposition. These are source presentation defects, not reader evidence that the kernel accepted contradictory proofs. Reader Figure3 check after independent visual review: the middle output weight is −.3. The network is ReLU(.66 ReLU(−x+.1)−.3 ReLU(x+.25)+.99 ReLU(.7x)+.1). Its four slopes on regions divided at−.25,0,.1 are−.66,−.96,−.267,.393, and its outer ReLU stays positive. Hence it is globally .96-Lipschitz, consistent with the positive call epsilon=.096,delta=.1. Inputs−.2 and−.1 produce .283 and .187, differing exactly .096; this refutes epsilon=.0959,delta=.1. These are exact reader calculations, not artifact execution. The earlier record misread the negative weight and has been corrected. Robustness encoding uses two halfspaces for |x1−x2|<=delta and a two-segment output absolute-value function; the paper reports equivalence to is_robust_1d. Robustness example was added during two-stage review after artifact evaluation. GitHub includes it, but peer-evaluated Zenodo artifact explicitly does not. It must not be described as checked in the evaluated artifact or as evidence that all published snippets compiled. Authors give O(2^n) network segments for n ReLU activations, O(n) constraints per segment, and O(2^(nr)) systems of O(rn) constraints when r network copies are combined. These estimates suppress complexity contributed by netIn/netSat and W, so should be read for fixed/simple specifications. FME has exponential elimination blow-up; no polynomial-time performance claim is made for the full prover. Replacement by a polynomial linear-feasibility solver is future work. title: Verified Progress Tracking for Timely Dataflow
what: Formalizes and proves safety of modern Timely Dataflow progress tracking in Isabelle/HOL by composing distributed progress exchange and worker-local propagation. Corrects an earlier TLA+ clocks model that excludes supported non-upright behavior and lets workers inspect/update global state. Sections 3–4 reconstruct the earlier clocks protocol, whose upright updates require introducing larger pointstamps while dropping smaller ones, then replace its global record field with worker-owned capabilities plus in-flight data. New capability creation is justified by local capabilities; a weaker justified predicate governs withheld progress updates. Sections 5–6 model weighted cyclic graphs, partially ordered timestamp summaries, frontier antichains and incremental worklists. The work_vacant-conditioned local safety theorem and implied-frontier equality compose with exchange under the could-result-in order; initialized workers’ downstream frontiers conservatively witness every existing pointstamp. The proof separates general assumptions with locales and uses signed multisets for finite-support integer counts. Section 7 compares proof engineering with the ported TLA+ proof and reports executable local-propagation comparison against Rust examples.
numbers: one person-week and about 1,000 extra lines to port earlier TLA+ safety proofs
assumptions_limits: Finite workers and locations, reliable FIFO progress-message queues, and partially ordered pointstamps. Timestamp summaries are nonnegative, monotone and compositional; every proper graph cycle strictly increments timestamps, and self-edges are excluded. Workers may fail-stop or pause indefinitely; the system retains safety but does not recover. Combined propagation runs to an empty worklist as one action only when it terminates. The paper explicitly does not prove general propagation termination or liveness/fair delivery. Safety covers progress tracking, not the whole dataflow runtime, user operators, or an implementation-refinement theorem for Rust. Proof sketches and more formalization details are in a separate linked extended report not included/read here.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to distributed-system verification, TLA+ proof/model fidelity and Rust-related research. It shows that a previously verified abstract model can miss valid implementation behaviors and worker-locality constraints, supplies concrete assumptions needed by cyclic dataflows, and distinguishes model safety, comparative testing and implementation correctness. It is not a Verus proof of the Rust code or an LLM-agent evaluation; those remain possible follow-on uses.

title: Tiramisu: Fast Multilayer Network Verification
what: Tiramisu verifies distributed routing configurations by building multilayer graphs of routing processes, VLANs, physical links and route attributes. It chooses a policy-specific algorithm: path-vector simulation for actual path selection, integer linear programs for quantitative path metrics, and graph traversal for potential path existence. A Yen-based accelerator avoids enumerating some failures. The paper gives conditional handwritten correctness arguments and performance comparisons on real and synthetic configurations. Records RAG tainting and TPG construction, L2 contraction, routing-algebra operations and convergence boundary, physical-failure correlation, complete ILPs and TDFS/TYEN listings, ACL repair example, all tables, detailed baseline conditions/core counts, unsupported feature combinations, and qualified printed-formula/listing/proof concerns rather than treating broad speed or correctness claims as universal.
assumptions_limits: §§4.1–4.2: A routing adjacency graph (RAG) is built per destination subnet. Vertices are routing processes and static-route holders; paired edges encode BGP/OSPF adjacency and directed edges encode redistribution. Route-origin vertices are tainted, propagating except across consecutive iBGP edges. This preliminary phase assumes active adjacencies and no filtering; traffic propagation graphs (TPGs) subsequently model those dependencies and filters. §4.2: A TPG is built per source/destination subnet pair. Vertices include process RIBs, per-device VLAN ingress/egress, source and destination. Edges encode physical VLAN-compatible links, L2 flooding, process dependence on L2 or OSPF routes to BGP next hops, and attachments to processes tainted for destination. VRFs replicate process vertices. Parsing/device configuration, topology, protocol settings and concrete advertised prefixes form the trusted input. §4.2: Prefix/neighbor route filters and source/destination IP ACLs prune edges. Other edge labels add/remove/block route tags or carry metric vectors (administrative distance, local preference, AS-path length, OSPF cost). Import/export actions are placed on importing-process outgoing edges. Traffic traverses opposite to route advertisements: blocked-tag information propagates toward tag-adding edges. Shared physical-link variables correlate multiple logical protocol edges under failures. §5.1: Layer-3 TPG contracts L2 paths whenever connectivity exists, combining non-overlapping labels. Routing algebra has signatures, a preference relation, labels, a composition operator and origination signature. Composition and comparison are per protocol: BGP sets local preference, adds AS-path length and uses OSPF tie-breaking; administrative distance mediates protocol choice. Full protocol implementation semantics and parser refinement are not mechanized. §5.1/Algorithm 1/Appendix C.1: TPVP starts destination with origination and other nodes empty, repeatedly composes neighbor paths/signatures and picks locally preferred paths in shared-memory order until paths stop changing. Theorem 1 is conditional on network convergence and supported routing algebras. Lemmas 2–6 argue permitted-path, contraction and ranking correspondence by node/protocol cases, then compare round-robin TPVP to path-vector protocol scheduling. Footnote 4 assumes the algebra has all properties needed for convergence; no general termination theorem for arbitrary configurations. Appendix C.1 qualified proof boundary: The scheduling argument says any ordering leads to a valid solution. That supports a stable solution under its premises; it does not separately establish unique outcomes across multiple stable states or equivalence to every possible concrete convergence schedule. Do not infer universal deterministic path selection from convergence alone without the requisite algebra/uniqueness assumptions. No Verus, Rust, TLA+ or proof-assistant development provided. §5.2/Appendix A: TYEN replaces Yen’s Dijkstra step with TPVP, forms candidates by root/spur perturbations and checks configured preference order. Acceleration requires strictly monotonic path-cost composition. Removing root vertices prevents loops; removing next edges excludes already enumerated paths. Candidate-specific eRemoved tracks these exclusions, not only realizable physical-failure sets. Category-i checks without acceleration may enumerate failures. Appendix A/Algorithm 3 qualified listing concern: The prose chooses the shortest candidate, but line 23 appends to the end of listB and line 26 removes its first entry. No sorting or priority-queue operation is printed. A FIFO list can choose a worse earlier spur candidate before a better later one. This is a discrepancy in the printed listing; the implementation was not executed or inspected to establish a tool failure. §6.1/Appendix B.1: KFAIL means reachability with strictly fewer than K physical-link failures. The ILP minimizes failed physical links, represents traffic reachability/propagation and reverse-flow blocked tags, ignoring irrelevant cost preferences. Theorem 9 is stated for no ACLs. Logical AND/OR are said to be expressible as ILP constraints; actual solver encoding/refinement and external solver correctness are trusted. Appendix B.1/Table 2/Eqs.4–5 qualified printed-formula defect: oNodes excludes both src and dst; Eq.4 constrains reachability only on oNodes, and Eq.5 constrains propagation only for edges entering oNodes. Rdst=0 therefore has no connection to incoming traffic. On a connected tag-free graph the literal formulas admit zero failures with Rdst=0. An incoming-flow/destination-reach constraint is needed. Theorem 9 proof invokes Eq.4 at dst although its quantifier excludes dst. This is about the published encoding, not an executed artifact counterexample. §6.1: ACLs can drop data while route advertisements still attract it. Authors explicitly show pruning an ACL path can overestimate resilience: P1 preferred to ACL-blocked P2 preferred to P3, all edge-disjoint; one failure of P1 causes a drop, whereas pruning P2 yields apparent min-cut two. Repair computes N for graph disconnection and L for choosing an ACL path, returning min(N,L). TYEN finds the first ACL path M, keeps the union of preceding M−1 paths, and min-cuts it for L. §6.1 qualified ACL proof boundary: Cutting the union of earlier preferred paths is not explicitly constrained to keep the first ACL path available; a shared cut might remove that path too. The paper does not separately prove that only the first ACL-bearing path suffices for arbitrary overlaps. Treat this reduction as needing a preservation/completeness argument, not a reproduced failure. §6.2/Appendix B.2: BOUND maximizes selected inter-device edges with unit source output, unit destination input, internal flow conservation and tag constraints. The text uses length ≤ K although Table 1 prints length < K. Equal Bound changes the objective to minimum length and compares extrema. No separate end-to-end mechanization proves ILP soundness/completeness. Appendix B.2/C.2 qualified printed-formula defect: Unit endpoint flow and internal conservation allow a valid src–dst path plus a disconnected directed cycle, all selected edges equal one. Maximizing their sum counts the cycle as additional path length. The printed constraints have no connectivity or subtour elimination condition. Theorem 10 proof incorrectly assumes every invalid selected flow must have an unbalanced node; a cycle is balanced. No implementation failure claimed. §7/Algorithm 2/Appendix C.3: TDFS first checks raw disconnection, then reachability with blocking edges removed, then blocking-edge-to-destination reachability with adding edges removed, then blocking/adding pair connectivity after removing tag-removing edges. Theorem 13 uses four path cases and claims exact always-unreachable classification. Supported tag treatment excludes multiple tags affecting the same destination. Description claims a constant number of DFS calls, while pair checks in the listing can scale with tag edges. Algorithm 2 line 7 qualified generic-listing concern: It searches from any blocking edge to dst without requiring a compatible prefix from src to that edge. A graph with sole src path s→b1(block t)→a1(add t)→d and an unrelated source-unreachable branch x→b2(block t)→d passes this check via b2 although the src path is blocked. A source-relevance invariant or prefix check is needed for the generic listing. Realizability under every TPG construction invariant is not proved here; no network or artifact test executed. §7/Appendix D: Waypoint checks remove the waypoint then test reachability; waypoint-chain checks remove nodes for each waypoint and search between preceding/following chain nodes. Multipath consistency retains multiple best signatures and compares best-path counts with/without ACL pruning. Blackhole checks consider ACL-attracting routers or static next hops without destination reachability. These inherit graph/model/algorithm assumptions; no arbitrary temporal or transient-routing property language. §9/Appendix C.1: Concrete external advertisements only; no existential/universal symbolic advertisement search, control-plane equivalence or quantitative prefix-count policy. IP-based ACLs only; port/protocol ACLs, ACLs affecting routing advertisements, community groups/AS-path filters and multiple tags affecting one destination are outside coverage. iBGP route deflection and local preferences/tag filters assigned to received iBGP routes cannot be modeled correctly; Appendix C case iii-d explicitly states this. §8: Real universities include VRF/VLAN and cannot be modeled by compared tools in that evaluation. Real datacenter and synthetic Zoo/Rocketfuel inputs support different feature subsets; no single baseline comparison covers all claimed generality. Plankton uses 32 cores versus Tiramisu one core. Baseline versions, complete runtime distributions, memory totals, seeds and confidence intervals are not given. No new real configuration bug yield or correctness differential count reported. §8: Results are author measurements: median over 100 runs for 100 different traffic classes, standard-deviation bars. This wording does not clearly establish 100 repeated trials per class. Faster per-policy verification does not quantify coverage of unsupported constructs or correctness of the published formulas. Abstract <2.2 s on large networks and Zoo <0.12 s refer to different described workloads; retain both rather than silently equating them. §8.3 calls one failure k=1 despite the strict <K convention elsewhere.

title: Encoding TLA+ set theory into many-sorted first-order logic
what: Presents the translation used by a TLAPS SMT backend to encode TLA+’s untyped ZF-style sets and functions into many-sorted first-order logic. A universal sort represents non-Boolean TLA+ values, Boolification identifies propositions, and preprocessing rewrites/abstracts non-basic constructs before SMT solving. The encoding handles heterogeneous untyped expressions, set membership and extensionality, partial-domain functions, tuples, records, arithmetic bridges between TLA+ values and SMT integers, and deterministic Hilbert choice. A sound terminating/confluent rewrite system normalizes operators; abstraction introduces fresh symbols for residual non-basic terms, while definition elimination reduces user definitions. The backend targets shallow non-temporal obligations common in distributed-algorithm safety proofs. Benchmarks cover Peterson and Bakery mutual exclusion, Memoir type/refinement proofs, and finite-set cardinality, comparing CVC4/Z3 with ZIP backends and typed/untyped encodings.

Quantifier generation can overwhelm SMT solvers; rewrite/abstraction may expand formulas. Arithmetic is linked through an injective embedding into a universal sort and relies on solver reasoning. title: Specification and Verification With the TLA+ Trifecta: TLC, Apalache, and TLAPS
kind: formal verification workflow and case study
what: Uses a TLA+ specification of asynchronous termination detection and Safra's ring algorithm to demonstrate complementary verification with TLC explicit-state checking, Apalache bounded/SMT and inductive-invariant checking, and TLAPS theorem proving, including refinement from the algorithm to a high-level state machine. The high-level module specifies active nodes, pending messages, termination detection, safety, liveness under weak fairness, and quiescence. Safra's algorithm adds white/black colors, message counters and a circulating token; termination requires an inactive node 0, no pending messages, white token/node, and zero accumulated counter. TLC finds 4,097 states for N=4,K=3 in the abstract model and 1.3 million (N=3,K=C=3,Q=9) or 219 million (N=4 with same bounds) in the algorithm model, exposing state explosion and a token-color bug. Apalache checks bounded prefixes, proves an inductive invariant for N=100 in 20 seconds, and checks quiescence for N=100 in 11 seconds. Refinement is checked for small N; TLAPS proves type, safety, liveness, and refinement for arbitrary instances, with an invariant proof taking about 230 lines and liveness/refinement about 245 lines. The conclusion recommends TLC first, Apalache for inductive invariants, TLC/random exploration for liveness, then TLAPS for higher confidence.

title: Improving BDD Based Symbolic Model Checking with Isomorphism Exploiting Transition Relations
what: Presents Transition Locality Exploiting BDDs (TLEBDDs), which represent component transition relations with a reduced BDD plus a mapping list, implicitly encoding unchanged local variables as identity patterns. A specialized AND algorithm combines TLEBDDs without expanding them, with optional immediate abstraction/shift during image computation. The system model is a finite interleaved asynchronous composition whose component reads/writes only shared variables and its own local state. TLEBDD removes identity patterns for other components and shares isomorphic subgraphs across replicated component relations; the mapping list maps reduced to actual interleaved variables. The paper derives recursive AND handling for identity-pattern levels and explains why immediately shifting target variables to from-state variables avoids large intermediate BDDs. It evaluates forward reachability in an adapted Sviss/CUDD checker and separately measures transition-relation construction, comparing ordinary partitioning, identity reduction, and TLEBDDs.

CCP 10: ordinary and TLEBDD time out; immediate shift completes in 12:32h with 67,822,819 nodes
Transition construction: MutexLocal 2047 uses 3,414,118 TLEBDD nodes while ordinary and identity-reduced forms run out of memory
assumptions_limits: Requires finite-state systems, interleaved asynchrony and transition locality; experiments use replicated components and concatenated variable ordering, one 2.4-GHz Pentium core with 3 GB RAM, and a 24-hour timeout. Gains vary by benchmark: Dining Philosophers has little memory reduction and slight slowdown at 22 components, and future work identifies other orderings/algorithms. The approach is a data-structure optimization, not a new correctness logic; reachability results inherit the checker/model assumptions.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant to formal verification of distributed/concurrent systems: it shows how symbolic representation choices determine whether exhaustive reachability is feasible and reports concrete protocol scaling limits.

title: Token Elimination in Model Checking of Petri Nets
what: Presents static and marking-dependent dynamic abstractions that reset irrelevant Petri-net place tokens to zero while preserving a target reachability property, reducing branching and duplicate markings. Static least-fixed-point sets S↑φ/S↓φ propagate visible positive/negative effects from the query; dynamic C↑M/C↓M/CFM first over-approximates future possible effects and fireable transitions, then computes refined visible sets D↑φ,M/D↓φ,M. Tapaal integration applies abstraction at every reachability node.

what: . title: Accelerated Bounded Model Checking Using Interpolation Based Summaries
what: Introduces Trace Inlining, a lazy BMC algorithm that alternates under- and over-approximation, extracts Craig-interpolant procedure summaries from verified traces, and reuses/refines summaries across call contexts; implemented as Saransh. The inlining tree tracks overapproximated, inlined, blocked and summarized call sites. A verification oracle encodes passified procedures as SMT VCs; a verified partial trace yields an interpolant summary that replaces a subtree. LIFO unblocking explores all relevant traces; when a reused summary is insufficient, a stronger context summary is conjoined. title: Infinite State Model Checking by Learning Transitive Relations
what: Presents Transitive Relation Learning (TRL), which learns transitive relational summaries while bounded-model-checking an infinite-state transition system, reducing its effective diameter until finite-depth unsatisfiability proves safety. TRL detects loops in SMT models, computes conjunctive variable projections and transitive projections from recurrence analysis, adds learned relations while forbidding consecutive use of a learned relation, and uses blocking clauses to prefer learned transitions over loops. Learned relations over-approximate for safety, so safety is sound but unknown may result; an acceleration-based under-approximation replacement reconstructs traces to prove unsafety. The implementation supports LIA relational formulas/CHCs and integrates Yices/Z3 in LoAT. The paper proves Theorem 22 (safe result implies safety) and correctness of linear-integer transitive projection, and details limitations, related interpolation/acceleration approaches, and a 626-problem CHC evaluation.
numbers: On 626 distinct LIA-Lin CHC problems with 300-second timeout and about 11GB memory, LoAT TRL solved 386 (267 safe, 119 unsafe), including 16 unique safe and 1 unique unsafe proofs (19 and 9 when ABMC is disregarded). Z3 GSpacer solved 373; LoAT ABMC solved 272. TRL was strongest overall and competitive in runtime, while GSpacer led safe instances and ABMC led unsafe instances.
assumptions_limits: The theory assumes a complete first-order theory with effective quantifier elimination; implementation is restricted to linear integer arithmetic. TRL may diverge because learned-relations generation/trace search is not guaranteed to terminate, and learned over-approximations cannot prove unsafety without acceleration. BMC unrolling can bottleneck large systems, although backtracking on loops mitigates this. Future work targets reals, bitvectors, arrays and temporal verification.
use_for_goal: A modern automated proof-search method for infinite-state safety that learns relational summaries rather than interpolants. It is directly relevant to formal verification automation and CHC backends used for Rust/C, but does not verify distributed protocols or produce Verus proofs itself.

title: Robustness Verification of Tree-based Models
what: Develops exact and anytime lower-bound verification for decision-tree ensembles under l∞ perturbations. A single tree is verified in linear time; an ensemble is reduced to maximum K-clique search in a K-partite box-intersection graph, and a multilevel clique algorithm gives progressively tighter robustness lower bounds. Each leaf corresponds to a d-dimensional axis-aligned box. Ensemble leaf tuples are feasible exactly when their boxes intersect, yielding a K-clique; Theorem 1 bounds exact verification by min{O(n^K), O((2Kn)^d)} for at most n leaves/tree and d features. The multilevel algorithm merges T tree parts into pseudo-nodes, preserving boxes and refining a bound level by level until exact. It also handles multiclass attacks, arbitrary query boxes, unimportant features and anchor-like analyses. Across nine datasets and standard/robust GBDTs (500 examples where feasible, 10-step binary search), bounds are close to MILP while up to roughly 3000x faster; for robust MNIST the reported bound ratio is 0.96 and 12.6s versus MILP hundreds of seconds.

title: Position: Trustworthy AI Agents Require the Integration of Large Language Models and Formal Methods
what: Argues for bidirectional LLM/formal-method integration: LLMs automate specification and proof work, while model checkers, theorem provers, SMT solvers, testing and runtime monitors constrain and certify LLM actions. The proposed six-stage pipeline starts from natural-language requirements, auto-formalizes them, runs model checking/theorem proving/SMT, tests edge cases, monitors executions and iteratively refines outputs. It sketches a Coq theorem-prover agent and a miniF2F even-number example. Sections 2–5 distinguish failure modes of LLM-only reasoning (hallucination, non-determinism, no traceability), FM-only workflows (specification effort, scalability and unpredictable environments), and hybrid trade-offs. The auto-formalization workflow creates a proof outline with placeholders, delegates algebraic gaps to external tools and revises failed proof steps. The model-checking discussion targets safety/liveness, deadlock and refinement; theorem proving targets machine-checkable proofs; SMT handles satisfiability; testing and monitoring cover behaviors outside proofs. Appendix A gives explicit Coq interaction steps and an Isabelle/HOL formalization attempt, making the proposal concrete but not an implemented benchmark. The implemented PAT prototype repairs GPT-4o car-lock modeling errors using model-checker traces: leavekey must require an open door, and locking receives explicit owner/key guards. Appendix A also gives Z3 meeting scheduling with missing unavailable-day constraints and a Dafny palindrome specification/implementation; these illustrate semantic alignment risks rather than measured success rates.

title: Efficient Two-Layered Monitor for Partially Synchronous Distributed Systems
what: Combines an efficient HLC γ-extension filter with an accurate SMT predicate detector. The filter controls false-positive/false-negative trade-offs; the SMT second layer checks only marked windows, yielding constant-size clocks and large monitoring-time reductions for partially synchronous distributed systems. The model assumes bounded clock skew ε but no message-delay bound, and expresses violations as predicates over process variables. ε-extension considers all states within skew to remove false negatives for supported predicates, while γ<ε reduces candidate windows at the cost of recall. The second layer encodes event intervals, causality, skew, and predicate truth as SMT constraints; batching 100 windows amortizes solver calls. Experiments simulate 10 round-robin processes (one million iterations each) and evaluate precision/recall across message probability α, state-true probability β, delay δ, skew ε, and duration ℓ, then test mutual exclusion in time-division multiplexing.
numbers: γ=0.045 setting: precision falls 0.929→0.295 as γ goes 0.1ε→ε while recall rises 0.009→1
for n=10, δ=10, ε=100, α=0.1: two-layer 3.1 s versus single-layer 81 s
average cost reduction 90%, minimum 85%; second-layer maximum 2.5 s
γ=0.25ε example costs 228 ms with false-negative rate 0.627
assumptions_limits: Partial synchrony and known (or estimated) ε are required for the accuracy guarantees; predicate detection remains NP-complete in general. HLC γ-extension cannot handle all predicates and may produce false negatives when γ<ε. The two-layer monitor has perfect precision because SMT filters false positives, but recall is only perfect at γ=ε and runtime may become a bottleneck if the filter marks too many windows. Experiments are simulations and one mutual-exclusion application.
use_for_goal: Provides a concrete distributed-systems verification/monitoring design with explicit soundness trade-offs, SMT witnesses, and quantitative overhead results; useful as an operational complement to formal proofs of distributed implementations.
