title: Practical, Low-Effort Equivalence Verification of Real Code
kind: symbolic equivalence checker and libc/toolchain evaluation
what: Presents uc-klee, which automatically gives two C functions symbolic inputs, lazily creates pointed-to data and cross-checks outputs/errors on explored paths; evaluates libc implementations, revisions, compiler optimizations and self-checks. §2 describes an automatic harness that snapshots memory, executes one function, restores original values while retaining constraints, executes the other, then compares escaping results or error type. User wrappers filter invalid inputs or canonicalize allowed output differences, exemplified by isdigit. §3 tracks referents in symbolic shadow memory so low-level pointer/integer casts and symbolic-index accesses work. Output comparison recursively follows return/argument-reachable memory, comparing data and pointer offsets while allowing allocation addresses to differ; unrelated globals are omitted. Lazy initialization handles unbound pointers through unique symbolic objects, constrained addresses, size-doubling from 8 bytes and nested-allocation depth limits. §4 distinguishes instruction coverage from path exhaustion and uses identical-code cross-checking to expose verifier nondeterminism and pointer-tracking defects. Comparing O0/O3 versions exposes a confirmed LLVM 2.6 memmem optimizer defect.
numbers: cross-library 143 checked: 66 verified, 57 different, 15 timeouts, 4 KLEE-limited, 1 uc-klee-limited; at least 7 actual bugs
revision comparison 203 checked: 84 verified, 20 different, 30 timeouts, 56 KLEE-limited, 13 uc-klee-limited; 2 new bugs and 5 patched bugs
optimizer comparison 622 checked: 335 verified, 70 differences, at least 1 confirmed LLVM defect
self-check 622 checked: 335 verified, 12 differences; median coverage 100%
150 function pairs verified up to fixed 8-byte input bound; lowest median coverage 90.1%
ffs 33 paths exhausted in 6.8s with 100% coverage; lazy object maximum 2KB
300 routines (150 distinct pairs) equivalence-verified by exhausting paths up to 8-byte input size (§1)
Lowest median statement coverage 90%; all other experiments 100% (§1)
Found a serious LLVM optimizer bug and numerous uc-klee errors (§1)
isdigit filter eliminated all mismatches for isdigit and 11 analogous routines (§2.1)
assumptions_limits: Equivalence holds only for the finite explored paths, bounded object sizes/depth, single invocation in isolation, chosen compiler and architecture. If both functions make the same mistake, cross-checking cannot detect it; matching error types count as equivalent even with different root causes. Lazily allocated objects cannot alias existing objects, missing overlap/circular-buffer behaviors; some address constraints cannot be realized. Unbound function pointers are unsupported. KLEE concretizes symbolic allocation sizes and floating-point operands, potentially missing other values; unresolved externals, symbolic external-call arguments, inline assembly and structure returns can make paths unverifiable. Global state is compared only when reachable through returned/formal-argument pointers. Reference behavior and filtering wrappers replace a formal intended-behavior specification, and differences are not automatically bugs.
use_for_goal: Relevant to evaluation of generated proofs and code changes: an independent implementation or previous revision supplies a differential oracle, while self-equivalence checks exercise the verifier/compiler chain. The paper demonstrates why coverage, bounded equivalence, confirmed bugs and intended functionality are separate claims. This can complement Rust/Verus or TLA+ validation but proves neither distributed behavior nor an agent’s ability to formulate a correct specification.

title: UCAgent: An End-to-End Agent for Block-Level Functional Verification
what: Presents UCAgent, an end-to-end LLM agent for block-level hardware functional verification using a Python DUT environment, configurable 31-stage workflow, automated stage checkers, and Verification Consistency Labeling (VCLM). The design converts Verilog/SystemVerilog DUTs to Python packages with Picker/Toffee, decomposes requirements through coverage and testcase stages, and enforces FG/FC/CK labels across artifacts. The implementation separates middleware, workflow management, validation, and execution modules; checker feedback drives retries. what: Implements verification and synthesis of heterogeneous networks of interdependent stochastic models: DTMCs, CTMCs, MDPs, POMDPs and stochastic multiplayer games. Models remain separate while properties of one supply probability or reward parameters to another. Defines dependency, external-observation and internal-choice parameters. title: Unbounded-Time Safety Verification of Stochastic Differential Dynamics.
what: Reduces infinite-horizon probabilistic safety for nonlinear polynomial Ito SDEs to finite-horizon verification. Exponential stochastic barrier certificates give an exponentially decreasing tail bound; time-dependent polynomial barriers and SDP then bound the selected finite interval. Defines the stopped diffusion and infinitesimal generator, uses vector supermartingales and Doob maximal inequality to prove tail bounds, and gives sufficient conditions for time-dependent finite-time certificates. The reduction picks a horizon after which the tail is below any requested epsilon. SDP templates synthesize both certificate types, while matrix exponentials handle vector certificates. The full paper evaluates three examples: scalar population dynamics, a noisy harmonic oscillator and a two-dimensional nonlinear drift system.

title: A Unified View of Piecewise Linear Neural Network Verification
what: Recasts major PL-neural-network verification methods as branch-and-bound optimization and introduces a benchmark suite for comparing their bounds, branching and search behavior. Boolean output properties become a scalar minimization/counterexample problem by adding linear and max-pooling layers. Reluplex, Planet, MIPplanet, BaB, BaB-input, BaB-relusplit and BaBSB are described as choices of bounds, splitting and search in one algorithmic template. The paper argues that rebuilding convex approximations after each split tightens bounds, proposes input-domain branching and Kolter-Wong smart branching, and releases CollisionDetection, ACAS and PCAMNIST benchmarks. Higher-level relaxations and non-PL activations are identified as extensions when suitable bounds exist.

title: Do Unit Proofs Work? An Empirical Study of Compositional Bounded Model Checking for Memory Safety Verification
what: Studies a systematic bottom-up method for compositional CBMC unit proofs. Analysts iteratively build harnesses, ensure termination, increase coverage, and refine models of unknown variables/functions from error traces; objective completeness requires graceful termination, full reachable-line coverage, and resolution of every memory-safety violation. The study selects 73 functional units from 89 known defects across FreeRTOS, Zephyr, Contiki-ng and RIOT. Initial harnesses set loop bounds to one; coverage gaps trigger larger bounds or allocation limits, while error traces drive minimal preconditions and function models. The blind construction protocol separates defect identification from proof writing. Analyses quantify model types, loop bounds, development/execution cost, comparison with engineer-authored FreeRTOS proofs, and generalizability to larger functions.

title: Vac - Verifier of Administrative Role-Based Access Control Policies
what: Vac reduces administrative RBAC user-role assignment reachability to program verification. It prunes policies while preserving the target-role query, then uses an integer overapproximation for safe answers or an exact bounded-user Boolean encoding for complete analysis and attack finding. It reconstructs attacks in the original policy after pruning. Default execution combines Interproc, CBMC and μZ. Details the k+1-user cutoff, abstraction direction, exact encoding, bounded-search Unknown outcome, original-policy attack reconstruction and backend routing. Reports 20 realistic-case variants and 30 synthetic policies, all heavily reduced by pruning. Large original input size is separated from the difficulty of the tiny residual verification problems.
assumptions_limits: §§1–2: addresses ARBAC-URA role reachability under the chosen administrative rule semantics. Privilege escalation and separation of duties can be encoded as reachability queries. This is a policy-model result, not a proof of permissions enforcement in SQL Server, Active Directory, SELinux or Oracle implementations mentioned as motivation. §2: input declares roles/users, initial assignments, Can-Revoke pairs, Can-Assign rules with conjunctive positive/negative role preconditions, administrators and target role. Supports any-user and specific-user target queries. Detailed model semantics referred to [8]; arbitrary policy languages or arbitrary Boolean precondition syntax are not established here. §2: pruning preserves target-role reachability, not every property or full trace equivalence. Six pruning actions and sufficient conditions remove irrelevant roles/rules/users. A two-step witness in an intermediate policy may terminate pruning early. Correct transfer to original policies depends on recorded pruning information and reconstruction. §2: cutoff theorem tracks at most k+1 selected users, where k counts administrative roles rather than administrators/users or all roles. Boolean encoding uses (k+1)×n role bits and nondeterministically simulates rules. This exact reduction depends on the theorem and ARBAC semantics in [8], not a generally valid cutoff for distributed systems. §2 Abstract Transformer: integer variables count users in subsets of role combinations; Interproc uses the box domain. Unreachable abstract error proves no target reachability. Reachable abstract error may be spurious and cannot establish an attack. §2 Precise Transformer: exact Boolean-model error reachability iff policy target reachable. Supports μZ, HSF, Eldarica, Getafix, Moped and NuSMV. Decidability and a complete theoretical reduction do not guarantee that every run finishes within finite practical resources. §§2–3: CBMC underapproximates executions. Found errors supply witnesses; no error gives Unknown. Default unwind=2 is a cheap bug search, not the k+1-user completeness theorem and not a proof that all attacks have depth two. Default falls back to μZ after failed bounded search. §2/Fig1: precise backends can report Error without the CBMC original-policy attack reconstruction path. Counterexample module specifically consumes CBMC output and pruning metadata. The figure also depicts Unknown for bounded failure and No Error for sound negative analyses; do not treat all backend YES/NO labels as identical query semantics. §3: C implementation depends on ANTLR3.2 for C, ROXML and CCL, plus external verification backends. Translation, pruning, parsing, solver semantics and trace lifting remain trusted. No formally verified implementation, proof certificate or source-to-policy correspondence checker is reported. §4: Table1 has four hospital, four university and twelve bank variants. Last four banks modified by the authors to add users and make two queries safe. These are realistic case-study models, not new audits of deployed organizations or 20 independent real systems. §4: Table2 contains three synthetic suites of ten policies, every target reachable. Residuals have only two to four roles and one to three rules despite up to40000 original roles/200000 rules. Results demonstrate effective pruning on selected structures, not solving equally large irreducible Boolean state spaces or balanced safe/unsafe synthetic cases. §4: Linux64, IntelCorei7-3770,16GB RAM; default pipeline. Table1 Reach time is overall analysis time, including pruning, not an additional duration to sum with the pruning column. Positive times include counterexample generation. Backend-specific counts, repeat variance, time/memory budgets and ablations are absent. §5: priority and performance comparisons with Mohawk, RBAC-PAT and asaspXL are author claims without a head-to-head timing table here. Separate-administration restriction discussed for Mohawk/RBAC-PAT is not an assumption imposed on Vac. Temporal RBAC is cited as prior application, not evaluated in this paper. No new in-paper cutoff/translation proof or mechanized theorem is supplied; core proofs cited in [7,8]. Software, prior proofs and benchmark files were not independently run/read. No Verus, Rust, TLA+ or LLM experiment is reported.

title: Validating the eBPF Verifier via State Embedding
what: SEV tests the Linux eBPF verifier with deterministic closed programs. It profiles accepted programs, folds their observed register states into R9, then inserts a conditional illegal operation that must be reachable under the observed execution. Accepting that transformed program exposes an unsound approximation. A one-month upstream campaign found15root-cause-distinct verifier logic bugs, including12soundness/3completeness bugs and two reported privilege-escalation cases;10were fixed at submission. This is empirical validation of a verifier, not a whole-verifier correctness proof. Records the self-checking containment oracle and paper-only argument, deterministic-input and trace-preservation assumptions, concrete folding/operator/tracer design, false-negative paths and lack of detection-equivalence proof, all bug class/location counts and overhead values, manual triage, precise sample failures/diagnostic errors and privilege conditions. Separates verified-component claims from incomplete specification/implementation correspondence and records no bugs found in tnum.c rather than treating that as proof.
assumptions_limits: §§1,3.1: Necessary soundness invariant is that every concrete execution state belongs to the corresponding abstract state. The testing oracle embeds an observed value with a branch to an invalid operation; a correct analyzer must consider that branch feasible. A rejected transformed program due to the sink passes this particular test, not every state/path or full verifier soundness. §§3.1–3.2: Inputs are accepted, closed, deterministic eBPF programs without external input/interactions so a single profile is repeatable. Correct interpretation/tracing, folding evaluation and transformed control-flow/register behavior are assumed. The method does not directly validate arbitrary nondeterministic production BPF workloads, concurrent shared map changes or every environment-dependent helper. §3.1 Proposition3.1/Corollary3.1: Paper argues embedding adds no invalid operation except the sink, using branch-state partition Ai=Aj union Ak and safety under subset Ak. This is a prose argument, not a mechanized proof of the generator/transformer/verifier semantics. It presupposes correct construction and original accepted program behavior; it cannot establish that all verifier rejections are bugs without diagnosing their cause. §3.1 folded variant/§4.5: Paper calls folded detection capability equivalent to direct embedding based on likely propagation over continuous campaigns. No injectivity or detection-equivalence theorem/probability bound is proved. §4.5 explicitly allows arithmetic to hide some non-contained states. Folding collisions/precision loss and missing generated programs can produce false negatives; longer testing is not a completeness guarantee. §3.2: R9 is reserved for folded state. One random ALU function is generated per basic block, then reused each time that block occurs in a loop trace; folded expected value is evaluated in execution order. Folding excludes division and unary operations and uses nonzero registers to reduce collapse to zero. These restrictions concern folding instructions, not necessarily every original generated instruction. §3.2/§4.2: Structured generator tracks lightweight register/stack types, encodings and control flow to make accepted tests likely. Tracer records instruction indices/register states at basic blocks using an internal buffer, virtual device and mmap. It does not snapshot all accessible memory; load/store issues are detected only if they propagate to observed registers or yield another diagnosed failure. §§3.2,4.1: Interpreter bpf/core.c is patched for tracing, so runtime ground truth is relative to this interpreter/instrumentation. No claim of testing every JIT compiler, processor or architecture follows. A verifier behavior not exercised by generated accepted programs may remain unchecked. §4.1: Campaign boots compiled upstream kernels in QEMU/KVM guests, restarts dead VMs, and retains original program/profile/transformed program. Root-cause analysis/deduplication is manual; automatic discovery does not mean automatic explanation, exploit construction, patching or independent validation. §4.2: Counts are15unique roots within one month and10fixes as of submission. These historical results do not imply all bugs are fixed today or each has a CVE. Two reported exploitable cases require CAP_BPF or CAP_PERFMON; they are not both demonstrated unprivileged-without-capabilities attacks. All15roots are reported in verifier.c, not arbitrary kernel-memory bugs. §4.2: Soundness bugs wrongly accept unsafe programs; completeness bugs wrongly reject safe ones. Rejection for a reason other than the sink prompts a completeness-bug diagnosis under valid transformation assumptions. A wrong diagnostic for an already-invalid program, as in Figure5d, is a logic-error case but by itself does not demonstrate acceptance of unsafe code or rejection of safe code. §4.4: Overhead comparison runs24hours and repeats measurements for each program, but does not report number of repetitions/programs, distributions, absolute throughput, confidence intervals, per-VM vCPU allocation or accepted-program rate. Total1.6%throughput impact is small partly because only infrequently accepted programs are profiled/transformed. No direct controlled bug-yield comparison with Syzkaller/BVF/Buzzer is shown. §4.5: No false positives observed is an empirical author report, not a proof of the whole oracle implementation. Accepted-program search diversity is the main acknowledged source of false negatives. Raw coverage refers to execution paths in generated programs and induced coverage to verifier code; optimizing induced coverage is left outside scope and no measured coverage percentage is supplied. §4.5: Directly inserting many sinks can halt checking early or fork repeatedly; verifier state pruning cannot remove these paths because precise registers have different ranges. One final folded sink avoids that multiplication. It also tests newly inserted arithmetic, which can expose a bug absent from the untransformed program. §5: Authors report range-analysis bugs in the same Linuxv5.19 version Agni claimed to verify and cite incomplete conditions/divergence issues. This challenges scope/specification correspondence, not validity of every formal proof. No bugs found in previously verified tnum.c (~200LOC) is a testing observation, not a newly proved soundness result. Agni range analysis is~2100LOC against~20000LOC overall verifier. §5: Compared with offline abstract-log comparison, the target verifier itself interprets embedded predicates, avoiding a second full abstract-state parser/reference verifier. This is a metamorphic testing oracle with a semantic containment requirement; without predefined per-component specs does not mean without any specification or modeling assumptions. §§5–6: Kernel-local case applicable to evaluating proof/checker trust and generated specifications. No distributed protocol, Verus/verified Rust, TLA+ or LLM-agent evaluation. A real adaptation to proof assistants/distributed verifiers requires a corresponding executable semantics, valid transformation and oracle; none is implemented here. No SEV repository/artifact appendix pointer in saved PDF; external references and bugs not replayed.

Useful benchmark pattern for LLM agents generating specs/proofs: retain original/runtime/transformed witnesses and classify soundness versus precision failures. Paper evaluates eBPF verifier logic, not distributed systems or Verus/Rust/TLA+/LLMs.

title: VEP: A Two-stage Verification Toolchain for Full eBPF Programmability
what: VEP separates eBPF verification into C-level symbolic execution and SMT proof generation in user space, compilation that translates code, assertions and proofs, and independent bytecode symbolic execution/proof checking intended for kernel space. Separation logic describes owned memory and helper-acquired resources. Annotations expose loop invariants and contracts unavailable to fully automatic verifiers. The paper reports acceptance/rejection, time, memory and annotation/proof sizes on 41 small programs, and claims Coq proofs of the separation-logic transformation properties. It does not present a mechanized soundness/refinement theorem for the entire executable toolchain. Records proof-generation/checking boundary, trusted helper specifications and bytecode semantics, assertion restrictions and conversion rules, compilation passes and source-property loss, safety versus intended functionality and termination proof limits, concrete string/list/socket examples, all Table 2–5 results and deployment/version uncertainty. Separates sample success from universal no-error/full-programmability claims; checks discrepancies in memory/speed/acceptance prose and proof-line terminology; preserves printed illustrative inconsistencies without claiming implementation defects.
assumptions_limits: §§2/5: Claimed small trusted computing base excludes the C verifier, compiler and SMT solver because bytecode is checked again. Guarantee still depends on correct executable bytecode checker, faithful eBPF instruction/memory/arithmetic semantics, actual helper contracts, and correspondence with kernel execution/JIT. The paper supplies no whole executable-checker soundness or code-to-kernel refinement theorem. §5 specifically reports Coq proofs for separation-logic transformation properties, not all these components. §§2.1/3/5: VEP-C computes strongest postconditions, eliminates spatial entailments, and uses its own SMT solver producing cvc5-style proof terms. VEP-eBPF independently symbolically executes bytecode and checks spatial/pure proof steps without solving. Checked proof terms remove the need to trust SMT answers only to the extent proof rules and their checker/semantics are correct. Kernel-space deployment is the intended architecture; evaluation does not clearly distinguish an in-kernel deployment benchmark from standalone checker measurements. §§2.2–2.3/7: Introduction and capability section claim functional correctness, but §2.3 explicitly makes user intent the user’s responsibility and §7 lists functional correctness as future work. The reported Key_connection annotations are expressly memory-safety-only. Accepting bytecode safety does not establish intended lookup/copy semantics or preservation of arbitrary source assertions. §2.2: Termination within finitely many steps is claimed. The shown loop reasoning uses invariants and exit conditions; no explicit general ranking-function, decreasing variant or fuel/step-bound rule is explained. Invariant preservation alone establishes partial correctness, not termination. This is a limit of the presented justification, not a reproduced checker counterexample. §§2.1/6.2/Appendix B: Full programmability and no false positives/negatives are author claims. Finite examples and annotations do not establish completeness for all safe programs; general entailment is acknowledged undecidable. Spatial-expression scope restrictions reject some natural quantified array assertions, requiring custom predicates. Appendix B DNF normalization can multiply branches, so approximate linear symbolic-execution cost in statement/assertion length excludes assertion-size growth and SMT solving. §3: Memory ownership uses disjoint spatial conjunction; duplicated ownership is inconsistent. Built-in helper contracts are derived from documentation, not proved against kernel helper implementations. Resource acquire/release soundness depends on their completeness and accuracy, including permitted null returns, flags and sizes. Contract variants are selected for supported contexts. §§2.3/4: Source C undefined behavior can compile into memory-safe bytecode. Early source rejection protects source semantics beyond kernel bytecode safety. Maliciously altered bytecode with a valid safety proof may pass without matching original program intent. Neither final safety checking nor an unverified compiler automatically proves C-to-bytecode functional refinement. §4: Compiler uses nanopasses, member-to-offset conversion, calling convention transformation, iterated register coalescing, and explicit stack frame preconditions. Few optimizations supported. Dead source variables become existential logical variables. Figure 14 deliberately turns a false source assertion x==1 after x=0 into satisfiable exists _x,_x==1; source assertion truth is lost even though bytecode safety can survive. §4 Figures 13/15, Appendix A: Printed illustrations contain apparent inconsistencies. Figure 13 sets R1=0 then asserts R1==*(R10-4)+1 while stack value is0. Figure 15 declares fields x,next but accesses l.head. Appendix A transforms forall n,v!=n*n into forall n,n!=n*n, which fails for n=0/1 and is not generally equivalent. These are source illustration issues; artifact behavior was not tested. Appendix A prose also describes x as a nonsquare although displayed condition constrains v with x=2*v. §3 Figures 4/6/9/12: An arbitrary owned output list proves initialized memory/ownership, not that memset filled every byte or strncpy copied/padded correctly. Figure 9 uses stronger repeat(v,n) content predicate; Figure 6’s displayed successful strncpy postcondition is weaker than complete C-library functionality. Keep actual predicate content when evaluating generated proofs. Appendix B: Internal assertions separate program-variable addresses, pure facts and owned memory; logic variables in spatial facts require permitted existential binding. Printed array-address conversion shows V(e1+e2) without explicit element-size scaling; semantics/type conventions would need inspection before inferring a compiler defect. §6: Evidence is 41 selected small C programs, not large production services or adversarial bytecode fuzzing. Linux Kernel5.15 and PREVAIL August2024 used. Hardware, trial repetitions, confidence intervals, human annotation time/user study and whole-tool LOC are not specified. No independent reproduction performed. §6 Tables 2–5: Passing rate means acceptance for safe cases and rejection for unsafe cases. All ten unsafe cases stop at VEP-C; compiler/eBPF columns are dashes. Thus data demonstrate C-front-end rejection, not independent final-checker rejection of ten crafted attacks. Safe VEP outcomes are 30 category samples plus one Key_connection, all accepted. §6.2: Linux 6/10 acceptance is for the PREVAIL sample category, not all safe programs; Linux category is9/10 and Stringlib3/10, with Key0/1. PREVAIL10/10,8/10,1/10 and Key0/1. Source attributes PREVAIL variability to SMT dependency/nondeterminism although introduction describes abstract interpretation; no experiment establishes that causal claim. Claimed version regressions30%/20% lack paired version tables, and no cross-version VEP study is shown. §6.1: Claimed predictable2–3MB VEP-eBPF memory is contradicted by Linux sample maximum8034KB (lathist); VEP-C maximum32569KB. Linux average.94ms applies to its accepted Linux sample subset, not all benchmarks, and Stringlib maximum2.69ms. Claimed3–5x faster than PREVAIL is not uniform: Linux category12.48/8.42≈1.48x, while39.46/8.42≈4.69x relative to VEP-C. Different acceptance sets complicate average comparisons. §6.3: Table3 labels proof counts as proof lines, while prose calls64840 proof obligations. Do not infer64840 independent obligations. Annotation lines are a size proxy, not measured effort or expertise. Key proof5819lines in table versus about5800 in text; preserve rounding. §7: LLM generation of annotations, broader functional correctness and advanced optimization support are proposed future work. No LLM agent experiment, Verus/verified Rust/TLA+ proof, distributed-protocol theorem or code execution reported in this reading.
use_for_goal: Useful proof-carrying-code case for evaluating generated specifications and proof checkers: distinguish user intent from safety, source UB from bytecode safety, proof generation from independent proof checking, and isolated Coq logic properties from executable-checker soundness. Resource ownership and translated annotations are relevant to verified Rust/Verus comparisons, but this is C/eBPF work and does not verify a distributed protocol. LLM annotation support is future work, not evaluated agent proof generation.

title: Scalable Deductive Verification of Data-Level Parallel Programs
what: Improves VerCors scalability for array/matrix data-parallel programs with three linked techniques: rewrite nested quantified array expressions into equivalent single-variable forms with usable SMT triggers, use unique type qualifiers to rule out array aliasing, and use immutable qualifiers to model unchanged arrays as mathematical sequences. Kernel-body extraction further reduces solver context. Section 2 explains permission-based separation logic, Viper translation and nested GPU parallel blocks through OpenCL XswapFast and PVL examples. Section 3 defines a bijective inverse for linear index expressions, states conditions for correctness, and reports a 2,500-line Lean 4 proof of the rewrite theorem; nonlinearity and unsupported modulo patterns remain limits. Section 4 explains Viper quantified heap chunks and snapshot comparisons, then defines immutable and unique typing, including struct/pointer examples. Section 5 evaluates CLBlast BLAS kernels, earlier Halide/HaliVer benchmarks and a Radio Telescope Pipeline containing the Padre algorithm. On an i7-11800H/32GB Ubuntu 23.04 machine, ten runs per experiment and one-hour timeout show all techniques up to 150× speedup, 8.5× total Level-1 and 10.8× Level-2 CLBlast speedups, more than 1.9× on earlier experiments, and previously unverifiable xger/xher2 and Padre cases becoming verifiable. The rewriter was essential for every reported experiment; gemm_3 failed because modulo is unsupported.

title: Storage Systems are Distributed Systems (So Verify Them That Way!)
what: VeriBetrKV verifies a single-threaded crash-safe B-epsilon-tree key-value store by combining ordinary Hoare code proofs with TLA-style state-machine refinement of program plus asynchronous disk environment. Reusable crash-safe/cache templates and transposition split journal and tree reasoning. A Dafny linear/shared extension coexists with dynamic frames and a trusted C++ backend; case studies measure reduced proof annotations and competitive but uneven performance. Records disk acknowledgment/corruption/sync contracts, full refinement decomposition and disjoint-region condition, linearity/BoxedLinear trust and borrowing rules, checkpoint/journal architecture, proof-latency discipline and its empirical caveats. Saves complete code/proof tables and printed benchmark values, including contradictory speedup and latency prose. Separates a general asynchronous-system method from an actual multi-node or CPU-concurrent implementation.
numbers: Table 1: 1210 spec, 6373 implementation, 44685 proof lines; the crash-safe map spec is 283 lines
assumptions_limits: §§1–3: Safety and functional correctness only; operations need not terminate. Implementation is single-threaded, with asynchronous I/O/pipelining but no CPU concurrency. Demonstration has one processing node and one disk. Multi-node/multi-disk/heterogeneous generalization is conjectured, and shared-memory thread concurrency is future work. IronFleet has distributed/liveness results, but those are prior work, not VeriBetrKV results. §2.1: User trusts a 283-line top-level dictionary/crash contract, environment/OS/runtime API specifications, build system, modified Dafny/verifier/Z3, C++ backend/compiler/toolchain and hardware behaving as modeled. Smaller specification size may aid review but does not prove the specification matches intent. The linear typechecker changes and BoxedLinear primitives are trusted rather than a separately proved compiler/type-system soundness theorem. §§2.1,3.1: The I/O bus can reorder requests/responses but cannot duplicate or drop them except during crash. The composed StorageIOSystem nondeterministically takes a program step, disk/environment step or whole-system crash. Crash resets volatile program state; acknowledged writes survive, while unacknowledged addresses may contain old, new or corrupt bytes. Arbitrarily many crashes at arbitrary modeled points are covered, including reboot/recovery states. §3.1.1: Disk corruption can occur at any time but cannot produce a valid-checksum block. CRC32C is trusted and referenced by the disk model. Invalid checksum aborts the current query, preserving no-wrong-answer safety at the cost of availability. A malicious disk that fabricates valid checksums, checksum collisions or stale valid blocks violates the assumed model. This is not an unconditional CRC integrity guarantee or fault-tolerant recovery from arbitrary corruption. §§3.1.2,6.2.3: Without crash/corruption the visible state is a dictionary with latest writes. Crash reverts the entire dictionary to a consistent prior snapshot no earlier than the last completed sync. Spec has ephemeral and persistent states; background steps can advance persistence. sync_start/sync_end ensure that at end, persistence includes the state at start or a newer version. Unsynced operations may survive or disappear as part of a consistent snapshot; this is not independent per-key arbitrary rollback or durability of every returned insertion. §3/§6.2: Hoare reasoning verifies synchronous local implementation handlers against the program machine. Environment behavior and crashes are handled by IOSystem refinement. General real-system theorem is conditional on the actual executable, trusted API interactions and environment matching those models. TLA-style refinement is encoded/proved with Dafny, not reported TLC model checking or proof of arbitrary storage behavior. §§3.2,6.2.2: Map→abstract B-epsilon tree with infinite-map nodes→finite pivot-bucket tree separates key semantics from representation. A hypothetical purely in-memory implementation is shown gray and is not an actual second implementation. Generic CrashSafe<T>/BlockCache<T> lifting says a refinement of node/tree contents lifts through a crash-safe cache/disk composition. §6.2.3 Figure 3: Tree IOSystem and JournalIOSystem independently refine CrashSafe<Map> and JournalViewMap. CompositeViewMap applies journal operations to map snapshots. ConcreteCache adds byte marshaling; Disk<byte> refines a partitioned typed disk. Transposition rearranges program/environment components only with an invariant that tree and journal access mutually disjoint disk regions. Their models cannot simply be separated if their effects overlap. §6.2.4: Executable handler invocations refine Next transitions of ConcreteCache; I/O labels are no-op, request or response and must match trusted API actions. Proving code-to-model is insufficient without the enclosing disk composition, while proving abstract crash safety is insufficient without this implementation connection. Recovery does not write disk (§8.1), avoiding a separate write-during-recovery proof burden without excluding repeated crashes. §4: Developer policy stops feature work when verification exceeds 20 seconds, then controls definition visibility, opacity/reveal and solver instantiation profiling. The discipline reduces search burden but cannot decide arbitrary verification, distinguish all timeouts from defects, or guarantee a fixed bound. Measured final passing definitions are not a distribution of failed proof attempts or controlled developer productivity. §5.1: linear means non-aliased mutable values and shared means temporarily borrowed aliased immutable values. Static checking forbids duplication and silent discard and restricts shared values to borrow scope; explicit free is allowed. Functional sequence semantics permit in-place C++ mutation without SMT heap-aliasing reasoning. Ordinary heap references still use dynamic frames, and can be held inside linear structures. §5.1 Figure 2: Trusted BoxedLinear<A> embeds a linear value in a freely aliased heap object. Take requires Has() and sets it false; Give requires no stored value. Borrow is restricted to pure functional callers so an imperative method cannot remove ownership during the borrow. SMT proofs establish Has() where ownership is not syntactically obvious. Thus the method combines type safety with proof obligations rather than enforcing all aliasing rules in a simple Rust-like typechecker. §5.2: Backend maps immutable datatypes to structs, heap arrays/classes to reference-counted objects and immutable sequences to shared storage plus offset/length. Linear sequences use in-place operations and explicit deallocation without reference counts. Mathematical integer executable code is rejected; refined machine integers must fit C++ types. Compiler and runtime correctness are trusted. §§6.1.1–6.1.2: Uses 2 MiB nodes on HDD, 128 KiB on SSD, fanout 8. Serialized lower nodes avoid conversion, while the root uses a mutable search tree for single insertions. A ghost per-index lseq_has sequence permits taking disjoint subsets of linear children during splits. Claims about Rust needing unsafe/Option are the paper authors’ comparison, not a general impossibility theorem about all safe Rust implementations. §6.1.3: LRU BlockCache tracks inter-block references and garbage collection. Persistent/frozen/ephemeral copy-on-write trees represent last completed checkpoint, checkpoint in flight and live updates. Logical-to-physical indirection uses linear-probing hash table; example 1 TiB disk requires 24 MiB table. Two alternating counter-tagged superblocks select the latest checkpoint. Correctness depends on modeled write completion and checksum semantics. §§6.1.3–6.1.4: Checkpoint writes dirty nodes, then indirection table, then a superblock. At checkpoint start dirty shared nodes become write-back-before-editing, preserving the frozen snapshot. A node write must be issued before modification but need not complete before modification; crash can recover the old checkpoint. Logical journal records each insertion; sync persists journal instead of repeatedly writing large nodes. Checkpoint reclaims journal space. §7.1: Table 1 implementation proof/executable ratio is about 4:1; including refinement proofs gives 7:1. These annotation counts are a proxy for final proof burden, not person-time, maintenance cost or specification adequacy. Authors observed no runtime correctness/data-loss bugs but did observe liveness/performance bugs; no duration or exposure denominator establishes a general failure rate. §7.1: Hash-table proof LOC 1678→1063 (about 37% lower), search-tree 2220→1531 (about 31% lower), with search-tree executable LOC increasing 289→373. This compares two author implementations and supports reduced annotation burden for those components, not a universal productivity effect. RocksDB test/production ratio 0.99 and BerkeleyDB 0.45 are not directly comparable correctness guarantees. §7.1 Figures 4–5: 98.3% final proof units under 10 seconds, 99.0% under 20; 37 exceed 20 seconds and 54% of those involve dynamic frames. Hide 308 definitions (18%), reveal 1403 times; 52 never revealed and 74% revealed at most five times. Visibility counts both overestimate and underestimate manual effort. Whole verification takes 1.8 CPU-hours, 11 minutes on 32 cloud machines, not 32 CPU cores in one machine. §7.1 reader qualification: Printed sentence says maximum verification time dropped 10s to 32s and 99th percentile dropped 1.3s to 4.8s. The endpoints increase in that order and conflict with dropped; the PDF visibly contains this wording. Do not silently reverse endpoints or claim a quantified speedup from this sentence without correction from source authors. §7.2: HDD/subcomponent runs use AWS d2.xlarge with four hardware hyperthreads, 2.4 GHz Xeon E5-2676 v3; SSD i2.xlarge has four hyperthreads, 2.5 GHz E5-2670 v2 and SATA SSD. All YCSB systems limited to one core and 2 GiB RAM; load 10 million operations/about 5 GiB, run phases 10000 operations. Reported medians and min/max over six runs, not confidence intervals. §7.2.1 Figure 6 reader calculation: Printed HDD Load medians are BerkeleyDB 233, VeriBetrKV-DF 5649, VeriBetrKV 5579 and RocksDB 44670 ops/s. Ratios from linear VeriBetrKV are about 23.9× faster than BerkeleyDB and 8.0× slower than RocksDB, matching abstract 24×/8× but not body/caption over 25× or caption about 9×. Preserve numerical evidence rather than reconcile by guessing different runs. §7.2.1: VeriBetrKV is slower than both other stores on most queries and roughly 4× below RocksDB, but HDD uniform U has RocksDB 35 versus VeriBetrKV 57 ops/s. SSD Load has VeriBetrKV 8986 versus BerkeleyDB 6664 and RocksDB 72645, about 1.35× faster/8.1× slower; body says 4× slower on SSD, inconsistent with printed load values. Workload-specific outcomes matter more than a universal performance claim. §7.2.1: Authors attribute slowdown to effective-cache reduction from fragmentation/conservative cgroup allocation, lack of overlap between CPU and flush I/O, and 1.5× more I/O than RocksDB, about half extra from checkpoint policy. Simulated 1.8 GiB cache exceeds 13K HDD insertions/s and matches 300K I/Os for 1M queries. These simulations/profiling attributions are not a measured optimized implementation. Query I/O usually 1.5 MiB versus RocksDB 4–8 KiB; future partial-node marshaling is unimplemented. §7.2.2: Microbenchmarks compare dynamic frames/linear on 64M random 64-bit-key hash operations and 8M search-tree pairs. Linear hash inserts and queries are faster but deletes slower; search inserts slower and queries faster. Authors suspect reference-count and reconstruction overheads; no isolated causal experiment is supplied. Dafny type extension is 1900 LOC (3%) and C++ backend 3100 (7.5%). Appendix A: Artifact Docker images include source, modified compiler, verification/performance scripts and graph generation. Any x86/x64 CPU with HDD/SSD, 20 GiB disk and several hours expected; source YCSB/config included. External proof bodies, compiler changes, durability implementation and benchmark scripts were not audited or replayed by this reader. No LLM-agent evaluation is present.
use_for_goal: Direct bridge between distributed-system TLA-style refinement and crash-safe storage, with a Dafny ownership discipline related to later verified Rust work. Contributes proof modularity, trusted-environment clarity, implementation correspondence and solver feedback metrics relevant to evaluating LLM-generated specifications/proofs. No Verus implementation, actual multi-node storage proof, TLC experiment or LLM benchmark is reported.

title: VerifAI: A Toolkit for the Formal Design and Analysis of Artificial Intelligence-Based Systems.
what: Introduces a Python toolkit integrating semantic scenario generation, black-box simulation, property monitoring, sampling search and counterexample analysis for AI-based closed-loop systems. Demonstrates autonomous-driving falsification/fuzzing, counterexample-guided neural-network data augmentation, cart-pole robustness testing and mountain-car training-parameter search. Formal models and temporal-logic monitors guide finite simulation; the paper provides no machine-checked correctness theorem or exhaustive safety certificate. Explains how one semantic feature representation connects six workflows: falsification, fuzz testing, counterexample analysis, data augmentation, hyperparameter synthesis and model-parameter synthesis. Scenic supplies conditioned scenario distributions; monitor scores guide adaptive sampling; feature-valued error tables support PCA and recurring-value analysis. Concrete examples expose perception-to-controller failure propagation and distinguish rewards, training settings and system parameters. Quantitative evidence is mainly a1000-sample cart-pole illustration with38violations; substantial augmentation/algorithm detail is delegated to prior publications.
assumptions_limits: Inputs are a simulatable closed-loop system(controller, perception and plant), a modeled environment and a property. Controller/perception can be arbitrary executable code. The simulator is a black box, so the evidence concerns simulations of this chosen composition and environment. No proof of correspondence to physical dynamics, renderer fidelity, implementation semantics or every possible environment is given. Semantic/abstract features describe objects, positions, headings, colors and parameters rather than raw pixel arrays. They can be hierarchical products of boxes/finite sets/structures/arrays or a Scenic probabilistic program. Scenic constraints condition the scenario distribution and a renderer/simulator creates concrete sensor inputs. This is a generative search space; the paper supplies no abstraction-soundness theorem covering every concrete image or real environment. Perception is assessed through system-level behavior because component specifications are difficult; the same classification mistake matters when it causes a closed-loop failure. This does not establish correctness of perception outside modeled/rendered contexts. Distribution assumptions and permitted agents/behaviors are designer choices, explicitly acknowledged as incomplete environment modeling. The initial release uses sampling, not exhaustive symbolic exploration. Listed passive methods are uniform random, simulated annealing, Halton and Scenic samples; active methods are cross-entropy and Bayesian optimization. The prose groups simulated annealing among no-feedback samplers; its specific implementation is not explained, so the record does not infer an algorithmic contract from that label. Directed/exhaustive and symbolic/adversarial methods are future extensions. Monitors accept MTL, objective functions or arbitrary Python code; MTL Boolean and quantitative semantics use py-metric-temporal-logic. A monitor score can guide search and identify a violating trace. The paper gives no formal monitor implementation proof, sampling-completeness theorem, stopping rule, discretization error bound or statistical assurance theorem. No discovered violation is not a proof of universal satisfaction. Error-table rows are counterexamples and columns are semantic features. PCA is offered for ordered domains and recurrent-value subsets for unordered domains, either offline for debugging or online for sampling. Correlation is the stated interpretation, not demonstrated causal attribution. The paper gives no numeric PCA output, significance assessment or validation of inferred feature importance. Communication is client-server over IPv4 sockets: VerifAI sends a configuration and the simulator returns trajectories, supporting multiple simulators. This is interoperability infrastructure, not verification of a distributed protocol, socket delivery guarantees or concurrency correctness. AV experiments use commercial Webots2018. Lane following uses non-ML line detection; squeezeDet-based perception estimates cone distance and initiates a lane change below15m. The MTL property requires cone clearance and avoiding overshoot, but its exact formula, clearance threshold, horizon and robustness normalization are not printed. First AV case varies object positions/orientations, disabled-car color, cruising speed and reaction time. The orange car is mistaken for cones, triggering a premature/incomplete lane change and crash. This is a concrete found failure, not a quantified search-efficiency comparison; sample counts, runtimes, seeds and baseline performance are absent. The acknowledgements identify a Titan Xp GPU used for the research, without specifying a complete machine or its assignment to this experiment. Second AV case models an occluded intersection accident with sampled initial positions. One car turns using an OpenStreetMap/Intelligent-Intersections trajectory; the other maintains velocity or brakes on a simulated smart-intersection warning. The authors say this can identify sufficient advance notice, but provide no numerical warning bound, exhaustive guarantee or experiment table. Figure3 is explicitly a partial Scenic program; missing world-model definitions and spot2 prevent treating it as standalone runnable code. Data-augmentation example renders road images for squeezeDet, then selects additions by random error-table samples, top-k closest samples or PCA generation. Figure4 shows two cars counted as one. Accuracy improvement and detailed results are attributed to reference9; this paper prints no accuracy values, held-out split, number of new images, retraining budget or comparative statistics. Prior-paper results have not been independently read here. Cart-pole controller is trained using PPO with100k training episodes. Test variations named in the prose are initial lateral position/rotation and pole mass/length; Figure5 visually plots pole length, cart mass and pole mass. Record retains that presentation difference without guessing an implementation error. Reward is described using2.4m displacement and12degree angle, then testing thresholds are said to be slightly modified without supplying values. Cart-pole Figure5 reports38violations among1000randomly sampled parameter configurations. Main text also says sampling was guided by reward; the precise sampling law is unspecified. Reader arithmetic38/1000=3.8percent describes this plotted set only, not a deployment failure probability, iid confidence interval or general robustness certificate. No runtimes, repeated seeds, statistical uncertainty, comparator or numerical failure coordinates are reported. Mountain-car experiment searches discrete training-algorithm choices and training-set size. It negates the goal-distance reward so falsification becomes finding settings yielding a successful learned controller. A table of safe hyperparameters and PCA sensitivity are claimed but neither values nor counts/results are printed. Safe here is simulation success in this study; no guarantee for all training randomness, environments or future policies follows. Novelty/first-tool claims concern integration and extension of prior methods. The paper explicitly delegates algorithms/formalisms to refs7–10,12,15,22 and augmentation results to ref9. It contains no formal theorem, proof, verified tool kernel or code-generating proof agent. Integration claims are author statements, not an independently established priority survey. Implementation/examples are linked at https://github.com/BerkeleyLearnVerify/VerifAI with expected outputs. No commit hash, full dependency lock, complete experiment hardware configuration, wall-clock results or reproduction is supplied here. Acknowledgements identify a Titan Xp GPU used for the research. The front page displays Artifact evaluated and Functional badges; this is published artifact-evaluation evidence, not this reader’s execution or independent replication of every experiment. CARLA and X-Plane interfaces already exist according to the conclusion, whereas applications and symbolic search are future work. No artifact source or simulation was executed in this reading. Relevance to specification/proof-agent evaluation is methodological: preserve the scenario model, executable target, explicit monitor, generated witness and training/test distinction. Sampling-guided repair and reward optimization can find improvements without supplying a proof. No LLM agent, Verus, verified Rust, TLA+ or distributed-system verification experiment is reported.
use_for_goal: Indirect evidence for evaluating formal-methods tooling and automated specification/repair workflows: a formal property monitor plus search can yield concrete counterexamples without a universal proof; semantic environment coverage, monitor fidelity and simulator correspondence must be recorded separately. Useful counterpart to verified solvers and proof-generating agents, but not evidence for LLM proof success, distributed protocol correctness, Rust/Verus or TLA+ integration.

title: Formal Analysis and Redesign of a Neural Network-Based Aircraft Taxiing System with VerifAI.
what: Presents an integrated VerifAI design workflow for an industrial Boeing TaxiNet aircraft-taxiing controller: Scenic models semantic runway environments, active search drives X-Plane closed-loop simulation, counterexamples are analyzed and targeted tests confirm causes, and retraining uses discovered failures. The TaxiNet requirement is expressed in Metric Temporal Logic (MTL). The paper extends Scenic with externally assigned parameters so active samplers can replace fixed probabilistic draws, and implements a VerifAI client/server interface to X-Plane datarefs. In the six-dimensional case study, 4,000 nominal runs found only 55.2% satisfying the eventually-centerline property and 9.1% leaving the runway. Visualization localized failures to dim lighting, cloud/time interactions, runway intersections around 1,450 m, and aircraft shadows; disabling shadows confirmed the hypothesized root cause. Replacing the neural net with ground-truth errors made every counterexample satisfy the property, localizing faults to perception. Generic, Halton, and specialized retraining raised satisfaction to 82%, 83%, and 86%, respectively, and reduced runway departures to 3.9%, 0.6%, and 0.5%; cross-entropy sampling learned a failure-focused distribution, but augmentation experiments sometimes regressed performance.

Tgeneric: 82% satisfy, 3.9% leave runway
THalton: 83% satisfy, 0.6% leave runway (15x departure reduction)
Tspecialized: 86% satisfy, 0.5% leave runway
cross-entropy sampler: ~1,200 runs; learned ~79% probability at 1,400–1,600 m
20-epoch augmentation: generic baseline 85%, cross-entropy 82%, intersection augmentation 73%
assumptions_limits: The study uses a prototype TaxiNet and X-Plane simulation, not a deployed aircraft or exhaustive proof. Search covers a six-dimensional scenario space, 30-second simulations, daylight/weather ranges, and a specified runway; failures outside those abstractions are not assessed. MTL robustness guides search but nonnegative/negative sampled results are not a universal safety guarantee. Retraining leaves a 14% specification-failure rate and depends on training-set size, simulator rendering, and controller/network architecture.
use_for_goal: A concrete verifier-in-the-loop workflow: formal scenario/specification, falsification, causal debugging, and retraining. It supplies realistic evidence about how simulation-based counterexamples improve an ML controller while showing that test/falsification results remain bounded by the modeled environment and are not a correctness proof for distributed systems.

title: A Methodology for Developing a Verifiable Aircraft Engine Controller from Formal Requirements
what: Presents a three-phase, requirements-driven methodology for developing and verifying an aircraft engine controller: elicit and formalize requirements in FRET, verify through FRET-supported Simulink/Kind2 and FRET-guided formal models, then assemble a traceable verification report. The paper details the fretish intermediate language, FRET-generated LTL and CoCoSpec contracts, the parallel Phase 2A/2B toolchains, and feedback loops that revise requirements when verification exposes errors. The industrial use case translates 14 natural-language requirements and uses 20 supplied test cases to add detail; the authors explain how combining independent designs can expose inconsistencies.

title: Foundational Verification of Stateful P4 Packet Processing
what: Builds Verifiable P4, a Coq program logic and semi-interactive verifier sound against formal P416 operational semantics, plus a proved-correct reference interpreter. Demonstrates source-level functional correctness of a sliding-window Bloom filter and a firewall no-recent-false-negatives policy, and adapts the proof to sliding-window count-min-sketch. Section 2 connects P4 control-block proofs to functional models, abstract time-window axioms, a per-packet process relation and its flow-level history closure. Hierarchical representation predicates and MOD clauses track only the rooted persistent-register subtree, enabling client/library proofs. Sections 3–4 define P4light, big-step stack/external-state semantics, nondeterministic partially initialized bits, a determinizing interpreter and a separate static instantiation phase with fully qualified paths and abstract methods. Theorem 1 proves SBF model axioms; Theorem 2 proves the P4 control implements the model; Theorem 3 proves program-logic soundness. Table 1 records P4-manual/compiler ambiguities and fixes. Sections 5–7 report proof sizes, saturating CMS adaptation and explicit boundaries for parsing, compilation, concurrency and probabilistic false positives.

dense-flow maximum gap about 100 microseconds
48-bit nanosecond timestamps with wraparound

about 600-line full P4 firewall example
assumptions_limits: The SBF’s no-false-negative flow theorem assumes dense monotone packet time with no gap over T/C (about 100 microseconds), enabling incremental clearing; correct switch timestamps are assumed, while 48-bit nanosecond wraparound is allowed by the proof. Parameters are T=60 seconds, k=4 panes, r=3 rows, S=2^18 slots per row. Packet handling is atomic for a single Tofino-like pipeline; multiple pipelines, recirculation and surrounding packet scheduling remain future work. The logic excludes packet parsing/deparsing although the operational semantics includes them. The P4 front end/type checker and deployed compiler are not proved correct here; architecture resource acceptance and compiler correctness are assumptions for executable behavior. The reference interpreter selects zero for undefined bits, proving one allowed behavior rather than exhaustively exploring nondeterminism. No small false-positive probability is proved. P4 type-soundness proof and broader interpreter test-suite validation are ongoing.
use_for_goal: Adds a concrete distributed-network infrastructure case and a method for lifting code-level register updates to temporal multi-packet policies. Useful for a Verus/verified-Rust or proof-agent study because it exposes representation predicates, modular pre/post contracts, time assumptions, source/compiler boundaries and the gap between a no-false-negative property and probabilistic filtering quality. This paper uses Coq/P4 and supplies no TLA+ or LLM experiment.

title: Verification of the Garsia–Wachs Algorithm
what: Dafny formalization of naive and optimized Garsia–Wachs variants returns an alphabetic binary tree of minimum weighted leaf-depth cost. Extracts a direct recursive one-phase construction from the Kingston–Knuth correctness proof: recursively solve a shorter reordered weight sequence, then split the proof-selected leaf to restore an optimum tree for the original order. Both present implementations remain quadratic; logarithmic data-structure refinements are proposals. Records unlabeled-tree representation and separate weight semantics, exact pair/insertion conditions, constructive W/X/Y/Z proof chain, zero-sum/nonnegative cyclic-shift proof, recursive and mutual-recursive termination arguments, overlapping2-descending interval invariant, and concrete performance bottlenecks. Distinguishes checked functional correctness from unimplemented asymptotic refinement and unmeasured solver/runtime behavior.
assumptions_limits: §§1/3–4, pp.1/6–7/13: mathematical introduction allows nonnegative weights; actual algorithm contracts use nonempty seq<nat>, so verified inputs are nonnegative integers, not arbitrary real frequencies. Cost helper accepts integer sequences, but optimization theorem is stated for naturals. Result is an unlabeled full binary-tree shape with exactly input length leaves; associating weights by inorder position gives original alphabetic order. No empty input or negative-weight algorithm contract. §3, pp.6–7: Tree=Leaf|Node(left,right), no stored leaf weights. Levels and CostSeq zip a separately supplied weight sequence with leaf depths, then sum. DeleteLeaf requires internal root and a valid leaf index; removes leaf and collapses parent into sibling. SplitLeaf replaces selected leaf by two children. This avoids relabeling many leaves during exchange proofs. Split cost identity combines adjacent weights before splitting and adds their sum. §1/§4.2, pp.2/8–9: select least k in1..n with k=n or q[k−1]<=q[k+1], equivalent to first locally minimal adjacent-sum pair. Earlier positions satisfy q[i−1]>q[i+1]. Insert combined q[k−1]+q[k] at greatest j<k with j=0 or q[j−1]>=sum; all j<=i<k−1 have q[i]<sum. Strict/nonstrict inequalities and leftmost choice belong in proof preconditions, including zero and tied weights. §4.1, pp.7–8: W says if q[k−1]>q[k+1], every optimum tree has l[k]<=l[k+1]; equality of weights gives some optimum with this relation. Exchange lemma applies to any suitable tree with l[k]>l[k+1], deletes leaf k and splits its successor, reducing cost at least q[k−1]−q[k+1] and making the pair siblings. Nonnegative subtree weights support this comparison. §4.2, pp.8–9: X first constructs an optimum tree with nondecreasing levels through k and l[k−1]=l[k]. Claim2 forces l[j]>=l[k]−1 by contradiction using delete/split and negative cost change; proof separates adjacent/nonadjacent exchanged leaves. Final witness satisfies l[j]=l[k]−1, or l[j]=l[k] with j a left child. Claim1 and Statement return witness trees, not only existential statements; Claim2 establishes a property of its supplied tree. §4.3, pp.9–10: Y transforms the specially selected X witness, not an arbitrary optimum tree. Deleting the appropriate sibling leaf produces shorter-sequence tree of exact cost c−q[k−1]−q[k], hence minimum shorter cost cprime<=that value. For case(b) delete j or j+1; for case(a) delete first index s at level l[k] (or sibling s+1). Level equalities establish unchanged outside costs and the combined coefficient. §4.4, pp.10–12: Z starts from any optimum shorter tree and chooses greatest s1<k at same level as its leaf j. SplitLeaf(tprime,s1) restores original input length and has cost<=cprime+combined weight; combine Y to get equality and optimality. Intermediate rotation of weights among equal-depth leaves preserves cost. CyclicShift2 proves the original order is no costlier than shifted order by telescoping coefficients and summing strictly positive weight differences times nonnegative level differences. No parity case split needed. §4.5.1, pp.12–13: original bottom-up nonalphabetic phase needs induction that its output is level-equivalent to an optimum alphabetic tree; author points out this reasoning was implicit in Kingston/Knuth. New variant recursively constructs the shorter optimum directly, then applies Z. It avoids intermediate nonalphabetic tree and level-equivalence postconditions; does not claim the original algorithm was mathematically incorrect. §4.5.2, pp.13–14: naive GWAlgorithm decreases sequence length, basecase one Leaf. LeastNumber and GreatestNumberLe are executable linear searches; k and j exist by final-index and zero fallbacks. Recurse on length−1 sequence, find greatest s1 between j and k−1 with equal level, split. Postcondition certifies minimum cost among all shapes with correct leaf count, not uniqueness of optimum shape. §4.5.3, pp.15–17: optimized GWAlgorithm takes1<=r<=length with2-descending prefix; initial r=1. Main method decreases lexicographic(length,length−r), Combine decreases(length,length−r,|ks|). Main passes overlapping interval lengths ks=[r] at a candidate pair. TwoDescendingIntervals recursively joins prefixes of length>=2 with exactly one shared position; each last pair is potentially locally minimal. Merging interval lengths removes repeated scans; sequence-shortening recursion preserves the semantic optimum postcondition. §4.5.3, pp.15–16: FindJ first binary-searches neighboring-weight maxima to exploit2-descending rather than globally descending weights. Combine handles no-longer-minimal pair by advancing main scan or merging first two intervals; actual reduction updates ks differently for j<=1/j>1 and k=1. It selects s1 with binary search only after proving monotonic equal-level prefix properties of shorter optimum. Published code omits ghost assertions/lemma invocations, which author says are numerous. §4.5.4, p.17: assuming array-backed immutable sequences and constant indexed access, FindJ logarithmic but concatenation/slicing copies linearly, computing leaf levels needs traversal/precomputation, and SplitLeaf traverses a simple tree. Present full algorithm O(n²). Rank-augmented AVL sequence structures, paired-neighbor weights, efficient leaf-position access or deferred output-tree construction could support O(nlogn); these are proposed refinements, not verified implementations in this paper. Complexity argument is prose, not a supplied formal cost theorem. §5, pp.17–18: about3600DafnyLOC for both versions, author report. Many calc hints and trial-and-error solver-resource tricks needed to obtain consistent verification; no verification time, timeout distribution, machine, solver/version configuration, runtime comparison, large workload or annotation ratio reported. One explicit compiled-example claim and explanatory traces support illustration, not a performance benchmark. §§2/5, pp.5/17: Dafny sends obligations through Boogie to Z3. Automation discharges index/slice safety, with assertions/lemma calls as hints. Paper does not provide kernel proof terms, verified compiler theorem, SMT trust audit or independently executed artifact. LLM declaration explicitly rules out GenAI production of article/artifact; this is a human-written verification case, not an agent benchmark.

Solver brittleness and extensive calculation hints suggest concrete evaluation axes for LLM proof agents, but paper supplies no agent data or automated proof-generation experiment. Sequential optimal-tree algorithm rather than distributed-system/TLA+ verification or verified Rust.

title: Verified Decision Procedures for Modal Logics
what: Lean formalization of terminating sound and complete tableau decision procedures for modal K, KT and S4, with histories for reflexive/transitive logics and verified backjumping for K. Returns an unsatisfiability proof or a constructed tree representation carrying evidence of a satisfying Kripke model. The S4 construction handles ancestor-loop requests by propagating invariants and fulfilling them at the root. Explains dependent output types, early-terminating dependent map for recursive transition branches, downward propagation of sequent invariants, upward propagation of partially constructed S4 models, lexicographic termination measures and responsibility sets enabling backjumping. Separates terminating search and semantic correctness from practical VM evaluation, explicit finite-model formalization and fully executable S4 model reachability, which remain qualifications.
assumptions_limits: Input is a finite list of propositional modal formulas in negation normal form, with natural-number atoms, atomic negation, conjunction/disjunction, box and diamond. A correctness-preserving translation from arbitrary negation is described as easy rather than developed here. No first-order quantification, temporal fixed points or arbitrary global knowledge-base assumptions are added to these algorithms. K permits arbitrary Kripke accessibility; KT requires reflexivity; S4 additionally requires transitivity. Satisfaction requires a designated state, so empty carriers cannot witness satisfiability. Logical model assumptions are the target specification, not claims about external distributed-system executions. Correctness/termination are Lean function/type-theory proofs. The paper says the functions could run with #reduce but this is too slow for direct use in a Lean proof; experimental evaluation instead uses #eval on Lean’s virtual machine. It does not establish verification of that VM or kernel replay of the experimental outputs. K output is closed with a proof of unsatisfiability or open with a tree state and satisfaction evidence. Tree models are inductive finite syntax with list-valued atoms/children; interpretation functions recover the Kripke structure. S4 additionally uses histories, signatures, ancestors, pending backward-edge requests and several proven invariants. K termination follows decreasing connective count. KT needs a pair: maximal modal-operator count in a formula and main-sequent connective count, with handled box formulas moved into history. S4 needs closure-bounded history/handled sets and a lexicographic triple; no formal runtime/space complexity bound is claimed. Backjumping implementation/proof is for K only. Extension to KT/S4 is future work even though the authors argue the closed-branch nature makes it portable. Other optimizations and alternative data structures are prospective. The finite-model theorem is explicitly not separately formalized. Authors infer it from finite tree objects. K/KT valuation and relation are computable; S4 semantic relation uses reflexive transitive closure, and explicit verified finite reachability computation remains future work. The returned S4 object should not be described as an already implemented finite adjacency matrix with an executable edge checker. Formal proofs rely on the supplied Lean/library environment. The paper reports no verified compiler/VM, independent proof audit or executable refinement to an external prover. Reader did not replay the scripts. A small benchmark is evidence of practical evaluation, not a complete assurance argument for all deployments.
use_for_goal: Proof-agent infrastructure example where termination, model validity and optimizations all require explicit invariants. Pending cyclic obligations are resolved by a finite well-founded construction rather than accepted as unexplained proof cycles. Reader inference: useful for specification/proof agents and trust-aware evaluation of returned certificates; modal knowledge semantics can inform distributed reasoning, but no distributed protocol, TLA+ checker, Verus/Rust verification or LLM evaluation is implemented.

title: Formal Verification of Agentic MLOps Protocols: Model Checking and Liveness Guarantees in Distributed Model Context Protocol Workflows
what: A gateway sits between an LLM agent and its tools (Model Context Protocol, MCP, a standard for LLM tool calls). Before each tool call it checks, against a hand-written state machine, that the call keeps three temporal-logic rules true: no deadlock, every GPU that is handed out is eventually returned, and no two agents write the same network folder at once.

reachable states at depth 14: 196,608 unconstrained vs 672 with guards (99.66% fewer)

title: Efficient Formally Verified Maximal End Component Decomposition for MDPs.
what: Mechanizes correctness of maximal end-component decomposition for finite MDPs in Isabelle/HOL, refines the algorithm through efficient mutable data structures to LLVM bytecode, and integrates it into the mcsta probabilistic model checker. Experiments show performance comparable to the prior unverifiable implementation and lower memory use. Defines MDPs, end components and MECs over finite states and support sets, then formalizes the iterative SCC/culling algorithm. Isabelle locales state nonempty branches, finite state sets and closed kernels; refinement relations and separation-logic assertions connect abstract lists/sets and bitsets to LLVM memory. The implementation reuses verified Gabow SCC code but adds deletion-capable graph structures. Integration avoids data copies. The evaluation compares verified, integrated and reference implementations, including QVBS, long-run-average and hand-crafted MEC benchmarks.

title: Towards Formal Verification of Password Generation Algorithms used in Password Managers
what: Surveys password-generation algorithms in Chrome, Bitwarden and KeePass and proposes an EasyCrypt reference implementation supporting length and per-character-set minimum/maximum policies. The authors formalize functional correctness and a game-based security property requiring indistinguishability from uniform sampling over policy-valid passwords. The reference generator samples required character classes, fills remaining positions subject to maxima, applies a random permutation and uses rejection-sampling RNGs to avoid modulo bias. EasyCrypt expresses correctness as probability-one policy satisfaction and security through RealRPG versus IdealRPG games; the paper also records implementation differences across 15 password managers.

three algorithms studied in detail
reference password length range 1–200
correctness target probability 1
uniformity security advantage required negligible
no runtime benchmark reported
assumptions_limits: Security assumes the underlying random-byte generator is secure and the policy-valid set is the ideal comparison domain. The paper presents formalizations and a reference algorithm rather than a proved extracted production implementation; future work includes Jasmin implementation, user-defined character sets and password-strength properties. Strict policies can still generate guessable strings such as P@ssw0rd.

title: Formal verification of Romanov’s triplet logic: A verified filter for sliding-window 3-CNF with application to structured formulas
what: Mechanizes Romanov’s Triplet Logic in Rocq, verifies translation/clearing/SVI operations, and extracts a verified filter plus exponential post-check for well-formed sliding-window 3-CNF. The work identifies a precise correctness boundary: SVI is a sound one-sided filter in general, while aligned intersection and a strong CTF predicate restore completeness for the structured sliding-window fragment. The VFR prototype combines machine-checked polynomial filter stages with post-check search and validates outputs against SAT/brute-force oracles.

General 3-SAT still needs external verified solvers/certificates.
