title: A Formally Verified Checker for First-Order Proofs
what: Presents VTV, an Agda checker whose kernel and first-order semantic soundness theorem are formally verified for TESC proof objects. The checker reconstructs omitted sequents while traversing an inductive proof, checks side conditions and supports theory-extension rules (currently equality axioms, relation definitions and choice axioms). A size-tracking tree replaces lists to make random access practical in dependently typed code. The paper explains engineering choices that make a verified checker usable: De Bruijn syntax, mutually recursive traversals accepted by Agda termination checking, indexed-functor freshness invariant, and a simple append-only balancing tree. Soundness is stated as verify-success implying sequent unsatisfiability, while parse-verify deliberately leaves equivalence between parsed TPTP and the original problem to an unverified parser. The empirical study filters TPTP to CNF/FOF theorem or unsatisfiable instances solvable by Vampire/E and compilable to TESC, then compares VTV with optimized Rust OTV. VTV checks 12,291/12,296 proofs within 16 GB, has 40 ms median and >97.4% under one second, but at least >64 GB is needed to check all proofs.

5 proofs exhausted 16 GB; at least >64 GB to verify all with VTV
VTV median 40 ms, OTV 30 ms

assumptions_limits: Soundness assumes the root sequent satisfies the good-sequent indexed-functor invariant and targets first-order equality semantics with an infinite-arity encoding. Input formulas must be closed because the unverified Rust parser rejects open formulas. The formal theorem covers the proof-checking kernel, not that parsed TPTP text is equivalent to the original problem. VTV has substantially higher peak memory than OTV and five largest proofs exhaust 16 GB (three still fail on 64 GB).
use_for_goal: A machine-checked certificate checker illustrates a small trusted kernel for proof-producing automation. Its explicit parser trust boundary and memory failures are useful when evaluating LLM-generated proofs or Verus/TLA+ proof artifacts: checker success is meaningful only under stated input and parser assumptions.

The checker function verify for Proof performs two tasks: (1) it constructs the omitted intermediate sequents as it recurses down a Proof, and (2) it checks that the conditions are satisfied for each inference rule used.

title: VyZX: Formal Verification of a Graphical Quantum Language
what: Presents VyZX, a Rocq-verified inductive library for ZX-calculus diagrams, semantics and rewrite rules, plus ZXViz visualization and circuit interoperability. VyZX represents variable-arity diagrams inductively with explicit casts for dependent dimensions, defines matrix semantics in QuantumLib, and proves proportionality/equality composition lemmas. It formalizes Jeandel et al.’s complete equational theory including connectivity, spider fusion, Hopf, bialgebra, state-copy and self-loop rules; proves scalar and matrix universality through diagrammatic scalar gadgets and controlizer-based addition; ingests SQIR circuits and verifies Bell-state preparation and peephole optimizations. ZXViz renders nested proof states in VSCode/rocq-lsp and automation handles color swaps, transposes and casts.

title: Weak Simplicial Bisimilarity and Minimisation for Polyhedral Model Checking
what: Introduces the weaker spatial logic SLCS_eta and matching weak simplicial/weak plus-minus bisimilarities, proves Hennessy–Milner characterisations and a semantics-preserving minimisation procedure for polyhedral cell-poset models. SLCS_eta requires the source point and intermediate path points to satisfy the reachability condition, making it strictly weaker than SLCS_gamma. The paper proves the continuous polyhedral and discrete cell-poset interpretations coincide (Theorem 3.20), then proves weak simplicial bisimilarity and weak plus-minus bisimilarity coincide with logical equivalence (Theorems 4.9 and 4.12). A three-step construction encodes a poset as an LTS, minimises by branching bisimulation (mCRL2), and reconstructs a Kripke model whose SLCS_eta formulas are preserved/reflected (Theorem 5.12). The prototype maps results back to meshes for visualisation.

title: Automated Hypersafety Verification.
what: Presents Weaver, a counterexample-guided verifier that simultaneously searches for a reduction of a k-copy product program and a safety proof of that reduction, thereby reducing hypersafety to ordinary safety reasoning. Programs are regular trace languages and proofs are finite assertion sets inducing regular infeasibility languages. Looping tree automata (LTAs) represent sets of sleep-set reductions; closure and emptiness enable decidable proof checking. The paper proves finite counterexample sets and strong progress under an interpolation assumption, proves every sleep-set reduction is sound and optimal per Mazurkiewicz class, and gives antichain and partition optimizations. Weaver implements total-order and partition algorithms, Craig interpolation and atomic-block abstraction, covering sequential, concurrent and stress benchmarks.

loop-free: 27 cases, 0.15 s average

proof sizes 4–298; refinement rounds 2–33
assumptions_limits: Input programs are regular trace languages over a finite statement alphabet with a sound, fixed dependence relation; D-reductions rely on semantic commutation of independent statements. General reduction existence is undecidable, so the LTA sleep-set class is sound but incomplete (partition optimization is additionally incomplete relative to all sleep-set reductions). Termination requires a proof for some explored reduction and an interpolation oracle that returns subsets of a target proof. Atomic-block optimization is sound but incomplete. The tool handles simple imperative programs without procedure calls and uses finite benchmark properties.
use_for_goal: Relevant to automated relational verification of concurrent/distributed code: it searches proof-friendly interleavings while proving reduction soundness, exposing explicit incompleteness and dependence assumptions important for trustworthy LLM-generated concurrent proofs.

title: Why Agentic Theorem Prover Works: A Statistical Provability Theory of Mathematical Reasoning Models
what: Develops a statistical theory for finite-budget agentic theorem proving. It models verifier-backed proof search as a deterministic finite-horizon reachability MDP and defines statistical provability as the probability that a specified prover reaches a verified proof within a verifier-call budget on a problem distribution. Under a faithful state abstraction, optimal MDP success equals budgeted syntactic provability. For offline depth-wise action-value regression followed by greedy proving, Theorem3.1 bounds the gap to the optimal prover by an occupancy-weighted sum of value-estimation errors; the multiplier is the learned prover’s average truncated proof length. Error terms separate approximation, training-region coverage geometry and Monte Carlo rollout noise, with a faster rate under an action-gap margin condition. Defines full proof states as multisets of open goals so branching remains Markov, deterministic verifier transition F, solved set G, hitting time TG, budgeted value V and average truncated length Len. Assumption3.1 requires compact concentration sets, Lipschitz optimal values and hypothesis classes, local-mass coverage of i.i.d. query pairs, conditionally independent binary rollout labels with mean Q*, and minimax regression. Theorem3.1 gives εt=approximation+covering term+Hoeffding rollout noise and regret 2Σ unsolved-mass×ε. A margin condition changes ε to ε^(β+1). Budget allocation balances Nt and mt under total labels nt=Ntmt. Appendices prove deterministic MDP, faithful abstraction, Bellman recursion, greedy regret, covering and uniform regression; truncation adds overflow penalty δW. Appendix C proposes representation selection by Bellman-certificate tightness and a complexity penalty; Appendix D interprets scaling through horizon, effective dimension and margins.
numbers: Main bound: best success probability minus learned prover's is at most 2 times (worst per-step value error) times the learned prover's average number of checker calls before success or budget end
Under an action-gap margin condition the dependence on error improves to a fast rate
assumptions_limits: Faithful abstraction assumes e(FR(r,a))=F(e(r),a) and exact preservation of solved states. The equality between optimal MDP success and syntactic provability follows this assumption; arbitrary learned embeddings need not be faithful. The theory is trace-local. Compact concentration Ct must cover both training queries and learned-prover comparisons, and the candidate region must retain at least one globally optimal action. The paper explicitly says a new prover leaving the occupied region is no longer certified without added coverage assumptions. Binary rollout labels are idealized verifier-backed success labels with conditional mean Q*. The paper says practical-target bias can be absorbed into ε, but the stated theorem assumes exact Q* labels and its approximation term is relative to Q*. Biased targets require an explicit allowance; reader derivation using the supplied minimax proof adds2bt when label means differ uniformly by≤bt. Repeating suboptimal-policy rollouts reduces sampling noise, not this bias. No empirical calibration is supplied. The exact minimax regression optimizer is an idealization. Numerical optimization error ξt can be added, but no practical learner, neural architecture or training algorithm is evaluated. The verifier transition is deterministic, while policy decoding, retrieval and exploration may be random. The theory addresses greedy proving; beam search, backtracking, top-k and decomposition need extra retention/suboptimality assumptions. The finite-horizon result does not remove undecidability, worst-case hardness or unknown proof existence. Statistical provability depends on q0, so a biased library workload can be easy while adversarial or uniform hard instances remain difficult. The effective dimension dt, coverage ct, Lipschitz constants, action-gap tails and occupancy curve are theoretical quantities. The paper proposes estimating them from traces as future work and reports no benchmark measurement. No Verus/Rust/TLA+/distributed-system experiment is supplied. Transfer to systems verification is an inference about replacing proof-state/verifier interfaces, not a measured claim.
use_for_goal: Directly relevant as a formal framework for evaluating agentic proof systems: use finite verifier budgets, workload distributions, occupancy curves, action gaps and trace-local coverage instead of only theorem existence or worst-case complexity. For Verus/Rust/TLA+ distributed verification, the candidate abstraction is to model verifier-accepted code/specification states as deterministic transitions; faithful abstraction, retention and label assumptions would need to be checked, so this transfer is inference.

title: From Width-Based Model Checking to Width-Based Automated Theorem Proving
what: Introduces a modular framework that converts width-based dynamic-programming model checkers into procedures testing graph-theoretic conjectures on bounded-width graphs. Defines treelike decomposition classes and treelike width measures, then treelike dynamic-programming cores with local witnesses, cleaning, invariants, coherency, bitlength, multiplicity, and deterministic state complexity. For coherent finite cores, inclusion of all width-k decompositions reduces to a finite refutation search; Theorem 23 combines cores for Boolean graph properties and gives a double-exponential-in-core-size procedure. The instructive tree-decomposition encoding realizes treewidth. Applications instantiate cores for coloring, connectivity, Hamiltonicity, flows, minors, and degree/connectivity properties, yielding explicit tests for Hadwiger, Tutte flow, and Barnette conjectures.

assumptions_limits: Graphs are represented by regular ranked-tree decompositions; coherence requires equivalent decompositions of the same graph to agree on acceptance and invariants. The strongest inclusion bounds require finite, internally polynomial cores and polynomial combinators. Bounds are parameterized by width k and core bitlength/multiplicity and are very high (typically double exponential); no implementation or empirical runtime is supplied. Results test conjectures on bounded-width classes, not unrestricted graphs unless an independent irrelevant-vertex argument supplies a constant width bound.

It is relevant to specification/proof automation methodology, but does not verify distributed implementations, Verus code, or TLA+ specifications.

title: Scaling Bounded Model Checking By Transforming Programs With Arrays
what: Transforms array-manipulating ANSI-C programs with large loops into array-free, loop-free witness-index programs so off-the-shelf BMC can scale. A nondeterministic witness index ia and scalar xa represent one arbitrary array element. Array accesses matching ia use xa; other reads become nondeterministic, writes are conditional, and loop headers are removed while modified scalars are nondeterministically reset. Structural Lemmas 1–3 establish state representation, expression over-approximation and statement preservation; Theorem 1 proves original assertion violations remain violations after transformation. Precision rules require full-array loops, iterator-indexed accesses and no relevant loop-defined scalar/array dependencies; Theorem 2 proves exactness for invariant assertions meeting those rules. The implementation supports 1-D arrays and is tested on SV-COMP ArraysReach and three real applications.

assumptions_limits: Formal language exposition restricts to one 1-D array, though implementation handles ANSI-C features and multiple arrays via a technical report. Transformation is generally an over-approximation: unsafe results can be spurious when precision criteria fail, and array accesses outside loops are not covered by precision claims. title: Not All Invariants Are Equal: Curating Training Data to Accelerate Program Verification with SLMs
what: Introduces WONDA, a verifier-filtered training-data pipeline: AST normalization removes semantic-preserving syntactic clutter, then an LLM proposes compact generalizations that are checked for inductiveness, sufficiency and speedup. LLM simplification is not semantics-preserving by assumption; every candidate is re-verified. Cast stripping can be unsound under overflow, so final verifier checks are essential. Evaluation is C programs/InvBench (219 programs expanded to 362 loops), with 123 hard instances selected by >15 s baseline and 20 hard timeouts; results measure verifier outcomes, not proof certificates. 80/20 training/validation split is by curated samples; the paper does not state program-group splitting, although multiple candidates may derive from one program. title: Hyperproperty-Preserving Register Specifications
what: The paper addresses hyperproperties of programs using concurrent registers, which ordinary linearizability does not preserve. It proposes WSR, a non-atomic shared-memory specification complete for write-strong-linearizable implementations: every such implementation forward-simulates to WSR, including single-writer ABD. It also defines decisive linearizability, weaker than write strong-linearizability, and a DR specification complete for this class; multi-writer ABD is shown to belong via a forward simulation. The motivating client programs show how scheduler-controlled interleavings can correlate coin outcomes and reads even when each implementation is linearizable.
assumptions_limits: Hyperproperties are evaluated under a strong adversary that observes execution prefixes and controls scheduling/internal nondeterminism. Programs communicate with objects through calls/returns; the extracted text gives motivating examples and definitions but omits most later formal constructions and proofs (the available file ends during the introductory example). Claims about WSR/DR completeness and ABD classification are therefore recorded from the paper's stated contribution, while detailed proof obligations and quantitative evaluation are unavailable in this extraction. The target objects are registers and crash-resilient ABD-style implementations.
use_for_goal: Makes precise why ordinary linearizability proofs are insufficient for randomized or security properties, and identifies forward simulation as a proof artifact for hyperproperty preservation. This is directly relevant when verifying concurrent distributed objects or evaluating whether a generated refinement proof preserves the intended probabilistic behavior.

title: Analysis of the XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol
what: Gives a formal network model and safety/liveness analysis of XRP Ledger Consensus Protocol (XRP LCP), a Byzantine agreement protocol operating with individually chosen trusted node lists (UNLs). Lemmas and propositions derive overlap conditions for ledger agreement: validation propagation through honest-majority support yields Theorem 8’s pairwise overlap bound. title: Zero-Knowledge Model Checking
what: Introduces zero-knowledge model checking (ZKMC), proving that a secret reactive system satisfies a public temporal specification without disclosing its transition relation, via explicit-state KZG commitments or symbolic Farkas witnesses and folded sigma/range proofs. The framework certifies LTL/ω-regular model checking by ranking functions for the product with a complementary Büchi automaton. The explicit-state scheme commits to secret initial states/transitions and batch-proves that public counterexample states cannot be in the secret model; its certificate is two group elements while prover work is quadratic in state count. The symbolic scheme restricts systems to linear guarded commands, translates initiation/step/fairness obligations to linear-inequality unsatisfiability, uses Farkas dual witnesses, Pedersen matrix commitments, zkMatrix multiplication, Bulletproof range proofs and a Salem–Spencer one-shot fold. The prototype tests handshake, DHCP and round-robin protocols and reports separate enumeration/setup/prover/verifier timings, showing complementary scaling regimes.
numbers: explicit-state runs up to about 2^12 states in the stated two-hour budget; symbolic runs up to about 2^20.9 states and 2^13.7 obligations
explicit back-end is preferable below about 2^11.8 states; e.g. exb_i4a3 prover 2 s versus symbolic 1 min
symbolic dhcp_10000_3_10 (2^20.9 states) completes in under half an hour while explicit enumeration times out
round-robin rr_5 reaches 2^10.2 states and 38,427 obligations; symbolic verifier is OOM
symbolic timings include 1–4 min setup, 1–41 min prover and 2–8 min verifier across DHCP/round-robin cases
assumptions_limits: Soundness relies on binding/hiding commitments, knowledge-sound zkmm/zkeq/zkrp, Fiat–Shamir random-oracle modeling and field bounds avoiding integer wraparound; Farkas completeness can fail when only rational or out-of-bound witnesses exist. Explicit-state verification exposes quadratic state-space costs; symbolic verification requires linear guarded-command models, integer coefficients and piecewise-linear rankings. Public specifications/certificates can themselves leak the secret model, and side channels are out of scope. A negative verification result does not imply the property is false.
use_for_goal: Shows how formal model-checking assurance can be made privacy-preserving, with explicit cryptographic assumptions, proof obligations and reproducible protocol benchmarks; relevant to formal verification systems and the limits of proof artifacts that hide implementations.

title: Specifying and Model Checking Workflows of Single Page Applications with TLA+
what: Presents a TLA+ modeling pattern for single-page application workflows: variables represent observable widget properties and actions represent user events; TLC checks reachability, liveness, invariants, and deadlock. The paper gives a complete math-exercise SPA module with Init, Input Answer, Check, New Question, Terminating, and weak fairness, then demonstrates diagnostic TLC results. Reachability of every question and eventual availability of New Question are proved; an initially plausible invariant is falsified and repaired to condition on a nonempty result; an off-by-one precondition creates a concrete deadlock. The mapping is deliberately practice-oriented and exposes implicit widget-state workflows.

assumptions_limits: The case study is a small finite-state model with a bounded maximum question count and nondeterministic answer correctness; weak fairness is used to prevent stuttering. It models user-observable widget states rather than implementation code, omits asynchronous communication and server activity, and does not evaluate an industrial SPA. The author notes TLC's finite-state limitation and proposes theorem proving and automatic AngularJS-to-TLA+ generation as future work.
use_for_goal: A concrete TLA+/TLC workflow for turning implicit UI state transitions into checkable temporal properties; useful as a small, auditable specification example for verification practice, though not distributed-protocol verification.

title: Zonotope Domains for Lagrangian Neural Network Verification
what: Introduces ZonoDual, combining zonotopic intermediate bounds with Lagrangian decomposition to produce tighter lower bounds for ReLU-network verification. The paper formulates verification with duplicated layer variables and dual equality multipliers, replacing independent hyperboxes by zonotopes that preserve neuron dependencies. A zonotopic ReLU program is equivalent to two-layer verification and NP-hard; coordinate partitioning gives tractable relaxations, with exact 2-D candidates computable in near-linear generator time. ZonoDual initializes DeepZ/IBP bounds, performs GPU-friendly 2-D dual ascent, optionally merges later partitions into MIP subproblems, and retains valid lower-bound guarantees. Stagewise use of tighter boxes further improves zonotopes.
numbers: 2-D zonotope evaluation O(dm) after O(dm log m) preprocessing
2-D zonotope has 2m vertices
CIFAR network 6,244 ReLUs/4 layers
MNIST-Deep 5,196 neurons/6 layers
MNIST robustness ZD 21.8–52.6% on listed networks
assumptions_limits: The core setting is scalar feedforward affine/ReLU networks and axis-aligned input boxes; the method is an incomplete bound procedure, not complete verification. Weak duality and sound pushforward bounds are required. Higher-dimensional ReLU programs need MIP or another incomplete solver, and stagewise optimization has substantial memory/parallel cost. Reported experiments are MNIST/CIFAR-10 networks and compare bounds, not end-to-end branch-and-bound completion.
use_for_goal: Combines relational abstract domains with dual proof bounds, a concrete design pattern for scalable but sound incomplete verification.

quotes.text: We provide an approach that merges these two threads and uses zonotopes within a Lagrangian decomposition.
When Z is a zonotope, solving a ReLU program over Z is equivalent to a neural network verification problem for a 2-layer network, which is known to be NP-hard.
Ultimately, our algorithm will always provide a valid lower bound to the verification problem so long as the dual function is evaluated appropriately.
